Report:
In a very deep prep shortstop class in 2023, Cholowsky stood out as having some of the highest projectability in the class with supremely impressive talent on the defensive end. His continued physical development hasn't cost him a step and it's elevated almost every part of his game. 

A blue-collar worker who leads by example, Cholowsky gets high marks from coaches, his teammates and those who operate in his proximity. The leadership qualities are top of the scale. After taking his talent and god-given abilities for granted a bit in high school, Cholowsky's mentality changed at UCLA. He began placing a greater emphasis on nutrition and the weight room. He's put on 20 pounds of muscle since arriving to campus, skyrocketing his physical and athletic traits in every area of his game.

Cholowsky is an average runner with fantastic first-step quickness on the dirt. His lateral range is among the best in the class and he's got the ability to make every throw from every angle with plus arm strength and athleticism to burn. Cholowsky is no stranger to the highlight reel play, converting outs in ways other are not capable. Cholowsky has all the traits of a future plus defender at the shortstop position. His frame is just about at peak physical state and likely shouldn't carry much more strength if he's to hang onto his premium athleticism. 

Cholowsky's physical transformation at UCLA has helped kick his offensive tools into an entirely new gear. What was once hitterish in the box is now far more impactful with more on the way. Cholowsky's exit velocities have peaked north of 112 mph and his barrel rate towers over most of his middle-infield peers. Cholowsky's plus raw power projection has the chance to output 25-homer campaigns as a professional. There are very few holes in this swing. That said, there are a few things to clean up to reach his eventual ceiling. At times, Cholowsky will feature a more pronounced barrel tip to compliment what can be a bigger leg kick. It can result in Cholowsky struggling to get the barrel to premium elevated velocity, especially on the inner-third. Velocity above the zone is just about the only area Cholowsky has shown a willingness to chase outside of the zone. Scouts would prefer to see his swing and quiet a bit as July approaches to ease any hit tool concerns at the next level. As his game continues to evolve and his understanding of how pitchers are trying to attack him continues to mature, Cholowsky has a chance to age into a complete hitter. 

Cholowsky grew up in a baseball family. His dad has been a scout for most of his life and it's made assimilating to the game and it's demands comfortable for Cholowsky. There's a case to be made that Cholowsky is the most complete draft-eligible college shortstop prospect since Dansby Swanson in 2015.

Emerson is what they look like. Offensively, it's pretty loud tools. Setup from a wide base, Emerson displays strong balance and rhythm in a simple swing with solid bat speed on the back end. Emerson's swing can get steep at times, but his attack angle allows him to cover and ambush pitches at the bottom of the zone better than most of his peers. The composure and mature nature in the box stands out. Emerson isn't jumpy or anxious. He sees the ball and reacts. It's power to the pull-side and a hit tool that stands out against upper-level competition. Emerson doesn't strike out, though he hardly chases walks either. The total product offensively has considerable upside with impact ceiling at the next level.

Emerson's contact quality can be streaky in tournament and showcase settings. There are times he'll look like a barrel magnet who simply cannot get out. Other times he'll roll over on breaking balls at a higher clip than you'd like with a general lack of slug on the baseball card. Emerson is still growing and maturing into what his eventual swing will look like. His bat-to-ball skills and bat speed stand out. He's as good a bet as anyone in the class to blossom into a complete hitter. 

Emerson is an above average runner with long strides and an athletic gait who should hold his speed as he ages. It's already a reasonably physical frame for his age, so he may ultimately settle in a solid average runner. In any case, he certainly won't be any sort of liability on the base paths and will likely add value in that department in some capacity as well. Emerson has an above average throwing arm with whippy action and carry across the dirt. It'll serve him well as he figures to stay on the left side of the infield. The glove projects above average at shortstop and potentially plus at third base. He's also been up to 90 mph on the mound. Emerson checks just about every box scouts look for in a player at this stage assuming the slug will come. There may not be an exceptionally loud tool on the report, but Emerson has the potential for five legitimate tools. Perhaps it's something of a Chase Headley outcome. He will be 18.5 years old on draft day.

Flora is as exciting a right-handed pitching prospect as we've seen in recent years. He still brings projection and a 6-foot-5-inch righty with a limb-wielding delivery and an explosive burgeoning arsenal. Flora has an up-tempo delivery with a higher leg kick. He moves fast down the mound with conviction. The arm action is loose and whippy. Command for the fastball continues to be an emphasis in his development as too often at this stage his misses are to the arm-side, largely because he gets moving too fast at times. That's improved in a dramatic way in 2026, now showcasing above average command on most occassions.

His fastball has been as high as 102 on radar guns but generally floats 96-97 with carry through the zone and an athletic finish through release. His lower slot and command for the top of the zone forces barrel to haplessly swing under his heater on most nights. It's every bith a 70-grade heater, and plays as such when he's hitting his spots. 

Flora possesses two breaking balls and they both flash plus upside. A more firm slider has good sweeping shape in the mid-80s with blossoming hand feel and command. Flora's willingness and confidence to back-door that pitch to left-handed hitters is a separator. He'll manipulate its shape at times, adding and subtracting depth depending on the situation. There's a big sweeper in the low-80s that exhibits huge shapes at times, too. 

Flora added a kick-change in 2026 and it's taken his menu of offerings to the next level. He's become equally as difficult to hit for left-handed hitters now. It's got excellent depth and depection, diving off the fastball tunnel late. Flora deletes spin from the pitch and creates awesome velocity separation in the 86-89 mph range. While he's still polishing up the ability to consistently create the same shape on a pitch-by-pitch basis, it's clearly an above average weapon, trending toward plus. 

Flora certainly operates like a starter and the strikes are improving. It's high-octane, MLB-ready stuff with the finer details and overall command being the last frontier of his development. If he performs at a high level throughout the 2026 season, Flora could blossom into an extremely high pick in 2026.

Lebron has a few legs up on the other college shortstops in this class. He's got an elite frame with more projection left in a hyper-athletic package. He's a whippy, lanky, lean middle infielder with a ton of filling out to do in his future, and present tools in every part of his game. He's an electric defender and as technically savvy as they come. Lebron fields the ball out in front of his body, showcasing plus arm strength across the diamond. He's proven capable of making every throw from every angle. Jump throws around the second base bag, submarine flips to first on balls he has to charge, back-hand pivot to side-arm tosses back to second base -- he's got every trick in the bag. Lebron has exceptionally quick hands and uses his momentum well when fielding his position. Better still, Lebron is a plus runner who flashes exceptional lateral mobility too. This is the easiest 'plus' grade on a glove in the class, and when all is said and done Lebron may end up one of the best defensive shortstops in Major League Baseball. Ironically, it's the routine play and/or Lebron chasing flair that can cause the few errors he's posted to this point in his career. Surely, most scouts will feel that can be cleaned up with reps. 

The aforementioned speed also plays in a big way on the bases. Lebron will be a threat to steal bases at the next level and could flirt with some 25/25 seasons if the hit tool continues to grow.  

Lebron has quick hands at the plate and he's shown marked improvement in terms of exit velocities over the past twelve months. What was once well-below average power is now looking more like the potential for plus raw power projection. Lebron peaked north of 110 mph and continues to add strength to his wiry frame. His build and feel for the barrel suggest he could grow into a bit more juice as he continues to physically mature. 

The hit tool has taken strides over the course of his Tuscaloosa career as well. Lebron sets up with a wide base and rocks and drifts back into a stacked back side. He folds his front knee and counter-rotates his front shoulder in his load, creating a move foward that, when on time and connected, is quite powerful. That front knee/front shoulder sequencing can at times result in Lebron opening up early with the front side, allowing him to get beat on spin off the plate. When he's right, Lebron hits behind a firm front side, rotating hard around his front hip pocket, creating awesome separation as he uncoils. Lebron absolutely hammers anything elevated in the zone and is particularly dangerous when he can get his hands extended on elevated velocity. Breaking balls and changeups at the bottom of the zone can still be a bugaboo for Lebron, however he showed more of a willingness to stay on those pitches as a freshman before regressing a bit in that area in 2025. Finding a happy medium between ambush hitting at the top of the zone and a more defensive approach in two-strike counts should help his offensive game blossom into a more complete package. For the time being, there's a bit too much chase and too many in-zone whiffs. Given his speed and feel for the barrel, it's unlikely he'll develop into less than an average hit tool guy at the next level, but there's work to do. 

If a team is looking for pure upside and ceiling, Lebron may carry more than any other name in the country. This is a potential 70-grade defender with at least a plus run tool and the arm strength to become a Gold Glove winner at the 6. There are very few developmental checkpoints left for Lebron to check off on the defensive end. It's impressive. Lebron has a path toward four 60-grades on his scouting report, however the hit tool will need to catch up if he hopes to become the No. 1 pick in July.

Following two award-winning banner campaigns at Duke, Gracia followed his head coach, Chris Pollard, from Durham to Charlottesville for his 2026 draft-eligible campaign. 

Gracia is a slugging corner outfielder with very present over-the-fence power and a highly-advanced understanding for how to backspin a baseball. He's a flyball specialist. It's well-above average bat--to-ball skills both inside the zone and outside of it, a particularly rare trait for players with his longer frame and levers. 

From a raw power perspective, Gracia actually took a small step backwards as a sophomore after flashing plus bat speed during his freshman year. All of his exit velocity metrics backtracked in 2025, flashing just average raw power. He lost two mph on his peak exit velocity and also saw his barrel rate drop slightly. It's still a frame built for big damage and most scouts expect he'll tap back into the juice he showed as a freshman going forward. 

Perhaps the best way for Gracia to improve his damage output and impact at the plate going forward would be to get more aggressive at the plate. He has consistently run lower than average swing rates and has a tendency to let the pitcher dictate the pace of an at-bat. That's gotten Gracia into pitchers' counts too often, forcing him to put borderline pitches in play late in counts instead of ambushing the cookie he may have received two pitches prior. Given his bat-to-ball metrics, ambushing pitches early in counts shouldn't hurt his ability to create more production. Gracia owns extremely low whiff rates regardless of the pitch location. In-zone, out-of-zone, spin, velocity, it doesn't really matter, Gracia's barrel can cover just about everything with the exception of velocity up and in on his hands, but that's to be expected from a player of his size with his levers. Taking a more aggressive approach to the plate and getting off more early-count A-Swings could help his offensive game jump back into Golden Spikes territory. 

Gracia checks a lot of the conventional boxes scouts want to see. It's a long, athletic body and longer levers that should add muscle and strength as he continues to mature. He's a solid average runner with a fringe-average arm strength in a corner. Gracia has a chance to develop into a 30-homer left fielder and a guy who routinely runs high on-base rates at the next level.

Lackey is one of the most well-rounded prospects in the 2026 class. A catcher by trade, he's got the flexibility, athleticism and arm strength to play the position as a professional. Lackey is a fairly average with regards to pitch framing; better stealing the north and south strikes than he is pulling the ball back into the zone when a pitcher misses arm-side or glove-side. Certainly a trait he can develop with further reps behind the dish. He's exceptional at blocking the ball in the dirt and is above-average throwing would-be base stealers out at second base. Lackey gets up and out of the crouch with impressive burst and flashes pop times that point toward an above average defender long-term.

It's hard to poke many holes in Lackey's offensive game too. He's well-above average from a bat-to-ball perspective and his peak batted-ball events have resulted in exit velocities north of 112 mph. There are components and traits here that suggest a plus hitter at the next level with the ability to perhaps run into 20 homers per year. He'll need to pull the ball with more frequency, and get the ball in the air more often if he's to realize his impact potential with the stick, but he's shown the raw strength and feel to get there when he chooses. Better still, Lackey has the athletic frame scouts like to see from a catcher who still has some strength gains on the horizon.

As if the defensive ability and hit tool upside weren't enough, Lackey is also a rare-breed catcher who has plus speed on the bases. He'll steal bases in buckets when the legs are fresh. 

Lackey has all the same traits that a player like Harry Ford showcased in the 2021 Draft that made him a top 15 selection. However, Lackey is doing it in the ACC against far more superior competition. This is top-ten pick upside.

Big time favorite of Georgia area guys due to an advanced feel for hitting, as well as finding the barrel, Burress is one of the more beloved recruits in Georgia Tech history. Explosive hips and big bat speed help Burress generate power well beyond what you might expect from a smaller frame. His exit velocities have approached 111 mph with at least above average raw power projection on the horizon. Burress has some drift in his swing and inconsistencies in terms of direction depending on where the pitch is. It's an operation that has allowed him to absolutely hammer anything at the top of the zone, however softer stuff at the bottom of the zone or below the zone can nullify some of his impact at the plate. He'll step in the bucket at times to sell out to his pull-side. It's an oddity, but Burress has been the most impactful player in the 2026 class across two seasons and it isn't terribly close. The raw power is legit and so are the tools. Until the quirks in his swing prove to be an issue, there's little reason to question his operation. 

Burress is athletic and runs well and has plenty of arm for center field. It's possible he's forced to left field if there's a more dynamic defender holding down the '8' in his organization as a pro. His solid-average speed also plays on the bases, however he's not inherently a base-stealer. He's still focusing on developing the little things necessary to become a stolen base artist. 

Burress' size will undoubtedly be a talking point as the draft approaches. That said, all he's done is perform. There have been very few hiccups along the way. At some point, the baseball card and under-the-hood metrics should supercede a player's physical stature.

One of the more dominant lefties in the 2026 class, Bolemon has long been a fiery competitor and performer on the tournament circuit. He's a composed, polished southpaw with mechanics that are refined and repeated well. He'll work up to 97 mph, living 91-94 with steep angle and natural deception. 

A power curveball with big vertical tilt is his primary out pitch, a breaker that lives deep into the fastball tunnel. It's firm, 80-84 with biting action, overmatching the opposition. A quality changeup rounds up his arsenal with high-level conviction and some tail. 

The entire package on the bump is more refined than most of his peers. Bolemon is a strike-thrower with one of the better deliveries in the class. There's some capabilities on the offensive side too with a short, compact swing and some pull-side power. Bolemon will be 19.3 years old for the draft.

Rojas is a lanky, long, left-handed pitcher with projection ahead of his frame both in terms of mass and strength. He has wider shoulders and a leaner midsection, two traits scouts like to see in younger pitching prospects. Rojas is a tough look for hitters with a wider approach angle and a lower slot. It's loose with very low effort and three pitches, free and easy.

Rojas blossomed over the last calendar year adding several ticks to his arsenal including a fastball that has brushed 98. He's mostly 92-95 but there's life and deception on his heater that allow it to play up. Rojas launches from a lower slot and absolutely blows hitters up at the top of the zone with the pitch. It's a high-spin offering with considerable arm-side run and he'll occasionally stay behind it to hold vertical action. 

Rojas' changeup is probably his best pitch as he really sells it and tumbles it off the fastball tunnel late with some parachute. There's also a upper-70s breaking ball that could ultimately end up his best weapon with top-tier spin rates and feel for shape. It's been a continuous up arrow next to his name. He's absolutely mauled the opposition this spring. He will be 19 years old on draft day.

Booth is a metric darling and it begins with his age. He will turn 18 years old just days before the Draft. He's a powderkeg outfielder with a ton of raw traits and tools that are beginning to surface into in-game production. At first blush he looks the part of a table-setter thanks to his 70-grade speed and twitchiness in the box and in centerfield. After taking in batting practice and a couple games of at-bats it becomes fairly evident there's tools in the impact category as well. 

Booth can swing it and presents 'plus' raw bat speed that shows out to the pull-side. That swing is a little more projectable and aesthetically pleasing in BP; his in-game hacks being a bit more inconsistent from a mechanics perspective. Booth has a downhill plane and can be placed into the "chop" swing at times. That said, he never surrenders at-bats and has consistently runs low strikeout rates throughout his amateur career. 

Booth is a strong defender who has a chance to develop into an above average glove that plays in all three outfield spots. It could become something of a Trent Grisham type of profile in due time.

When Jacob Lombard's older brother George was drafted in the first round by the New York Yankees in 2023, the bar was set. Three years later, Jacob has a chance to one-up his older brother. And likely will.

The tools here have a chance to be era-defining.

Lombard deploys an athletic, rhythmic setup at the plate with quick hands and a compact, short path through the zone. He has present power with big exit velocities to all fields and has been known to inside-out the ball into the right-center field gap with authority. This is a player who could grow into 70-grade raw power all whilst manning a premium infield position. 

Lombard's hit tool has continuously improved year over year. It's become one of the most advanced and polished swings in the class. He hardly ever expands the zone. It's big and loud and often in the air to the pull-side. The components are there for Lombard to become one of the more impressive slugging prospects any draft has seen over the last handful of years. There's physicality and projection in the offensive profile. Superstar traits. 

Lombard has become more physical over the past calendar year but it's hardly cost him a step on the dirt. He's a 70-grade runner with fluid and quick-twitch actions necessary to play shortstop as a pro. The arm strength is probably the tool lacking the most impact, but it's still squarely average and is on pace to fit the shortstop position as he matures. If it never comes, Lombard could still develop into an extremely potent centerfielder or third base profile. His instincts, actions, internal clock and hands are all befitting of a future '6' in the big leagues.

Lombard with his pedigree and bloodlines are on a short list of players with franchise-altering ceiling. He brings back shades of Manny Machado.

Hacopian was an absolute star for the Maryland Terps before transferring for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign to College Station. The offensive profile features very, very little holes. He's a complete hitter in a lot of ways. 

Hacopian has shown an exciting combination of elite bat-to-ball skills and plus raw power in his young collegiate career. He's among the most polished bats in the class at this early stage in the draft process thanks to a keen eye, a selective nature and terrific bat speed. He extends at-bats by spitting on pitchers' pitches and fouling off pitches on the black. He makes the opposition work. Hacopian is an adjustable hitter who rarely gives away an at-bat or a pitch for that matter. He's as tough an out as you'll find. 

Perhaps the only thing missing from his shining offensive profile is a greater emphasis pulling the baseball in the air. His ground ball rates are the only thing holding him back from being a Golden Spikes nominee and a potential top five pick in the Draft. Turning the ringing singles through the hole into blistered balls over the left field fence would elevate his profile into a new tier. For the time being, it's plus bat-to-ball skills, it's plus raw power, and it's a plus approach. Hacopian has a chance to be a special hitter at the next level if he can unlock just one more gear. 

The frame is mostly maxed in terms of physical projection, but he can handle third base at an average level with average arm strength. Hacopian played a great deal of shortstop at Maryland, but flipped to third base on the Cape leading into the 2026 season. He's a more natural fit at the hot corner. Hacopian has a tendency to throw across the diamond from a lower arm slot causing his throws to loop and tail back into the first baseman. It hasn't led to many throwing errors at this point, but it is a throwing style scouts generally scoff at at the amateur level. It's by no means a disqualifier of any kind. Guys like Nolan Arenado, Alex Rodriguez and Kyle Seager employed similar throwing styles for their entire careers. While Hacopian isn't a dynamic defender, he is deliberate with his technique and possesses a strong internal clock. He rarely rushes his throws and has strong feel for the game. 

While the bat shines and the glove does its job, Hacopian isn't a burner. He's a below average runner who clocks 4.50+ times home-to-first base. He's not going to add much value in the stolen base department and he will likely struggle to take the extra base at times. 

Hacopian has top-ten pick traits and tools. He's one of the better college hitters to come through over the course of the last couple of years. He'll need to continue to mash considering the limitations on the bases and with the glove. He's been one of the most consistent hitters in college baseball going back to his freshman year.

Bell was a second round pick by the Rays in the 2024 Draft, but went unsigned and ended up in the SEC where his bat has flashed the upside folks have long felt it possessed. He's a masher. Bell peaked as a freshman with an exit velocity of 111 mph. He averaged 90 mph and lifted the ball in the air to his pullside 35 percent of the time. It was a 15 percent in-zone whiff rate and a chase rate near 23 percent. He could be had with advanced breaking balls at or just below the bottom of the zone, but that's hardly a surprise for a player being exposed to college pitching for the first time. Above average bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate compliment his innate feel for providing impact and punch in the box.

Bell has changed physically and mechanically on campus. He's demonstrating looseness in his hands from the left side with loft built into his swing. He’s eliminated the barrel tip that would cause swing and miss, as well as timing issues in high school. He's also widened his stance and is leveraging his back-hip with far more authority, turning harder on the baseball.
 
The physicality has really ticked up over the last calendar year with added strength and mass, particularly in his lower half. His profile is buoyed by strong defensive actions, above average arm strength and a mature IQ on the field that should help stay at the shortstop position at the next level. Bell has the ability to throw from multiple angles. He's got quick, precise footwork with strong fundamentals. Bell can be a frenetic defender at times with a still-developing internal clock. Still, the components are present and he's got a good chance at developing into at least an above average defender. 

Bell's impressive resume landed him an opportunity with Team USA's Collegiate National Team after just one year in college baseball, a rare honor. He's revered for his workman mentality, seriousness and competitive edge on the field. It's remarkably obvious that Bell's first, second, and third priority in life is baseball, specifically winning. He will be a draft-eligible sophomore.

Strosnider is a gamer. He burst onto the scene like a bat out of hell his freshman year for the Horned Frogs running a .350/.420/.650 slash with 11 homers and 10 stolen bases. 

It's all coming together for Strosnider at the right time. He's grown into pull-side power on campus and is now flashing exit velocities north of 112 mph. His peak exit velocities can compete with just about anyone in college baseball registering hard-hit rates more than 50 percent of his at-bats as a freshman. He gets to it from a swing that creates big stretch and extension out in front of the plate. He's a twitchy athlete with strong hands and quick hips. Strosnider has been especially effective smothering pitches he offers at inside of the zone. His athletic testing and force plate output points to a guy who could continue growing into more and more power. 

Strosnider's aggressive mentality in the box has led to whiff and soft contact on pitchers' pitches. He can struggle to adjust and make contact on swings outside of the zone and is particularly aggressive swinging at breaking balls below the strike zone. Despite the nitpicking of warts, it was a remarkably impressive introduction into college baseball. Eye-opening to scouts. Assuming he makes one more noteworthy jump as a draft-eligible sophomore, his game could blossom. 

Defensively, Strosnider has plus speed and well-above average athleticism that will likely place him in a corner at the next level, but the arm has ticked up the last twelve months and could have a place in right field garnering plus grades. He's cycled between centerfield and right field for the Horned Frogs. There's a centerfield ceiling here if Strosnider doesn't slow down with more muscle, however he's unlikely to get full-time opportunities at the '8' with Chase Brunson flanking his right at school. He will be a draft-eligible sophomore, barely 21 years old for the Draft.

Becker is a big, strong, projectable shortstop in college that likely profiles to third base at the next level. As far as floors go, he has one of the safest in the class.

Becker's swing is pro ready right now. It's simple, grounded, balanced with very little wasted effort. He stays up the middle of the field and let's power materialize based on a pitcher's mistake. The hand speed stands out, as does his ability to consistently hit the baseball very hard thanks to elite barrel awareness. Becker lacks the twitch and explosive athletic actions of some of his peers, however he's growing into more strength and the raw power should come. There's already flashes over solid average raw power, and his feel for getting to the barrel is exceptional. Simply put, Becker knows how to hit. Perhaps the only concern on his overall offensive profile is a willingness to expand the zone at times. That said, he makes up for his aggressive nature with excellent adjustability and a knack for working deep counts. 

He plays shortstop now, but most believe he'll eventually land at second or third base as a professional. Should he stay at the position, Becker projects a solid average shortstop. He’s got good first-step quickness and an average arm that plays up a bit with his ability to throw from multiple angles. It’s quiet actions and good size that could add more physical tools with further maturation.

Reese entered the Houston lineup right out of the gates thanks to his impressive bat speed and present raw power. That gangbusters production landed him at Mississippi State in 2025 by way of the transfer portal.

It's a big, long frame with considerable pull-side power from the left side coming out of a compact move and fast-twitch turns on the baseball. Reese projects an above average hitter with strong in-zone and out-of-zone contact rates. He's an adjustable hitter that puts pressure on the opposition to make good pitches thanks to his athleticism in the box. Reese absolutely hammers fastballs and has improved each year seeing and reacting to spin. Despite slightly higher than average chase rates, Reese is ultra-efficient, lifting and launching the ball with impressive exit velocities to the pull-side. It's a slugging archetype with the bat-to-ball skills necessary to dispel any pigeonholing. 

Reese has bounced around on defense between third base and left field. His physical frame does threaten his ability to stick at third base long-term, but he's more than proficient handling a corner outfield spot. He's only a fringy runner with fringy arm strength. Should he shore up the overall hit tool in the coming seasons and establish value in the field, Reese has a chance to come off the board on day one in 2026.

Considered the premium pitching prize of the 2023 class, Peterson walked away from a lot of money to get to Gainesville. It's a premium fastball that sits 94-96 touching 99 with running life late and considerable carry. He fills up the zone. He can spin it and the pitch should trend more effective as he matures thanks to well-above average extension down the mound. Peterson has above average command for the heater and likes to live on the corners at the top of the strike zone.

His most effective pitch is a nasty slider featuring high spin, resting 84-86, up to 89 with deep, late break.  Peterson has shown the ability to manipulate shape and a willingness to throw it to righties and lefties. It's another pitch with a strong command track record. His misses are generally off the plate and his best offerings on the black low, glove-side. It's a breaking ball with some of the highest ceiling in the class. He flashes a changeup at 85 with tumble and a mid-70's bender as tertiary offerings. There's also a much bigger curveball, however his shapes and feel for executing that pitch presently lag behind his three better established weapons. 

This is a fairly north-south arsenal of pitches with an emphasis in changing the eye level of the hitter. Peterson has long levers, whippy, athletic actions, and a compact delivery with definitive starter traits. He throws strikes and battles on the mound. It's one of the more complete pitching profiles in the 2026 class.

Flukey is a lean, high-waisted, long-levered righty with significant athleticism and arm-speed for a guy his size. Already touching 98 and sitting 94-96 deep into starts, Flukey should consistently throw really, really hard as he continues to develop. 

The heater already projects a plus pitch going forward thanks to enormous carry through the zone. Flukey tends to throw his fastball to the glove-side rather than elevating it. As he grows more comfortable with commanding that pitch to the top of the zone, it's effectiveness should jump. Thus far, it's been effective getting hitters to expand outside of the zone, but not especially effective missing bats. For a guy with as much extension, velocity and induced vertical break as Flukey, the fastball should eventually be a much bigger weapon. 

He'll mix in an above above curveball with a bit of hump, though it features absolutely massive depth, generally thrown 76-78 mph. Flukey throws the bender nearly 20 percent of the time. He'll happily steal strikes with it or bury it in the dirt to get whiffs. And he's gotten a ton of whiffs with it thus far. His command for that pitch stands out. 

Flukey also throws a harder bullet slider in the mid-80s, though his command for that pitch is more average. It's got a high ceiling thanks to its depth and overall shape, however getting more value out of the fastball will unlock more upside for both breaking balls. He folds in a more traditional mid-80s cutter that possesses more bullet shape, bridging his entire menu of pitches together beautifully. 

He'll mix in a changeup as well, though he doesn't have great feel for the pitch right now. The shapes he's able to produce with it however point toward plus upside with the cambio. 

As Flukey adds weight and polish, his stuff should continue to pop. It's a remarkably athletic starting pitcher profile with limitless projection. Unfortunately, Flukey missed a huge chunk of the 2026 season with a stress reaction in his ribs. The ceiling on an arm like Flukey is someone like Logan Gilbert.

Kuhns became an enormous weapon for Tony Vitello down the stretch as a true freshman and hasn't looked back. He's a good mover on the mound with solid extension. It's a super loose and fast arm with whip and projection still forthcoming. Kuhns carries himself like a bulldog on the mound, unafraid of the big moment, intense. He features a lean, slender build with plenty of room for muscle and velocity. 

Kuhns operates with a traditional wind-up delivery featuring a high, tall gather, into a high leg kick and stride toward the plate. He demonstrates excellent balance through release. Kuhns has a longer arm stroke that doesn't inhibit his ability to throw strikes. He's always on time. There's some effort through release, but nothing worthy of any red flags. In fact, it should continue to iron itself out with more strength. Once he allows runners on base, he works with quick tempo out of the stretch, again throwing strikes at a heavy clip and mixing up his pitches. He's not predictable, and works with a pace that should hold runners in place. 

The fastball is a good one. He's been up to 98 and will sit 94-96 the second time through a lineup. Kuhns spins the heater particularly well and player development experts believe there's some low-hanging fruit to extract even more value from the heater. He's lowered his slot a few inches in 2026 and tends to work down at the bottom of the zone before electing to elevate as his outings wear on. Utilizing the elevated heater with its flat approach earlier in his starts to get whiffs and punchouts would conceivably up his effectiveness. Kuhns' zone-neutralized VAA is among the flattest in college baseball. 

Glove side, Kuhns works with a slider sitting 82-85 and a curveball at 77-80 that both spin near 2,500 rpm. The slider is the better of the two offerings and has been a legitimate put-away option when he shapes and buries it. The curve is still finding its way, more often used as a get-me-over strike-stealer than a put-away weapon. These are both pitches that a professional pitching lab is going to love getting their hands on. He's got the capacity for spin out of the hand, however repeating his shapes and executing those pitches will be a development emphasis at the next level. 

Arm side, the changeup is a putaway pitch right now. It runs 15 inches of horizontal break away from left-handed hitters, sitting 83-85 and touching 86 with good separation from the fastball. It's also generating big whiff rates. As is the case with most 21 year olds, there's still some polish in terms of consistently landing that pitch where he wants, but there's no denying its upside. This is a future weapon at the next level, and should have no issue getting to above average grades. There are nights it will likely flash plus. 

The story here is projectable upside, feel for spin, and fastball value that may not be fully extracted yet. It's a great blueprint for future success. Kuhns moves well and has proven capable of handling the bright lights. There are a ton of similarities to Bryce Miller in the whole package, with a bit more velocity upside. Kuhns is draft-eligible as a sophomore.

Clark is a tooled-up middle infield prospect with a chance to provide value on both sides of the ball. He's a legitimate prep prospect for the 2026 Draft, but his commitment to Duke may muddy the waters a bit in July. Clark comes from a family that values education in a big way. 

Clark is exciting. It's plus foot speed with a quick split out of the batters box from the left side occassionally flashing 70-grade run times home-to-first. Clark delivers a heavy barrel with active hands in the box. He's a slappy hitter as currently constructed with ground ball rates that can be prohibitive toward his ability to impact the game with his bat speed. Home runs don't decorate his baseball card yet, but scouts think the raw power projection and bat speed are there to eventually incorporate over-the-fence output into this bag of tricks. Clark uses his strong lower half well to generate ground force making hard turns on the baseball. It's advanced bat-to-ball skills with the chance to slug going forward if he makes a swing adjustment to get the ball in the air more often. 

Clark has active feet on the dirt and has the quick hands and actions necessary to play on the dirt as a professional. The range at shortstop is present, however as he continues to fill out and get more physical he may be tested at the '6'. His solid average arm strength plays just fine at second and third base. Feel for both of those positions lags behind his natural instincts at the shortstop position, however those actions should blossom over time with further reps. 

Given the foot speed, present strength, bat speed and feel for hitting, it's easy to dream on Clark developing into a bat-first middle infielder.

Schmidt checks just about every box you could ask for from a projection lefty at the high school level. He reclassified up from the 2027 Draft and won't turn 18 until a couple months after the Draft. He's big, strong, left-handed and controls his body beautifully down the mound.

Schmidt has all the components necessary to start at the next level. A terrific mover, he generates huge extension down the mound allowing his fastball to play up. He's routinely 93-96 and will grab 97 on occasion with strong tailing action. Schmidt's fastball doesn't possess dynamic shape, but he hides the ball and well and the velocity can sneak up on hitters with how close to the plate he releases the baseball.

Schmidt's two breaking balls are good ones. There's an upper-70s curveball with strong vertical tilt and some late darting action to his arm-side. He commands the pitch at an above average level. A more traditional low-80s slider has been a point of emphasis in his development this past year and he's reached a point where he can throw it in any count. It's a gradual breaker that will flash above-average upside, however it lives off the success and command of his fastball. 

The changeup has just as much upside as the breaker. Schmidt generates well-above average fading action to his glove-side and can sink the cambio too. 

This is a reasonably complete arsenal that really only needs a cutter or firm bullet slider to round out a four-pitch mix. Schmidt's age, size, handedness and body control should be huge selling points in the 2026 Draft. He's got the components to go very early.

A reclass up from 2027, Grindlinger is one of the youngest draft-eligible players of the modern era. He'll turn 17 years old just 3 months prior to the event. Grindlinger is one of the more impressive two-way talents the draft has seen in the last handful of years. He has the chops to become a first round pick as both a pitcher and an outfielder. 

Grindlinger's ceiling on the mound has scouts intrigued. His left arm has looseness to it and the ball jumps out of the hand free and easy.

He's an excellent strike-thrower with a fastball that run itself up to 97, launched from a deceptive slot. Grindlinger owns a reasonably generic release/launch profile from a height and angles perspective, however at his best he's creating moderate carry through the zone, complimented by above average tail to the fastball. His ability to spin the ball is also more average, however his slider is already up into the mid-80s at times with solid shape. Grindlinger's hand-feel for pitch design is impressive at such a young age.

Grindlinger has also flashed a changeup with big, dynamic shape. He kills spin better than most of his peers and has shown the ability to command it to the arm-side with relative consistency.

Grindlinger is already showing above average extension down the mound for his age and should grow into a bonafide starting pitcher operation. The strikes, athlete, arm action and looseness of it all is awfully tantalizing.

As mentioned, it's first round tools at the plate. He's got long levers and a keen understanding for how to catch the ball out front to create loft. Grindlinger is already flashing plus power projection and punishing the baseball. He uses the middle of the field beautifully. Grindlinger does a nice job anchoring his back hip into a positive forward move, rotating hard against a firm front side and creating significant bat speed. He lags the hands deep in his load creating huge torque, delivering a heavy load through the zone a la Matt Olson or Kyle Tucker with a flatter attack angle. It's a longer stride and a toe tap, both of which seem to consistently be on time. Grindlinger has very good hands and shows the ability to get the barrel to all four quadrants with adjustability that can be rare for a player with his length and levers. His whiffs, while rare, have generally come on elevated velocity. He has shown no issues dealing with spin and is generally unwilling to expand the zone. This is elite plate coverage, an excellent eye and an approach far beyond his years. 

Grindliner has some bounce in his step and is a long-strider underway. He's a above-average runner now, but has the look of a player who could slow down half-a -tick with added size and muscle as he matures. 

Grindlinger checks just about every box in the book. He's a premium prospect with a substantial ceiling, however whoever drafts him should be prepared to let him develop for several years in minor league baseball as he gets older, bigger and stronger. From this chair, the bat is too special to give up future offensive impact.

Carlon was a regular relief pitcher for the Sun Devils as a freshman posting 34 strikeouts in 40.2 innings. But he really stepped up his game in the Alaska League, dominating both sides of the baseball and winning league MVP honors during the summer of 2024. Most believe his future is on the bump. 

This 6-foot-5 southpaw has a strong two-pitch wombo-combo featuring a mid-90s fastball that's touched 98 and a mid-to-upper-80s bullet slider that’s a real swing-and-miss weapon. Carlon's has an exceptionally high launch creating outlier steepness for hitters; the slider being the great beneficiary of that trait. It's such a good breaking ball that Carlon actually throws it just as often as he does the heater.

He's folding in a curveball with more frequency this year and generating whiffs with that pitch as well. There's also something of a gyro kick-change that he's been working on building out to round out his arsenal. 

Carlon is a smooth, athletic mover on the mound with some projection left in his frame. He doesn't extend particularly well down the mound for his size, something that will likely always limit his fastball effectiveness at the next level. Carlon was honored with an invite to the Team USA Collegiate National Team this summer. If you squint, there's something of a Robbie Ray look here.

Spangler certainly looks the part. A 6-foot-4-inch infielder with long limbs and a high waist, Spanger went into the summer of 2025 with considerable physical projection and lived up to that billing over the winter. He put on more than 20 pounds and added the muscle scouts wanted to see. It's now considerable present maturity and strength, especially compared to his peers at this stage. He's got a sweet left-handed swing featuring plenty of bat speed and pull-side loft. There's a whole lot more in the tank on the way. Despite his longer levers and still-maturing frame, Spanger's ability to keep the hands tight and make compact turns on pitches all over the zone stands out. He's a controlled hitter who doesn't try to out-swing his frame. It's an even, wide base with a quiet load and simple swing that projects to hit going forward. This is a kid who could hit for both average and power. 

The numbers support the narrative. Spangler saw some of the best pitching anyone in this class over the last two years. He saw bigger velocity on a consistent basis than just about anyone. He still raked. A sub-15 percent chase rate combined with a 14 percent whiff rate and 7 percent whiff rate on swings inside the strike zone point to a distinguished hitter. While the slug is yet to materialize in his in-game production, at least on the bigger stages, few question he'll eventually get there. It may not be his carrying tool, but Spangler should have no issue getting to 20-homer output at some point. Spangler is going to hit and he's likely going to slug. He'll just need to develop the ability to get the ball in the air more frequently. 

Defensively, Spangler works well through the ball well. He possesses average arm strength and should be able to handle third base if he outgrows the shortstop position, especially considering his recent gains. Spangler does seem to have lost a bit of his looseness and flexibility with the added strength. It's quiet, confident actions with soft hands on balls hit right at him. His internal clock and tempo on the dirt stand out. Just a lot of polish here with physical impact upside on the way. Spangler is committed to Stanford, a school notoriously difficult to pay players away from. He will be 18.9 years old on draft day.

Townsend is one of the most fiery competitors in the 2027 class. He holds himself to a high bar that can come across in demonstrative ways on the mound. He's an audible competitor who isn't afraid to show emotion on the bump. He is a metric-darling with massive spin rates on the breaking ball and a high spin fastball. He'll work up to 98 with the fastball, resting 92-94 in later innings. While the fastball has strong spin and shape at times, commanding the pitch at the top of the zone will be an important development for Townsend going forward. Walks can get streaky for Townsend, and a lot of times fastball command is to blame. 

The aforementioned breaking ball is a hammer curve thrown in the mid-70s to low-80s with huge downer break and conviction. The shape of the pitch will vary at times, but at its best, it features sharp, late bite, spiked into the catcher's glove at the dirt. He'll grab north of 3000 rpm at times with it. The two pitches tunnel well off each other and represent a bit of a meta in professional baseball right now.

Impressively, Townsend added a mid-80s sweeper in 2026 launched out of the same slot as the rest of his arsenal. It's added a lateral element to his offerings, elevating his pro upside. 

Townsend's cutter has a chance to be a very good one. It's 86-89 with big vertical shape, up into the low-90s. It plays extremely well off the fastball. As if the stuff wasn't good enough, how it's contextualized into his arsneal is beautiful. He's also worked to refine a changeup that he's grown more and more comfortable throwing in games, flashing above average at times with spin-killing release. 

Townsend's control and command are still a work in progress and his composure on the bump is something he's worked hard to regulate at Ole Miss. Repeating his delivery, holding his strength deeper into games, and staying in the strikezone will be keys toward his future impact on the mound.

A tremendously decorated high school football player, Bowen has a lot of big believers on the diamond where his physicality and tools have him one of the top ballplayers in the state of California in 2026. 

A physical hitter with strength in his hands and core, Bowen is already showcasing some of the best raw power projection in the class. The hit tool has taken a big step forward in 2025 as well with healthy contact rates and a more selective approach at the dish. 

Bowen is an aggressive runner who looks more like a linebacker than an outfielder on the base paths, but still generates above average run times. His arm strength in right field (or third base) may be his best asset, and it could be some of the best arm strength in the class when all is said and done. He's your prototype power-bat/power-arm right field prospect who is still reasonably green in terms of training age. 

Bowen will need to make sure he doesn't get too big if he intends to keep the athleticism he's grown into over the course of the last year. He's extremely physical at this still young stage. Bowen will be 18.5 years old for the draft and has an up arrow next to his name.

Gaeckle has shown the ability to sit 95-96, touching 98, unafraid to locate in on the hands to righties, arm-side. He'll brush them off the plate. 

Gaeckle throws two breaking balls and both project plus or better. His better breaker is a 2800-rpm bullet slider that he pitches front-door to righties and can locate off the plate and bury to lefties to get punch outs. The curveball is an absolute hammer with impressive depth and velocity, up to 83 mph. 

A changeup has been a point of emphasis in Fayetteville and it's certainly taken huge strides. An 88-89 mph fader, Gaeckle has seen this pitch take flight in Fayetteville. He creates horizontal planes tailing the pitch away from lefties. It projects an above average pitch going forward, maybe more with continued refinement. It's a very "stuffy" profile capable of working north-south and east-west with hitters.

Gaeckle isn't the biggest guy in the world, and his body is already fairly maxed out muscle-wise, so skeptics may look at the frame and question where it goes from here, but the stuff is so *now* it's hard to argue with the upside. Gaeckle is on his second UCL after undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2020. He was a 20th round selection by the Reds in 2023, but elected to head to Arkansas.

Edwards has bounced around between relief roles and starter responsibilities at USC, in large part due to on-again, off-again injuries issues. That said, he's a starter through and through going forward.

Edwards is a good mover on the bump with a fluid delivery and an over-the-top slingshot delivery. He's shown feel to pitch and gets production out of a three-pitch mix, complimented by some natural oclussion and deceptive mechanical patterns. It's a drop-and-drive operation that looks prototypical until release, where Edwards gets his elbow high and launches from a slot well-above the average pitcher.

While the fastball is ordinarily just 91-93 mph, Edwards can at times reach back for 96 in side sessions showing his arm strength. Edwards does generate whiffs and chase outside fhe zone at an exceptional clip thanks to the aformentioned deception, however his shapes are awesome too. Edwards gets plenty of ride on the heater, and will ocassionally cut the baseball. It's a unique look for hitters, especially when you consider the 78-inch launch height -- a full ten inches higher than the MLB average. Edwards isn't a long-strider and doesn't generate great extension down the mound, instead relying on the factors above to generate value from his heater.

Edwards' breaking ball is an upper-70s slurvy bender that can climb into the low-80s when he chooses to shorten the pitch up a bit. He throws it for strikes at an impressive clip and has shown feel for landing it to the back foot of right-handed pitchers, and sweeping it away from lefties. Edwards has actually found more swing-and-miss success against right-handed hitters with the breaking ball, speaking toward is platoon-neutral splits for his arsenal. It's a pitch that tunnels the fastball very, very well with hitters swinging over the top of it with frequency. It's not a terribly sexy pitch from a Stuff+ perspective, but has been effective paired off that fastball. It's likely got an above average future. 

The changeup is actually Edwards' second-most thrown pitch, however scouts believe the breaking ball will ultimately unseat the cambio from a favorability standpoint. Still, the changeup posted enormous whiff rates across the last two seasons and presents enough vertical and lateral movement to project an above average weapon at the next level.

Edwards has yet to put together an extended sample in a single season due to bullpen usage and the fluky injuries along the way. If he can post a big innings total in 2026 and leave no doubt of his durability as July approaches, he's got Top-100 pick traits. He won't turn 21 years old until a couple days after the draft.

Everything about Vochko fits the "prototype". It's a 6-foot-4-inch, 225-lb frame with a cutting fastball that explodes generates weak swings and feeble ground balls. He's been up to 100 mph and will like 95-97, but has struggled to miss bats or induce chase with the heater throughout his collegiate career. Volchko generates huge spin on his entire arsenal and the fastball possesses some of the biggest spin rates of any fastball in the class. He throws a more conventional cutter with diving life as well, also high in velocity. 

He's got two breaking balls, a low-90s slider that used to produce more bullet shape is now showing true sweep in Athens. It's a potential plus-or-better weapon going forward so long as he's establishing the fastball where he wants to in the zone. He generates strong chase and whiffs rates on the sweeper thanks to its firmness and elite spin rates. 

He's shown good conviction and bite on a traditional slurvy bender too, however it lacks dynamic vertical depth and he doesn't throw it often. There's a bit more growing to do in the polish department, and the operation will tighten up as he gets older, but the arm is loose and the athlete is exceptional.

Volchko is throwing an upper-80s changeup a lot more as a Georgia Bulldog. It's critical for his ability to punch out left-handed hitters. For much of his amateur career, everything he's thrown has moved the same direction. That is no longer always the case. 

Volchko has struggled at times during his collegiate career, partially due to the aformentioned fact most of the pitches in his arsenal act the same. He struggles to create various pitch shapes and doesn't particularly move the ball in a loud way north-south or east-west. He jumped into the portal in large part because he needed his pitch mix and pitch design reworked for the 2026 season and that seems to have worked in a big way. His command is still fringy and walks can still shorten his outings. A high-leverage bullpen role as a professional is very possible. 

Volchko turned down considerable money in the 2023 Draft and now appears primed to do well in 2026.

Kevin Roberts Jr. is a physical two-way specimen with some of the most powerful upside of anybody in the 2026 class. It's an ultra-long 6-foot-6-inch frame featuring a high waist and lean, lanky strength spread throughout. Roberts has broad shoulders and a strong lower half that point toward further strength on the way. Scouts are split on where his highest ceiling lays. On the mound he's been up to 96 mph with loose, whippy arm strength and good balance for a pitcher his age. He'll flip in a budding breaking ball with solid depth as well. There's a fringier changeup that has been a point of emphasis in his development for the last year.

All that being said, the offensive tools may be simply too loud to take the bat out of his hands. 

Unlike many of the tall, physical towering high school bats before him, Roberts can really, really hit. He's feel for the strike zone and his ability to put the fat part of the bat on the ball, despite his levers, is exemplary. Roberts ran a 15 percent chase rate throughout the summer of 2024. That was complimented by an 11 percent whiff rate and a 9 percent whiff rate on swings inside the zone. The kid can really hit. Roberts sinks and drifts into his back hip, leveraging the ground well to create power. And it's already arrived. His .636 slug and.272 ISO as a high school sophomore across showcase and top-tier tournaments are evidence of the impact Roberts brings to the dish. So long as these tools and traits continue to translate as the level of competition continues to improve, there's no reason to think he can't eventually be labeled the top high school bat in the country. 

In the field, it's plus arm strength with solid average, likely destined for right field where he projects at least a solid average defender. There's something of a Jorge Soler profile here. A two-sport star, Roberts excels on the basketball court as well. He'll turn 18 years old right around the day of the draft. Models should push his profile up the board provided he continues on the positive linear ascent scouts have seen to this point.

A late re-class into the 2026 Draft, Brick was originally supposed to be draft-eligible in 2027. Brick is one of the most decorated bat-to-ball artists in the 2026 class with a hit tool some are already throw plus grades on at this stage. He's also got strong catch-and-throw skills behind the plate.

It's easy to dream on the offensive upside Brick could eventually bring to the dish. He has routinely run whiff rates in the single digits most years throughout his prep career. Better still, he's a polished hitter with a quiet approach, unwilling to expand the zone. Brick chooses to let the ball travel and tends to pepper the right-center field gap. Rarely will he elect to turn and burn as ambushing into his pull-side power hasn't been on the resume often. That said, the raw power exists in a very big way. Brick is capable of putting on a display in batting practice and has flashed plus bat speed. He's got extremely fast hands. There will likely be a point in his amateur career where he flips the switch and actively tries to become a run producer rather than a conga line contributor, and he's more than physically capable of making that switch. The building blocks of a decorated, distinguished hitter are quite present here.

While Brick has played some third base in his high school days, most foresee a catching prospect at the end of the day. He's quick and explosive out of the crouch with a strong, accurate arm down to second base. Brick has impressive athleticism behind the plate and possesses the ability to back-pick runners at first base, and even second base if they get too aggressive out there. He's got the components to develop into a revered defender if he continues on this linear trajectory. Brick projects a fringe-average runner at the next level. 

The hit tool, the power projection, the catch-and-throw and athleticism; Brick has an exciting array of tools and all the traits necessary to be a starting-caliber shortstop at the Major League level. He's arguably the top catching prospect to become available in the draft since Blake Mitchell in 2023. He will barely be 18 years old on draft day.

Scouts were enamored by Brunson's frame and whippy strength in high school, culminating in he being drafted by the Tampa Bay Rays in the 18th round. He went unsigned. 

Brunson has a line-drive approach with a gap-to-gap style of hitting, though he's begun to grow into more raw power and is exercising it to the pull-side for TCU. Brunson has already peaked with batted-balls registering north of 110 mph. Brunson doesn't inherently possess plus bat speed, but he swings a heavy barrel and knows how to drop it into the zone. He hits the ball hard and runs elite contact rates on anything thrown inside the strike zone. Contact quality on velocity in on his hands is an area of of improvement that Brunson has continued to focus on. That said, when he gets his arms extented on mistakes down the middle, especially elevated, he can be dangerous. 

Brunson could end up at any number of positions at the next level. He played a bit of catcher in high school but has been manning centerfield for the Horned Frogs over the last two seasons. He's a solid average defender at the '8' and has shown some feel for spacial awareness around the wall/warning track. He's an average runner with above average arm strength. The whole profile is more befitting of a right fielder at the next level when all is said and done.

Robbins has essentially been a full-time player for Seton Hall right out of the gate. He started 34 games as a freshman and hit nearly .300 in the Big East. He's parlayed that success into bigger and better results as the years have gone on with his prospects looking brighter than ever. Robbins transferred to the University of Texas for the 2026 season after spending two years at Seton Hall. 

Robbins hits the baseball very hard. He's a batted-ball merchant who generates significant production by way of his exit velocities. He's registered exit velocities north of 110 mph and will routinely sit well north of 95 mph. He absolutely pummels pitches elevated in the zone and has shown the ability to adjust to spin low-and-away. Robbins' entire offensive profile is built on his approach, an approach that doesn't include swinging at pitches outside of the strike zone. He's a disciplined hitter who generally runs low chase rates. He boasts strong contact rates on swings in the zone too. The only critique on Robbins at this stage is a general lack of extended looks at more advanced pitching. He's been productive on the Cape playing for Harwich, a feather in his cap for model teams looking for production with the wood bat. 

Robbins is an above-average runner with good instincts on the base paths. He's an active base-stealer and consistently looks to put himself into scoring position. A right fielder by trade, Robbins has average arm strength and takes good routes to the ball. Most scouts believe he'll eventually shift to left field as a professional, but it's average or better tools in the corner befitting of a player with the chops to stick out there.

Sorrell saw his name surge up draft boards in high school in 2023 after showcasing added physicality and athleticism in all facets of his game. Now at A&M, the speed has ticked up even more. The arm has ticked up too. His actions are more connected and fluid with his added weight. Sorrell possesses one of the better power-speed combinations in the college class this year, and it comes alongside a premium frame with a left-handed swing. Better still, he's a dynamic defender who will throw his body into harms way to make jaw-dropping plays. That profile checks a lot of boxes. A lower body injury kept him from flashing his dynamic playmaking ability in the field and on the bases in 2025, but many expect he'll be back to his old tricks as the 2026 Draft approaches. 

The hit tool and approach have taken noticeable steps forward. That said, his swing remains rigid at times and Sorrell has shown a willingness to expand the zone on breaking balls low-and-away. Sorrell is an aggressive hitter. He hunts fastballs. When swinging at pitches inside the strike zone he consistently hits the ball extremely hard. Putting himself into positions to get those pitches and generate that impact will be a developmental emphasis going forward. The breaking ball has evaded Sorrell throughout his amateur career, but the upside on the player is immense if that part of his game polishes up. 

The trajectory and runway here is awfully exciting. Sorrell is as tooled up as a guy like Jarred Kelenic. The latter has struggled to adjust to professional pitching but has long had star-level tools. Sorrell has every opportunity to blow through that comparison. If it all clicks into gear, Sorrell has top-five pick traits.

Peterson is a power-hitting third base prospect with a lofty left-handed swing built for damage. He doesn't sell out for power, but does get into it naturally. It's a quiet, composed swing from the left side that projects into impact. It's a pull-side emphasis with a lift mentality in his approach, though unlike most with a similar profile Peterson keeps his strikeouts down and draws his walks. It's an overall polished offensive profile with middle-of-the-order upside. There is above average raw power and Peterson could potentially grow into plus bat speed depending on how the frame matures. Peterson tends to shift his weight early and drifts through his plant leg a bit causing him to lose some of the leverage built into his back hip in his load. It's something he's been working to clean up and the move has been muted more often than it was even a summer prior. 

While third base is his primary home, Peterson could land at a number of positions at the next level. He already demonstrates the ability to handle the hot corner, though some scouts like his profile behind the plate where he features an athletic, quick release. He's also showcased a 91 mph arm on the mound with a promising slider and is serviceable in the outfield as well. Peterson is just the epitome of a ballplayer with gamer traits. Throw him anywhere and he'll find a way to provide value. Should the bat take another step forward as we approach the draft, it's first round tools and traits. Peterson will turn 19 years old just a couple weeks after the draft.

Hirschkorn is an long, tall, imposing righty who presents a ton of angle to opposing hitters. It's an effortless delivery with a compact, short arm action and some whippiness through release. He commands the ball well and is exceptionally deceptive with hitters being forced to sit on the fastball, often resulting in hapless swings against his secondaries. He'll work the fastball up to 97 and will is more routinely 93-94 with some carry and tail through the zone.  

Hirschkorn's breaking ball performs like a plus pitch, but it's metrics suggest it's close to above average. His ability to hide the baseball and tunnel his three-pitch mix from his fastball release results in hitters often looking lost and guessing. The breaking ball is a slurvy bender in the low-80s. There's also a mid-80s changeup that he's shown feel for commanding at the bottom of the zone, killing spin very well. 

Hirschkorn is still growing strength and developing consistency in using his lower half. There's a ton of low-hanging fruit to help his stuff explode into another tier. 100 mph is in the tank. It's a premium frame, a loose arm and pitching comes very easy. It's a sky-high ceiling if the development doesn't stall.

Curiel doesn't swing and miss. Like, ever. It's elite bat-to-ball skills from a 6-foot-3-inch left-handed hitter. The immediate thing that stands out is the calm, balanced rhythm about his game. He hardly ever expands the zone and runs strong walk rates because of it. Curiel also has super-advanced feel for the barrel and hits the ball hard consistently. He's got a sweet left-handed swing and never looks anxious or tense at the plate. For the time being, this is a hit-over-power profile. Curiel doesn't have much twitch, torque or subsequent bat speed at the plate and may not be a guy who ever hits more than 15 homers in a season as a professional. HIs peak exit velocity at LSU following the 2025 season was just a shade over 107 mph. That said, he's popped a couple 110+ readings after some offseason strength gains. The tide could be turning on what's been a slow burn on the power front for Curiel.

Curiel is a composed player with some standout tools. He's a solid average runner with long strides. He's been a left fielder most of his career at LSU, however he's getting full-time run in centerfield as a sophomore in 2026. Curiel takes solid routes to the ball and makes the plays he's expected to make. It's average arm strength. He could play centerfield at the next level, however most scouts seem to prefer the fit in left field ultimately. 

Curiel is a draft-eligible sophomore. A model-driven organization that value a high floor will place Curiel on a pedestal. He doesn't possess conventional middle-of-the-order traits, but should be a high-average, high-OBP hitter at the next level. He brings back shades of Andrew Benintendi at Arkansas. The 90th percentile outcome here is perhaps a 6-foot-3-inch version of Steven Kwan.

Comeau is also an impressive hitter with wiry strength to all fields and a quick, compact swing with fast hands. He hits for more power than many would expect and could be a guy who boasts above-average bat-to-ball skills with above average raw power projection. In some ways, his profile offensively compares favorably to 2025 second round pick Cooper Flemming, as well as 2024 Pirates second round pick Wyatt Sanford. 

Defensively, he'll need to find a home. A shortstop by trade, the actions are more befitting of a third baseman or perhaps a guy that ends up in left or field field as a professional. He's a solid-average runner that will be able to survive wherever he ends up. Should he prove capable as a shortstop, or even an infielder, to a front office as July approaches, it could impact his draft stock by a full round grade or better. 

Comeau can pitch a bit too. His long, tall, slender frame really stands out. It's long, lanky levers with loose, whippy athleticism and very little effort. Comeau generates huge extension down the bump with a long, whip-like arm action with tons of acceleration through release. Although he's only been up to 94 mph at this point. The fastball itself will vary in shape, sometimes sinking into right-handed batter's knuckles and other times carrying through the letters. His slider features sharp tilt with tunnel and conviction out of the same slot as the fastball. There's also a low-80s changeup that he commands well, though it's shorter shape for the time being with more depth than arm-side fade. 

Comeau is a ball player. Perhaps the icing on the cake is Comeau will be just 17 years old for the draft. He checks nearly every box models and scouts look for.

Hernandez has considerable upside offensively as he's shown feel to hit, advanced barrel awareness and already possesses plus raw power projection. It's a physical frame that should continue to add strength and polish, especially if he eventually gives up training reps on the mound (we'll get to that). Hernandez has registered exit velocities north of 111 mph and combines the bat speed with solid average bat-to-ball skills. There's some swing and miss in his game when it comes to the breaking ball, but he's gradually shown growth in that department on campus. Hernandez lets the ball travel and tends to focus his efforts on the right-center field gap. That's great for the batting average, but given his bat speed and physicality, teams would like to see him lean into the pull-side a bit more to extract more value from the bat. There's no questioning his maturity and polish offensively, however there's more in the tank from a production standpoint. 

He's smooth and consistent at second and third base as well. He's an average runner and possesses above average arm strength that will fit in the outfield as well should he be forced out that way at some point in his career. 

A two-way prospect, Hernandez is decorated on the mound too. He throws four pitches, all of which are usually controlled into the zone and commanded well to both left-handed and right-handed hitters. Hernandez has a tendency to let his front side fly open and land open to the plate so his stuff can on occasion spray to the arm side. His fastball rests 92-93 but will grab 94 at its peak. There's some darting action to his heat, dotted both glove-side and arm-side. The slider, changeup and curveball are all effective offerings as Hernandez mixes it up and pitches backwards better than most arms in the class. He changeup has flashed 70-grade shape and render left-handed hitters hapless when he's able to get to it. The curveball is also noteworthy and it's firm with hammer shape. Again, he just needs to get ahead of hitters to deploy it.

He's a bulldog on the mound who works quickly and repeats very well. The starter traits are reasonably obvious here from and operation and athlete perspective. He'll just need to find more consistency in commanding the baseball. It looks like the makings of an innings-eater who should be effective, a la Brady Singer if he doesn't end up a power-hitting corner infielder instead. He is a draft-eligible sophomore.

A high-octane righty with immense projection and pitchability well beyond his years, Sides has scouts in California gushing over where it could go over his high school career. The long, high-waisted, prototype right-hander has been up to 95 mph with an mid-80s slider. He's worked to integrate a bigger upper-70s curveball that flashes considerably deeper shape, a pitch he's shown a willingnes to throw more against left-handed pitching. There's also an upper-80s changeup for lefties, however it's clearly a fourth offering at this early stage in his amateur career. 

Sides absolutely hammers the strikezone and rarely ever surrenders a free pass. He'll throw from several arm slots, none of which are a dead giveaway on what pitch is coming. The result is varying shapes on his fastball and breaking ball; a master manipulator of his pitch mix. Sides is an artist on the mound. This is likely a guy who will be bumping into the upper-90s in short order. He will be 18.5 years old on draft day.

After a year at Stetson as a freshman, Hughes transferred to Texas Tech in search of bigger and brighter lights. That move paid dividends for Hughes and the Red Raiders as he immediately became one of the best hitters in the country as a sophomore.

Hughes just knows how to hit. Top to bottom, tip to tail, there are very few holes in his offensive game. He boasts well-above average contact rates regardless of the pitch and regardless of the zone. He handles spin, he handles velocity and he consistently hits the ball extremely hard. His batted balls hit north of 95 mph ranked among the best in the sport in 2024. Hughes has plus raw power and pulls the ball in the air with plenty of frequency. If there's any hitter in the 2026 class that has a case to be labeled a future plus hit/plus power guy, it's probably Hughes at this stage. Hughes looks like prime Max Muncy at the dish both aesthetically and from a production perspective. 

Hughes isn't any sort of dynamic defender it's a left field glove with fringe-average speed, below average arm strength and passable routes. The bat will do the heavy-lifting on the profile, but it may be strong enough to get him selected in the first round regardless.

Williams is one of the most purely talented athletes in the 2026 class and has projection ahead of him to polish up the unrefined areas of his game. He's already a plus runner and should hold his speed as he adds strength in his upper half. The arm strength is huge with double-plus projection on the dirt or in the outfield. Some scouts want to see what it looks like on the mound, but the offensive tools and lack of reps on the mound will likely keep Williams on the dirt. 

He's a right-handed hitter with bat speed actively works to lift the baseball. While that has caused some inconsistencies in barrel quality, his best cuts are loud with over-the-fence upside. It's impact projection and the chance to slug going forward. Williams could end up in any number of different positions on the field with his physical tools. If the overall hit tool ticks up as the draft approaches, it's first round tools and upside. 

Williams injured his ankle in the playoffs of his junior year resulting in surgery. That caused him to miss virtually the entire summer showcase and tournament circuit. Teams looking to draft him will have to do most of their evaluations exclusively off his play in high school league play. Still, the tools are quite obvious regardless of venue or level of competition. He will be 18.6 years old on draft day.

A massive, intimidating force on both sides of the ball, Borthwick's future is undoubtedly on the mound. He's an unbelievable mover and athletic tester for a player and pitcher of his size and stature. Borthwick's loosness, fluidity and ability to repeat with his frame is a rare trait. For these reasons, if inserted into the right player development program, his ceiling on the mound could explode. 

The bat aside, this is a pitcher. His size and stuff have both exploded over the past twelve months. Borthwick is an imposing, deceptive righty with a fastball up to 96 featuring tailing action and some funk. He's proven durable, capable of carrying 92-94 into the mid-innings. He'll carry the top rail and has shown the ability to sink the ball away from left-handed hitters low-and-away. He launches from a lower short-arm slot and creates unique angles and optics for hitters with an unconventional kick-step stride down the mound. That move does lower his extension to a mark shorter than most pitchers his size, however everything still plays up due to the uniqueness of the operation. Borthwick still has some inefficiencies in his lead-leg block and sequencing, suggesting he could be the type of arm that creeps toward triple digits in shorter order at the next level. 

Borthwick has solid hand feel and spin capacity for a slider that could eventually become a steady plus. It's a low-to-mid 80s breaker with late tilt, commanded with conviction to his glove-side and below the belt.
