There's some early seam mirror traits that allow it to play up with coupled off the fastball, too. As player development gets their hands on his breaking ball, it's likely to become his best weapon. 

Borthwick's two-pitch wombo combo is supplemented by an upper-70s curveball with above average spin, as well as a low-80s changeup that's taken significant strides since his sophomore year. His ability to kill spin stands out, and his shapes have steadily improved. 

He'll be just 18.3 years old for the draft and profiles as one of the more physical players in the class.

Rembert's added considerable athleticism and strength in the last twelve months and projects to stay on the infield with a frenetic nature about his game, soft hands and depandable actions. It's solid average foot speed and the actions to play on the dirt as a professional. He's a second baseman through and through. If he comes into an organization with a loaded infield, Rembert has proven plenty capable of handling left field as well. 

Rembert's bat-to-ball skills are solid average. He hammers fastballs and is aggressive on anything elevated in the zone. He's flashed above average raw power projection with exit velocities exceeding 111 mph. The contact quality does tend to take a dip against breaking balls and changeups, but Rembert's up-the-middle approach doesn't put him in a bad spot when those pitches are thrown in the zone. Rembert has a chance to develop into an above average hitter with solid-to-above average raw power.

Ballinger arrived to the College of Southern Nevada in 2024 as a two-way prospect. He tried his luck on the mound but coaches and scouts quickly realized how potent the left-handed bat could become. A .431 average as well as a walk-to-strikeout ratio north of two generated tons of interest in the first baseman in the transfer portal after just one season. He took his game to the University of Kansas for his sophomore season, 2025, and the hits haven't stopped coming. 

Ballinger doesn't have too many notable holes in his swing. He makes plenty of contact against both left- and right-handed pitching. He can, at times, be susceptible to sliders from advanced pitching, but he also hasn't been exposed to that kind of firepower at a high clip at this point in his career. As he continues to grow comfortable with Big 12 baseball, scouts believe his swing will nullify the effectiveness of some of those breaking balls. Ballinger has shown tremendous feel for the barrel with big average exit velocities and peaks high enough to suggest it's above average raw power in the tank. He's also a remarkably selective hitter who refuses to expand the zone and waits to pull the trigger on pitches that fit his heat zones. 

Ballinger is a hitter cut from the cloth of yesteryear. It's a quiet, compact, squatty stance at the plate with a closed front side and a high back elbow. He has very little rhythm, but rather triggers that he employs to explode through the zone when the pitch is thrown. 

Defensively, Ballinger is destined for first base where scouts believe he is passable if not average. His pure athleticism may get him into above-average range in due time, however his lateral range will not be an asset. Ballinger is a below-average runner.

Dietz is a highly physical lefty that eats up hitters on both sides of the plate with a lethal fastball/slider combination. The heater sits around 93-94 and will touch 97 on occasion, with big carrying life that plays big at the top of the zone. 

The slider sits in the 80-83 range with strong gyro traits, which plays very well off the fastball profile. He'll fold in a low-90s cutter to get hitters off the one-two combo.

Rounding out the arsenal is a high spin changeup that flashes good fading life vs right handed hitters, but is sparsely thrown and confidence in the pitch is still developing. 

The big lefty works from a near overhead arm slot that gives him that near perfect backspin on the four seam, but it's been a work in progress to control such an intentful delivery. The stuff has proven time and time again to play, so the ability to throw good strikes consistently is what will be monitored most moving closer to the 2026 draft. He missed the beginning of the 2024 season with a stress fracture in his elbow and will have a limited baseball card in July.

Tinney took an unconventional route toward college baseball stardom. A proud product of the state of Colorado, Tinney uprooted to Notre Dame for his studies. After seeming the field sparingly as a freshman, he became the full-time backstop for the Fighting Irish in 2025. That vote of confidence paid dividends as he immediately proved to be one of the most imposing power bats in the country.  Tinney transferred to Austin for his draft-eligible sophomore year.  

Tinney's bat can be boom or bust. Power is the calling card and he displays it in spades. Tinney has registered batted-ball events north of 115 mph and ranked inside the 99th percentile for average exit velocity in 2025; north of 94 mph. When he hits the ball he hits it with a ferocity few in the sport can match. It's every bit that of double-plus raw juice and he's showcasing it in games already. Tinney's hit tool leaves a bit more to be desired. He's a patient hitter but he gets exposed against breaking balls and his adjustability on pitches outside of the strike zone needs work. It's below-average bat-to-ball skills and Tinney may run a low batting average and high strikeout rates in professional baseball when tasked with hitting premium pitching on a nightly basis. Even if he's a .225 hitter, it's 35-homer upside, more than enough for Tinney to warrant the projection of a full-time player at the next level. 

Behind the dish, Tinney suffers some of the same woes as tall, big-body backstops before him. He struggles to get low in the crouch. Framing and stealing the low strike has been a challenge. He does have plus to double-plus arm strength and has been very strong throwing out would-be base-stealers. Teams have been aggressive trying to run against him and he's consistently posted some of the more impressive caught-stealing rates in the country.

Tinney is a well-below average runner who does not add value with his legs. It's a tough fit in right field if he's forced out from behind the plate considering the athleticism needed to cut balls off in the gaps. 

The jury is out on whether Tinney is athletic and/or flexible enough to warrant full-time catching duties at the professional level. The power and arm strength carry the water on the profile and should help him get selected reasonably early in July. There's something of a Hunter Goodman type of profile here.

The rare prospect hailing out of the great state of South Dakota, Radel has developed into a big arm for the Fighting Irish and has positioned himself to capitalize on his talent in the Draft.

Radel will work up to 97 from an ultra-high slot featuring carry and cutting action. It's not a fastball that's built to miss bats, but as Radel gets stronger and continues to add strength and velocity to his 6-foot-5-inch frame, he might be able to overwhelm hitters with velocity. Radel ranks among the best in college baseball at generating extension down the mound -- over 7 feet -- so he'll have the ability to bully hitters soon enough. 

Radel throws his slider about a third of the time and it's been effective. It clearly draws some value from his fastball shape. It's deep with big shape, especially strong out of his launch height. He sprays the breaking ball all over the zone limiting it's production and impact at this stage. As he continues to learn how to tunnel a trio of the fastball, a cutter and this slider, his arsenal could overmatch hitters, especially if he's commanding all three pitches. 

Radel worked hard to integrate a changeup into his repertoire in 2025 with mixed results. The shapes were just okay, and he struggled to miss bats with the pitch, however it was especially effective getting left-handed hitters to chase off the plate. 

Radel has a proven track record of throwing strikes and limiting walks. He's an exceptional mover with three or four pitches and better bat-missing days ahead.

A popular name in the 2025 Draft, Riojas pulled his name out of consideration to return to Texas for 2026. After two seasons at UT-SA, Riojas took his dynamic two-pitch mix to Austin to pitch for the Longhorns. But that two-pitch arsenal is no more. Riojas throws the kitchen sink these days. 

Riojas has seen a small velocity jump this year and is not reaching back for the upper-90s at times, resting 94-96 early in his outings. He does a nice job creating a flatter plane with the fastball, a high-carry four-seamer with big extension and hop through the top of the zone. Riojas's feel for the top rail stands out resulting in that flatter-than-average approach angle despite a higher-than-average launch. It's been a pitch that creates chase, whiffs and soft contact. Riojas has shown capable of cutting that pitch too. 

Riojas transformed what was previously an average breaking ball into a big, sweeping slider with firm velocity. It's effective generating whiffs from right-handed hitters and has the look of an above-average weapon, even if it doesn't perfectly fit some of the other seam orientations his arsenal has. Riojas creates steepness and late, sharp break on that pitch, his high release allowing it to play up.

Riojas scrapped a fringy changeup this spring and started throwing a deeper split-finger that has been diabolical when he commands it to left-handed hitters. It really plays well off the fastball tunnel. It serves its purpose beautifully in a menu full of well thought out weapons. 

Riojas also added a cutter in 2025 that has gotten even better in 2026. It's harder, sharper, and keeps righties and lefties off this fastball. It's been especially effective generating whiffs just below the zone. 

Riojas pulled his name from the 2025 Draft seeking another year in Austin to refine his stuff and pitch for the burnt orange. It's four pitches, and while none of them are necessarily plus, he should be able to get pro hitters out by mixing it up and showcasing various shapes.

A two-sport standout with a potential future on the football field as well, Ponatoski won Ohio Gatorade Player of the Year as a junior leading Archbishop Moeller as the starting quarterback. Ponatoski can do it all. 

He's a solid left-handed hitter with barrel that stays through the zone for an extended period of time. He's got strong hands at the point of contact and can deliver a heavy barrel to all-fields. There's polish in his approach, happy to let the ball travel and inside-out velocity when he's beat. 

Ponatoski was arguably the most impressive high school hitter over the course of the 2024 summer. In tournament and showcase settings, Ponatoski put together an 11 percent whiff rate against the best arms in his class and rarely expanded the strike zone. Breaking balls gave him a bit more fits than did the heater, but he more than held his own. When you extrapolate the summer to include his high school season, Ponatoski was one of the most potent hitters in the country. Across all events and close to 150 plate appearances, his .362/.500/.486 slash and .986 OPS stand out. He'll have to show the same level of success on a bigger stages as the draft approaches, but he's got the attention of scouts in Ohio and nationwide. 

Ponatoski is a sure-handed infielder with 70-grade arm strength and enough athleticism to handle the shortstop position at the high school and college level. His lateral mobility, foot speed and first step may ultimately push him to second base or, more likely, third base as a professional. Ponatoski is a fringe-average runner at this stage. 

If the bat and shortstop don't work, Ponatoski has experience on the mound too. It's effortless life and velocity on the mound, up to 93, arm-side run and some carry. There's a mid-70s big curveball that's been worked on over the last 12 months that has a chance to get to solid average. Ponatoski will need a third pitch if he's to reach his starting pitcher upside. He'll be on the younger side for the draft, just 18.3 years old on draft day. 

There remains real questions on whether Ponatoski prefers football or baseball.

Moore has been one of the more impressive hitters in the country this year with elite in-zone contact rates and the ability to fend off pitches just off the black. He's yet to flash much raw power, though his left-handed swing and lean frame point toward it blossoming into at least a threat in the future. Moore is a polished hitter who draws tons of walks and limits his strikeouts to minuscule levels. It's a top-of-the-order table setting profile who adds value on the base paths. 70-grade speed and a lightning quick first step help Moore steal bags at will. He's been one of the most decorated pillow thieves in college baseball across the last three seasons and figures to bring that dimension of his game to the professional ranks too. 

Moore is a dynamic centerfield prospect who takes crisps routes and projects to stay up the middle as a professional. It's a plus glove with average arm strength and a high IQ for situational baseball. Moore is among the higher floor prospects in the 2026 and could move quickly in pro ball.

Brown can do it all. An accomplished pitcher and right field prospect, most scouts believe more in the bat than the ability on the bump. 

Two-way upside is possible here. The bat-to-ball skills stand out. Brown doesn't swing and miss much on anything that's in the zone. He's a pure hitter with a swing that covers all four quadrants. Brown owns a solid approach at the plate, but when he expands the zone he has a much more difficult time putting the ball in play. If the pitch recognition skills improve in his third year in Baton Rouge, he could quickly develop into one of the better pure hitters in college baseball. Brown shows more bat speed and raw power in batting practice than he's willing to show in games. It's above-average raw power, however game power right now is more on the fringy end. 

Defensively, Brown shows strong routes to the ball and situational awareness. He has plus arm strength and has the ability to hold runners at bay. He profiles into right field as a pro. 

Should the bat fail him, Brown could conceivably get on the mound more often. Projection and strike-throwing ability here really stand out. The slider is the bread and butter here with depth and sweeping action, a real bat-missing weapon against left-handed hitters. Brown hasn't yet seen a velocity bump. He'll usually sit 89-91 over extended outings, touching 93 at his best. He projects a crafty southpaw who commands the baseball well and has the ability to manipulate shape. Brown was the Texas Rangers' 16th round pick in 2023 but went unsigned.

Molony earned full-time playing time with the Ducks as a freshman after he showed considerable impact in the bat and solid actions on the dirt. He was a star for the Ducks 2025 campaign positioning himself as a must-know prospect for the 2026 Draft. 

Molony is a strong hitter. He runs elite in-zone whiff rates and possesses an approach that keeps his chase rates down at a healthy level. It's fringy raw power projection and his feel for the barrel can be streaky. Molony hasn't shown the adjustability in the box scouts want to see from premium hitters yet, but his production has been steady thanks to the approach and feel for covering anything in the zone. Molony has a swing with very little wasted movement, a muted move forward and compact, quick hands. It's an operation that should continue to hit moving forward. Laying off those elevated fastballs above the zone and in on his hands would help his game take another jump forward. 

Defensively, Molony is an asset. A human highlight reel. Molony can make even the most difficult plays to his right look composed and under control. He's a plus defender with above average arm strength. Molony is going to play the shortstop position and he's going to play it at a high level. He's also an above average runner with the IQ necessary to snag bags once on base. 

If the offensive profile takes a step forward in 2026, Molony could hear his name called inside of the top ten picks. He's got plenty in common with 2025 first rounder Marek Houston and arguably has more twitch and first-step quickness than Houston.

Lowrance's length and body control stand out in the box. He's a confident left-handed hitter with a quiet move into the zone. He uses his levers well, holding the barrel inside of the zone for a prolonged amount of time before finishing long, maintaining his bat speed. The leverage and extension stands out in a big way. His offensive mechanics have helped produce above-average bat-to-ball skills with strikeouts yet to thwart his impact potential. Lowrance is still growing into an understanding of how to efficiently use his size to get to the pull-side with many of his base hits being ringing gappers into the opposite field. That said, he's hitting the ball very hard and there's considerable power projeciton on the horizon. Lowrance could grow into 30-homer output once fully matured. It's a good looking hitter with some hit tool floor and strong swing decisions to supplement the imminent strength gains.

Lowrance plays third base and can spell at shortstop for the time being. Added weight and strength will likely end those opportunities in the coming years. It's above average arm strength with the hands that should allow him to play the hot corner at the next level. He's an above-average runner with a stiffer, upright running style. Lowrance is a long-strider and will likely hold some run-tool value as a professional.

The bat is the calling card here, as is the projection. Lowrance could grow into lineup-defining raw power as he continues adding strength. That's an exciting blend of polish and projection to dream on.

Condon is a mortar shell shot out of a cannon with the electric personality and unapologetic grinding nature scouts love to see. He forces you to watch him play his game. It's an intensity and level of competitive fire that is rivaled by very few. 

Condon possesses above average bat-to-ball skills and can sneak up on pitchers with an ambush approach to the pull-side. It's unique timing triggers with an early load and occasional toe-tap. His swing is upright and a bit stiff at times. It's not a rhythmic swing, but rather reactive in nature. Explosive hands help him turn on velocity, but he can be exposed on better velocity at the top of the strike zone. Questions on the hit tool will follow Condon so long as he carries his present swing. 

On the field and running the bases, Condon absolutely shines. Condon is a true centerfielder who routinely posts 80-grade run times out of the box. He's a dynamic defender with a chance to grow into plus-or-better defensive in centerfield. Condon projects into a table-setter role with the physical capacity to lose a few balls into the seats each year. He figures to steal a ton of bases too.

Helfrick offers immense upside both behind and at the plate. A strong, athletic frame that offers plenty of projectability, Helfrick shows very strong hands and ability to get into his lower half creating huge power potential with the bat. His exit velocities have peaked north of 113 mph. That raw power does come with significant swing-and-miss concerns. Helfrick struggles to stay on the slider and can be quite susceptible to spin low and away. While he isn't known for expanding the zone, he can get over-anxious on velocity up and in and is willing to chase that specific pitch with frequency too. Helfrick does shorten up with two strikes and puts the ball in play at a pretty healthy clip when he's behind in the count, but he does sacrifice contact quality in order to put the game in motion. 

Helfrick is a very good defender and an exceptional athlete for the position. He presents some of the best pop times of his peers with explosion out of the crouch and a plus arm behind it. His very athletic profile that should stick as a catcher moving forward. His above average run times will also create opportunities on the bases.  

If Helfrick's bat-to-ball skills can take a sizable step forward in 2026, he's got all the components necessary to be a first round pick in the Draft. If he ends up more of a boom-or-bust, pull-side fly ball merchant with a big arm behind the plate, he's got some of the traits that made Mike Zunino an effective catcher at the MLB level for nearly a decade.

Marchand was a standout throughout the 2025 summer at the most premium events high school ballplayers could get invited to. HIs versatility and production provides impact in a number of different areas on the field. Most see Marchand a shortstop going forward, but he can pitch, too.

Marchand is unconventional in the box, but it hasn't inhibited his ability to put up gaudy numbers. He doesn't swing and miss despite a reasonably aggressive approach. Marchand drifts forward quite hard and hits over his front side. He lags his hands and the barrel behind his shoulder deep, creating big stretch and bat speed through the zone. Marchand rotates around a stiffer, upright position at the point of contact, however he hardly whiffs. The swing generates a flatter attack angle. That said, Marchand still finds a way to back-spin the baseball and get into his raw power. It's a wiry, elastic frame with a swing that feels cut from the cloth of yesteryear. 

Marchand is an ultra-aggressive hitter and generally runs swing rates higher than most. He tends to expand the zone at a heavy clip, however the bat-to-ball skills are such that he puts most everything in play. Strikeouts have not been an issue for Marchand at this point in his career. Skeptics will question whether the swing will work at the professional level, however the performance metrics, production and feel for hitting stand out. 

Marchand is a primary shortstop now and owns above average arm talent. His footwork is strong and he's shown the internal clock necessary to play the left side of the infield going forward. Marchand does have a longer stride that helps him get to tough balls in the hole, however his average run tool doesn't add additional value on the dirt. Those bullish on the profile believe he'll grow into a bit more speed thanks to his frame and wiry nature. 

On the mound, Marchand has been up to 92 mph and owns a pretty good breaking ball. He's a strike-thrower and has shown the ability to hold his velocity into the third and fourth inning of work. 

There's a lot to like on this player. Questions on the swing are unlikely to dissipate between now and July. So long as Marchand keeps hitting, the skeptics will continue to fade. He also has age on his side and won't turn 18 until two weeks after the Draft.

A standout freshman year at Rutgers led Natili to the transfer portal where he'd eventually commit to Cincinnati for his 2025 and 2026 campaigns. He's a power frame/power arm prototype catching prospect who derives most of his value with the stick in his hands.

Natili is a reasonably aggressive hitter who runs slightly higher-than-average swing rates. That said, his swing decisions are among the best in the country. He swings at just about everything that is in the strike zone and has run chase rates well-below the collegiate average. It's fringy bat-to-ball skills with some rawness in terms of the ability to get the hands up to elevated velocity or spin off the plate. As he transitions to the next level, he'll need to become a more adjustable hitter and make more contact on swings inside the zone. The power and bat speed are both above average with exit velocities exceeding 112 mph at peak. Pitching and stuff will only get more advanced, especially once reaching the Double-A level. Doing damage and making contact on those mistake pitches will be key if he's to reach his starting-caliber catcher ceiling at the next level. 

Natili has a chance to catch at the next level, however he's likely be a beneficiary of the new ABS system more than others. It's above-average arm strength more than befitting of a quality catcher, however the framing and lateral mobility behind the dish are a work in progress.

Duncan comes from a baseball family and it shows in how his body moves. It's fluid, smooth and very loose on the mound. 

Already up to 94, Duncan should be a guy that lives 92-95 in due time. He has three pitches with a fading changeup being his primary out-pitch. The slider has comes along in recent months and now projects at least an average offering going forward. Duncan's entire arsenal plays up thanks to well-above average extension and some unique angles created by his launch profile. 

He's an extremely high follow and will be barely 18 years old for the Draft. It's day one traits.

Koeninger is a legitimate two-way prospect who has seen his game blossom on the mound as he's matured. Scouts seem to be 50/50 when it comes to projecting whether Koeninger will be a hitter or a pitcher at the next level. He's as legitimate a two-way prospect as you'll find at the high school level. 

Koeninger shows good feel for tempo and repetition on the mound with a loose, over-the-top delivery, hiding the ball nicely before launch. He's been up to 98 with moderate carry and tailing action. He more comfortably lives 92-94 as he lathers into the second and third inning of work, but continued maturation and strength gains should see the Keller product sustaining mid-90s velocity deeper into his starts in due time. He generates exceptional extension down the mound, a big building block in developing a starting pitcher, however Koeninger lacks deception and tends to show the ball to the hitter early in his delivery. 

Koeninger's breaking balls are absolute weapons. His fastball quality set sup two bat-missing breakers that he'll throw to left-handers and right-handers alike. The curveball is big, sharp and sold with arm speed. It's generally 79-82 with impressive deep break. It tunnels off the fastball and can be a mollywhopper of a weapon when he's spotting the heater up in the zone. His capacity for spin with rpm approaching 2800 should get pitching development analysts excited. Ths slider above average in its own right, generally 81-83 with lateral tilt and some depth, late and thrown with feel to the glove-side. Koeninger has worked hard to try and fold in a low-80s changeup to left-handed hitters but it's clearly his third option at present. 

This is a big arm with a good frame and a strong delivery. There's enough strikes to suggest a rotation role going forward. The four-pitch menu speaks for itself. 

In the batter's box and on the dirt it's also exciting. A physical hitter with strength at the point of attack, Koeninger is an impressive all-around ballplayer on both sides of the ball. It's fast hands and hard turns creating an intriguing blend of power and speed. Despite some stiffness in the hands, Koeninger has very little wasted movements in his triggers and is short to the ball with some length through it. He'll at times drift over his front side and throw his front hip leaving him susceptible to better breaking pitches. It's comfortably plus pull-side raw power projection. Koeninger has used the whole yard throughout his high school career and consistently posts strong bat-to-ball metrics. He's just not a guy who has dealt with strikeout woes. 

Koeninger has tools and actions on the dirt with a chance to stay on the left side of the infield. He's an above average runner. Koeninger will be 18.8 years old for the draft.

As impressive a pitching prospect as you'll find in the 2026 class, Waechter gets high marks in several areas. Already up to 97 with sizzling spin rates, Waechter has the ability to punch tickets with one pitch at this stage. He'll ride his heater in all four quadrants flashing real pitchability and a bully mentality. Waechter has seemed to lean more on a two-seamer this spring with more sinker and tail than ride, however he's shown the more conventional four-seamer in the past. Both fastballs have impressive shape and will blow through barrels with above average command. Waechter comfortably owns above average heater projection and could be reaching for more as the velocity continues its upward trajectory. 

A mid 80s slider has come on strong in the last nine months, now a sharp two-plane banger with well-above average spin rates and command to his glove side. At times he'll go even more firm with this pitch, delivering an 89-90 mph cutter. 

Waechter folds in a mid-80s changeup with fading action that he's shown a willingness to throw to right-handed hitters and left-handed hitters alike. 

Waechter's operation is one of the best in the class. There's conviction and extension down the mound with solid direction and intent. Waechter's arm action is fast and works well as he finishes balanced and in an athletic position to field his position. It's a sky-high ceiling on the bump with top-of-the-rotation upside. 

Waechter has real starting pitcher traits. He will turn 19 years old a couple weeks after the draft.

Horn is a Stanford commit and that should immediately provide pause into his signability, but from a pure talent standpoint he's one of the most decorated in the country. An injury abbreviated his 2025. Had he played all year, he may have been ranked considerably higher early in the spring. 

He's an impressive hitter with great feel for the barrel and a willingness to take the baseball to all fields. The bat speed has ticked up considerably over the past twelve months and scouts now see a left-handed hitter who could grow into above-average raw power. Horn is a shortstop now but figures to shift to second or third base in due time where his actions play better. He's got soft hands and a strong throwing arm, though his lateral mobility will play nicely elsewhere on the dirt. Horn has grown in the run tool department and is now a plus runner, aided by quickness out of the box. 

Horn is also a talented pitcher with a fastball up to 95 mph, however scouts believe his future is on the dirt and in the batters box.

Ruiz might be the most exciting player in the class. He's electricity personified. On the infield, it's lightning-fast hands with a quick exchange and above average arm strength befitting of a true shortstop. Ruiz plays the position like a scatback. It's high-energy, frenetic in nature with exciting traits. Ruiz doesn't have the prototypical length or stride of some of his peers. Instead, he's forced to make plays leaning into his twitch. He makes every play, including the highlight reel play you'll rewatch on SportsCenter tomorrow night. Ruiz is plenty capable of sticking at shortstop and has the tools and instincts to be a 70 defender at the position. He's gotten run in centerfield too where he's looked like a potential above-average to plus glove there as well. Ruiz is also a solid-average runner. 

Ruiz has projection in his frame and should continue getting stronger helping to improve his offensive game. He's flashing some bat speed even if that won't be a big part of his game from the left side and while his feel for the barrel has been streaky it's fairly obvious how good the final package could get. He's a dynamic bat-to-ball artist who puts a ton of pressure on the defense and opposing pitcher. Quick-twitch hands allow Ruiz to make late decisions in the box and spray the ball to the opposite field with some authority when he's beat. There's a whole lot of tools and traits here, albeit lacking impact physicality. Ruiz has some of the same physical traits and athletic tools that could result in a Nick Allen type of profile. If he adds more strength, perhaps it could become more. He will be 19.3 years old for the Draft.

Reddemann made a great first impression as a true freshman in 2024 logging some of the most innings of any "diaper dandy" in the country. He had a 4.01 ERA with 66 strikeouts and only 19 walks in 76.1 innings. Those numbers had Reddemann named the WCC Freshman of the Year and he was also named to the All-WCC First Team. A rare feat for a first-year pitcher. That level of success across a larger sample landed Reddemann in the transfer portal after the 2025 season, electing to transfer to UCLA. 

An athletic righty with an up-tempo herky-jerky delivery, Reddemann brings some natural deception to the bump with his unorthodox movement patterns. His fastball is his best pitch, and it can grab 97 mph, impressively holding 93-95 deep into outings. Reddemann's fastball shapes are all over the place with no real consistent pitch design. But on the average, it's usually generic with a bit more value and perceived hop at the top of the zone. That said, his plus command and pitchability allow his velocity to play up. Reddemann compliments the fastball with a changeup, slider and curveball, mixing things up for the opposition. His bag of tricks makes him effective, however none of his pitches are remarkable in terms of stuff. The changeup is particularly impressive from an execution and tunnel perspective. It flashes above average.

Reddemann is a strike thrower and he'll keep hitters uncomfortable. He's got moxy on the bump and likes to work fast. He projects a back-end of the rotation arm capable of logging healthy innings at the next level. He could get up to a mid-rotation role if the breaking ball advances.

After two big years at Virginia, Ford found himself draft-eligible in 2025. He went unselected, though most of that was due to his concrete commitment to transfer to Tennessee. 

A big, tall, long frame, Ford has sneaky athleticism and has rotated between the outfield, first base and third base throughout his college career. He's been challenged more at the hot corner in Knoxville. He played some centerfield on the Cape this past summer too -- a testament to his sneaky athleticism and willingness to showcase his tools. His 6-foot-5-inch frame certainly projects to a corner in some capacity in the long run, but the actions are undervalued by the industry. Ford has displayed good route-running ability in the outfield and shouldn't be any sort of liability if he ends up in the grass.

Ford has easy power and uses every bit of his leverage at the plate. He's short and direct to the ball with impact bat speed, extension and feel for lift. The exit velocities support the eye test too. He has a tendency to step in the bucket and throw his front hip at times and that's affected his contact quality and his ability to get the ball in the air. He's an aggressive hitter who has shown a tendency to expand the zone. Still, Ford's impact on pitches inside the zone and relative absence of an enormous hole in his swing points toward a middle-of-the-order thumper at the next level -- especially considering his size and physicality in the box.

Staying in the outfield or at third base in some capacity will be especially critical for Ford's draft stock in 2026. Distancing himself from the first base label will be key.

When Blair arrived to campus coaches were drooling over the projection in his 6-foot-3 inch frame. He's already tacked on 25 pounds of muscle since arriving and the coinciding stuff continues to tick up.

Blair flashed a big future as a freshman. He was named to the CUSA All-Freshman Team and posted more appearances than any other Liberty arm on the season. Streaky control woes would derail his outings now and again, but the upside was fairly clear. He turned a corner in 2025.

Blair will sit 92-97 with his fastball and usually sits on the higher end of that spectrum in the early innings. It's an ultra-low three-quarters launch that induces serious arm-side action on the fastball. It's not necessarily a bat-misser, but Blair does get value from weak ground balls and some hitters expanding the zone as his sinker tails toward earth. The sinker sets up a cutter that neutralizes the opposition and generates feeble hacks. The sinker serves its purpose, however the cutter puts hitters away. Blair compliments the fastballs with a slider he's been working to find more consistency for. There's also a changeup that he's thrown a good number of times, however he's yet to generate the whiffs or chase you'd expect from a player with his unique arm slot and velocity in the tank. He's an east-west guy who relies on soft contact to get outs, but missing bats has trended upward annually.

Despite working in a starting pitcher role since 2025, Blair has more the look of a high-leverage reliever at the next level. He'll almost certainly work as a starter early in his professional career until the point he proves he'd be more valuable in the bullpen. That may never come. Time will tell. He holds his velocity well into his outings and he does possess three pitches so starting at the next level isn't a foregone conclusion.

Santarelli has been a meteoric riser in the eyes of scouts over the course of the last twelve months. The power and impact potential towers over most of his peers. Santarelli has a short, quick, compact swing. It's smooth and balanced with barrel control that plays to all fields. The move forward is short with hands that are direct to the ball with precision and impact. Some believe Santarelli will eventually blossom into an above average hit tool guy as a professional, however it's the aforementioned juice that'll take him up the ladder. Santarelli boasts exit velocities north of 113 mph at times. He looks different than anyone else on the field in batting practice and represents one of the most intimidating offensive packages in the class. 

Santarelli's bat isn't the only part of his game beginning to stand out. He's turned his body into an athletic vehicle now capable of posting average to solid-average run time home-to-first. Santarelli has soft hands and sound actions receiving the baseball at first base with a chance to develop into an above average defender at the position. He can play a corner outfield role in a pinch, however his routes can be scenic with inconsistencies in his first step and directness to the spot.

Santarelli's is a big, strong, ultra-physical player at this stage. He'll need to keep his flexibility and athleticism as July approaches but all signs point toward him being one of the more imposing bats in the class.

Yow is the fastest player in the entire 2026 class. He's lightning-quick out of the box and has flashed home-to-first times south of 4.00 seconds. And this profile is still trending up. Good muscle is still being added. 

Yow can do some things with a bat in his hand. It's solid average bat speed projection with a short, compact swing. Yow has quick hands and is direct to the ball. He doesn't create much coil in his swing, however his swing forward and length does create some natural stretch. Yow is unlikely to develop into any sort of slugger, but it's certaintly enough impact to turn doubles into triples and occassionally lose one over the fence to the pull-side. The speed puts enormous pressure on the defense with choppers to the left side of the infield often wreaking havoc on the opposition. 

Yow is still developing the body control to play the shortstop position at the next level, however the athletic tools obviously stand out. The range and stride-length both look befitting of a shortstop. That said, it's average arm strength that is tested when Yow is moving to his right. He's comfortable and smooth around the second base bag. It may end up at second or third base when all is said and done, however given his ascension physically and athletically in recent years, pulling him off the shortstop position early in his minor league career would likely be a mistake.

A two-sport superstar, Brody Bumila is a force on the basketball court when he's not toeing the slab. This is a massive left-handed pitcher who brings funk, deception and gasoline to the bump. From a pure stuff perspective, few arms in the country, college or high school, can match Bumila's peaks. It's an extra-large, long frame with a high waist and terrific athleticism for a player of his size and stature. 

Bumila has been clocked as high as 98 from a low-slot featuring arm-side tailing action and variable vertical profiles. At his best, he's staying behind the seams of the baseball and holding carry through the zone, obliterating hitters on the top rail with IVBs that will hover at or around 18 inches. That vertical shape, combined with his flat approach, complimented by what can at times be arm-side tail north of 15 inches, makes for a unicorn fastball in many respects. Bumila will commonly settle in more 92-93 after the second and third innings, but as he gets into professional baseball and begins focusing exclusively on baseball, scouts believe he should hover in the low-to-mid 90s. 

Bumila's best secondary is an low-80s changeup that he still broadcasts a bit. He'll need to continue to develop feel, conviction and arm speed on that pitch, but given his fastball shape and deception it could eventually transform into a 'plus' weapon. The movement profile on the cambio flashes nothing short of extraordinary with huge fade and considerable depth. 

Bumila throws a low-to-mid 80s slider that will at times short short, cutter-like shapes. He's also got a bigger, mid-70s curveball that he's worked to rein in, often losing it to he arm-side. Scouts will want to see a more refined breaking ball as the draft approaches if Bumila is to hear his name called inside of his Top-50 ceiling.

Bumila missed most of the 2025 season recovering from a minor surgery. For that reason, he'll be a fresh look for many Northeast scouts in this cycle. It's a sky-high ceiling if he can put it all together as July nears.

Sims is just scratching the surface of what he may someday be capable of on the mound. Already up to 100 with a "playing catch" delivery, Sims is unpolished clay with massive upside. The whole package is long, explosive and the secondary and tertiary offerings are budding. Sims' entire arsenal is tough to pick up out of the hand with his fastball/slider combination tunneling hard and late. 

The heater features arm-side tilt and last-second tail. It plays in every quadrant and has shown the ability to tie right-handed hitters in knots largely due to how difficult it is to track out of the hand. At his best, Sims will hold 96-97 into the third and fourth innings of work. Couple this with elite extension, sometimes delivering the baseball 7.5 feet out in front of the plate. Sims dunks the baseball on hitters giving them very little time to react. 

His slider is already a low-to-mid 80s hammer with darting action into the left-handed hitters batters box. It's a one-two punch that could project 'plus' on both accounts. He kills spin on a changeup effectively and has shown the ability to fade the baseball away from left-handed hitters. 

Sims is a streaky strike-thrower and has been effectively wild at times. When he's at his best, he's unhittable. When the strikes are there, he's shown to be reasonably untouchable. Continuing his development of the changeup as well as command of the zone will be paramount in determining where he fits in the Draft. All that's left to be determined is how effective those pitches will be. For the time being, it's largely a reliever look, but Sims makes everything look so easy that a future as a starter shouldn't be ruled out. It's unlikely whichever team drafts him will bail on his spot in a rotation until at least his Triple-A days.

Wiggins, brother of former Razorback pitcher Jaxon Wiggins, has shown tremendous arm talente grabbing 101 and resting 98-99 over multiple innings. The arm strength is without question and the fastball value will carry his profile, but the breaking ball has taken steps forward of late as well. He's been held back in the past by command and control woes, something he'll need to iron out as the Draft approaches in July. 

Wiggins is a good athlete and was a two-sport standout in high school. He's a hard thrower with bloodlines. He will be draft-eligible as a sophomore. Unfortunately Wiggins had to undergo elbow surgery in May of 2025 and won't get the opportunity to pitch many innings in front of scouts before July.

Lynch really saw his stock skyrocket of late when his velocity flashed into the mid-to-high 90s and held 91-92 over short outings. He generates huge arm-side tail on his sinker and strides way down the bump to help hide the baseball. 

He offers an mid-80s sweeping slider that flashes plus with considerable horizontal tilt. There's also a mid-80s changeup. Both pitches are power weapons and play nicely off the sinker. He's a ground ball pitcher who won't miss a huge number of bats with the fastball, but the stuff is real. 

Lynch is an athletic mover who produces impressive extension out in front of the plate with a super-quick arm and projection remaining in the pure stuff. Lynch could fill a number of roles moving forward, but there are traits to like in a starting pitcher here.

Williamson is on the undersized side of things but what he lacks in prototypical size, he makes up for in explosive actions in the box. WIlliamson has shown average raw power, though it's ticking up over the last calendar year. Part of that is due to added strength, but part of it is also due to some swing changes. Once a rather simple, quiet swing, Williamson has added some noise in his hands with a loud barrel tip that lengthens the swing and the bat path, but bat speed has ticked up as a byproduct of the move. Williamson has long shown fringy bat-to-ball skills and can struggle at times against spin. He handles velocity in the middle and lower-third of the zone, but elevating fastballs can leave him susceptible. He'll need to find a balance between hit tool and bat speed going forward if he's going to capitalize on what some believe is a potential top 100 pick.

Williamson has played all over the outfield with the corners being his primary roaming zones. He's a solid-average athlete with advanced instincts and he takes better-than-average routes to the ball. It's fringy arm strength. Williamson can play centerfield in a pinch and has shown the reaction skills necessary to do so as a pro.

A tremendously intimidating athlete in the box, Bailey might possess more raw power than anyone in the 2026 class. It's exceptional bat speed from the left side with a bat path built to do damage to all fields; his pull-side power being mammoth. There's some natural loft built into his attack angle, but Bailey lets the ball travel and can blister baseballs into the left-center field gap with authority. Bailey will likely always come with significant swing and miss in his game, but he swings at the right pitches. He struggles to identify and adjust to spin, instead relying on getting ahead in the count and punishing mistake pitches. He'll likely always be a high slug, high walk, high strikeout, three-true-outcome bat at the next level. 

The 6-foot-4-inch Bailey can play a little bit of third base but scouts like the profile at first base long term. Bailey is a below-average runner and most of his value will come by of the bat. He was a 20th round selection by the White Sox in 2024.

Kleinschmit assumed a starting role for Oregon State in 2025 and really hasn't looked back since earning the honor. He's been one of the more effective pitchers on the West Coast for the last two years. 

Kleinschmit's arsenal is built around a four-seam fastball that'll run itself up to 95, however he more commonly rest in the 90-91 bucket throughout his starts. Kleinschmidt induces above average carry on his fastball and generates considerable tailing action to the arm-side on the pitch as well. Some natural deception and a launch height several inches north of league average have allowed that pitch to perform at a high level, specifically producing impressive chase rates. It's at least an average pitch going forward and could creep into the above-average territory with a little velocity bump. 

Kleinschmit's sweeping breaking ball is comfortably his best pitch. It's an upper-70s frisbee that features huge action into the right-handed batters' box. Kleinschmit gets above-average marks for spin rates and his ability to put hitters away with the pitch. He does a nice job repeating his arm slot on the pitch too, allowing it to look like his fastball if only momentarily out of the hand.

A fringier changeup has flashed unique shapes, specifically deviating off the fastball's vertical plane late. Should he elect to start throwing that pitch with more frequency, it's got a chance to be above average. 

Kleinschmit has the making of two above average pitches at the next level with a fastball that could jump into that territory with further strength gains. Despite a longer arm swing and wide elbow spiral, Kleinschmit is a strike-thrower through and through. It's not a conventional look for a starting pitcher, but Kleinschmidt bucks that trend with his feel for pitching. He's got a pro frame with strength in his lower half and some projection left above the waist.

Prosek has long put up monstrous performances in tournament and showcase settings. His offensive tools are far more advanced than most of his peers and he often overmatches similarly-aged pitchers. The swing is short, repeatable and powerful to the pull-side. Short of a larger-than-average leg kick, Prosek has very few moving parts and finds a ton of barrels because of it. All Prosek has done is hit, hit and hit some more. 

He's a fringy runner with average arm strength destined for second or third base at the next level despite handling shortstop duties right now.

Harris is certainly how you build a pitching prospect. A high waist, long levers, broadness in the shoulders and strength in the lower half. He's already a well-built player, but figures to get stronger, and in a projectable way, over the next few years. Harris has a composed delivery with a loose arm, repeatable mechanics and plenty of strikes. 

Harris has been up to 96 mph and scouts believe there's more coming. He launches from a higher over-the-top slot and generates steepness downhill. The fastball possesses some carry but gets most of its value from angles and tail. He's shown a willingness to work inside to right-handers and will back-door the fastball to steal strikes. He's been a ground ball machine throughout his high school career. Given the athlete, the operation, the pitchability and feel for repeating, Harris has a chance to grow into plus command for the heater as he matures. 

The breaking ball continues to take big strides and is now flashing plus potential. It's 82-85 with short sweeping break. He's ripped through a few 3000 rpm breakers during his high school career and is routinely north of 2800 rpm. The capacity for spin and shapes stands out. 

Harris has mixed in an inconsistent changeup over the course of the last twelve months, but it varies in terms of velocity, execution and shapes. 

Harris has a shot to become a day one pick in 2026. It's three pitches, composure, strikes and feel for spin. Adding to the allure is the fact he'll barely be 18 years old for the Draft.

Maniscalco is one of the more alluring shortstop prospects in the 2026 class thanks to a bevy of tools on both sides of the balls, coupled with the projectable frame scouts like to see. He reclassified up from the class of 2027 and now finds himself as one of the youngest draft-eligible high school players in history. 

The glove is set to make Maniscalco a lot of money at the next level. He's one of the most dynamic draft-eligible high school shortstops in years. Most scouts are comfortable throwing a 70 on the defense with a select few convinced he's an 80 glove -- extremely rare in domestic scouting. The actions are butter. The hands, feet and adjustability stand out in an exceptional way. Plus arm strength supplements his ability to get to every ball and make every throw. Maniscalco is an above-average runner who's better underway than he is from a first-step perspective. 

Maniscalco is a talented hitter with solid bat-to-ball skills from both sides of the plate. The swing is a little crude, but it works. He employs a deeper hand set in his load with a flat barrel over his shoulder. That barrel set helps get his bat path on-plane quickly, staying through the zone for an extended amount of time. Maniscalco has some twitch in his hips and creates a decent amount of torque, firing the barrel with an up-the-middle approach. He has an abbreviated leg kick and can sometimes struggle with getting the foot down too early. Maniscalco is at his best peppering the opposite field gap and creating some loft on pitches when he's slightly out in front to the pull-side. Given his age, it's fair to think the offensive profile will polish itself out with maturation and natural strength gains. For now, it's hit-over-power. 

Maniscalco has a chance to blossom into one of the more complete prospect packages in the 2026 class in due time. He'll be young for the class, just 17.2 years old on draft day.

Following two strong years at Florida Atlantic, Beard hit the transfer portal and changed his address to Tallahassee for the 2026 season. 

Beard has all the metrics teams love to see. It's a four-seam fastball up to 94 with almost perfect spin efficiency and serious hop at the top of the zone. Elite IVB, up to 26 inches at times, averaging north of 22 inches on nights he's feeling it. Beard has an outlandishly high launch height, in large part due to an extremely short stride down the mound, that diminishes some of his innate fastball value, but it's certainly a unique, deceptive look for hitters. To date, Beard has generated huge chase rates on his fastball just above the zone. HItters simply do not expect a 6-foot-2-inch righty to launch from the sky and the ball never sinks or tails back into the zone. It's just a very outlandish look. The coinciding whiff rates are also well-above average.

Beard's slider is disgusting, especially when considering his launch height. He repeats his slot very well and creates considerable depth on a bullet spinner, 82-84. Beard doesn't inherently spin the ball well, but his feel for shapes stands out. In 2025 as a sophomore, Beard ran a chase rate north of 40 percent and a whiff rate north of 40 percent on the breaker. He was one of just 60 pitchers in the country to generate those metrics. 

Beard can turn over an upper-70s changeup with arm speed to get whiffs. His ability to execute that pitch inside and out ot the zone needs some refinement, but the clay is there for an above-average cambio. 

Beard has a lean body with projection remaining and a quick arm. It's a north-south arsenal of pitches that does well changing the eye level of hitters. Commanding the baseball and repeating his delivery will be a point of emphasis as he moves forward, but model teams will see the numbers here and think long and hard about what this looks like in a pro system.

Davis has enormous athletic tools that play all over the field. He's your prototypical spark plus with whippy bat speed and the wheels to create mayhem on the bases. 

Offensively he carries some of the same rhythm and foot-down mechanisms as Cedric Mullins. It's a shorter leg lift and the hips do most of the work. Davis does a nice job of taking the bat direct to the ball and using the whole field. Davis can get a little disconnected on spin and offspeed pitches with a propensity to get out on his front side too early, but the hands work so well he's able to flick the ball into both gaps when he's beat. Davis is a patient hitter who will draw his walks, though there's some swing and miss in his game when the barrel gets out in front of his frame. All of that should clean itself up over time with added strength. 

The tools should only continue to improve. Already an above average runner, Davis should soon possess plus foot speed to go along with what many consider one of the better throwing arms in the class. There's centerfield tools here with traits that profile into any of the three outfield spots. Davis will be 18.5 years old on draft day.

Following a gangbusters freshman campaign at Butler where he won Big East Freshman of the Year, Lewis hit the transfer portal and headed to Winston-Salem where his power and hit tool played immediately. The bat is certainly the selling point here. 

Lewis absolutely hammers fastballs left up in the zone. He covers mistakes anywhere in the zone, but is susceptible to softer stuff at the bottom of the zone and just below it. Spin on the outer-third can also give him fits. While he's still flashing the discerning eye that made him so successful in the Big East, Lewis is swinging through more pitches in the ACC and running a whiff rate considerably higher than what he did as a freshman. He's been an extremely patient hitter with anemic swing rates. If he's to go in the top five rounds like some believe he's capable of, being a more aggressive, impactful hitter will become paramount. That said, 'impact' isn't in question. Lewis has been north of 113 mph from an exit velocity standpoint. He can bang. 

Lewis is capable of playing third base but most believe his first step and hands will take him to first base as a professional. This, of course, will put further stress on his bat. Lewis is a fringy runner with fringe-average arm strength.

An east/west starting pitcher prospect, Kramkowski has been up to 97 with his sinking fastball. It's a torpedo heater with huge arm-side tailing action and significant bore into right-handed hitters' knuckles. Kramkowski generates huge extension down the mound and it allows his sinker to sneak up on hitters. He'll occasionally work to create more lift on that pitch sacrificing tail for some carry. That's made it a weapon up in the zone due to his low launch slot. 

Kramkowski pairs the sinker with an exceptional sweeping slider. It's firm, usually 82-85 with two plane break. Kramkowski is still working to hone in his command for that pitch, but when he's got it locked in it's consistently an above-average weapon. There's also a cutter in the low-90s that lives to keep hitters from guessing; effective in inducing weak contact. 

Kramkowski has a loose, whippy arm, generates considerable extension and has a full menu of pitches. He struggles to generate much variety in north-south pitch shapes, but his ability to work arm-side to glove-side is strong. 

This is a low-effort operation and a unique look for hitters. Kramkowski will need to continue refining his control and command, but if he finds the strike zone with more consistency he is probably one effective changeup or split-finger offering away from being a top-two or three round selection in 2026. He knows how to shape the baseball and checks the boxes.

Head is a wiry, athletic outfielder with a smooth lefty stroke at the plate and a quick first step. Head has fast hands and quick wrists, turning on heat on the inner third for impact consistently. Head is a plus runner who may ultimately grow into average power, however he's not consistently hitting the baseball hard at this stage in his career. His continued emphasis on adding strength and bat speed going forward will define his ceiling, but the approach and pure bat-to-ball skills are quite strong at present. 

Head's feel for centerfield has really taken a jump on campus. He seems to get to everything hit in his vicinity in the grass and is a highlight reel machine. He's a good bet to play centerfield as a pro. There's a good bit of projection remaining in Head's lean, long-levered 6-foot-3-inch profile. He is a draft-eligible sophomore.

Contreras has taken major strides over the course of the last calendar year. His athleticism and physicality has bumped up on the mound and he's now flashing some of the biggest pure arm talent of anyone in the class. It's unrefined, but the ceiling is growing. He's so advanced at this stage that he pitched meaningful innings for Brazil in the World Baseball Classic in March at just 17 years old. 

Contreras has been up to 100 mph with a fastball that darts and tails into right-handed hitters. There's occasionally some carry to the pitch, but it's often dictated by his release point, generally above the zone. He'll sit 93-97 over multiple innings. Contreras has a super-fast arm and could live at or near triple digits in a bullpen role at the next level.

The fastball is undoubtedly good, but his breaking ball has a chance to be a dynamic weapon with a litle more added shape. He rips through death ball slider at 85-89 and has been up to 91 with bullet action. There's huge arm speed and conviction in how he throws the pitch. Hitters have to be ready for the fastball given him propensity for velocity, so when he snaps over the breaker he often gets feeble swings. It's got a chance to be a true out-pitch in time.

Contreras will flash an low-80s split-grip changeup, sometimes characterized as a fork ball, and has shown a willingness to throw it to right-handed hitters and left-handed hitters alike. He's shown average feel for landing it at the bottom of the zone, however its shape and conviction suggest at least a plus pitch going forward, maybe better. It's got teeth and represents a true swing and miss weapon immediately. 

Contreras is a shorter-strider for his size who has a relief look to him at times. The middling extension will put considerably more pressure on his secondaries at the next level without the advantage of elevated perceived velocity. The control for strikes and command for landing those strikes is still a work in progress, however he's relatively polished for a player his age, with his levers, throwing the way he is. He's got late-inning leverageable upside and could eventually own some of the best pure stuff in the 2026 class. Combine that with his physical size and athletic gifts and it's easy to see why teams will covet his profile in July. He'll also be just 18.1 years old for the Draft. 

Contreras is the son of former MLB hurler Jose Contreras.

Dempsey is a bit of a spin merchant. His breaking ball earned him a tryout with Team USA's CNT during the summer of 2025. He'll routinely grab rpm north of 3000 with his sweeper. It's a 79-80 with enormous two plane break, late with the ability to miss bats against righties. 

Dempsey has solid arm talent with a fastball that'll tickle 96 mph with solid arm-side tailing action and moderate carry. His command at the top of the zone is among the best in the class, helping lead to one of the flatter VAAs in the class. He launches from a lower-than-comfortable slot for hitters to pick up. It's resulted in strong chase rates for the heater, too. 

There's a lesser-thrown changeup that's performed well, too.

To his credit, Dempsey is also a gifted offensive player with two-way upside, however his future is on the mound. The capacity for spin is impressive, but he'll need to develop a third pitch to get hitters out. He'll be young for the draft, and many evaluators and scouts believe his best stuff is ahead of him.

Zion Rose was a bit of a unicorn in high school. A catcher posting 70-grade run times with a big arm behind the dish is reasonably unheard of. That said, some of the finer details kept him from locking down that position at school. Louisville coaches elected to move his talent to the outfield in 2024 in an attempt to get his bat in the lineup every night and expose him to new roles, expanding his versatility. After all, the speed plays better in the grass than it does behind the plate. The results have been warranted as Rose has developed into a capable left fielder, although he's slowed to more of a plus runner with added strength. 

Offensively Rose has strong wrists and hands to manipulate the barrel. There's plenty of bat speed here, solid average raw power at this stage. He may grow into more. Developing more of a pull-side emphasis could unlock another level of impact for Rose. At present, he seems content lashing line drives and well-stung ground balls to the opposite field. The bat possesses near top-of-the-scale contact rates when he's swinging at pitches inside the zone. When expanding the zone, Rose has a keen ability to keep an at-bat alive by fouling off pitches off. That'll be an important trait as Rose is an aggressive hitter who will chase pitches at times. 

At present, Rose is a hit-over-power left field prospect with sneaky raw power and plus speed. He's not getting to his physical tools at the plate yet, but is a productive hitter and puts the game in motion at a high clip.

Carbaugh is a tough at-bat. A tall, lanky righty with considerable projection, Carbaugh comes at hitters from an ultra-deceptive low three-quarters arm slot. That launch results in considerable arm-side tailing action. He's shown the ability to back-door his fastball to righties at will and will front-door the heater to left-handed hitters too. Carbaugh has been up to 97 mph and has above average command for that pitch. That pitch should continue to perform thanks to its flat vertical approach angle and Carbaugh's willingness to move it both vertically and horizontally in plane. 

The sweeper will need to firm up, but it's presently an upper-70s frisbee with two-plane tilt; more sweep than depth. His spin rates will eclipse 2900 rpm at times; a terrific building block for the future. He's still working to find consistency with that pitch as he'll often get under the sweeper creating a hump in its approach. 

Carbaugh has worked hard to develop the changeup over the last twelve months and some believe it's got plus upside. It's made huge strides over the summer and now parachutes through the zone. His willingness to throw it against right-handed hitters also stands out. Couple in the fact he creates above average extension down the mound and there's pretty considerable upside of a starter at the next level. Carbaugh will barely be 18 years old in July. Excellent clay.

Lord certainly looks the part of a prototypical right-handed ace. At 6-foot-8, 200 pounds he's get immense projection ahead and the stuff should soon follow. For now he's up to 97 in a controlled showcase setting but he's more routinely 91-94. The fastball has some teeth at the top of the zone with some late life and considerable carry through the top rail. It's a difficult heater for hitters to get on top of as Lord features an outlandishly high launch. Lord creates plenty of steepness in his arsenal and it shows in a big way in his breaking ball and changeup. 

The breaker is a low-80s two-plane bender with more curveball shape than traditional slider traits. That pitch will firm up as he ages and matures into his frame. The changeup might be his best secondary right now featuring some darting action and tumble. He sells that pitch nicely and it projects into an above average weapon as a pro, however he doesn't turn to the pitch as often as scouts would like. 

The book on Lord is projection. He has a long way to go before he realizes his upside ceiling. He's yet to truly incorporate his lower half or natural strength into his delivery, something that could unlock a big new gear. As it all clicks into place Lord could end up with triple-digit velocity as well as a pitch mix and athleticism that mirrors someone like Logan Gilbert.

Nawrocki is an undersized southpaw with enormous stuff and a chance to shut down opponents at the end of games if he doesn't ultimately stay in the rotation. 

Nawrocki is a supreme athlete with a super quick arm. He generates huge hip-shoulder separation, well-above average extension and outlier scap load to deliver a mid-90s fastball capable of blowing hitters away. Better still, Nawrocki's sub-5 foot launch height allows his entire arsenal to play way up. He hides the ball late through his delivery, launching from behind his ear out in front of his frame. He's cross-body and closed at release creating more angles and occlusion for the opposition to try and fight through. It's enormous spin capacity with fastballs sizzling north of 2700 rpm at their best. He's shown the ability to manipulate shapes, however at his best he's holding carry and pounding the top of the zone. When he's landing the heater at the top of the zone, it owns the traits of a true 80-grade fastball. 

Nawrocki will sink and tail the fastball at the bottom of the zone when looking for chase. Nawrocki's control for the zone and command inside of the strike zone has taken a significant step forward over the last year. If he can get to average strike-throwing capacity, he's got a chance to be a starting pitcher at the next level with three disgusting pitches. 

The slider here is just nasty. Nawrocki has been up to 87 and lives 82-85 with spin rates in excess of 3300 rpm at times. His breaker is a traditional sweeper that buckles hitters. Left-handers stand little chance when he's commanding the pitch. Right-handers are often frozen when he's able to back-door it. He's also shown the ability to land a mid-80s changeup that has depth with spin rates near 1500 rpm. 

Both the fastball and sweeping breaking ball comfortably have 70-grade upside and both will occassionally flash outputs to suggest elite ceilings. Scouts are bullish he will be able to put the puzzle together to reach his ceiling.

Skelton exploded onto the scene moreso than ever over the course of the last twelve months with exceptional performances in big games and events in front of large buckets of scouts. The physical tools stand out in a big way on the offensive side of the ball. A well-built infield prospect with a barrel-chest and broad, sloping shoulders, Skelton has a legitimate chance to play third base at the next level.

The physical strength stands out in a big way. Skelton regularly registers triple-digit exit velocities from his teenage 6-foot frame. Skelton's swing is reminiscent of Alex Bregman. Simple, direct, short into the zone and extended through it. Skelton's triggers are quiet. He gets the foot down with the hands back, loaded and ready to fire. He stays locked behind a firm front side and rotates hard. Skelton is going to hit going forward so long as the swing decisions continue to remain sound. Thus far, they have. Skelton has the look of a hitter who could boast a strong hit tool and can provide impact in the power department as well. He's fun to watch hit. 

Skelton plays some shortstop now, but he'll end up at second or third base when all is said and done. He's a fringe-average runner at best with a heavy-footed gait. The arm is just average and his throws have a tendency to tail and sink at times due to his arm action and release. Skelton has reliable hands and gobbles up just about everything hit right at him. The tools are perfectly capable of playing second base at an average level so long as he doesn't get too big for the position. 

Skelton is a bat-first prospect whose offensive profile might just be too good for teams to pass up inside of the third or fourth round range. He will be 18.9 years old for the Draft.

Brock had a polarizing junior college career. It got him selected in the 14th round by the Brewers, but he elected to go to Oklahoma to improve his draft stock. 

Everything Brock is capable of is exciting. He can windmill dunk a basketball, he's posted sub 6.4 60-yard dash times, he's the all-time homerun champion at Southwestern Illinois by a healthy mark in just two years of play, and he stole 70 bags his final two season at SICC. The speed is legit with run times that will at times approach 70-grade marks home-to-first. His .431/.541/.844 career JUCO slash speaks to the damage he did. 

Brock employs a wide base at the plate and swings with some uphill plane. His swing path allows for the barrel to stay through the zone for a long time. He's short to the ball, quick, compact and cuts off his swing at the top. Contact quality has stood out at Oklahoma. The tools are loud, however he enters the 2026 Draft with an abbreviated baseball card in terms of reps versus premium competition. 

Brock has primarily played behind the plate where he's got a chance at the next level. Pitch framing is a work in progress, but solid average arm strength and athleticism out of the crouch are present. He's played some outfield across the last two seasons too, providing some versatility if he's forced out from behind the plate.

Noah Wilson is a polarizing prospect in that his raw tools are traits absolutely scream off the page, though his mechanics and athletic actions are unique. Wilson sets up with high hands and a slightly open base. His load is noisy with a back elbow that flies high and cocks into position for launch. That moves leads to something of a steep attack angle with intent for launch. Wilson really works to stay behind the baseball and deliver all his torque through his front side. It's fairly elite bat speed despite only possessing slightly above average rotational acceleration. Wilson isn't necessarily quick to the baseball, but when he's on a pitch he'll boast exit velocity and distance figures most of his peers will never touch. Curiously, Wilson's bat plane will sometimes normalize in game suggesting his batting practice sessions are, at times, him electing to drop scouts' jaws rather than put together a professional display of hitting. Nothing wrong with that. It shows what the body is capable of from a metrics perspective. Wilson has shown a good amount of swing-and-miss in his game at this stage, a hurdle he'll need to clear as July approaches if he hopes to hear his name called early. 

Wilson has flashed 80-grade speed and is light on his feet despite his physical frame. He's a burner underway. He will likely hold his speed and has a chance to stick in centerfield. It's fringy arm strength that will undoubtedly slide to left field should he be forced off the '8' by a more premium defender.

Following an up-and-down two years at the University of Texas, Gasparino transferred back home to Los Angeles to play ball at UCLA for his draft-eligible 2026 junior year. Gasparino is a big, long, tall outfielder with immense athleticism. A plus runner with a plus arm in right field. he has exceptional body control considering his size and long levers. 

It's plus raw power at the plate, though his bat path can get long at times. He shortened his stride and muted his leg kick, quieting his lower-body operation at the dish in 2025. It has unlocked more of a hit tool. Gasparino will continue to add weight and muscle. As he does, his swing will change and his eventual upside will become more clear. To date, he's struggled to catch up to velocity at the top of the strike zone and has shown an eager, aggressive approach bloating his chase rates. The impact in the bat is clear, but swinging at the right pitches will be the only route toward capitalizing on his enormous ceiling. As it stands today, he's a projection bat with exciting athletic tools, testing and body control despite some up-and-down in-game performances. The peaks are brighter than the sun, but he's got to find a way to show it more consistently. 

It's top-ten pick upside with some believing he could develop into a Matt Kemp-level prospect. But Gasparino has a ways to go to meet those hefty expectations.

Sdao turned down a ton of money in the 2025 Draft in order to return to College Station. Resetting his market after missing the 2025 season was a priority for the talented lefty. 

Sdao is a promising projection lefty with a live, loose operation and a wiry, electric frame. At 6-foot-3, 170 pounds, scouts expect Sdao will add close to 25 pounds before his development is over. His ultra-quick arm is already touching 97, and he'll sit 92-94 well into starts with bat-missing carry through the zone. Sdao spins the fastball well and generates slightly above average extension down the bump allowing his velocity to play up a tick or two. 

He features a low-80s sweeping slider that's been up to 86. He has a tendency to drop his arm slot to achieve his current breaking ball shape. To date, it's been highly effective missing bats and generating chase, however Sdao has thrown a huge sample of these in his abbreviated career at College Station. There's also a mid-80s changeup that's flashed above average upside in its limited look. 

Sdao had worked primarily in relief across 2023 and 2024. He logged just seven starts in his Aggie career, but pitched in 42 games and logged 92 innings before 2026. He was scheduled to take on a rotation role in 2025 before eventually succumbing to Tommy John in the fall of 2024. Sdao's handedness, fastball quality, projection and strike-throwing ability will still make him very sought after in the 2025 Draft. He has suitors as high as the second round, though a third round selection seems more likely at this juncture.

The first thing that immediately stands out about Ethan Bass is how all of the players on the field tend to gravitate towards him. He's a well-liked guy in the dugout thanks to his hair-on-fire mentality, easy going temperament and ultra-competitive gamer personality between the lines. Bass is a swing-tinkerer who is finally beginning to come into his own at the plate. There's been several variations of hand setups and leg kicks in his swing over the years. Of late he's been more upright in his setup, hands resting at shoulder height with a moderate stride and leg-lift to help incorporate his lower half. It's allowing him to tap into more of his natural raw power as ringing doubles and shots off the wall have become more prevalent of late. Bass generates whippy bat speed and has shown feel for getting to his pull-side with bigger and louder intent over the last calendar year. The hit tool has ticked up in the right direction over the last year too. Better still, Bass is a plus runner who will add value on the bases. 

With that said, when teams are buying this profile it is also because of the glove. Bass is a bouncy defender who is light on his feet with a gliding nature about his play. His footwork and natural feel for the dirt are rivaled by very few in the class. He can make just about every throw from every angle and makes playing the shortstop position look like an art form. He's shown capable of playing third base at a high level too if for some reason he outgrows the hot corner. There is the potential for a true plus-or-better glove here.

If the bat continues its rocket ship trajectory as July approach, Bass has first round tools. A true joy to watch play the game. For what it's worth, he can really pitch too. Already touching 92 with a flashy slider, there's multiple avenues for him to carve out of future role. Bass will be 18.9 years old on draft day.

DeCaro, originally a member of the 2024 high school class, reclassified into the 2023 draft class and will be barely 20 years old on draft day. He's got an athletic, physical 6-foot-5-inch frame and has recently seen his velocity tick up a bit. It's a big, durable frame that should continue to add more ticks too. 

DeCaro work up to 97 and rests 92-93 in multi-inning outings, and it's a definitive starting pitcher profile. His heater features impressive arm-side run with well-above average spin rates and will occasionally hold some vertical carry. It's been an effective pitch generating ground balls, but it doesn't appear as though it's going to be a swing-and-miss weapon.
