DeCaro has the innate ability to spin a breaking ball, though adding velocity to his secondary weapons will be a priority in his development, especially since he does not extend down the mound particularly well. Breaking ball quality will be a must since his fastball won't be relied upon to get outs on its own. 

The slider sits 81-82 and has been up to 85 with two-plane tilt. It's provided moderate value in the whiffs, chase and weak-contact department. The curveball is certainly his best pitch with huge shape, huge spin and enough firmness to get hitters out in front. It's a plus curveball, however he's not throwing it quite as much as he could, partially due to hitters not being intimidated by the fastball. 

DeCaro added a high-upside changeup in 2025 that flashes very interesting tunneling traits to go alongside the heater. It's performed very well and has a chance to eventually become his best weapon going forward.

DeCaro isn't a guy who is going to beat his opponents with sheer force or stuff. He's a master of craft and keeps hitters off balance with a bevy of offerings and buckets of strikes.

Mendes is a terrific athlete who shows potential both on the mound and at the plate. He's almost entirely scrapped his position player dreams, however. His future is on the mound. That's where he has placed most of his development efforts. 

He runs the fastball up to 96 from the left side and is capable of generating moderate carry and late tail with solid extension down the mound, improving his perceived velocity. Mendes isn't a hard-thrower and is more commonly 91-93. It's a solid average fastball that serves a purpose to set up the rest of his tricks.

Mendes pairs the heater with a nasty slider that gets good depth and some lateral tilt. It's been an above average weapon thus far and could take one more step forward if he begins throwing it just a bit harder. 

Mendes worked hard to develop a changeup going into his sophomore year and while his ability to land that pitch where he wants to the arm-side continues to be a focus, the shapes he's creating are truly dynamic. It's a plus changeup that fits his repertoire nicely.

There's a much bigger, deeper curveball to round out his arsenal as well that's performed nicely. It's got solid depth and dives off the slider tunnel late. 

Mendes has the full menu of pitches and his strike-throwing ability continue to improve. Scouts expect the velocity to make a jump too. If the strikes continue to improve and the stuff comes with it, Mendes has a chance to hear his name called in the first couple rounds.

One of the better hitters in the Peach State in 2026. Galason has a simple swing with very few moving parts. He gets the foot down and takes the barrel directly to the ball with quiet hands and good direction. He employs a wide base and works up the middle of the field with a line drive emphasis. Galason sticks his nose in the zone and has the look of a pure hitter. As one might expect, there's very few strikeouts and enough raw power to be dangerous, however he doesn't project a slugging threat as a professional. It's fringe-average raw power that he's still working to tap into more consistently. 

Galason has some bounce on the dirt and some rhythm in his hands. It might end up at second or third base when all is said and done, but the actions of a professional infielder are there. When tasked with showcasing in the outfield, he's flashed above average arm strength and could play in the grass as a utility type going forward as well. His above average foot speed will play anywhere.

Galason reclassified from the 2027 class into 2026 and will be just 18.1 years old for the Draft. He's on the smaller side from a stature perspective, but he has very few noteworthy holes in his game.

Norby has one of the best breaking balls in the 2026 class. He's produced exceptional strike-quality, two-plane break and velocity with that pitch that some scouts believe give it a plus floor at the professional level. Norby's sweeper has been up to 85 mph and will routinely rest 80-81 mph. He spins the breaking ball north of 3000 rpm with frequency. It's a real hammer. 

The fastball is Norby's second-best weapon, however it's got some development ahead. He's been up to 93 and is more commonly 89-92 with generic shape. Norby does spin the fastball well and extends well down the mound. It's an entirely different delivery with the heater than it is the breaking ball. Norby works much further down the bump with the heater and launches from a considerably higher slot. His two pitch arsenal is visible to advanced hitters. 

Norby has been effective as a college starter and throws a ton of strikes. He's undersized and will need to refine his ability to repeat the same operation on the bump if he's to gain confidence from scouts and pro analysts, but there's clay here for an out-getter at the next level.

Dowd has truly grown into his own as a collegiate ballplayer. Once entirely undersized and lacking impactful tools, added muscle and consistent reps have turned him into a spark plug with some sneaky tools.

After getting full-time reps at USC, Dowd was able to make adjustments in his sophomore year that led to some rather noteworthy jumps. He began pummeling velocity and getting the ball in the air at far healthier clips. While he's unlikely to ever boast better than 45-grade raw power, his hit tool could blossom into an above-average weapon as a professional. Dowd has seen steady improvements in his approach at the plate, his ability to get to his pull-side and his exit velocities. He's still susceptible to sliders just underneath the strike zone, but he's got time to right the ship there.

Dowd is a strong defender in centerfield who shows off plus run times. It's speed that plays better in the field than it does on the bases. He takes aggressive routes to the ball and has rangy athleticism that makes him capable of making highlight reel plays in the gaps. Dowd is still refining his technique on balls his directly over his head, and he seems to lose balls in the sun and in the lights at a higher clip than most accomplished centerfielders. These are things that could be polished over with time and more reps. Dowd has a chance to develop into something of a Brett Gardner type of table-setter. He's on the smaller and lighter side so much attention will be placed on his ability to provide impact with his legs and with his glove.

Johnson is a barrel-chested middle infielder with a loud stroke at the plate and budding power on the way. He aims to lift the ball and drive the ball over the left-center field fence every chance he gets, and the game power is already playing. Despite this approach, Johnson has shown a more polished approach at the plate than some of his peers keeping his strikeouts lower and his walks high. He hardly ever expands the strike zone and is more than happy to take what the pitchers gives him. The pull-side emphasis is certainly here, but it's more pull-side gaps than it is towering fly balls hit at the foul pole. Johnson plays a more mature brand of baseball than you'd anticipate watching his ringing batting practice sessions.

Metrically, Johnson will light up models. He keeps ground balls to a minimum and gets the ball in the air to left field at a heavy clip. He's showing the components of a future slugging infielder at the next level. 

In terms of the athletic traits, he's an average runner with an above average arm that more than carries through the first base bag. The body may ultimately force him to third base, though his tools play quite well at the hot corner. Johnson is a physical specimen who can make things happen at the plate. He'll turn 18 years old just a few months before the draft, making him an appealing model option in July.

One of the more famous names around the country in the 2026 prep class, Giles has long been considered a high follow prospect going back to the eighth grade. He's got a sweet left-handed swing with a natural understanding on how to backspin the baseball. He's short into the zone and long through it with fast and loose hands and the ability to catch mistakes out in front. Fast, twitchy hips create tons of torque. He can get locked up on pitches on the inner black and can lose connection on pitches on the outer black. He punishes mistakes. Giles figures to eventually grow into above average raw power and has a swing that should allow him to get to it. After struggling throughout parts of the summer in 2025, Giles got stronger and clicked into a new gear this spring. 

The physical tools elsewhere continue to improve with above average arm strength and above average foot speed that works better underway than it does in terms of first-step quickness. His defensive prowess is strong. It's fundamentally sound footwork coming through the baseball with an arm action that gets the ball in quick with carry to the target. There's a lot to like in this profile and he'll be a high follow as he continues to add strength. Giles will be 18.5 years old for the draft.

Washington has one of the more distinguished hit tools in the class at this stage. Some of the fastest hands in the class with an ultra-compact swing. Washington glides and drifts through the hitting zone and allows his hands and wrists to do all the work scorching line drives all over the field, peppering the right-center field gap against velocity. Washington is a bit of a swing-tinkerer with different variations of a leg kick and toe tap depending on the event. Regardless of what he deploys, the hits seem to stack in bunches.

Washington doesn't project to be a hulking slugger at the next level, but at the high school level he's been one of the most prolific power hitters in the country. In 2025 as a junior, Washington ranked among the top in the sport for homers. He was instant offense. 

A solid average runner, he's unlikely to be a huge base-stealer at the next level, though running will certainly be in his game to some capacity. Washington projects into centerfield if he doesn't slow down at the next level, though his game profiles just fine in left field as well. Quite a dynamic player with the floor of a hitterish spark plug. He'll be extremely young for the class at just 18.1 years old on draft day. There's day one upside here.

Mercurius and his brother Alexander have been popular names in the scouting community for a few years, both adding bigger and better stuff each time they're seen. Mercurius finds himself draft-eligible for the first time since high school in 2026 carried by a big breaking ball and burgeoning velocity. After spending two seasons at UNLV, he transferred to Norman for the 2026 season for the chance to play with his brother for at least one season. 

Mercurius pitches out of a traditional hands-over-head wind-up with considerable arm speed through release. He's already up to 98, and his shapes are rapidly improving. He's generating more carry on the heater in 2026, up into the plus territory. He's also shown fringy command for the pitch, relying on zone-percentage rather than actually throwing to specific locations. He added a more traditional sinker in 2026 to try and get more value from his four-seamer at the top of the zone, and that's helped a good bit. Mercurius has a "stock" release, so the secondaries need to flash. And they do.

The slider can be good. It's a low-80s bullet-spinning breaker with near perfect efficiency. He sells it with big arm speed and conviction. Hitters have a hard time picking it up out of the hand. It's a future above-average pitch, however analysts would like to see him get a bit more depth to his breaking ball.

Mercurius will fold in some plus changeups that could use a bit more tumble through the zone, but they do possess pretty strong arm-side fade. It's a pitch that continues to climb from an effectivness standpoint leading some analysts to suggest a consistent future plus outcome could be in the cards. It's got plenty of separation off the fastball and plays up thanks to some tunneling. 

Mercurius has an athletic delivery and throws enough strikes. He'll need to find a way to make his mid-90s fastball less hittable if he's going to capture what some believe is a no. 4 starter profile at the next level. The profile was strong enough to warrant a Team USA Collegiate National Team invite following the 2025 season.

A famous arm going back to his high school days, Johnson was a 20th round pick by the Cardinals in 2023, but went unsigned. He is a big, physical lefty up to 98 with plenty of arm-side run and sink coming out of a deceptive, low-launch slot. It's a barrel-breaking, ground ball inducing bowling ball. That said, Johnson has been held back for most of his collegiate career by control, command and execution woes. 

Johnson's fastball will flash. That low-launch release does make for effective value at the top of the zone, especially when he can hold some vert. More often than not, Johnson is coming around the fastball and sinking it away from right-handed hitters. Given his velocity and unique angles, he'll likely find more and more value with the heater if his command and strike-quality trend in the right direction. 

He's begun spinning a better breaking ball on campus, a weapon against both-handed hitters with deeper shape but it needs to be thrown more firm. There's also a changeup that he's thrown more and more to right-handed hitters. His shapes and command for landing the pitch have taken big strides in Norman. Scouts are split on whether he'll be able to start at the next level, but this is an out-getter with a big, strong, workhorse frame. If the strikes and production are there he could go very early in 2026, especially as a lefty. 

Metrically Johnson still has a ton to like. He's got the floor of a leverage reliever if the strikes don't improve.

McCoy has been a nice piece for the Gamecocks with his three-pitch mix and loud arm talent from the left side. It's a fast arm with fringy command, stuff over polish. McCoy works with an up-tempo delivery and pitches with aggression and moxy.

McCoy had a very solid 2025 season posting 60 innings for South Carolina en route to an invitation to the Cape. That's where his stock took off. McCoy pounded the zone with greater ferocity and challenged hitters in a starting role. He was striking out boat loads of batters for Harwich most of the summer. Because of that showing, McCoy boosted himself up into must-follow territory for 2026. Unfortunately, after breaking through, McCoy tore his UCL before the 2026 season began costing him his entire junior year. 

McCoy's fastball is a good one. He's been up to 98 and ordinarily cuts the baseball. McCoy will more commonly sit 92-94, but his exceptionally low launch height helps the fastball play way up to hitters. It's been awfully impressive at the top of the zone. McCoy isn't a big extension guy, but his unique fastball traits and components to his release make him an uncomfortable look for the opposition.

McCoy's slider has two plane of tilt and at it's best will sweep away from left-handed hitters aggressively. He throws it hard, usually 83-84, but he's capable of rushing it to the plate at 87 if he's willing to sacrifice lateral break for more bullet tilt. Adding to the allure of the breaking ball is McCoy's ability to occasionally approach 3000 rpm. The fastball/slider combo both have the chance to develop into plus pitches if his command for the zone continues to track upward. 

McCoy throws his changeup less than ten percent of the time and has confirmed it's a development that's he's focused on going forward. He's flashed some big shapes with the cambio every now and again, but it's fringy command at this stage. 

This is a pretty fun profile even if it isn't a prototypical starting pitcher package. It's three or four pitches with big fastball value when it's commanded. The breaking ball is already flashing plus and hitters are being forced to cheat and guess what's coming. McCoy has day-one stuff in July if the polish comes.

Reasonably unheralded coming out of high school, Levu locked down significant playing time immediately at UCLA as an option at first base and in a utility role. 

Levu has got advanced feel for the zone and keeps his chase rates at reasonable levels considering his age. Levu hits just about everything he swings at in the zone and has shown above average power, including to the opposite field. He's got excellent barrel controlled and has shown a unique ability to get the fat part of the bat to all four quadrants, as well as above the strike zone. Scouts would like to see him get the ball in the air a bit more, but considering this stage in his career it's hardly a red flag. This looks like a potentially potent first base stick with a well-balanced overall offensive profile. 

Levu is limited on the field to first base due to his fringe average speed and average arm strength but it is above average actions around the pillow with high marks in the IQ department. He can play third base in a pinch.

The pride of the great state of Utah, Murdock has been a development focus for the staff at UC San Diego since arriving in the fall of 2023. A strong-body righty with big metrics traits, Murdock has had to polish some of the roughness around the edges of his profile, but it's slowly all coming together.

The arm talent here noteworthy. Up to 97 with almost seven feet of extension, Murdock has the velocity and ability to move like a starter does on the mound. He's more routinely 92-95. It's a true cut/ride heater that creates plenty of weak contact and can generate some whiffs elevated as well. That said, fringy strike-throwing has slowed his ascent as a prospect. Murdock is very good at spinning the baseball and can snag rpm north of 2400 at times on the fastball.

Murdock owns three average-or-better secondaries in the slider, curveball and changeup. The slider has been expecially effective with enormous chase rates and firmness befitting of a professional weapon. It's a pitch that's more commonly flashing above-average or better upside, however Murdock can struggle to get to it with his fringy strike-throwing ability. Murdock's slider is more of a gyro bullet spinner with minimal horizontal shape and deep, diving action. That plays up from his higher slot. The curveball is very big, generally in the upper-70s. 

The changeup is in there, however it's squarely a tertiary offering and are often thrown only a few times each outing.

Given the body, the arm talent, and athleticism and feel for multiple pitches, Murdock has a chance to shoot up boards in the spring of 2026. Showing the capacity to work a bit more east and west would benefit his profile, especially if he can get those shapes from his changeup at times. He needs to throw more strikes and establish the fastball. If he does, there's some reason to believe he's a third or fourth round pick.

Broussard was lightly recruited out of high school with many college coaches and recruiting supervisors opining he needed to added weight before he was ready to compete at the D1 level. He spent his freshman season at San Jacinto College where he hit north of .400 and immediately re-garnered the attention of the scouting community. 20 pounds heavier with a baseball card to his name, Broussard transferred to his hometown Houston Cougars where he stapled his name in centerfield and didn't look back. 

After a slower start to his sophomore season in 2025, Broussard got ultra-hot and began putting everything in play. His plate coverage skills were impressive, as was his unexpected raw power. Broussard was long considered a slasher, but he was putting together exit velocities approach 110 mph as a 170-pound sophomore. He complimented the impact with speed to burn on the basepaths. It was an ever-present green light in 2025 and Broussard was always running. All of these traits and tools were elevated by borderline elite bat-to-ball skills. He showcased a reasonably strong approach, expanding the zone only when he could get the bat head to the spot. His in-zone and out-of-zone whiff rates were equally minuscule. Broussard is a sparkplug in every sense of the word with enough raw power and bat speed to make pitchers pay for assuming he's going to slap the ball line to line. 

Broussard is an exceptional centerfielder. He takes superb routes to the ball, consistently takes a strong first steps and glides in space. He's capable of getting to balls in the gaps few can. Broussard's double-plus run tools allows him to make the highlight reel play. He's a potential plus centerfielder as a pro. It's average arm strength. 

Broussard has tons of selling points. He'll also be just 20 years old for the Draft. The frame has more projection on the horizon and he's already hitting the ball harder than his current physical stature would suggest. He's one of the more impressive total package centerfielders in the 2026 Draft with a very real chance of hearing his name selected on day one.

Libbert was a steady performer on the high school showcase and tournament scene, including stops at Team USA tryouts and several standout performances with the Warriors Baseball program. After a brief stint at Missouri, Libbert transferred to Ole Miss where his stuff has ticked up a notch.

Libbert a high-launch lefty with a low-to-mid 90s fastball, up to 97 with solid carry occassional cutting action. There's some natural deception that gets swings outside of the zone. Libbert worked hard over the fall and winter to reinvent his delivery, upping his extension down the mound and slightly raising his arm slot to generate more lift on the baseball. The results have been encouraging. It can be difficult to find bigger shapes from left-handed starting pitchers. Libbert has some uniqueness to his heater.

Libbert's slider is above average, 79-81 with deeper, two-plane tilt and solid spin traits. He's scrapped his bullet slider from 2025 an instead now focuses on throwing a firm cutter in the mid-to-upper 80s that compliments the more lateral shape of his sweeper. It's helped bridge a more complete arsenal of pitches.

Libbert's changeup has been inconsistent, however his ability to kill spin, create depth and sometimes fade the cambio stands out. His ability to repeat his fastball's arm slot and deceive hitters with the pitch stands out. There's above average or better upside here if his feel for consistently creating bigger shapes takes another step forward. 

Libbert missed much of his senior year of high school recovering from TJ and didn't pitch for Missouri as a freshman in 2024. He logged a full season of work in 2025 before transferring to Oxford. Bouts of strike-throwing streakiness and inconsistent execution of his pitches has slowed his momentum at times, but the peaks here are awfully encouraging.

Shelar has the look of a prototypical right fielder with strength in his lower half and physical traits that show out in the box and in the field. His above average arm strength and direct routes to the ball look the part of a future corner defender with his solid average speed complementing those traits. 

Shelar is as you'd expect in the box. There's plenty of bat speed and raw power here. He's got explosive hand speed and swings with extreme intent. His swing is presently built with a top-spin emphasis, something that his resulted in huge exit velocities but not a lot of in-game over-the-fence power. There's some stiffness in Shelar's swing that could inhibit his ability to ever unlock true in-game power, but you'd be hard-pressed to find a more physical hitter right now at this stage than is Shelar at this age.

A bluechip recruit for the Demon Deacons in 2023, Morningstar is a premium body guy with huge stuff that's only gotten bigger on campus.  It's five pitches and an array of east-west as well as north-south options to keep the opponent uncomfortable in the box.

Morningstar has grabbed 97 with his four-seamer and sits 93-95, however a bit vanilla in shape. He's deceptive by nature which bolters the swing-and-miss on his fastball, but it doesn't inherently possess traits that stuff models favor. His sinker is a much more formidable weapon featuring impressive diving action. Morningstar gets more whiffs on his sinker than most. The existence of two fastballs makes each heater just a bit more valuable. It's just moderate extension for a pitcher of his size so owning the full accoutrement of weapons will be necessary to find success. Completing the full heater arsenal is a high-80s cutter that can be extremely valuable in terms of missing barrels of more formidable hitters. 

The breaking ball is a hammer. Morningstar has produced big whiff and chase rates on his curveball thanks to its huge shape and low-80s velocity band. He'll compliment the bender with a more firm slider in the mid-80s to keep hitters off their timing windows. The changeup is also a real go-to pitch and it plays very nicely off his sinking fastball. 

Morningstar has a whole menu of options to throw at hitters. It's mid-rotation upside and a day one pick in July.

A mid-major bat with huge offensive upside, Bogenpohl is the latest Missouri State product to boast big pro potential. At 6-foot-5, 240 pounds, Bogenpohl towers over most of his peers. He's extremely physical and carries his 240-pound frame athletically. He's light on his feet and moves very well for his size. 

The bat is the carrying tool here. It's perhaps 80-grade raw power projection and he's tapping into a lot of it already. Bogenpohl is registering exit velocities north of 117 mph at his peaks. He possesses a polished eye and hardly ever expands the zone. However, Bogenpohl will swing through elevated fastballs and spin inside the strike zone at an unsustainably high clip. He does enormous damage on pitches on the inner-third, but is susceptible to the slider or changeup low-and-away. His swing and miss on pitches outside of the zone is also quite high, even if he doesn't offer at them often. The crudeness of his offensive profile also bores out in his batted-ball data and spray charts. Bogenpohl hits the ball on the ground quite a bit and struggles to lift the ball to the pull-side. These are all development checkpoints that he's worked hard to iron out on campus The impact ceiling is absolutely enormous, it's just a work-in-progress to get to all of it.

Bogenpohl has gotten run at all three outfield spots though scouts believe left or right field will be the ultimate destination for his talents. He looks plenty comfortably in centerfield, and could stick at that position early in his professional career. It's solid-average speed with above average arm strength. He takes steady routes to the baseball. He projects a solid-to-above average defender who should be able to hold runners station-to-station with further development. 

The ceiling and upside here is substantial if it all clicks into place. There's a path toward a Matt Wallner type of offensive producer here, albeit without the same arm talent in the field. He will be a draft-eligible junior at 21 years old.

Weingartner's game has blossomed in a big way over the last calendar year. His frame and physical tools continue to tick up. Combine those budding traits with what was already a distinguised hit tool and it's easy to get excited about what the final package could become. 

Weingartner has a simple swing with simple triggers and an all-fields approach to hitting. He drops his hands back into a locked position at foot strike and takes a direct path to the ball. It allows Weingartner to hold the barrel through the zone for a prolonged amount of time. Weingarnter is growing into some raw power and could flirt with 15-18 homers per year if afforded a full-time role as a professional. For now, it's safely average raw power projection at the next level. 

A 70-grade runner, Weingartner adds value on the bases by putting pressure on the defense. He's quick out of the box and takes aggressive angles around the bags. Weingartner has played some infield, however most like his game in centerfield or right where the speed and plus arm strength plays up. 

Weingartner carries at least two plus tools and a bat that continues trending up. Weingartner's brother was a sixth round pick in the 2025 Draft.

It's not too common a prospect hailing from the great state of Vermont graces the top of draft rankings, but McCarthy has some of the components necessary to hear his name called early in 2026. Originally a member of the 2027 draft class, McCarthy re-classed up to 2026 and now represents one of the younger players available. 

An athletic 6-foot frame and violent arm speed, McCarthy looks the part on the hill. He creates big separation at foot plant and repeats his delivery very well. McCarthy is already running it up to 97 with with some tailing life and tremendous feel for the strike zone.The heater explodes out of his hand free and easy. He fills it up and dares hitters at this level to hit it. Often time, they do not. 

McCarthy's changeup is probably his best secondary at this stage, but it's close. There's conviction and feel for that pitch at a young age, including a willingness to throw it to the back foot of right-handed hitters. He effectively kills spin and creates tumbling action, hitting the brakes at the plate.

The slider is a very good breaking ball with bullet tilt and solid vertical depth. Again, McCarthy's advanced pitchability allows him to throw that pitch to both lefties and righties with confidence.

McCarthy's athleticism, strike-throwing ability, three-pitch mix and cold weather profile will catch the attention of scouts as the draft approaches. He's got some similarities in physical build and stuff as 2021 second round pick Calvin Ziegler of the New York Mets.

Jackson and his teammates James Clark represent two of the better position prospects on the West Coast in 2026. Jackson is one of the more exciting prospects thanks to his loud athletic tools. He's got a chance to play on the middle infield at the next level or perhaps in the outfield too. 

Jackson can fill up a scouting report. It's plus run times and an aggressive personality in the field. He chases the extra base and likes showing off the wheels snagging stolen bases too. He's an absolute burner out of the box with a quick first step, routinely beating out infield choppers, turning doubles into triples on gappers. Jackson has a chance to be a dynamic table-setter, but that may be underselling the impact in the stick.

The bat speed stands out here. Jackson has some moving parts in his swing, but they all come together thanks to electric hand speed. Jackson deploys a high-set back elbow with some trunk tilt forward. He makes explosive turns against his front side and generates most of his power from his torso and upper-half. It's bat speed that plays to all fields. Given the unconventional nature of the swing, there's some innate volatility in how the mechanics will handle more premium stuff as he works his way up the developmental ladder. 

Jackson is on the older side of this class. He's 19.5 years old in July and lacks much physical projection. It's a physically mature lower-half with tons of strength spreadout throughout his frame. What you see is what you get. It's possible he gets a bit stronger in professional baseball, but that may come with the foot speed losing a step.

Thome has really blossomed as an offensive player over the last twelve months and teams think he's got a chance to be an impact stick at the next level. That sort of label is to be expected from the son of Hall of Fame slugger Jim Thome. 

While Landon doesn't have the size and physicality that made power hitting come so easy for his father, he does have the swing and and feel for the batters' box. Thome swing is simple. He creates coil and counter-rotates to get to his bat speed. Thome uses the ground and his back hip to create torque and leverage. He turns tight and shows looseness in his hands to manipulate the barrel around the yard. Thome does aim to pull the baseball with impact. There's above-average raw power projection here despite lacking prototypical slugger size. It's a well-balanced offensive profile and a swing that should translate.

Finding a defensive home for Thome will be key as July approaches. He looks best suited for second base where his actions will most comfortably play. It's fringy arm strength, however soft hands and feel for throwing on the move come naturally. If he gets considerably more physical, perhaps third base is in the cards.

Thome has the look of a player who could eventually blossom into a Brandon Lowe type of impact stick. The bat will carry the profile.

Dunlap has a chance to be the prototype power-arm/power-bat backstop with the big, physical frame. It's impressive physical projection with more strength on the horizon. Dunlap has the broad, rounded shoulders and strong lower half that point toward a future run-producer.

Dunlap certainly looks the part in the box. It's an open setup with leverage into his lower half. He triggers forward, closing off to the pitcher and delivering a heavy barrel through the zone. Dunlap's swing can get long and outside of his body at times, velocity on his hands giving him trouble from time to time at certain events. When he's given the opportunity to extend his arms and take the barrel through the outer-half, the results are usually loud. Dunlap's swing should shorten up as he gets stronger. 

Dunlap's frame is more befitting of an outfielder or third baseman than it is a catcher, but he's shown plenty capable behind the plate. It's above-average speed with above-average arm strength that plays behind the dish and in the outfield. He's twitchy and explosive out of the crouch, with first-step abilities that would play beautifully in right field, or even perhaps centerfield to begin his career.

Schaffner has been a starting-caliber player since the day he set foot on a college campus. He ran a .337/.436/.421 slash as a true freshman and North Dakota State and complimented that with stellar defense at shortstop. He transferred to North Carolina for the 2026 season, his first draft-eligible campaign in college baseball. A three-sport star in high school, Schaffner is a strong athlete. 

Schaffner is a pure hitter through and through. He boasts elite contact rates both inside the zone and outside of the zone. His short, compact swing plays to all fields. That path has made it almost impossible to sneak anything by him if it's thrown in the strike zone. While has hasn't shown much raw power at this stage, his 6-foot-2-inch frame does have room for 15 to 20 pounds of muscle that could translate into game power. Players like Jacob Wilson and Luke Keaschall had similar wiry frames and eventually grew into some bat speed.

Schaffner is an above-average runner who can post occasional plus run times home-to-first. He's a head-down runner who should be a stolen-base threat as a pro. He's a strong defender up the middle, however it's only average arm strength and that could cap his ceiling as a glove. Still, he should gobble up everything hit in his direction.

Harris has huge offensive upside with more bat speed than most of his peers. It's plus raw power projection. He creates a ton of space in the box with a long stride and good direction with a hit tool and game power that plays to all fields. Harris has a projectable, physical frame that should continue to add good weight and physicality as he ages. He looks the part of a future middle-of-the-order bat. There's presently some swing and miss in Harris' game, likely stemming from inconsistent triggers in his swing and a stride that can create multiple planes for his upper half. That figures to sort itself out over time. 

Defensively he is a rangy outfielder with plus arm strength and plus foot speed. His footwork, routes and fundamentals are advanced. Harris has a quick transfer and release and has the makings of a potential plus defensive right fielder. He'll need to cut down on the strikeouts and overall swing and miss. If he does, it's tools that stack up with any high school prospect in the class.

Herst is one of the more premium physique prospects in the 2026 class with long legs, strength in his core, squared off shoulders and long levers, all of which point to serious projection on the horizon. Projection aside, Herst has very real *now* stuff with a fastball that's tickling the mid-90s. It's a short, deceptive, fast arm that stays behind the ball and generates some carry through the zone, however its shape often falls into the dead zone category. The fastball plays way up thanks to exceptional extension and athleticism on the mound. It's a tough heater for the opposition to pick up and it's feasted at the top of the zone. 

Herst whips in a low-80s slider with big two-plane tilt and feel both backdoor and front door. He's an above-average spinner of the baseball, but his feel for manipulating shape stands out. The changeup is his best weapon. Herst kills spin and tails the cambio heavy off the fastball tunnels featuring exaggerated arm-side fading action and vertical tilt. It's already flashing 'plus' upside. 

Herst commands all three pitches at an above-average level and has the look of a true pitcher in a landscape full of "throwers". He generates elite extension down the bump allowing the baseball to sneak up on hitters. When considering the frame, the strikes, the feel for three pitches, looseness and fluidity in his operation, his extension and ability to control the game, Herst screams starter going forward. He's one of the top arms in the 2026 class and has definitive day one upside.

One of the better hitters on the West Coast as a high schooler, Grahovac took his bat to A&M where he continued to pummel the opposition. After a gangbusters freshman campaign he missed much of 2025 with a left shoulder injury that required surgery. He's expected back at full-strength in 2026. 

Grahovac has an all-fields approach and an willingness to take velocity the other way. He's got a strong frame with tons of present game power. His whiff rates can balloon at times when he gets outside of his approach, but in general the trajectory of his offensive game has only continued to improve on campus. The bat carries here as many evaluators think he will be just an fringy defender at third base or in a corner outfield spot. 

Grahovac has dealt with bumps and bruises going back to his prep days so durability will continue to be an emphasis in watching his profile mature. The body and player are already physically peaking, so continued immediate impact and damage at the plate will be important. Grahovac has been one of the better hitters in the country since starting from day one in College Station.

Snow's fastball has been up to 96 and will sit 91-94 in his starts. He generates above-average carry on that pitch and can miss bats at the top of the zone. Snow's got a two-seam variety as well that he'll bring out to get ground balls. 

The breaking ball shows a capacity for spin with rpms approach 3000 at times, however commanding that pitch remains a developmental focus. It's an upper-70s/low--80s slider with lateral shape. He broadcasts the pitch at times and slows his arm speed to generate the shapes he's currently getting to. A mid-80s changeup rounds out the arsenal with tumbling, fading action. 

It's big stuff with strong fastball command. The secondaries continue to trend upward. Snow is a pretty good mover with moderate extension and the ability to repeat. He has a chance to develop into a good arm with more strength gains and reps.

McElvain saw a massive jump in stuff and physicality heading into college shoving 98, sitting 93-95 with carry on the top rail, commanded glove-side. His fastball has become effective boasting well-above average whiff and chase rates, however foul balls and deep counts have led to more walks than many scouts anticipated from the talented southpaw coming out of high school. It's plus fastball traits without the command to know where it's going some nights. 

He's worked into harnessing a low-80s slider with swing-and-miss potential, but he'll spray that pitch a bit at times. In 2026 he's opted to throw a low-90s cutter more often than the traditional slider, electing to elevate his arsenal rather than work for whiffs below the zone. McElvain does shape his breaking ball quite nicely featuring deeper, sharp break, but he'll go through cold snaps where it's uncompetitive. He's worked to integrate a changeup against right-handed hitters this fall, however his shapes are unpredictable. 

A big, downer, over-the-top curveball has become McElvain's primary weapon deep in count. It features bigger shape and plays well off the fastball. 

McElvain controls the body well and works down the mound with extension, intent and solid athleticism. He's struggled to command the baseball at times and it's affected his ability to generate momentum and traction on the college stage. He elected to transfer to Arkansas after his freshman campaign at Vanderbilt to work with pitching coach Matt Hobbs. 

There's a lot of runway ahead of McElvain to grow and establish himself as one of the top college arms in the 2026 class. He may ultimately be a reliever at the next level, but there's no questioning the arm talent and stuff.

Advincula has plenty of athletic tools with budding bat speed and the ability to play a ton of different positions. It's absolutely elite bat-to-ball skills with the ability to cover velocity, spin, and tumble both inside and outside of the strike zone. What raw power he possesses exists at the bottom of the zone where, especially out over the plate where he can get his arms extended. Advincula has no issue getting to the high ball, however his bat speed and barrel awareness backs up a bit up there. He is mostly a gap hitter right now, though most believe the body and bat speed with eventually lead to a guy who could flirt with 10-12 homer output if he strays away from what is presently a slappy swing. 

Advincula is a plus runner who runs the bases well. He's got a quick first step and his IQ allows for stolen bases to be in his bag of tricks. Advincula has exclusively played second base at the collegiate level and is an above average glove at the position. 

After two years at Cal, Advincula transferred to Georgia Tech for his draft-eligible junior season. He projects a slap-happy table-setter at the next level who should add value with his leather and legs.

Milam is a super bouncy, twitchy little infielder with some of the softest hands you'll find, especially in stateside scouting. He's only got an average arm, and his lateral range is tested with short choppy strides, but the hands and feet are so quick and so smooth. Milam can handle shortstop in a pinch, but best projects as an above average defender at second base. 

At the plate, there's not a ton of thump and doesn't project to much more as he matures, but there's serious feel for the barrel here with an all-fields approach and a track record of performing against both his age and upper class arms. It's especially impressive bat-to-ball skills both inside the zone and out of it. When Milam pulls the trigger, he's putting the ball in play. Despite a willingness to chase pitches out of the zone, Milam is hardly a risk to punch out. 

Milam is the exact type of player that scouts fall in love with because of his work ethic and floor. He's the type of guy who will always exceed the expectations put on him by prognosticators and evaluators alike. This is a big league caliber talent, even if he likely won't impact a team at the top of a lineup.

Ojeda took on a big role for the UC Irvine bullpen as a true freshman and has since seen his usage and role continue to blossom. While he doesn't possess the prototypical size and strength of a starting pitching prospect, Ojeda is a loose, athletic and generates elite extension down the mound with exceptional feel for direction. 

The ball comes out of his hand easy from a lower slow and natural ride through the zone. It's an effective fastball that should continue to improve with more velocity. He missed bats at a 30 percent clip with the heater as a sophomore in 2024 and generated a chase rate north of 30 percent as well; one of the few starting pitchers in the "30-30" club. He nearly repeated that output as a sophomore in 2025. He's already up to 96 will be just 20 years old for the 2026 Draft. It is to be assumed he'll be living 92-93 in no time and should reach for velocity bands a tick higher as July approaches.

Ojeda is fastball-heavy but will throw a low-70s curveball and a low-80s changeup that have both been effective in missing bats. He throws those pitches for strikes and has feel for commanding them, though pitch-shape quality isn't yet where it'll need to be at the next level. 

Considering his athleticism, arm talent and feel for the zone, Ojeda has a chance to develop into an early pick with pitchability and release traits that are impossible to teach. If the velocity takes a jump as July approaches, Ojeda could flirt with Top-50 pick projection.

Renfrow was a two-way player in high school but surrendered the bat in favor of a full-time role on the mound in Blacksburg. It's considerable arm talent with a fastball already touching 97 with some carry through the zone. He'll live 93-94 and carry his velocity deep into outings. 

Renfrow commands a shorter slider that's been up to 87 and is consistently 84-85 mph. His feel for landing that pitch to his glove-side really stands outs. Very few hangers. There's also a mid-to-upper 80s changeup that he broadcasts a bit lacking the arm speed and conviction toIt was highly effective this year and should continue to provide value playing off the effectiveness of his fastball. 

Renfrow has a starter's build with a thick lower half and a reasonably effortless delivery. He gets down the mound very, very well for his size, a testament to his athleticism. He's got the chance to develop into a starter at the next level if a tertiary offering ticks up. It's definitive feel for the hill.

In an era where so many players sell out for power and exit velocity, it's Brenner's polish and old-school mentality that stand out. Brenner's versatility plays big into his future value too.

Straight up, Brenner is one of the most decorated bat-to-ball artists in the country. He runs microscopic whiff rates, with pitch selection and plate skills that grade out among the best in the class. Brenner employs a short, compact swing showcasing strength in his hands and core. He makes hard, tight turns through the zone and elevates the baseball effortlessly. Brenner's hands are so good, when he's fooled, he's still capable of keeping the barrel back long enough to use the opposite field and flip singles down the line. His ability to keep the ball up the middle of the field is a major strength. His ability to cover every quadrant, as well as his ability to manipulate the barrel through the zone is exemplary. While the power tool isn't a major part of his game just yet (and some of that has to do with his approach), scouts believe he could ultimately tap into solid-average game power as a pro. There's 10-15 home run output in the cards here if Brenner leans into that part of his game.

An above average runner with plus arm strength, Brenner has been played all over the diamond. He's a talented catcher who stands the chance to stick behind the plate. He's flashed sub 2.00-second pop times and is an athlete behind the dish. His blocking skills still require some elbow grease and polish around the edges, but he looks plenty capable from a tools perspective of developing into the role. Brenner has played a good deal of shortstop in high school, but looks more fit to play third base at the next level. It's also not out of the question he receives some run in centerfield at the next level. Brenner could be utilized as a Swiss Army Knife as a professional; another feather in his cap from a value perspective.

There's plenty of intrigue around a player like this. He is clearly a talented hitter with a strong eye at the plate and solid fundamentals across the diamond. The athleticism is also ready for the rigors of professional baseball.

A year removed from Tommy John surgery, Garcia has seen his stuff trend back up in a big way this spring. The fastball is grabbing 96 at his peak, however in starts he's more 91-93. His heater has shape and late hop through the zone with real bat-missing characteristics. Garcia has a chance for a plus fastball at the next level, especially in a bullpen role where it will play up.

The changeup is a weapon. It's a mid-80s tumbler that Garcia has shown feel for. He kills spin and can shape and command it where he wants. There's also an over-the-top upper-70s curveball that's a strike-stealer. 

Garcia looks best served in a relief role at the next level, but he could tickle the upper-90s in due time.

Purify is an athletic infielder with gap-to-gap power, an all-fields approach and twitchy wrists in the box. He's got an adjustable bat plane that leads to a high number of line drives and singles. He's got solid bat speed, though he doesn't project to grow into better than fringe-average power. Purify's quiet demeanor in the box and hitterish disposition has scouts bullish he'll be able to hit at the next level. It's a relatively bigger leg kick and Purify can get jumpy against spin, but in general, he makes good decisions in the box. 

Purify's biggest strengths are in the field where he glides about the dirt and has a strong arm that can fire from any angle. Purify is also a very good runner who can be a weapon on the bases. It's plus foot speed and he's seemingly gained a half-tick in that department with strength gains on campus. As he adds weight and strength in his upper-half, his profile could drastically change. He'll be just 20.8 for the 2026 draft.

Ransom and middle-infielder battery mate Jet Berry represent two of the better infielders coming out of the state of Arizona in 2026. After impressing scouts with the hit tool throughout the summer in 2025 despite a lighter frame, Ransom tacked on 15 pounds of muscle over the winter and has begun impacting the baseball. Those offensive gains have really supplemented what what already an impressive glove.

Ransom projects anywhere on the diamond. He's an exceptional athlete that makes infield and outfield work look easy. On the dirt, he's one of the best in the class throwing from any angle and getting the ball out quick. Above average arm strength is up half-a-grade from where it was in 2025. Ransom has loose wrists and a natural softness on the dirt. He's got all the actions to play a plus infielder as a pro. Should he be forced to the outfield for any reasons, it's excellent technique and footwork, complimented by above average arm strength. Ransom has looseness and fluidity in everything that he does. It's awesome projection.

With the bat, Ransom is more hit over power. He gets the foot down early and can take the barrel wherever he wants. There's a natural flow and looseness in Ransom's hands and wrists at the dish, much like on the dirt. He looks like a natural hitter. Above average speed underway is an asset on the bases, however his swing does inhibit him to get out of the box quickly.

Ransom is a natural ballplayer. He can hit, he can run, he can throw, and he can do it just about anywhere on the diamond. He's growing into a bit more power and could be a home run threat as he gets stronger, though it's unlikely anything more than average raw power.

Marsten was formerly a Stanford commit but flipped to Wake Forest in the fall of 2023. Not that it made him any more signable in the 2024 draft. He missed most of his high school career with elbow and back injuries but got healthy as a senior to intrigue scouts. Marsten was working up into the mid-90s and tickled 100 mph in high school, however his stuff backed up a bit at Wake Forest as a freshman. 

Marsten logged just north of 10 innings in his first years on campus and never threw more than 50 pitches in an outing. Wake Forest and that staff allowed Marsten to work three full innings just once in his eight appearances on the season. The fastball grabbed 99, but more routinely. 93-97 with big tailing action. 

There's a slider and a curveball that project going forward as well, the former comfortably grading out above average with sweeping shape especially as he works a lather and gets into the game. The slider is firm, usually 83-85 with bullet shape. It can take him an inning or so to find bigger shape on the breaking ball. 

Marsten has one of the more put-together operations in the class and has a real chance to start and throw long outings at the next level. The projection and ceiling didn't flash as much as scouts were expecting in 2025 as a freshman, but there's runway ahead of him. He'll be a draft-eligible sophomore. It's a complicated draft profile, but arm talent that can be challenged by few.

After blowing the doors off of the Colonial Athletic Conference for two years with Stony Brook, Paulsen took his bat to the ACC and Chapel Hill. Paulsen is considered by some to be one of the more pure hitters in the Carolinas in 2026.

Paulsen is a talented left-handed hitter who makes his money pummeling anything and everything thrown inside of the strike zone. He possesses elite hand-eye coordination and get to pitches anywhere in the zone. He does a nice job using the whole field and can poke one out over the wall to his pull-side when he catches the ball out in front. Paulsen's swing has a significant amount of trunk tilt as he works to create loft and leverage with a steeper swing. It's a simple swing with very little wasted movement. A moderate stride and quiet hands make for a direct path to the baseball. Paulsen is going to hit for average going forward and should continue to grow into more raw power as he matures. For the time being, it's average bat speed with most of his over-the-fence production coming by way of efficient swing mechanics and an elite understanding of creating loft to the pull-side. If Paulsen can become just a tick more selective at the dish and focus on waiting for and swinging at pitches he can do the most damage on, he could transform into a terrifically impactful middle of the order stick for the foreseeable future.

Paulsen's value isn't limited to the bat, however. He is the reigning CAA Defensive Player of the Year. A decorated first baseball with oven mitt hands and a quick first step, Paulsen has a chance to be a plus defender at the pillow a a pro. He's shown a keen feel for picking short-hops at first base and smothers just about everything hit his way. His spacial awareness in foul territory stands out. 

Paulsen is a below average runner who is unlikely to create extra opportunities on the base paths. 

In some ways, Paulsen has a bit of Kyle Manzardo in him.

After redshirting in 2024, Govel took to a bigger role with the Trojans in 2025 logging 48.1 innings and punching 45 tickets. That success led to a full-time weekend role in 2026 where he saw his production begin to take off.

Govel is a thick, strong, well-built 6-foot right-handed that relies on bigger shapes and pitchability to get his outs. He's primarily a north-south pitcher in terms of shapes, however he tends to live at the bottom of the zone with his four-pitch arsenal. An up-tempo delivery with a fast over-the-top finish can be tough for hitters to track out of the hand. 

Govel has been up to 95 and will sit 91-93 with a heater that explodes out of the hand. Govel induces a ton of vertical lift on his fastball with exceptional value when he elevates the heater. His an assuming frame does look as though it can blow a fastball by hitters, until he routinely does. Govel's carry on the pitch will fall a bit with the professional ball, and he'll need to add a couple ticks to the velocity department to have the same effect and success in MLB, but he's still reasonably raw from an innings and development perspective, so that may come naturally. It's every bit that of an above average heater projection as is.

Govel offers a traditional curveball with big vertical break and horizontal break as well. It's in the upper-70s velocity band and relies on his fastball command to be effective. His feel for throwing the big bender for strikes stands out in a big was, as does his above average spin rates.

Govel's cutter is a weird one. It's 88-90 with considerable carry and enough horizontal break to look like a slider out of the hand. The ball just never really drops. It's kept hitters off the fastball, even though it hasn't naturally been a swing and miss pitch. 

He'll round out his arsneal with a changeup that can flash big shapes, however repeating his best versions of that pitch will come and go. At its best, it's tailing hard off the fastball and dying at the plate.

Govel will probably need to add some sort of gyro ball slider to bridge his fastball and curveball at the next level. He seems to be able to supinate well enough to get there. Still, for now, it's a solid four-pitch mix. He's that gyro ball and a bit of velocity away from being a potential top-two round talent. He is on the older side for the class and will turn 22 just a month after the Draft.

Willits comes from a distinguished baseball family; his father coaching at the University of Oklahoma after a career in the big leagues; his brother the first overall pick in the 2025 Draft. Willits is a slap-happy hitter who uses the whole field. He's revered for his polish offensively, rarely expanding the zone and taking his walks from the time he was a freshman on campus. He makes a ton of contact both in the zone and out of the zone and works long at-bats. He's one of the more proficient hitters in college baseball in handling spin and shouldn't ever be a player who strikes out much in his career. Willits doesn't project to slug much as he's posting below-average exit velocity figures and hits the ball on the ground a little too often. 

The frame is pretty maxed out at this point and Willits is already rovering between the infield positions. He lacks the typical range of a big league shortstop, however the tools play nicely at second and third base. He projects into a utility role at the next level and should hit at the bottom of a lineup as an integral cog in a "conga line" approach to roster building. Willits is an above average runner who generates a bit more value with a quick first step. He'll be a base-stealer at the next level, however he's not inherently a speed demon.

Beck has enjoyed an impressive two year run with Indiana State. He's also been a standout performer in the West Coast Baseball League for Saskatoon the last two summers. Built like a barrel of gunpowder, Beck plays an explosive, exciting brand of baseball on both sides of the ball.

Coiled up tight with fast hands, Beck rotates hard in the box in an effort to get to all of his pull-side power. It's above-average raw juice with exit velocities that'll exceed 111 mph at their peak. Beck can consistently get to the barrel too. His average exit velocity and hard-hit rates are far more befitting of a player larger than he.

Beck can hit tool. He's an aggressive swing who expands the zone a good bit, but his bat-to-ball skills drive steady whiff rates both inside and outside of the strike zone. In fact, his whiff rates inside the zone suggest a potential plus hit tool once fully seasoned. Beck doesn't have an obvious holes in his swing, velocity at the top of the zone only occassionally giving him a hard time. 

The athletic tools stick out too. Beck is an above average runner with a quick first step out of the box. He plays with his hair on fire in centerfield and isn't afraid to put his body in harms way to make a catch. Beck has a legitimate chance to play some centerfield as a pro.

There's something of a Daulton Varsho profile here.

Bryant had an outstanding summer as a rising junior and saw his stuff take a big jump with plenty of scouts in attendance. Bryant is up to 95 mph with a fastball that bores into the right-handed batters box. It's a super-quick arm that should live in the mid-90s band by the time he's draft-eligible. 

Bryant's slider is his best pitch; a low-80s sweeper that he'll front-door and back-door depending on the opposition and situation. He's also worked to fold in a mid-80s splitter that's shown a jump over the past twelve months. It's some of the best feel for landing an offspeed pitch you can find in the Southeast for this class. 

While Bryant doesn't yet create much extension down the mound, he's a very good athlete with a lean frame and flexibility that should help develop that piece of his game as he matures. There are starting pitcher components here is it all comes together and further development persists.

Johnson was ultra-effective coming out of the bullpen for the Chanticleers as a sophomore in 2025, but he's been stretched out for more expanded roles in 2026 with eyes on starting as a pro going forward.

Johnson has some natural deception in a delivery that features an exceptionally high leg lift and solid tempo working down the mound. He tends to land slightly closed and throws across his body, creating a difficult pick-up point for the opposing hitter. Johnson tends to throw off his back-side deep into his delivery and lacks the extension you'd expect from a player with his large frame. He relies on arm speed, scap load and hip torque to generate velocity. There's some low-hanging fruit in his operation to get him throwing a bit harder, mostly notably getting a bit more separation in his shoulders and throwing out over his front side. Those changes could cost him some of the deception he presently has, but it also could help prolong his career, improve his durabilty, and keep him in a starting rotation at the next level.

Johnson's fastball has real life. Despite only touching 94 thus far, he's generating considerable carry on the pitch. Paired with his deception, it's created big whiff and chase rates. Johnson also naturally spins the baseball quite well, so tinking with his mechanics shouldn't cost him his whole bag of tricks. 

Johnson's slider has the chance to be a very good one. He's consistently 82-84 with the breaker, generating vertical break bordering on elite. Landing that pitch in competitive spots, let along for strikes, has been a challenge for Johnson. He's a bit more comfortable throwing an upper-70s curveball, however that pitch doesn't fall quite as impressive on the "stuff" spectrum. Still very good shapes, but not the outlier traits of the slider.

Johnson has not yet shown a formidable changeup.

This is a funky lefty with a great frame, a big fastball, and some things to develop in terms fo the breaking ball. At worst, it looks like a leveragable reliever going forward; a guy who can work multiple innings and perhaps avoid the dreaded lefty-specialist label.

Peterson was draft-eligible as a second-year sophomore in 2025, but didn't hear his name called, largely due to arm strength that was still blossoming. He's up a few ticks in 2026 and has developed better secondaries, too.

Peterson is an excellent athlete on the mound. He collects with a stacked back-side and high-leg kick, striding deep down the mound and generating well-above average extension. His strike rate is up in 2026, and he's repeating his release point much, much better.

Peterson will run it up to 96 with carry and tail, launched out of a 65" slot -- slightly lower than the MLB average. He spins the ball exceptionally well with rpm north of 2500 on the fastball. He'll settle in 92-94 in the middle innings. Despite favorable metrics, his fastball hasn't been a bat-misser, instead a means to an end. It sets up a much improved breaking ball combination.

The curveball is Peterson's best secondary. It's firm, 80-83 with huge lateral action and solid depth. He'll spin that pitch north of 3000 rpm consistently, and has registered a few north of 3200. It generates strong whiff and chase rates, especially when he's tunneling it off his fastball velocity. Most importantly, Peterson is staying in the same arm slot this year as the fastball, making it far more difficult for hitters to identify out of the hand. There's a firm mid-80s slider here, too, however its shapes and execution are more of a work in progress. 

Peterson also has a mid-90s sinker that generates ground balls and gives hitters a different look. To date, he has not shown much of a changeup.

The lack of a third pitch, specifically an offspeed weapon, is a deterrant to Peterson's overall draft profile. Everything is moving in the right direction here and he could be one of the quicker 22 year olds off the board in July.

Barker wasn't often present on the showcase and tournament circuit throughout the 2025 summer circuit, but made his presence known on the scouting trail after the winter going into his senior year. He added a bit of weight and strength, adding impact and complimenting an already impressive athletic profile. 

Barker is sitll growing and tinkering with his swing. He sets his hands low and works to lag the barrel to create bat speed through the zone. It's a pushy swing at times with hands that can get outside of his frame. That said, at times he'll cheat and rotate hard, creating impact to the pull-side. As Barker adds more muscle and strength in his upper hands, the swing should become more connected on a more routine basis and his lashed doubles into the gap will begin jumping the fence. Barker has shown some swing-and-miss in his game at certain stops, but tracks the ball relatively well and stays inside of the zone. With 15 more pounds and continued maturation, he has the chance to grow into a bat that hits near the top of the order.

Barker is an excellent athlete. He's a plus runner who tests extremely well on force plate. It's already awesome tools with more on the way as player development sinks its teeth into his game. Barker is a primary shortstop with some lateral range. He may end up at second or third base when considering the present actions. Still, the athlete can play anywhere.

Teams are going to covet Barker's lean frame, excellent athletic testing and chances to stick on the dirt. He's got power upside in the bat and could transform himself into a big time performer as he matures. He'll be quite old for this class, already 19.5 on draft day.

Brody, the son of former Marlins manager Skip Schumaker, is much the same player his dad was during his playing career. After an encouraging summer in 2025, Schumaker went to work in the weight room and tacked on ten pounds of muscle, elevating his profile to scouts in Southern California. 

It's super polished bat-to-ball skills with a slap-happy approach and a grand willingness to keep the game in motion. There's some sneaky pop to the pull-side when he catches the ball out front. 

Schumaker is an active base runner and will take the extra base and get the green light on first base. It's 70-grade run times and that should hold over time with his hair-on-fire twitchy athletic actions. 

A shortstop now, Schumaker looks more the part of a future second baseman where his average arm strength and choppier gait will fit seamlessly into the puzzle that is a professional infield.

Lascelles became an interesting pop-up name coming out of Canada during the summer of 2025 after strength gains and physical maturity helped shoot his athleticism into another tier. A pure hitter, the added twitch has scouts intrigued by what the final form on Lascelles could be as a pro.

Lascelles has always been able to hit. He's a pure bat-to-ball artist who feasts on anything left in the zone. He's almost impossible to strike out as his hand-eye coordination on pitches outside the zone allows for long at-bats and pesky tit-for-tats with the opposing pitcher. He's a pest. Lascelles is a slasher and makes late reactions in the box. There's not much bat speed to speak of here, and he doesn't project to slug for much impact at the next level. Still, it's a top-of-the-lineup or bottom-of-the-lineup stick that could serve its purpose to keep the conga line moving. 

A shortstop now, Lascelles may eventually be pushed to second base if the arm strength doesn't improve. He's got good feet and the lateral mobility is more than strong enough to play on the middle of the diamond, but fringy arm strength may preclude him from playing the '6'. 

Lascelles is also a plus runner who will be valuable on the bases. 

Lascelles will turn 18 just a few months before the draft and has age on his side. He'll need to answer questions about offensive impact and/or the ability to play the shortstop position as a pro. There's day one traits if one of those two areas can take a jump before July. If not, he'll likely be a difficult sign away from Yale.

Gallaher is an athletic, explosive middle infielder with a flair for the big moment and a big time performer against staunch competition. Gallaher has bat speed and punch to all-fields with more juice to the pull-side considering his frame, though he primarily works the gaps at this stage. 

He's an above average runner with elite-level instincts on the basepaths. He's got an above average arm, though he's probably best suited for second base where his lateral mobility won't be tested like it would at shortstop.

Boshell has the look of a bruising middle-of-the-order bat with considerable bat speed from the left side of the plate. A big, broad, Amazon-box chest with wide shoulders and a physical frame, Boshell is going to be a masher. It's a swing plane built to do damage, and he's already proving plenty capable of just that.

Boshell's feel for getting to the pull side is exceptional. He ambushes pitches out in front of the plate, gets extended and violenty rotates his hips. Boshell is a fly ball hitter whose natural gifts with the bat allow for impact projection going forward. While he doesn't have a long track record of facing more premium pitching, his showcase and tournament resume consists of low chase rates, low whiff rates, and exceptional slug. Boshell will be scrutinized under a microscope as the draft approaches as scouts try and figure out if his offensive approach will work against bigger velocity and more consistent spin. 

From this chair, Boshell has a few things to clean up, however nothing glaring. He sets up with a rhythmic waggle, setting a firm base feeling for his back hip. He's got noisy hands in his pre-load, out away from his frame. He's often late to get his hands behind his frame into a firing position when the foot gets down, causing the swing to get long. The hands are forced to travel a long way, steering the barrel. Boshell also tends to throw his front hip before foot plant, eliminating the outer-third from impact potential. As Boshell goes through more player development and finds more consistency staying sync'd up, the offensive production could continue to climb. 

Boshell is an average runner with solid arm strength. His feel for routes in the outfield is a work in progress, but the athletic tools give him the chance to play out there as a professional working up the ladder. He's most comfortable at first base. He will be 19 years old for the Draft.

McNeillie's bread and butter is a plus changeup with 10 mph of separation off the fastball and legit conviction. The arm is loose and fluid, touching 99 but resting more 93-94. McNeillie can work the ball to both sides of the plate and isn't afraid to show the changeup to both righties and lefties. He prefers to work away from hitters with his entire arsenal. 

He's worked to develop a tertiary breaking ball to live off his two weapons. His slider has taken monumental strides since high school and is now a mid-80s bender that can flash with strong spin rates, but lacks command and consistent shape. 

It's enormous projection with at least 15 pounds on the horizon.

After an absolute dynamo freshman campaign at Stetson, Jones took his talent to the transfer portal and changed zip codes to Gainesville. Unfortunately for Jones and the Gators he missed almost the entire 2025 season dealing with a minor hamstring injury followed shortly thereafter by a shoulder injury he suffered diving for a baseball.

When healthy, Jones is a prototype spark-plug type with plus speed and an aggressive, borderline wild gait. Jones is constantly looking to take the extra base and routinely stretches should-be singles into doubles and doubles into triples. While he doesn't hit for much power at this stage in his career, his 6-foot-3-inch frame oozes projection. There's 20 pounds ahead of Jones where the raw power and bat speed should tick up in a meaningful way. Jones already possesses elite bat-to-ball skills with in-zone metrics and production against velocity that dwarfs most of his peers. Despite the length and long levers, Jones is still quick and efficient through the zone to the baseball. His profile is likely to transform with more muscle. 

Most scouts see a future in centerfield so long as he doesn't get too big. Jones takes solid routes to the ball and has a tendency to put his body on the line to make the play in the gap. He plays with his hair on fire and has one of the brighter futures from a projection perspective in college baseball.

When the University of Cal Berkeley recruited Matthew Thomas to come play ball for the Bears, he was a child. His freshman fall on campus he was 17 years old. Thomas played his entire freshman spring barely 18 years old. He's always been much younger than his peers. It's taken him time to mature both physically and intellectually on the baseball field. After two seasons at Cal in which he slashed .136/.167/.301 across 44 games, it was time for a change of scenery. Thomas headed to Northridge for his draft-eligible junior year, still barely 20 years old. 

Thomas' raw power has long been his carrying tool. His peak exit velocities and sheer bat speed are impressive. He's gone north of 113 mph at times, and the smattering of his top-end shots are close behind. Better still, Thomas has a natural feel for getting the baseball in the air. He's an efficient hitter, if not flawed. Thomas has long had swing and miss in his game, exacerbated by an aggressive approach. He isn't particularly snake-bitten by any specific pitch type, there's just been holes in his swing inside of the zone. Thomas lags his hands deep behind his frame in his load, creating big tension and torque. While that has created exceptional bat speed, it's also resulted in a bat path that can be uncontrollable and inconsistent at times. That's all seemed to improve in 2026 as Thomas is not only swinging at the right pitches more often, he's making far more contact as well. It may still only be a fringy hit tool, but if he can carve out a role at the next level where he's hitting .235 with plus power, he'll become a big leaguer.

Thomas is an above average runner underway and has shown capable of playing all three outfield positions. He takes good routes to the ball, and shows a general calmness in his play. Average arm strength fits anywhere on the diamond.

Thomas is still young for the class and won't turn 21 until a few months after the draft. He could return to CS-N and play out his senior year and try and bulk up the baseball card for scouts. Still, his name could surface inside of the top ten rounds if he continues his hot play as July approaches. He's clearly a different player this year than in years past.

Costello has long been a decorated hitter going back to his prep days at Cathedral Prep in Pennsylvania. The kid has always been able to impact the baseball and work impressive at-bats. That hasn't slowed at all since arriving to Winston-Salem. Costello got plenty of run as a true freshman in 2025 and showed swing decisions and bat-to-ball skills well beyond his years. He rarely ever expands the strike zone and does a nice job waiting for pitches he can impact in the fat part of the strike zone. Costello also flashes plus bat speed and innately possesses the ability to take the barrel to the ball. These traits have helped Costello routinely rank among the nation's best from an average exit velocity standpoint. Complimenting the swing decisions, bat speed and barrel awareness is a keen ability to meet the baseball out in front of the zone, generating fly balls and line drives to the pull-side at an elite rate. All of this evidence points toward one of the most polished hitters in the country. He's not entirely invincible however. Velocity up and away from his frame can give him trouble every now and again. Pitchers often try to go up there, miss, and pay the price. 

Where Costello's draft profile gets a bit muddy is on the defensive end. He's a below average runner with average arm strength befitting of a player who needs to play in left field. Costello will probably hold a bit more value to teams that can hide in in a stadium with dimensions less taxing to his limitations. Organizations like Houston, Philadelphia and perhaps the Yankees may find more value in the overall skillset. 

Ultimately, the bat is going to carry the water on this one. It's a good stick with an advanced set of traits suggesting he'll hit and hit quickly as a professional. Costello is a draft-eligible sophomore and will barely be 21 years old for the Draft.

The book on Christine is what it could become, not what it presently is. A projection southpaw with elite athleticism, Christine has the look of a long-term starting pitcher prospect. He generates elite extension and throws plenty of strikes for a player of his age.

Christine is only touching 90 mph at this stage, but he's comfortably 30 pounds shy of where he'll eventually sit as a professional. The fastball has real juice behind it with carry and some cutting action through the zone. It's got a chance to be a very good heater as he matures. 

Christine pairs a mid-70s curveball, as well as an impressive upper-70s changeup that he executes well to right-handed hitters. 

Christine will need to get more physical and add velocity before the draft if he's to capitalize on what some believe is 7-figure upside in the draft. All the components to dream on here are present.

Rangel has some of the most explosive stuff in the 2026 class, and there's a whole lot more on the way. The fastball is already touching 97 with enormous life and carry through the zone. Rangel boasts well-above average spin rates on all of his pitches, but the fastball really seems to benefit most from the rpms, skimming over barrels with conviction. 

The breaking ball is a low-80s slurve with huge depth and sweeping action. It's registered north of 3200 rpm at times, more commonly in the upper 2000s range; unhittable for right-handed batters with late life and strong tunneling attributes. There's a less-used upper-80s changeup too, a pitch he kills spin on well, flashing plus when he elects to pull it out of the bag. 

Rangel will spray the ball a bit at times and currently owns fringy control and command of his arsenal. He's got a chance to own three plus pitches with a high-leverage relief role as a bare minimum floor. This is a dynamic athlete with a real feel for the mound and one of the highest ceilings in the 2026 class. Rangel will turn 19 years old a couple months prior to the 2026 draft.
