He will be eligible once again in 2028 should he go unselected.

Relatively under-scouted during the summer of 2025, Cutshall has grown stronger and more athletic over the winter months, now pushing 190 pounds in a 6-foot-1 inch frame.

Cutshall still isn't a physically mature player. He's got growing ahead. But he's developed much more bat speed of late and his tools on the dirt seem to be blossoming as well. He's got a chance to hit with some pop-up performances against better arms over the course of the spring. He sets up with an open stance and high set hands. He gets the foot down early and turns hard on the baseball with burgeoning above average bat speed. The bat is still swinging Cutshall at times, but 15 more pounds of muscle and weight should get him controlling the barrel even better than he is today.

Cutshall is an average defender on most days, but can look a half-grade better than that at times. He's got above average arm strength that should get to plus as he adds the aformentioned muscle and mass. There's a decent chance Cutshall ends up at third base, but his offensivel profile fits the hot corner just fine. He's an above average runner with an athletic gait that should hold with weight.

Cutshall has believers in the scouting industry and could hear his name called as early as the third round, but may be a more comfortable fit for teams in the fourth or fifth round as an over-pay. He'll be reasonably young for the class, turning 18 just two months before the draft.

Martin has a wide setup at the plate with explosive hands and a line drive approach. He's got above average bat speed and certainly has the ability to put one in the seats. Martin has peaked north of 111 mph in terms of exit velocities and has the tools to hit 20 homers per year at the next level. He has a tendency to get out on his front side a bit early, and it can lead to streakiness in terms of contact quality. 

The biggest critique on Martin at this stage is his approach to hitting. He's among the most passive hitters in the country with swing rates outlandishly low. He never expands the zone and is one of the more decorated pitch-selection artists in the 2026 class, but analysts and scouts agree that's more a product of his passivity than it is pitch recognition skills on most nights. He'll need to ambush pitches more often as a pro, or he risks falling into pitchers' counts a ton. 

Few bats in the country can match Martin's effectivness against the fastball. He absolutely pummels velocity and does damage when he gets ahead in counts. The hit tool still has some unanswered questions, however few doubt it's a big-league quality stick.

Martin has a long, lean frame and is growing into his "adult strength". Martin has a strong arm and has the look of a Major League third baseman on the dirt. He has the range, actions, and the first step to get a shot at shortstop as well. 

It's a smattering of exciting tools with a bat that is blossoming as his draft approaches. He's a scout favorite in Southern California.

Sharman has some components to his operation that will undoubtedly appeal to pro organizations. He's an exceptional mover on the mound with above-average extension through release with good direction and balance, finishing over his front side. He's a strike-thrower with the ability to pitch backwards and work both sides of the plate. He's worked hard on his frame, carving out lean muscle and more flexibility over the past couple seasons. The broad shoulders and long levers stand out. The work ethic and dedication to his craft are apparent. 

Sharman launches his fastball a full five inches lower than the Major League average. He lacks dynamic shape on the fastball, however when commanded at the top of the zone, a flat approach does provide value in terms of generating whiffs. Sharman has been up to 97 in the past, but more commonly sits in the 92-93 bucket, showing durability and the stamina to go deep into ballgames. Sharman has been up into the mid-90s going back to his sophomore year, plateauing in some ways as he's made his way through high school. 

At his best, Sharman flashes a plus changeup with extremely heavy fading shape and parachuting depth off the sinker tunnel. His changeup is of the hig-spin variety, pronating hard around the baseball to create shapes. Hitters swing right over it when executed below the zone. He's thrown the cambio to lefties and righties alike; pitchability well-beyond his age. 

Sharman's primary breaking ball is a low-80s sweeper that features above average lateral shape and solid depth. Like his entire arsenal, his spin rates are at or slightly above average. There's more than enough clay here to mold an above average breaking ball. 

Sharman has polish, pitchability and a strike-throwing mentality that can take him an awfully long ways. He's proven capable of moving the baseball east, west, north and south. The only question on the profile is just how much value he'll be able to get out of his fastball at the next level. If a team believes the can tinker with his fastball shapes to get to 'plus' production, he's likely a top-two round arm. He can also swing the bat a little bit. He'll turn 19 two months after the draft.

A table-setter in the most fitting way, Berry is a chaos merchant who puts pressure on the opposition with exceptional bat-to-ball skills and one of the highest IQs in the class. 

Berry's hit tool stands out. He puts the ball in play at a high clip and uses the whole field. He's an awfully aggressive hitter who tends to expand the zone -- walks not a big part of his game. To Berry's credit, he works hard to get to his pull-side, however it's fringy raw power projection at best. His greatest asset in his ability to get on base. Once on, Berry likes to run. He's a pest. He's a plus runner with the knack for getting under the pitcher's and catcher's skin. Berry seeks the extra bag and is capable of scoring from first on a ball hit meekly to the wall. 

Berry will need to figure out where he's most valuable on defense. He's played a good deal of left field and second base and is capable of spelling the shortstop in a pinch. Fringe-average to potentially average arm strength.

Andersen is a top shelf talent on the mound with loose athleticism and easy rhythm. Andersen makes pitching look very easy. He works to bully hitters with the fastball. 

He's already up to 98 with fuzz and arm-side life. It's been an effective fastball on the tournament circuit, though it isn't necessarily a bat-missing offering at this stage. 

The changeup is probably his second-best weapon with late tumble and some fading action off the fastball tunnel. He really sells it too. There's a loopier downer breaking ball with slurvy shape here as well. It's been effective when landed buried deep glove-side. In total, it's three efficient pitches with average-or-better projection. 

Tack on the fact this is a clean operation and a good frame and Andersen's day one upside is pretty clear. He'll need to generate a bit more extension down the bump to reach what some believe is mid-rotation upside at the next level. If that isn't achievable, a more productive breaking ball will likely be key. Andersen will be 18.5 years old on draft day.

Hansen has been a starter for UC Irvine since stepping foot on campus on day one. He's a strike-thrower and a competitor that brings a menu of pitches to the bump, aquipped to get left-handed and right-handed hitters out. It's not overpowering stuff, but there's still a bit more projection in his frame to come. 

Hansen is a short-extender to the plate, instead electing to launch from a high slot creating steepness. His fastball tends to hop and jump out of the hand with above average carry through the zone, generally in the low-90s. Hansen has been up to 94 at his peaks. It's a solid average fastball, carried by its shape.

When Hansen is landing his fastball, his slider plays up in a huge way. It's an absolute hammer with gyroscopic spin and heavy, heavy diving action. Hansen's slider acts more like a prototypical death ball than it does a traditional slider. At times it's classified as a curveball. It's thrown in the low-80s and falls to the earth like an anchor. It's a pitch that's induced a ton of swings outside of the zone, but hasn't generated whiffs like its shape would suggest. If he can add a bit more velocity to the pitch, it could make a jump in effectiveness. 

Hansen is adept at killing spin on an average changeup that possess strong fading action, again generating swings outside of the zone. 

Presently, Hansen's profile is held back by an inability to create much glove-side movements to his arsenal. Adding a cutter or something that can get moving the other way would elevate his effectiveness, especially against right-handed hitters.

Roberson is as tooled up as they come in the 2026 class with a sweet left-handed swing built to do damage to the baseball. He's been a consistent performer on the tournament circuit for a couple years now boasting a strong hit tool and budding power that's begun to show up in games in the form of rockets into the gaps and off the wall. Roberson has a swing that should lend well toward hitting the ball over the fence in due time, a steep attack angle with pull-side intent in BP. He'll need to prove that swing can survive the test of higher velocity pitching up in the zone as he and the pitchers he faces get stronger, but to this point he's dominated the opposition. 

Roberson is already a plus runner and has posted run times that suggest he's getting faster. It's also plus arm strength in the outfield with a chance to be a real weapon out there. Roberson has played centerfield and right field in tournaments, and scouts seem to prefer him in a corner at this point. That said, the foot speed will certainly have teams giving him every opportunity to stay in the middle of the field at the next level if he doesn't outgrow his quickness. 

The true test of time here will be the hit tool, but it's a smattering of premium athletic tools and a swing that could eventually tap into average game power. An exciting player to watch. Roberson will be just 18.4 years old on draft day.

Harrington is one of the more premium athletes in the 2026 class buoyed by double-plus speed and plus arm strength; both of which really show up on the field. It's not just frontline speed either; Harrington has an electric first step both on the dirt, as well as coming out of the batter's box. 

At the plate he shows off fast hands with a quick stroke and a line drive mentality into both gaps. It's a wide base with a rhythmic cadence and long athleticism through the zone. There's something of a Nolan Arenado feel to his mannerisms and operation in the box. It's average power projection, though a ton of Harrington's future value is already rooted in his speed and defensive prowess. Harrington can get into some trouble in games when he gets pull-happy, but for the most part he's shown a polished, mature approach toward hitting. The whole package here is very exciting and refined with projectable twitch and upside in the athlete. Harrington is committed to Stanford and will be 19.2 years old on draft day.

One of the loudest bats in the 2026 class, Harwood has physical tools that few can replicate. The bat is for real, but it'll take some adjustments to unlock what could be prolific game power. The bat-to-ball skills are strong, as are Harwood's pitch selection skills. It's plus raw power projection, maybe more, but Harwood has struggled to showcase it at all in games. He pounds the ball into the ground and struggles to get to his pull-side. Despite his significant bat speed and physical strength, it's currently a hit-over-power profile. Harwood has put on serious muscle in the last couple years and has lost some of the twitch and athleticism that made him especially dynamic in his early high school years, but he's still a solid average runner that can handle a corner.

Harwood has pretty good feel for left field. He's got a shot at being a fringy defender in the outfield, though there's certainly first base risk too. If Harwood can keep his athleticism and stay in the outfield as the 2026 draft approaches, he's got Top 100 pick traits with the bat. If the body and frame back up to a full-time first base profile, he'll have to really bang in the months leading up to the draft. Harwood will turn 19 just a week after the draft, so models will expect a loud, polished, present bat. 

Ultimately, Harwood may be one swing adjustment away from making himself considerably more money.

A well-traveled pure athlete, Longo spent time at Spokane Community College and Utah Valley University before landing in Tempe for his fourth year of college baseball. He's a versatile player with burgeonging physical and athletic tools that should lend well toward him carving out a role at the next level.

A long-time third baseman, Longo made the swing to centerfield for the Sun Devils in 2026 to take better advantage of his speed. He's a plus runner and closes space in the gaps with impressive pace. Longo plays fearlessly. His arm strength is average, so holding runners won't be a strength, but also far from a liability. Longo has taken to centerfield well, however his first step on balls hit right at him can still be hit or miss. In totality, Longo looks as though he could eventually grow into at least an above average defender out there.

Longo is the rare patient hitter that shows a willingness to expand the zone. He's eager to get the bat head moving on elevated velocity, and has been known to try to pull his hands in on fastballs off the inner third. He's cut those tendencies down a smidge in 2026 playing on a bigger stage. Longo prefers the ball up. It's his natural bat path and the part of the zone he does the most damage. He can, at times, struggle to handle soft stuff at the bottom of the zone. Longo is flashing solid average power in 2026 and far more control of the barrel. He's consistently hitting the baseball very hard and posting impressive batted-ball efficiency rates with respect to pulling the ball and getting it into the air. Considering his 6-foot-3-inch frame and still developing strength, it's not out of realm of possibility he grows into above average game power to supplement his above average defense and plus speed, however the latter could fall a half-grade with much more strength. 

Longo is a good hitter when he's swinging at pitches in the zone. He's got bat speed and the right approach to hitting. So long as he's not expanding the zone, he's got a chance to become a solid average hit tool player. That will be more than valuable enough given his value elsewhere on the field. Longo will be 22 years old in July.

Veras certainly looks the part off the bus. A big, tall, athletic 6-foot-6-inch right-handed hitting outfielder, Veras is more than just physical upside. There's legitimate tools on the player. 

Unsurprisingly, Veras' raw power projection is his greatest trait. He'll routinely flash exit velocities north of 105 mph in games and has shown some feel for turning and burning to his pull-side. Veras employs a quiet, balanced, wide base with very little wasted movement into the zone. He's got twitchy hips and rotates hard, delivering a fast, heavy barrel. There's some whip in the swing and serious intent, too. Veras has dealt with a good amount of swing-and-miss in his high school career, however it's improving as he adds strength and his approach matures. 

Athletically, Veras will occassionally flash a plus run time but is more commonly above-average down the line and in the outfield. He's impressively light on his feet for a player of his size and gets a fleet first step out of the box. It's also plus arm strength that plays in a big way in right field. 

Veras is a prototype right field prospect with the speed and athleticism to perhaps play centerfield early in his minor league career. If the hit tool ticks up as July approaches there's nothing stopping him from being selected on day one. It's huge tools, a tremendous frame and suprisingly athletic tools.

Marohn isn't an overpowering southpaw with a fastball that generally just lives in the low-90s, but it's his supplementary weapons that draw rave reviews from scouts. 

A low-80s slider with big depth has been tough on lefty bats, and a mid-80s changeup does throw on the brakes at the plate and miss bats under the zone despite lacking prototypical separation off the fastball. Marohn has solid tempo and a feel for pounding the strikezone. It's a considerable floor with present polish.

After a year at Mount St. Mary's, Sheerin transferred to LSU for his sophomore year, however he missed all of 2025 with a torn ACL. 

A mountain of a man, Sheerin already towers over the competition with big, broad shoulders, a workhorse frame, barrel-chested with very real stuff. He's immediately taken to an extended role for the team in 2026, up to 99 with carry through the zone and late life. There's a ton of deception thanks to a drop-and-drive, crossfire delivery. It's plus traits and performance. 

Below average command and strikes limits his leveragability. He's flirted with a two-seam fastball as well, though it's dead-zone shape and performance thus far suggests it may ultimately get scrapped. Sheerin holds 93-95 into his second inning of work, though he's yet to get stretched out in a starting role so durability and velocity control may be tested as he matures into expanded responsibilities in college ball. 

Sheerin's slider is the true gem, a mid-80s gyro bullet with big depth and a touch of lateral tilt. It's already a plus pitch, and performing as such. There's a nascent curveball, as well as a changeup, though they're both currently under construction. Sheerin presently has below average control and walks have been a bugaboo, but the stuff, age, body and peripherals are all well-liked. He'll have to iron out the delivery into a more efficient mold by the time he's draft-eligible if he hopes to suggest a starter's future, but chances are this is a late-inning leverage bullpen profile. It's a good arm with upside.

Following a solid year at Wichita State, LaPour transferred to TCU for the 2025 and 2026 seasons. He's been nothing if not reliable for the Horned Frogs. While not a big-time punchout artist for much of his career, he's taken steps in 2026 to get more value from hsi fastball, elevating his arsenal as a whole. LaPour also does a very nice job controlling the game and working long innings.  

LaPour is a big, tall, physical righty with broad, rounded shoulders, a barrel chest and thick lower half. It's a durable frame that is a shoe-in to start as a professional. LaPour has been up to 100 and rests 94-97. Despite his velocity, LaPour has struggled at times to miss bats with the fastball, however he does limit hard contact. He's shown progress on that front in 2026 thanks to a bit more flexibility, athleticism and extension in his lower half. It's helped the heater sneak up on hitters. 

He'll show a mid-to-upper 80s slider and an upper-80s changeup, both of which project at least above average at the next level.

The question on LaPour is just how much fastball value can he generate with the pro ball. He's added some vert to the heater in 2026 and now could get to moderate carry with the big league ball at the next level. The velocity is big, but the ability to miss bats with the arm strength has been streaky. He's a terrific athlete that grades out well from an extension and force plate testing perspective, so perhaps there's some small changes that can be made to make his arsenal more effective. At worst, he's a back-end starting pitcher prospect. Some may view his upside a tick better than that. 

An elbow injury dampened LaPour's 2026 early on.

Armed with a tantalizing fastball/slider combo, Taylor jumped into the Bearcats rotation immediately as a freshman in 2024 providing value and stuff to the staff. He's been up to 96 with a reasonably generic fastball in terms of pure shape. He'll generally settle in closer to 92-93. There's upside in the pitch as Taylor demonstrates well-above average extension down the mound and the repeatability scouts look for in a delivery. It isn't a pitch that's missed bats to this point, something he'll need to tinker with as the draft approaches to provide helium to his profile. 

Conversely, Taylor's slider can be plus. It's a mid-80s bullet spinner with considerable vertical plane. That pitch has touched 89 mph and it plays well off his fastball. Taylor has the chance to feature one of the better breaking balls in the class among legitimate starting pitcher prospects when considering velocity, shape and execution. 

He's worked hard to incorporate a changeup into his arsenal, and it's come a long way. It's dives and fades off the fastball line with solid fading action, however he alters his arm slot and release point to get to his shapes. 

Taylor is an intriguing arm with the look of a starting pitcher at the next level. He lacks much supination value and his fastball doesn't possess unique traits, but he's going to fill up the zone and has a way to get both left-handed and right-handed hitters out. He profiles as a back-end starter if he cannot develop a plus offering or more fastball value.

Ritchie is a physical left-handed hitter with a budding raw power and a future in the outfielder thanks to surprising athleticism for his size and build. Oklahoma State has given him some run at third base as well where his arm strength could also profile. 

The bat carries the profile. Ritchie's hit tool has continued to blossom in Stillwater, however it will likely always come with an aggressive approach and swing-and-miss. His athleticism in the batters box stands out. It's a manueverable barrel and a lower-half that allows him to get to pitches in all four quadrants. Ritchie flashes above average raw power with bat speed that's tracked up from the left side. He's a barrel magnet, albeit with plenty of miss in his game. 

Solid average foot speed and instincts in a corner outfield role add value.

In the same way Chase Meidroth's and Justin Reimer's bat-to-ball skills helped get them selected in the fourth round by the Boston Red Sox in consecutive years, players like McDaniel should have suitors at some point in the meat of day two. While he doesn't have the shortstop chops of his two aforementioned predecessors, he may be just as good a hitter. 

McDaniel is an elite bat-to-ball artist with a unique setup at the dish. It's a wide, squatted, open orientation to the pitcher with especially low hands. McDaniel drifts back in his load and anchors into his lower-half, creating some leverage. His hands are active and unorthodox for a hitter of his pedigree. He pushes his hands up behind his back shoulder as the pitch is being delivered. Stranger still, McDaniel tips the barrel toward the pitcher in his loading phases. His hands continue to drift backward and upward even after his abbreviated stride forward has finished and his front foot is down. McDaniel clears his hips and shoulders simultaneously, dragging the barrel wherever he desires. Ultimately, he almost never misses. 

McDaniel consistently run nearly invisible whiff rates both inside of the zone and outside of it. He's a slasher, using the whole field to his advantage, however that has come alongside a high ground ball rate. McDaniel doesn't present much raw power, his max exit velocity barely exceeding 106 mph. However, the max exit velocity from both Meidroth and Reimer sat in that range as well. That said, those players did have a bit better feel for the barrel and hitting line drives. McDaniel is going to put the game in motion, and he's going to draw his walks thanks to his selective nature in the box. Just how much impact he creates is the question.

McDaniel is an above average runner who gets out of the box with some pace. He'll steal some bases, but it won't be an enormous part of his game. He shines on the defensive end with fantastic range to his left and right. He's got fast hands, a quick transfer and well-above average arm strength for a second baseman. His arm plays comfortably at third base when called upon. McDaniel has the chops to be considered one of the better defensive second basemen in baseball if he can earn the at-bats to claim such a title.

Lacking reps at shortstop will be a limiting factor in McDaniel's draft profile, as will his raw power. He's a very good baseball player with a path toward helping a ballclub win games at the next level, even if that's at the bottom of a lineup. There's something of a Luis Rengifo to McDaniel's aesthetic.

All Doty seems to do at every stop is hit. The Mississippi product has a flatter bat path with real strength in his hands and at impact. Doty employs a deep hand set with very little extra movement. He's quick to the ball with no wasted hitches. He pummels velocity, though there's been some streakiness against spin. Doty will gladly work to the opposite field, though all of his power is to the pull-side right now. It's a strong, athletic frame that figures to add a bit more raw power in the coming years. 

Doty is already a physical kid and an above average average runner. There's tools on the dirt, though he's likely to end up at second or third base as he gets more physical in the lower half. His above average arm strength will play anywhere on the field. Doty is buoyed by an awfully impressive hit tool and average athletic tools all over his scouting report. He's a joy to watch play the game. Doty will be on the older side for this draft at 19.5 years old on draft day. He's revered by area scouts for his disposition and attitude toward the game and his teammates.

Bonds is the nephew of all-time great slugger Barry Bonds and possesses some similar traits to his namesake. It's enormous raw power projection with peak exit velocities reaching north of 113 mph. He'll need to prove capable with the hit tool and polish around some unrefined edges, but the pure tools are huge.

Bonds originally committed to Campbell and got into 36 games in 2024 with the Fighting Camels. He ran a .267/.341/.427 slash with five homers and garnered enough interest from hometown Rutgers when he hopped into the transfer portal to relocate.

Bonds' hit tool took a considerable step forward in 2025 when he ran a sub-20 percent whiff rate and showed adjustability he hadn't as a freshman. There's still stiffness in his swing and he struggles to rotate through his shoulders. That biomechanical mechanism has been at least partially to blame for poor contact-quality consistency. He's hitting the ball a lot more often, but not necessarily hard all the time. He can be very, very dangerous when pitchers allow him to gets his arms extended on fastballs or breaking balls on the outer third. It's huge damage in those zones. That said, when Bonds is forced to pull his hands in and get the barrel to velocity on the inner-third, he has tended to roll over to the left side of the infield. Bonds is also an aggressive hitter who tends to expand the zone at a high clip. His size allows him to barrel-up pitches off the outer-third. It's pretty impressive the impact potential he can flash on pitches outside of the zone at times. 

Bonds is currently a centerfielder with above-average foot speed and a lumbering running style. He tracks the baseball well but can show some clumsiness in his lower-half when forced to turn his hips on a ball hit over this head. He also has solid average arm strength.

Bonds profiles as a right fielder at the next level as he likely slows down with continued maturation and added muscle. He won't turn 21 years old until a week after the Draft, so age is on his size. When you're already an extremely physical, brutish athlete, age/training-age isn't as big a feather in your cap.

The pride of Olympia, Washington, Overbay is a player development success story. After two years at UNLV and significant efforts in the weight room, Overbay hit the transfer portal and relocated to Arizona State for the 2026 season. His stuff has taken off, and so have his pro prospects.

To date, Overbay has largely worked in a relief role. His fastball will sit 95-97 and can snag 98 early in his outings. It's a high, over-the-top delivery with above average lift through the zone, generating whiff and chase at the top of the zone. Overbay spins the ball well, and has shown enough command to work plate appearances as he pleases.

One ahead, Overbay employs a firm low-90s cutter and a bigger sweeping slider in the mid-80s to get outs. The latter will flash above average traits. Perhaps his highest upside secondary is a changeup he's hardly throwing. It dives and fades off his fastball, cutting over 10 mph of velocity off it. If that pitch comes into full focus, he's got at least a small chance of breaking into pro ball as a starter.

Overbay still has plenty to prove at the next level. The offspeed pitch is a big part of that, but as is his control for the zone. If a team believes he can get there, he likely debuts at High-A starting games. 

Overbay is the son of former MLB standout Lyle Overbay.

An immediate starter as a true freshman with the Bruins, Dugger is a polished left-handed bat with a long, projectable frame and excellent bat-to-ball skills. Dugger is yet to show game power, though he sprays the ball to all fields and should grow into his frame and more bat speed in time. Finding more barrels will ultimately dictate where he fits in the draft. 

Dugger has awesome athletic tools behind the plate. It's 70-grade arm strength with repeatable mechanics that lend well toward his ability to consistently put the ball on the second base bag. He frames well, blocks well, and shows the components necessary to not only catch at the next level, but perhaps put himself in the conversation for a Gold Glove if the smaller, finite parts of catching come to him at the next level. 

Dugger will need to unlock another gear with the bat to hear his name called in the top ten rounds in 2026, but it's a solid floor with a chance to sneak into the 7-10 round range if he continues his hitterish ways.

Knaak has been one of the better performers in the 2026 draft-eligible class since arriving to campus. He immediately stepped into a starting role at Clemson and hasn't looked back, nor has he really faltered yet either. He throws a four-seam fastball with late life through the zone, up to 96 but more ordinarily 92-93. There's an upper-70s over-the-top breaking ball he'll use against against righty bats as well as a traditional sweeper he'll use for a unique look in the low-80s. Both pitches are above-average weapons. But it's his changeup that catches the headlines. He'll throw the cambio and induce extreme tail and diving action generating significant whiff rates. It's a pitch that's generated well-above average results. He's shown a willingness to throw it to lefties and righties alike. It's a 'plus' pitch when he's landing it below the zone, but Knaak will have a tendency to lean on that pitch too frequently and when it's left in the zone hitters have done damage. It's one of the better changeups in the 2026 class when he's mixing things up. 

Knaak has been a really, really tough look for lefty hitters especially. He has a short arm-swing with a compact delivery. He's a good athlete and and represents one of the higher-floor starters in the class. Knaak possesses at least one "plus" pitch and plenty of solid-average or better offerings to go alongside it. And he throws strikes. That'll get him selected early in 2026.

Burns began his career at Arizona State where he flashed big stuff before shoulder tendinitis ended his freshman campaign early. He's no longer in Tempe, but the stuff that made him appealing to scouts out the gates is still present. 

Now a Longhorn, Burns has been up to 99 and will rest in the mid-90s. It's a fastball that possesses elite carry and cutting action. Burns lives at the top of the zone and dares hitters to get the barrel above the baseball. His outlandishly high release height is a unique look for hitters.

He can snap over a nasty upper-70s bender and can flip in a mid-80s changeup -- likely his best secondary. There's also a cutter that's been put into his operation to bridge the three pitches together. 

It's a workhorse frame with four pitches. Burns has more routinely shown fringy control for the strikezone and may end up a leverage bullpen arm at the next level if he can't string together more consistent secondary offerings a second time through the lineup. He's an adrenaline junky that lives for short spurts.

Bayles enjoyed immediate success as a freshman posting 50 strikeouts across 42.1 innings. He parlayed that success into earning the Saturday role at Santa Clara. 

Bayles' best pitch is his low-to-mid-80s slider. He's a slider-heavy starter who is more than willing to throw the breaker to both left- and right-handed hitters. He'll back-door, back-foot and front door the pitch depending on the situation. He has an advanced feel for the pitch and has shown the ability to make that pitch bigger and smaller to keep hitters off balance. It's an above average weapon that Bayles is working to compliment with another offering. 

While Bayles' slider is impressive, his fastball has a bit less value right now. It's generic in shape, best when sinking and tailing away from left-handed hitters. Bayles needs to find a primary fastball shape with bigger deviation from what he currently has if he hopes to have better than a 40-grade heater. 

Bayles has the frame and strike-throwing ability to warrant starter consideration. That said, there's effort and a lack of a second and third pitch if he hopes to pitch into a lineup for a second time as a professional.

Jackson was a sleeper in the Peach State for much of his high school career but saw his draft stock take a jump after the summer of 2024. While swing-and-miss is still present, Jackson has a ton of physical growth in front of him in terms of putting on muscle and mass. It's s simple swing with a wide base, quiet hands, a high-elbow set in his load with a moderate barrel tilt. He's always on time and produces a compact path through the zone. Jackson projects into a slasher who boasts plus run times down the line. 

The bat is behind the glove. He's a twitchy infielder with good athleticism from both sides of the plate. It's above average arm strength and the chance to blossom into an above average runner too.

The pride of Reno, Nevada, and a product of McNeese by way of Mesa Community College, Nachtsheim has grown into his own in college, adding significant weight and strength to his 6-foot-4-inch frame. The stuff and strikes have continously progressed year over year, reaching an apex in 2026 with dominating performances up and down the spring. 

Nachtsheim is reaching back for 96 these days and has proven capable of sitting 92-94 with the heater. He's got excellent glove-side command for that pitch and likes to pepper the corners at the knees, elevating to generate his whiffs. The fastball exhibits plus carry and cutting action, complimented by almost 7 feet of extension. 94 might look like 97 to hitters. The fastball is generating impressive whiff and chase rates this spring. It has the look of an above average fastball at the next level, especially when command for that pitch is taken into consideration. 

Nachtsheim is relatively fastball-centric, but will the a cutter, slider and changeup to mix things up. 

the slider is comfortably his most used secondary. It's 82-84, sometimes firm, short, and relies on his fastball command to be effective. The cutter is more 85-87, also short, but holds vert well for the college ball. Nachtsheim's changeup is very generic. 80-84 mph with middling shape and results. 

Nachtsheim can throw his entire arsenal for strikes and likes to pitch ahead. He's punched tickets at an awfully impressive clip this spring considering how often he's in the zone. Walks have not been an issue either.

Nachtsheim is already 22 years old and doesn't hold much leverage in the Draft. He's also relatively filled out and physically mature, so whoever drafts him will likely have to be okay with what he is presently from a velocity and arm strength perspective. There's a ton to like here, even with some of his limitations. At worst, he's a "day three" pick and is more likely going to hear his name called in the top ten rounds as a money-saver type of move.

Holcomb is a big, athletic plaer with considerable raw power, however he's had a difficult time consistently tapping into it in games at this early stage of his career due to some chase and whiff to his profile. His size and physicality have made his profile famous going back to his high school days. Showcasing more of that power in games will come down to whether his pure bat-to-ball skills can improve. It's a boom or bust bat projection, however a move to centerfield in 2026 could elevate his role projection. 

Holcomb showed signed of improvement on the Cape in 2025 with an improving approach and better overall hit tool. It may never be an average hit tool at the next level, but if Holcomb can get to a place where he's a fringe-average hitter with his raw power, he could boast a few 25-homer seasons, provided he gets the at-bats to get there. 

His solid defensive actions and near top of the scale arm strength will keep him on the field for the long term, though he's been spread out across first base, third base, left field and centerfield to this point. He's an average runner. It's more of a prototype right field profile at the next level. 

In total, perhaps Holcomb can prove to be something of a Hunter Renfroe kind of player at the next level if the hit tool can get to a steady place.

Aloy spent his first season stateside at BYU before transferring to Arkansas in 2025 to play with his brother, Wehiwa. 

Aloy is less dynamic than his older brother but maybe more impactful in the box. It's plus raw power to the pull-side, anything left on the inner-third in danger of being punished. Aloy feasts on mistake pitches but can be exploited on breaking balls low and away. He's a rather selective hitter who does a nice job staying inside the zone. A lot of Aloy's success can be attributed to waiting for his pitch and ambushing it. Ultimately, it's likely a fringe average pure hit tool once he begins seeing pitchers that can spots their secondary pitches on the corners. Still, there is almost nobody in college baseball that runs hard-hit rates like Aloy does. He has definitive 30-homer upside if he's provided the plate appearances to get there. 

Perhaps his biggest hurdle in getting there is a lack of defensive value. He got just four games of action at first base at BYU in the first two weeks of his freshman year before being limited to designated hitter duties the rest of the way. The Razorbacks have been working hard to get him comfortable and consistent in right field, and he's made considerable strides with some scouts throwing average grades on his routes and instincts. He'll need that defensive value if he hopes to capitalize on his top 100 pick upside. Aloy does have plus arm strength that shows up on film. 

This isn't a completely unprecedented situation. LSU outfielder Ethan Frey barely played in the field at all in 2025 and ended up being selected in the third round. Teams are willing to look past the limitations if they're convinced a player is going to bang. 

Aloy has the raw power and bat speed to make a name for himself at the next level but cleaning up the fine details of the hit tool and finding a defensive home will likely dictate just how high he can go in July.

The 2025 MAAC Player of the Year and all-time single season RBI record holder for the Rider Broncs, Tiroly had a season for the ages as a sophomore last year. A .377 hitter with an OPS north of 1.200, Tiroly was a lineup anchor and did everything a coach could ask in the middle of the lineup. As mentioned, his 70 RBI bests the Rider program all-time. He hit 18 homers along the way. That substantial production landed him in the transfer portal prior to the 2026 season where he relocated to Charlottesville. 

Tiroly mashes. His pitch selection skills are sublime. His bat-to-ball performance even better. As if the building blocks of good hitting weren't enough, Tiroly has ranked near the top of college baseball in terms of average exit velocity and peaked north of 112 mph. He hits the ball a lot, he hits the ball hard, and he hardly ever lets pitchers win an at-bat. Tiroly pulls the ball, he lifts the ball, he draws his walks and he controls the zone. At times, he's looked like the total package offensively.

In terms of the athletic tools, it's mostly average. Tiroly is an average runner with a heavy-footed running style. He'll steal the occasional base thanks to his high IQ and reasonably nimble first step. He's an average defender at second base who has some lateral ability to his left. He can struggle to make the play on balls up the middle to his right. It's a second base profile at the next level and could eventually shift to first base if he gets too much bigger. Tiroly is a stout-framed kid with broad shoulders and a thicker lower half. It's a physical frame. There's something of a Dan Uggla appearance to his game.

A broken foot in the winter slowed his come-up in 2026. He'll need to keep hammering the baseball in 2026 should he hope to capitalize on what some believe is a top-three round ceiling.

After spending his first collegiate year at LSU, Kucherak hit the transfer portal seeking more opportunities and extended playing time. That took his game to Northwestern where he's blossomed into one of the more exciting 2026 Draft prospects in college baseball. 

Kucherak is a tooled-up shortstop with plus bat speed projection and the athletic ability to make a difference in every aspect of the game. He's power-over-hit right now, but Kucherak has flashed bat-to-ball skills in streaky ways leading bulls of the profile to believe he'll age into a more consistent player. Kucherak doesn't get cheated. When he makes contact it's among the highest hard-hit rates of anyone in the country regardless of position. It's a hot stick. 

Kucherak plays the shortstop position under control with a good tempo and internal clock. He's got an above average arm and can make most plays from the '6'. He's a solid average runner with the potential to add more speed with some training and development. The entire profile isn't too dissimilar from a player like Seattle Mariners super-utility Dylan Moore.

Moroney has started nearly every game at Rhode Island since his freshman year in 2024, compiling a steady stats on the back of his baseball card whilst providing value with the glove at the shortstop position.

Moroney can hit. He's got exceptional bat-to-ball skills and has the pitch selection skills necessary to work deep at-bats. He's works long counts and takes a slasher approach toward putting the game in motion. Moroney isn't affected by velocity and doesn't have any warts inside the zone or outside of the zone against spin. His apporach obviously limits strikeouts and drives up his walks, but groundballs and a lack of physical strength do limit the impact he can provide with the stick.

Moroney is a plus runner who will occassionally snag a 70-grade run time to first base when he gets out of the box hot. His speed plays in a big ways from a stolen base perspective, and it's also helped elevate his range playing the shortstop position. Moroney has solid average arm strength and is a reliable defender who is capable of the dynamic play moving up the middle to his left. He's a bit more tested moving to his right in the '6' hole. 

Moroney's bat-to-ball skills and speed give him value at the next level. He's a glove that could play the critical utility role at the next level, however his size and lack of bat speed may preclude him from ever developing into a full-time starter in the big leagues. It's a Role 40 type of player who will likely be a priority later into the draft.

Kerce is a solid infield prospect who can do a little bit of everything well, but likely isn't dynamic enough to play the shortstop position as a professional. It's above average arm strength, however the first-step quickness leaves something to be desired from a prototype middle infield prospect. Kerce is reliable and comfortable on the dirt. He'll always make the routine play, but will be challenged with balls hit harder with faster runners at the professional level. He's likely destined for second base, or perhaps third if he adds more power to his profile.

Kerce can really hit. It's elite bat-to-ball skills, especially on pitches thrown anywhere in the zone. He's a polished hitter who refuses to expand the zone and does a nice job handling spin and elevated velocity. Kerce is going to hit, but for how much impact? His 108 mph max exit velocity speaks to fringe average raw power. Kerce is more of a conga line contributor, capable of moving runners over and running lower slugging percentages. He's a useful, versatile player who can play in multiple spots and won't hurt your offense with strikeouts.

An exceptional mover and athlete on the mound, Dudan presents starter upside featuring a mid-90s fastball that's grabbed 99 and a hard, tight-spinning slider that's been up to 89 with 3000 rpm at peak. The fastball ordinarily settles in a few ticks lower than that, but it plays up at every velocity band because of his low slot. Dudan's heater is reasonably generic from a release and shapes perspective, but he added a sinker to his arsneal in 2026 to help create different looks for hitters. He's unlikely to ever miss many bats with the fastball, but it can be effective setting up that plus breaking ball.

Dudan has also worked to integrate a changeup a times in 2026, however it's very raw at this point. 

Dudan saw an enormous velocity jump upon arriving to campus and has been one of the more impressive arms in college baseball from a velocity perspective since arriving to Raleigh. He'll need to wrangle in the strikes and develop a reliable third pitch to get the most of his ceiling and starter upside, but there's reasons to dream. He's been an especially effective reliever when deployed in that role, primarily in 2024 and 2025.

Kennedy is an impressive athlete with a lot of twitch in his hips and tremendous athleticism in his actions on the field. A plus runner with a whippy arm on the dirt, Kennedy projects an above average defender wherever he lines up on the diamond. 

Offensively, there's some juice, but he's more of a gap hitter right now with projectable upside in a twitchy frame. Kennedy will need to work on staying connected in the box if he's to tap into what he's capable of offensively, but the tools are fairly obvious. Some added weight this past winter has bring his offensive profile together. Kennedy's biggest strength in the batters box is his selective eye and willingness to work counts deep to get the pitch he wants to pull the trigger on. He should earn plenty of walks at the next level, complimenting his foot speed on the bases.

From a pure scouting lens, Hernandez checks so many boxes. He's got long limbs, a higher-set waist, and strength in his upper-half pointing to more impact on the horizon. It's a 6-foot-5-inch frame with the athleticism necessary to play on the dirt at this stage in his baseball career. It's above-average arm strength with throws that carry through the bag. Despite his size, Hernandez is a very good athlete who posts plus run times with an aggressive, athletic stride. He's going to hold his run tool deep into professional baseball so long as he stays healthy. 

Hernandez boasts plus bat speed projection and a hit tool that continues to trend in the right direction. There's swing and miss in Hernandez's game, but that's to be expected of a player this size at this age. He's already flashing game power with pull-side juice and the ability to shoot ringing extra-base hits into the right-center field gap. Hernandez's feel for getting to the pull-side stands out. It's real power projection out of a premium frame. The hit tool will be tested up the ladder, but all the components are present for an impact hitter going forward.

While Beaty isn't the biggest guy in the world, what he lacks in pure size he makes up for with polish and fluidity. Beaty has a buttery operation that he repeats well, peppering the strike zone with a four pitch mix and command well beyond his years. The fastball has grabbed 94 with some carry and life on the top rail, however in general it possesses fairly generic shape. It's not true bat-misser, but thrown with confidence to all four quadrants the pitch seems to play up.

A high-spin slider is thrown in the upper-70s, front-door and backdoor with sweeping shape and some late two-plane tilt. His shapes will wobble as his starts progress. It's an average breaking ball with the chance to get to above average in time. There's a mid-70s curveball that he'll flip over against right-handed hitters and a changeup with late tumble and arm speed. The latter has a chance to be an average-or-better offering. 

Beaty is among the top pure competitors in the 2026 class with moxy and leadership skills that go beyond the bump. He does have Tommy John in the rear-view mirror, and he likely won't ever develop an arsenal that represents top-of-the-rotation stuff. It's more of a back-end of the rotation profile carried by pitchability. He will be 18.8 for the draft.

Evasco is an extremely long, broad first base and/or outfield prospect with tools generally reserved for players smaller in stature. A solid average runner with an impressive first step on the bases and in the field, scouts give Evasco a shot to play left field at the next level so long as he keeps his athleticism. It's fringy arm strength. Evasco gets high marks for his athletic traits, but if teams buy, it'll be for the bat. 

Evasco makes tight, compact turns on the baseball, a trait that is seldom seen from players his size. He hasn't yet fully realized his raw power, and is mostly an average in the game power department presently. Evasco does a nice job battling at the plate and keeps his strikeouts low, though he's in no hurry to draw many walks either. He's an aggressive swing who expands the zone at a red-flag worthy rate. In order for Evasco to get to that frame, bat speed and raw power, he'll need to swing at better pitches. When he does swing at pitches in the zone, he shows plus bat-to-ball skills. He'll likely have to take more advantage of his size and levers and create a big more stretch in his load if he's to develop into what some believe could eventually become plus game power. 

An approach change would unlock a new gear for Evasco. He clearly has solid hand-eye coordination, and the frame to dream on more impact potential. He's a draft-eligible sophomore.

New, a reasonably unheralded southpaw out of the small, 1A Hesperia High School in Southern California, saw his stuff take a big jump when he arrived on campus, touching 96 in the spring and settling in 90-92 with above average extension on the bump. 

New is a strike-thrower with two breaking balls and a starter's operation. The curveball and slider are both putaway weapons. New has a shot at starting at the next level, pitching in the 91-93 range over multiple innings with a solid breaking ball. He's got a strong frame with a sturdy lower half and a reasonably loose, easy delivery.

Segura is a sinker-slider righty with mirror traits that turn teams on to his profile. He'll primarily operate in the low-90s bucket, though he's been up to 97 with heavy spin and sink. As he fatigues, Segura's fastball flattens out a bit and morphs into a deadzone, vanilla fastball. That should iron itself out over time under the instruction of OSU coaches. 

The breaking ball flashes plus with two-plane tilt and strong sweeping shape. Segura has shown a changeup now and again, but it lacks consistency, though feel for shaping the pitch seems to be present. He possesses a starter's operation with ease and repeatability, though it may never be a prototypical bat-missing profile.

The cherry on top of Seguar's profile is a below-average launch height and above-average extension down the bump. He has every tool in the bag to start at the next level.

A table-setter with a slick glove, Cleary has led the Broncos is several statistical categories the last two years thanks to his extreme polish and reliability at the dish.

The kid can really, really hit. It's a squatted, slightly open setup with a heavy emphasis on rotation in his swing. Cleary sets his hands low and keeps the path to the ball as short as possible. He will lag the hands back a bit in his load, but never outside of his frame. Cleary prefers to read the baseball out of the hand and work into the opposite field gap. He knows the type of hitter he is, rarely selling out to pull the baseball. The result is an exceptionally low chase rate, elite bat--to-ball skills and very, very few holes in the swing. Whoever drafts Cleary will have to live with the opposite field approach and heavy ground ball profile. He's sessentially Jose Iglesias or Jake Mangum with a bat in his hands.

Cleary is an average runner with average actions at the shortstop position. He's not a dynamic defender, but he'll convert everything hit his way. It's average arm strength, elevated by a quick release and feel for clock. He'll bounce the ball into first base when necessary. There's IQ, even if athletic and physical tools aren't elite.

Cleary is a nice player with a really good shot to play the shortstop position all the way up the ladder. He's unlikely to win any Gold Gloves, but he'll get the job done. He's athletic and versatile to play anywhere on the infield. Just how much impact is in the bat is yet to be determined. As it stands now, his approach would represent one of the largest oppo-ground ball swingers in the sport.

Proskey bucks the trend of hard-throwing right-handed pitchers that draw the attention of scouts. Instead, it's his pitch shapes, pitchability, and competitive fire that garners attention.

Despite owning a fastball that's only ever tickled 94 mph, Proskey's heater delivers strong results. He pounds the zone with the fastball and has posted elite chase rates above the zone with the pitch when he misses. The latter is due in large part to well-above average ride through the zone, at times living north of 22 inches of IVB. Proskey spins the baseball very well, and his higher-than-average launch height is a unique look for hitters. All this being said, Proskey operates more comfortably in the 90-92 bucket throughout most of his starts; an underwhelming velocity band for a pro prospect. 

A mid-80s slider is his go-to secondary. It's been up to 87 and possesses short, bullet shape. That shorter shape is actually quite effective when considering what hitters are looking for after seeing the fastball hop through the zone. It's been effective generating chase below the zone, however Proskey isn't yet utilizing the gyro slider in a manner that gets whiffs. 

Proskey's changeup will flash too. He's excellent at killing spin on the baseball, and has shown capable of registering spin rates under 1000 rpm. His feel for landing the fastball in the zone when he needs to is a bit shaky, but when he's got feel for it, the pitch can neutralize left-handed bats. He's also shown willing to throw it to the back foot of right-handed hitters. 

Proskey is a strike-thrower and dares the opposition to hit his stuff. He keeps his walks low and has proven capable of going deep into ballgames. His 6-foot-3-inch frame does look flush for adding more velocity, but at this point he seems to have hit a bit of a velocity plateau. Couple the middling velocity with what is below average extension down the mound and there's real reason to question whether his fastball will perform at the levels it has in pro ball at the next level. Guys that struggle to extend down the mound generally have to live heavily off their secondaries to leverage bigger movement profiles. Proskey's ability to either add more velocity before July, and develop a bigger, harder breaking ball to get more whiffs, will dictate where he goes in the Draft. 

Given his polish, size and three-pitch mix, it's safe to assume Proskey will likely have a home in rounds 11 through 20 as a floor. If any of the peripherals take a jump this summer, he could work his way up into the 5-8 round range.

Titsworth saw his role expand during a sophomore getting the opportunity to start for the Tigers. He's long had the durable, strong frame to hold up over long innings. The arsenal and operation and finally coming together to support the physical tools.

Titsworth's best pitch is the fastball. It's 92-95 and will tick up to 97 with reasonably generic shape. Titsworth launches from an exceptionally low slot allowing said shape to play way up. Whatever vertical carry he's able to hold onto the fastball innately produces value on the pitch at the top of the zone. He does throw two fastballs. The four-seamer showing big value elevated. A running two-seamer doesn't get the whiffs, but succeeds in generating ground balls and chase outside of the zone. Titsworth isn't the athlete that a guy like Bryan Woo is, but does possess some similar traits in how he's able to shape the baseball from his slot. 

Titsworth's slider has a chance to be a good one, however he hasn't thrown it much. It's a true bullet spinner, 81-84 with occassional late, short horizontal tilt. That pitch has generated strong whiff rates and has been effective inducing swings out of the zone. His feel for throwing that pitch for strikes will come and go. 

Given his unique slot, Titsworth's changeup may eventually end up being his most effective secondary offering. For now, it's crude, unpolished and rarely deployed. There's solid velocity separation off the fastball, however he's not yet consistently showcasing bat-missing shapes.

Titsworth has things that can be impossible to teach. He's shown capable of starting capable of starting and his athleticism should warrant that role at least to begin his major league career.

Guevara, a Panama-born infielder, had an underwhelming freshman season with Auburn in 2024. However, he made a significant impact with a remarkable sophomore campaign in 2025. Standing at 5-foot-11 and weighing 210 pounds, he is a right-handed hitter with a powerful swing. 

In 2025, he showcased his skills by slashing .331 with a .388 on-base percentage and a .556 slugging percentage. He hit five home runs and 11 doubles during that season. Guevara is known for his contact hitting and has a keen sense of the barrel, particularly when it comes to fastballs. He sets up with a relaxed and open stance, which allows him to make quick adjustments to the ball. It's average bat-to-ball skills with some batted-ball peaks that suggest he could grow into 20 homer power if he carves out a full-time role as a pro.

Matt Scott is a mountain of a man, standing tall at 6-foot-7, 231 pounds. He has all the traits teams look for in a future starter at the next level. He's a strike-thrower with a beautiful operation, fantastic body control and the stuff to carve through a lineup two or three times over. 2025 was a bit of a step back in terms of his control for the zone, but evaluators believe he'll still be able to fill the box as a pro. He elected to transfer to Georgia for the 2026 season to try and re-find his upside. 

The fastball will grab 98 with carry through the zone, however he's generally in the low-to-mid 90s. It's effectiveness is nullified a bit by his high release point, steepening his approach angle. He's still extremely tough to square up at the top of the zone. He throws a traditional cutter to try and generate more production from the fastball bucket. Interestingly, Georgia raised Scott's release point almost six inches in 2026, creating more carry and cutting action on the four-seam, as well as bringing his release profile into a very unique territory with names like Trey Yesavage and Justin Verlander. 

Scott throws a firm slider in the mid-80s with short two-plane tilt. It's been effective against right handed bats. He'll also mix in a splitter to lefties, and he's had some success in that department too thanks to late, deeper break and strong tunnel attributes off his heater. 

For now, Scott's fastball is his carrying pitch, the his two secondaries will flash solid-average, the slider being more potent. That said, when you consider the body, the mechanics, the athlete and the development ahead, this is a reasonably elite prospect with a high floor.

Jackson was a monster as a true freshman for the Wofford Terriers. So much so that he took his talents to the transfer portal and changed zip codes. Now an SEC bat, Jackson is a certified thumper with real feel for the fat part of the bat. His average exit velocities rival anyone in the countre. It's comfortably plus bat speed and his barrel awareness is supreme. Jackson combines loud impact with above average bat-to-ball skills and a polished approach. He does hit the ball on the ground more than scouts like to see, but loft could come with maturation and further understanding of his swing. 

Jackson possesses a strong frame with strength distributed through his upper and lower body. It's a physique reminiscent of Henry Davis at Louisville. Jackson has a strong arm and is athletic out of the crouch. Lateral mobility, framing and blocking remain areas of concern long-term for his ability to stay behnd the plate. That said, Jackson is an above average runner and can play both corner outfield spots. He's got a shot to stick behind the plate long-term, but there's some work ahead.

Jorgensen is an interesting pitching prospect with real unique abilities in his right arm. He's got a heater that has touched 97 that carries through the zone with reasonably elite metrics and presents just enough arm-side tailing action to stay off the barrel if he leaves it in the zone. He's no stranger to IVB marks north of 22. Better still, his 6-foot frame generates well-above average extension, sometimes approaching seven feet. Jorgenson's fastball will be every bit that of a plus heater at the next level, and will generate whiffs at heavy clips if he's landing it at the top of the zone. 

He folds in a low-80s slider that's inconsistent and short and relies on his ability to land the fastball for strikes; and he generally does just that. The slider will sometimes melt into curveball shape when he comes over the top of it. It's nothing better than average for the time being, however his capacity for spin should help a player development team get his breaking ball to above average over time. For now it's a two-pitch mix with a low-80s changeup-splitter being a distant third offering on the menu. 

Jorgensen has a composed delivery and repeats very well. It's an over-the-top action with some early leak in his front side to achieve it. He's shown feel for tempo and extension and has components to a starting pitcher profile if he can fold in a third pitch. A bit undersized, Jorgensen makes up for his shorter stature with bigger stuff. He missed much of his junior year and coinciding summer recovering from an ACL injury. Ultimately, this has the look of a high-leverage reliever with three pitches and the ability to get outs with the fastball alone. Jorgenson has 8th inning upside.

Following two seasons in Tempe where he struggled to earn much playing time, Lettow departed Arizona State and transferred to San Diego State where he was immediately greeted with more innings and chances to prove his mettle.

Lettow is a true five-pitch artist who relies on sequencing and pitchability to generate whiffs and punch outs. The fastball will climb to 94 mph, but more comfortably sits 90-92 with solid carry and tail through the zone. He's shown average strike-throwing ability with the heater, but does get a good bit of whiff and chase on the pitch. He also spins the ball particularly well; a good reason to believe in his projection going forward.

Lettow spreads the menu out with a cutter, sweeper, curveball and ocassional changeup to lefties. The sweeper has a chance to be pretty good. It's thrown in the low-80s for now with better than 13 inches of sweep. The curveball and cutter are reasonably generic, stock pitches. The changeup is very inconsistent from a shapes and strikes perspective.

Lettow's pitchability is a strong suit. He's still very young for the class, and is growing into his own. He's a project and might not currently carry an above average pitch outside of perhaps the fastball, but there's clay to work with in the pitch plot and ability to create shapes.

A 17th round pick by the Pirates in 2023, Cuvet has been on scouts' radars for some time now. Cuvet fits the prototype power corner-infield profile in a nutshell.

It's an imposing, high-waisted frame with elite bat speed and plus-plus raw power that will play frequently in-game. Cuvet is an ultra-aggressive hitter who expands the zone at unsustainable rates pushing his whiff rates north. He shortens up in two-strike counts and does a nice job of maintaining a healthy strikeout rate despite the aggressiveness. Cuvet may never be the type of hitter who runs a high batting average or walk rate, but the slugging potential should make up for those woes. 

Cuvet plays light on his feet for his size and has the ability to attack the ball with confidence and arm strength behind it. He shows a real chance of sticking at 3B long term, with high level power projection if the frame doesn't get too physical. Cuvet has already received a bit of run at first base at Miami, though that's largely been a byproduct of roster design and getting younger players into the fold. Still, it's something to monitor and something scouts will be keyed in on as July approaches. 

Scouts want to see Cuvet continue to refine the overall hit tool in order to meet his ceiling of a middle-of-the-order hitter, but the impact he's shown since arriving to Miami is first round talent.

Freshcorn was a huge draft target for several teams in the 2024 Draft but went unselected due to signability concerns. He's an explosive right-handed pitcher with dynamic athleticism on the mound and tons of projection in terms of velocity. To date, he's up to 96 with considerable carry, launched out of slot just north of five feet. 

He'll bully hitters with a high-spin cutter touching 90 with two-plane tilt and tunnel. His sweeper is a wipeout offering that has plus potential at the next level. 

Freshcorn is an electric mover and gets down the mound with strong extension for his size. He's a strike-thrower who pounds the zone with his three-pitch arsenal. Scouts will want to see him flash a changeup/splitter in 2026 before his draft. If he does, it's the potential for day-one stuff.

The pride of the state of New Hampshire, Fennell burst onto the scene for the Commodores in 2025 after transferring into Nashville spending his freshman season throwing the ball for Dayton. He attacks the strike zone and gets ahead of hitters. Fennell possesses an intriguing blend of release traits, pitch shapes, deception and athleticism that has scouts bullish on what the final product could become. 

It all begins with the fastball and it's a metric monster. Fennell launches from a 55 inch slot, over a foot lower than the average release height in major league baseball. Fennell generates huge extension down the bump and is able to maintain a reasonably vertical spin orientation on his fastball creating some carry and unique late hop. It's a fastball release, shape and approach angle hitters don't ordinarily see. Fennell gets roughly 14 inches of vertical carry and 14 inches of arm-side tail on his fastball with a sub -4 degree vertical approach angle. The pitch is very unique. That all being said, there is some room for growth. Fennell will tickle the low-90s but generally pitches more comfortably in the 87-89 range. It's not velocity that will work against major league hitters. He'll need to find another gear before he reaches the Double-A level. Still, the foundation is here for something exciting.

Fennell is fastball-heavy but does throw a dynamic changeup to left-handed hitters, and he throws it often. He creates tons of vertical depth on that pitch and elite fading action. It's more than 10 mph of separation off the fastball too. It's a 60-grade cambio. 

Fennell throws a traditional cutter with stock shapes and traits. There's also a sweeping slider in the low-70s that he'll use to right-handed hitters. 

Fennell is a strike-thrower with a unique set of traits and tools to get hitters out. He doesn't spin the ball particularly well and has yet to grow into the velocity necessary to find immediate success in pro ball. If he finds another few ticks in the velocity department, he's got a chance to go in the top few rounds.

Belyeu has enjoyed a very nice career at Auburn, showcasting a power-speed combination that can be difficult to find in the college ranks. 

Belyeu has been the primary centerfielder at Auburn going back to his sophomore year. Most scouts believe his eventual home will be in a corner, however he'll almost certainly begin his professional career up the middle. It's above average speed and strong routes in the field. 

As noted, Belyeu also brings power to the plate. He's peaked north of 111 mph and has shown an innate ability to hit the ball in the air. Belyeu is still working on finding more consistent barrels, as well as getting to his pull-side with more authority, but the physical tools flash plenty often. His swing plane can get him in a little trouble when he expands the zone, but he's an accomplished bat-to-ball aritst when swinging at strikes. 

Belyeu made waves during the 2025 season, hitting a big solo home run in the sixth inning of Auburn's season-opener just hours after losing his mother to cancer. He's an easy player to root for, the tools are the cherry on top.

Weinstein has some of the highest level bat-to-ball skills in the class with a smooth, calm-and-collected playstyle, always looking to put the game in motion and do the small things well. Weinstein can take the barrel to any ball in any quadrant regardless of whether he's out in front or late on a pitch. He's got strong hands and possesses the ability to make ultra-tight turns on the baseball to keep it inside the white lines. Weinstein feel for getting to his pull-side stands out. He delivers a heavy barrel with a flatter attack angle, an operation geared to pepper line drives all over the yard. While power isn't totally in his profile yet, there is some sneaky pull-side juice when he gets out in front of one and yanks hard on it down the line. He figures to grow into impact in due time. Weinstein, uniquely, elects to wear a batting glove only on his bottom hand.

It's hard to oversell just how strong the hit tool is here. Weinstein ranked at or near the top of the entire 2026 class during the summer of 2024 and 2025 in just about every hit tool metric you can find. His chase rate sits south of 20 percent. His whiff rate sits south of 15 percent. Even more impressive, his in-zone whiff rate sits south of 10 percent. As one might expect, Weinstein hardly ever strikes out. This sort of production is generally reserved for slappy hitters. Weinstein bucks that trend posting impressive slug and ISO numbers. 

Weinstein has some natural infield actions and has a chance to play second or third base at the next level, most scouts leaning toward the latter. Weinstein has some oddities in his mechanics and how he moves at times so an eventual home at first base isn't out of the question if he continues to add strength and slows down. Weinstein won't apply too much pressure on the basepaths with what many consider fringy or a tick below foot speed, but he's a high IQ player whose been known to take the extra base. As far as high school players go, this is a reasonably high floor with the "gamer" label written all over him. Weinstein will be 19.4 years old on draft day.

A year after his brother heard his name called on day one of the draft, Ebel is pushing his way up follow lists for this class. A well-rounded prospect with ways to add value on both sides of the ball, Ebel has fans in the Southern California scouting scene.

Ebel possesses well-above average bat-to-ball skills and has begun growing into some bat speed. He's shown the ability to get to his pull-side in games and could eventually own average game power at the next level. A demonstrative hitter, Ebel can often be found talking to himself in the box after each pitch, processing the information from the at-bat pitch-by-pitch. Ebel may end slightly favoring the hit side of his game over the power tool, but he's a good bet to add value with the bat through some avenue. He's just remarkably pesky and consistently a difficult out. 

Ebel has average tools at the shortstop position, however his game is elevated by natural feel for the position and a high IQ. His situational awareness stands out, as does his internal clock. It's average arm strength and average foot speed befitting of a player who likely ends up at second base or third base, but fundamentals may keep Ebel at shortstop as he works up the ladder. Ebel has some similarities to Nationals fifth round pick Trey Snyder from the 2024 Draft. Snyder got a signing bonus reflective of a Top-70 pick that year. 

Just 17.8 years old for the Draft, Ebel will have models screaming his name. That said, there's not a ton of training-age projection on the frame, so organizations might not buy the upward projection that a younger player in the draft might ordinarily possess.

Mendoza is a gap-to-gap hitter with solid bat-to-ball skills and burgeoning juice. It's mostly all bat-to-ball traits carrying the profile for the time being, but Mendoza's bat speed has ticked up since arriving to Austin from Tempe. Now a Texas Longhorn via the portal, Mendoza has continued to flash his hitterish way. He's an aggressive hitter who tends to expand the zone, but is so talented he'll foul off pitches off the black to keep an at-bat alive until he gets a cookie mistake. Some scouts believe he's blossoming into fringe-average raw power and exit velocities approach 110 mph would reinforce that notion. 

Mendoza is the quintessential second base prospect with a fringy arm and average range. He's played some third base as well. The bat will carry the profile, but some scouts believe he's got a shot at becoming an above average hitter with double-digit homer upside as he gains strength.

Kozeal does everything on the diamond with fluidity and ease. He's a solid average runner with a solid average arm and strong footwork on the dirt. He works well around the bag and projects to stick at second base even if he's only an average defender. 

At the plate, he has a chance to shine. There's still a good bit of swing and miss on the profile, and he's an aggressive swinger that will expand the zone at times. But if the polish comes, there's significant impact projection on the bat. Kozeal has peaked north of 112 mph from a batted-ball perspective. He can really put a charge into the baseball.

From the moment Marsh stepped on campus he carved out significant playing time and impressed scouts with his baseball acumen and hard-nosed playing style. He's added 25 pounds of muscle since graduating high school and now look the part of a true MLB-caliber prospect with burgeoning exit velocities. 

Marsh has a quiet, balanced setup at the dish with a neutral hand setup and reasonably narrow stance. His load and positive move forward are understated relying on quick-twitch hips and hand speed to generate power. To date he's shown a balanced offensive profile swinging at the right pitches and making a lot of contact. Marsh can be susceptible to softer stuff low and away but it's hardly a hole in his swing at this point. The bat-to-ball skills are strong, especially for his limited track record in college ball. 

Marsh has primarily handled left field duties for the Cardinals where his average arm strength is most appropriate. He takes efficient routes to line drives and ground balls into the gaps and gets it back into the infield quickly. His routes on fly balls into the gaps can be scenic at times, however he's gradually improved his level of comfort out there with continued reps.

Marsh is a very solid player with a steady bat and some athleticism on the basepaths. He's got a shot to fill a Role 5 profile at the next level at a corner outfield spot.

A big helium prospect during his sophomore campaign at Iolani, Ota has the size, speed, strength and projection that scouts fly in to see. It's legitimate left-handed power with more coming. Ota has flashed big bat speed and impressive exit velocities in game settings. 

Ota is already seeing his size slow him down a tick but he still projects every bit that of an average runner with average arm strength destined for a full-time role in the outfield. The hit tool will flash, though finding consistency against more premium competition will be key down the stretch.

It's taken Winslow some time to adjust to the college game, but he arrived, finally, in full force in 2026. His understanding of the strike zone improved, his bat-to-ball skills improved, and he started hitting the ball harder than ever. It's above average raw power with a developing hit tool, however he can be susceptible to better spin low and away.

Winslow is extremely talented behind the plate with fantastic pop times, a strong arm and revered understanding of the game according to his teammates. He's got a very good chance to stay behind the plate going forward.

A 19th round selection by the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2023 Draft, Morton elected to attend Texas A&M in 2024 and 2025, but struggled to throw strikes. He transferred to Minnesota for the 2026 season, his hometown school, and immediately carved out a starting role and found considerably more success. 

Morton is a tall, angular right-handed pitcher with a strong lower half and repeatable mechanics. The fastball has been up to 97, but typically sits in the 92-93 bucket with some serious heavy sink and life late in the zone. It's a high-spin heater that's done well creating groundballs. He has feel for an mid-to-upper 80s slider that he prefers to backdoor on lefties and run away from righties. It's routinely sits north of 3000 rpm and features massive two-plane tilt with considerable sweep. It's an absolute haymaker of a pitch and one of the best breaking balls in all of college baseball when he's commanding and pairing it off the sinker. 

Morton added a changeup to bridge his two weapons that move in opposite directions, and it's been excellent at limiting hard contact and giving hitters a unique look. 

He's worked to develop a consistent changeup, and it's certainly improving. He'll broadcast the pitch at times, but the conviction behind it has taken strides over the last couple years. 

Morton had been limited to relief opportunities before arriving at Minnesota, in large part to below average control and command. That seems to have taken a step forward with the Golden Gophers.
