He's a unique arm with the innate ability to shape the baseball. He could be a fun player development project and, at worst, a mid-leverage reliever when all is said and done.

It's not too common the state of North Dakota produces big league talent. In fact, as of 2025, only 20 players in MLB history had been born in North Dakota. Recent examples include Matt Strahm and Erik Swanson. The most famous names produced in North Dakota are Darin Erstad and Travis Hafner. Koenig hopes to see that list grow.

An imposing 6-foot-6-inch righty hailing from Portland, North Dakota, Koenig spent the first two years of his collegiate career at North Dakota State where he racked up 87 strikeouts in 106.1 innings against 43 walks. After tacking on 25 pounds of muscle and adding athleticism, Koenig's pitches jumped. The stuff and pitchability ticked up in a big way in 2025, leading to his pursuit of the transfer portal and eventual relocation to Ole Miss.

Koenig is good clay. It's obviously an elite frame, but Koenig's body control and feel to shape the baseball stand out too. He's been up to 98 mph and has shown the ability to create vertical hop through the zone. Koenig's fastball shape is diluted a bit by his higher launch height, but his ability to land the fastball at the top of the zone has helped produce strong whiff and chase rates in his amateur career. Perhaps the cherry on top, Koenig is a good mover who generates solid extension down the mound. He also spins the ball better than most. Given his size, arm speed, physicality and age, it wouldn't surprise if he eventually flirts with triple digits and hold mid-90s velocity.

Koenig throws a firm mid-80s slider that is a true bat-misser. He throws it for strikes, and is already producing big-league quality shapes from his breaker. Koenig innately spins the fastball better than he does the breaking ball, but his feel for shaping the baseball and throwing it firm allows the slider to play up. It comfortably projects above average going forward, and has a chance to get to plus if Koenig can generate more swings outside of the zone. 

Koenig doesn't throw his changeup often, but when he does he's shown it capable of being a real weapon. It's 84-87 with some feel for creating depth. It doesn't mirror the fastball yet, but he's proven capable of deleting spin off the pitch and generating some tumbling action. Koenig throws the pitch for strikes. It should become a bigger part of his arsenal at the next level. 

Koenig has some low-hanging fruit in terms of ironing out his mechanics that should help the command of his entire arsenal. An emphasis on tampo and arm action repeatability should unlock his next gear. He could fill multiple roles at the next level, but most scouts would like to run him out as a starting pitcher in the low minors.

Fisher was a late riser in his high school draft cycle, and because of the lack of runway, ended up at Arkansas. A two-sport star who was highly decorated on the gridiron, Fisher's future is on the mound where his low-90s fastball and low-80s curveball both project at least above average offerings moving forward. He's been up to 94 with sink and tail.

Fisher's aforementioned breaking ball is dynamite. He's had trouble throwing it for strikes at times, but when he's in and around the zone it's enormous whiff rates and two-plane shape that few can mirror in the collegiate game. It's a low-80s sweeping curveball that dives and slashes away from left handed hitters. Because of his unorthodox slot, hitters see fastball out of the hand. 

There's a changeup here as well, though it's more fringy than his primary two-pitch mix. He'll need to generate more fastball quality go capitalize on what some believe is top-100 pick upside.

A massive, imposing right-handed with a diabolical 1-2 combo, Jasa has a fastball that'll touch 98 mph with sizzle up through the zone. He's shown feel to land the heater to the glove side and will elevate the pitch to get whiffs. 

The curveball is a lock-up artist mirroring the fastball with late, sharp over-the-top break. Jasa's steepness and downhill plane can make the breaking ball tough for hitters to track out of the hand. He's added a changeup that'll flash upside in 2026 as well. 

Jasa has the loose, free delivery you want to see from a player of his size and stature. He repeats well and has traits you want to see when projecting a starter at the next level. That said, controlling and commanding the baseball have been a struggle as walks can mount. 44 walks in 45 innings throughout the college baseball season and the Cape in 2025 left much to prove, but he seems to have turned something of a corner this spring. He's likely blossom into a punch out artist in due time, but until he starts throwing more strikes his ceiling will be limited.

Nelson can really hit. He's consistently run low whiff rates with a willingness to use the whole field and take what the pitcher gives him. The swing has some uphill plane, but Nelson's feel for timing allows him to catch barrels and hit the ball hard. He'll likely never be a guy that slugs, but the efficiency of the swing could allow him to flirt with a ten-homer season or two at the next level if he's afforded the plate appearances to get there. It's sneaky pop, and Nelson knows how to pull the baseball. 

An average runner now, Nelson does have an athletic gait and could add a half-grade to the run tool with some added strength. He's unlikely to ever become a burner, but he won't hurt a team on the bases, that's for sure. 

Nelson shows off the athleticism on defense. He looks plenty comfortable at the shortstop position. His first-step quickness stands out, as does the internal clock. Nelson’s arm action at the position is a lower three-quarter slot causing his throws to tail and sink as they arrive to first base, but he's consistently on-target and never rushed. Nelson may be moved to second or third base by a more premium, physical shortstop, but he'll certainly play the position in college or the low minors. 

The hit tool will carry the water on this profile, but Nelson doesn't have many glaring holes. He's not overly physical, but his polish and feel for the game help bridge the gap between him and more explosive players.

One of the youngest players in the 2026 class, Brady won't turn 18 years old until after the regular season comes to an end in October. The stuff is already beginning to blossom for the New York product. 

Brady has touched 94 mph but his velocity gains of late have been a rocket ship. Brady was up to 90 as a high school junior and is now consistently living a couple ticks higher than that in games. It's not a bat-missing heater, more tail and sink than ride, but Brady throws strikes and generates ground balls at a high clip. 

Brady's slider is more of a cutter at this stage, 84-85 with shorter tilt and late slight depth. The changeup has been a developmental emphasis, but it's still not at a place where it's being used in games a whole lot. 

Brady is good clay with size, arm strength and youth on his side. He has a balanced delivery with the looseness and whip that projects well for adding velocity. He's also an athletic mover in terms of loading into his scap to generate shoulder speed. If a team believes they can get his secondaries to average-or-better at the next level and quickly, he's a decent bet to hear his name called with something close to a 7-figure bonus attached.

Following a big freshman season at Baylor where the Bailey logged north of 50 innings as a teenager, the transfer portal came calling and Bailey received overtures from most schools in the SEC. He ended up committing to Texas A&M, however a late change of heart landed him at McClennan CC making him draft-eligible as a 20 year old in 2026. 

Bailey has big arm talent. The fastball has been up to 98 from the left side with some tailing action, however too often the heater's shape falls into what analysts would call the "dead zone". It's a fastball that has identical vertical and horizontal movement allowing the hitter track the pitch to the plate. Because of this, his mid-90s fastball has struggled to generate whiffs and hitters can generally avoid chasing it off the plate too. Still young, Bailey has plenty of time to tinker with his grips and shapes as he matures. The arm talent and strike-throwing ability is most important at this juncture. 

Bailey's low-to-mid 80s bullet slider has the chance to be a diabolical weapon. He generates elite diving action on the pitch and launches from a slot four or five inches higher than the MLB average. At a minimum, Bailey will be a groundball artist. He's had plenty of success missing bats with the breaker too. Bailey doesn't get terribly far down the mound with his stride so generating value from the breaking ball will be paramount toward him finding prolonged success as a professional, especially if he expects to work through a lineup for a second or third time. He's certainly armed with the traits of a good one. 

Bailey also throws a changeup and it's flashed some potential as well. He's shown a willingness to throw it early and often to right-handed hitters and has shown the ability to kill spin and deaden the ball as it approaches the plate. Bailey gets huge depth on the changeup and enough fading action to convince hitters it could be the fastball just long enough. To date, he's produced strong chase and whiff rates on the cambio as well. 

Bailey will likely deviate into a sinkerballer in due time to get the most out of his arm talent and slider/changeup combo. His arsenal works best at the bottom of the zone. He's unlikely to ever be a strikeout-artist, but Bailey projects as an effective arm in any number of various role fits at the next level.

Johnson, a contact hitter with impressive on-base skills, is the rare third base prospect whose speed is his greatest tool. He's got sneaky pop, however he projects more into the hit-over-power bucket as a professional. Johnson's whiff rates are impressive and despite a reasonably aggressive approach, he puts the game in motion. 

Johnson is a formidable defender at third base with above-average arm strength for the position. His 70-grade speed may play better in centerfield than it does in the dirt, and his arm strength would be a true asset out there. Given his tools and potential versatility, Johnson is a good bet to come off the board earlier than public boards anticipate.

McKay graduated high school from the prestigious Orchard Lake St. Mary's and immediately earned the starting second base job in Lansing. After an impressive freshman campaign where he OPS'd .690 with nearly a 1-to-1 walk-to-strikeout ratio, McKay's game exploded in 2025.

The bat carries the profile here and it's distinguished. McKay is one of the best bat-to-ball artists in the country. It's next to impossible to sneak anything by him. Sliders, fastballs, elevated, buried, sweeping or fading, there just simply aren't holes in his zone. McKay is a patient hitter too. He doesn't expand the zone. Better still, he's not a slashing ground ball merchant either. McKay understands how to find the barrel despite possessing well-below average raw power. He's unlikely to ever develop into any sort of power hitter, but McKay can set the table or keep the conga line moving at the end of the order. His solid-average speed and quick first step are also assets on the bases.

McKay is a second baseman through and through. It's fringy arm strength and short, choppy steps on the dirt. He's got a chance to be an average glove as a pro. If the bat stays at this breakneck bat-to-ball pace, he's got a chance to be the 2026 version of Chase Meidroth.

The son of a former decorated NFL fullback, Lane brings similar physical tools to the baseball field. He's a steady defender in the outfield with solid average arm strength and a smooth, laid back brand of defense. Lane has played some second base, though most scouts seem to prefer the future profile in a corner outfield spot. The entire package is probably an average defender when all is said and done. 

Despite some noise in his loading phase and swing, Lane can really hit. He's been a standout in tournaments. Lane employs an open base with low hands in his setup, resting the bat on his shoulder and exploding through the zone on-time. Lane has some of the fastest hands at the plate and best raw bat speed projection in the class. He's routinely shown it off with blistering exit velocities into the gaps. Lane does a nice job limiting his strikeouts and has been more than willing to take his walks as well. He's been a high-level performer for several years and figures to be one of the more complete bats in the 2026 draft. It'll be interesting to track whether Lane's swing mechanics will translate against more premium arms as he and his peers mature. He will be a model darling as well, turning 18 years old just a week prior to the draft. This is one of the best overall impact sticks in the class.

Barczi found himself draft-eligible as a second-year sophomore in 2025, but went unselected as he was mostly a part-time player for the Commodores behind the plate. An offseason spent in the weight room elevated his bat to levels unseen in 2026.

Barczi is a power-hitting, power-throwing backstop that fits the prototype big league catcher in today's game. It's huge pull-side power from the right side with occasional opposite field power too. He does have some swing and miss in his game, however it's a comfortable trade-off for the impact he brings into the box. The throwing arm rates among the best in the 2026 class, though footwork, technique and foudational skills behind the plate looks like more of a work in progress at times. 

Scouts would like to see Barczi work to get a bit lower in the crouch to give his pitchers a lower target at times. Still, with the direction baseball is going and robo-umps on the horizon, Barczi should have no problem staying behind the plate in the modern game, and could represent the prototype moving forward.

Barczi is the ideal modern catcher. While he's still developing some polish for the roughness around the edges of his defensive abilities, his bat speed and arm talent make for awesome foundational tools to build around.

Potestio is one of the better bat-to-ball artists in the 2026 class. He projects one of the more polished batting-average archetype middle infielders in the draft with a sound approach and exit velocities that continues to trend upward.

Potestio has long been revered for his hand-eye coordination. He's run impressively low whiff rates at every stop of his amatuer career. Potestio can be a bit passive in the box but that helps keep his chase rates in check. It's elite bat-to-ball skills on pitches inside the strike zone and Potestio has shown the ability to catch up to upper-tier velocity when he sees it. This season his peak exit velocity numbers have edged more toward 40-grade power, a step in the right direction. He's always had good feel for back-spinning the baseball and hitting the ball to the pull-side. This combination has scouts bullish Potestio could eventually be a guy who runs into 10-12 homers as a professional. Still, he'll make his money by putting the game in motion while hitting in the back-third of a lineup. 

Potestio has played all over the field at different stops the last couple years. A primary shortstop at USD, Potestio took to the outfield on the Cape and showed versatility and an aptness for tracking the ball. It's solid average foot speed and some feel for situational awareness in the outfield. Potestio has shown well at the shortstop position, however, and projects to stick on the middle infield as a professional, perhaps moving to second base if there's a more premium glove in place. 

Potestio is a high-floor prospect who will serve as a conga line generator in a lineup. He's a sound glove with versatility and enough foot speed to warrant late-inning consideration off the bench. He's not too dissimilar from Arizona State second baseman Kyle Walker from a year ago, however Walker was a better runner and Potestio has a bit more power projection.

Parker is a physical left-side of the infield defender with the actions befitting of a player destined to stay there. The physicality with the bat stands out as well.

Parker doesn't have the same robust sample of at-bats against premium pitching that some of his peers do, but when tasked with putting together strong at-bats in big settings against big arms, he's often delivered. Parker shows good bat-to-ball skills against velocity and covers anything within the strike zone. It's short, quick and loud into the zone with a cut-off finish. His hand speed and luxury of late reactions in the box stand out. Parker aims to lift and drive the ball to the pull-side, however when tasked with hitting velocity he'll often choose to shoot the ball the other way. This inconsistent approach will likely polish itself out over time. Parker isn't yet showcasing consistent in-game power, however the frame, bat speed and physical projection suggest it'll eventually come and should be a big part of his game at full maturation.

Parker has some athletic tools to dream on as well. He's a solid average runner with an athletic stride that could get a bit better as he matures. He's a confident defender with solid-average arm strength. His throws carry through the bag. He's rangy enough to stick at shortstop for the time being, but his actions look destined for third base where he could be an asset. 

Parker won't turn 18 years old until a week after the Draft. He's got some model-friendly traits that could surface his name in high regard to teams in July.

Springall isn't the biggest player in the world, but he gets the most out of his tools and brings a level of polish to the field that'll be an asset for wherever he plays next. The bat has taken strides over the last calendar year and is showing signs of burgeoning bat speed. 

This is a very twitchy player. Springall shows a good feel to hit with a line-drive centric approach. He finds the barrel with a heavy frequency and can be a doubles machine peppering the gaps. It's a simple swing with a moderate leg kick, getting the foot down on time, repeating his triggers and consistently being in a position to hit. Springall has grown into average raw power projection thanks to quick-twitch rotational hips and fast hands that fly through the zone. His feel for getting to the pull-side stands out. He gets the most out of his physical tools. Springall is unlikely to be much of a power threat early in his professional career, but he'll likely grow into it with age.

Springall is a shortstop now, but his range and arm strength will likely land him at second base or in the outfield as a pro. He's got exceptionally fast hands and certainly looks the part of a future above average defensive infielder. He is an average runner who could get a bit faster with his wiry, projectable frame.

Leguernic is a low-slot lefty with funk and deception. The fastball works in the low-to-mid 90s, up to 96 with armside run and some sink. He's worked over the last twelve months get generate a bit more carry on his fastball in an effort to get whiffs at the top of the zone. While streaky, there are outings that flash impressive fastball upside.

His best pitch is a disappearing low-to-mid 80s slider with depth and considerable sweep; an impossible task for left-handed hitters. It's a pitch that's generates enormous whiff rates across this career at Clemson. If Leguernic is forced out of a rotation role at the next level, his breaking ball could be a massive weapon in specific spots. 

He'll show a changeup to righty bats that has promise. Leguernic has very little effort in his operation and scouts think he's got a shot to start at the next level. He'll be extremely young for a college prospect in the 2026 draft and won't turn 21 until October.

Something of a hidden gem for the class, Long saw a big jump in stuff this spring with a fastball that's now cresting north of 95 mph with carry and late tail. Long will mix in a two-seam to get ground balls and chase from left-handed hitters as well. 

Long's breaking ball is an upper-70s slurvy bender with middling spin traits. It's gradual and will hump when left elevated. There's components here to build an average breaking ball, however he'll have to start throwing a bit harder if he hopes to approach above average or plus grades.

The changeup is a real weapon. It's thrown in the mid-80s with advanced feel for zone control. Long will dance that pitch away from lefties and bore and fade it into righties. His comfortability with it stands out at this stage. It's got a chance to get to plus. 

Long's delivery is sound, controlled, on-time and repeatable. He throws enough strikes to start his career in a rotation and see where the breaking ball goes from there. He'll be young for the class, too. Just 18.1 years old.

McHugh began his career at VCU where he earned immediate playing time as the starting first baseman in 2024. He bashed six homers and OPS'd .775 in the A10 conference. That success landed him in the transfer portal that fall. He made his way to NC State for the 2025 season, his sophomore campaign, where he'd parlay his success from the year prior into even gaudier numbers in the ACC.

McHugh is a slugger with a distinguished hit tool you don't find in players of his archetype all too often. He absolutely hammers left-handed pitching and has shown enough feel for the barrel and eye for the strike zone from the right side to earn a full-time spot in the lineup. It's plus raw power with exit velocities north of 113 mph and McHugh will pepper the entire field splashing screaming line drives into the gaps and punishing scoreboards in right-center field. He absolutely owns the inner-third of the plate and will make pitchers pay when they try and work in on his hands. That said, he can be overly-aggressive at times with those pitches and has a tendency to chase pitches well in on his hands at times. His eager nature, mixed with his inconsistent attack plane, has had a tendency to generate more ground balls than you'd like to see from a slugging corner infielder. The whole package has a chance to become an average hitter with the potential to hit north of 25 homers at the next level if he develops more consistent ability to back-spin the baseball. 

McHugh may not be done adding strength and muscle either. He's got projection left in his lower half and has the broad frame necessary to carry more muscle. This is a very strong player who will carry considerable strength as a pro. 

Despite the size and archetype, McHugh can scoot. He's an above average runner down the line and has an extra gear around first base. Conventional wisdom suggests he'll slow down as he continues to mature, but the athleticism stands out at this point in his career. He is a bit more heavy-footed on the dirt. McHugh has shown softness in his hands and the ability to smother balls hit to him at first base. He's got a legitimate chance to develop into an above-average defensive first baseman.

Kemp is the nephew of MLB great Matt Kemp. He has some of the same loose, fluid actions his uncle had. It's an athletic, lean frame with smooth, twitchy traits. He's shown quick hands, and heavy barrel with the same long follow-through his uncle had. Kemp has some loft in his swing that has produced in-game power at this very early stage in his career. He does a very nice job staying up the middle of the field and has shown hitterish tendencies. 

Kemp is already a plus runner and is beginning to flash '70-grade' run times as he's gotten stronger and more physical. He's got an athletic gait that looks as though it'll hold his athleticism going forward. He's flashed above average arm strength at tournaments.

Battista simply looks like a hitter when he enters the box. The rhythm, waggle and setup are befitting of a confident hitter that expects to succeed. He employs many of the mechanical traits that some of the better hitters do. And the athletic tools in the outfield stand out too,

Battista sets up with a closed front shoulder, his weight anchored into his back hip with a moderately high hand set. Battista has a moderate stride forward and does a very nice job staying behind the baseball and his front side in his swing. He lags the barrel well and creates impressive bat speed, rotating hard and late. There's some power projection in Battista's swing, and he's beginning to show it as he's matured into his frame. He's quick, twitchy and explosive through the zone with some feel to use the opposite field. At his best, the whole operation is reminiscent of a player like Jake McCarthy. That said, finding consistency in his swing on a day-to-day basis will be important in his development going forward. 

Battista is a plus runner who gets out of the box and up to full speed with pace. His speed plays in the field too. It's above average arm strength that fits in any of the three outfield positions, however centerfield will likely be his home until the speed and/or instincts are replaced by a more premium player. 

Battista is an exciting prospect. There are some unpolished components, but the athleticism and tools are fairly apparent. He's a bit undersized, but the hand and bat speed are certainly impressive for a player of his build.

Dugan is a talented and projectable shortstop prospect with strong actions on the dirt and elite athleticism. He's a plus runner who can add some value on the bases and in the field with his range. He's got a bigger, longer frame, and may end up at third base when all is said and done, but the athlete and untapped potential in his profile leaves the potential for him to stick at the 6 as a professional. 

Dugan does a nice job putting the ball in play and keeping the game in motion despite inconsistencies in finding the barrel. It's a balanced, simple left-handed swing that works. He's mostly a gap hitter at this stage, but his frame and feel for the game suggest he could grow into a bit more power as he matures. 

Dugan is also an exceptional tester when it comes to force plates and explosiness scores. He's a terrific ball of clay, and a player pro organizations will want to sink their teeth into. Whether teams will be able to get over his struggles from the showcase and tournament circuit during the summer of 2025 will be the million dollar question. One feather in his cap -- Dugan is beloved by scouts in his area for his attitude, disposition, bloodines and love for the game.

Morse is an intimidating two-way talent with powerful traits on both sides of the ball. 

Most like the upside on the mound where he's already touching 98 with a fastball that jumps on hitters. At 6-foot-7, Morse towers over the opposition and presents deception and steepness in his delivery. His fastball has some natural cut and can be thrown to both sides of the plate. 

Morse throws two breaking balls that melt together, most preferring his mid-70s sweeping slider over a deeper curveball that gets broadcast a bit. There's a low-80s changeup that doesn't yet possess definitive shape, but is sold with conviction. Morse is bit, tall, loose and effortless in his operation if not a bit raw with his mechanics. 

Perhaps the biggest hurdle Morse will face at the next level is a lack of spin across his entire menu of pitches. He may have a difficult time shaping new pitches, making him a bit "stock" from a player development perspective. This comes with more relief risk. 

As Morse gets stronger and continues to evolve as a pitcher, we're talking about a guy who could live in the triple digits in a bullpen role.

A 14th round selection by the Dodgers in 2023 and 9th round selection by the Mets in 2024, Jelkin has continued to elect to bet on himself in the hopes of improving his stock. He pulled his name out of the 2025 Draft after nursing an injury for most of the season in the hopes of turning himself into one of the premier senior prospects in this draft.

Jelkin is about as projectable a body as you'll find in this draft, and the stuff and athleticism really continues to trend upwards. He's always been an explosive mover, but everything is much more under control these days, and he's throwing more strikes because of it. He'll work up to 99 with late run and some carry, though too often it's a deadzone fastball. It's a deceptive pitch that really sneaks up on hitters due to the slot, but he'll want the shape to go in one direction or the other at the next level. 

His low-to-mid 80s slider tunnels well and induces quite a bit of swing and miss featuring big depth and slight gyro sweep. There's a bigger curveball that he's struggled to command consistently, but he'll offer it to right-handed batters at times. Jelkin underwent Tommy John surgery during the 2024 campaign and really hasn't been back to full strength until 2026.

Gomez is a big, physical, barrel-chested catching prospect with tools on both sides of the ball. He's one of the more well-rounded catching prospects in the country with a chance to contribute in more way than one. 

Gomez has power projection with a physically maxed out frame. He's got big strength distributed all over his player. Gomez has solid bat-to-ball skills and has shown capable of catching up to premium velocity. Changeups in the dirt can give him issues every now and again. 

From a splits perspective, Gomez isn't particularly decorated from one side rather than the other. He is a more aggressive hitter from the right side with much higher chase rates, but those swings haven't blown up his contact skills.

Gomez's tools with the glove are strong. It's plus arm strength with pop times that can appoach 1.90 at his best. Gomez is up and out of the crouch with tempo and quickness. He's a very skilled defensive prospect. 

There's not really many directions Gomez's frame can go from here. He'll need to be sure to make sure he doesn't get too big and outgrows his athleticism. As things stand, his rare ability to provide value with both the bat and the glove will have teams interested in July.

Tryba carved out an extended role for the Gauchos immediately upon arriving in 2024 logging 47 innings as a true freshman punching 65 tickets and issuing just 14 walks. He continued to work primarily in a bullpen role in 2025 and continued to punch tickets at a very high clip.

Tryba is a very unique looks for hitters. It's a super-low launch with a fastball he's still able to hold some vertical carry on. The fastball has produced impressive whiff rates up in the zone. His changeup gets hitters to expand outside of the zone at unhealthy clips and generates strong whiff rates, however Tryba is still at a place in his career where he's only throwing it less than ten percent of the time. Given his fastball and release traits, finding better feel for that pitch would truly elevate his bag of tricks. The slider is his favorite weapon and he throws it often and for strikes. It's a big sweeper that can generates close to a foot-and-a-half of lateral action with some late diving action.

Tryba has a deep arm swing with impressive scap retraction and some inversion at foot plant. That has led scouts and analysts to forecast a relief role at the next level. If Tryba continues to throw strikes and develops a strong feel for three or four pitches, it's likely he starts his big league career in a starter role until he proves he cannot fit that billing.

A draft-eligible sophomore barely 21 years old in July, Aceves is one of a number of MLB-quality arms at UC Santa Barbara for the 2026 season. A three-pitch mix and quality fastball metrics make for a firm foundation for player development to sink its teeth into.

Aceves doesn't have the same runway with Andrew Checketts at the Santa Barbara pitching development program that names like Bremner and Flora have flourished out of the last few seasons. He's in year two at school and thus is still getting his feet wet with this level of competition. That said, it's easy to appreciate what he's already bringing to the table. It's a pro-ready frame with big strength, durability and athleticism baked in. Aceves is on the bump playing catch with his battery mate, not overexerting himself or out-throwing his operation. He pounds the zone with the fastball, too.

Aceves' heater will grab 96 but more commonly sits in the 91-93 range. He generates above average carry through the zone and gets considerably more arm-side tail to his heater than most with hop profile he creates. Aceves has generated a healthy number of whiffs on the fastball, and hitters have shown a willingness to expand the zone against his primary offering too. Most of this is done through deception and hitters picking up the baseball late out of the hand. Aceves doesn't get very good extension down the mound, and his capacity for spin on the fastball is rather ordinary. Given its production and performance metrics to this point, it's fair to assume another velocity jump would comfortably place his fastball in the above average category, and it could jump into the plus tier if Aceves finds a way to live more mid-90s rather than low-90s going forward.

Aceves splits his secondary usage equally between a big slider and an impressive changeup. The breaking ball is fringy from a strikes perspective, but its enormous vertical profile does generate whiff in the zone. It's not a pitch he's gotten much chase out of, and some of that goes back to his ability to spin the ball and create sharp break. For now, it's mostly an average slider, but could take a jump with a bit more velocity. It's currently usually a low-80s offering.

The changeup has a bit more exciting profile. Aceves gets significant arm-side tail to his changeup and gets almost a foot of vertical separation off his fastball vertically. It's a weapon that's generated huge chase rates and respectable whiffs too.

Aceves didn't get a ton of opportunities to start as a freshman, but will likely jump into more rotation opportunities in 2026 with innings available to him. He'll need to show a tick better control, but the peripherals here are exciting for a player as green as he is.

A rocket ship up arrow arm during his junior year, Webb has been up to 98 mph in showcase events and will hold 90-93 in game settings. Webb has some effort and recoil through delivery but is generally around the zone generating whiffs at the top rail with moderate carry. He's a good extender down the bump allowing his fastball, and the entire arsenal for that matter, to play up above its 'stuff'. Webb does have some whack and effort through release, perhaps the biggest barrier toward starting at the professional level. 

Webb throws two breaking balls; a bullet slider and a bigger, firm over-the-top curveball. The slider is ordinarily 81-85 with some lateral tilt and sharp hammer biting action downward. The curveball is a bit sharper, generally in the upper-70s and low-80s with heavier vertical break. Both breaking balls flash plus upside. There's also a changeup but he rarely goes to it. 

Webb has starter traits, a good, durable frame and pitches with tempo and conviction. He does a nice job holding runners with a quick delivery out of the stretch.

Colin White has some of the best stuff from the left side in the country. He's up to 96 with carry and arm-side run, the ball exploding out of his hand. He's got a chance to throw very hard, and the shapes to supplement the heater into becoming a true bat-missing weapon. 

The fastball likely won't end up his best pitch and a huge, sweeping breaking ball has plus or better upside written all over it. It's two-plane tilt with late, sharp break. The whole story with White will be whether he improves his strike-throwing ability. The frame is very good and he projects to become quite physical in time. There's some effort at release and that's caused his walk rate to balloon on him at times. If he gets to the point where he can command the strike zone, there's the upside for two plus pitches on the menu. 

White will be 19.6 on draft day and will be expected to dominate the opposition in the months leading up to the event.

A talented two-way prospect and a bit hidden at Glynn Academy, Sammis isn't a player who was terribly present on the showcase and tournament circuit in 2025. He's always been a performer, however scouts have had limited opportunities to see him play aside from league player for Glynn. That said, he's a bit stronger this spring and scouts have rushed in to see his growth.

Sammis has good size for a shortstop. He's got a 6-foot-1-inch frame, broad shoulder and some strength in his upper-half. There remains some projection in his levers, however he's likely approaching his peak athletic and physical form. 

At the plate, Sammis employs a wide, squatted base with neutral hands, an upright barrel and some frenetic waggle in his setup. He loads into something of a rigid state with almost no weight transfer, instead using ground force to develop tension. Sammis has a moderate leg kick without his head changing plane. He's direct through the zone with some natural loft to his swing; a line drive hitter with the capacity for some back spin. Sammis' ability to separate the hips from the shoulders helps him uncoil solid bat speed -- a major part of his developmental growth this past winter. For now, Sammis looks like a well-balanced hitter that may be able to get into some game power at the next level.

Sammis is a steady infielder with some range. He's got excellent footwork, rounding through the baseball and taking his momentum toward the first base bag whenever possible. He's got above average arm strength and has enough athleticism to make the play moving to his right. That said, Sammis isn't a great runner, posting fringe-average times home-to-first more often than not. Considering his frame, he's unlikely to ever be extra value with his legs. Still, the tools and athleticism are here for at least an average glove at second base or third base, and perhaps shortstop if he doesn't get much bigger.

Sammis has been up to 95 mph on the mound with a developing breaking ball as well. Most scouts prefer his game with a bat in his hands, but the arm talent does speak toward some of his ceiling and versatility.

An undersized lefty that works from a composed, deliberate operation on the bump, Davis is an advanced thrower of the baseball. He's got strength in his lower-half and operates with balance and polish. It's a three-pitch mix, plenty of strikes and some projection to go in his upper-half.

Davis will run it up to 94 mph and will routinely live in the low-90s with a fastball that tails and sinks at times. It's a pitch that sets up his breaking ball/changeup combination.

The breaker is a bigger with two-plane break. His comfort throwing the pitch stands out, landing it to right-handed bats and left-handed bats alike. It's a little light, generally in the upper-70s, but Davis has a quick arm and could grow into a tick more velocity in the coming years.

The changeup has good shape, arm speed and conviction, however Cutshall does broadcast it at times, lowering his slot. A relatively easy fix as a pro.

Davis' undersized frame will cap his upside in the draft, but left-handed pitchers with projection, three pitches and strikes are generally a popular demographic.

Scolari spent two seasons at San Diego and tacked on considerable weight and muscle in his time there. Draft-eligible in 2025, he went unselected despite overtures in the first five rounds. Scouts were worried they would be unable to sway the second-year hurler away from his commitment to Oregon. 

This is as prototypical a starting pitcher prospect as you can find. He boasts well-above average extension from a simple, repeatable, effortless delivery. Scolari throws strikes and has two pitches that can miss bats. 

Scolari boasts a fastball that's been up to 96 mph with carry and cutting action. At his best, Scolari can boast fastball shapes few in the sport can. His ability to miss bats with the fastball stands out.

Scolari pairs the fastball with a sweeping slider in the mid-80s with more lateral tilt than depth. It plays nicely off his fastball when he's cutting the heater as mentioned. Scolari struggles to repeat his breaking ball shape, but the hope would be he polishes that part of his craft up in professional baseball. There's a mid-to-upper 80s changeup, though it's largely below-to-fringe average at this stage.

Where he fits in this Draft will largely depend on how much further teams believe he could blossom with professional development.

A three-pitch specialist with burgeoning control and command for his arsenal, O'Brien has been a player development success in Spokane and now has the eyes of scouts.

This is a drop-and-drive delivery with a low-launch for a pitcher of his size. O'Brien's fastball is a traditional four-seamer that has been up to 97 mph. He creates flat angle to the plate thanks to his release height and ability to stay behind the seams of the baseball. At times, O'Brien can hold enough vert on the fastball to approach 15 or 16 inches of IVB; a devastating shape at the top of the zone for a player with his underlying release traits

Both his slider and changeup induce swings and misses and moderate chase outside of the zone. They both side in the low-to-mid 80s and both are executed into the zone at average rates.

O'Brien's ability to repeat his delivery with three unique pitches and unique metrics under the hood should help him hear his name called on day two of the Draft.

After a dominant year in the Oregon State bullpen, Palmer left Corvallis seeking the opportunity to start and showcase his durability and stamina in a weekend role. He transferred to Cal Poly for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign. 

Palmer saw a meteoric rise in stuff this spring with a fastball that jumped up to 96, resting 91-93 in just about every showing. An elite mover, Palmer gets well-above average extension through release and generates above-average carry on the heater. He cuts the baseball quite a bit, effective at the top of the zone, especially considering his 63 inch launch height and 6-foot-6-inch frame. Palmer gets a ton of scap load and projects to throw quite a bit harder as he gets into pro development, some foresee triple-digit upside. Palmer's big body and athleticism are quite evident.

Palmer's slider is a mid-80s two-plane breaker with some shortness at its crest. It's a pitch that'll need to sharpen up and get later break to reach what some believe is a plus ceiling on the pitch. There's also a changeup he hardly ever deployed, a pitch that lacks dynamic shape at present.

There's some low-hanging fruit to unlock more velocity here, and scouts rave about his makeup off the field. The breaking ball may dictate his draft ceiling, but the components to dream on are terrific. Palmer was the Texas Rangers' 20th round pick in 2023, but went unsigned.

Skowronski originally enrolled at the University of Kentucky coming out of high school, but a lack of playing time resulted in him transferring to Winthrop for the 2025 and 2026 seasons. He's left an impression on scouts with his size, tools and physical projection. 

At 6-foot-5 and 220 pounds, Skowronski certainly looks the part. He's well-built with physical tools that cannot be taught. Despite his size, the strength and frame are not yet resulting in raw power. Skowronski's exit velocities are on the fringier side, however he's got fast hands with some twitch providing him the luxury of making late decisions to swing. It's resulted in strong chase rates -- he forces the pitcher into the zone. 

Skowronski's hit tool has some intruiging traits. He covers anything and everything elevated in the zone, and has shown no issues whatsoever handling velocity. For now, his biggest issue is softer stuff low and away. Skowronski aims to pull the ball with authority, so covering the bottom-third quadrant on the outside corner can give him some fits. Overall, his bat-to-ball metrics are on the fringier side -- however most of his whiffs come outside of the zone. He's solid average when swinging at pitches inside the strike zone.

Given Skowronski's size and feel for getting to his pull-side, it's hard to imagine he won't eventually tap into more bat speed and raw power. For now, it's something of a tweener hit/power profile. 

A primary corner outfielder, Skowronski moves well for his size. He's a long-strider, reasonably light on his feet. It's plus speed. He tends to track the baseball well, however his comfortability is clearly tested on the road in unfamiliar outfields. Skowronski can get a bit timid around the wall, and he'll sometimes struggle to convert the tougher play into an out. All of the physical tools are here to suggest an above average defensive corner outfielder could eventually come to fruition, but for now there are moments of inconsistent play. He's got above average arm strength. 

Skowronski will need to tap into more raw power as July approaches to realize his top-five round upside. There are strong physical tools on both sides of the ball, just unrefined.

Bowen is certainly an up-and-comer in the 2026 class with athletic tools across his entire game. He plays with an athletic flair that is hard to miss. A solid average runner with a wide, athletic stride, Bowen figures to not only get faster as the months pass, but should hold his speed into his professional career. 

Offensively it's a hit tool that has really surged over the last calendar year with added strength and reps. Bowen has a whippy stroke with show-off hand speed, direct to the ball and holds no biases to the pull-side. The bat continues to improve and is slowly becoming one of the more noteworthy sticks in the region. 

Defensively, Bowel plays with range and tempo up the middle of the diamond with enough arm strength to project at shortstop going forward, though an unorthodox arm action and inconsistent arm accuracy may encourage him to second base over time. Bowen plays low to the ground with quick hands, fast transfers and bounce in his step. 

He's an exciting young player who continues to get better. Bowen is on the older side and will be 19.5 years old on draft day.

Mansbery is essentially how you'd draw up a very solid ballplayer if plugged into ChatGPT. He doesn't everything well. He may not be spectacular in any one area, but the sum of his parts is a potential future big leaguer that can play any number of positions as a professional. 

Mansbery's demeanor at the plate is stoic. There's no waggle, no unnecessary movement patterns, no ribbons or frills. Mansbery sets up in an upright athletic position with a slightly closed front shoulder, high hands and a moderately wide base. He picks the foot up in his load and puts it right back down. The stride is abbreviated and serves its purpose. Mansbery can at times get the hands going forward before his rotation begins, diluting some of his raw power and bat speed, but his 6-foot-3-inch frame is oozing with physical projection and strength gains on the horizon. As he gets stronger and locks into a firmer front side, the bat speed and power production should take a considerable jump. For the time being, he's a doubles machine with a line drive appoach. He keeps the barrel through the zone for an extended amount of time and uses the whole field quite well. It's hit-over-power for now, however there's obvious reasons to believe his potential for slug is coming.

Mansbery shines on the defensive side of the ball. He's shown plenty comfortable at the shortstop position where he glides across the dirt and never appears rushed. The internal clock stands out. Mansbery's length and stride help his range both to the left and the right. It's solid average arm strength that plays best coming in on the ball and moving to his left, however he can make the highlight reel play moving into the '6' hole on occassion if the runner isn't a burner. Mansbery himself is an average runner, though considering his frame and athleticism, a speed bump with strength gains shouldn't be ruled out of the equation.

There's a lot to like in this player from a traditional scouting lens. Mansbery is easy to dream on, and he's already showcasing the defensive prowess necessary to hold a big league role.

After redshirting as a true freshman in 2024, Johnson carved out a decent sample in 2025 for Cuesta JC hitting .346 and being named to the All-Western State Conference First Team. That afforded him the ability to transfer into Northridge for his draft-eligible 2026 season, a season that's led to more success.

The bat is the headliner grabber. Johnson has a moderate leg kick with some waggle and counter-coil in the load. He doesn't overswing to get to his bat speed and relies on uncoiling his lower half, using ground force to do the heavy lifting. There's some tip in the barrel and occassionally some excess hand action in the load, but it hasn't inhibited his ability to get barrel to ball yet. 

Johnson consistently hits the ball hard and has awesome feel for getting to the pull-side. He makes plenty of contact, however he can be a bit aggressive at the dish, expanding the zone at a relatively high flip. When he does swing outside of the zone, he hasn't yet shown much adjustability to fight off those pitches for foul balls. Johnson hammers velocity and hasn't struggled with spin in the zone either. There's above average raw power projection here with a barrel that stays through the zone for an extended amount of time, flashing exit velocities north of 111 mph. 

Johnson is an average runner with a wide, long stride that could conceivably get a tick faster in pro ball with development. He's a rangy defender with the ability to throw from multiple angles. It's above average arm strength with carry across the diamond.

Johnson's overall hit tool and pitch selection ability will be highlighted as the draft approaches. He's clearly got some tools in the box and on the dirt to carve out a role. He'll turn 21 just a month prior to the draft.

Omidi generates easy bat speed and has tremendous feel for the fattest part of the bat. His pull-side raw power projection is his biggest selling tool, however the hit tool has demonstrated the polish necessary to see the power come through in games. It's a simple swing with a short, direct path to the ball, compact into the zone with fast hands/wrists. Omidi gets to loft with selling out to get to it. A bigger leg kick helps him stay into his legs and drive the ball with authority.

Omidi is a shortstop by trade but will likely end up at second base, third base or left field as a pro. It's fringy arm strength and actions more befitting of a player outside of the middle of the field. He is an average runner who is unlikely to gain much more speed on his physically muscular frame. 

Omidi will turn 18 years old just a month before the draft so he has age on his side. His training age is probably more age-appropriate. He's a good looking stick who could add offensive impact to his future employer's lineup.

An impressive hitter with a flair for the dramatic, Murphy always seems to be involved in the big moment. His swing is balanced and controlled, quiet and compact. Murphy creates space in the box and transfers his weight efficiently. He's on time for velocity and spin and puts the ball in play with intent. He really projects to hit going forward. The frame should grow into some more raw power in time as well. 

Murphy is a plus runner with above average arm strength. The speed plays better on the bases and in the outfield than it does purely home-to-first. With a long follow-through in his swing, Murphy is often out of the box delayed. It's easy to fall in love with the traits. He's not just a showcase guy either. Murphy has performed at the biggest tournaments the sport has thrown at him. He's got a chance to play centerfield at the next level and profiles a well-balanced impactful player. Murphy will be 18.7 years old on draft day.

The word "raw" can be taboo in scouting circles, but James certainly fits the bill. It's unpolished, inexperienced, and a work-in-progess, but the crude traits that he'll flash are remarkably impressive. He's dramatically changed his delivery over the last year, now showing more refined timing windows and sequencing. Because of it, he's blossoming. 

James has been a been of a rocketship prospect over the course of the last twelve months as he's seen his stuff absolutely explode. The fastball has gone from 90-93 during the spring of his junior year, to now brushing 98 with sink and exceptional tailing action. Better still, it's a low-launch missile that can miss bats at the top of the zone or generates ground balls away from right-handed hitters. He'll still spray the heater a bit, but the arm talent and prospective value of the pitch is exciting if he can harness his command. The cherry on top? James is an elite mover who can flash extension numbers north of 7 feet at times. 

Perhaps more important, James has flashed (rarely) elite slider metrics. He's routinely 84-86 with the breaker, but he's shown a couple low-90s sweepers with a willingness to throw it at the back-foot of right-handed hitters. Again, James doesn't entirely know where it's going yet. It's a breaking ball with enormous upside, even if he's not consistently getting to its best shapes or velocity bands. 

Everything about James is being flashed in small samples. He's got lockdown late-inning reliever stuff that's already very present. He'll need to prove capable of throwing strikes and holding his velocity across multiple showings as July approaches, but the ceiling is fun.

Hudson is a polished, confident athlete on the bump and really knows how to pitch. Alpert has brushed 94 with a fastball that's launched out of a deceptive high three-quarter slot. There's carry and some tail on his heater with big spin rates. He'll generate whiffs when landed arm-side to righties. Alpert can really get down the mound too with plus extension allowing his velo to play up. He projects to add velocity too thanks to his frame, quick arm and loose, fluid athleticism. 

The slider is his go-to put-away pitch. It's a low-80s frisbee with more sweep than vertical plane, though Alpert will tinker with its shape depending on the situation. It's an above average breaker and could end up in the 'plus' category as he gets stronger and generates more fastball value. He'll flip in a changeup that he's working to develop, but at this stage he's hardly needed it. There's starter clay here.

Wood is an exciting shortstop prospect who, while undersized, has proven capable of playing above his weight class. 

Wood's athletic traits stand out in a big way. He's a 70-grade runner who routinely takes the extra base. It's a scatback running style with short, choppy steps with feet that can start a fire. He's a very strong defender at the shorstop position with above-average arm strength and throws that carry through the bag. His lateral mobility stands out for his size. Wood always seems to be in the right position on the diamond at any given time as well.

Offensively, the bat to ball skill stand out in a big way. He puts the game in motion and has sneaky bat speed capable of occassionally losing one. He more likely projects a doubles and triples hitter who generates his offensive value with stolen bases. 

"Firecracker" seems to be a strong label for his game. He'll be 19 years old for the Draft.

A big, physical left-handed hitter, Hearn represents one of the better athletic prospects in Southern California for the 2026 Draft. While there is still some figuring out to do with regards to where he'll play in the field, some of the traits he possesses should make for an enticing development project for a player development team.

Hearn's profile is anchored heavily by the bat. A 6-foot-4-inch left-handed hitter, he brings bat speed and the potential for serious impact into the batters box. Hearn deploys an upright stance with some waggle and counter-rotation in his setup. It's a short, flat, compact stroke with heaviness in his hands. Despite some stiffness, Hearn generates plus bat speed and has the frame and projection to suggest 70-grade raw power on the horizon. There's some rawness and polish necessary to get Hearn into positions to find more consistency and repeatability in his operation at the plate, but there's athleticism and some feel for timing here that will make for molding the player easy. Hearn shows a natural ability to get to his pull-side helping drive the narrative he'll get to his raw power in games. 

Hearn's approach has been steady. He doesn't expand the zone and keeps his whiffs rates in healthy ranges. There's still too many ground balls in his profile, but Hearn's speed does help ensure those aren't automatic outs.

Hearn can burn down the base line. He's routinely clocked home-to-first times under 4.2 seconds despite often times being slower out of the box due to his swing follow-through. Underway, it's 70-grade run times. He's got a chance to be a base-stealer as a pro.

Hearn will need to find a defensive home. It's below-average arm strength in the outfield with mechanics that can be prohibitive toward arm accuracy and arm strength gains. Hearns routes to the ball in the field are solid. He looks comfortable tracking the baseball. He's played all over the outfield, but likely profiles in left field as a professional. It's possible he ends up at first base at the next level if some of the athletic tools in the outfield don't come along, however that would certainly be a waste considering his foot speed.

Hearn has similarities to a player like Luke Raley. It's big, strong and athletic with a blue collar approach to at bats. It's fast and physical in the outfield, if not unconventional. He'll probably be able to unlock the ability to play in the outfield as a professional, however he may never necessarily be a value-add out there. Hearn will be 18.5 years old for the Draft.

Zdunek is a prototypical right field prospect with a burgeoning bat, space to fill out the frame and enough athletic tools to provide impact on both sides of the ball.

The hit tool stands out in a big way for Zdunek. It's a tall setup with some counter-rotation in his load. Higher set hands are quiet, loaded into a powerful position, firing with little wasted actions into the zone. He employs a simple leg lift and moderate stride forward with a pull-side emphasis and some feel for generating loft. Zdunek tends to flatten his path as the velocity he's facing trends upward causing more ground balls. He also predictably struggles to get to the pull-side as he faces harder throwers. Zdunek doesn't have any glaring holes in his profile from a bat-to-ball perspective. He's handled spin just fine. That being said, he is an aggressive hitter who expands the zone at a healthy clip causing contact-quality woes every now and then. Still, it's hardly resulted in any strikeout issues at all. This is a player who puts the ball in play consistently. 

Zdunek has the frame and bat speed to project above average bat speed and raw power projection. The frame is going to add 10 to 15 more pounds of muscle before he's reached his peak form. Given his feel and desire to get to his pull-side, the game power should come naturally in time.

Zdunek has some tools in the outfield, too. He receives the ball soft and out in front of his frame. The footwork is solid and he looks the part of a guy who will stay in the outfield. Zdunek has solid-average arm strength with an arm action that doesn't project to add too much more oomph at the next level. He's a fringy runner who could gain a half-step with speed training to get the stride moving quicker. 

The bat is the standout tool for Zdunek. He could eventually become an above average hitter with above average raw power. His arm strength will play in either corner. From a model perspective, he will barely be 18 years old for the Draft.

Moore was a draft-eligible second-year sophomore at the University of Kansas, buit Nate Yeskie and the LSU Tigers came calling in the transfer portal giving Moore enough leverage to return to the college scene for another year. It's not a prototypical power starting pitcher profile, but the pitchability and arsenal of offerings stand out. 

Moore's fastball will grab 96 with awesome sinking shape out of a very high slot, especially from a player just 6-feet tall. Moore works best when he's getting around the pitch inducing horizontal tailing action to the arm-side. It's one of the steeper fastballs in college baseball. Despite its middling velocity, it's remarkably effective for what it is. Moore doesn't spin the ball particularly well and doesn't miss many bats with the heater, but it acts as a means to an end to generate soft contact and get to his secondaries. 

The changeup is his best pitch, and it can be disgusting when parried off a well-commanded sinker. It's 83-85 with tunneling shape generating big whiff rates. It's every bit a plus changeup when he's landing his pitches where he wants. 

Moore has shown a decent cutter that will back up on hism at times in the upper-80s. The sweeper and curveball have both taken positive steps at LSU, although finding consistent shapes, especially from the sweeper, is a work in progress. Moore is more adept and getting left-handed hitters to strikeout, however soft contact from right-handed hitters is typical. 

This is four or five pitches and tons of strikes with dynamic arm-side shapes. He's undersized and lacks fastball swing-and-miss value, but there's some velocity and definitive feel for the zone.

It's been a rocket ship twelve months for Holden Herring who finds himself considered by many one of the top junior college prospects in the country. After originally commiting to play baseball at Texas Tech in 2026, he flipped to Weatherford College in an attempt to once again garner the attention of scouts. It worked.

In high school, Herring flashed a 95 mph heater toward the end of his prep career, but mostly sat 90-92 after the second inning on most nights. Fast-forward to his freshman year on campus and Herring is now brushing 98 and is more routinely living in the 92-95 bucket as he lathers. Hering's fastball gets whiffs thanks to above average extension down the bump and moderate amounts of ride that play well if he's commanding at the top of the zone. He's been in the zone a bunch as a freshman.

The secondaries are a little less daunting, but the clay is here for development. The curveball is generally 77-80 with some hump, but there's capacity for spin. Hering also throws a low-80s changeup that will flutter and fade late, however he utilizes that pitch inside the zone too frequently. Its shape is plenty conducive for whiffs with better command. As his sequencing and execution for the secondaries improves, so too will the strikeout totals.

Hering has many of the prototype starting pitcher markers. He'll need to throw more strikes, and more quality strikes, but considering the age, the body, the stuff and the feel for shaping a baseball, it's easy to dream. He'll barely be 19 years old for the Draft. He's essentially an older draft-eligible high school senior touching 97 facing stiffer competition. Hering has a case to be the first junior college name off the board, and could go inside of the top five or six rounds.

Tronstein is a fearless hitter with an aggressive nature about his offensive game. He's a rhythmic hitter with super fast hands and an ability to cover the inner third against premium velocity. It's twitchy hips with the ability to create space and separate at the plate. There's some power projection here that he's begun to tap into in batting practice sessions clocking exit velocities north of 108 mph at times. Tronstein has some variability and moving parts in his swing that includes several different leg kicks and some hand and barrel triggers. To this point his quick hands and compact swing have covered any concerns with projecting the hit tool. 

It was a difficult summer for Tronstein in 2025 as he struggled to find consistency in the batters box due to those variable triggers in his swing. He worked hard throughout the winter to make some swing changes and those changes seem to have made a big difference in his production this spring. 

Defensively he can really go get it in centerfield. He takes strong routes to the ball and tracks/closes on the ball nicely. It's above average speed with plus arm strength that is a real asset in any outfield spot. Tronstein has also played a good deal of shortstop throughout different point of his high school career. It isn't out of the realm of possibility he begins his professional or collegiate career on the dirt. High level tools here. Tronstein will be 18.4 years old on draft day. He's expected to be a difficult sign away from Vanderbilt.

Riordan is a bat-first middle infield prospect who possesses enough athleticism to potentially stick on the dirt as a professional. But as is the case with most prospects, his ceiling will be dictated by whether or not his bat continues to blossom. 

Riordan has seen a nice rise in his abilities offensively over the course of the last twelve months. He's added bat speed and twitch in the box, allowing him to keep up with more premium pitching, however he still struggles to catch up to the velocity of the better arms. There's still a decent amount of swing-and-miss in his game, but Riordan does well staying inside the strike zone, consistently spitting on pitchers' pitches. While his approach can at times get a bit passive leading to streaky strikeout woes, he balances those trips back to the dugout with plenty of walks -- and the extra base hits have ticked up too. Riordan will likely continue to get better as he adds strength. His swing currently gets disconnected at times, primarily due to his lower half rotating quicker than his shoulders. The twitch stands out, but to his detriment at times for the time being. He's a bit undersized, so it's unclear just how much impact he'll ultimately be able to grow into, but pound for pound, the bat speed at this stage stacks up nicely next to most of his peers.

Riordan is a shortstop now, however he'll likely end up at second base, or perhaps third base, when all is said and done. He's got soft hands and some bounce in his step, but the arm action is more befitting of a player that moves off the '6'. Riordan is an above average runner, but he gets good breaks out of the box and can on ocassion stretch the legs and snag above-average run times home-to-first.

It's easy to dream on Johnson and his 6-foot-3-inch frame. It's top-end athleticism with projection on the way. The peak offensive tools stand out. 

Johnson can put a thump into the baseball. The package comes with some swing and miss, but his batted-balls are so efficient, teams will happily take the impact in exchange for some whiffs. Johnson's adjustability in the box stands out in a big way. He puts together competitive at-bats and has shown plenty capable of impact pitches that aren't in the strike zone. He does a very nice job matching his plane with the pitch as it comes in. The game power projection because of it stands out. It's comfortably above-average raw power projection, with plus not out of reach. It's bat speed that is already showing itself in game settings. Johnson has an exciting top-end offensive projection if some of the polish around his plate appearances irons itself out as he works deeper into bigger and better levels of competition.

Johnson is a solid-to above average runner who seems to be picking up steam in the run tool department as he's gotten stronger. He can play all three outfield spots. He's played centerfield at times for his travel ball team, but will rover between left and right field as needed. Johnson owns an average throwing arm.

Meyer is your prototypical huge stuff, scattershot command righty with a mid-90s fastball that's been up to 98, settling in closer to 95. His whole arsenal possesses high spin rates highlighted by a massive slider that can get a little squirrely. It features enormous two-plane tilt with elite sweeping action and huge depth. He'll bump 3300 rpm on the breaking ball, and it's been up to 88 in the past. If Meyer ultimately ends up in the bullpen, the breaking ball will be a neutralizer in short outings. 

At his best, Meyer can be a dominant two-pitch guy. The slider flashes double-plus and is almost impossible to hit for righties. When he's not on, Meyer can walk a lot of batters. This is an electric arm with good athleticism on the bump and a huge ceiling if/when it all clicks. Because he has a tendency to change his release point to achieve a multitude of shapes, most scouts and analysts see a future in a bullpen for Meyer at the next level. 

Meyer was kicked off the West Virginia roster in early March. He pitched just 3 innings in 2026.

Minick is a solid player in the box. He’s tall and sets up with an open front side with high hands. His leg lift leads into a small stride. The whole operation is controlled. While Minick is unlikely to ever become a decorated bat-to-ball artist, his exit velocities suggest a slugging archetype with impact too all fields is in the cards at the next level. 

Minick is an efficient hitter too. He has feel for getting to his pull-side and elevating the baseball. He's a launch magnet and gets into his above-average raw power with ease. 

Minick has previously been a primary third baseman with solid average arm strength befitting of a player at the position. He's made the move to centerfield in 2026 in an effort to let his speed provide more value on the field. His first step in the grass and lateral quickness is above average, and his hands are also just okay on the dirt. The tools simply play better in the outfield. His versatility may provide some extra value in the draft.

Following two dazzling seasons at Western Kentucky, Whalen hit the transfer portal for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign. He signed on to pitch for War Eagle and brought his big fastball and dynamic changeup to the Cotton State. 

Whalen has a good fastball that's been up to 96 mph. It's elevated by exceptional extension and above-average spin rates. He also launches from a slightly lower than average slot allowing the heater to generate some extra value at the top of the zone. Whalen has a generic four-seam shape and probably won't miss buckets and barrels as a pro, but there's enough fastball value here to project a solid-to-above average heater if he can find just another tick or two in the velocity department. To date, he's missed bats and forced hitters to expand the zone at above average rates. 

As mentioned, Whalen's cambio is a good one. He throws it a ton and misses bats inside and outside of the zone at heavy clips. There's enormous depth on his changeup and he kills spin very effectively. Whalen repeats his arm slot beautifully and sells the pitch with big arm speed. He also generates close to 10 mph of separation from his heater. It's every bit that of a plus pitch and he figures to rack up strikeouts at the next level with it. 

Whalen does have a fringier slider that he'll throw now and again. It's firm, 83-84 with two planes of break and a bit more lateral action than depth. He's struggled to land the pitch for strikes but has produced good results when it's in/around the zone. 

Whalen has a durable frame, a bulldog mentality and a go-to out pitch. There's some effort through release and his strike-throwing ability to date has been fringy. There is some relief risk on the player, but given the feel for three pitches and ability to hold his good stuff into the fifth and sixth innings, Whalen is likely to begin his big league career as a starter until he proves incapable otherwise.

Wachsmann has tacked on strength and size over the course of the last calendar year and is pumping some of the best stuff in the 2026 class. It's three pitches, strikes and a workhorse frame.

Wachsmann has touched 96 and will rest 91-94 as he works a lather into the third and fourth innings. He's got aptitude for spin and can generate some interesting shapes with his arsenal. The fastball is tailing missile launched from a three-quarter slot, barreling in on right-handed hitters' knuckles late. It's got some life and extra value at the top of the zone. 

The changeup is the best secondary and it's got upwards trajectory. Wachsmann's fastball shape and look out of the hand makes it easy to tunnel and pitch off of. He'll fade cambios away from left-handed hitters with some late tumble when he rolls off it. There's impressive velocity separation on that pitch as well.

The breaking ball has components to build on, especially above-average spin rates. For now, it's a curveball in the upper-70s with slurvy tendencies. It relies a bit on command to be effective at this stage. Placed into the right professional organization, elevating the metrics and production of that pitch shouldn't be too difficult.

Wachsmann has size, stuff, a loose arm and enough strikes to warrant considerable draft attention. He'll barely be 18 years old for the Draft, however he is said to be a tough sign away from Wake Forest.

Tryon is a balanced player who doesn't have any one tool that jumps off the page, however his consistency and translatable traits should make the jump to pro ball easier than most.

It's hard to poke holes in Tryon's game. He boasts above average bat-to-ball skills with the pitch selection skills and approach that allow his impact to play in games. Tryon handles velocity and isn't fazed by spin or pitchers that can command to all four quadrants. He's adjustable and can survive long at-bats. It's loose hands in the box and some whip in the barrel. Tryon can hit, and with a few adjustments, he may be able to unlock a bit more power.

Tryon employs a setup at the dish stolen from the 90s. It's slightly hunched over the plate, the barrel resting on his back shoulder. He has an understated leg kick and forward move built to use the opposite field. He's short into the zone and takes his hands directly to the baseball. He sacrifices the leverage his lower-half can create in favor of spraying the ball all over the yard. That said, if the opposition leaves him something soft in the lefty-loop zone, he's shown plenty capable of turning and burning. It's solid average bat speed that plays to the opposite field fence. Should Tryon make a few adjustments with his lower-half, he could tap into above average raw power and the potential for a few 20-homer seasons at the next level. He's a sneaky athlete capable of making those changes. 

Tryon has plenty of experience playing the corner outfield spots, however most believe he's best at first base. He's an average runner and does get a quick first step. His arm is average and plays comfortably in left field.

Some scouts like Tryon's profile to that of Kyle Manzardo during his time at Washington State. It's an old school look  with a polish about his game.

Robertson was a hidden gem in the 2025 MLB Draft out of Walters State CC. A 13th round selection by the Texas Rangers, Robertson elected to test his luck at Virginia Tech as a draft-eligible junior for the 2026 campaign. He is still on the younger side having turned 21 years old just two months prior to the Draft. 

Robertson led the JUCO ranks as a sophomore in 2025 in the strikeouts department. He's a big data guy. It's a low-launch righty with a fastball capable of hopping over the barrel featuring tailing action and some late sink. When Robertson holds vert and elevates the fastball, it can be brutally difficult for righties to make contact.

Robertson throws a tight slider in the mid-80s with lateral tilt and some sharpness late. He can occassionally get in trouble when he leaves that pitch up, creating a hump in its approach. 

Robertson's longer arm swing does lead some the question his ability to start at the next level, but it's put-away stuff and a potential leverage arm floor in the bullpen if he stays healthy.

Loew is an interesting infield prospect with a power-over-hit profile that could one day slug for considerable impact at the next level. He projects to get more physical and considerably stronger in the coming years thanks to a stacked lower half and muscled-up core. 

Loew's greatest strength is not his hit tool. It's what he can do to the baseball when he's on time and on the barrel. Loew is as efficient a slugger as you can in the country when he's right. Loew's ISO in 2025 was a remarkable .240. That will happen when you're as strong as he is and you're producing a fly ball rate of over 43 percent -- good for second-best in the country among players who posted at least 70 plate appearances. Better still, his feel for extending and catching the ball out in front stands out. Loew produced a healthy 23 percent Air PULL% this past summer. 

That said, swing and miss and strikeouts have nullified his bat too often in high school circuit play. 

There's reason to buy stock now before Loew unlocks a new gear offensively. His innate ability to create stretch and coil in his swing is hard to teach. He stacks into his back hip better than most at this age. Loew lags the barrel in a way that creates serious torque and whip through the zone. According to Blast Motion, Loew ranks in the 92nd percentile among high school hitters on the Over-Slot draft board for average rotational accleration. He ranks in the 83rd percentile in hand speed among that same bucket of hitters. The raw bat speed is also comfortably plus.

For Loew, it's a sequencing issue. His timing and his triggers are inconsistent. During his load, he brings his hands in tight to his core, mirroring a leg lift to build energy on that stacked back side. As he makes his forward move, the hands are still moving backwards. He'll often get his front foot down before his hands are in a firing position. Because of this, the swing sequencing gets disconnected, making it awfully difficult to get on-plane on time. Marrying his hands and his move forward, specifically when the foot gets down, will help him stay on time against better pitching as he works his way into professional baseball (or in Baton Rouge).

An LSU commit, Loew is going to have two senstational options when the draft comes around in July. By all accounts, he's got a great head on his shoulders and comes from a humble, supportive family. Loew has all the tools on the field and off the field to turn himself into a mashing infield prospect as July approaches. He's a name to keep tabs on. 

Loew is an above average runner with a solid average arm in the field. His future likes sits at third base where his lateral mobility and physical frame will be less tested than it would at the '6'. Loew will turn 19 a couple months after the 2026 draft and would be eligible once again in 2028 if he ends up at LSU.

A reclass up from the 2027 draft, Arnold is one of the more exciting prospect to come out of the state of Rhode Island in a handful of years. 

Arnold has some strength to him in the box. He sets up with a moderately wide base, knees slightly bent with the barrel laid back on his shoulder.
