He drifts back and anchors into his back hip in the load, dropping his hands into a slot to fire. That move gets him quick to the baseball. There's a good bit of uphill loft in Arnold swing. There's an obvious emphasis to hit the baseball in the air, and the results support it. Arnold's 64 percent Air Contact% was among the best of any high school hitter in 2025. There's strength in Arnold's hands with some natural feel to get to the pull-side. He hasn't been tested with bigger velocity yet, and that could pose some issues for a hitter with his swing plane. He's had some in-zone whiff issues at times on the circuit, but nothing to suggest a terrible red flag. To Arnold's credit, he's shown a mature approach to hitting and hardly ever expands the zone. He's not in much hurry to walk, and strikeouts have been a part of his game, but those have come alongside slug, a difficult combination to find in a shortstop. 

Arnold is a fringy runner but does have some range to his left on the dirt. His athleticism and fluidity on the dirt can be tested moving to his right. Arnold does have above average arm strength and has proven quite capable of playing third base when asked. He's particularly impressive charging slow rollers/choppers and firing across his body. Ultimately, the hot corner will likely be his full-time position at the next level, perhaps second base.

Rivers is an ultra-strong, physical catching prospect with a barrel chest, broad shoulders and strength well-distributed about his frame. He shows burst and athleticism behind the plate, especially out of the crouch. He could stand to get a little deeper into his hips, but he's already a big, physical kid so that's rare from a frame like this. It's a strong throwing arm too, though his arm action can get a little "hitchy" and long in the back at times. He's shown fundamentals behind the plate, and has a shot to stick back there at the next level. 

At the plate, Rivers operates from a wide open, upright stance, but puts himself in a good position during his load. There's considerable bat-speed here, and Rivers extends out well driving the ball to all-fields, locking in to a firm front side. It's at least plus bat speed, however his swing plane as presently constructed creates more top spin. He'll be the first to admit he can get pull-happy, but the swing works in-game to cover line-to-line. The entire profile isn't terribly dissimilar from a guy like Kyle Schwarber, and there will be pressure on Rivers behind the plate like there was with Schwarber. Ultimately, the bat (like most prospects) will carry the profile. Rivers will need to stay on his flexibility as the body continues to get stronger.

Harris certainly looks the part of an imposing 1B/OF slugger at the plate with tangible strength and power plainly observable in his frame. Harris has the enormous bat speed you would expect from a player of his stature and has routinely posted elite exit velocity figures in practice sessions. It's comfortably 70-grade raw power, and he'll get it in the air. 

Harris is held back a bit by something of a grooved swing. He can struggle to adjust on pitches he offers at outside of the zone. Scouts would like to see him use left-centerfield and develop some hitterish trends as he matures toward July. Bat-to-ball has been a point of emphasis in his development. Getting to it in games will be key. It's a three-true-outcome type of profile.

Nelson is a hitterish shortsop prospect with a sound left-handed swing built to pepper the opposite field gap and keep the game in motion. He doesn't possess much slug at this stage, and doesn't present as the type of player who will eventually impact the ball with consistency. The hit tool will drive the prospect value.

Nelson is a sure-handed defender at shortstop with above average lateral range and plus foot speed underway. He's got average arm strength with quick hands. It's second base tools, however Nelson will likely begin his professional career at the shortstop position until he's forced elsewhere.

Piech missed all of his freshman season due to Tommy John surgery but has burst onto the scene since. 

It’s mostly a two-pitch mix with Piech, primarily using a four-seam fastball and big curveball against both-handed hitters. His changeup is still a work in progress. The fastball has plenty of desirable traits. Due to his high slot, Piech’s fastball tilt can eat hitters up. The pitch has elite ride and primarily plays at the top of the zone, complimented by strong command for the top rail. Piece is sitting 91-94 but can reach back for 96 early

The curveball tunnels perfectly off his heater, working from the top shelf into the bottom of the zone. The pitch can garner freeze early in counts and panicked swings late in the count. The velocity difference is stark, with the vertical separation from the fastball forcing hitters to constantly be in between.

Piech built in a gyro ball slider this season in the mid-80s that's bridged his arsenal together nicely. He's shown steady command for that pitch as well. 

There are clear questions that Piech needs to continue answering if he wants to start as a pro. He needs to show a changeup and the ability to combat left-handed hitters with something more than spin. He's young for the class, and reasonably green to college pitching. He'll turn 21 years old after the Draft.

Georges added a ton of physicality over the past 12 months recovering from Tommy John surgery. The stuff has really come on. It's a pro frame with a broad upper body and sturdy lower half. A lot to build upon. 

Georges has been up to 96 mph and likes to pitch at the top of the zone with considerable carry and arm-side run on the fastball. Georges spins the ball well and will routinely rip fastballs north of 2350 rpm. He'll mix in a low-80s breaking ball with bullet spin, occassionally tilting the pitch laterally away from right handed hitters. It's been north of 2800 rpm. 

The changeup in particular has taken a jump since his injury. Georges shows feel for shaping that pitch and will tumble it away from left-handed hitters deep in counts seeking swing-and-miss. His strike-throwing ability has been streaky, though the recently added size and weight seems to have taken much of the inconsistencies out of his delivery that troubled his early high school career pre-injury. 

With an elbow injury already on the medical report, Georges will always have to fight that wart in draft war rooms. That said, the frame and the stuff are more than befitting of a top 100 pick in July. He will be 19 years old on draft day.

Nickoli is an intriguing shortstop prospect who has seen his game and his name blossom over the course of the last calendar year. The tools have really begun to come on of late.

Nickoli is a switch-hitter with good hand speed and a tight, compact swing from the left side. He has burgeoning raw power by way of added strength in his frame translating into more twitch offensively. The same can be said about his swing from the right side, however the swing can get just a little longer with some extra length in his triggers. It's still far from prohibitive in his ability to make solid, loud contact. Nickoli has run strikeout rates that are a tick higher than scouts would like over the course of his amateur career, and ground balls have had a tendency to thwart his offensive upside in game settings. He seems to be turning a corner in those departments with the added muscle. 

Nickoli isn't the biggest, most imposing physical specimin, but he does look like a guy who could grow into above-average raw power over time. 

Nickoli is a dynamic mover. He's posted sub-4.10 splits from home to first and projects to be at least a 70-grade runner at his peak. Nickoli moves very well on the dirt with a quick first step and some lateral range. He's likely destined for second base as a professional, but can play the shortsop position when asked at a proficient level.

Amalbert entered the 2025 summer as a well-liked arm by scouts in the Northeast, however strong bat-to-ball skills across multiple events raised eyebrows. Amalbert has played all over the infield and in the outfield at times -- his versatility a plus in his tool belt. 

Amalbert's up-the-middle approach stands out. He has a knack for hitting the ball hard back where it came. He's not inherently a powerful player yet, but the frame does have more room to fill out and scouts believe there's the potential for solid average raw power once he fully matures. That muscle should supplement what is already solid feel for the barrel.

Amalbert has some athletic tools that play nicely at myriad positions. It's above average arm strength that plays better in the outfield than it does on the dirt. He's an above average runner too. He's capable at several positions, his versatility likely a major selling point for his profile at the next level.

Mataczynski was a late pop-up prospect in the summer of 2025 after showing out at WWBA in Jupiter, Florida. 

Mataczynski oozes projection. It's a long 6-foot-3-inch frame with long, wiry levers and twitchy strength. He employs a wide base at the plate and leverages his back hip in his setup and load. The swing is a bit crude and unrefined, but there are components to dream on. For now, Mataczynski has an exaggerated forward move and swing across his front side. It's a flat path built to pepper the gaps with line drives. There's zero questioning the bat speed and raw power projection, but as presently constructed it's a slashing hit-over-power profile. 

Mataczynski is a swing tinkerer. He's altered his leg kick, stride and swing path a number of times over the last couple of years in high school baseball. Adjusting to professional instruction and swing changes at the next level shouldn't be difficult. 

The athlete, although unrefined and unorthodox, stands out in a big way. Mataczynski is a plus runner with a sprinter's stride. He reaches full-speed faster than most. It'll play on the bases. 

Defensively, Mataczynski shows the ability to throw from multiple angles and hold his plus arm strength in just about any circumstance. When moving to his left, it he can dial it up even more. He's a bouncy defender with some range that comes by way of his stride length. Matacyznski can play a bit out of control at times and his clock can speed him up, but all the tools, traits and projection are here for a dynamic defensive player. 

The cherry on top, he's been up to 94 on the mound. 

Mataczynski is an exciting ball of clay. As he gains strength, the whole package will likely become more clear. As it stands, he's certainly a player development gem.

Adetuyi missed his entire freshman year at FAU recovering from Tommy John, but returrned as a redshirt freshman flashing a big breaking ball and enough velocity to suggest a future pro role. Now a year old, stronger, and distanced from the surgery, his stuff continues to trend up.

Adetuyi is primarily a three-pitch guy these days. The four-seam fastball is quite generic from a shapes perspective, but he has been up to 93 mph, complimented by nearly 7 feet of extension. It performs better than its metrics might suggest it should Still, it's likely an average, perhaps a bit better, pitch at the pro level.

Adetuyi makes his bread with the breaking ball, and it's a good one. An low-80s sweeping slider, Adetuyi gets huge depth and solid horizontal break on the pitch. He's generated impressive whiff and chase rates on it, as well. This is a guy that keeps hitters guessing with deception and a wider arm angle.

His changeup has really upside, too. It's got enough vertical separation off the fastball to be productive, and can fade a bit as well. 

Adetuyi likely profiles as a mid-leverage reliever that specializes in getting left-handed hitters out. He could use a tick forward in the velocity department, but as he gets further away from the injury that may come. He will also be just 20 years old for the Draft.

A metric darling, Harpster is going to miss bats. He's a 6-foot righty with a long arm swing, some deception in a slight cross-fire delivery, and he throws strikes. Harpster will lead with the fastball, but his secondaries are coming along.

Harpster makes his money with the fastball. It's 91-94 with a low release height and enough carry to sizze over the top rail, missing barrels. His feel for commanding the top of the zone is also strong. Harpster's middling velocity is elevated a bit by well-above average extension, especially for his size. Better still, his capacity for spinning the baseball helps his heater hop late. Given his strike-throwing ability, this should play as an above average heater or better at the next level. 

Harpster throws a nasty changeup that gets plenty of ground balls. It's only four or five ticks slower than the four-seamer, but he does have to drop his slot a few inches to get to his shapes. Professional hitters will likely identify that change out of the hand, so he may need to tinker with how he deploys an offspeed pitch as a pro. 

Harpster throws a mid-80s cutter with lateral shape, as well as a sweeper with much larger sweeping action in the low-80s. Like the changeup, his secondaries usually rely on dropping his arm slot.

Harpster has a chance to start at the next level due to his strike-throwing ability and his feel for shapes out of the hand. Carving through a lineup a second time with how he's currently altering his delivery might be a tall ask. Still, it's fastball value as a foundation and strong spin rates. He'll be a popular name if he makes out of the top ten rounds for any reason.

LaFavor has the makings of.a starting pitcher going forward. It's a long, wiry frame with a whippy arm action, enormous extension and far more velocity on the horizon. LaFavor is still learning how to most efficiently use his physical traits, but he's already got a strong lead-leg block, elastic scap load and exceptional contralateral trunk tilt. 

LaFavor is at least 20 pounds away from his eventual playing weight, so there's much more in the tank. That said, he's already touching 92 and can hold 88-90 in his high school starts. The fastball will flash intriguing carry through the zone, however his release orientation is inconsistent and his shapes will vary, especially as he fatigues. As mentioned, LaFavor's extension is borderline elite. He'll approach 7.5 feet at times. This makes his middling velocity play up a few mph to the hitter's eyes. If LaFavor continues to add strength and the fastball jumps into the mid-90s as July approaches, it's a profile that will skyrocket to scouts. 

LaFavor is throwing a slurvy breaking ball in the upper-70s. It's got two plane break and will flash above average components, however LaFavor is presently dropping his arm slot considerably to achieve his breaking ball shape -- something hitters will pick up on at the next level.

His changeup is likely his best secondary,. It's more consistent than his breaking ball and possesses more dynamic shape. LaFavor will approach 20 inches of arm-side fade with the cambio, but again drops his arm slot to get there.

If LaFavor becomes more repeatable with the operation on his secondaries and his velocity spikes, he's got traits to hear his name called in the first few rounds of the Draft.

Following two dynamic seasons at Kent State, Bean transferred to Louisville for his 2026 campaign.

Bean is a terrific mover. He gets tremendous extension down the mound with tempo, looseness and fluidity. He's what scouts draw up when looking for the athlete that'll succeed in professional baseball.

To date, Bean hasn't gotten the value he'd hope from his fastball, but there are components to it that should improve with further development. He's been up to 96 and has shown the ability to hold 91-93 into the mid-innings of his starts. Bean gets moderate carry on the pitch and tends to tail it a bit as well. It's been effective getting hitters to expand the zone, but not it missing bats. 

Bean's curveball is an absolume. A mid-80s bender with two planes and enormous shape, firm with late, sharp tilt. It's every bit that of a plus breaking ball and it'll flash 70-grade traits when he's commanding it. 

Bean's got a slider and a changeup, both of which will flash at times. 

The potential here for a four-pitch mix and a double-plus carrying weapon sell the profile. Combine the pitch grades with the mover on the bump and it's easy to get excited about Bean's future.

It's been a gradual ascent for Todd over his four year collegiate career. After redshirting to get bigger and stronger at Dallas Baptist in 2023, he got his first game action as a redshirt freshman in 2024. He was limited to just 11.2 innings. He then logged 13.2 innings in 2025 as a sophomore, but walks curtailed a blossoming arsenal. Seeking more opportunities, Todd transferred to Pacific for his redshirt junior year, earning a starting role.

Todd owns a fastball that can be awfully unique. He's a drop-and-drive guy who generates well-above average extension, launching from a lower slot, generating solid carry. Todd has developed the ability to command the ball at the top of the zone, and his walks have come down, too. It's elevated his profile, garnering plenty of whiffs. To date, he's been up to 94 and more comfortably lives 89-92.

Todd has a menu of pitches that all possess lift. His cutter sits 83-84 with prototypical cutter shape. His sweeper, on the other hand, is something of an outlier. It's 79-80 mph and will consistently sit north of 10 vert. It's a frisbee slider that never falls. There's also a rarely used changeup that, when he's generating drop, can be effective.

Todd's middling velocity will likely limit his opportunities in the draft, especially being 22 years old already. He does have some uniqueness to his secondaries, and perhaps he'll carve out a relief role at the next level because of it. He's a day three bullpen prospect, and perhaps a money-saver.

Willoughby is on the older side for the 2026 class. He'll turn 19 a couple months prior to the draft and will find himself draft-eligible once again in 2028 should he go unselected.

The fastball has been up to 96 and will live 93-95 in one-inning outings. Willoughby is more commonly 91-93 after the first inning of work. His fastball has tailing action and Willoughby has shown the ability to pitch front door and back door with that pitch. 

The changeup is his best secondary. A dive-bomber with some late fizzle, Willoughby gets solid velocity separation off that pitch. There's conviction in his arm speed too. 

A firm slider in the 82-84 range is his best breaking ball. He has a tendency to drop his slot a tick to achieve the vertical shape he's currently getting. Some hitters identify that out of the hand rendering the pitch less productive.

Willoughby is a very good mover with a loose arm, strong extension, and strength projection in his upper half. He'll likely reach back for 97 or 98 in due time.

Dierks is funk and filth. It's a high leg-lift with deception, some cross-body action, a closed front side and an already fully optimized front block. He's got elite direction down the bump with balance and intent through delivery. There's some effort through release and his ability to repeat his release point can at times waver, but the strikes are palatable and the feel for landing his arsenal exists. It's solid extension and a launch height few hitters will find comfortable; especially high. 

Dierks is already up to 98 mph and will generate a lather in the 92-94 bucket. He's generates cut and carry through the zone with a supinator profile. Dierks gets whiffs with the fastball alone. 

He bridges two breaking balls with an upper 80s cutter that keeps righties off the barrel and generates weak ground balls. The slider is presently a low-80s bullet-breaker that will at times back up on him. He pairs a mid-70s 12-6 bender off to create diving action.

Rounding out the arsenal is a mid-80s changeup that dives toward the plate; especially effective out of his high launch.

This is four or five pitches, plenty of strikes, at least average command and physical projection. It's unique release traits and a bully mentality. Tons to like.

Moutzouridis was one of the most impressive pure hitters on the West Coast as a freshman in 2024. He possesses above-average to plus bat-to-ball skills and brings an advanced approach to the plate, unwilling to expand the zone. It's fringy power at best and Moutzouridis doesn't project to grow into much more muscle. 

He's a strong defender at both shortstop and second base and has the look of a full-time regular at the next level who hits toward the back-third of a lineup and keeps the conga line moving. One of the higher floor prospects in 2026.

Duer represents one of the more exciting senior draft-eligible prospects in 2026. Already 23 years old when he's selected, Duer won't have much leverage in the draft and will likely have to take a significant under-slot deal regardless of round. After stops at TCU and Florida Atlantic along the way, Duer has found his footing in College Station.

There's a lot to like about the hitter here. Duer has consistently walked more than he's struck out, and swings at the right pitches. He runs well-below average whiff rates and has begun to flash average raw power in games. He's unlikely to ever become a real slugger, but this new element in his game has dramatically raised his profile. Duer is a pure hitter with solid average speed and can add some value on the bases, too. 

Duer has played all over the outfield, but right field seems to be his calling. He's an instinctual defender with a strong IQ and takes good routes into the corner. He's got slightly above average arm strength and is capable of holding runners station to station. 

Duer really doesn't have a weakness. He's not a prototypical slugger, but he'll ambush mistakes these days. He's a sum of his parts type of role player with a strong hit tool and enough value every where else on the field to become a Role 45 performer as a pro.

After a year in Gainesville, Philpott hit the transfer portal and landed in South Carolina seeking rotation opportunities. 

Philpott saw a meteoric jump in his stuff from the time he arrived onto the college scene. The fastball jumped from what was a low-90s heater to a real weapon touching 97, maintaining 93-94 after the first inning. He produces huge spin rates on his fastball and can generates 'plus' carry through the strikezone at times as well. Philpott is a very good mover and generates above average extension down the mound. Philpott has thus far shown average control for the zone and walks can get streaky on him as he fatigues. 

Philpott throws an average slider that's firm and tight, occasionally showcasing some depth. There's also a changeup that will dive to the arm-side when he stays behind it. Both pitches need to show more consistency and/or bigger shape traits to project to the next level. The changeup is currently his best secondary and will flash above average in-zone traits. An injury slowed his 2026 considerably.

Brzustewicz hits everything. He's an accomplished bat-to-ball merchant who does have a tendency to expand the zone, but the hand-eye coordination is so strong he still puts the game in motion. That aggressive offensive mindset has limited his impact potential, something he'll certainly need to rectify as a first base prospect with size being on his side.

Brzustewicz has bat speed and he does a nice job leveraging the ground to create leverage and game power. But his willingness to put pitchers' pitches in play has diluted his exit velocity output. If he's to capture his top-ten round upside, he'll have to find more barrels. 

Brzustewicz is a fringe-average runner with a more lumbering running style and figures to slow a tick in professional baseball.

Alicia is your prototypical sparkplug profile that gets inserted into the top or bottom of a lineup and keeps that conga line moving. He's a frustrating at-bat for the opposition and refuses to give away an opportunity. 

Alicia won't be the guy providing much thump or slug. He's a slasher with an opposite field approach. It's borderline elite bat-to-ball skills and the passive approach that allows for long counts and selective triggers. Alicea won't swing at pitches outside of the zone, and if he ever does, he's fouling that pitch off or slapping it into play. Alicea profiles as a high-OBP machine with the athletic tools to make him meniacal.

Alicea's plus speed plays in a big way offensively. He tends to slash the baseball to the left-side of the infield, forcing long throws, tested by his pace down the line. Once on, he's not in any hurry to stay at first base. 

Alicea can handle both second base and shortstop at the next level. His physical tools are more befitting of the former with arm strength being the biggest challenge when tasked with handling the '6'. That said, he's a scatback defender who gets more out of his tools than most. He can certainly play shortstop up the minor league ladder and man the position in a pinch at the big league level. 

Alicea has the type of tools that are sought after on day three of every draft. He's got a high floor and middle of the diamond traits.

Scott is an intriguing catcher with a strong, thick catcher's frame and more strength on the way. He's an athletic mover who has displayed above-average lateral mobility and burst out of his crouch. The defensive tools standout as he projects a reliable backstop who will stay behind the plate. Arm strength has ticked up to above average and Scott has showcased pop-times in games under 2.0 at times. He'll flirt with 1.8 in showcases. 

Scott is something of a confounding offensive profiel. He's ultra, ultra, ultra passive in the box and works himself into pitchers counts without swinging. He's also had an issue with watching strike three go by. That said, when he's pulling the trigger, there's reason to believe this is actually a pretty darn good hitter. Scott possesses exceptional bat-to-ball skills and consistently puts the ball in play when he offers at the pitch. Whether inside the zone or outside of the zone, Scott has the hand-eye coordination to battle. Ground balls have had a tendency to pull down his slash line. 

Scott could end up a power-over-hit profile when all is said and done. He's got plenty of bat speed and rotational torque, but needs to get the ball in the air more often. He exhibits enormous pull-side power in batting practice. 

An approach overhaul could unlock a what some believe is one of the best high school catchers in the class. Scott plays a physical brand of baseball with polish not seen in many of his peers. Young for the class, he'll be just 18.1 for the draft.

Pompey has played all over the infield in his collegiate career but looks best suited for the third base in the long run where his physical frame and arm strength will play nicely. After two seasons at Texas Tech, Pompey transferred to Arkansas for 2026

The bat has taken a considerable step on campus with more raw power and a better approach. Pompey burst onto the scene as a true freshman showcasing significantly more strength and over-the-fence power than was forecast in high school. It's plus bat speed and at least above-average game power at the next level. All that said, Pompey has what some consider to be a grooved swing. It present lacks adjustability and feasts on mistake pitches in his hot zones. He struggles to foul pitches off that he's fooled on and struggles to identify spin out of the hand. Those components to his offensive profile lead some to believe he may only ever peak as a below-average hitter at the next level and will rely heavily on his raw power to derive production on the offensive end. Pompey has all the physical tools in the world and a great frame to grow into but until he makes adjustments to his swing his impact may be capped to boom-or-bust outcomes. 

Pompey moves really well for his size and has some lateral burst. He is still growing into his frame and strength. The quirks in his swing could iron themselves out naturally as he gains body control. His athleticism and foot speed will keep him playing at least an average brand of defense wherever he lands on the field.

Hull was a popular draft-eligible sophomore playing for George Mason in 2025. A big year was parlayed into NIL opportunities at North Carolina, another year for Hull to continue proving his impact potential in a bigger conference. 

Hull's bat took an enormous step forward in 2025. He got remarkably stronger and it unlocked athleticism that required more muscle and mass to access. Hull makes plenty of contact both inside the zone and outside of it. Hull is more of a slasher that swings across his body and prefers to put the game in motion rather than leaning into his size and strength to create impact to the pull-side. His swing currently creates far too many ground balls with opposite field rates that leaves something to be desired from a player with his physicality. Hull's peak exit velocities point toward a plus with plus raw power, but his contact quality and approach at the plate are currently resulting in 40-grade game power. A few adjustments here and there and Hull has the look of a guy who could transform into something like Luke Raley. But he's got work to do to get there. 

Hull is an above average runner, however his first few steps are Flintstone-esque; choppy and short to get up to speed. He's an aggressive runner who will use his speed on the bases to steal bags. He almost exclusively played right field at George Mason with future fifth-round pick James Quinn-Irons flanking his right in centerfield. As a Tar Heel, he's been taking centerfield by the horns. Hull is moving even better than he was as a draft-eligible sophomore and now looks the part of a capable centerfielder. Average arm strength supplements long strides and steady routes. 

Hull has components few in this class can match. It's size, it's solid speed, it's burgeoning bat speed and it's left-handed. There are only a handful of players in this class that can match those traits and tools. He is draft-eligible for the second time in two years.

One of the faster players in the 2026 class, Danza is a burner who has the luxury of carrying that speed in a premium 6-foot-1-inch, 205-pound frame. Danza has physical and athletic tools that could help take him to his impact ceiling. 

Danza's swing is unconventional. There's moving parts including an early counter-rotation, a late, handy load, a moderate leg kick and some inconsistencies from a timing perspective. Danza engages his lower-half well to generates torque and coil in his swing. It's plus power projection with a hit tool that has played well at Clearview High. He's got feel for turning the barrel heavy and hard. If Danza can quiet down the operation, he'll get to his bat speed and raw power with more frequency.

Danza can play the shortstop position with impressive lateral range and the athleticism necessary to throw from multiple angles. The arm strength and arm action may ultimately be more befitting of a third baseman or an outfielder when all is said and done. 

The athletic testing, foot speed, raw power and frame are all exceptional here. If it all comes together, it's high-ceiling impact upside.

Following two seasons operating in a relief role for the Texas Longhorns, Harrison got the opportunity to start full-time in 2025 and thrived. The biggest reason for the added responsibility? His walks plummeted. He ended up pulling his name from the 2025 Draft in search of one more tangible jump to improve his draft stock. 

Harrison features a four-seam fastball he'll run up to 94, but more commonly rests in the 90-91 bucket. It's not a dynamic pitch in terms of shape, release profile or spin, but Harrison hides the ball and releases from the wide side of the rubber creating deception for the opposing hitter. His feel for landing the fastball to the glove-side stands out, creating a wide horizontal approach angle for hitters to track. It's been effective missing bats at moderate levels in 2025. It's unlikely better than a 45-grade pitch at the professional level unless Harrison can add more velocity.

He's worked to fold in a sinker with more frequency and that's a pitch that exhibits more dynamic shape. That said, Harrison is forced to drop his arm slot close to five inches to achieve it. Pro hitters may pick up on that, especially in a starting role. 

His best pitch is a sweeping breaking ball. It's firm, up to 89, but more commonly 82-84 mph. He generates a good deal of lateral action on that pitch. It's been especially effective generates whiffs. It's got the components necessary to be an above average offerings eventually at the next level. 

Harrison changeup is also formidable. While it hasn't missed as many bats as you'd like to see at this stage, the shapes he's producing suggest there's some small tweaks that can be made to get more impact out of the pitch. 

This is four or five pitches and improved strike-throwing ability. Harrison probably won't hear his name called until "day three" unless one of his pitches suddenly becomes truly dynamic. He's draft-eligible for the second year in a row, however this summer he's a definitive pro prospect.

Thomas walked away from day-two money in the 2025 Draft as a draft-eligible 21-year-old throwing for Hawaii. His production and arm strength landed him in the transfer portal where he'd commit to TCU for the 2026 season. He'll play the entire season at just 21 years old.

A big, tall, prototype-framed righty with a starter's build, Thomas certainly looks the part and then some on the bump. He uses his body extremely well, generating 7.3 feet of extension down the mound. He's essentially dunking the baseball on hitters. And it shows in how the fastball performs.

Hitters are forced to make a decision early on his low-to-mid 90s heater. Thomas has been up to 96, but lives 91-94. He's generated enormous chase rates at times throughout his collegiate career. It's a heater that moderately hops and tails into the right-handed hitter. 

Thomas has been fastball-heavy for most of his collegiate career, however he'll fold in an upper-70s slider that's slurvy in nature. He'll flipped over a handful of mid-80s changeups too.

The 2026 Draft will be a birthday present of sorts for Thomas. He'll turn 22 years old just days before the event.

One of the top high school prospects to come out of the state of New Mexico in quite some time, Del Angel has physical tools including one of the best throwing arms in the class. Del Angel is also a plus runner with a long, athletic gait that figures to hold true into the next level. His athletic testing also ranks among the best of his peers and it certainly confirms the eye test. 

Offensively, there's some unconventional loading triggers and setup at the plate, but he gets the foot down and has performed in front of scouts. Quieting the hands and weight transfer in his swing will likely come in time. The tools here are sensational, now comes the time to try and make it look pretty. It's not like unconventional swings haven't been drafted high in the past. Outfielder Benny Montgomery had a severe hand hitch in his load and was still a top ten pick in 2021. Del Angel will be 18.9 years old for the draft.

After spending a year at Saint Leo University, Sandefer transferred to UCF for the 2025 season where he brought his fastball-heavy arsenal to the Knight's bullpen. He then transferred to Gainesville for his draft-eligible 2026 season. 

Sandefer is up to 96 with sink and tail. He hides the fastball well and generates considerable arm-side late running action. Sandefer generally sits 92-93 and has shown the ability to hold that into the fifth and sixth inning of his starts. 

Sandefer's breaking ball will flash big stuffiness, however landing it for strikes is streaky. He's 80-83 with the sweeping breaking featuring spin rates that'll exceed 2800 at times. Sandefer drops his arm slot and tends to shorten his stride on the breaking ball, something big league hitters can pick up on. He'll need to work toward repeating his delivery for his entire arsenal if he hopes to lather through a lineup for a second or third time as he moves up the minor league ladder. 

Rounding out the arsenal is a nasty changeup with heavy fading action. It's 81-83 launched out of the same slot as his slider. Sandefer generates big chase and whiff rates on the cambio and some scouts believe it's a future plus pitch, however he needs to generate more depth on that pitch for it to take another step forward. 

This is primarily an east-west profile with a ground ball emphasis. The slider is a true weapon. Getting stretched out and showing the ability to pitch a big innings load in 2026 will help Sandefer cement himself as a potential Top 100 pick in July. He's got three pitches, strikes, stuff and the athletic, wiry frame scouts covet every summer.

Wright blew up during his sophomore campaign at Bowling Green establishing himself as one of the most intriguing young catching prospects in the 2026 Draft. His performance vaulted him into the transfer portal where he'd relocate to Knoxville. Exceptional defensive skills and a burgeoning bat, Wright has the chance to eventually develop into one of the more well-rounded two-way backstops in the country.

The 2025 MAC Defensive Player of the Year, Wright caught 36 games behind the plate and logged 22 more games in the outfield as a sophomore. His athleticism and feel for the game play best in left field. Wright threw out 14 of the 30 would-be base stealers as a sophomore, a testament to how quickly he gets out of the crouch, as well as his solid-average arm strength. His pop times routinely sit in the 1.95-2.00 range. Wright has a tendency to put the ball right on the pillow when throwing down to second. He also allowed just three passed balls on the season. Wright has a chance to catch at the next level with an outfield corner being a suitable backup plan. 

At the plate, Wright is a bat-to-ball specialist with elite in-zone whiff rates and enough adjustability to extend at-bats fouling off pitchers' pitches. He's an aggressive hitter who isn't afraid to expand the zone, and that's stymied his contact quality at times. Wright doesn't hit the ball particularly hard and will need to focus on pulling the trigger on more damage pitches as July approaches. It's below average raw power and underwhelming barrel skills, but if Wright can change his approach to hitting it's possible he finds more impact in the slugging department. He does have feel for catching the ball out in front of the plate and pulling it in the air, however the pitches he is putting in play are rarely mistake pitches. For the time being, Wright profiles as a low strikeout, low walk hitter. He may run a reasonably healthy batting average, but his on-base percentage at the next level may suffer and he doesn't own the bat speed to make up for that wart in the slugging department. Wright is also a solid-average runner who isn't afraid to snag the occasional extra bag if the opposing pitcher isn't paying close enough attention. 

Wright's defensive versatility and prowess brings a floor scouts will surely appreciate. He needs to develop a more impactful offensive identity as the Draft approaches if he hopes to capitalize on a top-five round ceiling.

Long considered a premium defender with true shortstop traits, Durnin struggled a bit on both sides of the ball at Wichita State in 2025. He had Tommy John surgery in 2024 that not only created rust in his game, but muscle atrophy also slowed his recovery and ultimate return to the field. Finally back to full strength following the spring of 2025, Durnin took his talents to the Appalachian League and dominated for Kingsport to the tune of a .407/.519/.662 slash. He hit six homers and stole ten bags in his 40-game sample. Once again, the lights were shining bright for Durnin and his prospect helium. 

A Missouri product, Durnin elected to transfer home from Wichita State for the 2026 season to play for the hometown Tigers. He brings a steady calm on the dirt and a leadership quality about his game. The oldest of three brothers, Durnin has worn that quality with pride throughout his young life. Players gravitate toward him. 

The aformentioned defensive prowess stands out. It's a plus glove with above average arm strength and the lateral range to stay at the '6' going forward. You know what you're getting from Durnin on the dirt.

Offensively, the bat-to-ball skills and approach are sound. He swings at the right pitches and doesn't expand the zone. It's gap-to-gap power, with enough juice ot run into 8-12 homers per year. He's a solid average runner who gets a bit more value out of his speed that one might expect due to his baseball IQ.

Bastian is the classic case of a player going to college, getting bigger and stronger and blossoming into an entirely new version of himself. He arrived to Jacksonville a 5-foot-10-inch outfield prospect weighing just 174 pounds. He's tacked on close to 20 pounds in college, much of it coming in his lower half. The results are showing up all over his scouting report. He elected to transfer to Florida for the 2026 season, seeking bigger, brighter lights and the biggest stage in college sports, the SEC. 

Bastian's hit tool is still coming on but scouts are bullish on the trajectory. His bat speed and hand speed have both increased considerably over the past 12 months and he's getting to pitches at the top of the zone he once struggled to get to. The bat speed and raw power are now in the plus category. There's still some streakiness in Bastian's ability to impact the breaking ball, but that too has shown improvement. To his credit, Bastian is a patient hitter who doesn't expand the zone and generally swings at the right pitches. 

Bastian consistently posts 70-grade run times. His wheels play a bit better on the basepaths than they do in the field at present. His routes in centerfield can be a bit wonky and crude with his lower-half getting out of whack when tracking fly balls, however his athleticism does make up for some inefficiencies. Bastian has a history of making the highlight-reel play. He does a very nice job staying behind the baseball and setting himself up to throw out runners looking to advance on a fly ball, supplemented by above-average arm strength. Bastian also always seems to throw to the correct base. Given the athlete and the foot speed it's possible he has a chance to develop into a plus centerfield defender, however at present there's polish to come. Bastian certainly profiles as a defensive asset.

Bastian suffered a nasty injury during fall ball once he arrived to Florida -- a compound leg fracture that required surgery. It delayed his ramp up with the team.

Jindra is a well put together infield prospect with present strength well-distributed throughout his frame. He's got strong legs, broad, rounded shoulders and the makings of a barrel chest. Jindra's 6-foot-1-inch frame doesn't have much projection left in it, however his present strength and filled out frame look the part of a player who will own the appropriate size for pro ball. 

Jindra's best tool is the bat. He's got a rhythmic setup with active hands and timely triggers, consistently putting himself into the hitting position at foot plant. The hands and leg kick work well together with simple triggers. Jindra has lower set hands and an understated forward move with a perfectly-still head through contact. Most of his bat speed comes by way of hand speed and rotation. He's not a twitchy mover, but he delivers a heavy blow through the zone with strong hands. He has the look of a player who will be a consistent hitter going forward, especially as he's exposed to more and more premium pitching.

Jindra hasn't hit for much power on the showcase and tournament circuit, but the average bat speed in the tank should lend well to the ocassional homer, especially if he works a bit harder to get to his pullside. Jindra is already hitting the ball in the air, but he's struggled to turn through the baseball when faced with more advanced pitching. His plate approach also stands out. Jindra is happy to take his walks.

Jinda has the physical tools to stay on the infield, ever if his actions are more befitting of a third baseman when all is said and done. He does a nice job of getting low to the ground fielding the baseball, and has shown some feel for tempo. Jinda's lateral mobility and time to throw would be challenged at the shortstop position, however his plus arm strength and carry on his throws would play beautifully throwing across the diamond from the hot corner.

Jindra is a solid-average runner, trending toward above-average run times as he's gotten stronger. His run tool should be valuable in all facets of the game.

A feather in his cap, Jindra is also up to 92 mph on the mound with a breaking ball that can be a weapon.

Three years at Tyler Junior College resulted in just 26 appearances as Brasch dealt with injury during a majority of his JUCO career. That said, he was able to hop on the mound nine times in 2025, starting seven games. It was enough to encourage him to hop into the portal and move into the D1 spotlight.

Brasch landed at Louisiana where he turned into one of the hardest throwers in college baseball in 2026. He can reach back for 99 when he needs it, and he'll sit 94-96 with moderate carry through the zone. He does get a bit more value from his fastball thanks to above average extension down the bump, too. Commanding the pitch is another story. It's fringy feel for the strike zone, however he'll rack up whiffs when it's anywhere close. 

A mid-80s slider is his primary weapon. It's also fringy from a strikes pespective, but does generate some swing and miss thanks to some late break, two planes. Neither the slider, nor the fastball force the opposition to expand outside of the zone much.

Brasch's future role is tricky. He's started at Louisiana, but with mostly two pitches and fringy control and command, he likely profiles as a hard-throwing mid-leverage reliever that can handle middle innings. He'll be 22 for the Draft.

The second Teel to grace prospect boards, Aidan's brother Kyle was the 14th overall pick by the Red Sox in 2023. Aidan missed that 2023 season due to injury, but has looked strong since returning to the mound and the outfield. Aidan was draft-eligible in 2025 but went unselected and chased more opportunity in Starkville. 

While not the biggest player in terms of stature, Teel more than makes up for his size with stuff on the hill. He'll work up to 95 with darting action in on righties and some tail away from lefties. Teel flashes a promising slider with considerable sweeping action in the low-80s; a pitch that has been highly effective against right-handed hitters. There's also a bigger curveball with depth and some sharpness. Teel hides the ball a bit with a shorter arm action and a tight elbow spiral in the back. Although he's thrown longer outings in school, scouts are split on whether he fits best in a bullpen or in a rotation at the next level. 

Teel boasts above-average bat speed and a simple swing from the left side with an upright stance and an quiet move forward when the ball is pitched. Most of his power is to the pull-side, however the bat speed plays into the opposite gap. Teel is an aggressive hitters who looks to make things happen, however average bat-to-ball skills and a willingness to work deeper into counts after an ambush approach balances the profile out a bit. He's susceptible against spin, especially against left-handed pitching, but feasts on fastballs and has shown the ability to flip off-speed stuff the other way. 

Teel presents plenty of value in the outfield where he has the look of a solid-to-above average defender in center with plus speed and plus arm strength, both of which help limit the opposition from taking the extra bag. Although it's a smaller sample or work, this years' version of Teel took good routes, especially into the left-center field gap on tough fly balls. He's a defensive asset that should earn stock in draft rooms with the glove. 

That versatility, abbreviated baseball card and variation in role projection make Teel a polarizing prospect. He's likely valued heavier as a bat than an arm at this stage, but could get draft consideration on both fronts.

Conover spent one season at Cowley CC before transferring into Stillwater for the 2025 and 2026 seasons. His offensive game exploded after his prep days. Added muscle and a surge in athleticism took him from a tweener profile to a guy who can now handle all three outfield roles depending on his team's need.

There's almost nobody in college baseball who can claim the consistency in hard contact that Conover can. He's a barrel magnet with significant impact to all parts of the yard. Conover is slightly better than average in terms of getting to his pull-side but it hardly affects his ability to generate impressive exit velocities. This is a guy who's going to slug at the next level. The bat-to-ball skills and pitch selection/swing decisions are both slightly below average at this early stage in his amateur career. Conover can be streaky identifying breaking balls out of the hands and he's merely average from an adjustability standpoint. Scouts are bullish on the simplicity of the swing and think he's got a chance to really take off as he continues to get exposed to more advanced pitching. Ultimately, strikeouts will likely always be a part of his game, but the impact production he projects to unleash on the opposition going forward should mask the inconsistencies he'll show time and again with the hit tool. The entire offensive package isn't too dissimilar from Andrew Fischer at Tennessee in 2025. It's efficient, it's consistently loud, and it's a swing that dominates pitches inside of the strike zone. 

A solid-average runner, Conover can handle centerfield and does have the instincts and route running ability to cover everything routine hit his way. He's even capable of the occasional highlight reel play. That said, his tools play better in a corner. The arm strength and sprint speed are probably more befitting of a left fielder at the next level, but he'll likely get his start as a pro in right field.

Wentz is a barrel-chest, physically matured infielder with impressive bat speed and plenty of athleticism to handle the dirt right now. He has more raw power from the left side, though he can struggle to get to it at times with a loud load causing timing issues against more advanced competition. Wentz settled in throughout his freshman season at Wake Forest and began getting to his pull-side with more frequency as the spring wore on. 

The uphill nature of his swing path will likely always leave him susceptible to elevated velocity and more premium breaking balls, but when left a cookie he's often deleted those pitches from both sides of the plate. Swing-and-miss will always be a balancing act for Wentz, but if it comes with significant impact, strikeouts won't matter so much. Wentz does have some margin for error with his timing at the plate thanks to his bat speed and raw power. He can get away with being late and is no stranger to the opposite field homer. 

Wentz arrived to Wake Forest a shortstop and has above-average athleticism with above average arm strength. He profiles to second or third base at the next level, and he's played those two spots with the most frequency in Winston-Salem. Wentz will not turn 21 years old until a week after the draft. He'll have models on his side, especially if he mashes ACC pitches for the second year in a row.

It's been a winding road and a tumultuous journey for Bryans who finds himself draft-eligible for the fifth year in a row. Bryans spent two seasons at Jones County JC before transferring to Alabama for the 2025 season. Struggles to throw strikes landed him back in the transfer portal, this time heading to Jacksonville State. 

Bryans first year in the SEC was a challenging one. A year removed from posting a 3.00 ERA with 14 strikeouts and six walks for Bourne on the Cape, Bryans control for the zone evaded him. He waslked 15 batters in just nine innings of work for the Crimson Tide, limiting his opportunities to establish a role. His feel for the zone has improved in 2026, or so early returns have suggested.

Bryans is something of a metric anamoly. A southpaw with a release four-and-a-half feet wide of the rubber. Launching 54 inches outside of the center, Bryans' release would be the widest launch in the big leagues, besting Hoby Milner's 52-inch release angle. This trait alone will generate draft interest as players that present unique look for hitters are always coveted. As expected, it's an ultra-low launch as well, just 58 inches off the ground. 

Bryans isn't just a fun trivia answer. He can bring it. His fastball has been up to 98 mph and will routinely sit 93-96 in his showings with considerable arm-side tail. Bryans gets plenty of whiffs and chase on the fastball, however finding the zone with that pitch over the years, as mentioned, has been the emphasis.

A sweeper in the mid 80s is his best secondary. It's got all the ingredients to become a true weapon and a wipeout offering if he can get his arsenal to even fringy control. There's also a very seldom used changeup.

Bryans is on the older side and doesn't have a long track record of success in college baseball. He's flashed at times, but teams will want to see some better feel than what he's been thus far. There's a reasonably good chance he'll be selected as a money-saver at some point in the draft. If he goes unselected due to strike-throwing concerns, he'll be a priority add for a team looking to sink their teeth into him.

Big, tall, funky and mean. Grulkowski brings moxy and a bully mentality to the bump. The hard-throwing righty has some metric tricks up his bag, easy to forecast a future role in the big leagues.

Grulkowski will run his fastball up to 95 mph, but more routinely sits 90-92. It's a low slot, slingshot delivery with some natural deception and life late. He creates a flat approach angle with some late tail, ocassionally generating enough hop to miss bats in the heart of the plate. If the velocity continues to trend upward, Grulkowski could possess a plus fastball in relief looks.

The slider is the real weapon here. It's a 3000 rpm frisbee thrown with conviction and real nasty shape. Grulkowski sweeps the breaker hard and late away from right-handed hitters, commanding it with finesse to the glove side. It's got the makings of a plus offering as well. 

Grulkowski lacks a third pitch, at least from a usage and confidence perspective. It's a relief look for the time being, however if he works to fold in a changeup or splitter in the years to come, the opportunity to start exists.

Gilligan has proven consistently proven to be one of the better catch-and-throw backstops in the 2026 class. He's a surefire catcher with a chance to be a true defensive asset as a professional. The bat isn't far behind either. 

Gilligan's plate appearances stand out. He's not a jumpy hitter and his takes on pitches just off the plate are impressive. He seems to have a distinguished eye and a willingness to take his walks. Gilligan isn't afraid to pull the trigger either. He's shown some bat speed to his pull-side and can put the game in motion. It may not be the offensive tools necessary to become a full-time player at the next level, but we'll let time dictate that outcome.

Gilligan has a hose behind the dish. It's at least 70-grade arm strength with exceptional jumps out of the crouch. He fires seeds. He'll hold runners at bay at the next level.

Surowiec is an excellent hitting prospect. It's big strength and physicality with considerable rotational force at the plate. His power really plays. Surowiec delivers a heavy barrel through the zone and stays compact through the entirety of his swing. He was an absolute force on the tournament and showcase circuit as a rising high school senior, but curiously couldn't find much playing time for Ole Miss as a true freshman. The lack of opportunity led to his decision to transfer to the University of Florida for the 2026 season.

Surowiec blistered the baseball in the Northwoods League this past summer the tune of a .385 average with a .472 on-base percentage and a .792 slug. He hit 20 homers in just 58 games, leading the Northwoods League. His 68 RBI also paced the pack.

Defensively, Surowiec is capable of playing first base and left field, and has third base sparingly on his baseball card. He does have a strong arm and moves laterally well enough to get some innings at the hot corner. Fundamentally, he likely fits best at first base. He's also an average runner with a strong first step.

McGuire has long been a pitchability guy with a favorable operation and considerable projection. He added weight and strength over the last twelve months, elevating his arsenal into true leverage stuff. He's now reaching back for 97 and resting 93-94. It's a heater that has considerable carry through the zone complimenting the natural deception his delivery offers. 

He'll mix in a sweepy, deep slider and a fringier curveball, though both pitches lack consistency. McGuire has a quick arm and should continue to polish his operation as he ages. There are some starter traits here though he's largely been used as a multi-inning reliever where his stuff shines. When drafted, he could initially be deployed as a starting pitcher in the low minors.

Oshinskie struggled over the first two years of his career at Brown, but seemed to have turned a corner on the Cape this past summer. His 38 strikeouts in just 28 innings of work were complimented by just 8 walks and an ERA under 2.00. Oshinskie has primarily pitched out of the bullpen in college, but that may change as July approaches.

Oshinskie has been up to 94 mph with a fastball that features moderate carry and above-average tailing action. He generates well-above average spin rates on the pitch, a driving factor in the horizontal shape he induces on the heater. Oshinskie isn't the most electric mover on the mound and owns below average extension, however his profile is secondary-centric -- an archetype that should help negate the ineffectiveness of his fastball.

Oshinskie's breaking ball has a chance to be pretty dang good. It's 79-82 with huge vertical tilt and some gradual lateral break. It's routinely run big whiff rates and Oshinskie has done a nice job getting hitters to expand the zone with that pitch as well. He'll likely need to throw it a little harder in professional baseball, but the components are here for a potential plus breaker. Oshinskie also throws a more prototypical over-the-top curveball. It's 77-80 with even bigger downward action, again posting enormous swing-and-miss metrics.

Rounding out the menu is a changeup that also possesses plus upside. It's 79-81 with elite horizontal darting action. That pitch has also generated huge whiff and chase rates.

Oshinskie's lack of fastball value is a bit moot in some respects. He's got two dynamic breaking balls and is talented pronator with the ability to get the baseball to go the other direction. It may behoove him to lean into a sinker-baller profile with the fastball to get the most out of his release traits. 

Better still, Oshinskie has physical projection on his side. He can comfortably add 20 more pounds to his 6-foot-3-inch frame without losing his athleticism. He'll turn 21 years old just days before the Draft. It's a model-darling scouting report, and a name that could surprise in July. Oshinskie has top-five round upside. An injury delayed his start to the 2026 season.

Jennings certainly looks the part off the bus. A 6-foot-5-inch, 215-pound outfielder with the athleticism to go get it in centerfield, it's easy to dream on what Jennings could one day become if it all comes together. There's some physical maturity and polish still to come, but if it arrives before July, Jennings could hear his name called early. 

Despite his size, Jennings isn't the raw power projection slugger one might expect. His exit velocities are more commonly in the average range, however he does hit the ball hard with steady frequency. He's also shown feel for lifting the baseball and getting to his pull-side, so the innate traits to become a power hitter are there. Getting more efficient with his swing and growing into his 'adult muscles' could unlock a bit more production. Jennings is slowly learning how to leverage his size and frame to generate bat speed, and it's showing up in his burgeoning batted-ball data. 

The power will need to come as Jennings isn't a terribly decorated pure hitter. It's fringy bat-to-ball skills, however supplemented by a patient approach, unwilling to expand the zone. Jennings has run healthy walk rates, and his strike out rates have never ballooned. It feels as though he's a tinker here or a tinker there away from becoming a very productive impact hitter. 

Jennings is a very good outfielder. He tracks the ball very well and his routes to the spot rarely fall short of what's expected in either center or right field. He's fearless around the wall and has shown a willingness to give up the body to make an out. He's ultimately going to slide to right field as a professional where his physique and above average speed play best. It's average arm strength.

Vaughn has been something of a breakthrough star for the Crimson Tide in 2026 after missing much of the first two years old his collegiate career. He played in just eight games as a freshman and then missed all of the 2025 season nursing an injury. A primary catcher, Vaughn has experience at first base and left field as well.

Vaughn is 6-foot-2 and still has some projection across his entire frame. He sets up at the plate with a relaxed, upright stance, slightly open to the pitcher. Vaughn sinks into his legs in the load, counter-coils with relatively quiet hands. There's rhythm and waggle in his load, creating tension and torque. Vaughn has a tendency to throw his hips open ever so slightly early, losing some of the raw power he's built up in his swing. Still, he's peaked with exit velocities that suggest at least average raw power. More could be on the way with that aformentioned physical projection. Vaughn has thus far displayed sound pitch selection skills and the bat to ball skills to survive as a professional hitter, albeit with a slightly passive approach. He hits the ball in the air with frequency and appears to be an efficient hitter from a launch and pull perspective.

Vaughn's defensive chops are mostly average, however his athleticism and blocking do stand out. Framing and arm strength on more on the average side. Coaches rave about his leadership capabilities. 

With such a small baseball card, Vaughn will have to leave little doubt in SEC play that what scouts are seeing is real. He's got upside inside of the top ten rounds. Still young for the class, he'll be barely 21 years old for the Draft.

Sosa boasts a very well-rounded profile behind the plate. Advanced receiving and blocking with arm strength that plays up due to plus accuracy. Tools to stick long term at catcher. Fringy bat-to-ball skills with budding raw power from the left side are buoyed by an advanced approach at the plate. Making more contact on swings inside the strikezone will be paramount as July approaches. Has already shown above average exit velocities for someone his age. A rising profile. 

Sosa transferred from NC State to Miami for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign.

Rintaro Sasaki has been a bit of a global story long before ever picking up a bat in Palo Alto. A top-ranked player in high school at Hanamaki-Higashi High School, Sasaki was expected to be the no. 1 overall selection in the 2023 Nippon Baseball Draft as a teenager. He instead elected to trailblaze a path for Japanese high schoolers going forward by enrolling at Stanford pushing his professional eligibility off until 2026 when he'll be eligible for this Major League Baseball Draft.

Sasaki's tools on the diamond are carried by plus power that he effortlessly gets into in games. He's already physically maxed and produces gaudy exit velocity figures, especially for a player of his stature. The pure hit tool isn't quite as impressive as the bat speed he showcases, but scouts are awfully bullish on where it may end up by the time he's draft-eligible. For now, Sasaki can struggle with getting to elevated velocity above the belt. Sliders and changeups have also given him fits at times. It's been an adjustment period for the international star, but he's continued to adjust and has shown gradual improvement. That said, he works mature at-bats, doesn't expand the zone, and has seen his comfortability continue to improve in the states over the course of the last two years. 

Defensively most anticipate Sasaki being a full-time first baseman when all is said and done. He does have above average arm strength, however his footwork, technique and subsequent arm accuracy do require considerable work if he's to man the hot corner as a professional. He could potentially end up in right field in a pinch, however his below-average foot speed will likely preclude him from playing out there regularly. 

Sasaki's bat speed and raw power are fairly unmatched especially for his age. He has the potential to become one of the bigger sluggers in baseball if the roughness around the edges of the rest of his offensive game polish themselves out as he ages and matures.

Barney's size and athleticism are both ascending in a positive way at the right time. He's shown strong body control for his size and age and his athletic tools have ticked up too. The size and swing both suggest offensive impact. 

Barnes has a sound swing from the left side. He makes tight turns on the ball and stays behind his front side, creating leverage and loft. Barney's size naturally creates strong exit velocities and he projects to grow into plus raw power as he adds more strength. It's a frame ripe for more muscle and mass. 

Barney is a primary first baseman, but may be a good enough athlete to play left field. He moves well and plays above his fringe-average straight-line speed. It's fringe-average arm strength that will be tested in the outfield if he ends up going that route.

Barney's bat will carry the water. He'll need to hit and show offensive impact projection as July approaches to capitalize on what some believe is a top-three round profile.

A physically advanced left-handed pitcher from the state of Tennessee, Beaird is only 6-feet tall but comes with mature strength in his lower half and shoulders. Beaird pitches exclusively out of the stretch and generates energy with a bigger leg left, significant torque and hip hinge. He uncoils with a wide hand-break, a longer arm action and separates his hips and shoulders to get to his velocity. 

Beaird fastball has been up to 95 in short-inning settings with tremendous value coming by way of riding shape. Beaird has feel for the top of the zone and gets plenty of whiffs on his heater in game settings. It's every bit that of a plus heater and could jump into the 70-grade range if the velocity continues to come. 

An upper-70s/low-80s breaking ball will flash hammer shape but is more commonly slurvy in nature. It's got above average upside, potentially more. His upper-80s changeup lags behind his wombo-combo one-two punch, but does have a chance to get to at least average value with a grip change. 

Beaird has some effort through release and doesn't have the prototypical starting pitcher frame. It's a relief look now, but one that could eventually possess two plus pitches his velocity bands continue to tick up. It's leverage stuff. There's some similarities to what Gage Jump was in high school on this profile, however Beaird is more physcially mature at this stage. Beaird will be 19 for the draft.

A 19th round selection by the Brewers in 2022, Noot went unsigned and made his way to Baton Rouge. He was draft-eligible in 2025, but did not get selected.

Noot has some of the easiest velo in the class. He's been up to 99, but the ball just explodes out of his hand. His velocity has backed up a bit since arriving to LSU, now more 92-95 on most nights with the ocassional 96. It's a heavy fastball with big arm-side run. Works well at the bottom of the zone. His changeup probably has the most upside as it's firm with solid vertical traits. Shows feel for a mid-70s curveball that he can throw for strikes. 

Noot makes it look easy on the bump and has definitive starter traits. He dealt with some arm fatigue during his freshman season, something teams will have to monitor.

Niu has had an adventurous career. He spent the first two years in college at New Orleans where he bounced all over the diamond. Niu played every outfield spot, as well as second base and third base in 2023 and 2024. Seeking stability and more opportunity, he transferred to Marshall for the 2025 season. The adventure continued. 

Niu played the entire 2025 season as the starting shortstop for Thundering Herd. The results with the glove were good, not great. He's not a natural shortstop. But then came the summer where he was inserted as the full-time centerfielder at Falmouth. His game blossomed. Niu is a centerfielder. End of story. It landed him in Fayetteville for the 2026 season despite receiving some late draft interest in 2025 after his showing on the Cape.

An above average runner who will occassionally click into plus run times underway in the field, Niu is a natural in the grass. He takes crisp routes and gets the ball in with urgency. It's plus arm strength proficient at hitting the cut-off man with pace or threatening advancing runners at any base. Niu is unlikely to play on the dirt again, but if he does it will be in a utility measure and not as his primary home.

The bat is power-over-hit right now. Niu is an aggressive swinger who expands the zone looking to make things happen. It affects his contact quality and draws down his slash line. When Niu is swinging at pitches inside of the zone, he's doing damage. He hit a ball 113 mph this season and flashed batted-ball peaks that point toward above-average or better raw power. It's going to take further seasoning and reps against advanced breaking balls and pitches just off the black to improve his overall hit tool, but the impact potential is in the tank if he ever gets to it.

Mechanically, Niu is a rhythmic hitter. He has a few triggers in his load that get him into place for the fastball. Adjusting off those triggers can be a challenge. Getting his hands to the top of the zone and keeping his front hip and weight back on spin will be a developmental checkpoint. He's a very good athlete and more than capable of the adjustments necessary to succeed. Inserted into the right player development system, Niu could find another gear in the box score department pretty quickly.

If you squint, there's a path for Niu to turn himself into a Jake Meyers type of producer. The defense should provide a floor and there's enough impact in the stick to occassionally change the score of a game. He'll be 22.5 for the Draft.

Following two dynamite years at Kennesaw State, Rhudy hit the transfer portal and headed to Knoxville for the 2026 season; his first draft-eligible campaign since high school. Rhudy is capable of handling multiple roles, however most foresee a future in the bullpen for the talented righty out of Georgia. 

Rhudy throws the fastball a lot and it's a good one. Up to 93, Rhudy will sit 89-91 with moderate carry and considerable cutting action. He launches the heater from a low slot and misses bats in buckets when he's landing the pitch at the top of the zone. It's one of the flatter vertical approach angles in the SEC. Rhudy also spins the fastball with elite metrics and generates above-average extension down the bump. All of those components have helped generate enormous whiff and chase rates over the course of his collegiate career. 

Rhudy spins the slider at close to 2700 rpm, generally 77-79 mph with two plane of break. There's more lateral tilt than depth on the breaking ball, however he's hardly thrown the pitch at this stage in his career; just ten percent of the time. He also has a tendency to drop his slot further and cuts nearly six inches off his delivery to achieve the shape he's currently producing. It's a breaking ball that needs work, but coaches at Tennessee are convinced he's got the clay to eventually own an above-average breaker. 

Rhudy's got some effort and whack at delivery that will likely preclude him from starting at the next level. That said, it's an exceptionally unique fastball and breaking ball traits that can be molded into a leverageable bullpen profile.

An interesting lefty with unique metrics traits, Holloway does things with a baseball most cannot on the bump. It's a near-perfectly efficient vertical release with big carry through the zone and steep angle. Holloway generates above average extension and can blow a fastball by hitters at the letters. Holloway continues to add more velocity presently sitting in the 92-94 bucket most nights (up to 97). 

Holloway throw a hard, mid-70s 12-6 bender that's mostly average. The changeup is above average, 82-84 with some late tilt at times. His upper-80s cutter can get right-handed hitters off the barrel. He will be 18.8 years old for the draft.

Melaerts has a case to be the top junior college prospect in the 2026 Draft. His stuff has exploded at Blinn and he's continued to blossom the secondaries on campus.

The immediate thing that stands out about Melaerts is just how different he looks from his high school days. He's tacked on 20 pounds of muscle and has redefined his athleticism on the mound. Melaerts is moving much quicker than he did as a prepster, and his arm speed has taken a dramatic jump. It's swing and miss, punch-out stuff. The last box on his checklist of to-do items is to improve his control for the zone and command for his fastball.

Melaerts' heater has a chance to be a good one. He's up to 97 with late life through the zone. The baseball explodes out of his hand and has real value at the top of the zone. Melaerts is creating shapes with the fastball that will get outs at the professional level. To date, he's only been tasked with mutli-inning outings and hasn't been stretched out across larger inning loads, but in long relief showings, he's settled in 92-93 mph. 

Melaerts best secondary for the time being is a mid-to-upper 80s splitter with heavy diving life and conviction out of the hand. It's the definition of a put-away weapon when he can get to it. There's also a mid-80s bullet slider that can melt into the look of his splitter at times. Melaerts has proven comfortable and capable throwing both pitches to left-handed hitters and right-handed hittesr. He doesn't have split preferences with either offering. 

Melaerts purportedly has a low-to-upper 80s curveball that he'll throw consistently in bullpens and side work, however it's not a heavy-usage pitch in games. 

The cherry on top here is Melaerts' athleticism. He tests well with force plates and, given his 6-foot-5-inch frame, likely has some low-hanging fruit to extract more velocity on the bump.

The jury is out on whether Melaerts will be able to start at the next level given his current strike-throwing abilities. That said, it's some of the best stuff in the country regardless of level. Melaerts will be just 20 years old for the Draft.

A rare three-year development project for the Buccaneers of Blinn College, Ekdall has really begun growing into his own in 2026 and is flashing bigger and better stuff than ever before. Just 5-foot-11, 170 pounds when he graduated from Lake Creek, Ekdall now stands 6-foot-1, 185 pounds and owns the frame and operation necessary for the rigors of professional baseball. He's hardly pitched, though. He redshirt his freshman year in 2024 and got just one appearance in 2025 before his breakout campaign this spring. Tommy John was sandwiched into those first two years on campus. 

Ekdall operates exclusively from the stretch with a reasonably quick move to the plate. It's a true four-pitch mix with a fastball that generates above average carry and some late hop. Edkall has touched 97 this spring, but more commonly pitches in the 91-94 bucket. 

He parlays the heater with a cutter, changeup, sweeper and curveball. None of the breaking balls are particularly consistent at this stage, and most are firm with shorter tilt. The changeup will flash some pretty exciting metrics, especially from a depth perspective. 

Ekdall is a true junior, 21 years old for the Draft. He's committed to play ball at Texas A&M in 2027 and could be a difficult pull away from College Station.

August elected to stay home and pitch for Delaware as a freshman, though his metrics and stuff were so good he eventually landed in the portal after that season ending up at VCU. After one year, he transferred once again, this time to Liberty for the 2026 season. 

August generates impressive carry on his mid 90s fastball out of a low-ish slot. He's been up to 98 and feasts at the top of the zone. Commanding the fastball at the top of the zone is a strength, even if controlling it consistently in the zone will come and go. There's effort in his drop-and-drive operation with a ton of scap load. His arm will occasionally be late with some inversion. His extension and flat approach, coupled with his arm strength could get his fastball into plus territory in a bullpen role at the next level. 

He'll pair an above average changeup off his fastball to get lefties out, however August has become fastball-reliant of late as his outings have gotten shorter. His breaking ball is still a work in progress. At its best, he creating bigger depth and locating that pitch below the zone, however it needs more velocity if it's to become a weapon. 

His whole arsenal comes out of an interesting slot featuring plus extension. August will need his operation, effort and feel for the zone come together if he's to realize his eventual ceiling. It's a ton of interesting traits lacking present polish with a bullpen role likely in his future at the next level.

Slanker enjoyed a breakthrough sophomore campaign at Ohio where he slashed .302/.422/.720 with 21 homers. That move forward prompted him to jump into the transfer portal seeking bigger, brighter lights. He landed at Louisville. 

If the slash wasn't evidence enough, Slanker can hit. He's a selective hitter who possesses average bat-to-ball skills, but he's efficient. When Slanker puts the ball in play, it's very often lifted to the pull-side. While the raw tools may not support the slash line from his sophomore year, there are traits here to believe he can hit as a pro, especially if he gets stronger. The raw power is mostly average right now. 

Slanker is a primary right fielder who takes solid-average routes to the ball and gets the ball in quickly. It's solid-average arm strength. The profile is more befitting of a left fielder at the next level.
