Slanker will have to up his bat-to-ball skills or up his game power if he hopes to capture his Top-100 pick upside. He's a remarkably productive college hitter who owns some traits scouts like to see.

McKee is a power-righty up to 95 with an extremely quick arm. He could throw really hard in due time. It's a lean frame, and he's still growing quickly, so that velocity jump could happen sooner rather than later. He throws two fastballs, a four-seamer and a sinker, the former being a slightly more effective pitch with heaviness and some tail. 

McKee throws a short, firm, power-slider in the mid-80s that's seen its velocity jump in recent months and now showcases swing and miss upside. There's some effort here and his directional cues can change from outing to out, so McKee may ultimately be a reliever, but it's a leverageable profile with some projection on the horizon. It's certainly not too late to alter his role projection.

Barrett appeared poised to be the next Andrew Checketts arm to come out of UCSB, but a torn UCL limited him to just seven innings over the 2024 and 2025 seasons. After a massive freshman season in 2023, it's been a hard road back. Seeking a fresh start, Barrett jump in the portal after the 2025 campaign and enrolled at Oklahoma State. He's once again missed time in 2026. 

It's a big, long lefty frame with a fastball that'll carry up to 95, though he sits a few ticks below that most nights. While controlling the baseball and commanding the baseball will continue to be a point of emphasis moving forward, Barrett has been effectively wild to this point. All three of his offerings, the fastball, slider and changeup, draw huge chase and whiff rates when batters off at them. If Barrett can learn to command his pitches, the fastball especially, with more conviction, he's got the upside of a potential future top-five round pick.

Adams was draft-eligible in 2025 as a second-year sophomore, but pulled his name from the Draft to chase bigger overtures in 2026. 

Adams is considered one of the more promising left-handed pitching prospects in the 2026 class with projection and present stuff. The velocity has ticked up over the last two years, now brushing 96, sitting comfortably in the low-90s deep into his outings. Perhaps the biggest wart on Adams' report, however, is the general lack of fastball value. He doesn't miss many bats with the heater and relies on speeding up and slowing down hitters with his secondaries. 

Adams has a promising big upper-70s curveball that he commands well with big shape and projection thanks to its current velocity and Adams' arm speed. It's a true 12-6 breaker and will flash, especially when he's getting some value from his fastball at the top of the zone. He's folding in a low-80s slider this year as well and it plays nicely across his pitch charts. Adams has worked to integrate an upper-80s cutter that he's demonstrated strong command of as well. It'll flash above-average traits in games and works nicely tunneled against the fastball and slider combination. He'll mix in a changeup as well, though it's presently tertiary and is used seldomly against RHH. 

Adams is a strike-thrower with the whole menu at his disposal. He profiles as a No. 4 starter at the next level, but will likely post some higher-production outings when he's landing four or five pitches where he wants them on any given night. The kid just knows how to pitch and get outs.

Rein has been a steady force on the showcase and tournament scene going back to his freshman year. He's grown into considerable impact on the offensive end, and scouts havn't given up on the upside on the mound either.

Most scouts like Rein more with a bat in his hands than on the bump. He's a right-handed hitter with good size, a strong frame and big, impactful bat speed. Rein sets up wide and showcases a strong lower-half. He uncoils with explosive torque and creates plus raw power with more on the way. Rein isn't unfamiliar to exit velocities north of 110 mph. Rein's swing has some loft to it, and he has a tendency to swing across the baseball creating top-spin in games. He's so strong that those top-spinning line drives still clear the left-field fence. Rein swings with max intent and tries to hit the baseball as hard as he can. It can lead to mishits and a susceptibility against spin, but few can put on the display he can. Rein may be a guy that strikes out at a healthy clip, but it should come with considerable slug if the hit tool and understanding of how pitchers are attacking him develops alongside his strength. 

Rein is a primary shortstop, but he's played all over the diamond showing versatility. He's an average runner, but it's plus arm strength that profiles at third base and into right field. Rein isn't a natural outfielder yet, however he doesn't have the reps under him to make a fair critique on his ability to grow into it. For now, it's short, choppy steps more befitting of a third baseman. On the dirt, Rein plays with an upright nature and relies on his arm strength.

The bat carries serious water on Rein's profile, however it has a chance to hit in the middle of a lineup going forward. He'll have to establish firm residency somewhere defensively.

A former two-way standout, Horn dropped the bat at Nebraska to focus on pitching full-time. The athleticism he showed in the field and at the plate has translated beautifully toward him elevating his stuff on the mound. It's some of the more intriguing stuff in the Big 12, even if dominant results have yet to show up in box scores.

Horn has the full menu at his disposal. It's a four-seam fastball, a cutter, a slider, a curveball and a changeup. Horn has been up to 98 with a reasonably generic fastball; generally more 92-94. His fastball has generated solid, not spectacular results. Horn added a bit more carry to his heater in 2026, and it's seen an uptick in effectiveness.

The changeup is his go-to secondary against left-handed hitters. Again, a solid offering. There's not enough velocity separation from his fastball, and it's not the most dynamic shape for a cambio you'll find in the country. It'll flash above average. 

A combination of a cutter and a sweeper, as well as a curveball, represent his secondary weapons against right-handed hitters. Both present more lateral action than depth. He'll get some chase and some whiffs on those pitches. Again, both are usually average in value. There's also the aforementioned cutter, however it's largely used to keep hitters off the barrel of the four-seamer and not effective in missing bats. 

Horn has an athletic delivery and is an above average strike-thrower. He doesn't miss a ton of bats at this stage and projects as a fringy strikeout artist as a pro. The stuff continues to tick up in the right direction as he's distanced himself from his two-way days. He'll need to develop one of his secondaries into a better out-getter to drive down the amount of base runners he's currently surrendering. There's back-end rotation upside here if he can take another step with the Draft approaching.

Solid hitter, good bat-to-ball skills, a selective approach and has shown some impact to all fields. Patient hitter, plenty of foul balls, works long counts and is more than happy to take his walks. Some projection left in frame, but reasonably undersized from a physicality perspective.

Sound defender, above average arm strength, can throw from multiple angles and looks the part of a utility player that can play anywhere on the dirt. Definitive infield prospect.

Pellegrin is just a good baseball player in every sense of the word. He's polished on the defensive end, and seems to hit at every event he attends. Pellegrin may not be the flashiest player in the class, and he may not have a ton of physical projection, but he knows how to play the game, and play the game the right way.

Offensively, Pellegrin sets up with a neutral base, lower set hands, squared up to the pitcher. Pellegrin has a moderate stride with some push his his hands, however he's pretty consistently on time. Pellegrin's swing plane will vary, ocassionally collapsing his back shoulder in an attempt to get to loft. This is not frequent. He's got some twitch in his hips and rotates through a lower half that does a nice job staying behind the baseball. To date, Pellegrin has shown some swing-and-miss against velocity inside the zone. Interestingly, he seems to perform better when tasked with taking the barrel to fastballs outside of hte zone. Pellegrin seems to thrive when he can get his arms extended. He's added weight this spring that should help the hands catch up with better fastballs in the heart of the plate and in on his hands. Still, he'll have to prove as much to scouts. To his credit, Pellegrin hardly ever expands the zone.

Pellegrin is not a thumper and doesn't not project to hit for much power, however it's possible he grows into enough strength to run into double-digit homers if given the plate appearances to amass that total.

Pellegrin is an average runner with a strong first step out of the box and in the field. He's a primary shortstop whose actions are befitting of a player who will play the position up the ladder. He may be forced to shift to second base as he approaches MLB with more dynamic athletes flanking his right. 

Pellegrin is a solid ballplayer who should blossom with added strength. He'll be 19 years old for the Draft.

Carson Lane has blossomed into a hard-throwing starting pitcher at UNLV after being a lightly recruited hurler out of Huntington Beach as a prepster. Lane is up to 97 these days and will rest 91-93 after the first inning or two of his outings. He possesses a high launch and works up in the zone with his entire arsenal. 

The fastball is his best weapon as currently equipped. He naturally cuts the baseball and at his best he can generate north of 20" of vertical break with near 0 horizontal break. It's a pitch that works up in the zone, but he'll need to unlock more consistent velocity if it's to miss bats at a high clip in the high minors. And scouts think he will. Lane has longer levers and a loose, whippy arm action. The ball jumps out of his hand. There's arm speed here on a frame that can hold more velocity. Lane could live in the mid-90s soon enough and should at least flirt with triple-digit readings as his peak. 

The rest of his arsenal melts together as Lane's secondaries are unrefined. He likes to throw a mid-80s slider that consistently demonstrates short, cutter shape. It's has been effective in getting hitters off the barrel when they're picking up his fastball, but it's not dynamic enough to be a true out-pitch at the next level yet. He's working to establish a bigger, more consistent breaking ball. That'll be necessary as Lane projects a north-south arm who will require big velocity to generate whiffs. 

Projection is the allure here. If Lane begins throwing harder as July approaches and develops a bigger, deeper breaking ball he has the look of a guy who could go in the 4-6 round range.

John Stowers can really swing the bat. It's a quiet left-handed swing with consistent triggers and a bat path that projects to hit for both average and power. The latter is the calling card right now as Stowers generates natural loft with his swing showcasing pull-side power rivaling players much older than he is. He's got physicality in his hands and wrists at the point of contact with twitchy hips and more power on the horizon. He's been a steady performer on the tournament scene and while swing and miss on elevated velocity has been streaky in-game, most scouts like the swing and see a path toward cleaning up his ability to handle the top rail. 

Stowers is athletic behind the dish with a quick transfer and the arm strength necessary to stay behind the plate at the next level. It's a full arm action that could eventually be shortened over time to improve his pop times. He is a below average runner who likely won't add extra value on the base paths, though few full-time catchers do. Stowers will be just 18.2 years old on draft day and profiles well in draft models. He's graded out extremely well in pre-draft interviews and organizations are a big fan of his leadership qualities.

One of the most slept-on starting pitchers in the SEC, Cleaver has been a model of consistency for the Wildcats since arriving onto campus in 2023 as a freshman. He ranks among the top inning-eaters in the SEC over the last two years, and his stuff is beginning to evolve into bat-missing pitches.

Cleaver isn't a hard thrower yet, but he hasn't had to be. The four-seam fastball will tickle up to 92 mph, more commonly sitting 88-90 with moderate carry through the zone. Despite his tepid arm speed, Cleaver still generates a healthy amount of whiffs with the heater, and he's been known to induce quite a few bad swings up and out of the zone when he's commanding the pitch to the arm-side. Cleaver's fastball is certainly aided by nearly 7 feet of extension and  the natural ability to hide the ball behind his body deep until release. 

Cleaver also generates some value on his four seam fastball by mixing in an upper-70s/low-80s cutter that possesses short vertical break with near perfect bullet spin. It's not been a pitch that gets whiffs on its own, however hitters tend to chase this pitch outside of the zone as well. It's been especially effective at the top of the zone against left-handed hitters. 

Cleaver's bread and butter, without question, is a low-70s breaking ball that he's shown exceptional feel for from an execution, consistency and command perspective. It's got big downward shape some late glove-side tilt. Cleaver doesn't spin the ball particularly well, instead relying on command and feel to land his breaker in the spots necessary to freeze hitters, or get swings in the dirt. His curveball has generated exceptional whiff rates and a chase rate many in the sport would envy. Slower over-the-top curveballs are something of a lost art in Major League Baseball. It remains to be seen if a pitch in this velocity bucket would be effective against professional hitters.

To round out a robust menu of pitches, Cleaver throws a low-80s changeup that's got roughly 15 inches of horizontal fading action to the arm-side. It's served its purpose to show hitters a unique look, however it has not been used to get whiffs. 

Cleaver is a lefty that'll throw the kitchen sink at hitters. It's five pitches, tons of strikes, feel for shapes, a starter's operation and more. He may never be better than a back-end of the rotation starter if he never finds more velocity, but he's a good bet to find success as a professional thanks to his polish, pitchability to moxy.

Landon Schute is built like you want a starting pitcher to look. It's a broad frame with a workhorse physique and strength distributed throughout. He's angry on the mound with a bulldog mentality. The fastball has brushed 95 with carry and life through the top rail. The heater is what scouts call "here it is, I dare you to hit it" stuff. 

Schutte flashes a low-80s downer curveball with conviction and tunneling traits. When thrown in the zone it's been tough to handle, though he'll often lose it glove-side. There's also a mid-70s changeup that he's been reluctant to throw unless he has to against more premium left-handed hitters. It's a work in progress, but shows teeth. 

Schutte is an explosive mover who works with tempo and intent. It's all of the starter traits scouts look for. Highest level upside. First round stuff. Schutte will be 18.8 years old on draft day.

Chavez made his presence known at the 2026 Super 60 event this spring. His left-handed swing, loose hands and bat speed stands out to scouts. Chavez has had a streaky career at Mount Carmel with the bat, including posting a strikeout rate north fo 25 percent as a junior and being reasonably absent on the showcase/tournament circuit the summer immediately following. 

That said, the potential for slug stands out here, as does his asthetically appealing swing. Chavez tests extremely well with Blast sensors posting bat speed and hand speed marks that rank among the top of his peers. 

Chavez is a surefire first base prospect who is an average runner. He's got age on his side and will turn 18 years old just a week prior to the draft. Teams that believe he's just now beginning to grow into his physical upside may take a shot on him in July.

Novak is a polarizing prospect in that scouts and analysts are split on whether his approach to hitting will translate to the next level. A big 6-foot-3-inch, 210-pound corner outfielder, Novak has the tools to be more impactful at the plate, but instead chooses to play a passive brand of baseball.

Novak isn't in a hurry to swing the bat. He runs outlandishly low chase rates, but his swing rates and leave rates on fastballs in the zone leave something to be desired. He's flashed above-average bat-to-ball skills and strong hard-hit rates, but those often come deep in counts when more hittable pitches have passed by. Thus far, he's shown average raw power with the ability to naturally lift the baseball without selling out. There's an impact slugger in here, however it remains to be seen how much that will come out at the next level if Novak allows the opposition to dictate at-bats at the high clip he does.

An average runner with the ability athletically to play all three outfield positions, Novak is likely destined for a corner as a professional.

You cannot start a conversation with Sullivan anywhere but his fastball. Already touching 98 and resting 93-96, Sullivan is an intimidating at-bat for the opposition. When he stays behind his fastball he can cut and carry the heater but often he'll send his front side flying open and leave the pitch to tail into the right-handed batters box. His control and command have both continued to improve seemingly on a monthly basis as he's gotten stronger over the last twelve months. 

Sullivan's delivery and athleticism stand out in a big way. It's whip-crack arm speed with one of the fastest shoulders in the class. While he's not the biggest guy in the world, his phenomenal twitch and range of motion should allow him to hold this level of velocity into the next level so long as he stays healthy. He's had bumps and bruises that have kept him off the mound at times in his amateur career. 

The breaking ball is firm and sharp and effective even when spiked in front of the plate. Sullivan's changeup, while only average on most nights, is a workable third pitch. 

There's day one traits here. If he settles into more of a high-leverage relief projection he'll likely fit somewhere in the middle of day two or he'll end up attending Alabama. Sullivan will be 19 years old for the Draft.

A two-way talent with legitimate traits on both sides of the ball, Sampson's bat has caught more headlines as he's gotten bigger and stronger. There's impact projection if the hit tool continues it's linear path toward viability. 

Sampson has size, handedness and physicality on his side. It's a sweet left-handed swing with bat speed and efficient plane. Sampson drops a heavy barrel through the zone and has shown the ability to flash exit velocities at this age that point toward the potential for plus raw power projection. Elevated velocity and advanced spin can give him trouble inside and outside of the zone, but that's trending in the right direction as he's aged. Sampson is still learning how to impact the baseball to his pull-side, but that should come with time and maturation. 

On the dirt, the hands work and are capable of playing the hot corner at a steady level. He's unlikely to ever become a highlight reel regular, but Sampson will likely be trusted over there with further seasoning and reps. He's an average runner with average arm strength tested by a mechanical, deliberate arm action. Sampson will need to continue working on the fundamental and operational aspects of playing the infield, but softness in the hands a strong interal clock give him a chance. 

On the mound he absolutely pounds the zone and hardly ever issues free passes, a trait hardly ever seen with players at this age. He doesn't throw particularly hard just yet, up to 91 mph and usually resting 87-88 with tail and sink. There's a changeup and a mid-70s breaking ball that he likes to manipulate depending on the handedness of the batter. Both pitches show solid command and can be thrown early or late in counts. Sampson has a big, physical body with starting pitcher traits. He's not the most explosive mover and doesn't have the fastest arm in the class, but this level of polish oozes floor. If Sampson is living in the low-90s by the the time draft rolls around, he's got Top-100 pick upside. There's also offensive upside here with a sweet left-handed swing and some hittability and bat speed. A lot of avenues for this kid to make an impact going forward. He'll be 19.2 years old on draft day and will be draft eligible again in 2028 if he ends up at school.

Curry is a physical corner profile with easy bat speed and natural feel for launch. He's a natural hitter with the ability to get the barrel into every zone. He has a calm demeanor in the box and looks relaxed against premium arms. Curry is still developing what figures to be a pretty impactful offensive game. He can still drift and get out over his front side inhibiting his ability to tap into his raw offensive tools, but those inefficiencies haven't stopped him from generating impactful performances with the hit tool. 

He's a fringy runner at best and is best suited for a corner outfield role or first base at the next level. Curry is also up to 92 on the mound with a good little slider. Ultimately, this is a power-profile with a high floor hit tool.

Clatur has a lot of things going for him in MLB draft war rooms. He'll barely be 18 years old for the draft, and he's already showing some big traits. 

This is a fastball that jumps on hitters in a big way. Clatur has been up to 97, but more commonly sits 91-92 with serious hop through the zone. Some of the better hitters in the country were consistently late against Clatur's fastball last summer. He gets buckets of whiffs on the heater and can get away with misses in the heart of the plate at times due to his shape. Given his frame and age, it's not out of the question to assume Clatur may find 97 some day and sit more 93-94 at peak.

The slider is his primary weapon at this stage. It's a 77-81 with impressive depth. It's a breaking ball that'll need to firm up as he works into the next stage of his baseball career, but his feel for shaping the baseball stands out despite a lack of natural ability to create spin. A low-80s changeup rounds out his arsenal. Again, Clatur has feel to shape the ball, however he's not inherently blessed with the ability to delete spin. Most of his arsenal comes out of the hand in the same rpm bucket. 

Clatur has the foundation of a young righty with a frame to build on. He owns natural fastball value and can play a little yo-yo with his secondaries.

Hill certainly looks the part of a big league arm. His massive 6-foot-5 frame is physical and there's even more strength on the way. He's up to 96 with darting life. Hill mixes in a tough slider in the mid-80s with sweeping shape as well as an upper-70s changeup that lags behind the rest of his arsenal. 

Hill has some inefficiencies in his delivery that could clean up some of his strike-throwing inconsistencies. Plenty of time for those components to come together. The clay is here for a potential top 100 pick if he can get his profile into a more polished version of what it is today. He'll be super-young for the class, just 18.2 years old on Draft day.

A converted catcher, Garza's arm strength and athleticism he showed behind the plate have translated in a big way to the mound. 

Garza has a fastball that has seen its velocity continue to trend upward as he's become more focused on pitching. He's touching 96 these days with carry and some late tail to the arm-side. He fills up the zone with the fastball and has shown a willingness to change planes based on count leverage. It's certainly got above average potential, perhaps more if the velocity continues to climb.

Garza's slider is his crown jewel. Already a mid-80s frisbee with hard, late break, it's every bit that of a future plus breaking ball, and perhaps is already suggesting as much on stuff models right now. It's a wipeout secondary that he's proven capable of landing to the glove-side just off the plate to put hitters away. It's a pitch that features very little hump of broadcast out of the hand, jumping out of his fastball's tunnel late and in dynamic fashion.

A low-to-mid 80s splitter rounds out the arsenal, and while he hasn't thrown it a whole bunch, he has shown he can land it in competitive locations even if his command for the pitch is mostly fringy at this stage.

Garza is a riser in this draft class thanks to his winter gains and continued comfort on the mound. He's a terrific mover with the chance to start at the next level, so long as he proves durable enough for the challenge. He's still rather green to the art of pitching, so he'll have to check off some boxes with scouts as July approaches.

A massive lefty with a Dontrelle Willis-esque delivery, Cope has been one of the more famous arms in the 2026 class going back to his freshman year. The iconic high leg kick and high handset/break bringing back visions of Willis and pitchers of yesteryear. Cope has been up to 95 with a deceptive low release and a bit of a slingshot release on a fastball that features arm-side tail and carry. Cope has shown the ability to hold his velocity deep into starts and will routinely rest 91--94 into the fourth and fifth inning. 

He'll raise his slot a bit and get a tick more vertical on a short upper-70s gyroscopic slider. There's a low-80s changeup that Cope has been reluctant to show, a work in progress that could play well off the fastball with above average fading action. He's shown solid average command of the baseball and does a nice job limiting walks, bullying the opposition with angle and funk. 

Cope is the highest level follow in the 2026 class and has a chance to throw real fuzz. He'll be 19.3 years old for the draft, so scouts will want to see present stuff in the months leading up to the event.

Walk is a lean, wiry, downright skinny outfielder with a slappy approach to the game and blistering run times on the base paths. 

A switch-hitter, Walk is a better bat-to-ball guy from the left side with a polished approach and a willingness to take his free passes. His game has often been characterized as "annoying" by the opposition as he's been known to create chaos when given the opportunity. 

Walk doesn't possess a whole lot of power, but could develop into a table-setter who plays centerfield at the next level.

Just two years removed from being one of the more tantilizing physical specimens in the 2024 Draft, Quigley finds himself draft-eligible once more in 2026 with a bigger and louder sample under his belt. Seldom-used at South Florida as a true freshman in 2025, Quigley transferred to NFSC to get more playing time and attention from scouts. 

Quigley is certainly one of the more physically imposing players in the box. It's a long, strong frame with serious bat speed. Quigley is short to the ball and has natural loft in his swing, however he's yet to translate that loft and bat speed into game power at a high clip. Some scouts see the potential for plus game power as he matures into the game. Quigley has tinkered with his swing, varying between a more upright, athletic stance and a more leveraged back-heel focus, the former generally like the more comfortable setup. The latter has led to better results in the approach and swing-decision department. 

Quigley was more of an outfield prospect in high school, but finds himseld at shortstop and third base these days. He's an above average runner with a long stride -- good for stealing bases, and he's willing to show it. The short-form here is scouts really like the bat and the physically imposing frame. The offensive upside is tantalizing.

Brown is a talented two-way player with a physical frame. He routinely over matches the opposition on both sides of the ball.

Brown's biggest upside probably sits on the mound where the stuff and physicality continues to tick up. 

Brown has has begun to show more of a starter look this year featuring a true three-quarter slot and a bit of a slingshot arm action. He lands open and tails his arsenal away from left-handed hitters. He's added more sink to the baseball this year, generating weak contact aplenty. He doesn't extend down the mound well, a roadblock toward his ability to start as a professional, but his three-pitch mix ties hitters in knots. 

The fastball will grab 97 with considerable sink and occassional arm-side tail. Brown's changeup is very clearly 'plus'. It possesses huge depth and parachutes into the right-handed batters box. It also lives in the fastball tunnel late as it approaches the zone. 

His slider will vary in shape but also tunnels well off his arsenal. It's mostly average, sometimes morphing into a firm cutter. Brown doesn't yet possess great feel for landing his menu of pitches to the glove-side, instead allowing everything to tail away from left-handed bats. That'll be a piece of his development that will dictate if he can start at the college level. It's an awfully uncomfortable at-bats with hitters consistently being forced to guess what pitch is coming.

With the bat in his hands it's 'plus' raw power from the right side of the plate and a true feel for the barrel. It's a bit more hitterish with noisy hands from the left side. Most scouts believe he'll ultimately hit right-handed full-time at some point in his career. Brown can hit and he delivers a heavy blow to the baseball. 

Perhaps more impressive are Brown's actions on the dirt. He projects to third base due to his size and lateral mobility, but Brown has ultra-soft hands with loose wrists on the dirt. He's technically sound and demonstrates a slow heartbeat on balls hit his way. He supplements the glove with above average arm strength. He's a big frame so there will be an emphasis to stay mobile if he wants to stay on the left side of the infield.

Brown will two-way in college if he gets there.

Putnam is a big arm talent and a big mover on the mound who could end up throwing real gas someday. 

The fastball has been up to 100 mph in side bullpen sessions. Putnam has some durability too, importantly grabbing his best radar gun readings in the fourth and fifth inning of work. The control and command for the zone is streaky. Putnam is an electric mover whose delivery should shore itself up with strength gains in due time. It's an over-the-top delivery with big extension and carry through the zone.

Putnam throws an upper-70s breaker with curveball shape, more depth than horizontal tilt with some hump still present. Putnam does have feel for spin and shaping the ball, but refining that breaker will be crucial if he's to turn into a starter going forward. 

The velocity, arm strength and stamina will wow scouts. Polishing the edges, throwing more strikes and advancing the pitchability will eventually elevate the draft profile.

A bit of a hidden gem up in the Northeast for much of his high school career, Brown opened the eyes of scouts and baseball evaluators during the summer of 2025. A 6-foot-5-inch righty with age, traits and metrics on his side, Brown has fans in the scouting community.

An exceptional mover, Brown generates nearly seven feet of extension down the mound. His athleticism helps generate an arm slot that is just slightly lower than MLB-average despite it coming from such a long frame. Brown usually sits 80-92 and will grab 95, however his velocity plays up in a major way thanks to his extension and fastball shapes. Brown has a vertical carrying heater and can induce north of 21 inches of vertical break at his peaks. That's impressive considering his moderate velocity capacity at this stage. As he throws harder, that should only improve. Brown's fastball has a chance to be special as he adds strength and stuff in the future. 

There's a low-80s slider and a low-80s changeup that are both deployed sparingly at this stage. They've both shown at least average upside and play nicely off the uniquneness hitters have to prepare for with the fastball. 

Brown is a pure projection play. He could blossom into a big time talent in college if he isn't signed away from Penn State in the draft first. He'll be 18.5 for the draft.

One of the premier bat-to-ball artists in the 2026 class, what Moore lacks in physical stature he more than makse up for with his polished approach and pesky nature. A draft-eligible true sophomore, Moore can contribute to a team in multiple ways. A versatile player. 

Moore employs a slightly closed setup at the plate with a front shoulder closed to the pitcher as well. He has quiet hands and a simple move taking the barrel to the ball with quick hands and a slasher mentality. Moore uses the entire field and takes what the pitcher gives him. His approach has resulted in a high ground ball rate; something that may dilute his batting average as a professional. In college ball, it's helped produce a high batting average to go alongside a healthy on-base percentage thanks to a willingness to draw walks. Moore simply refuses to expand the zone and because of it consistently runs minuscule, elite chase rates.

An above average runner, Moore gets good breaks out of the batters box and tends to beat out 50/50 choppers on the infield. His speed should allow him to at least be a stolen base threat at the next level, even if he's not a particularly dynamic threat. This is a bottom-of-the-lineup slasher who will put the game in motion. A true conga line mentality. 

Moore almost exclusively played third base for the Hoosiers as a freshman and has rotated between the hot corner and second base of late. The arm action and arm strength both probably fit best at second base. It's average arm strength, but Moore's feel for game tempo and his internal clock are both plus. He's certainly comfortable at third base and despite lacking prototypical third base tools, plays above-average defense and gobbles up everything routine. The tough in-between hop is just about the only thing that can give him trouble.

Moore's versatility on the dirt, his above average speed, and his polish at the plate are all selling points. His 5-foot-9-inch frame and lack of much power will likely push his profile into the 11-20 round range, but there should be buyers. He fits what the Guardians and Nationals scouting leadership like to target in drafts.

Latham is a sturdy-built righty with strength and mass even distributed across his 6-foot-1-inch frame. He lacks much more physical projection. Broad shoulders and a thicker, stronger lower-half suggests durability going forward. 

Latham delivers from a high three-quarter slot. There's some effort and moderate whack at release, specifically when he throws the fastball. It's a high leg-kick with a deliberate, sometimes late gather. Latham's arm swing is on the longer side featuring some urgency and tempo to get into his launch position. He generates average extension down the mound and relies on arm strength and arm speed to get to his velocity.

At present, Latham has been up to 94 but more comfortably pitches in the 90-92 range across multiple innings. Latham will at times flash effective carry, coupled with above-average arm-side movement. It's likely a solid average fastball going forward.

Latham's secondaries consist of a curveball, slider and changeup. He spins the baseball well, exceeding 2800 rpm on the curveball at his best. The curveball is presently his best weapon, however he has a tendency to vary his release points and broadcast the pitch a bit at times. His slider is firm, 82-84 with shorter vertical tilt and some sweep. His ability to land that pitch for strikes can be streaky from night to night. A low-to-mid 80s changeup is a high spin offering, presently lacking dynamic enough shape off what his fastball does. 

Latham has four pitches and throws enough strikes to perhaps start at the next level early in his career. It's not a prototypical starting pitcher build, and he may not create shapes that can manuever through a lineup more than once. His capacity for spin gives him some building blocks to play with from a player development standpoint, however his ceiling may be limited given his frame. There's certainly talent and traits here, however teams may want to see how he performs as Southern Miss before investing in the Draft.

A winding road has led Quarles to Florida SouthWestern. Originally an Ohio State commit coming out of high school, Quarles instead enrolled at Bryant & Stratton College where he'd run an OPS over 1.250 as a freshman. That got him noticed nationally, once more transferring zip codes, this time to FSW.

The athleticism and notariety on Quarles' name has jumped into a new tier. He's getting noticed by scouts and writers on the amateur seen at a heavy clip. The speed stands out in a big way. He's a stolen base merchant and tracks fly balls with reckless abandon. While the routes can be crude, his athleticism and range more than makes up for what any shortcomings fundamentally. Quarles is a centerfield prospect through and through. If he's forced to left field as a pro, it'll only be because there's a more fluid, consistent ball-tracker flanking his left.

Quarles has super-fast hands at the plate. He's learned to integrate more loft and backspin into his offensive profile since high school. He's catching the ball out front and getting to his pull-side with a bit more frequency, even if he still tends to pepper the opposite field. Quarles' plate skills and approach are a solid with some work still ahead at this stage. He has a tendency to expand the zone against spin and offspeed weapons, but not quite at red-flag levels. Still, as the level of competition gets tougher, scouts will wonder if the chase rates will bloat. The bat-to-ball skills are also average without any clear trends or specific holes in his offensive profile. Breaking balls generally result in the highest clip of whiffs for Quarles.

The whiffs may be something teams can deal with when considering the run tool and raw power. It's above-average raw power that's trending toward plus. It plays to all fields too. Quarles will need to continue showing off the bat speed as July approaches to ease concerns over some hit tool concerns.

Quarles is exciting. He's certainly one of the top junior college position-player prospects in the 2026 Draft. It's a power/speed combo with some shortcomings in the polish department. He won't turn 21 until after the Draft and hasn't yet been challenged with elite pitching.

A big, tall, physically imposing right-hander, Norman towers over the opposition with a 6-foot-7-inch frame and a repertoire of pitches that continues to expand. A former Georgia State standout, Norman transferred to Coastal for brighter light in 2026.

For the time being, Norman is mostly a two-pitch guy. He runs the fastball up to 96 and will sit 91-94 with carry and occassional cut. It's big extension down the mound that should help his heater plus up a bit, but to date it's been a pitch that's been hit around at times. Norman does get swings outside of the zone from the opposition, but they're often fouled off. 

A low-to-mid 80s slider is his go-to secondary featuring solid two-plane tilt. He repeats his release point well and sells the pitch with solid spin rates and arm speed. It's been effective, however he's struggled to get to it at times. 

Norman has been working to fold in a deep changeup that he'll need if he hopes to start at the next level. 

The frame and arm action really work here. Norman is a good mover, a good enough strike thrower and should have three pitches with the ability to work north/south and east/west soon. It's a project in a lot of ways, but good clay.

Lanman burst onto the scene as a true freshman earning Freshman All-American honors from a number of publications after shoving 72.1 innings and punching 79 tickets as a teenager. Lanman has a deliberate delivery with a short-ish arm-swing, exploding through release with conviction. Lanman cuts the hell out of his fastball with carry and lift. Despite only topping out at 95 and living a few ticks lower than that, Lanman posts above-average whiff and chase rates on a pitch that could eventually land 'above average' at the next level. 

Lanman's slider is along the same lines, a cut-heavy bullet slider that he'll elevate and lift more than a conventional slider. Commanding that pitch where he wants it has been a work in progress as it generally gets hit pretty hard lower in the zone, but as he lands the breaker at the top of the zone (a la Cristian Javier) he should begin to find more and more success parlaying it off his fastball. Lanman's most-used secondary is a traditional 12-6 curveball in the mid-70 velo band. With time he'll add more oomph to it and eventually iron out the hump. For now, it's largely a fringy pitch that is most effective at freezing hitters and/or getting ahead of hitters early in counts. At this stage it hasn't been a dynamic swing-and-miss pitch. 

Supplementing the arsenal is huge extension down the bump. He's a great mover. 

Lanman's workhorse frame, repeatable arm action, extension down the mound, his strike-throwing ability, and unique release traits make for an intriguing pitching prospect at the next level. He'll need to figure out some way to generate some east-west threat to hitters, perhaps a splitter at the next level.

Kiker owns a compact build and strong lower half. His delivery involves a longer arm swing that generates velocity in the low 90s, up to 95 mph. Kiker's delivery is loose and easy with conviction. He's shown advanced pitchability, changing the tempo of his delivery and keeping hitters off balance. Kiker has a tendency to land slightly open, at times sling-shotting the ball to the plate. There may be a bit more velocity in the tank as he learns to stay closed through his stride, as well as firming up his lead-leg block. For now, the arm talent is so exceptional on its own, he's dominating the competition without being totally efficient. 

His slider is a low-80s bullet-breaker with strong vertical traits. Kiker throws the fastball and slider with equal weight making it difficult for hitters to sit on any one pitch. There's also a bigger, deeper slurvy breaking ball that does well when spiked in the dirt, tunneling his fastball/slider combination. 

Perhaps the most interesting part of Kiker's arsenal is a mid-70s knuckleball that he's shown incredible feel for at this stage in his baseball career. His knuckler dances all over the place before generally landing in and around the zone. It's consistently generated hapless swings from opposing hitters. 

Kiker will probably need to add a changeup or a splitter to the arsenal to become a true starting pitcher prospect, but he's got time. If the velocity spikes up into the mid-90s by July, Kiker is an obviousl day-one pitching prospect.

Cooney certainly looks the part and acts the part of a big league infielder. It's the high waist, long strider with athletic actions across the board the teams really target as future middle-of-the-diamond stalwarts. 

Indeed, Cooney can pick it and has a strong arm that fits fine at shortstop. He's been forced off the position often due to the existence of Maddox Molony, but he'll likely get a shot once again in pro gall. There are questions on the impact in the bat, but this is a solid frame with plenty of projection to come and the building blocks of a really talented infielder at the next level.

One of the more explosive arm talents in the 2026 class, Hamilton possesses release traits and pitch shapes that make hitting his stuff a real pain in the ass for the opposition. The pure velocity hasn't arrived yet, but if it ever does, Hamilton has a chance to develop into a high-leverage weapon at the very least. 

Hamilton is a short-strider who will lull hitters to sleep with his slow, deliberate operation. He's not a fast mover, but the arm speed at release will catch hitters off guard. It's a longer arm action with some mild inversion as he works down the mound. Hamilton lands slightly closed and cross-fires his arsenal, hiding the ball behind his back shoulder long enough to create considerable deception. The heater blows up at the top of the zone thanks to a lower launch and unique carrying traits for his slot. Hamilton fires from a wider angle and could generate even more fastball value against right-handed hitter if he were to ever setup on the third-base side of the rubber. The heater has been up to 94 and will sit 89-92 after the third and fourth innings. There's occassionally some tail to the pitch, however its value is primarily derived from its vertical approach angle. 

Hamilton folds a mid-70s slurvy sweeper to right-handed hitters and throws a bigger, more exciting low-80s changeup that fades and tumbles hard to his arm-side when there's a lefty in the box. 

Given the lack of extension, Hamilton will likely need to develop a harder breaking ball if he's to start at the professional level. It's a leverage relief look for the time being. If Hamilton works to incorporate a sinker and/or a cutter and gets the sweeper moving faster through the zone, he'll certainly develop through the minor leagues as a starting pitcher prospect. It's a good frame, three pitches, strikes and fastball quality. An excellent foundation. Hamilton will be 18.6 years old for the Draft.

A big, tall, imposing righty with a workhorse frame, Albanese transitioned from high-leverage bullpen opportunities into a more extended bridge reliever as his sophomore spring rolled on. He tossed more than 50 pitches just twice as a second-year hurler, but most expect he'll see chances to start in 2026.

Albanese's fastball is his bread and butter. He's a good mover who generates elite extension toward the plate, some of that in large part due to his already lengthy frame. He pounds the zone with a heater that'll live 92-94 and touch 96 at peak. Albanese produces moderate carry through the zone, but the pitch has a tendency to sneak up on hitters with how close he launches to the plate. Supplementing the velocity and extension is a natural ability to spin the baseball at a high clip. Albanese has an plus heater that produces exceptional results at the college level.

Albanese throws one breaking ball with big two-plane shape. It's much fringier feel for commanding that pitch into and out of the zone. He also has a tendency to broadcast the pitch to hitters because he cuts off his stride more than six inches down the bump. At 79-80 mph, it's a pitch that needs to firm up and add sharpness if he hopes to get pro hitters out with it at a consistent clip. For the time being, it's a fringy secondary that'll flash above-average traits when he's got feel for throwing it with conviction and command.

Albanese has the big frame, the ability to throw strikes and inputs teams will like to see from a fastball perspective. There's some effort through release that may preclude him from pitching in a rotation at the next level, but it's arm talent that can likely carve out some sort of role.

A big imposing left-handed hitter, McQuillan has plus raw power projection with the bat-to-ball skills necessary to show it off. He swings a heavy barrel and has shown capable of turning around premium velocity to the pull-side. McQuillan's big, physical, durable frame stands out, as do his fast hands and whippy barrel in the box.

McQuillan isn't a burner but he moves better than most players his size. There's some stiffness in his gait but he still amps up to solid-average run times and making tight turns around the bases. He's an extra-base hit machine who likes to show off the wheels.

McQuillan has received plenty of time at third base, but most believe he's a corner outfield stick or first base thumper at the next level. The bat will carry the water here, but it's a loud one. McQuillan will be 19 years old for the Draft.

Shadek went reasonably unheralded coming out of high school, in large part due to undergoing Tommy John surgery as a senior. He took 2024, his freshman season, as an opportunity to get bigger and stronger and rehab his arm strength back to full health. And that path paid off. Shadek turned himself into one of the hardest throwers in the Big Ten. That caught the attention of schools elsewhere, eventually landing him in the transfer portal where he'd relocate to Georgia Tech. 

It's a true five-pitch mix for the big righty out of New Jersey. He's been up to 99 with a fastball that features some hop and tailing action. Shadek spins the heck out of the fastball and should be able to generate some dynamic shapes with further tinkering and seasoning on the mound. As presently constructed, the velocity is responsible for whiffs produced. 

Shadek will throw the kitchen sink. His slider is firm, up to 86 with shorter break, occasionally sweeping into the glove-side box. He'll fold in an even shorter cutter in the same velo band that probably needs to firm up if it's to serve its purpose. A big, deep curveball flashes plus shape and stuff. He'll also mix in a changeup to lefties now and again that lacks dynamic shape at this stage, but Shadek does kill spin nicely. 

Shadek isn't yet the punch out artist that he could become. He's very green on the mound and his best baseball is ahead of him. Feel for four or five pitches, huge extension, strikes, and a workhorse frame has scouts and evaluators bullish on the final product.

Voegele, a 20th round selection by the Arizona Diamondbacks in the 2023 Draft, is an athletic righty with a quick arm and stuff that has really exploded over the last 12 months. 

Now up to 97, Voegele will sits 93-94 with arm-side run and moderate carry. The fastball has been effective despite him being a short-strider to the plate with a generic release profile. 

He mixes in two distinct breaking balls. There's a mid-to-upper 80s slider that will vary in shape, but at its best possesses very strong depth and some late tilt. The curveball is shorter, firm with some teeth. 

Voegele has also messed around with a changeup from time to time, but it's inconsistent. Scouts love his willingness and ability to pitch inside on right-handed hitters at such a young age. 

Everything Voegele does is athletic and easy. The arm action is a little long, but he repeats well and has a track record of filling up the strikezone. He'll need to continue to prove his fastball value isn't a mirage. If he puts together another banner year in 2026, he's got Top-100 pick upside.

Montgomery is a physically intimidating force in the box, but he's far from a one-trick pony. Pound for pound, this is one of the more exceptional athletes in the 2026 class. It's plus run times, above average arm strength and a burgeoning hit tool in tournament settings. Montgomery, of course, has the plus raw power you'd expect from a player of his build.

As if the present tools weren't enough, Montgomery tests extremely well with force plates and proponents of the profile believe there's even more tools to be extracted from his 6-foot-5-inch frame. A brutish slugger with serious weight behind his hands at the point of impact, Montgomery has a shot run into 30 homers at the next level and steal 30 bags if the hit tool ever gets to a point where his athleticism plays in a bigger way on the field.

Cash Scarborough is one of the more unique pitching prospects in the 2026 class. He's an analytic darling with huge stuff that can explode through the zone when he's at his best. Undersized, Scarborough will fight the reliever labels throughout his career, however he's got the arsenal to fend off doubters for some time.

Scarborough has a chance to own a special fastball. He's been up to 97 mph, launched from a 60 inch slot. At his best, Scarborough is holding 15 inches of IVB on his heater with VAAs well under -4°. When he's landing the heater at the top of the zone, and staying behind the baseball, it's at least a plus offering, closer to a 70-grade weapon when the velocity comes along with it. Scarborough compliments the four-seamer with a low-90s sinker that often melts into his four-seam shape, but does generate a bit more arm-side tailing action.

The cutter and sweeper here have some upside. The cutter in particular is launched out of the same slot as the four-seamer and generates considerable depth and horizontal movement to the glove-side. It's a low-to-mid 80s weapon and often resembles a slider more than a cutter, but whatever he'd like to classify it as, it's a very good pitch. It's a barrel-beater and a whiff generator when he's landing it off the plate. The sweeper gets big numbers behind it, but Scarborough drops his arm slot considerably to accomplish those shapes. Professional hitters will pick up on that quickly. Still, his ability to supinate like that and creates shapes is moldable at a minimum.

There is a changeup here as well. Scarboroguh is capable of getting the baseball to move the other way. His shapes are very inconsistent here, as is his feel for landing it anywhere competitively.

The undersized right-handed high school pitcher is always a difficult demographic in the draft. From a stuff perspective, few in the class can match Scarborough's peaks. His capacity for spin is excellent, his delivery is sound and reasonably free and easy. The arm speed is very impressive. If he can prove to even one team he's a starting pitcher prospect, there's a chance he goes and gets top-three round money. If teams believe he's a reliever, he'll likely be offered six figures somewhere after day one. Should he make it to Stillwater, he'll be a very real weapon for the Cowboys.

Consiglio was impressive as a true freshman for NC State in his limited looks earning an invite to play with Team USA. It's a cross-fire delivery with plenty of deception and upside in the secondaries. His low-90s fastball isn't overwhelming and has only been up to 94 featuring reasonably generic shape. It performs well as hitters have struggled to pick it up out of the hand, but metrically it isn't a pitch that will light up analyst alarms. 

Consiglio's changeup is probably his best pitch; a mid-80s tumbler that he's shown solid average command for. It's produced strong whiff rates and can induce some chase outside of the zone as well. It has a chance to become plus if he develops a more effective fastball and better command of his arsenal.

There's a loopier curveball and a cutter-esque slider that have both been effective in smaller samples, but lack feel for command. Consiglio has an up arrow next to his name.

After an on-again, off-again freshman year at UCLA, Randall has become more reliable for the Bruins in 2026 and now represents one of the more intriguing metric darlings on the West Coast. A great mover, Randall possesses awesome extension and athleticism on the mound. The strikes have continued to improve, upping his leveragability to role projections at the next level. He's yet to start a game in college, but some scouts believe he should get that shot in pro ball. 

The thing that immediately sticks out with Randall is how easy he moves on the bump. It's an explosive, under-control body operation with a vertical three-quarter arm slot. The high leg kick and impressive ride down the mound allows his pitches to sneak up on hitters. The arm action itself can be a little late at times, leading to wobbling control. 

The fastball has been up to 98 and will sit 94-96 in his bullpen outings. It's a heater that presents above average carry through the zone with high spin rates. It's a fastball that'll grab whiffs. 

His go-to secondary is a tumbling changeup that plays 7-8 mph off his heat with shorter break, aided by arm speed and conviction. It relies on its velocity separation as its break doesn't vary too much from the fastball. He'll bury a bullet slider over the plate in the upper 80s, though it's been an inconsistent weapon in showings. There's also a shorter low-8s curveball.

Randall doesn't yet have a secondary weapon he can rely on to get hitters out. He's a fastball-first reliever at this stage with a big arm and blossoming velocity, although fringy control and command has limited his upside in big spots. He's a good arm with some strong traits that remains considerably unrefined.

Dorsey had a big up arrow on his name in 2025 before an injury ended his season after jsut three outings. After a spectacular two years with the University of South Florida, Dorsey transferred to LSU for his draft-eligible junior season where he continued to show off his exceptional arm talent. It was all for naught.

Dorsey relocated to Central Florida for the 2026 season seeking new voices, bigger opportunities and a fresh start. 

Already touching 99 with above-average spin rates, Dorsey can get by throwing the heater early and often. He's got a high slot, carrying and cutting the fastball over the barrel of opposing hitters. He relies heavily on shapes and velocity due to middling extension. 

If nothing changes at the next level Dorsey will be forced to throw his sweeper at a much greater clip, but it's a very, very good one. He's flashed spin rates north of 3000 rpm at times and will routinely rest in the 2900 range. Dorsey's sweeper is firm, usually 83-84 mph and up to 87 mph at peak. He generates plenty of two-plane tilt with the pitch and it's performed very well to this point. 

Dorsey will need to rein in the control and command a bit as walks can spike on him at times, but it hasn't been an enormous red flag at this point in his career. There's a chance for two above average pitches here with the innate arm talent to stretch one of those offerings to 'plus'. He'll need a more polished changeup if he hopes to start at the next level, but this is a workhorse frame with an exceptional ability to manipulate the baseball.

Charlie West might have the most circus-trick fastball in the country. A 5-foot-11-inch lefty, West delivers the baseball with full intent and effort. It's below average control and command, but there are four pitches here and a shot at a big league role if his feel for the zone improves.

That fastball is ridiculous. Despite his stature, West launches from a slot four or five inches higher than the MLB average. His extreme over-the-top supination delivery results in enormous carry and occassional late hop through the zone. While he's only touched 93 mph, he's consistently generating north of 24 inches of IVB. It's a fastball that's produced impressive whiff rates, especially for its velocity band. Again, controlling the baseball, let alone commanding it to a specific zone or quadrant is a work in progress.

West tends to drop his arm slot for his secondaries, but he does have three different weapons to work with. The changeup has been his most effective pitch outside of the fastball. West gets impressive depth and tumbling action on the pitch, resulting in huge whiff and chase rates. It's also his most efficient pitch from a strike percentage perspective. If West can ever get command for his heater, the changeup may start flashing plus. 

A slider and curveball both serve their purpose, but aren't terrible effective at this stage. The slider is a low-80s breaker with deeper tilt and some late lateral break. The curveball sits in the mid-70s and dives roughly half a foot more than the slider. 

West is an athletic mover with good extension and secondaries he's shown relative feel for. It's a reliever look with a Yuki Matsui type of arsenal. West will be very young for the draft and won't turn 21 until after the 2026 season concludes.

Underhill changed zip codes in 2025 after two intriguing seasons with Eastern Kentucky. He landed at Austin Peay. 

Underhill has explosive arm speed and can reach back for 97. A mid-80s slider is his most effective weapon. Underhill has worked hard to fold a changeup into his repertoire and it's flashing some above-average. He generates above average extension down the mound and launches his entire assortment of pitches from an extremely low slot. It's athleticism and uniqueness on the bump with a heater that's been difficult for hitters to touch at the top of the zone. 

His tools aren't limited to pitching either. He's also a smooth right-handed hitter with heavy hands at the plate. Above average runner too. 

Underhill is the type of prospect organizations love to take a shot on given his intangibles and untapped potential. The whole package may not have come together yet, but there are components to dream on from a player development perspective.

Bell was draft-eligible as a 21-year-old in 2025 but, to the surprise of many, went unselected. 

Bell swings a heavy barrel. His hard-hit rates and exit velocities have consistently ranked among the best in college baseball in his three-year stint with the Bulldogs. While his peak exit velocities are more befitting of a player that possesses above average raw power, his feel for the barrel will likely drive up his homer output at the next level if the hit tool can survive more advanced pitching.

Bell's got some swing and miss in his game, and he's an aggressive swinger who will expand the zone when presented with spin. Pitches left inside of the zone haven't been a huge issue. Bell sets up with an open stance and employs an exaggerated leg kick to get to his bat speed. Bell actually switched from a toe-tap to a leg kick during the 2025 season to try and improve his power output. It's very real juice with proven power to all fields, including over the right-center field fence. As the months have progressed, the entire operation at the plate has continued to quiet down more and more. The handsy load and sequencing issues seem to be behind Bell. He's blossomed into an impact producer that fits in the middle of a lineup.

A primary right fielder, Bell is an above average glove in a corner with solid range at the athleticism to make the tough catch. He's got solid average arm strength and can hold runners at bay in most scenarios. There's been some run at third base over the course of his collegiate career as well. If enough scouts believe he can play the hot corner as a professional his name could be pulled into the top five or six rounds as a money play. 

Bell is a good player who's coming into his own. If he can cut down the swing and miss on the breaking ball, he'll blossom into one of the top position player prospects on the West Coast for 2026.

Smaldino and his 6-foot-6-inch frame earned immediate playing time in Berkeley as a freshman and parlayed that into a full-time starting role as a sophomore in 2025. He elected to transfer following that year and played his draft-eligible junior year in Tempe for the Sun Devils.

Smaldino is an imposing presence in the box regardless of his stature. He sets up closed to the pitcher with lower set hands and some spine bend, slightly leaning over the plate. His load involves pressing the hands back. tipping the barrel slightly to create more length through the zone. When he gets the foot down, Smaldino is locked into a stretched position generating coil, using his frame very well. He stays behind his front side, rotating hard over his front hip, demonstrating excellent hand strength through the zone. It's enormous bat speed, however Smaldino's ability to control the barrel in-zone will waver as his swing plane can jump all over the place, especially when presented with spin. He's certainly built to do damage, and he gets the ball in the air at a healthy clip, but more premium arms with big secondaries can give him fits.

Smaldino is a primary first baseman who moves well around the bag and projects to stay at the position. He's an average runner. It's a boom-or-bust profile with 70-grade power. If the hit tool catches up with the raw power, he's got a chance to develop into a 30-homer threat in the big leagues, however the polish isn't there yet.

Buettenback, a former standout high school running back, carries himself with the same level of physicality and impact that his shoulder pads delivered as a prep. A stout 6-foot-1-inch, 215-pound right fielder, Buettenback brings the power to the box you'd expect from a player with his pedigree and stature. But he's ditched his aggressive gridiron nature and plays with a level of calm and maturity each time he steps into the on-deck circle. 

After hardly playing as a freshman, Buetteback headed out to the Northwoods League in 2024, winning League MVP with a .395/.504/.605 slash with nine homers and 30 stolen bases. The stage was set for a massive redshirt freshman year in 2025. Unfortunately, an illness made his playing time yo-yo for much of the season. Buettenback performed admirably, but many felt as though there was more meat on the bone from what he was showing. 

Buettenback's underlying metrics support the notion there's more in the tank. He ran average contact rates supplemented by an above-average approach with healthy chase rates and strong in-zone swing rates. His bat-to-ball skills on swings inside the zone were well-above average, however a lack of adjustability on pitches outside of the zone hurt his slash line and strikeout rate. His willingness to swing and pitchers' pitches does neutralize some of his raw power and contact quality at times. Buettenback pulled the trigger against fastballs consistently and got to his pull-side nearly half of the time, smoking line drives with a heavy frequency. 

It's at least above average raw power with exit velocities that have ticked north of 110 mph. His average exit velocities are more middle of the pack. A short, compact swing plane with some natural loft should help him get to most of that power in games, eventually. This is an intriguing bat, if not yet fully optimized or efficient in the box. 

Buettenback is an above average runner underway who moves exceptionally well for his size. He's got a smooth stride that should mature well as he ages into professional baseball. Buettenback has the look of a solid average right fielder. He takes reasonably good routes to the ball. His spacial awareness, feel for the wall and the warning track presence is a work in progress, but he generally makes the play. It's solid average arm strength with a mature game IQ. Buettenback will rarely hurt his team with his defensive play, however he's unlikely to provide excess defensive value. 

Buettenback has a chance to develop into something of a Kole Calhoun type of player at the next level, especially if his defensive traits tick up. The bat is intriguing, as is the athlete. A year removed from his illness, Buettenback has a chance to take a jump as July approaches.

A left-handed hitter with a powerful swing, Corley deploys an open stance with high set hands. He's displayed an advanced hit tool and a simple move to take the barrel to the baseball. He'll vary leg kick and strides in the box depending on the situation, but can really ambush a pitch when ahead. Corley has fast hands with adjustability. He's been one of the better hitters in this class on getting to velocity on the top rail. Corley should get more physical and incorporate his lower half a bit more as he matures, but the pure bat-to-ball is impressive at this stage. He's a fringe-average runner with a physical, upright gait, unlikely to ever be a burner on the bases. Corley displays strong reads in the field with a compact arm swing and average arm strength. He's likely destined for left field at the next level if the arm strength doesn't improve, but the selling point on this profile, at least as currently constructed, is the bat. 

Some believe Corley has a chance to pitch going forward. He's been up to 93 mph and moves well on the bump. Loose arm, good extension and a lower-slot helps his three-pitch mix miss bats. The sliders is 79-83 with sweeping shape. A low-80s changeup rounds out the arsenal. Corley has a good bit of head-whack at release. As he gets stronger and continues to refine his mechanics, that should iron itself out. He doesn't overthrow the baseball. He will be 18.8 years old for the draft.

Alaniz is a local favorite of scouts in the state of Texas thanks to his do-it-all attitude, polish, and versatility. While undersized and lacking a carrying tool, Alaniz does the little things that don't stand out in a box score but help his team to a win. 

A primary shortstop at Trinity, Alaniz has proven capable of playing all over the diamond on the travel ball circuit. He's plenty capable of playing shortstop, and at an above average level. It's average arm strength, soft hands and quiet actions all befitting of a middle infielder. His best defensive home may ultimately be second baes as a professional.

Alaniz's bat is hit-over-power. He peppers both gaps and can turn singles into doubles with solid average foot speed. He's a good baserunner and is aggressive and witty enough to take the extra base. While he's not likely going to be an impact hitter in the lineup, he'll be a conga line performer.

Alaniz is something of a budget Dylan Moore. He doesn't quite have the bat speed Moore does, but he can play all over the field and provides defensive value. He also runs enough to provide value.

Kyle and his brother Kolby have been punishing the college baseball landscape for the better part of the last five years. Where Kolby is more of a slugging middle infielder, Kyle is a bat-to-ball merchant with speed to burn on the basepaths. 

Branch carved out an immediate starting role with the Sooners upon arriving to Norman. A primary second baseman, Branch can rover around the field and handle a number of roles. He's smooth and dynamic at second base. Soft hands and quick feet allow him to make just about every play hit in his radius. Branch and the highlight reel play are quite familiar with one another. The actions may eventually force him to shortstop where his average arm strength and athleticism should probably be given a chance to sink or swim. In any case, it's a surefire up-the-middle defender.

Branch's hit tool is very strong. While he doesn't possess much slug, Branch does put everything in play allowing his above average speed to be put on display.

Branch has a chance to be a plus hitter with above average speed and plus defense at second base. He's a very talented ballplayer even if homers are unlikely to ever become a part of his profile.

Holton is a high-octane righty with an up-tempo delivery and a fastball that he likes to blow by the competition. He's been up to 96 and he'll tinker with shape; sometimes running the ball into righties, other times carrying it through the top rail with a bully mentality. He'll scatter the pitch around the zone and currently features below average command for his arsenal. 

Holton also flashes a low-80s slider with depth, though he broadcasts that pitch at times and it can be identified out of the hand. He's got a tremendous frame with a high waist, long, lean levers and projects still coming. He's a guy that could eventually sit in the mid-90s in a bullpen role. If the strikes improve and a third pitch comes along, Holton could get a shot to start. He is revered by coaches and his peers for being a baseball junkie and a pitching "nerd".

Perhaps the most unique athlete in all of college baseball, Ishikawa has a decorated backstory and brings unique talents to both sides of the ball. After just one season at the University of Seattle in 2025, Ishikawa hit the portal and transferred to Georgia where his stock took a sizeable jump.

Ishikawa can do it all, but he'll likely be drafted for his ability on the mound. Despite his smaller frame, Ishikawa's athleticism and exceptional movement patterns allow him to throw pretty hard. He'll work up to 96 mph and has shown capable of holding 91-94 mph across several innings. He's a strike-thrower and will manipulate the shapes of his fastball to keep hitters at bay. He's at his best when he's cutting the heater into the knuckles of right-handed hitters. The University of Georgia deserves some credit here. Ishikawa was mostly 88-91 in 2025, touching 94. His stuff took a considerable jump under the tutelage of Wes Johnson. 

Ishikawa throws a mid-70s curveball with bigger downward shape. It's effective at the college level, but will likely mostly be used as a strike-stealer at the pro level. There's a low-80s slider and a mid-80s changeup that he'll lean on to get whiffs. 

This is four pitches, it's strikes, it's polish and it's athleticism. There's all the makings of big pitching prospect here, just scratching the surface of player development. 

Ishikawa plays centerfield when he's not pitching. He's hit leadoff for the Bulldogs and works long, annoying counts from the opposition. 

Ishikawa is already 22 years old and was selected by the Orix Buffaloes in the sixth round of the 2025 Nippon Professional Baseball Draft Conference in Tokyo on Oct. 23, 2025. He has options after this season to go in several different directions.

The second in the Flora line, Hudson's older brother Jackson is/was a premium draft prospect for the 2026 class coming out of college. Hudson is a much different player, but decorated in ways of his own. 

One of the more premium bat-to-ball artists in the class, Flora is almost impossible to strike out. He's a selective hitter that likes to put the game in motion; not yet blossoming into impact power to project into the middle of a lineup. Flora has good size and a sweet right-handed swing. Power should come at some point, if only fringy at best. Flora is certainly a bat-to-ball artist, and one of the best in the class, even if many of those balls in play are hit on the ground. 

Flora is a solid average receiver with enough arm strength to project behind the plate. He's still growing into baseball muscle and athleticism, so his story is likely not yet written defensively. Ultimately, he'll likely grow into above average arm strength as at the next level. He is a solid average runner and projects one of the better runners for his position in the class.

Shouse is a two-way player with upside on both sides of the ball, and scouts are split on what side of the ball his future lays. That said, of late, it seems the growing sentiment is favoring the bat. 

Shouse is an extremely impressive athlete on the mound with sublime body control coming out of a longer arm action, attacking hitters. The fastball works up to 98 and is commanded well. There's real deception here. The ball jumps on hitters with late carry. While it's not presently exceptional command, Shouse has shown flashes of dominance in the zone and there are plenty of scouts who like the upside as a starter. 

He's worked to develop more depth on a low-80s slider, and that's seen real progress over the last year. There's also a changeup that he'll offer to left-handed hitters. 

Offensively, it's twitchy raw power with a exit velocities that suggest plus bat speed. He's shown average bat-to-ball skills and an aggressive approach. It's also a double-plus throwing arm in the outfield. His routes and ability to track the ball continues to be a work in progrese as he's new to the role being a shortstop for most of his amateur career. Shouse has played some first base as well. Scouts will need to see more refinement on the pure hit tool, but everything about the player flashes upside.

After two slugging campaigns in the ACC playing for the hometown Pittsburgh Panthers, Zuckerman was sought in the transfer portal and traveled south to Georgia Tech for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign.

Zuckerman certainly looks the part. He fills out a uniform and looks like a pro off the bus. And the tools match the frame. Zuckerman has plus raw power and delivers heavy hands through the zone with a short, abbreviated swing. He finds barrels at a heavy clip when he's making contact, however swing-and-miss has thwarted his ability to consistently translate the bat speed into game production. Zuckerman has what many would call a "grooved swing". He pummels pitches in his hot zone, however adjusting to pitches outside of the zone or pitches on the black gives him fits. It's certainly a slug-over-hit profile going forward, but also a profile that could conceivably be an adjustment away from being productive.

Zuckerman can handle third base at an average level and certainly owns the arm strength for the position. His big, physical frame may eventually push him to first base if he loses athleticism and/or lateral mobility.

It's something of a Ryon Healy type of profile, with a bit more whiff than Healy showed at Oregon.

Following a big freshman year at Cal State Fullerton, Johnstone hit the transfer portal seeking bigger and brighter lights.

He's an accomplished bat-to-ball specialist who boasts minuscule whiff rates combined with impressively small chase rates. It's a polished approach and one that projects to hit for average and on-base at the next level. Johnstone is an adjustable hitter. He handles pitches inside and outside of the zone and can make a pitcher work. He can, at times, be a bit passive in the box, but he hardly gives away at-bats. Johnstone to date has shown below average raw power and slug isn't a big part of his game. He's an average runner who will occasionally snag the extra base. 

Johnstone has shortstop roots and moves well at third base. It's a smattering of average tools at the hot corner with the chance to play there or at second base at the next level. He is the brother of Vanderbilt hitter Logan Johnstone and elected to join him at Vanderbilt for the 2026 season.

Ruiz was a legitimate draft prospect playing for Lamar in 2025 but went unselected due to his commitment to transfer to Arkansas. Ruiz is a fiery player who plays with a ton of energy. He personifies the sparkplug label and tends to elevate those around him. He can play a bit hot sometimes and his composure can be tested in big moments when he comes up short. That said, he's almost always a net-positive in the dugout and keeps his teammates mentally and emotionally checked in throughout the game. 

Ruiz is a pure hitter. He works mature at-bats and tends to draw long counts. He's consistently run steady walk rates and limits his strikeouts well below league average raets. Ruiz puts the game in motion, even if he may not own better than below average raw power. He prefers to pepper gaps and find any way on base to highlight his tools. He's a plus runner and has more than a willingness to take bases off the opposition.

Ruiz is a primary left fielder with above average arm strength. Given his athleticism and arm talent, he can probably spell all three outfield spots when asked.

Ruiz brings traits to a lineup that cannot be measured. He's a winner and works hard to bring others with him.

Following two impressive campaigns at Cornell and a loud summer on the Cape, Quatrani elected to transfer into Notre Dame for the 2026 season. The Fighting Irish had a gaping hole behind the plate with the departure of Carson Tinney to the University of Texas.
