While Quatrani doesn't have the same name recognition as his predecessor, the tools aren't terribly dissimilar.

Quatrani can absolutely murder a baseball. His exit velocities have peaked north of 113 mph, and that raw power was on full display on the Cape where he max exit velocity ranked 8th in the league. Better still, his 90th percentile exit velocity of 102.9 bested every other player. 

Quatrani brings a reasonably polished approach to the plate. He stays inside the zone at a healthy clip and almost always swings at a fastball when he gets one inside the strike zone. There's a lack of adjustability in his swing, and he can be neutralized if pitchers force swings outside of the zone, but it takes premium stuff to get Quatrani out of his spots. It's probably a fringe-average hit tool at the next level, but if Quatrani finds a path toward being a .240 hitter as a professional, his raw will more than justify the swing and miss.

Quatrani has a chance to stick behind the plate, however average arm strength and meager pop times will put pressure on his ability to control the run game. He's slightly above average from a framing perspective.

Even if Quatrani ends up at first base or in left field as a professional, the offensive tools are more than loud enough to justify consistent lineup time. He'll turn 22 years old just after the season ends.

Dillon Moss is a wiry, explosive catching prospect with twitchiness in his swing and athletic actions. He's a guy that really leverages hard into his back side, transferring his weight with authority and getting violent through the zone with spring-loaded hips a la Andrew McCutchen. He's tinkered a bit with his swing and setup of late, but hardly ever gets cheated and seems to always put a charge into the baseball. There's power to the opposite field too. He'll shorten up and lace pitches into right-center with two strikes with quick wrists that can get to every quadrant. There's a comfort and quiet confidence Moss presents in the batters box that really makes it difficult to pitch to him. 

He's an average runner now, but that is likely to change in one direction or the other as he continues to add mass and strength in his lower half. Moss is the younger brother of 2025 star draft prospect Dean Moss. He will be 18.7 on draft day and is expected to be a difficult sign away from Stanford, as most Stanford commits tend to be.

After two years at St. Louis University, Kelly transferred to Ole Miss in search of brighter lights. 

Kelly is going to be a force for model teams when the draft comes around. Armed with a fastball up to 96, a launch height under 6-feet, and more than six-and-a-half feet of extension down the mound, Kelly has the makings of a metric monster. His fastball often sinks, but he can at times hold vertical carry when he's looking for it. If he can stay behind the ball just a tick more as July approaches he could end up possessing something akin to what Bryan Woo brings to the mound. That's a high bar, but Woo was a fourth round pick and Kelly could get drafted above that by precedent alone.

He's not a one-trick pony either. Kelly throws a strong sweeping slider that comes off his fastball tunnel. He commands that pitch beautifully to the glove-side. It's got a chance at becoming a 'plus' pitch going forward. Kelly also throws a deceptive change-up with plenty of arm-side diving action. It floats to the plate and never stops looking like his heater until it's in the catcher's mitt. He's struggled to command that pitch and will decelerate his arm speed at times, but there are components to build on. Kelly will throw any pitch to any handedness of hitter. If there's one wart to his game at this early stage it's the gopher ball. Kelly has had a tendency to surrender the homer on fastballs he leaks to his arm-side with more tail than hop. As he continues to refine his craft and emphasizes creating carry through the zone, that should happen far less often.

There's so much to like here. The operation, the strikes, the secondaries, the competitor, the frame. It all checks out. Kelly has a chance to go very early in 2026.

Seuferling committed to Wake Forest back in the summer of 2025 having reached back for 94 mph at a couple of tournaments along the way. Clearly Tom Walter and that coaching staff saw something in him along the trail as his stuff exploded over the winter.

Seuferling is up to 99 mph these days and has shown the ability to hold 95-98 in side bullpen sessions. He can hold moderate carry on the pitch, however it's his deception that provides the value. Seuferling has a short, tight arm spiral with a pushy release. It's a reasonably stock release and launch profile, however the ball does jump out of his hand, holding moderate carry and some tail. 

Seuferling best secondary is an upper-80s changeup that will flutter and sink to the plate. He sells it well, however it does lack dynamic shape, relying instead on tunnel and command to miss bats. There's a mid-80s slider that owns cutter-like shape.

Seuferling doesn't have a prototypical starting pitcher's release and will need to see his secondaries blossom before he can work through a lineup more than once. It's a big arm and a big fastball with a big future in college baseball if he doesn't get paid away from Winston-Salem.

Driffill is a well-built righty with an athletic delivery. He moves with intent and bottled violence. It's a drop-and-drive operation with impressive separation at foot plant. Driffill rotates hard through his delivery, uncoiling fast to create arm speed and velocity. There's some inversion when his lead leg gets down. Driffill can be a streaky strike-thrower, but when he's living in and around the zone, the stuff plays in a big way with swing-and-miss stuff. 

The fastball is up to 97 and Driffill will live 92-94 with some carry and considerable tail to the arm-side. Driffill has a longer arm swing, deep in the back with some natural deception. It's a lower launch with fastball value as he climbs the ladder in and above the zone. Driffill's misses tend to be high and to the arm-side, specifically when he fatigues and sends the front hip open early. 

The breaking ball is a mid-to-upper 70s sweeper with some sharpness and tunnel when buried down and away to right-handed hitters. He'll need to firm that pitch up at the next level, but feel for shape and creating spin, as well as execution is present, even if not entirely consistent at this stage.

This is a good mover with present stuff, some feel for spin and athleticism very present. There's definitive relief risk, but it's high-leverage, end-of-game projection.

Roman is a physical right-hander with a fast arm and more velocity on the horizon. Already touching 96, most scouts see a mid-90s relief profile in due time. The fastball will get a lot of whiffs as it explodes out of the hand with some deception and flatness in its approach. Figueroa is a good strider down the mound and creates solid extension.

He'll fold in a sharp slider as his put-away pitch, but often times the fastball will do the heavy-lifting. There's also an occasional cutter to bridge the gap, as well as a bigger curveball and changeup that'll dance all over the place at this young age. 

Figueroa will be 19 for the Draft.  If the ease of operation and strikes continue to develop in a positive way, he's got a chance to become a very effective right-handed pitcher. It's a full mix of pitches, an innate ability to shape the baseball, and release traits that'll excite teams.

Super twitchy, unreal athlete. Tests off the charts athletically. Has a chance to be a two-way guy. Ortiz is awfully cerebral in the box. He's a barrel magnet with the ability to spray pitches to all fields. Ortiz has shown plenty capable of slugging against velocity and spin at the college level and demonstrates a polished approach in the box keeping his chase rates in check. There's some streakiness against secondary weapons from more advanced pitching, but that's to be expected as this early stage in his amateur career. He has a tendency to slow the game down and features tools in all areas of his game. Ortiz is a dynamic defender at second base and possesses the first step and average arm strength necessary to play shortstop in a pinch.

Ortiz missed much of the 2025 season due to injury, but got back on the field on the Cape for Yarmouth-Dennis. It's first round tools if he can prove more durable as July approaches.

LSU has had a knack for landing elite talent out of the state of New Mexico in recent years but they have have a difficult time getting Blomker to campus. It's big stuff, a big frame, a butter operation and more in on the horizon.

Blomker boasts some of the easier 98 mph heat you'll ever see. The arm works great with looseness and considerable arm speed. The ball jumps out of the hand with sizzle and some late life. Blomker lives 92-94 in his starts and has shown the ability to ramp velocity back up at the end of his tank. Better still, his spin capacity for the heater stands out, routinely north of 2400 rpm. Command for the fastball has been streaky with glove-side misses common, pulling across his body. 

Blomker's breaking ball jumps out of the hand and trails the fastball at crest. It's two-planes and sharp biting action late. Blomker's command for the breaking ball is fringy, but effectively wild at times thanks to the juice on his fastball. It's got the makings of a plus bender. 

He'll flash a fading changeup that he hardly needs to throw at this stage in his baseball career. It's dances to the arm-side and usually relies on tailing action rather than depth to induce unique looks/whiffs. In time, the changeup will be a weapon. The components are present.

Blomker checks just about every box a scout is looking for. It's size, it's stuff, it's projection, it's fastball value and propensity for spin. Only 20 players born in New Mexico have been drafted and made it to the Major Leagues. Blomker sure has the look of No. 21.

Under-recruited and under-scouted as a high school senior, Naess was a standout for the Laguna Beach baseball and basketball teams before arriving to campus at Cal Poly. Standing at 6-foot-6, 175 pounds as a freshman, Naess had a ton of physical projection and needed to get into the weight room if he was going to find success at the college level. Now ten pounds heavier and stronger in his lower half, Naess is beginning to realize some of his upside, even if there's considerably more on the horizon.

In his second year as the Cal Poly Friday night ace, Naess has been steady. He'll run the fastball up into the low-90s, however he's more commonly 88-90 with some deception, buoyed by above average command. Naess brings a high slot and some steepness to the bump. He hides the ball well, in part because his arm action can be a tick late at times. Despite living in the upper-80s, Naess should throw harder some day. He gets good separation between his lower half and shoulders, and isn't yet utilizing his legs as much as he will some day in his delivery. Forecasting some mid-90s velocity in the future isn't out of the question.

Naess owns an above average changeup that he'll throw early and often. It's elevated by the command of his fastball, as well as the conviction in his arm speed. There's also a mid-70s curveball he'll mix in to lefties and righties alike.

Naess is a difficult prospect to gauge from a draft perspective. He's not a hard-thrower, and doesn't possess a plus secondary. That said, he's 25 pounds shy of where he'll eventually sit one day, and perhaps a team will be willing to buy into that upside now.
Strike-throwing issues in games.

Matthews has some interesting hit and power upside. He's a back-hip hitter who anchors hard into his backside to load and strides through the zone with a big, high leg kick to generate bat speed and space. There's some waggle and various triggers in his load that allowing him to get on time. The hands work really well with a track record of getting to pitches in any quadrant. Matthews has great size and is a demonstrated performer on the showcase and tournament circuit. 

Melt in the fact he's a left-handed hitter with above-average speed and scouts will flock to see the North Carolina product all spring. As if the offensive tools weren't exciting enough, he's also got a plus throwing arm from the outfield and has at least a chance to play centerfield going forward assuming he doesn't get to big for the position. He profiles well in right field. 

There may come a time when pitching gets so advanced that he'll need to quiet everything down at the plate, but for the time being Matthews has shown the ability to handle velocity, spin, and multiple planes. It all projects well. Matthews will be 19 years old for the draft, so scouts and analysts will want to see the bat outperforming his peers in the months leading.

Carns is one of the more impressive catchers coming out of the state of Florida in 2026 thanks to a well-rounded game and some projection with the bat. The hit tool is solid here. It's a short, compact stroke with a line-drive focus and an awfully quiet load. There's a real feel for the barrel. Carns has enormous bat speed with considerable stretch in his load and should hit for big power as he continues to develop. 

He's presently a plus runner, a rare trait for a catcher at any level. It's an athletic frame too, and should hold some twitch as he matures. He's a strong blocker behind the plate and has showcased soft hands and above average arm projection at showcase tournaments throughout the last calendar year. 

Carns is an aggressive hitter with a well-balanced game and athletic traits on every tool. He was a 20th rounder by the DBacks in 2024 but elected to go to Florida State.

Breyfogle has insane tools in his big, athletic frame. It's huge data but rough around the edges. He's a lefty stick with considerable raw power and bat speed. The swing is unorthodox with an unusual setup and tons of moving parts and extra motion in the box. That's left Breyfogle exceptionally liable against premium pitching.

Defensively, Breyfogle is a plus runner and can go get it in the field, however his routes and first step can be hit or miss. 

Breyfogle was a well-liked prospect coming out of HS but missed getting selected, instead electing to head to Tucson. It's a sky-high ceiling if the hit tool meets expectations in school. Breyfogle missed almost the entire 20256 season with a shoulder injury.

While Grant doesn't yet possess one standout pitch, his ability to land the fastball, slider and changeup combo for strikes makes him an awfully difficult at-bat in the high school ranks. 

He's been up to 96 and will rest 90-92 setting up his bullet slider and changeup to do the heavy lifting later in a battle. The changeup projects the best offering. He will turn 20 years old near Opening Day 2027; on the older side for his class.

"Rookie" can really hit. That's abundantly clear when looking at his baseball card. It's tremendous bat-to-ball skills with an all-fields approach. He really lets the ball travel deep into the zone and has been known to pepper the left-center field gap with authority, especially against velocity and backdoor spin. It's likely no more than fringe-average power, but the hit tool combined with above average foot speed wreaks havoc on opposing pitchers. Most simply don't have an approach toward getting him out. Shepard can get himself in trouble at times against pitchers that throw a heavy ball as is demonstrated by a bloated ground ball rate, but he puts the game in motion and makes the pitcher work. 

Shepard doesn't have a definitive defensive home at this stage, though most scouts tend to slot him in at second base or the outfield at the next level. He's played his fair share behind the plate and at shortstop, though neither is a natural fit in pro ball. Shepard has a good internal clock and soft hands and can throw off multiple planes. From this chair, he looks like a natural fit for second base. Shepard is a good athlete with twitchy actions and budding athleticism. He'll derive his value from producing high on-base numbers and batting averages at the next level, sprinkling in some impact in other ways. Shepard will be 18.7 years old on draft day.

Harmon is the prototype projection arm with big upside if the physicality and velocity eventually comes along. It's two distinguished pitches with a third developing in the lab.

Harmon and his 6-foot-4-inch frame currently live in the upper-80s on most nights, touching 93. His fastball plays way up thanks to elite extension and big vertical shapes, at times going north of 22 inches of IVB. Harmon can miss bats with the best of them at the top of the zone thanks to his release traits and shapes. He'll need to make the jump into the low-90s on a more consistent basis if he's to garner the signing bonus he'll want in the draft.

Harmon's primary weapon when he's ahead is an upper-70s changeup that he'll throw to both left-handed and right-handed hitters. It flutters and dives at the plate with spin rates that can drop under 1100 rpm. Harmon will need to develop better feel for spinning a breaking ball and/or improving his capacity for spin if he's to see his slider or curveball take a step forward.

Harmon looks like a no doubt SEC arm. He could occupy a weekend spot after a year of development in Oxford. If he goes pro, strength gains and breaking ball development will be the two priorities right out of the gate. Harmon does things you can't teach with the body, the operation and with his fastball. He's a very intriguing prospect.

Stone began his collegiate career at Johnson County CC before transferring into Columbia, South Carolina for his sophmore year in 2025. He was a pitch-to-contact righty a year prior, but appears to be unlocking better swing-and-miss stuff in this, his draft-eligible junior campaign.

Brandon Stone is awfully difficult to square up. He doesn't give up a lot of barrels. He's unlikely to ever become a strikeout artist, but his three-fastball mix makes for an effective ground ball specialist. The sinker is his go-to heater; a low-90s torpedo that jets into the hands of right-handed hitters. It's been effective limiting hard contact, as well as getting hitters to expand the zone. Stone has worked hard to integrate a low-90s cutter into his arsenal, and it's shown effective getting left-handed hitters to swing over the top when placed under the hands. 

Stone's slider is perhaps the pitch that's taken the biggest jump year-over-year. He's now 82-85 with a bigger, deeper breaker that compliments the sinker/cutter combo nicely. It's still not a big whiff machine, but it keeps hitters off the barrel.

Stone will also chuck in a mid-80s changeup that has bigger depth and some tailing action, however hitters seem to identify that pitch out of the hand better than they probably should considering he's naturally a sinker-baller. That said, he kills spin very well and shows some of the traits necessary for a player development program to tap into. Some of the ineffectiveness can likely be attributed to Stone's underwhelming extension and lengthened timing windows for hitters to react.

Stone is an intriguing arm in that he can do things to the baseball that can be tough to teach. He's got feel for manipulating shapes and spin, but will need to reign in the command on the corners if he's to reach his back-end of the rotation upside at the next level.

Howell is the quintessential scouting story. A big body, big-armed righty enrolled at Memphis as a true freshman in 2024 and took the entire year to refine his craft -- a redshirt. He made his debut for the Tigers in 2025 tossing 26.2 innings of relief, showing big stuff and scattered command. It's up arrows across the board.

While still a relief look on the mound, Howell is gaining confidence in his operation and throwing more strikes. His tempo has improved considerably on campus, as has the athletiicism. He's an impressive mover for his 245-pound frame. He generates impressive extension down the mound, and moves with intent. He'll still struggle with streakiness from a strikes perspective, but when he's locked in it's been bat-missing stuff.

Howell's run the fastball up to 97 with carry through the zone and some cutting action. He presents a high-slot for hitters and some natural, hiding the ball behind his shoulder before release. Howell is more routinely 92-95, however the velocity continues to trend up with maturation. It's moving in the direction of what could soon become a plus heater, so long as he's in the zone enough to allow the pitch to play.

Howell's slider is also impressing scouts. It's dive-bomber with strong vertical traits that play well off his high launch. It's generated big whiff rates throughout his amateur career. Howell has also shown more feel for landing the slider for strikes than he has the fastball. It's been up to 85, and more commonly sits 81-82. Howell will likely need to firm the pitch up just a bit in pro ball, but this is a weapon.

Howell has also thrown a handful of changeups in his time at Memphis, but currently it's not a reasonable offering at the next level.

Whoever drafts Howell may give him the chance to start in his minor league career given the chance for two plus pitches and the aformentionted athleticism. There's traits to dream on here, with a leveragable floor in the cards.

Coaxum certainly looks the part in the box. He's built like a premium prospect with long legs, lean levers and broad, squared-off shoulders that all point to considerable strength on the horizon. Coaxum operates out of a wide base and has doesn't utilize a leg kick, instead opting to shift his weight with pure twitchiness coming out of his lower half. The athleticism in his hips and shoulders is elite. He leverages and anchors into his backside with serious strength and makes hard turns on the baseball. As he's gotten older he's begun standing taller and taller in the box, now presenting himself a far greater slugging threat than a year prior. Coaxum projects to get to 'plus' raw power and could eventually get to it in games as he works to avoid the swing and miss currently in his game against spin. 

Take all the projectable offensive tools and tack them onto what is already double-plus speed in the outfield and you have the potential here for a complete five-tool player if the polish missing from his profile continues to develop.

Dunwoody's strength gains in the summer entering his senior year helped elevate his profile to Four Corners scouts. The physical traits, alongside what he's capable of doing to the baseball, has him firmly positioned as a potential priority names in the 2026 Draft.

Dunwoody tacked on more than ten pounds this past winter and saw his fastball jump from the low 90s up to 96 this spring. He's long had the ability to spin the baseball too. His fastball will sizzle north of 2500 rpm at times. Dunwoody also has the unique luxury of being able to make the heater move in both directions. He's a natural supinator, his more comfortable fastball shape featuring cut and carry. It plays very well at the top of the zone. He does ocassionally tail the heater to the arm-side, unclear whether that's a second fastball grip or just release variations.

Dunwoody's slider will creep into the mid-80s with bullet tilt and some seam mirroring traits that work well naturally off his fastball. It's a pitch that gets whiffs when buried low and away. There's a bigger low-80s curveball that still has a bit of hump in it, but the raw spin and feel for shaping the pitch are intriguing. Dunwoody will also flip over a mid-80s changeup that's he's still struggling to control and execute consistently. 

Dunwoody's operation on the mound has also improved with the added muscle. There's still some whack through release, but it's a balanced delivery, finishing tall and ready to field his position. It's moderate extension through release and a reasonably generic launch profile.

Dunwoody has the menu to become a rotation piece going forward. His control for the zone has been fringy for much of his high school career. Showcasing the ability to get ahead in counts and avoid walks will be critical in determining where he goes in the Draft.

Rispoli finds himself draft-eligible for the second year in a row, barely eligible as a redshirt freshman in 2025. He went unselected, but purely due to his short baseball card and undersized profile. Another year under his belt, he's proven one of the more steady shortstop prospects in the country with supplementary tools that should help his name get called inside of the top ten rounds in July.

Rispoli's undersized nature is on full display in the batters box. He's not a power hitter by any means, but he makes a ton of contact and tends to put the game in motion. Scouts have been critical of his passive nature in the box, skeptical whether falling behind in counts as much as he does will translate to the pro game without impacting his slash line. Rispoli would be served well to go into ambush mode here and there. For a guy with his exemplary bat-to-ball skills, he has no business running the strikeout streakiness he does now and again. 

Rispoli drives up his batting average with a plus run tool, ocassionally popping 70-grade run times when he breaks the box with momentum to the right side. He's a base-stealer and should provide value on the bases at the next level from the jump. He's at least an above average defender at shortstop, however more steady than dynamic on most nights. He's got solid-average arm strength that'll flash a tick better than that moving to his left. 

Rispoli profiles as a Role 45 shortstop at the next level that can serve the table-setter role or perhaps the late-inning pinch runner or defensive substitution. His lack of bat speed and impact will likely curb his ability to carve out many 450 plate appearance campaigns as a pro, but he's got a chance to play in the big leagues for a very, very long time given his strengths and middle-infield profile.

A draft-eligible redshirt freshman, McCraine is a rare breed in many ways. He didn't appear in a single game for the Tigers in 2025, but turned in an exciting summer in the Perfect Game Collegiate League as a 20 year old. He parlayed that into a strong performance in the fall, carving out playing time as a second-year player in 2026.

McCraine looks the part. He's 6-foot-3, athletic and projectable in his frame. He's got some waggle in his setup, an open orientation to the pitcher with some bend in the knees. There's some noise in his hands in the loading phase, but he's usually on time for the fastball with quickness in those hands. The operation at the dish looks similar to what Mitch Haniger used to employ.

With such an abbreviated baseball card, it's difficult to know exactly what McCraine is at this point. Scouts believe there's at least average bat-to-ball skills here, and the approach should lend well toward modest walk rates and healthy strikeout rates. There's above-average raw power projection, however he's still likely 15 pounds away from realizing those gains. McCraine is a plus runner capable of stealing bases, and it's a part of his game he enjoys to flex.

The versatility may be his best calling card. McCraine is a good enough athlete to play centerfield or shortstop. His home will likely be the outfield as a professional, however it's possible he gets some run at the 6 in the low minors to test his ability. 

McCraine is polarizing as something of an unknown. He's a draft risk, but a fun lottery ticket at a minimum.

Seibert finds himself draft-eligible after transferring out of Knoxville following the 2025 season. Elbow surgery almost entirely limited his development at Tennessee. 

Following along the long line of Blue Valley SW arms to come through the draft the last few years, Siebert may be the best of the bunch. A standout arm in the 2024 class, Seibert a 16th round pick by the Tigers but decided to go to Tennessee to chase more upside. He's already up to 99 in side sessions, living 92-94 with a firm, mid-80s slider. 

A massive, imposing figure on the mound, Siebert works downhill with authority. The ease of his operation really stands out, and his ability to control all the moving parts of his frame at such a young age is fairly rare. As he continues to develop and puts together a reliable third pitch, Seibert could realize his mid-rotation upside, maybe more if the breaking ball takes a significant step forward in professional development.

It's been a winding road for Alonso and his draft journey. Once eligible as a high school senior coming out of Rabun Gap Nacoochee, Alonso went unselected in large part to being almost 20 years old on draft day. Following a freshman year at MTSU and a sophomroe campaign at Columbia State CC, Alonso transferred to Troy. After years of development, his stuff has blossomed. He's now considered one of the more intriguing 22 year old prospects in the country.

Alonso is an athletic mover, especially for his durable size. He gets down the mound with conviction and showcases big arm speed with some deception out of a high three-quarter slot. Alonso's fastball will run up into the mid-90s, paired with a hammer curveball in the low-to-mid 80s. Alonso technically throws a slider and a curveball, however they will at times melt together. He's worked hard to establish a changeup/split, however it's not a big part of his arsenal at this time.

Alonso has a chance to own two above average pitches with the innate ability to fill up the zone. If a team believes there's a third pitch that could be low-hanging fruit, he could hear his name called in the middle rounds of the draft. Alonso doesn't have much leverage considering his age, so he may be a more popular under-slot option than many other pitching prospect ranked in his bucket.

Draft-eligible in 2025, Hartman went unselected after missing three weeks with injury down the stretch of his junior year. Hartman is a projectable left-handed outfielder who continues to add muscle and size onto a lean, long frame. Hartman seems to add more and more athleticism as the years go by. The continued added strength gains have translated into higher production at the plate, and his defensive abilities in the outfield continue to blossom as well.

Hartman's swing has improved dramatically since enrolling in at Washington State. His feel for generating loft, as well as his ability to get to his pull-side continue to improve year-over-year, if even marginally. Hartman has fringy bat-to-ball and barrel skills. The components are there to build a more productive hitter, but thus far his approach has slowed his momentum. He has a tendency to expand the zone and hasn't yet flashed the adjustability necessary to work long at-bats swinging at those pitches. Should Hartman grow into more bat speed, that aggressive approach may work, but to date his over-the-fence impact has been muted. 

His frame, bat speed and athleticism point to a player who could eventully tap into solid-average raw/game power. Hartman's steep plane and subsequent barrel accuracy also produce heavy ground ball rates drawing down his average exit velocity over larger samples. He'll need to polish the entire offensive profile at the next level, but there's clay to build upon.

On the defensive side of the ball, Hartman projects into left field as a pro. He's an above average runner with an athletic stride and a flair for making the highlight-reel play. He's got good range in either corner and is plenty comfortable making plays at the wall. He's an above average defender, however a fringe-average throwing arm will almost certainly limit his reps to left field in the upper-minors and the big leagues.

Hartman is a giant ball of what-if clay at this stage. The frame, the swing, the athlete, it's all very intriguing. Translating those traits into on-field success in the batters box will be the next box to check.

Liggon and twin brother Ezra and both excellent prospects in the 2026 class. Both possess bat speed, foot speed and the ability to impact the game on defense. Caleb has the feather in his cap of an infielder at this stage, while Ezra gets the advantage offensively being a left-handed hitter.

Caleb has plenty of fans in the scouting community. His long, athletic frame gets high marks from scouts with the bat in his hands. Liggon sets up tall and wide, hands outside of his body, neutral to his frame. His load is a minimal sway back into this back hip, the hands pushing back into place before the front foot gets down. Liggon drifts ever so slightly through his front side and rotates across his front hip. It's a compact swing that stays tight to the frame, but he can get disconnected when fooled by spin. Liggon finishes short and cut off at the top with two hands. 

Liggon is an aggressive hitter who takes it to the opposing pitcher. He doesn't wait long to try and attack. That approach comes with some swing and miss, primarily when offered slow stuff. Liggon does a nice job getting to his pull-side, and has shown a willingness to get velocity on the outer-half the other way. He'll need to make some adjustments to his swing and approach if he hopes to keep up with the breaking balls he'll be faced with at the next level, but the offensive tools are certainly present to become an impact bat.

Liggon's talents aren't limited to mashing. He's an above average runner with the run tool trending up. He gets very good breaks out of the box. The defense at third base is fringy, with footwork and lateral range being areas of emphasis going forward in his development. Liggon will need to develop a better first step and stride moving to his left. He's got very good hands with a quick exchange and the internal clock necessary to play the infield. The arm strength is above average and his throws carry through the first base bag. In total, Liggon looks capable of becoming an average, or perhaps slighly better, defensive third baseman with time, reps and professional development. 

Liggon will turn 19 years old two months prior to the Draft.

Following one single year at Everett Community College, Queen transferred into Oregon State for his sophomore year where he posted up nicely in a hybrid starter/extended relief role. Across 47.2 innings, Queen struck out 61 batters and wakled just 19. He was as steady as they come. Queen is once again pitching in multiple roles in 2026 with slightly bigger stuff.

Queen is sitting 92-94 with the fastball and generating strong chase and whiff metrics thanks to its exceptional carry and tailing action out of the zone. He launches from a slot slightly higher than most pitchers, so that horizonatal action he's getting out of the hand can surprise hitters. Queen has been up to 96.

The slider is his best pitch; especially dynamic in 2025. It's firm and it's dynamic with big vertical break. Queen's bullet slider sits 84-85 and will touch 88 on occassion with diving shape that supplements the fastball nicely. It's a stellar one-two punch with both pitches have a chance to be above-average or better at the next level. 

Queen will mix in a bigger low-80s curveball and has been working to develop a more consistent changeup to round out his arsenal. If he shows it's a usable pitch, he'll likely be drafted as a starting pitcher prospect and has a chance to go in the 4-7 round range.

Wiggins is a physical force in all aspects of the game, though without a doubt it's most noticeable in the batter's box. He's shown advanced barrel feel and a true all-fields power threat. Wiggins is an extremely patient hitter; some calling it downright passive. His swing rates rank near the bottom of the league. While that will help buoy his chase rate, it's negatively affected his ability to do damage on mistake pitches early in counts. 

In terms of the raw power, his peak exit velocities routinely sit toward the top of his class. That said, to maximize his tools, he'll need to clean some things up in his offensive game. Wiggins has some moving parts in his swing that can cause some inconsistencies in timing triggers and swing plane, but he's a high-IQ player whose swing should mature the deeper he gets into baseball. Presently, he runs extreme ground ball rates because of his inexperience and inconsistencies. Wiggins has struggled to hit the breaking ball in college, an adjustment he'll need to make quickly as his draft year approaches.

He is an average runner who most likely fits in an outfield corner long term where the bat still plays. Wiggins has arm strength that'll play in right field and his routes have continued to improve behind the scenes on campus.

Wiggins spent the first two years of his collegiate career at Indiana before changing zip codes for his draft-eligible 2026 season.

Coppola, the brother of Florida lefty Pierce Coppola, brings similar size and intimidation to the mound. He'll work up to 93 but sits a tick or two below that in most cases with unique angles and steepness. Coppola naturally cuts the baseball and doesn't have a route toward generating carry. Coppola's turned himself into a true supinator profile. He throws varying breaking balls, all of which sweep hard. This looks like a reliever profile at the next level. He is draft-eligible for the second time. He is on his third school in three years.

Kerrigan has been one of the steadiest hitters in the state of Georgia over the course of the last twelve months. Tommy John surgery kept him off the showcase and tournament circuit for much of his rising junior year, but a gaudy summer in 2025 has helped revive his profile for scouts in the Peach State.

Kerrigan can hit, there's little question about that. He possesses some of the best bat-to-ball skills in the class and has been tested with some of the better pitching the country can throw at him to drive the point home. It's a simple, rhythmic left-handed swing with elite feel for lifting the baseball and getting to his pull-side. Kerrigan is as efficient a hitter and you'll find in the Southeast. He does possess some raw bat speed, however it's generally reserved for batting practice. Kerrigan is usually unwilling to let it eat in games. Showing more ISO and slug in games will be a critical piece as July approaches should he hope to capture the second or third round ceiling that some evaluators believe he's worthy of.

The rest of the profile is solid. It's a corner profile, likely left field at the next level. He's an average runner with fringe-average to potentailly average arm strength, however that part of his game is still coming back from the injury. It possible he grows back into solid average arm strength and proves capable of handling right field too. For now, he's best positioned at the '7'. 

Perhaps the biggest hurdle on Kerrigan's profile is his age. He'll be 19.5 years old for the Draft and lacks the track record on the showcase and summer circuit many of his peers possess. It's an abbreviated baseball card for an older high school prospect. Kerrigan will want to show more thump in games against top-tier pitching as July approaches so scouts can feel comfortable he's more than a hit tool left field prospect. Players with the hit tool that Kerrigan has are very good prospect, but it may not be enough to get him paid away from Auburn. He would be draft-eligible in 2028 if he goes unselected/unsigned.

Bennett missed draft-eligibillity by just three days in 2025 and likely would have heard his name called had that been the case. A big, hulking, mashing catcher and corner outfielder, Bennett gets high marks for his approach to hitting, as well as his sheer raw power.

Bennett's got a lot of moving parts in his swing. There's plenty of waggle and Bennett is handsy as the ball approaches the plate. It's power-over-everything. 

Bennett is a strong dude. It's perhaps 70-grade raw power that he'll get to in games when he's swinging at the right pitches. There is some swing and miss in his game, particularly against breaking balls both inside and outside of the zone. That said, Bennett has shown the ability to stay inside the strike zone when he elects to pull the trigger. Interestingly, it's the breaking ball that comes into the zone from left-handed pitchers that has given him the most trouble throughout his DBU career. He'll need to quiet down his swing mechanics and work toward a bit more hit tool if his pure bat speed is to play in MLB.

Bennett is capable of playing the outifled and catching behind the plate, but his athletic abilities on both fronts is fringy to perhaps below average. He's also a 40-grade runner.

Bennett will turn 22 years old just two weeks after the draft and represents an offensive prospect. He's likely a day three pick.

Santos was something of a pop-up in the state of Georgia throughout the summer entering his senior year. While the product isn't finished, there's reasons to believe he's coming into his own as a ballplayer.

Santos is a swing tinkerer. He looks different in the box every time you see him. There are nights he utilizes a short stride forward move as his trigger. Other nights he'll employ a bigger leg kick. Then other times he's sink into his hips when the pitch is thrown before hardly picking up his front foot at all and letting his coil and torque create the swing. Wade also has something of a drift-back and kick-step forward in his swing to get loaded. It's unconventional and noisy, but Wade's bat speed makes up for any timing issues that may exist. It does beg the question whether he can find success against top-shelf velocity or better breaking balls. 

Wade shines with the glove. It's above average actions at the '6' with rangy athleticism and above average arm strength and twitch that shines on the dirt. Santos is a plus runner who can click into another gear on the bases. 

Given his athletic frame, twitchy actions on both sides of the ball and his ability to run, Wade has a case to be selected in July. The swing is unconventional, but it's working. He also tests extremely well with force plates, meaning there may be more in the tank from a raw power projection standpoint. If a team believes they can get Wade hitting against good arms, he's a sleeper in this class that could get drafted by an aggressive model-based organization.

Crane has a big, durable, bulldog frame and pitches with tempo and intent. It's a fast arm, a powerful frame and more velocity coming on the horizon.

Crane has been up to 98 and the ball jumps out of his hand. He's more commonly 92-93 after the second innings of work, but the life and lift on his fastball allows it to play up above its velocity band. 

A low-80s kick changeup is his favorite secondary, however he'll fold in a cutter in the mid-80s to get the ball going the other way a bit. It'll likely melt into a true slider at the next level, and it has a chance to be above average. A supinator by design, Crane has bat-missing stuff.

Kuglitsch has upside on both sides of the ball but his talents on the mound have really begun to blossom of late and scouts seem to think that'll be his eventually calling. It's a real easy operation with a loose arm and the baseball really jumps out of the hand. Kuglitsch has been up to 94 with ride and cut through the zone, settling in 89-90 as he moves deeper into his appearances. His control and command waver at this young stage in his amateur career, but added strength and maturity should see those traits uptick. 

Kuglitsch throws a slurvy breaker in the low-80s that projects with solid spin rates and some feel for spin. There's also a developing changeup in the menu. 

With the bat in his hands, it's an uphill swing with intent. Kuglitsh is also a plus runner.

Just about the only thing holding Collazo back from being a more premium prospect in the 2026 Draft is his size. But considering his age, there's more weight and impact on the horizon. As he continues to get stronger and more impactful, the tools will follow suit. The best is yet to come.

Collazo has consistently played above his weight class. Just 17.5 years old for the Draft, he's constantly in the box facing pitchers a year and a half older than he is. Collazo has shown considerable swing and miss in tournament settings, but it's improved over the last calendar year as he's added weight and strength to his 5-foot-11-inch frame. Collazo has a nice swing. He stays behind the baseball and leverages the ground hard to create bat speed. The load can get handsy at times, but that's improved as he's matured. Collazo flashes average raw projection and could contribute at the bottom of a lineup at the next level if the hit tool takes the next step. 

Perhaps Collazo's best tool is his athleticism. He's a 70-grade runner and it plays out of the batters box with a quick first step. Collazo also owns 70-grade arm strength, however his throws have a tendency to tail up the line effectively disarming the potential impact of the tool. He'll need to continue his development through reps to make the arm talent an true asset. Better still, Collazo tests through the roof from a force plate perspective. Model teams will see that and believe there's more bat speed, impact and first-step quickness in the tank through development.

As noted, Collazo will be just 17.5 years old for the Draft. He's one of the youngest draft-eligible players in the class and owns big physical tools and projection depending on the eye of the beholder.

Reeves is a physical force who swings a heavy barrel with tons of strength at the point of impact. He's an offense-first catcher who possesses pull-side juice that is already playing in games. Reeves has shown some swing and miss in his game, but that's a tradeoff most teams will accept considering the impact potential in the back. 

Reeves is nimble and quick for his size behind the plate. He's a fluid mover who gets out of the crouch well and flashes quick transfers. To this point he's shown above average arm strength with good accuracy to the bag. He's a player who is peaking physically and doesn't have much strength gains on the horizon.

The annual Colorado prep arm that surges up draft boards as July comes near, Garrison is a big, physical right-handed pitching prospect with the arm strength to go along with it. 

Garrison stuff saw a jump over the winter as he's now brushing 98 mph. He'll sit more comfortably 92-95 in games after the first inning or so. Garrison's fastball command is average, relying on a bully mentality and dare-you-to-hit-it approach to the heat. His fastball possesses moderate carry and some tail. It's a reasonably stock release and shapes profile on the pitch.

Garrison's secondary have come along with the added strength. His slider is now in the upper-70s and will brush into the low-80s with more lateral movement than depth. He tends to broadcast the pitch and bit, short-striding and releasing from a slightly lower slot to achieve his shapes. There's also a low-to-mid 80s changeup that will likely become his best weapon. He kills spin and creates shapes that mirror the fastball out of the hand.

Garrison is an arm-strength righty with a big fastball and burgeoning secondaries. He lacks prototypical extension and athleticism to suggest a surefire starting pitcher outcome at the next level. That said, given his size and budding velocity, him developing into a triple-digit reliever shouldn't be ruled out.

Morris has been one of the more consistent hitters on the showcase and tournament circuit over the last twelve months. He showed out at Area Code Games as an underclassman and elevated his name to scouts in the area. Morris is a twitchy mover with projection in a leaner, wiry frame. He's a line-drive hitter with feel for the pull-side gape with a knack for extra-base hits. Morris does a nice job limiting his strikeouts and posts above-average whiff rates. He's an above average runner but could grow into some value on the bases as he gets stronger. 

Morris has played a good bit of catcher for Clayton Valley, but he's a future shortstop going forward. Morris shows strong lateral mobility with some of the softest hands in the class. The actions are befitting of a middle infielder going forward. Above-average arm strength and the ability to throw from every angle supplements his efforts at the '6'. 

Morris will be extremely young for the class, barely 18 years old.

An infield prospect with good size and actions, Neal has several avenues toward positive value going forward. His swing creates space in the box with budding bat speed and a demonstrated ability to impact the baseball to the opposite field. Neal pounds fastballs and can adjust to spin despite getting out on his front foot a bit. There's real power projection in the offensive game. 

Time will tell if he can stay at shortstop with his size and strength, but his entire profile plays very well at third base. It's plus arm strength with carry across the dirt. It's not a foregone conclusion Neal is a hitter either. The upside on the mound is intriguing too. He's up to 94 with a loose, athletic motion, filling up the zone. An upper-70s slider really flashes with two-plane tilt and some sharpness. Neal will be 18.7 years old on draft day.

The calling card on Deion Cole is top of the scale elite bat speed and impact projection going forward. It's considerable raw power and power ceiling, especially to the pull-side. Cole will sell out to extend through the zone and try to lose one over the left field fence more often than not. When he does, it's very loud. With that approach does come quite a bit of swing and miss in the profile. It's an area of his game that will need to polish itself out as the draft approaches. That said, in general, when Cole puts the ball in play he usually finds himself on base. It's some of the biggest pound-for-pound exit velocity readings you'll find in 2026. 

Cole will routinely find himself in the outfield or at second base depending on the lineup construction that day. It's average arm strength on the dirt with a bit more natural athletic ability in the outfield. He posts solid average run times and should hold his speed early in his professional career. The name of game here is the hit tool. If it takes a step forward as we approach July 2026, it's comfortably first round tools and big draft upside. Cole will be 18.7 on draft day.

Garcia is a loose, wiry athlete with a power-speed combo coming out of the cold-weather Northeast; a popular demographic in the Draft of late. He's an above average runner with an upright gait, better underway than out of the box. 

It's average raw power projection all generated from a frame begging for 15 more pounds of muscle. Garcia is short to the ball from a higher hand set with a plane that easily generates backspin. He's a fluid defender at shortstop and has a shot to play the position if a more premium athlete doesn't shift him to the left or right on the dirt.

After a dazzling sophomore year at Wake Forest in 2025, Gunther curiously hit the transfer portal seeking more opportunities, specifically the chance to show his stuff in a rotation role. Given the depth of arms in Winston-Salem, that was always going to be a difficult role to crack. South Carolina landed his talent.

Gunther has a lot going for him on the mound and much of it has to do with how he launches the baseball. A 65 inch release height is a few inches lower than the average slot in Major League Baseball. Combine that low launch with an innate ability to hold vertical carry through the zone and Gunther is able to generate flatter approach angles than many of his counterparts in college baseball. He's been up to 96 and has shown the ability to hold 93-95 across bullpen outings. Despite his 5-foot-11-inch frame, Gunther generates close to six-and-a-half feet of extension down the mound letting his four-seamer play better than it already does. He's produced well-above average whiff rates on the heater with a moderate ability to get hitters expanding outside of the zone. 

Gunther's secondaries are very good. He annihilates hitters with a mid-80s cutter featuring impressive depth and some late lateral tilt. His ability to back-foot that breaker and play it off the four-seamer stands out. It's a plus pitch and fits his arsenal beautifully, supplementing his fastball and changeup perfectly. That changeup is his go-to weapon against left-handed hitters and he's produced enormous whiff rates with it too.

Gunther has a low-effort delivery with good extension, direction and conviction. He has shown fringy control and strikes can get away from him at times, but in general he has the traits and DNA of a guy who should pound the zone with more frequency than he currently does. Developing the ability to consistently land the four-seamer on the top rail will unlock a whole new gear in his effectiveness. This is also probably the only route for Gunther to start going forward. 

If the fastball is landing in 2026 and Gunther shows the ability to hold his stuff through a lineup a couple of times he's got the potential to go inside of the Top 100 picks. It's big stuff.

Horn finds himself draft-eligible for the second year in a row after going unselected in the 2025 Draft. He's got a good arm and will flash big stuff, however some things out of his control hold back his allure from a draft perspective.

At 5-foot-11, 185 pounds, Horn doesn't have prototypical size for a starting pitching prospect. That lack of length in his frame does correlate to below average extension down the bump. Pitchers with a lack of extension tend to have to rely on breaking ball quality to get whiffs and weak contact in professional baseball. Horn may be up to that challenge.

Horn has touched 98 mph with a fastball that, at its best, carries through the top of the zone and features moderate arm-side tail. Despite the velocity, Horn has generated middling whiff rates on the fastball in college, in large part due to that lack of extension and muted perceived velocity. Hitters simply pick it up earlier than with most pitchers. A 72-inch launch height does make for a unique release profile for a player of his size, and Horn has generated impressive chase rates above the zone because of it. At his best, he's launching the fastball from a high slot and riding it high just above the zone. In the zone, however, it hasn't been a heater that's provided much extra value. Interestingly, Horn spins the fastball (and his entire arsenal) extremely well. 

Horn's rpms are the envy of much of college baseball. The curveball will routinely sizzle north of 3000 rpm with true sweeper shape. It features impressive vertical depth with some of the better two-plane tilt you'll find on a breaking ball in the class. It hasn't been a pitch that's illicited much chase outside of the zone, but hitters certainly struggle to hit it in the zone. There's also a shorter cutter-like slider that bridges the fastball and sweeper nicely.

Horn's changeup has the chance to be a good one as well. He throws it for strikes at a high clip and gets whiff as it fades heavy and hard to the arm-side. It's a seam-shifted wake cambio as Horn actually struggles to kill spin on his offspeed pitches.

The exceptional spin capacity here and feel for shaping the breaking ball give Horn a shot at a big league role. It may be a reliever when all is said and done, but if Horn can live steady in the mid-to-upper 90s in short innings spurts, and compliment the velocity with his secondaries, he's got the stuff to succeed. Horn has proven to be an average strike-thrower and limits hard contact very well.

Horn will be 22.8 years old in July and lacks the leverage of many other draft arms. He's an under-slot target for teams in the 6-10 round range, and would likely be a priority on "day three" if he were to make it that far.

At 6-foot-6, 250 pounds, Marshburn is an intimidating force of gravity on the bump. He casts a shadow on hitters, and brings a level of physicality that can be unnerving to someone in the box. Hitters are almost always surprised when they see Marshburn deliver the baseball. He begins his delivery upright, gathers upright, breaks his hands up near the letters, and hinges like any prototypical 6-foot-6-inch righty would. He brings the arm up high behind his head, but suddenly, as if calling an audible at the last second, drops his arm into a slingshot low-three quarter pocket and whips the baseball to the plate. Almost instantaneously, Marshburn goes from a run-of-the-mill arm action to a guy flirting with a 90 degree arm angle.

That tremendously unique operation results in tremendously unique metrics. Marshburn delivers from a 64 inch release height and generates almost 20 inches of horizontal break on his fastball. Better still, he's getting just 4 inches of IVB on the sinker. It's a heatseeking anvil.

The heater sneaks up on hitters thanks to his above average extension and obvious deception. Marshburn is living 91-93 most nights, and will tickle 94.

Marsburn throws an above average sweeper and has worked to get his changeup to a place where it'll stump hitters, but it still a work in progres. 

At a minimum, Marshburn will have a role at the next level as a sixth or seventh inning ground ball specialist. He's a truly funky look, and an arm to circle later in the Draft.

Davis is a large and imposing force on the mound with an athletic frame, rounded shoulders and a strong lower half. He'll work the fastball up to 97 with considerable arm-side run to both sides of the plate. His slider is a real weapon, a gyroscopic bowling ball with considerable depth and swing-and-miss characteristics. 

Davis likes to throw a budding changeup to lefties too, and it's been effective in exhibition settings. There's also an upper-70s curveball that he's worked to integrate into his menu of pitches, but he doesn't seem to trust it yet.

It's a good operation. He's consistently on time both with his hand break and getting the arm up. Davis has starter traits and should continue to improve his overall arsenal as he gains reps and matures. Scouts want to see him bring more moxy to the mound and not be fearful to throw his stuff in the zone.

Reynolds has a sound approach at the dish with a short, compact, explosive swing with pull-side over-the-fence power. He's packed on plenty of muscle on campus and now has the look of a middle-of-the-order bat. He's got lightning quick hands and a consistent path to the ball with a real feel for the barrel, though he's struggled at times with pitches low and away. Strong upside at the plate in this profile. Reynolds is a fringy athlete in the field with an average arm, likely destined for left field at the next level.

Long, wiry and ultra-projectable, Liggon has the type of frame scouts look for when trying to forecast impact potential. It's 6-foot-4 and 200 pounds of whippy, wiry strength. The impact is beginning to show at the plate, and the athletic markers continue to trend upward. 

Liggon generates whippy bat speed and natural loft in a burgeoning left-handed swing. He employs the classic high back elbow to generate barrel lag and some natural steepness in his attack angle. A natural counter-rotation helps Liggon generate torque and bat speed. Liggon keeps his hands tight to the body and works to pull the ball in his at-bats, however the swing can get outside of his frame when tasked with handling spin and offspeed pitches on the outer-third. Liggon's timing windows and triggers tend to vary depending on the level of competition he's facing. He can get a bit handsy against soft-tossers. As he continues to get looks at more premium pitching, and the level of competition begins to normalize, his swing should iron itself out too. There are components here to dream on a hit tool, however the power projection will be the featured trait on most of Liggon's scouting reports.

The pure athlete continues to impress. Liggon is now a 70-grade runner -- an outlier grade for a player of his size. He's continually posted home-to-first bolts of 4.1 seconds and hustles on every play. Liggon takes comfortable routes to the ball and doesn't look phased by the demands of centerfield. It's above average arm strength, trending toward plus. Liggon's situational awareness is still a work-in-progress. He'll too often allow runners to advance by trying to make hero throws to home plate in situations that don't call for it. These granular details of playing the position will come with time. 

Perhaps Liggon's biggest wart is his age. He'll turn 19 years old two months prior to the Draft. Still, it's legitimate power projection, 70-grade run times and arm strength that's big league quality.

A two-year stay at Folsom CC led Kenney to the University of Washington for the 2026 season. He's a well-built righty with some arm strength and arm speed. Those bullish on the upside believe there's more in the tank.

Kenney moves well when he's throwing the fastball. He gets good extension and delivery the ball with conviction. He works behind the four-seamer, generating considerable lift and IVB with some occassional cut late. There's big spin capacity on the heater, too. Kenney's ability to command the fastball borders on average most nights with his misses usually pulled, glove-side. He'll run it up to 95, and sits 88-92 after the early innings of most starts. It's got the chance to be an above average heater if he can find either more velocity or better command. He does well with shapes.

The slider and changeup are his two go-to secondaries. The changeup is particularly effective with better command than the fastball and deep, fading life. It's 84-86 and Kenney does well to eliminate spin on that pitch. The slider is fringier, 80-82 with middling spin rates and shorter shape. He cuts that pitch off early at the top and broadcasts it to the hitter at times. 

Kenney will also throw a curveball and cutter, however both pitches melt into variations of the slider. 

Therer's some uniquenes to the fastball and some arm strength here to dream on. He'll need a more dynamic breaking ball at the next level, and more strikes and/or velocity from the heater. He's an interesting lottery ticket for an analyst in rounds 11-20.

Scouts loved Branch in the 2022 Draft, but he was 19.5 years old and projects as a second baseman. For that reason, nobody was willing to throw enough money at him to sway his talent away from Baylor. Branch was a hellion for the Bears making a loud, immediate impact upon arriving as a true freshman. He transferred to Georgia for the 2024 season and has been draft-eligible once again the last three years.

Branch has grown into his own in Athens. He's grown into above average bat speed and will occassionally pop exit velocities that look more like plus. He's extremely patient at the plate and stays inside the zone consistently. Baseballs jump off his barrel a bit different than his peers. Scouts want to see the bat continue to progressively tick upwards as we approach the 2026 draft, as well as keeping the athleticism he's grown into moving in the right direction.

A decorated pure hitter with elite bat-to-ball skills and an all-fields approach. Farber made an extremely loud debut to his collegiate career hitting everything pitchers threw at him. His production backed up a bit in 2025 as hit contact quality hit the skids. In search of a new start and brighter lights, Farber transferred to Auburn for the 2026 season. 

Farber isn't much of a slugging threat. His exit velocities are well-below average. A high flyball rate combined lackluster bat speed limited his offensive impact as a sophomore. He's at his best when he's spraying line drives around the yard. Farber can handle both infield positions up the middle of the dirt with some twitch and is a plus runner on the base paths. He profiles as a table-setter.

An impressive righty with an athletic delivery and the ability to repeat his mechanics at such a young age, Maxon checks the boxes scouts look for in a future starting pitcher at the next level. Maxon shows good understanding of tempo, sequencing and pitchability in his craft. 

He'll fun the fastball up to 94 with carry through the zone, hiding the ball well until release. A low-80s slider is a swing-and-miss weapon with depth and late tilt.

Maxon is an imposing hitter too. It's exceptional raw power projection and athletic testing that supports the notion Maxon is an especially explosive athlete. 

He's a fiery competitor with a chip on his shoulder out there. It's also a tremendous frame to dream on. Maxon will be 18.7 years old for the draft.

Ballew is a quicky, fidgety-handed hitter with twitch in his game at the dish. He's got an anxious demeanor in the box quiets things down as the pitcher begins his motion. The load features a minimal leg lift with little wasted movement. His hands fire through the zone late with a line-drive approach into both gaps. Ballew can drift over his front-side, lunging for the ball and sapping the power from his swing. That generally only exists when he's fooled and out in front on a breaking ball or offspeed pitch. He'll stay back on the fastball and pull the ball hard across his frame to get to left field. It's a contact-over-power approach that has served him well as he's performed at a high level throughout his high school career.  Ballew has flashed plus bat speed from time and time and scouts in the state of Texas believe there's more raw power in the tank than what he chooses to show on most nights. 

Defensively, Ballew has tools. He's a composed defender who brings the ball in quietly. It's a steady internal clock with good footwork especially to balls hit at him and to his left. Ballew can get a bit more flat-footed on balls hit to his right and will occasionally take the extra hop to get moving back toward first base. It's above average arm strength befitting of a player primed to stay on the left side of the infield. 

Ballew is an average runner.

Sheets is a bat-first middle infield prospect with an up-arrow next to his name after an impressive summer with the stick. The son of MLB-great pitcher Ben Sheets, Miller brings the same level of competitive fire and steadiness that his father brought to the mound.

Sheets' bat is what catches the headlines. His 6-foot-2-inch frame continues to add strength and is filling out in a way that suggests impact on the horizon. Sheets is a good mover in the box. He does a very nice job loading into his back hip and counter-coils his front shoulder to create bat speed and intent in the box. Miller's power projection comes from his ability to uncoil at foot plant, creating rotation and torque in his swing. He stays behind the baseball and can flash exit velocities into the opposite field gap -- a promising sign going forward. There's still some roughness around the edges in terms of keeping his head on a steady plane through the baseball, and Sheets' timing and triggers can vary and wobble depending on the quality of competition he's seeing. These are all reasonable things that can be worked out with reps and time. 

Sheets has feel to get to his pull-side and is a reasonably selective hitter. Ground balls have diminished his offensive production at this point in his amateur career, but that wart can often be ironed out. The inconsistencies in the swing have led to a some swing and miss in his game, but when he stays inside the zone Sheets shows off the traits to potentially project a solid-average hitter at the next level. 

Sheets is a shortstop now, but the arm action, lateral mobility and arm strength may all be more befitting of a third baseman when all is said and done. He's a fringe-average runner with average arm strength for the left side of the infield. 

Bloodines and pedigree have done well in the MLB Draft in recent years, and it feels as though the hit rate with guys coming from baseball families has been higher than the alternative. Sheets may not be a fast-mover at the next level, but his left-side of the infield tools and his impact projection with the bat could get him selected in the third or fourth round if a team falls in love with the person and the player. Sheets will be 19.2 years old for the Draft and will draft-eligible once again in 2028 if he makes it to Baylor.

A rare prospect hailing from the great state of Idaho, Orloski was a 20th round selection by the Boston Red Sox but went unsigned in the 2023 MLB Draft. Orloski is a wiry, athletic righty with a bit of effort in his delivery, though he throws plenty of strikes. It's a super-vertical release with a fastball that carries through the strikezone in the low-90s, up to 98. Orloski cuts the hell out of his fastball and gives hitters a look they rarely see. It's generated impressive whiff rates to this point despite lacking top-end velocity. He's also an exceptional spinner of the baseball. Orloski's launch height is way above league average. It's up there in Logan Gilbert territory. 

Naturally cutting his fastball opens the door to a big changeup and a breaking ball that eats from that slot. The mid-80s changeup has great feel featuring late dart away from lefty bats. The upper-70s curveball is thrown at-will, though it presently lacks definitive bite. Still, it's steepness makes it effective. Orloski could fill a number of different roles on the mound going forward, but does possess the athleticism to potentially develop into a starting caliber arm at the next level. His uncle, Joe, played in the Blue Jays organization.

Graves is a smaller-bodied southpaw with an electric arm and bat-missing stuff. The fastball will touch 95, though he'll generally sit 91-93 in relief appearances. 

Both the slider and curveball show promise, though the latter projects a potential plus offering with fantastic depth and a track record of inducing whiffs. He's fastball-heavy for the time being as he continues to refine his secondaries. 

Graves is likely a reliever at the next level, but scouts pretty unanimously agree he'll be able to get out with authority and could throw up into the mid-90s in no time.

Big-bodied catcher who to this point has shown considerable raw power to the pull-side and up the middle of the field. Has shown a polished approach with low chase rates and solid bat-to-ball skills. 

Harrison is one of the best sluggers in the class when it comes to launching the ball in the air and getting to his pull side. Some athleticism in the swing with rhythmic waggle and whip. May be close to physically peaked. Could end up at first base or third base.

Turlij is something of a hidden gem in the Northeast, but probably shouldn't be considering the ferocity of his stuff, frame and mentality on the mound. 

Turlij is a fast mover on the bump with high leg kick and aggressive tempo. He's been up to 97 and will rest 94-95 in short-inning outings. Turlij has proven capable of holding 91-94 in four and five inning starts. He's been one of the best punch out artists the state of Pennsylvania has ever seen buoyed heavily be the fastball quality. 

Turlij throws a low-to-mid 80s slider with plus upside if he continues to add firmness to that pitch. To date, there hasn't been much of a third pitch shown to hitters. 

Mechanically and athletically, Turlij looks like a starter. He tests extremely well with force plates and proponents of the profile believe there's even more in the tank on the way. He'll need to develop a third pitch that moves the other direction to take that next step in professional baseball.

Roman has some of the best arm-talent you'll find in the 2026 class featuring a fastball that'll peak at 97 with carry and tail out of an uncomfortable arm slot. It's a heater that will induce whiffs, however he's too often been uncompetitive from a control and command perspective. When Roman is right, he'll punch tickets up and down lineups, but cold snaps can result in walks stacked on top of each other. 

He's not a one-trick pony. There's a bigger low-80s curveball with considerable depth and some sharpness when he's on. He'll also float a high-80s changeup away from left-handed hitters. 

Roman's floor is a guy who's selected toward the back-half of the Draft thanks to arm-talent alone. If he proves he can land three pitches for strikes and can do so over multiple innings, he's every bit that of a potential top 100 pick.

Thomas is a prototype lefty with a big, athletic 6-foot-4-inch frame and a barrel chest. He's been up into the mid-90s, however he more commonly sits 89-91 with moderate carry and tail. The fastball has struggled to miss bats despite owning close to seven feet of extension. When Thomas is hot, he's dunking the fastball on hitters. 

His low-80s cutter/slider has been a real whiffs machine and projects really well moving into pro ball. if he can land it in the zone or in the shadow zone with more frequency. There's a sweeper and a changeup in here too, but his two primary pitches and naturally deceptive arm-slot has been enough to stump would-be hitters. 

Thomas is a very good mover with an excellent frame. He's got starter traits if the velocity takes a jump and one of his secondaries establishes itself as a true weapon.

It's impossible not to see Tre' Morgan when scouting and evaluating Minnatee. An LSU commit like his predecessor, Minnatee aims for a bit more game power at this same stage than did Morgan. He's uniquely armed with some of the same bat-to-ball skills, however.

Minnatee hit nearly .500 as a high school junior and showcased considerable bat speed and juice to the opposite field. He creates space in the box and stays back through the baseball letting the barrel do handle the hard work. The twitchiness, hand speed and overall violence in the swing stand out. Minnatee has a chance to hit for a big average and certainly some power going forward. The finished product may compare favorably with a player like Josh Naylor.

Minnatee is a below average runner who will play first base at the next level. He's got soft hands around the bag and the clock necessary to handle first base at a high level as a pro.

An underwhelming sophomore year at Oregon State pushed Caraway down draft boards in his draft-eligible sophomore year. Seeking a change in scenery, Caraway hit the portal looking for a new zip code. 

Caraway has a ton of strength in his hands that allow him to manipulate the barrel to all fields depending on whether or not he's out in front of spin/velocity. A violent hitter with power to every gap, Caraway is an offensive threat to do damage every time he steps in the box. He's already posting exit velocities north of 113 mph, and did so as a true freshman in Corvallis. It's 'plus' raw power even if he never fully gets to it in game settings. Contact quality has been struggle at times for him. Caraway could eventually develop into a 25-30 HR threat at the next level if some adjustments are made to the swing and attack angle.

Thus far there's been some swing and miss present in his game and his ground ball rates are higher than scouts would like to see. He's a streaky hitter who can carry a lineup when he's hot. 

The bat is going to have to carry water this spring. Caraway has a good throwing arm and can run a bit too, but fringier hands and actions might push him to the outfield over time. While the run tool can post average times now and again, Caraway has a stiff, upright running style that scouts believe will slow early in his career than some of his more athletic peers. Caraway is a good athlete and has every opportunity to prove his mettle on the dirt as July approaches. Skeptics look at stiff actions in the box and on the bases and question how the frame matures. It could end up a Jake Burger-esque player at 25 years old, however Caraway is considerably stronger and better build than Burger was at this same stage.

Following two seasons at Seminole State College, Dahl transferred into Louisiana Tech for his draft-eligible 2026 season armed with a three-pitch mix and the means to get both left-handed and right-handed hitters out. He's got some unique traits and could appeal to analytically inclined pitching development programs.

Dahl is a three-pitch arm with a release height a full eight inches lower than the MLB average. His fastball possesses a relatively flat approach angle when he chooses to elevate the baseball, an approach he's focused on with his craft. Dahl has shown the ability to miss bats with the heater despite it routinely living 92-94 with modest carry. Above average extension and those release traits do the heavy lifting. It's certainly at least an average fastball at the next level, and may have nights where it flashes and performs a bit better than its grade.

Dahl's best secondary is a tumbling low-80s changeup that he can really sell. It's got significant drop and his ability to command it where he wants stands out. It's an above average weapon on nights he's commmanding the fastball.

Dahl's sweeping slider is more on the fringy side. It's a low-80s breaker with average spin traits and a shape profiles that seems to live somewhere in between a true sweeper and a generic slider. He'll need to tinker with that pitch at the next level. 

Dahl could use a fourth pitch, preferably a firm curveball that provides a bit more depth to his arsenal. For now, his approach to pitching is fastballs and changeups to lefties. Righties get the fastball and slider. From that perspective, it's a fairly stock profile. That said, given the uniqueness of the fastball and his ability to work the ball in both directions, he could be a day three project for an organization that believes there's a bit more life in that engine.

Yamaguchi was a notable draft prospect coming out of St. Louis School in Hawaii as a prep in 2024, but went undrafted over concerns of his eventual defensive home. He's all but squashed those concerns whilst on campus, showing a hit tool and impact few in the industry forecast as he transitioned to campus. The 2025 Mountain West Freshman of the Year is a true middle-of-the-order slugger on the collegiate scene.

Yamaguchi is among the most aggressive hitters in the country. He runs high chase rates and his contact quality will suffer now and again because of what he's swinging at. That said, it's exceptional bat-to-ball skills and heavy hands that deliver a blow through the zone and outside of it as well. Yamaguchi runs very ordinary contact rates, in large part due to his approach. That said, when he's swinging at strikes, the whiffs are kept to a minimum. His hard-hit rate on pitches in the zone is impressive. Despite his 5-foot-10-inch stature, Yamaguchi is still delivering exit velocities north of 111 mph at his peak. Should he ever develop more refined discipline, he's got a chance to become a pretty strong hitter at the next level. However, if he continues to swing recklessly, his approach could get surgically picked apart once he reached Double-A.

Perhaps one part of Yamaguchi's game inhibiting his ability to make late decisions at the plate is his swing. His setup includes hands set below the letters and out away from his frame. There's noisiness in his hands and his triggers as the pitch is thrown. Yamaguchi sells out to generate energy in his core. That has helped produce some gaudy slugging numbers at the expense of pitch recognition and diminished timing windows. Make no mistake, Yamaguchi is a good ballplayer.
