He can really hit and takes his hands to the ball better than just about anyone in the country. He's adjustable on just about anything he can physically get the barrel to. 

Yamaguchi is a good athlete, especially for his size. While he's received run at shortstop, most believe he'll eventually play second and third base as a professional. 

Yamaguchi is a very good ballplayer. He's a natural hitter despite the overanxious desire to make things happen. He also plays with an edge and competitive fire that can be tough to find. This is a player that loves the game.

After two years at the University of Texas and a failure to get consistent footing underneath his game, Farmer transferred to UC Irivine for his third collegiate campaign. Draft eligible in 2025, Farmer went unselected, but he's still young for the 2026 Draft; barely 22 years old.

Farmer IV is interesting from a pure scouting perspective. The player is athletic, strong, posts double-plus run times, and he's shown flashes of a hit tool, though he hardly had the runway at UT to prove himself. Now getting consistent run, those traits still ring true. Scouts and evaluators alike value the upside. 

There's size, tools and traits to like here from a projection and role perspective. Farmer will need to prove his mettle as July approaches if teams are to buy into the clay on draft day. There's obviously some ceiling here if the pieces come together, but given the smaller sample size it'll be difficult for teams to feel complete confidence in his game transitioning to professional baseball without consistent, steady performances in 2026.

A big 6-foot-4-inch backstop, Madrid gets high marks for his ability to handle a pitching staff, steer his pitchers into advantageous positions both mentally and mechanically, as well as control the run game. His energy level behind the plate stands out, and his willingness to get dirt and block balls in the dirt is a plus. Madrid's larger size does create some challenges physically with regards to those blocks, as well as stealing the low strike, but his commitment to his craft has never wavered.

Offensively, it's plus raw power projection thanks to exceptionally strong hands and wrists in the box. Madrid can get his bat speed to all four quadrants and is especially apt at getting the barrel to the inside pitch. He's a willing recipient of walks, and strikouts haven't been an enormous problem for him at this stage, however there is some swing and miss in his game. He profiles as a big-body masher with a chance to play catcher or perhaps right field to compliment what is solid average arm strength. Madrid is also a solid average runner and will jump into another gear to steal the extra base when provided the opportunity.

Chrisman is comfortably one of the most intimidating bats in the 2026 class. His large stature and muscular frame show out in a big way in the batters box. It's huge bat speed with game power present and feel for loft and launch. This is at least double-plus raw power projection and it's growing into elite. When Chrisman is on time his shots to the pull-side are majestic. There's some waggle and rhythm in his hands during the loading phase that can get him late at times against better arms, but adjusting is all a part of the development process. Swing and miss and strikeouts will always likely be a part of his profile, especially due to his aggressive nature, but if those warts come alongside middle-of-the-order impact potential, it's a worthy trade-off. 

Chrisman is a bit more limited on the defensive end. While he's received reps at third base, most foresee a future at first base. He's a below average runner. Chrisman is on the older side, 19.3 for the Draft.

Following two impressive years at Sacred Heart, Foster went chasing bigger and brighter lights. He landed at South Carolina for the 2026 season. 

Foster has some of the most unique data you can find on the mound in the 2026 class. Frankly, it almost doesn't make sense. He's a low-slot righty launching out of a 5-foot slot with a fastball that generates 20 inches of IVB at peak. He's just 6-feet tall and generates ludicrous amounts of extension toward the plate; a key variable in his release height and ability to keep his fastball so vertical. Foster has already been up to 97 mph and he lives 90-92. Foster still scatters his fastball at times and dialing in his control and command will be a point of emphasis in his development over the next couple years, but there are traits here you simply cannot teach. 

Foster's best secondary is without question his changeup. He commands it well to his arm-side, but it still buckshot most nights in terms of where he'll land it. It features huge fading action and he can eliminate spin fairly well for his age. The slider isn't a good pitch at this stage and will require further development both in terms of learning how to spin the baseball as well as how to shape it. It's a relief profile at the next level, but a profile that could move up boards if Foster learns how to spin the ball.

Foster is the rare draft-eligible third-year 20-year-old prospect. He won't turn 21 years old until a week after the Draft. He'll still hold some leverage in July and arguably has more development on the horizon with just one year in the SEC under his belt.

A well-traveled fourth-year right-hander, Brainard spent the first two years of his collegiate journey at Northeast Community College where he'd start 15 games and rack up innings and experience. Brainard took to pitching full-time at Brainard, putting down the bat and allowing his second base glove to gather dust. After those two season, he transferred to Regis where he'd throw 56.2 innings, striking out 60 hitters. It was enough to garner the interest from Nevada in the transfer portal that summer. Now 45 pounds heavier and stronger than he once was as a high school senior, Brainard is growing into his own physically, and his craft has blossomed alongside his newfound strength.

Brainard is a four-pitch guy with a fastball that's been as hot at 98 mph. He generates solid extension down the mound from a traditional stacked back-side delivery. He throws from a full wind-up with nobody on base. Brainard finishes high with a slight fall-off toward the first base dugout. While 98 is in the tank, Brainard more commonly sits 93-96 with above average carry through the zone, as well as some tail. He spins the ball well-above average with heaters that will at times crest 2500 rpm.

Brainard doesn't lean on his velocity like many might expect. He throws a slider, curveball and changeup at heavy clips relative to the rest of college baseball; especially to those arms who throw hard like he does. It's a solid mix with variable shapes. His ability to repeat his delivery and release point is a strength.

Brainard's changeup has a chance to be his best pitch, however he'll need to find more consistency from a shapes perspective. He's adept at killing spin and can, at times, kill vert on the pitch, however he too often leaves that pitch up with middling shape. There's an above average changeup in here if he can begin throwing the best version of his offspeed pitch more often than not.

Both of Brainard's breaking balls are firm. The slider is 85-87 with shorter tilt and gyroscopic orientation. He'll throw a handful of 0 vert slider in his velocity band and, when thrown competitively, will get whiffs. The curveball is thrown in the low-80s in the ballpark of -10/-10. It's been effective at the college level and could be used as a professional if he generates a bit more depth.

Brainard's inherently ability to spin the baseball, throw strikes and generate velocity are all strengths of his. He hasn't been much of a strikeout artist relative to his stuff at the college level, so it's fair to question if he has much deception in his operation. He'll be 22.5 years old for the Draft.

Stops at Riverside Community College, UNLV and Long Beach State led Roblez, a fifth-year senior, to Corvallis. He's a metric darling with some of the more unique pitch traits on the West Coast. It's a definitive reliever profile, but a unique look for hitters no less.

Roblez is a guy that lives in the low-90s, but generates elite vert on his fastball thanks to significant contra-lateral spine tilt. He gets the arm up, way over the top and induce perfect backspin at release. He also cuts the fastball with his supination release profile. Roblez's operation also leads to an exceptionally high release height, close to 80 inches -- remarkably strange for a player stretching to measure in at 6 feet tall. Despite the unorthdox traits and release metrics, Roblez isn't generating a ton of chase or whiff on the heater, and is fringy from a control perspective.

The changeup, however, can be devestating. It's only 5 or 6 ticks slower than the heater, but it drops off the table and peters out thanks to spin rates that will approach 1000 rpm. When Roblez is establish the fastball in the zone, the changeup plays at least above average.

A cutter, slider and curveball represent his spin profile, however none are terribly consistent from a shapes or strikes perspective. The cutter serves the best purpose playing off the fastball, but most of the breaking balls here are fringy.

Roblez profiles as a fastball/changeup mid-leverage reliever at the next level. He needs to find a breaking ball he can throw to get hitters off the changeup. He'll be 23 years old just two weeks after the draft, and will likely be a small-dollar money saver.

Quincy Bright has long had extraordinary arm talent. At the age of 15 he was already grabbing 94 mph and he'd sit 90-92 over multi-inning starts for Salisbury. That said, Tommy John surgery slowed him during his high school career forcing him to much of his high school career. 

He's now peaking in the mid-90s launched from a lower slot. It's fairlly genereric from a shape perspective, however the flatness in his approach does allow the pitch to play up. 

with a mid-70s slurvy slider he'll deploy against LHH. Bright has been working to fold a changeup into his arsenal to keep RHH off the barrel and it's come along in the last six months. He sells the pitch with arm speed though generating more definitive shape continues to be an emphasis. 

Bright is a tremendous athlete who boasts good extension down the mound with a super fast arm. Scouts liken the whole package to big league lefty Taylor Hearn. Bright will be 18.6 years old on draft day.

Ross is one of the better defensive infielders available in the 2026 Draft. A shortstop by trade, Ross projects best at third base where the actions, footwork, hands, and fundamentals play up in a big way. Ross has a chance to develop into a 70-grade leatherman with plus arm strength to boot. 

Offensively, Ross can be passive at the dish thwarting some of the physical traits he possessess. It's average bat speed from both sides, however Ross has struggled to consistently get to his pull-side. 

Whoever drafts Ross will certainly be selecting the exceptional floor with the glove, but it'll be the bat that eventually dictates how high his ceiling can climb.

Loggie is exactly what scouts picture a starting pitcher looks like off the bus. A high waist, long levers, some broadness in the shoulders with strength in his core and lower half. Loggie has the prototype frame you look for on the mound. Couple that with advanced body control for a player of his stature and it's easy to dream on what the finished product could look like in short time.

Loggie's fastball is a low-90s offering with late life, some tail and dart through the zone. He's been up to 95 and routinely sits 89-90 as he works a lather into later innings. Loggie's capacity for spin stands out, at times jumping north of 2700 rpm with the heater and consistently living in the 2450 range. Loggie's ability to create angles and steep plane is very tough for the opposing hitter. At present, it's fringy control for the zone with the fastball and below average command. He'll spray the pitch a bit and finds most of his success being effective wild on certain nights.

Loggie throws two breaking balls, a tighter, compact low-80s slider being the better of the duo. He'll back-door and front-door that pitch to lefties and righties alike and has shown comfortability sweeping it away from left-handed hitters. There's some feel for shape here, but again, the strikes and command inside the zone is a work in progress. 

Loggie's low-80s changeup has a chance to be very good. His ability to throw that pitch to right-handed hitters and play with it to the arm-side off the tunnel of his fastball has it flashing above average traits with execution soon to follow. 

Loggie uses his frame very well and gets down the mound with conviction and tempo. The arm action works and the stuff is plenty big enough to project forward. If the strikes and strike-quality take a jump as July approaches, Loggie could hear his name very early.

Collins certainly looks the part on the mound with an arm stroke that really works. It's loose, composed and on time with plenty of strikes. Collins will touch 95, but routinely sits 90-92 with carry and late life through the zone. Supplemented by close to seven feet of extension, it's as explosive a heater as you'll find in this velocity band. It's a fastball that blows hitters up. 

Collins' best secondary is an low-80s split/change with tremendous sell and hard brakes and fade at the plate. It's routinely above average and will flash 'plus' when the fastball is landing at the bottom of the strike zone. A low-80s breaking ball is mostly average right now, though he does spin the baseball nicely and it's a pitch that projects solid-to-above average in due time. 

Collins is a strike-thrower with a great frame, a strong operation, big extension and three pitches. It's a loose arm with some length and healthy intent. It's definitive starter clay. The velocity will need to trend up as July approaches, but it's certainly a big-signing bonus stuff.

Left-handed and projectable. Evans looks the part. This fastball has bat-missing shape and an sizze with high-octane rpm at the top of the zone. For now, he's been up to 96, but it's more commonly 90-92. 

Evans has demonstrated the ability to rip through a 78-81 mph slider at 2600 rpm. It's a true out-pitch when landed and commanded. The changeup is in the tank, but feel for execution and shape lags behind his better two offerings. 

Evans is a fringy strike-thrower who seems to have different feel for the zone depending on the day. He's flashed average feel for the zone at times, but walks can get away from him at times limiting the effectiveness of his good stuff. If he can throw together a handful of better outings as July approaches, it's certainly day one stuff.

A unique two-way talent with switch-hitting ability at the plate, Rose seems to be able to do just about anything on the baseball field he wants. Despite his tools with the bat and in the outfield, most expect his future is on the mound. 

Rose has an arm action that really works. He's loose, athletic and shows good direction and balance in his move down the mound. He's shown some extension, however beings he's had very little formal training, it's fair to think he'll develop a good bit more in professional baseball. 

Rose's fastball is generally 89-92 and will tickle 93. It's got some carry and late tail that can keep hitters off the barrel. His command stands out. This is three pitches with a changeup that will flash above average upside. He's not flipping over many breaking balls that shape better than average, however his spin rates are well-above average and should be conducive toward pitch design and development at the next level.

Scouts rave about Rose's makeup and personality. He's a fiery competitor with a limitless thirst to get better. There's a humiliity about his disposition, too. Given his size and leaner frame, there's limited physical upside, however the polish and pitchability could get him to a back-end profile with time and patience in pro ball.

A 20th round pick by the Red Sox in 2025, Sumner returned to Provo for his fourth year of college baseball hoping to improve his draft stock. He's done just that.

After peaking at just 93 mph in 2025, Sumner touched 97 as a redshirt junior, resting more comfortably in the 91-94 range. His fastball possesses some late carry and does a nice job generating chase at the top of the zone, however below average extension does limit Sumner's ability to miss bats with the fastball. His capacity for spin, however, stands out.

Sumner's slider is a good one. A true bullet-spinner with almost no lateral tilt, Sumner can generate whiffs below the zone when he's showing the fastball and working counts deep. It's been up to 85 and breaks off the fastball tunnel very late, causing hitters to swing over the top with steady frequency. If the fastball quality improves at the next level, and hitters are forced to sit on the heater, Sumner could eventually develop plus performance metrics with the breaker. 

Sumner also throws a changeup with impressive vertical tilt and enough horizontal fading action to get whiffs. It's average from an execution perspective, but there's upside here if the heater continues to upward climb.

Sumner has traits, size and an easy operation. His lack of extension will be an uphill battle in terms of staying in a rotation as a professional, but he may be able to carve out a multi-inning role with some of the secondary weapons he possesses.

Cazares has shown well across multiple events as an amateur touching 96 mph. He can spin the baseball too featuring spin rates north of average. He's a high-intent arm with a repeatability in his delivery and natural deception coming out of a longer arm action, launched well-below a prototypical hurler. 

The slider is his best secondary and it's got wipeout traits. He'll sweep that pitch away from righties inducing plenty of whiffs. The changeup is coming along. He kills spin pretty well and has the ability to pump the brakes on that pitch to hitters, though it's squarely trailing his fastball-slider combo in terms of pure upside and present value. 

Cazares has strength in his frame and a fast arm that point to a guy who could soon flirt with upper-90s velocity. He'll need to pull the reins back on effort at release if he hopes to start at the next level, but there's components to his profile that point toward the ability to work multiple innings going forward.

Stokes saw his stuff take off his senior year of high school after focusing on basketball for much of his prep tenure. He went undrafted but received plenty of interest in 2023. After spending the 2024 and 2025 seasons at Oregon pitching primarily out of the bullpen, he transferred to Florida State for the 2026 season. 

Stokes got into eight games as a true freshman but struggled with command. And that's has continued to this day. It's a live arm with big stuff but finding the zone will be a developmental key if he's to reach his big league ceiling.

Stokes sinker is an absolute bowling ball. Stokes launches from a slightly lower-than league average release height despite his 6-foot-6-inch frame. He generates enormous sink and tailing action with steepness coming naturally from his frame. Stokes has been up to 99 and will sit 95-97 with above average extension in bullpen appearances. He has a tendency to miss high and to the arm-side, throwing his front side open early. It's presently well-below average fastball control and command. 

Stokes has slightly better feel for a low-to-mid 80s slider. It's been a true bat-missing weapon, mirroring the sinker seam orientation deep after release. It's a breaking ball that has all the makings of a future plus weapon, but it plays down a tick due to a lack of fastball command. 

Stokes is a former two-sport star with a basketball background and the athleticism shows up on film. His whippy arm and projectable frame has scouts excited as to what it could eventually become. Developing a changeup and throwing considerably more strikes are first and foremost.

DiMartini began his collegiate career at Penn State in 2024 where he earned just six at-bats in 13 games played. He was primarily used as a defensive substitute. That lack of opportunity landed him in the transfer portal where he latched on at Dayton and has become a bit of an offensive force. DiMartini then hopped into the portal once more, this time heading to Duke for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign. 

DiMartini can play all over the diamond but he found a home in centerfield for the Fliers and continues to get run at the '8' as a Blue Devin. He's an above average runner and clocks reasonably strong reads in the outfield. His game may be best-suited for left field as a professional, but few doubt his ability to play the '8' in a pinch at the next level. 

DiMartini's bat is what's collecting the headlines. He bludgeoned the baseball in 2025 with borderline elite batted-ball and exit velocity metrics. It's at least above-average raw power, but some scouts question whether all that juice will translate to professional baseball. DiMartini has a unique swing. It's a flatter path that he cuts off abruptly shortly after contact. It's something of a lumberjack tree-chop swing, but he makes it work. DiMartini does struggle with swing-and-miss woes, primarily against spin inside and outside of the strike zone. That's to be expected from what is considered a bit of rigid swing. He can also be challenged to get to better velocity at the top of the zone. DiMartini needs to become more adjustable as his draft approaches. He's a cookie-killer right now who clearly has the physical and athletic traits to be an impactful player if he proves he can hit. 

DiMartini figures to add value on the base paths too. He's got great instincts, a strong first step, and an aggressive all-or-nothing approach toward running the bases.

Autrey is a power-hitting corner infielder with a big left-handed swing. Power comes easy for the Texas A&M commit. It's 70-grade raw power that has a chance to pound 40 homers at the next level if the hit tool allows it to play.  He's got tremendous feel for the barrel and is short, quick and compact to the baseball registering huge exit velo figures. Autrey actually hit a 544-foot homer at the Power Showcase World Class at Glove Life Field in 2025, breaking an LED board on the jumbotron. It's prodigious raw power.  

It's a really physical stack. Autrey won't provide too much value on the bases and could eventually shift to first base as he matures. Scouts think the bat could be special with impact at the next level. He'll be 18.9 years old on draft day.

After spending the first two seasons of his collegiate career at Duke, Johnson followed his head coach, Chris Pollard, to Virginia for his draft-eligible 2026 season. 

Johnson is a really talented do-it-all prospect with tools scattered all over the field. He's been up to 97 on the mound from the left side, generating plenty of whiffs and ugly swings outside of the strike zone. His athleticism is obvious in how he rides the mound and generates solid extension for his size. Johnson is working to develop a more dynamic breaking ball, but what he's shown thus far flashes 'plus' production. Hitters have an awfully difficult time picking his arsenal up out of the hand. 

Most think his future will be on the bump, but at the plate he posts impressive exit velocities with the bat, though his game performances have been streaky. Johnson has put on muscle since arriving to campus and has slowed down to just an average runner. In the field, it's a plus throwing arm with strong routes in both left and right field. While he consistently hits the ball very, very hard, Johnson's swing-and-miss woes may ultimately preclude him from swinging the bat at the professional level. 

Tons of tools, tons of avenues toward impact. Defining how it all works best is next on the horizon.

The fourth brother in a line of Southisene's to become draft-eligible in the last three seasons, Troy brings some of the same traits his older siblings did to the game. He's a gritty hitter with an insatiable appetite for competition. 

Troy doesn't have the same size that Tate or Ty had, but what he lacks in physical stature he makes up for in hustle and fundamentals. He's a pest with a bat in his hands too. Southisene is a contact hitter. He's very difficult ot strike out and uses the whole field as well as anyone in the class. Southisene tends to get the hands going a little early and can get disconnected at times in the box -- this move clearly an effort to make contact rather than get his 'A-Swing' off. He picks his spots. Southisene will go into ambush mode when he gets ahead in the count, but more often than not he's gearing up to put the game in motion. Southisene's swing path keeps the barrel through the zone for an exceptional amount of time. All these traits are supplemented by a flatter bat path than most of his peers. This is a hitter first and foremost. Southisene's approach is moderately aggressive with pitches off the outside corner making his eyes light up more than most zones. Still, his hand-eye coordination helps create long at-bats and frustrating experiences for the opposing pitcher. Given his size, Southisene will likely settle in as a hit-over-power prospect.

Defensively, Southisene gets half his run at shortstop and the other half in the outfield. It's solid average arm strength at both position, the fundamentals and footwork being slightly more advanced in the grass. He's an above average runner who gets good jumps with high-level instinctual awareness. Southisene is as steady as they come.

Southisene is a high floor prospect with multiple avenues toward a big league role.

Bland is your prototypical power-hitting left-handed first base prospect. He sets up wide at the dish, anchors his lower-half hard, creates ground force with a steep swing to create loft and slug. There's a lot of moving parts and variations in his timing and triggers that can make repeating his swing difficult. That said, when he's synced up, few in the class can deliver the blow to the baseball Bland. An aggressive swinger with an eager disposition in the box, Bland is susceptible to strikeouts, but the impact is the major selling point. 

Bland is a fringy runner who has enough lateral mobility and first step quickness to play first base going forward, so long as he doesn't get too big and physical for the position.

One of the stars from the Canadian Junior National Team, Kitura is one of the more interesting bats available in the 2026 Draft. 

Kitura swings a heavy barrel. It's above-average raw power that's continued to grow alongside his frame. Kitura has strong hands with the ability to keep everything inside his body; a compact operation with a pull-side emphasis. Kitura generates loft naturally and is capable of back-spinning the baseball to the deepest part of the yard. His longer frame is high-waisted with a bit more projection coming in his lower half and levers. Kitura has flashed some adjustability on pitches at the bottom of the strike zone. The hit tool remains unpolished and inconsistent at times, but there are components here to suggest he'll hit enough to let the power play.

Kitura isn't an explosive mover and lacks twitch in the field and on the basepaths. He's a long-strider who makes up ground with an efficient running style rather than quickness in his actions. It's average run times, however the run tool could go in either direction with player development. On one hand, if a team gets his athleticism moving quicker he could conceivably gain some speed. But if he continues to add weight and muscle, that long stride could slog more into a heavy-footedness on the base paths. Still, he's be no means a liability on the bases or in the field as he exhibits good body control and fluidity. 

Kitura is a one-handed infielder who tracks everything into his glove and will occasionally pin his throwing arm behind his back while bringing the ball in. He demonstrates solid direction on the dirt and rounds through the baseball showcasing above average arm strength befitting of a third baseman. His arm action and arm strength play up in right field. The fundamentals with the hands and actions on the dirt will probably have to improve should he hope to play the hot corner as a pro, but he's got some of the lateral ability and tools necessary to begin his pro career on the dirt.

A well-rounded shortstop prospect with some burgeoning power, Martinez can do a little bit of everything well. He's an above average runner with the green light on the bases. Martinez has played shortstop and second base, the former being hims most comfortable home. It's a lean frame with physical projection and some length in his levers. 

Martinez has average bat to ball skills, however he works good at-bats and doesn't chase outside of the zone.

Wisener enjoyed a breakout during the summer entering his senior year. The stuff took a jump and so did his attention from scouts. 

The fastball is a mid-90s hopper with value at the top of the zone. Wisener has proven capable of holding 94-97 when tasked with throwing just one or two innings. He supplements the heater with a big hammer curveball with significant downward tilt, 80-82, tunneled when spiked.

One of the more premium arms coming out of Canada in the 2026 class, McDowell provides of a blend of size, physicality, pitching projection and present stuff that should have scouts excited about his prospect status going forward. It's a big, durable frame built to log long innings here and now. 

McDowell is already touching 96 mph and shows the ability to hold 92-93 over multiple innings. He's got a difficult release point for hitters to pick up -- much lower and wider than would conventionally be expected from a player his size and stature. It allows the fastball to play up a bit better than its metric and velocity. There's some carry and late tail through the zone. 

McDowell throws two breakings balls. His low-80s sweeper has solid-average projection, maybe a bit more. His feel for tunneling that pitch and executing it into locations that will garner swings is a work in progress. A bigger high-70s curveball is the more tantilizing of the two breakers. It's got more depth and plays off the fastball in a more natural, deceptive way. 

McDowell's training age doesn't line up with his physical age. He's got plenty of develop in front of him with strength and intellectual gains still on the horizon. This could be an arm that lives 93-95 in due time, with the feel for secondaries necessary to start at the next level. He is expected to be signable away from his North Florida commitment.

Acevedo is extremely raw in many areas of his game, but few players in the class can match the size and athletic upside that this player brings to the table. It'll take a while for him to reach his ceiling, but a team willing to play the long game should have Acevedo's name circled in the 2026 draft.

Offensively, the 6-foot-4-inch frame and athletic build immediately stands out. Acevdeo has tremendous size and a ton of physical projection remaining in his 220-pound frame (as difficult as that is to believe). The swing and offensive tools in-game have a ways to go. Repeating his swing will need to be a priority going forward. Acevedo mixes up his leg lifts and toe taps. He also significantly varies his stride length on every pitch. Sometimes he'll stay behind his front side, other times he'll drift through the baseball. It's a very crude operation, but one with athletic markers and flashes of obvious ability buried within a green ballplayer. The bat speed and raw power projection could be a 70 on the scouting scale. If Acevedo can ever figure out a way to consistently get to it, he could be featured in the meat of a lineup.

Acevedo is an aggressive hitter and a free-swinger at the plate. He's shown a willingness to expand the zone at hyper-anxious rates, especially against back-foot sliders from right-handed pitchers. That said, his whiff rates aren't terribly extreme, but they are something of a yellow flag warning. As his pitch recognition and plate approach skills improve, so too should his production.

This is as prototype a right field profile as you'll find. Acevedo is a fringy runner, but plays through the ball well. His crow hop and transfer is quick, getting the ball out with pace. As he matures into his adult frame, Acevedo could grow into plus arm strength -- the mechanics and comfortability are there.

While it may take some time, Acevedo is an exciting prospect and ball of clay. He's extremely young for the class, barely 18 years old for the draft. He moves well, and has shown flashes of offensive production to suggest polish could eventually come one day. There are risks on the profile, but for the right number, he's a fun lottery ticket in the draft.

James is a wiry, well-built, wound up middle infielder with considerable projection in his frame. A switch-hitter, James shows big bat speed from the right side and boasts impressive exit velocities to all fields. From the left side it's a bit more subdued with an opposite field approach and less whip. If he can tone down his swing and miss streakiness and strikeout rates, James has a chance at developing into an impact bat with game-altering tools. 

His 70-grade speed is an asset both on the bases and ranging to the middle of the diamond on difficult plays. Defensively it's average arm strength with twitch and bounce in his game on the dirt. He's got a shot to play shortstop at the next level if he doesn't outgrow the position. There's also a humility to the player that can be difficult to find on the showcase and tournament circuit. 

The narrative on James will be the approach and bat-to-ball skills. If those tick up in the right direction, it's day one upside. He will be 19.2 years old for the draft.

Deome is one of the more mature, polished hitters in the 2026 class with an approach built to put up big slash lines. It's a quiet, relaxed look in the box, never selling out for power or lunging into the baseball. Deome has shown the ability to hit the ball to all fields and will routinely pepper the left-center field gap for doubles. It's above average raw power that he should get to without forcing to it. He projects a high average, high on-base hitter with 20 homer upside. 

Deome has some real ability at third base with fluidity and soft hands that allow him to gobble up the routine play with ease. There's carry across the diamond too, although it's mostly average arm strength maybe a tick more. Deome is a below average runner who won't add a ton of value in terms of range or on the basepaths, but the bat and hands/fundamentals are so good he's certainly got a good shot to stick on the left side of the infield at the next level.

Bratton is one of the more unique pitching prospects in the 2026 class with some disgusting stuff on the bump. He's been up to 92 mph with a low-three quarter delivery featuring considerable tail and sink. His misses are generally to the glove-side as he likes to pitch away from righties and work more 'middle' to left-handed hitters. The heater sets what at times is a diabolical sweeping slider featuring north of 3000 rpms. It's a true sweeper in every sense of the word and it's regularly tied right-handed hitters in knots. Bratton's hasn't yet polished up a third pitch to work away from left-handed hitters, but he's shown a willingness to back-foot the sweeper, albeit with less consistency and comfort than the latter.

Bratton's delivery is simple with a high leg kick, sinking in to his hips and riding the mound toward average extension for his length. When he works a lather it seems as though he's playing catch out there. Bratton needs to throw more strikes and establish a third pitch if he's to start going forward. He currently has the look of a leverageable relief prospect who could pitch in big spots at the next level, and a velocity jump is to be presumed in the coming years.

After a fairly limited role as a freshman in 2024, Yost took over a full-time outfield role for the Gators as a sophomore in 2025 and never looked back. 

At his best, Yost is slashing balls into the gaps and flashing what is above-average raw power. He can be an aggressive hitter and tends to expand the zone at times, more specifically on elevated velocity. He handles anything on the inner-third with ease, though his swing can get long on pitches on the outer-half causing more whiffs. Yost has an efficient swing plane and can battle deeper into counts, though he'll likely need to add a bit more weight to control the barrel like he appears capable in the future. There's plenty of room in his lower-half for more muscle. 

Yost is a good athlete who leverages the ground nicely in the box. He's going to grow into more raw power as he matures. Yost in an average runner with tighter gait. He takes strong routes in the outfield but only profiles as an average defender at best, destined for left field. 

Much of Yost's draft value will come by way of the bat. If he adds the weight and strength necessary to tap into what some believe is a promising offensive future, he could climb as high as the third or fourth round.

A big-game performer with impact tools across his reports, Browning is a scout-favorite in Texas. He's a well-built infielder with a wide frame, broad shoulders and strong lower-half. Browning has raw offensive tools that can be streaky in game settings but there's certainly pull-side power that ranks among the best in the class, potentially above-average or better when all is said and done. He'll need to clean up the approach and swing and miss as July approaches to get the most out of his physicality and athleticism. 

He's currently a plus runner that is adding value on the bases and on the dirt. Browning has strong actions at shortstop but could eventually shift to third base as he outgrows the middle of the field. Browning will be 18.7 on draft day.

Priest is a decorated power hitter with considerable bat speed and an attack angle built to do damage. He possesses fringy bat-to-ball skills, but the approach is strong as he hardly swings at pitches off the black. When Priest chooses to swing, he consistently hits the ball very hard.

Priest is likely destined for first base where his hands and first step will work best. The bat, however, is the clear carrying tool here.

Belding's comfort and swing stand out in a big way in the box. He looks like a hitter before the pitch is thrown, and that's something scouts look for. It's a balanced setup with a direct path to the ball with very little wasted actions or eye wash triggers. Belding has the look of a true hitter and has the physical freme to project raw power on. 

Belding is a catcher by trade. His receiving skills and catch-and-throw has some development ahead, but there is some athleticism back there to build upon. The pure arm strength stands out and is plenty strong enough to stay behind the plate if the footwork, framing and receiving takes a jump. Belding has played some outfield and first base as well to keep his bat in the lineup. He is a fringy runner.

Boaz went unselected in the 2023 and 2025 drafts, mostly due to age and signability, but once again finds himself draft-eligible in 2026 as a third-year hurler for UNC. 

A big, linebacker-body lefty, Boaz worked into the low-90s in high school and has ticked up a notch at Chapel Hill thus far touching 96 at peak. He throws a sweeping slider with elite vertical plane that's performed extremely well in the ACC. He'll have to fold in a third weapon as July approaches to reach his Top-100 pick upside, however he's continued to improve year over year and represents one of the better left-handed pitchers in the country.

A 16th round selection by the Brewers in 2025, Coil decided to head back to Fayetteville for another run at it in 2026. 

Coil is generally your prototype pitchability lefty with deceptive stuff and a free-and-easy motion. He can get amped up at times in short outings and has touched 94 mph in 2025. That said, he's more comfortably 90-92 on most nights. It's his operation and consistency that have teams interested. Coil is a tremendous strike-thrower out of the bullpen. Despite being a short-strider without dominant velocity, Coil gets plenty of fastball value with his ability to hide the baseball. His frame points toward a future with a bit more ticks on the radar gun too. Coil also does a nice job avoiding hard contact by folding in a low-90s cutter that moves like his four-seam but keeps off the barrel.

Coil works down in the zone with all three pitches. He prefers to pitch to his glove-side. He's sweeping breaking ball will flash plus with huge spin rates. There's a changeup that mimics the action of his heavy fastball. The upside here is tremendous, especially if the velo bumps as most anticipate it should.

The book is going to write itself. A catcher named Catcher. It's too good to be true. But it's not just a fun coincidence. Hopkins is a legitimate catching prospect with some of the tools behind the plate to stay back there at the next level. And the athletic and offensive tools aren't far behind. 

Hopkins is explosive athletically. He's up and out of the crouch with tempo delivering a strike to second base with plus arm strength. His arm strength translates to right field too. An above average runner, Hopkins has straight line speed and has shown a willingness to dive on grenades to save his pitcher. He moves well laterally and has a frame that can stay behind the plate too. There's still plenty of strength projection in his lower half. His receiving skills continue to improve. The hands are getting softer and the forward stabbing motion is becoming less pronounced.

Hopkins has an upright stance with some waggle from the left side. He counter-rotates with a moderate leg kick and aims to pull the ball with intent. Hopkins has a tendency to step in the bucket at times, though some of that comes from a slightly open stance in his setup. From the right side it's slightly more compact with a line-drive swing plane. From this chair, the chance to hit from the right side currently outpaces the hit tool from the left side, however the latter presents more impact potential.

Hopkins is a dynamic defender with tremendous arm strength. He's one of the better defensive catching prospects in the 2026 class and has offensive tools to trust going forward. Better still, he can run. Hopkins will be 19.7 years old for the draft, certainly a hurdle he'll have to overcome for model-driven teams.

Fisher has impressed scouts along the trail with some of his tournament and showcase performances going back to 2024. A sure-handed shortstop with size and projection, it's easy to dram on Fisher eventually developing into an impact player going forward.

Fisher is still adding strength to his longer, wiry frame. His weight distribution stands out. Broad shoulders, strength in his core and hips with lean strength in the levers. Fisher has room for 15 to 20 more pounds and should run into more impact as he fills out. 

The swing has components and pillars that will be easy to work with Fisher struggles to repeat his swing and triggers at this early stage in his career; not uncommon. The bat speed stands out, as does his ability to lift the baseball and catch it out in front. The book isn't quite written on what Fisher can become with the bat in his hands, but it's easy to dream on a decorated hit tool with impact bat speed.

Fisher has the actions of a potential shortstop at the next level. He still plays a bit taller than scouts generally like to see from a shortstop, but as he works to get into his hips on the dirt everything should come together. The hands, actions and footwork are all very sound. Fisher's arm action allows for carry across the diamond too. The pure arm strength right now is solid average, but it's easy to see more juice behind his throws coming with the added strength.

Adding to what is already a strong case for a projection name, Fisher is an above average runner with a athletic stride. It's not the quickest first step and stolen bases may never be in his bag of tricks, but he'll add value as a whole on the bases.

Tarkenton is a bit crude in terms of the whole package, but may have some of the best upside of anyone in the class. It's big athleticism, exceptional athleticism and unique release traits that could make for good starting pitcher clay as he matures.

Tarkenton is only up to 94 at this stage but will carry the fastball over the barrel and generates whiffs. It's a prototype four-seamer with value elevated. He'll eventually need to show more velocity if he hopes to garner the signing bonus demands to pull him away from North Carolina. 

Tarkenton's slider throws a low-80s slider that features more depth than lateral tilt. It's effective tunneled off the fastball and has been known to get whiffs both inside and outside of the zone. There's also a mid-80s changeup with spin-killing traits. 

Tarkenton isn't the most physical right-handed pitching prospect. There's plenty of projection on the horizon. Considering the looseness of the operation, the arm speed, the present fastball value without overwhelming velocity and his feel for spin, Tarkenton has a chance to blossom into one of the better pitchers to come out of the 2026 high school class, even if that eventually comes by way of becoming a high selection in the 2029 Draft.

Saunders has a super stuffy arm with some of the metrics and traits teams like to see to project a starting pitcher going forward. It's a loose, athletic, whippy motion with some key biomechanical indicators to suggest there's even more velocity on the way. Saunders generates north of six-and-a-half feet of extension, allowing the whole profile to play way up. 

Saunders' fastball has touched 96 mph and he'll hold 91-94 over five or six innings of work. It's a hopping heater with a vertical release creating whiffs at the top of the zone. Saunders works with an up-tempo delivery with the aforementioned big extension causing his stuff to really sneak up on hitters. He's a bully. 

Saunders' slider will flash above average shapes and metrics. It's generally 79-83 with some gradual shape, more depth than lateral tilt. Saunders also throws a low-to-mid 80s changeup that he's shown a comfort landing below the zone.

Watkins is an enormous right-handed hurler with interesting pure stuff and untapped potential left in the tank. He is a natural supinator and creates huge cutting action on all of his pitches. The fastball has been up to 95 with zero arm-side tail. It's a cut-ride heater, though Watkins supinates so aggressively he actually ends up losing almost all of the carry on the pitch. The result is a very cutter-esque heater. It's been largely average whiff rates despite above-average velocity and outlier shape. If Watkins can generates a few more inches of hop through the zone to couple with his natural cut he could end up with one of the more enticing four-seam fastballs in the 2026 class. It's essentially Hurston Waldrep's fastball coming from a slot six inches higher. Watkins should be able to eventually unlock more fastball value thanks to his outlier 80-inch release height and near 7-feet of extension. Everything about his size, delivery and fastball shape are unique. 

As one might imagine, Watkins' slider is his best pitch as it presents considerable steepness and seam mirroring off the cut-fastball. He's been up to 87 mph with the breaker, though he's mostly 83-85 with two planes of tilt and inconsistencies in shape. It's at it's best when firm and bullet-like. 

Watkins' curveball has 'plus' upside featuring huge downer shape and natural 12-6 traits. He's still developing feel and command for that pitch, though when it's been spotted at or below the strikezone it's produced hefty whiff rates. It's thrown in the mid-70s. 

With Watkins' metrics and uniqueness on the mound he's a fairly solid bet to get selected on day two of the Draft as a floor. He's got day one upside if more velocity comes and he finds a way to get the baseball going the other direction with a splitter or circle-changeup. It's definitive starter upside. Unfortunately Watkins suffered an arm injury the fall leading into the 2026 season and hasn't had much chance to showcase his arm talent to scouts this year.

The twin brother of fellow prepster James Clark, Miles missed almost all of the 2025 summer recovering from a hamate bone injury. Fully healthy, he's closed the gap on his brother in the eyes of scouts with plenty of tools of his own.

Clark is a primary outfielder who can handle second and third base in a pinch. It's above average speed and plus arm strength that plays in all four spots; centerfield likely his calling early in his career going forward. Clark's footwork and fundamentals stand out. 

Clark's bat has shown impact and bat speed, however the hit tool has been streaky going back to 2024 and early in 2025 before the injury. He's looked far more physical this spring playing for St. John Bosco and some scouts believe he's blossoming into a more complete player with a bat that will belong somewhere near the meat of a lineup in due time.

Burdette has some of the best raw power in the class. Draft-eligible as a second-year sophomore in 2025, scouts wanted to see what one more year of Burdette at the college ranks could turn into. The power has always been prodigious, but cleaning up the at bats will be critical in redefining his draft position.

Burdette can really compress a baseball. He's posted exit velocities north of 117 mph and owns some fo the best batted-ball data of anyone in the country. That said, swing-and-miss has neutralized his raw strength too often. Whiff rates and chase rates that far exceed national averages have left scouts wondering if the hit tool can survive in professional baseball. There's not a specific wart here either -- in-zone, out-of-zone, sliders, elevated velocity... it can all give Burdette issues depending on the day. That said, when Burdette is a bit more passive at the dish and forces pitchers into the zone, his success rates jump. There's little question this is at least 70-grade raw juice, but proving he can get to it at the next level will be the question he must answer down the stretch.

Burdette isn't a one-trick pony. He's an above average runner with a thundering stride. The speed and athleticism plays in right field where his above average arm strength also fits nicely.

Rounds 11 through 20 are the floor for Burdette, however if he hits more than he has down the stretch, he could hear his name called as early as the fourth or fifth round.

After spending two seasons in Starkville at Mississippi State, Stevens transferred to the University of Oklahoma for the 2026 season after Bulldogs Head Coach Chris Lemonis was let go.

Stevens is a talented outfielder with violent bat speed and pull-side juice from the left-handed batters box. There's some length in his swing and a bit of negative space created in his load, but he's still been a steady performer when he's gotten on the field. Small nagging injuries have interrupted his collegiate career from time to time and its affected his ability to generate much momentum with the hit tool, but to this point he's shown enough to suggest it's at least a 40-grade hitter going forward. Batting average and on-base will likely never be Stevens' calling cards, however he's got the chance to hit 30 homers per seasons if he continues to work and learns to get the ball in the air with more frequency. 

Stevens has manned the first base pillow and the outfield throughout his collegiate career, most believing he's athletic enough to play left field in a full-time capacity as a professional. A below-average runner, he'll need to stay fit and spry to hold that projection. 

If things go awry with the bar, Stevens has some talent on the mound. He's up to 93 with arm-side run, showcasing a darting slider that he commands well to the back-foot of RHH. He's worked to fold in a changeup, though that will be a work in progress and won't need to be rushed at this early stage.

Weaver found himself draft-eligible in 2025, but went unselected after an uninspiring year for Duke followed by a tough showing for Trenton in the MLB Draft League. That said, the arm talent is undeniable.

Weaver screams projection with plenty of strength and stuff to come. The fastball has been up to 98 with juice at the top of the zone with some cary and cut. He's a high-slot righty that creates steep angles for hitters with his secondaries. The slider is firm and short, 85-87. Weaver isn't the best spinner of the baseball, instead relying on hand-feel to shape the his pitches.

Weaver will throw a low-80s changeup that can be effective when commanded, best when tailing away from his cutting fastball tunnel.

It's been a slog trying to throw strikes on a consistent basis for Weaver. He's got a great frame, a big arm and some feel for shaping the baseball. Whoever bets on him in the draft will be dreaming on upside and further projection. He doesn't have much leverage left and will be 22.2 years old as a senior-eligible prospect.

Guyette enjoyed a big breakout year in 2025 for Kansas State out of the bullpen vauling him into the spotlight. His efforts landed him an opportunity to pitch for Team USA CNT in their training camp. He profiles as one of the better shutdown relief arms in the country for the 2026 Draft.

Don't let the ERA fool you, Guyette is a tough look. He's stingy allowing hits and only tends to get in trouble when issuing free passes. 

Guyette lives 91-93 and will grab 96 when he's feeling loose. It's a remarkably low launch height with considerable arm-side tailing action. Guyette gets way down the mound with impressive extension and has some of the components necessary to miss bats with improved command. He'll spray the fastball a bit but tends to live arm-side as his pitches run so hard out of the hand. It's a good fastball with some ceiling if the polish and feel tick up.

Guyette throws a sweeping slider and a changeup, both of which perform at extremely high levels. He's more comfortable landing the sweeper for strikes. It's 81-83 and will rush up to 89 with depth and some sharpness. To date, Guyette has generated very healthy chase and whiff rates with that weapon. The changeup performs better than the slider when it's offered at, but finding the zone or the shadows of the black can be streaky. In time, given Guyette's unique fastball shape, the changeup probably has the higher ceiling. 

If the walks come down and velocity ticks up, Guyette could quickly become the most dominant reliever in the 2026 class. It's a full arsenal with uniqueness, athleticism and the fiery disposition necessary to get big outs.

It's not often you see a player recruited to play in Oxford from the state of Arizona, but Long is so talented, the SEC came calling. A 6-foot-3-inch righty who continues to grow and add muscle, Long has seen his stuff steadily tick forward over the last twelve months, culminating in newfangled velocity he's using to punch hitters out.

Long is up to an effortless 95 mph and there's more on the horizon. He's got a loose arm, strong tempo and big athleticism in his stride down the bump. His fastball sneaks up on hitters and carries over the barrels of the opposition thanks to above-average ride. His low-80s slider has made a jump this year with more vertical plane and conviction out of the hand. It plays well off the shape of his fastball and could eventually become an above-average weapon if he continues to firm it up. Scouts believe his changeup could become his best pitch in due time. His willingness to throw it and execute the pitch to both left-handers and right-handers stands out. He'll throw it early and often to steal strikes and to put away hitters as well. 

Considering the three-pitch mix, the size, the athleticism and pitch metrics here, Long has a chance to develop into a weekend starter in the SEC if he isn't poached by a Major League club in July first.

Miles Young is a physical monster and a tremendous athletic tester who projects to continue to add impact and offensive tools as he matures into his already stacked frame. It's mammoth bat speed and huge torque through the zone. Some of the most standout raw power in the class. 

Young is also a distinguished defender at shortstop with strong actions around the bag and lauded situational awareness. Young is an above average runner who can shift into another gear underway. The profile may ultimately shift to third base or into the outfield as he continues to add strength, but there's a lot of explosive elements to the player. He will be 18.9 years old on draft day.

Geertsma is a bat-first infield prospect with size and physicality. He's shown flashes of true impact at the plate with a powerful right-handed swing. While there's still some polish on the profile that will be required, it's easy to see why scouts believe in the future upside.

Geertsma is currently a power-over-hit bat who has shown swing and miss in his profile. He's an aggressive hitter who has shown a willingness to expand the zone, compounding the whiff streakiness. Elevated velocity is the biggest culprit in Geertsma's woes. It's an area of his game that can be cleaned up. The strength and bat speed on the player stand out. Geertsma is capable of hitting the ball out of the yard to the pull-side. 

The future defensive home likely won't be shortstop, his current primary position at Governor Livingston. Geertsma has rotated between third base and first base in game settings. Geertsma's hands are solid and he's shown a calmness at the hot corner. He's got a chance to stick at the positon if he doesn't get too much more physical. He's a bit heavy-footed by nature, so lateral mobility is unlikely to ever be a strength. Anything hit right at him is gobbled up and converted with routine ease. 

Geertsma's most likely outcome in July is ending up at the University of Virginia where he will have the chance to transform himself into a power-hitting ACC staple. He will be 18.8 in July.

Martinez really began growing into his athletic frame over the last 12 months and has seen his tools and production take a major leap forward. A two-way standout with opportunities on both sides of the ball going forward, scouts seem to be leaning more toward bullishness on the mound over his offensive prowess. 

As a pitcher he's been up to 91 mph with a fastball featuring well-above average carry through the zone. It's a super-fast arm and an explosive delivery as a whole. Martinez could soon flirt with numbers in the mid-90s. There's also a budding breaking ball with big downer tilt that he commands well to his glove-side. It's largely average for the time being. 

Martinez is flashy all over the field as an above average runner with plus raw power. He's even faster underway and falls into the category of one of those guys who has another gear rounding the bases. Martinez may ultimately come off the shortstop position and end up in the outfield where his fringier arm strength may more appropriately fit, but this is a high caliber performer with major helium. Martinez will turn 19 one month after the draft.

The fastball will grab 100 and settles in 96-98 over multiple innings. The heater will show moderate carry and tailing action with the ability to miss bats when elevated. 

He'll flash a low-to-mid 80s slider with tunnel forcing uncomfortable late swings from the opposition. There's also a changeup that has promise, but is largely inconsistent at this early stage. Stephens currently has below average control and command of the baseball and has been streaky with his walks this spring. He does possess punch out stuff but he'll need to work on throwing better strikes if he's to capitalize on arm talent. 

Stephens has a longer arm action with moderate extension. It's a super fast arm with a high leverage ceiling if he can extract a bit more value from the fastball in short showings.

Royer is a long, lanky, projectable right-hander with a really fast arm. Considering his size, Royer controls his body well and showcases impressive core strength and torque working down the mound through an aggressive finish. It's reasonably controlled aggression with some effort at release and some whack, but nothing looks terribly difficult or over-done. Roger generates elite extension and has an arsenal that benefits from delivering the ball so close to the mound. 

Royer's fastball has been up to 96 with carry through the zone and some natural cut, though he'll vary the shape of the pitch depending on the heater. He'll generally rest 91-93 over multi-inning appearances. It's a very fast arm that could have him tickling triple-digits in due time. 

Royer features a tilted slider with depth in the upper-70s, occasionally tickling the low-80s bucket. His delivery and tempo provide some natural deception, the fastball being especially difficult for hitters to pick up. Scouts would like to see the effort continue to tick down as he adds weight and strength approaching the draft, but there are few pitchers in the class that can match the projection, athleticism and present stuff that Royer possesses. 

Royer began his career at Georgia Tech but struggled to carve out a significant role as a freshman. That led to his transfer to Kennesaw State for 2026 where he finds himself draft-eligible as a second-year sophomore. There's certainly some reliever risk here, but the upside could be significant. A 20th round selection by the Yankees in 2024, he elected to go to school.

Pettitte, the son of MLB-great Andy Pettitte, brings the same level of moxy and production that has dad once did. It's a bulldog frame with a bulldog reputation on the bump. Pettitte is going to throw strikes and dare you to beat him.

The fastball isn't overwhelming, but it's been ultra-effective. Pettitte launches from an extremely high slot and can reach back for 94 at his best. He moves well with above-average extension down the mound. He throws his heater for strikes at a high rate too. It's a launch profile that has resulted in impressive chase rates from hitters and enough swing and miss to potentially project his fastball an above-average weapon at the next level if the velocity trends upwards. 

Pettitte's slider is also a good offering. It's 83-86 with short tilt, just enough to get hitters to swing over the top of it. Geared up for buckets of strikes, hitters are consistently in swing mode and tend to expand the zone on both the slider and fastball. Pettitte rounds out his arsenal with a lesser-thrown changeup, firm with middling shape. 

Unfortunately, Pettitte blew out his elbow while pitching on the Cape in 2025. He was exceptional before the injury, but with only 11.1 innings between 2025 and 2026, it's a tough baseball card to sell to scouts and front offices. He isn't expected to pitch in 2026, but could get healthy enough to showcase his talent at the Combine prior to the Draft.

Shull is a bat-first, power-over-hit outfielder who can play a little second and third base in a pinch. He provides plenty of bat speed from the right side with a more hitterish attack angle from the left side of the plate. It's a quiet operation with balance and extension through the zone with juice to all fields. The hit tool continues to advance as he's aged, leading some to believe he's one of the more enticing offensive prospects in the class. 

Shull is a fringe average runner with an upright running style, likely destined for left field or third base as a professional. He's continued to add muscle over the last twelve months and is now one of the more physical looks in the class. He does have an above average arm. He will be a draft-eligible sophomore at 21 years old.

Duncan is a former top prospect from his high school days. He's bounced around a bit, but has found him home at Wright State and seems to be getting some footing underneath his game. A 19th round selection by the Astros in the 2023 Draft, Duncan has made stops at Florida State and Tallahassee State College before finally arriving in Dayton, Ohio for the 2026 season. 

The speed stands out in a big way here. It's elite, 80 run-times with true centerfield skills. Duncan is hitting the ball a bit harder this spring and now looks like a guy who could live gap-to-gap with just a bit more strength. He'll likely never be more than a 40-grade raw power guy, but when combining his run tool and potential bat-to-ball skills, there's a path toward a Role 40 fourth outfielder at the next level.

A former hidden gem coming out of the state of Utah, Edwards arrived to Corvallis a two-way player, but has since dedicated his time to the mound. He's a potential back-end of the bullpen reliever with big stuff.

Edwards will work 94-96 and has been as rich as 98 with tremendous cut and slight vertical tilt. It's as hard and nasty a cutter as you'll find in the country. Edwards has been working to maintain the cutting action he gets, however generating a bit more carry through the zone could take his heater to plus.

Edwards' slider is usually more of a sweeper. It's got frisbee shape and lacks vertical depth at times, instead relying on lateral break to get whiffs -- and he's gotten plenty of them. It's 82-85 and will grab 87 mph. The spin on his breaking ball has improved from 2025, and he's throwing it for strikes aplenty. 

Edwards has chucked a handful of changeup into the zone over his Beaver career, but it's fringy command. For what it's worth, he's rarely put in spots where he needs to throw the changeup when his cutter can neutralize a left-handed bat at just as efficient a clip. 

Credit to Edwards, he takes on any role he's assigned and tackles it head-on. His ego doesn't preclude him from being successful in the bullpen, and that should take him far at the next level.

Burnham is technically a two-way player with some talent at the plate and a left-handed swing that can get into some power, however most scouts prefer the total package on the mound where a big fastball and makings of a curveball raise eyebrows. 

Burnham has been up to 95 mph but will more commonly settle in as a guy chucking 90-92 mph darts. It's got the makings of a plus pitch featuring well-above average carry through the zone -- a bat-misser in every sense. Burnham has a longer arm stroke with some serious intent in his delivery. He can open early at times and lose his fastball high and away, but when spotted at the top of the zone it's an out-pitch.

The breaking ball has traits and conviction in the low 80s. There's solid depth on that pitch, however executing it with consistency is a work in progress. 

Burnham has a relief look in his operation and isn't yet flashing a reliable third pitch.

Phelps is a bat-first profile with juice to all-fields featuring speed and instincts on the base paths to be a very real weapon in every offensive facet of the game. He's an above-average runner.  Phelps will need to carve out a defensive home in professional baseball as he hasn't been able to find firm footing anywhere on the diamond at Georgia. A bit surprising for a player with his foot speed. If teams decide he's a designated hitter at the next level his draft stock will surely slump. While it may be a day one bat, being unable to provide value in the field is important. 

He's been one of the best hitters in the country going back to his freshman year where he boasted impressive contact rates, fantastic barrel awareness, an innate feel for launch the ball with the tremendous ability to avoid strikeouts. Phelps is close to a complete hitter in terms of how he's presented himself to this point. Showing value in the field as the draft approaches will be critical. Phelps was draft-eligible as a sophomore in 2025 but pulled his name in an effort to continue developing his tools.

Burns was a 17th round pick by the Royals in the 2024 Draft out of Prosper High School. Burns actually took a gap year after graduating high school in 2023 and became draft-eligible in 2024 because of it. He enrolled in Starkville in the Fall of 2024 and finds himself draft-eligible after just two years on campus. 

It's size, it's left-handed, it's release traits, decent strikes and and solid extension. Burns checks boxes. 

The breaking ball is his best weapon and it's got a shot to be plus at the next level. Burns has feel for commanding the sweeper and usually throws it in the 77-79 bucket, however he's been up to 81 in the past. It's two planes and considerable depth. Burns has produced enormous whiff and chase rates with the breaking ball in his two years on campus and scouts believe it to be one of the more effective pitches in the SEC. 

Burns' fastball has been up to 95 however he's primarily 91-93 with sink and fading action. He's got feel for landing the sinker for a strike low and to the arm-side, away from right-handed hitters and under the hands of left-handed hitters. It's an average fastball that's produced average results. 

Most of Burns' career has been from out of the bullpen in large part due to his fringy control for the zone and lack of a third pitch.

Lopez enjoyed a nice freshman campaign at Long Beach State where he thumped eight homers and stole 13 bags in 54 games. He transferred to Southern California prior to the 2025 season where he's continued to show scouts some things. Despite going undrafted last year, there's still plenty of reason to be bullish on Lopez as he enters his age-21 junior year. 

While there's still considerable swing and miss in Lopez's profile and a general lack of rotation, but the physicality and projection remaining in his frame can be difficult to come by, especially in a player who projects to stay on the middle of the diamond. Lopez swings with his arms right now, especially when his hands get outside of his body. Developing more twitch and strength should unlock another gear at the plate. Lopez can handle shortstop at an above average level with bounce in his step and lightweight actions moving laterally. He showcases a slow heartbeat and grace around the bag. It's average arm strength, but his transitions and actions more than allow Lopez to make most plays. His draft stock will be dictated by the strides he makes with the bat in his third collegiate campaign.

Hart will be one of the more difficult looks any hitter in the 2026 class will see leading up to the draft. It's a 6-foot-6-inch frame coming down the mound with a cross-body delivery and tons of angle. Hart features a long arm action with enormous separation of his hands after break into something of a stab into his scap load. It's a very unique delivery, though he does a nice job of getting himself into an athletic position when the foot goes down. It's a low three-quarter delivery with some deception baked in. Hart has been up to 94 mph with sink and tail. 

He's shown promising command to all four quadrants with the fastball and plays a nasty upper-70s sweeper through the zone to get whiffs. As the changeup comes along, there's the makings of a dynamic arm here. 

Hart will be 19 years old for the Draft and will be draft-elibile in 2028 if he goes unselected.

Marin is one of of the more accomplished defenders in the class with fluidity and rhythm to his game on the dirt. He has smooth actions both with his feet and hands, as well as an athletic throwing arm. He's as good a bet as you'll find to stick at the "6" in this class so long as he doesn't outgrow the position. Marin is an average runner but his instincts do allow his tools to play up a bit on both sides of the ball. 

For now, he's a line-to-line hitter who has shown some grown over the spring in terms of impact punch at the plate. The swing and frame projects to add a bit more with maturity. Marin has a swing that's quick to the ball and his approach at the plate appears to have improved as well. He's a player to watch as the Draft approaches, especially playing in the SEC.

Krewson is an impressive athlete, especially at the plate where he extends well and gets solid stretch out of his 6-foot-2-inch frame. The accompanying barrel speed is big with serious whip through the zone; above average raw power with exceptional feel for backspinning the baseball and creating launch. It's a borderline elite approach with miniscule chase rates. 

Krewson is an average runner, best suited for a corner outfield role, though his above average arm strength projects in either corner. Krewson cut down his swing and miss rates a good bit this past spring. He spent his freshman season with Duke before transferring to Orlando for the 2025 campaign and Rutgers in 2026.

Lavey enjoyed a bit of a breakout on the Cape during 2025 after a few solid seasons for GW. He's always been a strong hitter, however physical maturation and brighter lights may have elevated his game with July in focus.

Lavey has been a consistent producer for two seasons on campus hitting over .300 each of the first two seasons. Lavey hasn't tapped into over-the-fence power on campus, but the raw juice is in there, as is evidenced by his 109 mph exit velocity with a wood bat on the Cape. Lavey has a tendency to hit the ball the other way and isn't pulling the ball with authority yet in his career. That has resulted in middling batted-ball data with a composite bat in his hand. It's been solid bat-to-ball skills as well as a reasonably polished approach at the plate. Lavey does have swing and miss in his game, particularly when he falls behind in counts and is exposed to more spin. The major takeaway with his bat is he'll need ot show more impact on a consistent basis as the Draft approaches. 

A primary catcher, Lavey has been deployed in left field at times where he held his own defensively. He's an average defensive catcher and has gotten more physical in the last calendar year, leading some to ask the question whether first base and left field is his eventual home. Lavey is also a 40-grade runner.

Still just 20 years old for the Draft, Lavey will have his proponents in the industry who believe he is still learning (and capable) of developing better feel for pull-side launch. He'll need to find it, as the defensive profile is more on the tweener side.

Arvidson pulled his name from the 2025 Draft during the event to chase a bigger outcome in the 2026 Draft. He got hot toward the end of his junior year and looks to be one of the more interesting relief prospects in the 2026 class. 

The name of the game with Arvidson is deception. He hides the ball particularly well. It's an ultra-high, over-the-top delivery with a supination release generating moderate carry and occasional cutting action. It's a pitch hitters haven't had much luck producing damage on this season. Arvidson will live 92-94 and has been up to 95. Most scouts believe there's a few more ticks coming. He generates a ton of ground balls and has been able to get some whiffs on his fastball too. 

Arvidson's bullet slider generated huge whiff and chase rates thanks to its substantial depth complimented by that aforementioned launch height. Hitters swing over that pitch and chase it into the dirt more than most breaking balls in the class. Arvidson doesn't generate much extension down the mound for a guy his size, so he'll have to lean on that slider more and more as he moves up the ladder. That said, a near-70 percent strike rate in 2025 suggests he's got more than enough feel for the pitch to do just that. 

A big, banger curveball is cast to the plate in the mid-70s, tunneling the fastball out of the hand. It does break off the fastball plane earlier than most traditional high-slot tunnels, but it's been an effective strike-stealer and it works in the dirt. His upper-70s changeup is a really brutal look for right-handed hitters, but seldom thrown.

He's got high-leverage upside out of the bullpen at the next level if the velocity continues to trend upward.

It's been an adventurous, winding road for Ralamb who now finds himself at his fourth school in four years. That said, he seems to have turned a corner in some ways at Bellarmine. It's certainly a reliever profile, but perhaps a good one.

Ralamb, plain and simply, has one of the best breaking balls in college baseball. It's a low-80s breaker with plus horizontal break, complimented by huge vertical shape, too. Ralamb gets to these shapes with spin rates that will at times exceed 3000 rpm. It's every bit that of a plus breaking ball, and moldable at the next level.

His sinker is his primary fastball. It's 91-93 and will tickle 95 with exceptional arm-side break. That said, he struggles to land it for strikes.

Ralamb is a two-pitch guy right now and will need to land his heater in the zone more often to capitalize on his traits. He's a late day-three pick or undrafted free agent. He'll be 22 years old for the Draft.

King originally committed to play college baseball at South Carolina, but a late switch took his talents to Volunteer State where he elected to refine his craft before re-entering the world of Division 1 baseball. King would pitch just 10.2 innings for Volunteer State as a freshman, but it was enough to garner the interest of coaches at MTSU.

King played some ball for Trenton in the MLB Draft League before laying down roots in Murfreesboro. He struggled to throw strikes and his stuff didn't miss bats like it had at Volunteer State. That said, everything is trending in the right direction once again.

King is a very good mover for his size. He generates solid extension and has a loose, whippy delivery down the mound. 

The bread and butter here is a low-80s sweeper with impressive two-plane tilt and command. King has struggled to get to that pitch, but it's a swing-and-miss weapon when he's looking for a strikeout. 

The fastball is a high-launch heater that's commonly 91-93 and will get up to 95 with some carry and tail. He's struggled to get ahead of hitters with that pitch, and will need to command it with more authority should he hope to continue starting at the next level.

King throws a bigger curveball and has shown flashes of a solid changeup.

The size, length and athlete here are all noteworthy. King has things organizations can dream on. If the velocity and control/command take a jump as July approaches, he could very well hear his name called in the top ten rounds. King is just 20 years old for the draft as an eligible second-year sophomore.

A two-way guy whose bat has begun to ascend in the last few months, scouts are split on where Hardcastle's best path to a pro role might be. He's shown a developing hit tool and the potential for plus raw power projection, however the tools on the mound might be too good to pass up. 

A big, broad, barrel-chested righty with a ton of strength in his frame, Hardcastle is one of the purest competitors in the 2026 class. There's an edge about how he pitches, a chip on his shoulder. He looks to punch hitters out in a very dismissive, albeit respectful competitor type of way. The fastball has been up to 94 with some carry and arm-side run, usually on the top rail. Hardcastle likes to play with different vertical planes and it starts with the heat.
