An upper-70s curveball shows hammer traits and will flash plus upside. Feel for commanding the breaker is still coming, though he's generally in and around the zone. Both the fastball and curve show above-average spin rates. There's also a low-80s changeup that seems a bit more naiscent in development, but has promise. 

Hardcastle is an impressive performer who will vary his delivery. He can get a bit erratic at times when riled up causing him to broadcast the breaking ball a bit, but to this point it's hardly affected the outcomes the at-bat. 

When right, Hardcastle pounds the strikezone with big stuff, projectable stuff, and a bully mentality. His physical build and starter's frame should help him stay in the role at the next level. If the stuff takes a jump before the draft, his name could rise. Hardcastle will turn 19 one more before the draft.

Following a freshman year at Pearl City CC, Robertson transferred to Ole Miss for the 2025 season but didn't pitch as a sophomore. Instead, he redshirt his first year in Oxford in an effort to gain weight. That paid dividends as the stuff ticked way up. 

Robertson has a live arm. He touched 97 this summer in the Northwoods Leauge and pitched to a 2.65 ERA across 54.1 innings. That’s a pretty significant feat considering how the balls flies in the NWL. Robertson punched 65 tickets in his 54.1 innings this summer, walking just 27. A low-to-mid 80s slider supplements his big heater.

Robertson is capable of pitching in multiple roles, and has shown as much for the Rebels this season. He lacks a reliable third pitch at this stage, but it's big stuff that is, at a minimum, leveragable in relief.

While Tatum is raw in many part of his game, the physical tools standout in a big way. He's a high follow for scouts not only for 2026, but certainly beyond as he continues to fill out his frame and learns to appropriately use his body.

The offensive tools shine. Tatum is a long left-handed hitter with strength in his hands. He's got broad shoulders, squared, with a higher-set waist and strength in his lower-half. He's a rhythmic hitter with some waggle and looseness in his wrists moving into his load. Madden creates space in the box and turns hard on the baseball showing above-average bat speed and plus power projection ot the pull-side. There's some steepness in Tatum's swing built for loft. While the hit tool has been streaky at times, the power and patience at the plate seems to always been present.

Tatum has some rawness at third base. He fields the ball deep and has a tendency to stab at ground balls. He's a good enough athlete to continue getting reps at the hot corner until he proves he can't play the position among his peers. Below average foot speed will be tested on the infield.

Tatum is also a big pitching prospect with a fastball that has been up to 94 with carry. He moves well and generates solid extension. He'll flip over a bigger mid-70s breaking ball to chase whiffs.

A big riser throughout the spring of his junior year. Charboneau has grown into louder tools as he's filled out his 6-foot-4-inch frame. 

Charboneau's offensive tool package is exciting. He employs a big leg kick and lands closed creating some natural counter-rotation in his swing. He turns hard through the zone and flashes big bat speed with feel for catching the ball out in front and pulling the ball with authority. It's a swing geared to produce loud top-spinning screamers to left field, however his plane does back-spin the baseball to the opposite field, especially when he can get his arms extended on a pitch out over the outside corner. Charboneau creates a ton of torque and stretch in his swing, lagging the barrel and violently letting it catch up to his hips through the zone. It is an unconventional swing with some moving parts in the load, but if Charboneau can continue to stay synced up throughout his amateur career, he's going to hit for serious power. Strikeouts may always be a part of his game, but you'll take that with the impact potential in the stick. It's plus bat speed and the potential for 25+ homers at the next level if the hit tool gets to a spot where his raw power can fly.

Charboneau is an above-average runner and a long strider who has a chance to grow into a bit more speed as he gains baseball strength through development. He's a corner outfield defender who can spell your centerfielder in a pinch. It's plus arm strength and average routes in the field with some natural feel for the position. He projects into solid-average glove in right field at the next level.

Ickes, a 19th round selection by the Texas Rangers in the 2023 MLB Draft, is a hitterish middle infielder with a smooth stroke and an all-fields approach. He's a gap hitter who makes the most out of his hit tool with average speed on the bases. Ickes lacks top-end bat speed, but is an efficient hitter who gets to his pull-side and understands how to backspin a baseball. There's 14-18 homer upside in the stick. His polish and desire to be great and lead really stand out. Ickes works long counts, draws his walks and gets the job done when he's called upon. 

Ickes is a strong defender on the dirt. He's capable of playing the shortstop position at an above average level and certainly has the floor of a defensive standout at second base. He's shown good lateral range with the ability to throw on the run from multiple angles. While the arm strength is mostly just average, his adjustability and athleticism allows that tool to play up. 

Ickes is a well-rounded player who can do a little bit of everything. He's proven himself valuable up the middle of the diamond and should gorw into enough impact to capture a Role 45 label at the next level.

McMannis is something of a metric freak on the mound. It's rare you find a player with McMannis' size and length capable of launching out of such a low slot. His 61-inch release height is ten inches lower than the average 6-foot-5-inch pitcher in Major League Baseball. He creates unorthodox angles that hitters are rarely ever exposed to. McMannis is also an elite mover with borderline elite extension down the bump. It's a pretty nasty look for hitter to adjust to. 

McMannis has been up to 96 in bullpens and 95 in games. It's more routinely 91-93. He naturally sinks the ball and creates some tailing action late. McMannis doesn't spin the baseball particularly well, so elevating the baseball and creating lift can be difficult. He's a big-time strike-thrower with the fastball and likes to challenge hitters. That said, he needs more weapons as hitters can sit on the heater right now. 

McMannis throws a fringy bullet slider that's mostly 81-83 featuring average spin. It hasn't been terribly effective at this point, but his ability to repeat his slot and create depth with the breaking ball suggests the pitch might have an above average future. 

He also throws a changeup that he tends to cut just a tick, but he kills spin well and generates enough velocity separation to get some chase outside of the zone. To date, his changeup has not been a bat-missing weapon. 

McMannis began his collegiate career at Maryland and transferred to Oklahoma for the 2026 season. His lack of secondary value has limited his ability to miss bats and it has also elevated his walks as hitters can lay off of everything but the heater. There are unteachable components to his game that a player development system would love to sink its teeth into. It's starter clay, but an unfinished product.
Up to 100 with cutter traits that could develop the pitch into a true plus weapon.

Hinojosa is yet to see his stuff explode like many scouts expect it will, but the ease and fluidity of his game on the mound really stands out. His fastball is touching 96 with huge carry through the zone. He'll continue to throw harder and harder thanks to rather elite scap load/looseness in his shoulder. 

Hinojosa throws a curveball that has some tunneling attributes coming out of his fastball slot. It's projects an above average weapon at the next level. Hinojosa is already pretty physical is stature and stands at just 6 feet tall. He's got a shot to start if a third pitch comes along.

Ahu is the next in a long line of talented bats to come out of the Hawaiian islands of late. At 6-foot-4, 200 pounds, Ahu has some similar physical traits that Aiva Arquette had in high school. It's long, lean, projectable and athletic in every part of his game.

Ahu's bat will carry his profile. He possesses above average raw power in a swing that stays remarkably compact through the zone. He has innate feel for creating backspin on the baseball and has shown present pull-side power at a young age. He's an average runner, though that could creep up a half-grade as he adds proper weight through physical maturation. 

Ahu is a shortstop now, though he may end up at third base in time. His actions fit that of an amatuer shortstop where average arm strength, long strides and lateral mobility are sound. He'll simply likely be pushed to his left by a more premium athlete as a professional. Ahu has a chance to be a 45-grade glove at shortstop or a solid-average defender at third base. He will be 19 years old for the Draft and is expected to be a difficult sign away from Stanford.

Swank has a physical frame and throws plenty of strikes, leading with the fastball and parlaying a curveball and changeup off the heat.

Swank is up to 95 with a fastball that presents multiple shapes. At his best, Swank is holding carry on the heater and slightly cutting the baseball. He's more commonly 90-92. It's a longer arm swing that can be tough for hitters to pick up. 

Swank's curveball looks like the fastball out of the hand. His slingshot delivery makes for excellent tunnel on his secondaries. The breaker is a low-80s hammer curve that he's shown willing to throw to lefties and righties alike. There's also a mid-80s changeup, however he doesn't use it much. 

Swank has the frame and strike-throwing ability of a starting pitcher, but has the operation of reliever. Time will tell what role he settles into. Should be eventually become a starter, he'll need more development with the changeup.

An elastic right-handed pitcher with exceptional athleticism and looseness in his 6-foot-1-inch frame, Sabater moves very well on the bump and has the look of an arm that could throw into the mid-90s at full maturation.

The fastball has been up to 95 with slightly above average carry through the zone. It's easy out of the hand, effortless through delivery with strikes filling up the zone. The athleticism and ease of which he throws the heater stands out. 

Sabater's breaking ball is a low-80s bullet spinner that will occasionally flash more lateral tilt to the glove-side. He sells the pitch with good arm speed and conviction, however he'll drop his arm slot a tick to achieve his shapes. Sabater's breaking ball possesses solid depth and can be late to break at times. 

It's two quality pitches, effortless mechanics, a loose arm and athleticism to build a final product on. Sabater has a good ceiling and could throw big numbers with more weight and strength. He will turn 19 right around the time of the Draft.

Jenkins transferred to Florida for the 2025 season after one year at Santa Fe CC. He's got a terrific frame with room to grow, already touching heavy velocity numbers and missing bats in buckets both inside and outside of the zone.

Jenkins has had a hard time generating momentum in Gainesville. An injury took him off the mound for seven weeks as a sophomore in 2025 just as he had begun to get loose. Once back, walks plagued his ability to work any sort of lather out of the bullpen. Jenkins' fastball has been up to 97 and he'll hold 93-94 with huge carry through the zone. He's a terrific mover too with a long-stride down the mound. Jenkins produced a 36 percent whiff rate on the heater alone as a sophomore. It's an uncomfortably high release point for hitters to track with some natural deception in his delivery. The deception comes from an arm action that can be late at times. While it does help confuse the hitter, it also leads to spraying the baseball at times.

Jenkins' secondaries have a chance to be very good. His low-80s sweeper features strong lateral action and solid depth too -- another pitch that registered a whiff rate north fo 35 percent as a sophomore. But again, with spotty strikes. The changeup may be his most formidable weapon, a low-80s cambio featuring significant arm-side fading action. It lives in the fastball tunnel late and darts arm-side with sharpness. Jenkins is a bit more apt to throw that pitch for strikes. The changeup has generated enormous whiff rates both inside and outside of the zone. If it's competitive, it can be devastating.

Jenkins will have to carve out a defined role as July approaches but at this stage it's hard not to slap a relief role on the tall righty. The stuff is huge.

Stieg was the Seattle Mariners 18th round selection in the 2025 Draft, but elected to return to Virginia Tech instead. He did not pitch in 2025 recovering from TJ. 

Stieg’s sinker is a hell-seeking missile. His launch height is slightly lower than average, and his approach angle is also on the flatter end of the spectrum. What separates Stieg is the elite amount of tailing action he generates with the sinker. There were times he induced more than 23 inches of lateral action on his heater. He averaged north of 20 inches squarely placing him in a small bucket of pitchers both in the amateur and professional ranks. He's been up to 97 and routinely sits 92-95.

Stieg’s sinker needs to get more productive going forward. As it stands, his heater does not project to miss bats at-or-below the belt. Stieg does keep hitters off the barrel by flashing a solid-average sweeping slider and an above average changeup with diving action. 

Stieg has the look of a high-octane reliever at the next level. It’s difficult to get through a lineup twice if you can’t miss bats with your fastball inside the strike zone. His three-pitch arsenal and strike-throwing ability gives him a shot, but he’ll likely need to be a guy who throws all three pitches with equal usage should he hope to find success the second time through the lineup. Stieg is a fast-mover with a quick arm who could conceivably throw harder in shorter outings.

From this chair, Stieg belongs in the fifth to eighth round range in July. He could sneak into the late-third or the fourth round if a team buys into his chances to start as a pro. They’ll need to specifically have a plan for generating more value from the outlier shape on his sinker.

Big, broad, barrel-chested righty with thickness in his lower half and mature build. Effort through delivery with spine tilt. It's a definitive closer profile. Incredibly high launch height allows Marmie's sinker to create significant steepness. Marmie has been up to 97 and can sit 93-94, however his fastball has been hit around a bit. 

His cutter has the most upside. It produced a .140 average and a .220 wOBA in 2025. It generated an arsenal-high 56 percent ground ball rate and an impressive 27 percent in-zone whiff rate. Marmie’s cutter is a good one – up to 92 with six inches of vertical separation off the four-seamer. Better still, it’s got north of a foot of lateral differentiation.  

He's offered a reluctant changeup on occasion against LHH.

Marmie had Tommy John surgery in the fall of 2025 and won't pitch until 2027.

Following two dynamic seasons at Seton Hall where he smashed 17 homers, 16 of which came as a sophomore in 2025, Milewski hit the transfer portal for the 2026 season and headed to Starkville. A big, physical, power-hitting backstop, Milewski has a chance to provide premium punch from behind the plate if his defensive chops hold court over time. 

There's little question what kind of offensive player Milewski can be. It's plus raw power that's translating in a big way to game setting already. Milewski has been north 113 mph from an exit velocity perspective. His 90th percentile exit velocity of 108.6 as a sophomore ranked among the best in the country. Milewski has some growth ahead in terms of consistently getting his swing into a launch position, but that should come over time.

The hit tool is a bit less refined than the power. Milewski is an aggresive swinger who is willing to epxand the zone. He's particularly susceptible to breaking balls -- strikeouts mounting in streaky ways at times because of it. Milewski can also be susceptible to premium velocity above the hands. It's a grooved swing in some ways. This is a hitter who will punish mistakes better than most, but developing adjustability in the box will ultimately dictate how high his role can climb at the next level. In Milewski's defense, it is a short, compact, explosive swing. He has the luxury of reacting late to the opposing pitcher. That said, he'll need to continue refining his pitch selection skills going forward. 

Milewski has a strong arm behind the plate and at his best can keep the pop times at or around 2.00 seconds. The big, physical frame can take some time to jump out of the crouch leading some to question if the catch-and-throw will survive the rigors and demands of professional baseball. Milewski's caught-stealing rates in college baseball have been below average. To his credit, pitch framing is slightly above average -- an achievement in and of itself considering the requirements to frame pitches below the zone for a tall catcher.

Milewski has some traits to like. It's big power, a reasonably strong arm and some natural feel to frame. He'll have to prove the hit tool is moving in the right direction as July approaches, especially with the questions surrounding his permanent defensive home.

Martinez gives off hitterish vibes at the plate with loose, rhythmic hands, an aggressive swing and a swing plane geared to pepper the left and right field gaps. He's shown feel for finding the barrel and lets the ball travel. Martinez has strength at the point of contact with a two-handed finish. Martinez has muscle in his offensive profile and could eventually grow into above-average raw power with the bat.

Behind the plate, it's a slow pulse with loose, easy actions. Martinez has solid average arm strength and gets to it without selling out his throwing motion. A former shortstop, the athlete stands out in a big way behind the dish. Martinez has a chance to catch going forward.

Guth was draft-eligible in 2025 but surprisingly went unselected. It was a huge development for the Vanderbilt program as they returned their most dominant bullpen piece to Nashville for 2026. Guth has been a stopper for the program the last three seasons. 

Guth leads with the slider. It's a death ball with enormous depth, 82-84 with above-average spin traits. Guth's breaker generated a whiff rate north of 50 percent in 2025 and was one of the most effective breaking balls in college baseball, despite a reasonably small sample. 

The fastball lives off the idea the slider could be on the way. Guth is up to 95 but more routinely sits 91-93 with moderate carry, best when he's inducing cutter action to mirror the slider. Guth spins the fastball exceptionally well and that's helped him produced elite chase rates and fastballs just above the zone. 

Guth also turned over a handful of mid-80s changeups this season and showed the ability to kill spin and create both velocity and depth separation off his primary two pitches. It's hard to know how consistent Guth is capable of executing that pitch with such a small sample, but the shapes are intriguing. 

A shorter strider, Guth has a relief look going forward. It's leverageable with swing-and-miss stuff; a potential seventh or eighth stopper at the next level. The ceiling is perhaps Griffin Canning or Jason Adam.

Kozera has good size for a right-handed pitcher with physicality and strength in his lower half and shoulders. He's a bulldog on the mound. The fastball is his bread and butter. It's a heavy-usage four-seamer with some carry and arm-side tailing action, up to 96. Kozera can get in trouble when it melts into a dead-zone shape, but for the most part he's able to keep lift on the ball late in the zone. It's a fastball that's produced solid whiff and chase rates as he seems to hide the baseball fairly well. Kozera's slider has promise, though it's buckshot for the time-being limited it's consistency and effectiveness. It's thrown firm and could eventually evolve into an above-average breaking ball with time and repetition. 

Kozera lacks a consistent third pitch, though he's worked to develop a changeup that has shown promise and some feel. He features below average extension down the mound. There's upside here and potential to start going forward if he can develop consistency in the secondaries. 

Kozera missed much of his first two years in college due ot a neck injury and lingering ailments in 2025. He transferred to North Florida for the 2026 season chasing a new start.

Very few players in the 2026 class project to hit for as much average as Coleman. He features an advanced barrel with manipulative hands that can get to any quadrant. His outcomes are consistently rocket line drives into the gaps. The bat speed projects a bit too as Coleman could eventually tap into average raw power. 

On the dirt it's smooth with rhythm and a slow heartbeat. The hands are soft and the arm strength projects average going forward. He's got a shot to play shortstop in college with his actions and could play any one of the three infield positions as a pro. Coleman is a solid average runner and an athletic mover with a ton of fans in the scouting community. Coleman will be 19.5 years old in the 2026 class and will be draft-eligible again in 2028 if he ends up at LSU.

Originally an Arizona State commit, Davies decommited from the Sun Devils and proceeded to keep his talent local at Salt Lake CC. Formerly a decorated two-way prospect, his capabilities on the mound have blossomed in a way he's put down the bat and focused on the bump.

Davies has big stuff. He's been up to 97 with a shorter arm action and natural deception, blowing hitters up at the top of the zone. His fastball shapes will vary, but at his best he's carrying the baseball through the zone and tailing that pitch away from left-handed hitters. He's more commonly 92-94. It profiles an above average fastball going forward.

The slider is probably his best pitch, a low-to-mid 80s shorter breaker with swing-and-miss traits. It's a bullet spinner with some depth characteristics. It's a breaker that plays well off the threat of his velocity. There's also an upper-80s changeup that lags his two primary pitches, but does flash some upside.

Davies is physically maxed at this point but does have the look of a mid-leverage reliever. He'll be young for the Draft, not 21 years old unitl 2027.

Dowell is one of the more impressive athletes in 2026 with a smattering of loud tools. It starts with the bat where bat speed and hand speed really stand out. Dowell has strong hands and wrists and stays compact through the zone with the ability to muscle pitches he's beat on to the opposite field. The pull-side power speaks for itself. Dowell is generally consistent with his ability to time the opposing pitcher, getting his foot down on time and setting his triggers to swing. He shown the ability to create variance in his bat path showcasing more loft on pitches down in the zone and slashing ringing extra-base hits on velocity on the top rail. Skeptics of Dowell's offensive game point to inconsistent performances against spin and a reluctance to draw walks. Those aspects of his profile could improve over time. 

Dowell is an above average runner underway who may settle closer to average or solid average as he continues to add strength and his body matures. He has plus arm strength and profiles as a right fielder at the next level with the potential to play centerfield if he stays lean and light on his feet. Dowell will be just 18.2 years old for the draft.

A 19th round selection by the Baltimore Orioles in the 2025 Draft, Anderson skipped out on going pro and instead honored his commitment to Heartland CC, deciding to stick around for a second year. He's become noticably stronger without losing his bounce on the dirt over the last twelve months, resulting in a commitment to play baseball at Kentucky in 2027 if he goes unselected/unsigned once more. 

Anderson stands tall in the box with his front shoulder closed off to the pitcher. It's a moderate leg kick with a minimal forward move, sinking slightly into his legs to create torque and tension. Anderson violently rotates through his center of gravity. Anderson has tremendous feel for getting to his pull-side and showcases good feel for getting the barrel to the baseball. He's a line drive machine that will flash average power projection, even if it's not a big part of his game at this point. Anderson does have some projection remaining in his lower half and has steadily added bat speed the last three years. 

Anderson has some range to his left and some natural feel for playing on the dirt. He's got softness in his hands and shows good tempo in how he plays the baseball. The athletic traits may ultimately push him to second base as a professional, but he's capable of spelling a more dynamic shortstop when called upon. Anderson is an above-average to plus runner once underway. 

The bat wil carry this profile, but feel to hit stands out, as does feel for the barrel. The run tool will help raise the floor as well. Anderson profiles nicely as a Role 45 second baseman at the pro level.

This will be Fontenot's fourth consecutive draft-eligible year in college. At 24.2 years old, he's one of the oldest players expected to be selected in July.

Stops at McLennan CC, LSU Eunice and Texas led him to Baton Rouge for the 2024, 2025 and 2026 seasons. He's pitched in a limited capacity across his Tigers career, but the stuff has ticked up this spring after years of injuries derailing his momentum. 

Fontenet is up to 99.8 mph this sseason with solid extension and a flatter approach. He generates chase outside of the zone despite a reasonably generic fastball shape. He spin the ball exceptionally well. Fontenot folds in a short, firm gyro slider and will flirth with a generic -10/-10 curveball in the low 80s. His control and command are fringy.

Given the arm talent, Fontenot will likely be a $5,000 money-saver in rounds 11 through 20 in July. He should be expected to go to Double-A immediately.
Up to 97, good curveball and the makings of a potential changeup. Good mover but below average strike-thrower. A project.

There are plenty of traits to buy into with Plunkett, especially at the dish. Physically, he's got broad shoulders and strength in his lower half. He moves well and has proven capable of creating separation and impressive rotation speed with the bat in his hands. He's an athletic right-handed hitter who sets up moderately wide in the box. He sets his back elbow high and throws a heavy barrel through the zone. There's steepness in his swing that can inhibit his ability to cover all four quadrants, but when he catches the ball out in front of the zone and extends, his raw power shines. Plunkett has quickness in his hands and strength and the point of contact. Contact quality will likely be inconsistent given his current swing path, but a few tweaks to the operation could unlock an impactful bat. Plunkett may ultimately end up a power-over-hit profile. 

Plunkett is a sure-handed defender who gobbles up anything hit right at him. He tends to field the ball deeper into his body than is preferred, and will field balls hit to his left outside of his frame with one hand. Still, his actions are quiet soft, and composed. While some of the technical fundamentals may ultimately need some clean up, Plunkett looks up for the task and development. A shortstop now, he projects to third base at the next level where his solid average arm strength and internal clock play best. He is an average runner. 

Plunkett is also a decorated basketball player for his high school team.

This is a player that looks the part in a uniform. He's got physical tools and athleticism that should keep him on the dirt as a professional.

Fitzgerald, a 23-year-old senior lacks leverage and projection, but threw together some good outings for the Nittany Lions and elevated his stock to scouts in the Northeast. Fitzgerald spent four years at Maine before transferring to Penn State for the 2026 campaign. 

Fitzgerald will work up to 97 with a four-seamer than sits 93-95. It's a cut-ride shape that gets whiffs at the top of the zone and can stay off the barrel of left-handed hitters. His true cutter/slider has improved this year and now sits 89-90 with lift and firmness. There's a low-80s curveball he'll flip over for striikes, as well as throw to the back foot of left-handed hitters.

Fitzgerald has thown a handful of changeups in his collegiate career, but with his supinator profile it has been slow developing.

Fitzgerald likely projects a "day three" pick and a money saver.

Mendez projects as a utility-type of player with bat speed and a track record of hitting solid pitching. He pounds fastballs and has shown far more pull-side power in spurts, leading some to believe there may be a bit more in the bat than originally forecasted. 

Santa Barbara seems to produce impressive infielders by the dozen and Mendez could be the next in a long line of them. Mendez's speed is limited, squarely a fringy, maybe even a below-average runner, but he does make up for it with a solid average arm and the hands necessary to handle third base. Mendez could end up at second base or third base at the next level, or potentially left field.

Jackson was draft-eligible in 2025 as a true sophomore, but teams elected to let him play another year in college due to rawness in his game. The ceiling is awfully intriguing, but the pieces need to fall into plate for Jackson to transform into his upside. The size and athlete stand out. 

Jackson's big frame and long levers have flashed plus raw power. When he keeps his hands inside his frame and turns on the baseball, he can really put a charge into a ball. Often times the swing gets long and Jackson takes an opposite field approach to the plate. That has impacted his contact quality at a high clip. Jackson is currently a rotational hitter who relies on his frame to generate impact. As he learns to get into his legs and use his strength in a different way, he could unlock a whole new gear at the dish. The sort of light-bulb moment happened for James Quinn-Irons in 2025, perhaps it will happen for Jackson in the near future.

Jackson's value extends outside of his offensive upside. He's a centerfielder by trade. It's above average run times with above average arm strength too. There's some rawness in his routes and actions in centerfield, but he gets to his spots and makes the plays he's supposed to make. Jackson currently projects as an average defender, but could see his game continue to blossom and/or elevate if he's asked to move to right field.

This is a moldable ball of clay. Perhaps Jackson is a new swing-coach and a strength and conditioning program away from seeing his game take flight.
HOLY CHANGEUP

Mizell is a line-drive hitter with an up-the-middle approach and a feel for the barrel. Right now, the game power hasn't quite arrived, but given the frame and bat speed, it's coming. The hit tool is quite distinguished here with strong whiff and chase rates, as well as feel for the barrel few can mirror. 

Mizell is slated for a corner outfield role where his fringy athleticism and run times fit, however he's been used as a designated hitter quite often in Tuscaloosa. He's got something in the neighborhood of an average throwing arm as well.

It's been a unique, winding road for Grossman. A product of King Kekaulike High in Maui, Hawaii, Grossman committed to the University of Utah out of high school and spent his freshman year there before transferring to Salt Lake Community College for his 2025 sophomore campaign. He then transferred to Oklahoma for this, his draft-eligible fourth-year junior. 

Grossman has seen his stuff blossom as he's added weight -- up 35 pounds since high school. Now 220 pounds, Grossman has a fastball that'll touch 97 and sits 93-95 in bullpen and single-inning showings. He's exceptional at spinning the baseball and can create dynamic shapes when his seam orientation is most efficient. Grossman's best secondary is a low-80s slider with shorter tilt that's effective when he's landing the fastball for strikes. The arm talent here is fairly obvious, though Grossman has a very limited track record in terms of showing his stuff to scouts in game settings to this point in his career.

Moss lives 91-94 and and will occasionally grab 95 with a fastball that tails a bit into the right-handed batters box. It's largely used to setup the rest of his arsenal and most scouts don't believe it's better than a 45-grade heater. That said, Moss generates well-above average extension down the mound and evaluators and analysts believe there's more fastball value to extract at the next level with added strength, velocity, and a couple tweaks in terms of his pitch grips. 

The slider is comfortably his best pitch and nobody can hit it. Moss will struggle to throw the breaking ball for strikes from time to time but his misses are always to the glove-side keeping him out of danger. It's a true sweeper with enough vertical plane to play with the hitters eyes, especially when taking into account his above-average extension toward the plate. Moss throws the slider 80-81 mph and it'll shorten up a bit on him when he tracks higher than that, touching 84. He'll also mix in a cutter to marry the fastball and slider a bit. 

Moss' changeup has the making of a dynamic bat-missing weapon but he struggles to sell that pitch with conviction right now. It's got big shape and separates well from the fastball, but for the time being hitters seem to identify it out of the hand better than they should. 

He represents one of the more interesting reliever-to-starter conversion candidates in the 2026 class. He's barely 22 years old.

Langdon has a ton of pure arm talent with a fastball already up to 95 mph and a tough breaking ball for both left-handed and right-handed hitters to square up. There's deception and angles here that are tough for the opposition to track. Langdon commands the strikezone and does a very nice job limiting base hits. 

He's had moments in tournament settings where he's lost the zone, but in general he eventually finds it and dominates the outing. While the arm action is free and easy, scouts would like to see the head whack ironed out of his delivery as July approaches.

Kellis has the big body and strike-throwing ability of a typical Northeast arm that hears his name called reasonably early in the Draft. The fastball continues to tick up and his secondaries in particular have taken a big jump over the last twelve months.

Kellis has snagged 96 in the first inning of his starts. He'll sit 90-94 with with sink and tail. It's a heavy fastball launched from a higher slot. Kellis has a long arm action and has something of a trebuchet launch. The ball explodes out of his hand and sneaks up on hitters. 

Kellis' slider has improved, but still has some hump to it. It's a low-80s bullet spin, best buried in the dirt. The changeup has a chance to be above average with tumbling actions and brick wall brakes in the dirt. 

Kellis has solid average control for the zone but tends to scatter his arsenal. It's average command thrown all over the plate. It's a starter build with three pitches and the chance to eventually become a ground ball specialist with some swing-and-miss stuff for left-handed hitters.

Guzman is a powder-keg infielder with a barrel chest and powerful lower half. He's played all over the dirt, including an average shortstop in summer ball play. Most scouts believe he'll eventually end up at second base or left field at the next level, two positions he's played extensively in Morgantown. 

Scouts laud Guzman for his hit tool and quiet left-handed swing that has peppered the gaps going back to his high school days. Guzman has fringe-average raw power and probably won't be a guy that is a big slugging threat at the next level. An above average runner who projects to add value on the bases, Guzman could be a nice Swiss Army Knife prospect at the next level that could fill a Role 45 spot on the bench of a competitive team.

Originally a standout at St. Bonaventure, Tharnish took his game to the SEC in 2026 and transferred to Kentucky for a chance to showcase his tools on a bigger stage. 

Tharnish has a lot of traits to buy into. It's a long, 6-foot-3-inch frame and excellent athleticism. He's a 70-grade runner and glides in the oufield. It's true centerfield components; a plus glove at the '8'. Tharnish's speed plays in a big way on the bases. He'll add tremendous value in the field and when his team needs an extra bag.

Tharnish is an aggressive hitter who expands the zone and a high clip. When he's swinging at pitches in the zone, his plate coverage is above average or better. But breaking balls off the plate have given him trouble. He's got a chance to own an average hit tool if pitch recognition and selectivity take a half-step forward. 

Tharnish doesn't project to hit for a ton of power, however his frame does lend some enthusiasm toward the idea strength gains and a couple swing changes could unlock something. 

Tharnish was draft-eligible in 2025, and will turn 22 years old just a couple months before the 2026 Draft.

Bucciero is a bat-first prospect who finds himself draft-eligible for the second year in a row.

The whiff and chase rates have both plummeted into ranges scouts and analysts can get excited about. He's hitting the ball harder than he ever has and finding the barrel with enormous consistency. Bucciero is no longer struggling to hit the breaking ball and is even making considerably more contact on pitches he offers at outside of the strikezone. One wart on his offensive profile is a ground ball rate that has spiked to unhealthy levels this year. Bucciero is employing a bit more steepness and loft in his swing plane in 2026 causing him to catch the top of the baseball with more frequency when he's out in front. Bucciero is a reverse-splits guy who can struggle from time to time against left-handed pitching. He may be able to hit a bit at the next level, and the exit velocities suggest a player who could flirt with 20-homer seasons if he gets sufficient at-bats. 

Primarily an outfielder, Bucciero exhibits some athleticism and a strong arm, receiving above average grades, giving him the ability to play right field effectively at the college level and potentially in pro ball. He tracks balls well and isn't a liability on balls in the gaps, however his below average speed does limit the plays he can get to.

Arguably the best prep outfielder coming out of the West Coast in 2023, West has always had an electric bat and the ability to create chaos on the bases. He's an above average defender in centerfield as well and could stick out there moving forward. Below average arm strength will likely land him in left field as a professional, but there's some wasted athleticism in a corner. 

West's tools and aptitude for the game earned him something close to a full-time role with the Bruins right out of the gate as a freshman. He's direct to the ball, slappy at the plate with more punch in his stick than most would expect. He can be a passive offensive player though. It's helped West post strong walk rates and strikeout rates that few can match, but his propensity for impact in games is limited. West also hits the ball on the ground at an extreme rate, too. If he's to ever capitalize on his ceiling, he'll have to find more loft. If he continues to get stronger, some believe West could go early in 2026. The upside here is a regular at the next level.

Lane learned under the tutelage of Marcelo Mayer as a high schooler and was plenty talented enough to start alongside him on the dirt. While he may not be quite the defender of his predecessor, he's not far off.

Lane has a sound right-handed swing and will flash above-average exit velocities at the plate coupled with rather impressive contact and chase rates. He knows what pitches to swing at and he puts those pitches in play. His profile is a bit muted by higher-than-preferred ground ball rates, however. A swing change could unlock more game power, but as presently constructed it's hit-over-power.

Defensively it's good actions, solid hands and a strong arm for the infield. Lane may eventually outgrow the shortstop position, though the bat profiles to either second base or third base, too. 

The entire profile isn't too dissimilar from what Kristian Campbell brought to scouts on his scouting report following the 2023 season. The Red Sox obviously ended up unlocking a new gear with Campbell thanks to a swing change. Maybe a similar career trajectory is in store for Lane.

Following two impressive years at Frank Phillips College and one year at New Mexico in 2025, Oriach hit the transfer portal and landed at the University of Georgia. Oriach received considerable scouting attention from evlauators in the Four Corners thanks to his size, handedness and rather impressive hit tool metrics for a guy his size, but went unselected. 

Oriach's batted-ball data and size are ultra-intimidating. He's an aggressive hitter who isn't afraid to expand the zone and chase a bit, however his hand-eye coordination and subsequent bat-to-ball skills have allowed him to showcase adjustability at the plate. It's rare a player with Oriach's levers can control the bat head against more premium competition, but he's bucked that stereotype. Scouts believe that if Oriach continues on this linear development path, his pitch selection may improve and the slugging should jump even further as he elects to pull the trigger on more damage-pitches going forward. It's 'plus' raw power and the frame and bat speed suggest he could get to even a bit more juice as he continues to mature.

Oriach is a below average runner who has played a majority of his games at DH, occassionally hidden in left field. It's a bat-over-everything profile, but an offensive talent that could slug his way to the big leagues.

Lindsey is a a big, physical, left-handed hitting first base prospect with strong bat-to-ball skills. It's a compact swing that stays tight to the body. He wraps the barrel and lays it back behind his frame, shallow into the zone with the ability to stay through the zone for an extended amount of time. It's a swing that really plays even if it's not built to hit for power as presently constructed. 

Lindsey can play a little third base and outfield, but the physical nature of his frame will likely move him to first base full time at the next level. He's a below average runner. 

The hit tool and power projection will need to carry the water on this profile, but Lindsey has proven he can hit.

Chee-Aloy immediately earned a starting nod with the Fighting Illini upon arriving to campus. He's a twitchy, spark-plug outfielder with a quiet setup at the plate. He creates good space with a short leg kick and a moderate stride keeping his head on plane throughout his swing. Chee-Aloy has a strong base with a muscular lower half and some projection to come in his shoulders and upper-body. He's a fairly anxious hitter who posts heavy swing rates and will chase outside of the zone. There's some raw power in his frame and he's flashed over-the-fence impact in Big 10 contests. He's an above average runner who possesses sneaky arm strength, solid average at worst. He gets good breaks on the ball and has a quick first step out of the box as well. This is a well-rounded player who makes things happen on the field.

Kelley reclassified up from the 2027 class in an effort to get his collegiate (or professional) career going a bit early. His physical frame and athletic tools were too advanced for his original draft class, now certainly more befitting of a draft-eligible high school prospect. 

Kelley's entire profile is reasonably balanced, with work to do on both sides of the ball to reach his full potential. He's demonstrated average bat-to-ball skills despite an aggressive approach that can get him in trouble against more advanced pitching. He's shown a willingness to expand the strike zone against all pitch types, his pitch recognition skills being an area of emphasis going forward in his development. Kelley can at times look like he's guessing which pitch is coming, rather than identifying it out of the hand. This bores out in his in-zone whiff rates and his universal chase rates. Still, the swing plane creates loud contact and consistently produces hard hit ball with backspin in the air. If Kelley can iron out his ability to put the ball in play during his plate appearances with more consistency, he's got a chance to be a player that lashes extra base hits in bunches. 

Defensively, Kelley is a primary shortstop. He's got athletic actions and quick hands with plus arm strength to boot. He tends to field the baseball deep into his body, something he'll want to clean up as the lights get brighter and the ground balls start getting hit harder. He's gotten significant run in the outfield as well; his arm strength impressive in both centerfield and right field. Kelley is an above average runner.

Perhaps Kelley's biggest selling point is his age and the way he fills out a jersey. He's got plenty of strength in his frame with the rounded, broad shoulders scouts look for to project more physicality on the horizon. There are plenty of reasons to buy this player in the draft, even if he's unlikely to move quickly through a minor league system.

Tremendous size and physicality. Broad shoulders, a high waist and strength in his upper-half and forearms. Big bat speed projection. Looks the part of a five-star quarterback. Above average run tool and athletic gait suggests he'll hold dynamic upside. Above average arm strength befitting of a prototype right fielder.

Boyle struggles with swing-and-miss despite possessing a refined eye. Pitch selection skills are very strong. Feel for the pull-side is strong as well. Swing and miss exists both inside the zone and outside of the zone. Handles fastballs just fine, but struggles to identify and put bat-to-ball against spin. 

Tremendous clay, big tools, pro-ready frame, but polish is required to reach impact potential.

Thompson is among the tougher at-bats in the 2026 class coming the the plate with a nasty arsenal and unique release traits. He creates a whole bunch of angles and can manipulate his arsenal to keep hitters uncomfortable.

It starts with the fastball. Thompson has been up to 93 out of low arm-slot. He'll generally tail that pitch away from righties with sink though at times he'll cut the pitch a bit and maintain some late carry through the zone. It's a pitch that misses a ton of bats despite what is presently largely average velocity. Thompson is mostly 90-91 and has shown strong control of the zone and will show streaky pinpoint command for the all four quadrants. 

Thompson likes to bury his low-80s slider and dance that pitch off his fastball tunnel. It features late tilt. He'll play with the shape of his breaking ball and has shown a willingness to back-door it to righties as well as bury it on their back foot. A changeup in a similar velocity band plays well off the fastball as well. It's a complete three pitch mix. 

Thompson's delivery is smooth, loose and fluid despite the quirkiness of his slot. It's a long arm swing with considerable scap load in the back and whippiness out in front. It's reminiscent of Madison Bumgarner. Thompson is an exceptional athlete and does a nice job separating his hips and shoulders on the mound. He's likely to flirt with mid-90s velocity in due time and should end up more 92-94 once fully mature. It's a starter profile despite his shorter stature and lack of overwhelming velocity.

Durham can do a little bit of everything and represents one of the better-known prospects in the 2026 class. A left-handed hitting shortstop with a projectable frame, Durham has shown flashes of advanced traits both offensively and defensively against top competition in big tournaments and showcase events. 

Durham employs an open stance and a slasher mentality at the dish. He's an aggressive hitter who does present some swing and miss in his game, specifically when faced against more premium competition. That said, he's long been a big-game performer with an impressive baseball card featuring big slash lines and more slug than one might expect from a player of his physical stature. Durham has average raw power projection and has shown it from time to time in games. He's no stranger to home runs. That said, ground balls have limited his consistent game power, a byproduct of his flatter bat path. 

Durham is an average runner with average arm strength. His physical tools may eventually push him to second base full-time, however the bat will ultimately carry the profile, and it's got a chance to be one of the more balanced offensive profiles in the 2026 class.

DeVaughnan stands out for just how easy he makes pitching look. He'll grab 96 from an effortless delivery. It's a fast arm and with the ability to pitch to both sides of the plate. He's got a curveball that jumps out of the hand and project solid-to-above average if he gets it a bit firmer. There's also a changeup he's mixed in at different tournament showings that scouts seem to like. An arm to watch approaching the draft. A lot of positive runway and helium on if/when this kid takes his whole game to another level. He will be 19.5 years old on draft day, so scouts will want to see his stuff jump to another level approaching the draft as he'll be facing players mostly a year younger than him.

A strong-body right-handed hitter catcher prospect, May checks a plenty of the prototype traits teams look for in their future backstops. 

The bat carries this profile. May has heavy hands and delivers and big blow through the zone. It comes with considerable swing and miss, however May swings at the right pitches and doesn't get beat by junk. It's short, tight swing with hands that stay inside the body through the zone; long on the follow-through. The operation at the plate projects to hit more than he has thus far in his amateur career, however May will need more reps to find his timing and a more consistent plane against premium pitching.

May has a chance to stay behind the plate. It's a big, durable, physical frame built for the rigors of catching full-time. He's got above average arm strength, however it's a three-quarter arm slot that can occasionally spike the ball to second base. He innately tails the ball into the receiver at second base more than most catchers. This isn't a disqualifier behind the dish, however it is uncommon. For what it's worth, Walker Janek had a similar release profile when he was selected in the first round in 2024.

May will need to close some of the holes in his swing before July to hear his name called in the top five rounds. He's a firm commitment to Kentucky and will be reasonably young for the class.

Campbell has taken a winding road to the point he's at now. He'll be nearly 24 years old on draft day, but is finally in a position to hear his name called given the the bright lights and constant exposure the SEC provides. After two years at Chattanooga State CC, a redshirt season at Charleston Southern, and finally a redshirt junior year at USC Upstate in 2025, Campbell transferred to Kentucky for his fifth collegiate season. 

Campbell got considerable draft attention in 2025 at Upstate, but ultimately the level of competition wasn't great enough for any organizations to pull the trigger. He's shown solid average bat-to-ball skills despite an aggressive approach in the box. Most of his warts revolve around velocity above his hands. That said, it's a fast bat with exit velocities reading north of 112 mph at times. His feel for consistently finding the barrel is a work in progress, and he hits the ball on the ground too much, but the peaks are inspiring. 

Campbell is a true centerfield who posts 70-grade run times. The speed plays on the bases too. It's also average arm strength. 

Campbell's uphill battle is his age and lack of experience on the biggest collegiate stages. He's got a chance to hear his name called as a $10,000 money saver at some point in the Draft. If that doesn't happen, he's likely an org-filler undrafted free agent. The tools are there. The leverage is not.

Cade Allen is a high-octane righty with a long, full arm stroke and an full intensity delivery. There's certainly some intent and effort in how he pitches, but the results speak for themselves. Allen has been up to 95 with big cut & carry; a fastball built to miss bats. 

He throws a traditional upper-70s 12-6 curveball that works off the fastball as well. Allen's changeup has a chance to get to plus as his feel for deleting spin and shaping to the arm-side stands out.

Julian Sabourin has some arm talent and feel for pitching that can be tough to find at this early stage in an amatuer career. His slider and changeup both project above average pitches and his feel for landing those offerings is advanced. The breaker is a low-80s bullet spinner with late life at times, playing well off his fastball. The changeup is an even better pitch featuring considerable arm speed, conviction and tumbling late life. It's got the makings of a potential 'plus' cambio in time. 

The fastball has been up to 93 but features generic shape. It's a potential average heater. Sabourin has three pitches, looseness in his arm, ease about his operation and a pretty good frame. He's got back-end of the rotation upside and projects to throw a bunch of strikes as he matures. Sabourin has age on his side, just 17 years old for the Draft.

There were real fears at South Carolina that Scobey wouldn't make it to campus in 2025 after receiving considerable draft interest. Those overtures never came to pass on draft day and the Gamecocks had a brand new starting infiedler on day one. 

Scobey certainly looks the part. It's a well-developed frame with boxy shoulders and strength built into his lower-half. He's demonstrated above average arm strength and the lateral mobility necessary to play the hot corner at an above average level. Scobey has quick hands and has a quiet nature about his actions on the dirt. He profiles as an above-average, maybe even plus defender at third base.

Offensively the profile is carried by above-average raw power and he seems to be growing into a tick more as he adds more strength. Scobey's swing has a hitch in the load where he pulls his hands backwards into his body. That's affected his hit tool and contact quality on campus. This combined with an anxious nature and a willingness to expand the zone has pushed his batting average and on-base south.

Scobey projects to become a prototype big arm/big bat third baseman going forward. He's got the bat speed to hit 20 homers at the next level but he'll need to make more contact to carve out a role that will allow him to get those at-bats.

A high-energy, hard-working table setter, Offing is an exciting prospect whose physical, athletic tools always seem to be in play in game action. 

Offing's profile is buoyed by a plus run tool that he likes to show off in centerfield and on the bases. He's quick out of the box and aggressive as hell in the field tracking fly balls down. Offing does have a good deal of experience at shortstop as well, however most scouts think a full-time transition to centerfield is in the cards immediately once he reaches pro ball. 

There's some raw power here, and Offing can tap into it every now and then. It's a flatter bat path built to pepper the gaps, but he'll occassionally back-spin a ball to the pull-side that gets out. Still, his physical tools and athleticism suggest he could be capable of flirting with double-digit homers as a professional. 

Offing is a streaky hitter who will go through bouts of swing-and-miss and mounting strikeouts. When you catch him on a heater, he can take over a lineup for a weekend.

The Area Code Games Player of the Week in 2025, Traylor has shown a feel to hit in big tournaments against good pitching. His physical frame and prospect pedigree both point to even brighter production on the horizon.

Traylor is growing into more power. He's flashed above-average raw power projection and does own a swing plane built to do damage. Traylor has heavy hands and rotates hard through the zone. Swing and miss can be streaky, but Traylor generally swings at the right pitches, providing a floor for his slash line.

A shortstop now, Traylor's 40-grade speed and lateral mobility will fit best at third base. He employs a wide base and works low to the ground, seeing and fielding the ball out in front of his frame. It's just average arm strength, but he's deliberate and foundationally strong. Traylor rarely misses his target throwing across the diamond.

Schmidt has been a bombastic performer in the ACC for the Yellow Jackets the last two seasons. He can really, really hit. But it's a bit of a tweener profile as it pertains to projecting him to professional baseball. 

A physically maxed first base prospect, Schmidt makes his money with excellent bat-to-ball skills and a strong approach. He's consistently run elite whiff rates both inside the zone and outside of it. He has no issues catching up with velocity and breaking balls are hardly an issue at this stage. Schmidt is going to hit. But for how much power? Schmidt owns below average game power and hasn't shown a great deal more in pre-game batting practice. His 106 mph max exit velocity does leave something to be desired from a first base prospect. To his credit, Schmidt keeps the ball off the ground, but tends to pepper the opposite field gap more than ambushing a pull-side fastball right now. He'll need to show more thump as July approaches if he hopes to capture what some believe is top-three round offensive projection.

Schmidt can play the first base position at an fringy level. His first-step quickness is okay. He does have soft hands and vacuums up whatever he can get to. He is a below average runner.

Church is the perfect Swiss Army Knife in the 2026 class. He's athletic enough to handle second base and the outfield, but also plays a mean defensive back and wide receiver at West Forsythe. He's just a sensational athlete who can do a little bit of everything in an exciting way.

Church's offensive game could blossom one day, but it's still a bit crude right now. His swing changes on a weekly basis with varying strides and hald-loads depending on the game. His feel for timing and getting the foot down on time is a work in progress. All that being said, when Church is on-time there's real bat speed that plays to the pull-side as well as the opposite field. That's supplemented by plus foot speed and more athletic projection on the way in his 6-foot-1-inch frame. Church is a burner down the line and can be a stolen base merchant if given the green light. 

Church likely profiles as a utility type. He hasn't yet stapled down consistent position on the diamond. The speed and athlete feels like a good fit for centerfield or second base. 

Church is an excellent athletic tester and boasts big force plate data. There's more in the tank here, but some elbow grease and another coat of polish will be necessary for his to let his tools shine in the way they're capable of at the next level.

The Sooners were awfully nervous they'd lose Catalato in the 2024 Draft, but lucked out when he went unselected. His 122 strikeouts in just 68 innings as a high school senior in Texas should probably have received more buzz than it did.

Catalano's has a starters' profile with s simple, shorter arm action, launching from a three-quarters arm slot. He generates his power on the mound from a sturdy lower half. He'll work 92-95 and can brush 96 when he's hot. Catalano throws two breakings balls, an upper-70s curveball being the more polished option of the two. He's a great mover with impressive extension and arm strength.

A hitterish first baseman with upside on the mound as well, Adams can add value to the game on both sides of the ball and presents a polished overall profile. It's a coin flip on whether he'll hit or pitch at the next level, however it's unlikely he'll give up either if he ends up at LSU. 

Adams has a simple left-handed swing with quick, loose hands. He takes his hands to the barrel to the ball with loose wrists and peppers the ball to all fields. Adams doesn't doesn't sell out for his pull-side and prefers to take what the pitcher gives him. That said, when he gets into ambush mode he'll flash above average power projection with real present bat speed. The polished approach serves the hit tool well. Adams doesn't have some stiffness in his hands in his load and a slight negative move, a mechanism that may be tested as he sees bigger velocity. 

Defensively, Adams is an average runner who has played first base and can be thrown into a corner outfield spot when needed. 

Adams has been up to 92 and will hold 89-90 into the deeper innings of his starts. There's a quality slider and changeup, both of which flash feel and quality. Both pitches are low-80s weapons.

DuBose owns all the components you could ever ask for from a shortstop prospect at the high school level. Remarkably quiet actions on the dirt, soft hands, big lateral range and the internal clock necessary to play the position at a high level. He still plays a bit tall fielding ground balls, and that's something that has impacted the consistency of his hands at times, but as he develops and works to get into his hips more, the entire package will likely come together in a polished form. The routine play, a part of his game that has been streaky, will likely clean itself up over time. 

DuBose is lean and wiry with a projection frame, considerably more strength on the way. He's got broad shoulders with narrower hips. DuBose will add good weight. 

The frame is already showcasing some whip and bat speed. DuBose has struggled with swing and miss and subsequent strikeout woes during parts of his career at IMG Academy. He's not a player in a huge rush to take his walks and pitchers have a tendency to come right after him. It's a hit tool that will likely blossom into something entirely new with the aforementioned gains in the gym. 

It's easy to dream on what DuBose will eventually become. There are checkpoints in his amateur career that he's yet to reach. As those physical pillars begin to arrive, scouts should have a better feel for what he's capable of.

Quevedo is mostly a one-tool bluechip right now with absolutely enormous raw power that allows his profile to stand out among his peers. It's 70-grade bat speed with a hit tool that lags a bit. 

He has some tools at third base including 'plus' arm strength, but scouts are split on the footwork and some believe he'll end up in right field in pro ball. Quevedo is an average runner.

A standout performer on the tournament circuit, Tucker is a big-body infielder with the athleticism to stay on the left side of the dirt. The bat is going to carry the profile from a pro perspective. 

Tucker is a left-handed hitter with very real bat speed. He's gets on-plane quickly and delivers a heavy blow through the zone with a path geared for slug. He's a physical hitter who leverages the ground to create raw power. the impact plays to all-fields and Tucker has been known to pepper the left-centerfield wall.

Tucker gets high marks on defense has hasn't been forced off the shortstop position yet despite his size. Above average arm strength is his most potent tool. He's a fluid mover with quiet actions and strong fundamentals. Tucker's size and strength can make it difficult for him to stop and throw when moving with pace to his right, but the arm strength does mask that at times. 

A lot of tools to like here. Tucker has the pro frame, the present bat speed, left-handed power and actions that suggest he'll stay on the dirt as a pro. He's also reasonably young for the class at 18.3 years old. Easy to buy in.

One of the most projectable swings on the high school circuit in 2026, Abate makes it look easy in the box. A smooth operator with tight turns, organic loft and length through release of the swing. Abate has strength in his hands and can get to his pull-side without selling out. There's very little wasted movement in the swing. It's fluid, it's fast, and it's performed in the showcase and tournament settings he's been given the opportunity to participate in. Abate doesn't have prototypical length in his frame, but in the same way Brandon Lowe and Kerry Carpenter have generated power over the years, so does Abate. 

Abate is an average runner who makes the routine plays in left field. He can play some third base in a pinch as well. Most of his value will be derived from the bat, but he's far from a liability elsewhere.

Murrietta is an advanced catcher with a real simple approach at the plate. It's a quiet swing with a flat bat path with a willingness to take the ball foul line to foul line. Murrietta will shorten up with two strikes to ensure the game gets put in motion. There's strength and bat speed under a more reserved approach to his offensive game, some suggesting a breakout is in the cards as the months pass and Murrietta gets to see more and more arms gaining comfortability. 

He's unlikely to add much value on the bases, but fans of the profile see a potential platoon catcher with average arm strength who can tackle first base or third base in a pinch. Either way, the bat will do the heavy lifting here. Murrietta will be 19.3 on draft day.

Bechtel struggled to get ample opportunities to play for the Wolf Pack in his two seasons at NC State. He was provided just 22 plate appearances across two seasons. Chasing more playing time, Bechtel elected to hit the transfer portal this summer, committing to UNC – Wilmington.

Playing in the Northwoods Leauge this past summer, Bechtel put the scouting world on notice. In 62 games, he slashed .304/.397/.545 with twelve homers. He added 28 stolen for good measure. Bechtel may always have some swing and miss in his game, but if it’s coming alongside middle-of-the-order thump, teams will happily trade one for the other.

Bechtel is a big, physically imposing player. It’s a 6-foot-5-inch, 230-pound frame that he carries well. He hasn’t outgrown his athleticism and doesn’t look like any sort of liability when tasked with playing left field. He's a solid-to-above average runner now. The looks are limited, but he's comfortable in the field. The arm strength and arm accuracy back into the infield, as well as the fundamentals necessary to hold runners at bay still needs a polish and fresh coat of lacquer, but he looks capable of growing into the role.

Call is a sublime athlete who turns in double-plus run times and some evaluators believe he's only going to get faster as he adds muscle and professional development. He can play shortstop, but his profile plays best in centerfield where he takes solid routes to the ball. The throwing arm is also plus, another feather in his cap in the outfield. 

Call is mostly a gap-to-gap hitter right now, though he possesses twitch at the plate and evaluators do believe he could eventually run into double-digit home run strength as a pro. He'll need to show more impact in the bat as July approaches to capitalize on his day-one tools. Call was a day three pick for the Boston Red Sox in 2023 but went unsigned.

Harrison Didawick is an imposing left-handed outfielder who gets down into his lower half and leverages the ground and his size in his swing beautifully. Didawick does a good job of sitting into his hips and makes tight turns on the baseball producing lots of torque. He uses the whole field well and has shown above-average pull-side power. The power comes with plenty of swing and miss exacerbated by an aggressive approach at the plate. He projects a below-average hit tool profile, but above-average game power could elevate his overall offensive production. When he finds his way on base, Didawick also uses his above-average speed to steal bases. 

Didawick is a good athlete in the field too, likely a left fielder moving forward due to his arm strength and the likelihood of a more premium defender playing up the middle. He often shows a good first step, taking strong routes to the ball and he has some highlight reel grabs on his resume. 

The power projection here is pretty loud, and the hit tool is coming along. He is draft-eligible for the third time. Refining his approach and pitch selection skills could get him drafted in 2026.

Kapa enters his sixth year in collegiate baseball with some of the better stuff in the ACC. He's yet to fully put it all together, but the strides he's made at UVA stand out. It's been a winding road. Kapa began his career at Alma College before transferring to Davenport College in 2024. That led him to Eastern Michigan for the 2025 season before transferring to Virginia for his grad student 2026 campaign. 

Kapa has been up to 97 from a lower slot He's generates well-above average extension down the mound and misses bats in buckets when he's commanding his heater at the top of the zone. Kapa's holds vert through the zone too, sometimes upwards of 20 inches of IVB. He also cuts the ball a great deal. It's a very unique fastball profile, albeit one that at times has lacked the command and execution necessary to get the results he's capable of.

Kapa's slider has a chance to be a real weapon. It's 82-84 with some depth and bullet shape. It's been a bat-misser. Kapa also has the components in place to develop at least an average changeup.

Control, command, consistency and execution have been pieces of Kapa's profile he's struggled to harness. It's a relief profile, but there's the ceiling here for a leverage arm that can be deployed toward the back of a bullpen if polish keeps coming. 

Kapa will turn 23 years a couple months after getting drafted. He'll likely be tested with an immediate High-A, or even Double-A assignment in 2027.

An ultra-physical left-handed hitting outfield prospect, Powell carries a fully-mature frame to the field, bringing the big tools to go along with it.

Powell has a quiet disposition in the box. It's a neutral setup with a moderately wide leg base. He rests the barrel hovering over his back shoulder and employs an abbreviated move forward in his load. He delivers heavy hands through the zone and can put a charge into the ball when he's locked in. 

Powell can be late to get going at times, rushing to get the barrel through the zone on time. It's resulted in mis-hits and weak pop-ups on the tournament circuit. That said, with further development and some refinement in his swing process, he stands the chance to mature into a hulking left-handed slugger. 

To date, swing and miss has slowed his game. He's shown a selective eye, but can get out over his skiis on soft stuff below the zone. To his credit, Powell has shown plenty capable of getting to his pull-side, and his feel for getting the ball in the air does suggest some natural feel to slug. Although raw mechanically, there's plenty of reason to believe he'll blossom into a potent middle-of-the-order bat.

Powell carries his strength well in the outfield. He's a fringe-average runner who could get a bit quicker as he trims into a more athletic version of himself with natural maturation. It's above average arm strength built for a corner, and the footwork necessary to perhaps play average defense.

Powell will turn 19 years old just before the draft and will be eligible in 2028 should he go unselected/unsigned.

Long, loose and highly projectable, Wheeler has the look of the prototype Florida Gator pitcher that goes on to do big things. Already touching 94, Wheeler possesses a bat-missing fastball with vertical traits and considerable carry through the zone. He can live on the top rail and throw cheese over barrels. 

There's a slider that flashes average and could get better as the physicality and arm speed of the whole profile improves. It's a pitch that features depth and a bit of sweep, but he's still working to iron the hump out of it. For now, it's primarily two pitches with a nascent changeup as a work-in-progress. 

Wheeler's operation is clean, repeatable and effortless. He throws a ton of strikes and has the makings of a future weekend starter in Gainesville if he ends up on campus. The highest ceiling here. Wheeler will be 18.9 years old on draft day.

Gavyn Jones saw a big jump both in stuff and draft projection over the past 18 months. He's no stranger to scouts having been selected by the Mets in the 18th round in 2023. Jones decided against attending Texas Tech, his original school of choice, and headed to McLennan for 2024 in the hopes of getting drafted higher a year removed from 2023. He went unselected in 2024, instead electing to pitch at Oklahoma in 2025 and 2026 before being eligible again this July. 

Scouts believe it's only the beginning for the loose, live-armed Texan. He'll grab 96 with considerable life late in the zone, mixing in two distinct breaking balls along the way. The first is a shorter slider that comes off the fastball tunnel late thrown in the mid-to-low 80s. His second weapon is a upper-70s downer curveball with considerably more depth and life. There's some length and inversion at the back of Jones' delivery, and scouts have commented on that in the past, though he's on-time at foot plant and Jones hasn't had too many issues throwing strikes. 

Given his handedness, present stuff and projection to throw harder, he's a good bet to get popped once again in July so long as he stays healthy.

Leffew's game has taken a jump since arriving to school. A year in Winston-Salem followed by a year in Austin, Leffew looks like one of the better strikeout artists southpaws in the 2026 class. 

The heater can touch 96, and he's held that velocity, but there's some effort in the delivery and the secondaries lag behind the sex appeal of the fastball velocity. Leffew has shown tremendous command for the top of the strikezone with the fastball allowing it to play up like a plus pitch. There's above average carry on the heater. 

Leffew throws a cutter, a slider, a bigger curveball and a changeup, all of which have flashed promise at one time or another, though consistency has thwarted his consistent upward trajectory. The slider has the making of a plus pitch with impressive diving action at the plate. 

Considering his handedness and *now* stuff, Leffew could end up a first round arm if the secondaries take one more step and he's stretched out to a point where teams believe he can start at the next level.

Larson's best tool is the bat, and it's very good. After impressing in the SEC as a freshman Larson took his stick to the Cape as a teenager and tore up the competition. His ability to change swing-planes with loose wrists and upper-body strength allows Larson to cover every zone. He's got the prototype turn-and-burn zone low-and-inside as a lefty bat, with pronounced loft and impact in that go-zone. Larson is a fringy runner with a fringy arm, likely destined for left field or first base where the bat will be the critical piece in deciding his role. 

Larson has drawn comparisons to former LSU outfielder Daniel Cabrera. Larson was a 20th round pick by the Twins in 2023, but went unsigned. He transferred to Texas for the 2026 season after spending two years in Baton Rouge.

Vigue had some late helium as a high school pitching prospect but was pushed to Michigan as one of the oldest draft-eligible preps in his class. He went undrafted in 2025, instead electing to transfer to Georgia to try and up his stuff for the 2026 Draft.

The stuff has really blossomed. Vigue is a supinator profile who continues to impress. Vigue will touch 97 and naturally cuts the baseball. He'll flip back and forth between a cutter and a slider, the latter being in the mid-80s with spin and teeth. The cutter has been elite in its purpose, up to 93 with darting glove-side action. It's extremely effective keeping hitters off the barrel. 

Vigue has the delivery and track record to project a starting pitcher going forward. Should he ever learn to throw a circle-change or splitter he could vault himself into first round consideration. He'll be a draft-eligible sophomore, but on the older side. He'll turn 23 before the start of the 2027 season.

After enjoying a gaudy freshman year at San Diego State where the local product slashed .361/.417/.582 with four homers, Turner elected to jump into the transfer portal where he took his talents to Ann Arbor to play ball for the Wolverines. Turner is mostly a contact-oriented hitter who boasts an impressive track record of putting the bat on the ball, especially against top shelf velocity. He does have budding bat speed that has been unlocked since eliminating a sizable hitch in his swing going back to high school. He's an aggressive hitter who tends to expand the zone at times, but gets away with it thanks to impressive bat-to-ball skills regardless of pitch-location. Scouts now see at least fringy raw power with the chance to develop into an average thumper in the college game. A third baseman by trade, Turner has laced up the cleats at second base and in the outfield at times during his collegiate career and could be moved around in a utility role when necessary. He'll need to continue his torrid hitter-ish ways to realize his top-100 pick ceiling, though unlocking more game power will need to come alongside his innate traits as well.

Greis is an exciting two-way talent who has dominated the competition in Southern California since arriving to the high school scene. A lean, athletic infielder with fluid, smooth actions, he's got a chance to stick on the left side of the dirt at the next level. He's shown soft hands in workouts with quick transfer skills and a strong throwing arm. The hands really work at the plate with strength at the point of contact. He's a line drive hitter who generally takes what the pitcher gives him and doesn't try to force anything to the pull-side. He's got legitimate helium on both sides of the ball with a fastball up to 91 supplemented by a curveball and a changeup, the latter flashing at times and dancing off the fastball tunnel. Greis will be 19.2 years old for the draft, so model organizations will want to see present impact come July 2026.

Mabeus is an impressive switch-hitting catcher with big catch-and-throw skills and considerable strength and bat speed from both sides of the plate. A 6-foot-4 mountain of a prospect, Mabeus has shown big game power from both sides of the plate, though there's more present loft from the left-side and a bit more blistering line drive doubles juice from the right. Either way, scouts like the hit-ability from both sides and think he's got a shot to hit and hit for power as both a left- and right-handed hitter.
