The arm strength and pop out of the crouch really stand out for Mabeus as well. His transfers are lightning quick. There's some technical work in terms of directional efficiency behind the plate, but most believe he's got a solid chance to stick back there at the next level; pretty impressive considering his size and physicality. A fringy runner now, Mabeus will draw most of his value out of the bat and up-the-middle role. Mabeus is lauded for his leadership qualities in the dugout and in handling his arms. He's assertive, confident, and drives the bus for his team.

Given the big arm strength and durable frame, Moser has always flashed starting pitcher potential going back to his junior year in high school. The polish has continued to tick forward year over year, with secondaries finally beginning to blossom as his draft approaches. 

Moser has been up to 94 mph some carry and tail. He's more commonly 89-92 in his starts after the first inning. GIven his size, arm speed and age, Moser is likely to live in the low-to-mid 90s at full strength and should flirt with upper-90s velocity in his peaks. 

A spin-killing changeup is his best secondary weapon. There's feel for some fading action and Moser's organic feel for tunneling the pitch off of his fastball works well. The slider is more of a work in progress, but it's firm (82-84) with shorter tilt. Commanding that pitch will be important in his development as for the time being it's mostly fringe-average around the zone. 

Moser will barely be 18 years old for the Draft and is expected to be a difficult sign away from Duke.

Following a big year at Central Arizona in 2025, Stagg played for the Edmonton Riverhawks in the WCL. That got him noticed enough to transfer for the 2026 season, landing at UC Santa Barbara for his second draft-eligible campaign. Yet another talented ballplayer out of Australia, Stagg has some tools to build on. 

Stagg is an above average runner with a physical frame that can at times flash solid-average raw power. He's grown into more foot speed as he's tacked on muscle. It's a quick first step with the ability to steal bases once on base. Stagg has a discerning eye and takes his walks too.

Stagg's setup in the box helps him eliminates whiffs and control his strike out rate. He sets his hands very low as the pitch is being delivered and has quiet triggers. The barrel gets into the zone quick and stays through the hitting zone for an extended amount of time. It's a flatter attack angle geared to hit line drives. 

It the field, Stagg's arm strength is his best asset. It's above average with carry through the bat. He's capable of playing centerfield, but may be best-served in a corner as a professional.

Heiberger is a talented lefty who owns some fastball value and secondaries that project into the next level of baseball. 

Heiberger throws two fastballs; a four-seamer and heavier two-seam fastball. He's shown better feel for landing the two-seamer for strikes and tends to throw it far more often. Heiberger doesn't spin the baseball particularly well, but does sink and tail the heater better than most. It's resulted in steady results with strong chase rates and more whiffs than one would conventionally expect from a natural sinker-baller. Heiberger doesn't extend down the mound like his 6-foot-3-inch frame would suggest, but does induce plenty of soft contact.

Heiberger relies on the changeup to get outs. It mimics the sinker and has nearly identical shape traits to the heater. He gets roughly 7 mph of separation off the fastball and it helps to generate whiffs and chase outside the zone. He'll throws a low-80s cutter to left-handed hitters too.

Heiberger has the look of a swing man or a front-end of the bullpen piece.

Labbe is a really solid athlete with a potential future behind the plate and on the dirt. He's got actions at both spots and have the tools befitting of a player who can handle either role. 

Labbe's quick feet, quiet actions and directional feel at the shortstop position all stand out. He works low to the ground and always seems to be moving toward the target. It's only average arm strength and that may limit him to a utility role on the dirt, but his feel for the game should necessitate that versatility. Behind the dish, the arm strength plays up a bit. There's carry to the second base bag. It's a quick transfer with balance, composure and tempo. From this chair, Labbe looks more capable of developing into an above average defensive catcher than an infielder. In any case, the athleticism stands out when he's got a glove on his hand.

Labbe stacks his stance into his back-hip and drifts forward in his load. He stays behind the baseball when he gets a fastball, but can sway over his front side when he's fooled on spin. Labbe has feel for the pull-side and aims to impact the baseball to left field. It's a line drive swing with fringy average bat speed and a chance to run into 10-12 homers per year if given 550 plate appearances as a pro. Slug will likely never be a huge part of his game, but there's enough raw power to be dangerous.

Labbe is a good ballplayer. He does a lot of things very well. If he ends up on campus, he's the type of glue that college programs desire. At the pro level, he's got a chance to play for a decade with his skillset.

Boop put together a very nice winter entering his senior year, tacking on strength and muscle and getting his frame into a more athletic state. His tools have trended in the right direction.

Boop has plus raw power and will ocassionally showcase it in games. There's still some inconsistencies in his bat path, and lazy fly balls are something he's working to iron out of his game. There's some feel to hit with improving timing and triggers. It feels as though he's a tinker or two away from unlocking something offensively.

Boop has a strong arm, above average on the infield with third base actions. He can spell a shortstop if needed. He's a below average runner.

Boop's bat will need to continue surging as July approaches if he hopes to get a shot to play pro ball out of high school. He's been a late recruiting focus for schools in California.

Big physical tools from Delaney. It's major bat speed from the left side with considerable intent on every swing. Delaney has raw power projection in his 6-foot frame. The hit tool, pitch selection and bat-to-ball skills continue to be a developmental emphasis, but there's little doubt on the upside if it comes together. He's a barrel of gunpowder in the box.

Delaney is an above-average runner with a strong first step. He's got average arm strength and is likely destined for a corner at the next level.

Olivares can really, really throw barrels. He's got extremely heavy hands that deliver a load through the zone few can match in the class. There's considerable strength at the point of impact with easy plus raw power. The swing is short, compact and quick through the zone. Something of a Mitch Garver stroke. 

Olivares has some tools behind the plate including an average throwing arm, though the possibility exists where he shifts to third base or left field at the next level to land a more superior defender with the gear on. The arm strength seems to play better at third base than it does behind the plate. He is a fringy runner who will derive most of his value from the bat. But it's a big one. Olivares will be just 18.3 years old for the draft.

Arcamone was a draft-eligible sophomore in 2025 but went unselected with pro organizations fearing his commitment to transfer to Georgia would be too strong.

Arcamone makes plenty of contact and stays inside the strike zone at impressive rates. His unwillingness to expand the zone has led to more barrels and bigger exit velocities. It's above average raw power with a swing geared to get to it. Arcamone creates big coil in the box bringing his hands tight to his body and exploding through the zone. There's very little wasted movement in his move forward, his hands staying neutral until he fires. He's shown the ability to take the barrel to all four quadrants, his impact slightly lesser on pitches on the outer-third. He is a below-average runner who has a tendency to throttle down on ground balls hit to the right side. Arcamone has a chance to hit for average and power at the next level with a sweet left-handed swing scouts admire. 

The catching is a bit more on the fringy side. Like many catchers at his level, Arcamone struggles to frame the low pitch and is just passable getting low into the crouch. His framing on pitches at the top of the zone is slightly above average. He does have above average arm strength, however his exchange and pop times are below average as he's a bit clunky out of the crouch.

Montanez was a 20th round selection in the 2025 Draft out of Puerto Rico, but went unsigned by the Reds. At that time, he was still uncommitted on where he'd play college baseball. Still, he wanted to chase a better pay day and elected to go the JuCo route in 2026. 

Montanez is well-regarded for his defensive traits. He's got solid-average arm strength and jumps out of the stance with tempo. The arm action can be  a bit long at times and his footwork has some polish coming in the future. Scouts believe he has a chance to catch going forward.

Even if he doesn't stay behind the plate, the bat will be forced to add value. There is a long track record of hitting and Montanez has flashed above-average raw power projection from the left side.

Abraham carved out an exceptionally large role as a true freshman in 2024 logging 34.1 innings for the Seminoles punching 42 tickets in his teenage debut to the ACC. He's maintained a bullpen role as a sophomore but his stuff is ticking up.

It's a prototype four-pitch mix. The four-seam fastball is a bit generic in shape, however he'll cut the pitch at times making it a tick more dynamic. Abraham has been up to 95 but more commonly sits 91-94. He generates considerable spin rates leading evaluators to believe there may be some low-hanging fruit to extract some more value out of his fastball. Abraham's high release height and vanilla shape will need to deviate into a more specific direction in pro ball.

The fastball is complimented by a very good cutter with high spin and bullet spin. Abraham has been able to miss bats in buckets with that pitch, forcing hitters to expand the zone at well-above average clips. His changeup is also formidable. Abraham kills spin and generates depth and tail on that pitch leading to missed bats and zone-expansion. His bag of tricks is rounded off by a big breaking curveball with impressive two-plane tilt and huge spin rates approaching 3000 rpm consistently. 

Abraham has the full arsenal but with below-average control. Walks have been his bugaboo. He'll whiff his way out of uncomfortable baserunner situations but that isn't sustainable at the next level. His pure stuff probably provides a floor as a guy who gets a shot into a bullpen at the next level at some point in his career but if the strikes don't improve he risks only ever being an up-and-down guy.

For the time being Hoffman is mostly a one-pitch specialist with a fastball that flirts with metrics seldom seen. He's only touching 95 for the time being but will grab spin rates in the elite category causing the fastball to explode at times. 

There is a slider here as well, but the spin profile isn't quite as dynamic on that pitch and he buckshots the command for that pitch on most nights. He's 80 percent fastballs on most occasions. It's a sturdy frame with a steady arm action and there's plenty of strikes to utilize his profile in a number of different roles. He'll need to iron out the slider and develop a changeup if he's to capitalize on what is arguably Top 100 pick pure stuff.

Hamilton has some interesting stuff and pounds the strike zone. The fastball isn't over-powering - 90-92 touching 94 at peak. He bores the baseball into right-handers knuckles generating soft contact. He can occassionally get swing-and-miss from left-handed hitters, especially up and away, out of the zone. Hamilton isn't overpowering and doesn't own a fastball that expects to be a true out pitch at the next level, but his sweeping breaking ball has a chance to be above average.

80-82, Hamilton's breaking ball features strong lateral tilt with some diving action through the bottom of the zone. He throws it for strikes at an exceptionally high clip and can generate both whiffs and chase with that pitch. From this chair, the pitch needs to be thrown more often to left-handed hitters at the back-foot. Hamilton insteads elects to throw his 82-84 mph chnageup when there's a lefty in the box. It's a fringy offering as currently constructed.

Hamilton has three pithes, one of which has the makings of an out-pitch at the next level. He's an average athlete with moderate extension on the mound. He may end up a mid-leverage reliever at the next level who will rely on soft contact in split-dependent matchups.

Williams has a ton of metrics that point toward future success. While he's not the biggest guy in the world, most pitchers envy the positions he can put his frame in to find value and miss bats.

Williams usually lives in the upper-80s with his fastball, but he's reached back for 92. It's an ultra-low launch created by considerable extension down the mound. Williams' fastball misses bats in buckets when he elevates it to the top of the zone. He creates an exceptionally flat approach angle up there with his launch traits. 

Williams supplements the fastball with mid-70s curveball he'll use to steal strikes. There's a low-80s changeup and a slider he's been working to incorporate in the upper-70s to bridge his arsenal.

Carver is your prototypical strong-armed, big-power backstop. His hit tool has come on in recent years as he's worked to understand his swing and his frame. Carver has quieted down the hands and lower-half in his load allowing him to track the baseball better to the dish.There's still a pretty substantial barrel tip and stride in his move forward, but scouts are more bullish than ever he's got a chance to survive in pro ball. 

Carver has the fire hydrant catcher's frame with plus arm strength and some pop out of the crouch. Carver can struggle to steal the low strike and will need to work to get lower in the crouch at the next level.

Rivero has had an interesting path through high school baseball. Originally a Los Angeles Dodgers international free agent target, Rivero was denied eligibility as an international free agent in 2025. He'd worked hard training in Venezuela in the hopes of being international eligible, but MLB shot that down. He instead maintains his Rule 4 eligibility as a domestic 18-year-old high school prospects playing in Arizona.

Rivero is highly regarded for his glove. The defensive actions and arm strength have both ticked up over the last twelve months. It's above average arm strength with a quick release and explosive mobility out out of the crouch. Rivero is capable of back-picking first base and has been a menace throwing out base-stealers at second base going back to his junior year at Canyon del Oro. 

Rivero is a contact hitter with a short swing he cuts off at the top. It's a simple swing with very little counter-rotation and some stiffness in the lower-half. He peppers the gaps and has some feel for back-spin that could result in fringe-average raw power as a professional. 

Rivero was set to sign with the Dodgers for between $600k and $750k. He could still get that in the 2026 Draft.

Long, lean and very athletic, "Trey" Barnes oozes projection. He's got traits in all three phases and has a chance to grow into complete ballplayer.

Barnes is unrefined offensively. His swing involves an exaggerated forward move and he tends to swing across his front side. It tends to be linear in nature. He throws his hands through the zone and isn't yet incorporating his back hip or lower half like his frame suggests he should. Barnes has a read-and-react approach to hitting. When he begins using the leverage he's naturally blessed with, his impact at the plate could take off. Barnes has clocked exit velocities north of 108 mph. The juice and bat speed are in the tank, but getting to it is an inconsistent exercise presently. 

Barnes is an aggressive swing who takes his cuts. Because he relies on his hands so much with his currest swing, he tends to believe he can get to anything. That's bloated his swing rates and his chase rates. A fresh coat of polish and paint in professional ball should help iron this out, but it'll take time. 

Athletically, there's a lot to like. Barnes is an above average runner whose growing into plus speed. He'll likely get there in short order. It's centerfield tools, however he may eventually end up a corner if he gets too big and/or his routes don't develop like some believe they can. Barnes' arm strength is fringy presently.

Barnes is something of a project. There's work to do offensively from a timing and swing mechanics perspective, but he possesses traits you simply cannot teach. He's got good size, is a good athlete, and has a natural feel to swing the bat. He's as good a day three prospect on the high school side as you'll find, assuming he can be signed away from his commitment to Southern Miss.

Krenek's big durable frame stands out. He's ready for the rigors of pitching at the next level. He should be able to carry a workload whether his next stop is Austin, Texas or professional baseball.

The frame comes alongside a longer arm action with a moderate arm swing in the bag, some scap load and a whip-like follow-throw. It's a three-quarter delivery that generates east-west movement on his pitches. Krenek can work to all four-quadrants and plays catch outside of the zone when the circumstance calls for it. 

Krenek's pitchability and strikes stand out. He's long been a strike-thrower with the ability to mix things up on hitters. The fastball has tickled 93, but Krenek's ability to hold 89-91 over long outings is a strength. He'll need to add more velocity at the next level, but his stamina on the mound is already a plus. 

The aforementioned fastball is a true sinker with huge arm-side running action and late sink. He'll work it arm-side and glove side and has shown capable of generating whiffs under left-handers hands, as well as elevated up-and-away from righties. It's unlikely to be a swing-and-miss pitch at the next level without more velocity behind it, but the utility of its ground ball potential still should be considered an asset.

Krenek throws two breaking balls. The slider is a low-80s bullet-breaker with downward tilt and cutter-like action. A mid-70s curveball is much bigger with two planes of break and considerable downward action. Both pitches compliment his arsenal nicely.

Krenak has shown an upper-70s changeup, however it lags in the grand scheme of his menu.

Krenek is unlikely to ever overpower the opposition, but his ability to generate ground balls and weak contact stands out. He'll be a blue collar worker on the bump and can eat innings. There's role projection here.

Lawson is a shot-put short-arm hurtler on the bump with a fastball that'll grab 94 with hop and deception. There's a bigger curveball in the upper-70s that plans well off the tunnel of the fastball as well. That two-pitch mix has racked up strikeouts in buckets when he's commanding the baseball in and around the zone. 

It's a reliever look, but potentially one with two plus pitches if the fastball velocity takes one more step.

A talented two-way prospect who has some skills and thump with the bat, most foresee a future on the bump where arm speed and athleticism lead the way.

Lange is a fast-mover on the bump with a balanced delivery, stacking his back-side and striding down the mound with intent and an aggressive nature. Lange turns his head away from the target and gets the opposition uncomfortable with a Luis Tiant-esque look-away and counter-rotation. He explodes out of his hand break and delivers a trio of weapons. 

Lange's arm speed is helping him flirt with mid-90s velocity, however he is more commonly 89-91 after the first inning of his outings. There's some late juice on the heater and it sneaks up on hitters. It's especially effective elevated and Lange has shown some feel for commanding the fastball both at the top of the zone and to his glove-side.

Lange's breaking ball is a swing-and-miss pitch with bigger depth. It's a traditional bullet slider featuring good conviction out of the hand. It'll need to firm up as he matures, but there's components and feel for shape that can be difficult to teach at this age.

Lange will be young for the Draft, just 18.1 in July.

Czarniecki has seen a steady rise in his region thanks to consistent loud performances both in league and showcase/tournament settings. He's an above average runner with above average raw power and the ability to play any position on the field. Most scouts like the profile in centerfield or left field when all is said and done. There's solid average arm strength and solid reads.

Some of the highest level upside you'll find in the 2026 class. Bradley is tall, long and lean with explosiveness and twitch on the mound. He's moves way faster than most prospects built this way. 

Bradley is up to 93 mph with a high-spin arsenal; the fastball flirting with 2500 rpm at times. His fastball has carry and tail, especially effective under the hands of right-handed hitters. 

The slider is firm for his age, an upper-70s two-plane breaker that's touched 83 mph. Bradley is still developing sharpness and later tilt on the pitch, but his innate feel for shape and spin stand out at this early stage. There's also a mid-80s changeup that remains a work in progress.

This is a high-level mover with tons of projection in the tank. It's a shorter arm action with some cross-body in his operation that creates deception. Bradley is consistently on time. The effort at release is moderate and scouts believe he'll eventually iron that part of his game out with added strength. Bradley currently features fringe-average control. He'll be young for the class, barely 18 years old.

As Schuman has continued to add weight and strength since reaching high school, his athletic tools have taken a considerable jump elevating his profile to scouts. It's still a bit crude around the edges, but Schuman's linear trajectory raises eyebrows.

Schuman is a heavy counter-rotator tucking his front shoulder back in his load to create coil. Schuman gets to his bat speed and raw power with hard, heavy turns through the zone delivering a firm barrel to the baseball. Schuman has proven capable of hitting the ball with authority to the pull-side, throwing his front hip early and emphasizing getting the bat out in front. It's a swing that may struggle against premium spin commanded low-and-away. Schuman has time to make the adjustments necesary given his age and athletic prowess.

That athleticism comes out in a big way away from the batters box. Schuman is an above average runner who gets better underway. He's an explosive, twitchy mover with fantastic force plate testing. That should point toward more impact from a first-step perpsective as he gets stronger. It also points toward considerably more raw power projection on the horizon. 

Schuman's offensive mechanics need some polish, lacquer and a fresh coat of paint. He's without question capable of making those adjustments. If he does, it's a 3-8 round profile.

Cupp was seen by some as the top shortstop in the 2023 class, but went to Mississippi State due to signability concerns. He transferred to DBU for the 2026 season. He has a great frame with long levers, a high waist, and broad shoulders that suggest more impact on the way. He glides on the dirt, but he's not a strong runner and relies more on his actions around the ball. He could swing over to second base or third base as he develops. Cupp shows quick hands and a solid average arm. The hit tool is the carrying trait here, some calling it a potential plus bat with fringy present power and an ability to drive the ball to all fields at the plate. Considering his foot speed limitations there will be a lot of pressure placed on the bat as Cupp moves up the ladder, but if he proves capable of sticking at shortstop all the while providing an above average hit tool, it's day one characteristics.

Myatt was arguably the top hitter in junior college baseball in 2025 at Walters State CC. His .484 average and 31 homers clobbered just about all of his peers, and by a wide margin. His production led to him being named the 2025 JUCO Player of the Year. As one might expect, that quickly landed him in the transfer portal where he quickly signed on to play in Knoxville with the hometown Tennessee Vols.

Myatt is a pure hitter. It's a quiet setup with a moderately high leg kick, a minimal move forward, a still head and a compact swing with a path that stays through the zone for a long time. Myatt has definitive feel for the pull-side and launching the baseball. He looks a bit like Max Muncy in the box. The art of hitting comes very naturally to him. 

Myatt's defense isn't quite as revered as the bat. He's been forced into a DH role at times in his career. Myatt has fringy arm strength and his footwork and hands can be clunky and get disconnected at times. He's got the athleticism to potentially develop into a third baseman or first baseman going forward, but there's work to do if he's to play on the dirt as a professional. He's an average runner. 

This is a pretty special bat. His draft stock may be diluted a bit by the lack of value on the dirt and marginal value on the base paths. Hitters hit and they rarely last long in any given draft. Myatt will need to continue to bang as July approaches.

Troxell is a well-built right-handed pitching prospect with strength throughout his frame and strength that it beginning to manifest itself into velocity on the mound. He's been up to 94 but more commonly sits 90-91 with a high launch and tough angles for the opposition to track out of the hand. 

Troxell's primary weapon is a big low-80s curveball that shows deeper shape, best buried at the plate. It plays off the fastball and gets uncomfortable swings from the opposition. 

Primarily a two-pitch guy right now, Troxell will need to incorporate a changeup as the draft approaches should he hope to capitalize on his seven-figure upside. He's a fringy strike-thrower who is more effective because of his stuff rather than his pitchability at this tage.

Bucholz is a back-foot hitter who hinges to create loft and plane through the zone. Bucholz drops the back shoulder and drifts into his lower-half to generate an uphill swing aiming to do damage. A big, strong player, Bucholz generates above-average bat speed and could eventually tap into above average game power as he continues to let his frame mature. 

A catcher by trade, Bucholz has received more and more playing time in the outfield as his athletic tools have ticked up. He's a fringy runner with above average arm strength befitting of a right fielder going forward. 

Bucholz is an exceptional athlete with tremendous force plate testing scores and grip strength. Teams buying into the profile will have to believe the bat and power projection will continue to trend upward as he learns to more efficiently and effectively use the explosive nature of his athleticism to his advantage.

Green finds himself draft-eligible for the second year in a row after going unselected as a second-year sophomore in 2025. 

Green is a fantastic left-handed projection arm with size, physicality and he pounds the zone. It's not overpowering stuff, but Green has produced in the SEC. It's mostly fastballs and sliders for the Nashville product. He throws a heavy sinker with some steepness that's induced a lot of soft contact. Green has only brushed 93 at this stage, but he holds his velocity well and will sit 90-92 deeper into outings. 

The sweeper is a true 'plus' pitch with elite depth and routinely showcases north of 15 inches of lateral tilt. It's been a swing and miss pitch for Green and should continue to improve as he adds firmness to that pitch. For now, it's largely thrown 79-80 mph. There's also a changeup he'll whip out for tough right-handed hitters that's been effective in garnering some chase, but in the zone it hasn't been a weapon that is especially effective. It's also largely below-average in terms of control and command.

Fairchild has been an arrow-up prospect for the better part of the last year as his athleticism has slowly caught up with his innate ballplayer abilities. He's grown into some strength with broadening shoulders and more muscle in his lower-half. 

Fairchild is a rhythmic hitter who has moving parts in his setup, load and swing. He employs an early toe-tap and strides forward late. The hands move into several different planes before setting low and narrow to the body before firing. Fairchild is a barrel magnet. While his swing is a bit prohibitive in his ability to get to his raw power, that may come with some adjustments over time. 

Fairchild is a smooth defender at the shortstop position. He may outgrow the position, but his feel for the dirt and his actions will certainly fit at second or third base. He's an average runner.

Lorenzo certainly looks the part. It's a long frame with a high waist, long levers and a quiet, athletic demeanor in how he plays the game. Lorenzo's game can be described as steady across the board. He's reliable and solid with some burgeoning offensive tools in an intriguing prospect package.

Lorenzo's story really hasn't begun to be told just yet. His 6-foot-3-inch frame is still at least 15 pounds away from where it will eventually sit. At the plate, is a tall, relaxed setup with moderately high hands, some waggle for rhythm and a repeatable swing. It's fast hands and a steeper attack angle built to get the ball in the air. At this stage, Lorenzo's lack of strength is inhibiting his ability to turn line drive and fly balls into slug. It's also forced most of his balls in play to the opposite field. As he tacks on weight, the box scores should change in his favor. To his credit, Lorenzo swings at the right pitches on most ocassions.

Lorenzo's fluid athleticism is a plus. He's a good defender and projects an above average runner as he gets stronger. He's got a chance to play the shortstop position; a sure-fire infielder once fully mature.

Lorenzo's game will be capped until he gets a bit more strength on his frame. Once that happens, he could blossom into an exciting prospect. For now, the uncertainty in his physicality may force him to make a decision on bonus overtures in rounds 11 through 20.

Bixby has long been a name on the scouting trail, a 6-foot-7-inch righty with immense projection. As you might imagine, considering his size and length, Bixby has long-limbs and has a ton of room for weight and muscle. He's largely been 92-96, grabbing the occasional 99, though he's yet to really hit his velocity jump that so many have expected. It's an awfully unique heater with cutting action and some carry. Still, the upside and future velocity here could end up considerable. 

Bixby struggles to repeat and throw strikes, a common plague for pitchers his size. It may take time and seasoning, but this is a good arm to bet on as he matures. A change of scenery from TCU to Oklahoma in 2026 was made in the hopes to accelerate that development.

A 14th round selection by the Mets in the 2025 Draft, Smith has exciting two-way potential with athleticism and arm talent to burn. The sky is the limit for the 6-foot-5-inch bluechip. 

Smith has tools on both sides of the ball but teams seem to like him most on the mound. He generates above-average extension and has a loose arm, up to 96 mph. He'll rest 93-94 in bullpen showeing and is a fringy strike-thrower. 

Smith's slider has the highest upside of any of his offerings. He'll throw it firm, 83-85 with downward tilt out of a high slot. He's generated huge whiff rates on that pitch despite struggling to land it in or around the zone with much consistency. It's got plus upside and represents a real put-away secondary.

In the field, Smith is a long-strider with above-average feel for centerfield. He's flashed plus bat speed with exit velocities exceeding 113 mph at peak, however his feel for the barrel and consistency finding the fat part of the bat is a work in progress. He's also an above average runner.

Smith has avenues toward a big league role. A pro organization could deploy him in a number of ways. It's a project, but an exciting one at that.

Addari found himself draft-eligible after his first season at Illinois State -- 2025 -- but went unselected due to a lack of performance and innings. The stuff is intriguing, he's just been unable to transfer the scouting report to the back of the baseball card at this point.

Addari is purely a relief profile. It's scattered control and command, and walks can stack on him at times. Addari has reached back for another gear in 2026, now touching 96 at times with a wide angle, a lower slot and bordering on elite extension. His fastball shapes won't get analysts' attention, however he's mostly ditched the four-seamer these days in preference of a sinker that's taken a step over the winter. If his command improves, he's proven capable of missing bats in the zone. Addari generally lives 92-94. 

The slider is his go-to secondary, sharp at 81-84. His wider release helps generate lateral action. 

Addari is mostly a two-pitch guy, and all signs point toward a future in a pro bullpen. His 6-foot-6-inch frame and loose, whippy are suggest he could throw a bit harder in professional ball with strength gains. He will be 22 years old.

A long, lanky, lean 6-foot-6-inch righty, Shrum has a ton of weight and added strength gains on the horizon. For now, it's all projection. Up to 95 mph, the fastball has moderate carry and can sneak up on hitters at the top of the zone. Shrum pitches with an effectively wild style and can spray the fastball at times. It's streaky command that relies on tempo and deception to generate whiffs with the heater. 

His best pitch is without question an upper-70s changeup with parachute action losing all life at the plate. It comes off the fastball tunnel late and routinely has hitters offering foolish swings. It's a future plus offspeed weapon, maybe better. There's a fringier breaking ball that continues to be an emphasis in his development. It's a loose operation, a good athlete who moves fast on the mound and is routinely in the strike zone. The best baseball is ahead of Shrum. He will be 19.2 years old on draft day.

Lynam is an exciting infield prospect that continues to get better every time scouts see him. What was once a loud, noisy, complicated swing has quieted down considerably entering his senior year. A ferocious barrel tip, big leg kick and forward trunk tilt has been replaced with a more steady upright stance and balanced move forward. Lynam has always done a fairly nice job staying behind his front side and rotating hard. It's big, whippy, leveraged bat speed that gets to the pull-side with authority on a regular basis. Lynam has the look of a guy that could grow into above-average or better raw power thanks to fast, whippy, wiry strength and bat speed. 

Lynam plays the shortstop position for Gloucester Catholic, however most expect a move to third base at the next level. Lynam has plus arm strength and throws that carry through the first base bag. The first-step quickness, lateral mobility and actions as a whole are more befitting of a player at the hot corner. 

Lynam is an average runner. Most of his value at the next level will come from the bat. Should he make it to college, Lynam has been up to 91 on the mound and could get more run as a reliever for Auburn.

Romero is a lean right-handed pitching prospect with a super quick arm and longer levers who could eventually throw cheese some day. For now he lives mostly in the low-90s, up to 95, from an over-the-top arm slot creating riding action through the strike zone, as well as some late tailing action. It's a pitch that does well missing bats. 

Romero features two breaking balls, the slider currently the better of the two offerings. It's aa low-to-mid 80s bender that he does well snapping over the plate for strikes generating whiffs inside and outside of the zone. There's a bigger, loopier curveball that has been effective in stealing strikes and occasionally generating whiffs when bounced in front of the plate. There's some tunneling characteristics on that pitch that mirror the fastball and to a certain degree the slider that allows it to play up. 

Romero does things awfully easy on the bump and while there's a little effort and whack at release, scouts believe that should iron itself out over time with added weight and polish. It's a super loose arm, a good mover down the mound and high-level athleticism. Romero will need to continue throwing strikes if he's to reach his mid-rotation ceiling, but this is good clay and there's certainly a whole lot more coming.

A two-way talent, Rice has seen his impact on the mound surpass his offensive game, most scouts now believe his future lies on the bump.

Rice is lean, wiry and whippy on the mound with one of the fastest arms in the Southeast. Despite being conventionally undersized for the position, his arm speed and conviction has scouts in Georgia intrigued. There's some feel for pitchability here, varying tempos and deliveries depending on the baserunner situation. Rice also throws plenty of strikes.

The fastball generally sits 89-991 with some cutting action. He's run it up to 93 at peak. Rice's feel for keeping the baseball away from right-handers and boring the ball into left-handers' knuckles makes for plenty of soft contact. 

The slider is his best weapon, an upper-80s sweeping breaker that lives in the cutter tunnel for an extended period to the plate. Rice's command for the glove-side with both pitches forces some terrible swings from the opposition when he buries the breaking ball low and away.

For now, this is mostly two pitches, however he's worked to fold in a changeup/split against a few left-handed hitters. It's rarely deployed.

Rice's size may price him out of the 2026 Draft, however he'll likely be an immediate impact name at Auburn in 2027.

Ellis is a bit of a wunderkind on defense with fantastic actions on the dirt and arguably the best throwing arm in the class. Not many could rival arm strength readings posted by Carlos Correa at the high school level, but Ellis checked that box. Couple his defensive talents with plus speed and you've got a really dynamic athlete here. The bat is still a work in progress presently lacking the impact you'd like to see at this stage, but Ellis continues to get stronger and add good weight to his lean frame. He'll be a fun project for South Carolina who believe in the upside in the frame and the stick.

Be it not for a devastating knee injury in 2025, Takats probably doesn't return to school. He was highly regarded several weeks into that season but became too risky a draft asset for teams to select in 2025.

Takats has had a rather winding adventurous career to this point. Recruited as a two-way guy out of high school, almost everybody in the industry regarded Takats an intriguing left-handed pitching prospect entering the 2024 Draft. And most thought he'd stay that course at Bowling Green. But that wasn't to be. Takats bat immediately became the buzzy tool around campus earning him 36 starts for the Falcons as a true freshman. The physicality and tools bumped up entering his draft-eligible true sophomore campaign this spring. 

Takats immediate selling point is the 6-foot-5-inch frame and projectable length and size. He's long and wiry with fluidity in his athleticism. He's still learning how his frame works at the plate. The hit tool has components to dream on. Takats boasts average bat-to-ball skills and will flash above-average raw power leveraged by his size. His path is generally on the more shallow side and he can at times struggle to get to loft. When he catches the ball out in front and gears for loft.his production to the pull-side can be loud. Getting Takats into a more consistent mechanic place with his swing will be an emphasis in pro ball. It's in there, if not raw and unpolished. 

Takats does fight an uphill battle given his level of competition at Bowling Green as well as his limited sample in college baseball. There's also the issue of no track record with a wood bat. Takats has performed at a respectable level when faced with good spin and bigger velocity. He more than holds his own. But just about every aspect of his baseball card has been just good, not great, this year, and that's an issue when you're playing in the MAC. At least in the eyes of scouts. 

Takats gets high marks for his centerfield range, routes and footwork. He's got a shot to play centerfield, although Vegas odds would certainly suggest a more dynamic mover/athlete shifts him to a corner. His above-average speed will play anywhere.

Takats has similarities to 2024 draftee Eli Serrano out of NC State. You have to dream on the future and pay less attention to the present-day production. He's still just a third-year player, but it's been quite a path to this point. 

He missed the second half of the 2025 season with a significant leg injury. He's also already undergone Tommy John during his career as well as ankle injuries.

Steele split time with Ike Irish behind the plate for War Eagle in 2025 after transferring into the program that fall prior. He's a big-body backstop with physical tools. It wasn't enough to get him selected in his first draft-eligible year last summer. 

Steele immediately became a star in the SoCon League winning Coaches Freshman of the Year in 2023. He showed considerable power as a teenager blasting 16 home runs as a freshman. That diaper-dandy campaign vaulted his prospect status and eventually led to his transfer from Samford into the SEC and Auburn. Steele's power is legitimate. The exit velocity figures are loud and it's juice to all-fields. That said, few in college baseball can lift the baseball to the pull-side like Steele can. His understanding for launch and leverage truly stand out. 

Steele is a below average runner, though his burst out of the crouch is good and his average arm strength may allow his profile to stay behind the plate. Though he and Ike Irish swap back and forth behind the dish at Auburn. This is a fairly well-rounded player who has a chance to go on day two if a team buys into the ability to catch and survivability of the hit tool.

Mattison has really impressed, pounding the strikezone and handling his business on a consistent basis. The delivery is athletic and repeatable featuring a high leg kick and solid drive toward the box. The fastball lives in the low-90s with some armside run. 

Mattison began his career at Grand Canyon before departing for Kentucky for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign. 

His bread and butter is an upper-70s changeup that tunnels his fastball beautifully, dying and diving at the last second, locking up hitters on a consistent basis. Mattison doesn't yet spin a formidable breaking ball, but the two-pitch combo he currently possesses gets batters out and it's easy to dream on the athlete.

Baynes has the chance to own one of the best fastballs in the 2026 class. There's some polish in the control and command category that will be necessary to reach his ceiling, but it's legit stuff.

Baynes has already touched 98 mph, but it's not the sheer velocity that has scouts excited. Baynes launches from a 62 inch release height out of a 6-foot-3-inch frame. Combine the launch traits and velocity with the fact he's been able to sustain induced vertical breaks north of 17 inches at times and it's a potential unicorn fastball. Baynes also spins the fastball at above-average rates leading analysts to believe his stuff will translate to the pro ball. Strikes have been the bugaboo here, but when he's in or around the zone, whiffs have come in buckets. 

Baynes doesn't throw his slider often, but when he does it's generated considerable chase from opposing batters. It's firm, 84-86, with bigger two-plane break, occasionally morphing into a traditional sweeper.

He also hardly throws his changeup. When he's shown it there's been well-above average fading action and serious depth to the pitch too. 

Baynes has high-leverage traits. If the whole package comes together and he gets to a point where he's even effectively wild, he could be a priority reliever target in July.

Sefcik is an physical specimen on the dirt with thunderous bat speed in batting practice and a well-rounded game on the dirt. In terms of the offensive tools, while Sefcik showcases mammoth exit velocities in batting practice, he's yet to translate those gaudy figures to the field. A flatter bat path has limited his in-game power, more often ringing ball into the gaps for doubles. He avoids ground balls, but isn't a proficient hitter at backspinning the baseball yet. He's an ultra-aggressive hitter who tends to expand the zone at times causing his strikeout rates to bloat during cold streaks. Sefcik is a barrel-chested infielder with broader shoulders, and he lacks much physical projection left in his game. He's a couple tweaks away from unlocking pretty substantial in-game offensive upside. Teams will needs to decide if his physical frame and the adjustments needed are worth the investment now.

Williams has immense physical tools featuring double-plus run times and the projection of a future above average hitter/tone setter at the top of a lineup. 

While swing plane issues presently exist, Williams makes contact with most pitches thrown in the strike zone. Ground balls and woes against spin have diluted him impact, but there are athletic tools to tap into if the right team gets their hands on him.

A reasonably unheralded outfielder coming out of Ladera Ranch, California in 2023, Freeman immediately carved out a full-time role with Northwestern and flexed his muscles offensively. It's above average raw power with a tremendous feel to launch. That combination resulted in a surge of homers at times as a true freshman. Freeman has taken some time to adjust to the college game with his bat-to-ball skills showing streaky tendencies, especially against velocity. He's held his own against spin and the profile has an up arrow as he works deeper into his amateur career. 

It's a toolsy player with length and projection. Scouts like him.

An undersized right-handed pitching prospect, Ramsey has a big arm and the type of mentality that is required to pitch at the next level. He's been up to 96 in bullpen looks and will run a low-90s fastball by hitters consistently at the top of the zone. 

An upper-70s breaking ball is his best weapon, though he'll mostly only show it to right-handed hitters. There's also a shorter, cutter-like slider in the 84-85 range that he's shown more of a willingness to back-foot and back-door to left-handed hitters. 

Ramsey's control has been fringy along the tournament and showcase circuit the last two years, but seems to be taking a step in the right direction as he's gotten a bit stronger.

Williams is a smaller player with a slasher approach as a switch-hitter. He's got a ton of burst and bounce in his game, good for making tough plays on the dirt and getting big jumps out of the box and on the basepaths. He's got a shot at becoming a menace and a table-setter at the next level. Almost exclusively a contact hitter, Williams doesn't possess a ton of juice at the plate, but when he shoots balls down the line and into the gaps, his double-plus speed is capable of taking the extra base. Williams can truly hit from both sides of the plate and his overall profile reminds scouts of former Auburn second baseman Ryan Bliss. He is draft-eligible for the second time after getting selected in the 19th round by the Dodgers in 2024 but honoring his commitment to Florida State out of JUCO.

Lim is a crafty lefty with above average feel for four pitches. He'll mix it up and work to both sides of the plate to lefties and righties. The fastball will work up to 91, but generally sits 88-89 with tail and he'll occasionally sink the pitch. Lim likes to work away from lefties but we'll scatter the fastball a bit against right-handed bats. It's not a terribly dynamic fastballs and Lim doesn't miss a ton of bats with the pitch, but it serves its purpose in terms of working to get ahead in the count. His best secondary is the changeup and it's a good one featuring impressive whiff rates and chase rates generally reserves for breaking balls. Lim commands the pitch beautifully and does an exceptional job keeping the ball down and missing the fat part of the zone. It's a potential future plus pitch if the whole arsenal ends up ticking up a few notches in the velocity department. The slider and curveball melt together a bit, both thrown in the upper-70s. He likes to throw both pitches outside of the strike zone, but his misses can be dangerous at times. Both pitches have been effective in creating swing-and-miss, though neither pitch is above average yet; the curveball showing the most upside. Lim will need to continue pounding the strike zone as he lacks explosive fastball value. He's the type of college arm that carves for three years and finds himself selected in the first few rounds of the draft.

Following a big freshman year at Dayton where Lujo slashed .361/.415/.556 with nine homers and 17 stolen bases, he hit the transfer portal and headed for Athens in search of a bigger stage.

Lujo is a bat-to-ball artist who consistently runs borderline elite contact rates on pitches inside and outside of the strike zone. He's an aggressive hitter who will expand the zone now and again, at times sacrificing contact quality to put the game in motion. He has very few, if any, holes in his swing and can cover velocity, spin and offspeed pitches regardless of where they're thrown. He employs a slightly open stance with good balance and a calm demeanor at the plate. Lujo has flashed average bat speed and some believe he's capable of 15-18 homers as a professional if provided the opportunity and at bats.

Lujo was a primary shortstop in high school and brings athleticism to the hot corner. He moves well on the dirt with active feet, attacking the baseball. His hands and actions have improved as he's received continued reps. The arm strength is fringe-average with a lower slot featuring throws that tail and sink into the first base line. Errant throws are something Lujo has battled when forced to make plans on the move. Lujo is a capable third baseman, but might be forced off the position if the reliability of his throws doesn't improve. He looks to have the actions necessary to play a solid second base as well. That versatility would improve his draft stock.

Camacho will be awfully young for the class as a third-year collegiate. Just 20.7 years old, Camacho has put together an extremely impressive three-year stretch at Pacific and the University of San Diego that has scouts taking notice. 

The bat will certainly be Camacho's money-maker. A sweet-left handed swing, Camacho hit .307 with seven homers as a teenage sophomore in 2025 despite battling a gnarly thumb injury for most of the year. He boasts above-average bat-to-ball skills and has flashed plus raw power with peak exit velocities exceeding 112 mph. Camacho shows adjustability in the box, fouling pitches off and wasting pitchers' pitches, drawing long at-bats. There aren't any obvious holes in his swing at this stage, either. Camacho hands spin, he handles velocity and can take the barrel to all four quadrants, as well as putting balls outside of the strike zone in play with some authority. As a primary first baseman, he'll need to show more impact in games to hear his name called inside of the top five rounds, but scouts do like the hitter and the projection of the bat.

Camacho has feel around the first base bag and shows an understanding of game speed and urgency on balls hit at him. He handles foul territory well for his age and has the look of a first base prosect who could eventually be above average at the position. He is a fringe-average runner. 

Considering Camacho isn't yet 21 years old and has some physical strength projection in his frame, it stands to reason a team may take a shot on the left-handed slugger in July. That said, given the NIL landscape and Camacho's leverage, him returning back to school or transferring may end up just as financial advantageous.

Antigua can really, really hit. The body isn't very projectable and he's a bit positionless at the next level, but it's hard to argue with just how good the bat has been. He's got a shot at being a fringy defender at a number of positions going forward. There's the potential here for a plus hit tool, and that's certainly worth considerable value as we evaluate.

Kranzler is an exciting young right hander with a promising breaking ball featuring two-plane tilt in the low-80s, some throwing future plus grades on it. He's an explosive mover with a fastball that sits 91-93 and can grab 94, though it sits in a dead zone in terms of movement profiles. Kranzler gets high makeup and competitiveness grades. It's a profile that will likely be breaking-ball heavy and could end up in a bullpen role without capturing more value out of his velocity.

McLaddie really burst onto the scene late in high school, showing hitterish tendencies and a sweet, left-handed stroke. McLaddie will be awfully young for the 2026 class and has a chance to stick on the dirt thanks to some bounce in his actions and a quick-twitch first step. If the bat continues to progress forward, he's got a shot to be a hit-first gap-hitter with occasional pop.

After going unselected in the 2025 Draft, Story returned to High Point for a second go at it in 2026. He began his career at Wingate before transferring into High Point for the 2025 season. He's got a big arm with a fastball up to 97, routinely 92-93. It's a bit dead-zone in shape, but Story does generate value from his heater by way of a lower release and affinity for the top of the zone. 

Story's mid-80s changeup is arguably his best secondary, but a low-80s slider has come along the last twelve months too and scouts believe it'll ultimately unseat the changeup as his best weapon. Both pitches could conceivably become above average at the next level. The sweeping slider in particular is already flashing that kind of shape. 

Story will need to clean up with is fringy control for the zone if he's to prove capable of starting at the next level. Story generates above average extension down the mound and has unique release traits that should help bolster his draft stock.

Hartman is a barrel-chested, broad shouldered hurler with some projection left, though his present skillset is enough to sell scouts on the impending value. Hartman works up to 95, though he's ordinarily 90-93 over long outings with tremendous ride through the zone. The command for the fastball is still a work in progress, though he's largely in the zone. Hartman mixes in a two-plane breaking ball and a tumbling changeup, both of which show the ability to become eventual weapons. Commanding the baseball going forward will be important for the Lebanon, Ohio lefty.

A fourth-year outfielder for the Vols in 2026, Chapman went unselected in 2025 despite flashing some of the best raw power in the country. There's some rawness to his game, but he's taken a step each consecutive year on campus.

The bat speed stands out for Chapman. It's above average raw power and some of the best feel for the barrel in the SEC. His hard-hit rates and average exit velocity always stand out. That said, it's an aggressive approach with heavy chase rates and whiff rates that lead to questions of whether he can survive against advanced pro pitching. Most of his whiffs come outside of the zone with adjustability has been a problem. Chapman has something of a grooved swing. He's a healthy hitter on swings inside the zone. 

Chapman has played all three outfield positions but is more capable in right field where his above average arm strength and routes fit more comfortably.

Logar is an east-west starting pitcher prospect who relies primarily on a sinker/sweeper one-two punch. It's an interesting looks for hitters. A super-high leg kick and a big, long arm swing makes for a difficult time picking up the baseball out of Logar's hand. 

Logar's sinker has touched 95 and features considerable arm-side tail and sink. Logar holds his velocity well and routinely sits 91-93 into later innings. He relies on working the ball in and out of the strikezone as his lower release negates his shapes a bit. Logar refuses to elevate his fastball and tinker with a four-seam grip, something that might generate a bit more fastball value and a unique look for hitters. 

His sweeper is his best pitch and it dances hard off the sinker tunnel. It's been up to 86 with big sweeping shape and depth as well. It's got a chance to be plus in a bullpen role. Logar has thrown some cutters to keep hitters off his two primary offerings, and they're in a unique spot considering his pitch designs, but he'll likely need to throw that pitch a bit more firm with more sweep if it's to become an effective third pitch. 

Logar spent the first two seasons of his collegiate career at James Madison before transferring to Starkville.

Simay finds himself draft-eligible for the second time in two years. A fourth-year junior, he's looking to prove what he accomplished in 2026 was no fluke. 

Simay begun his collegiate career at Ole Miss where he played in just four games across two seasons tallying two hits. The lack of opportunity drove him to the transfer portal where he'd enroll at Calhoun Community College for the 2024 season. After posting a .363 average with 12 homers, Simay once again relocated, this time to Southern Illinois where he's been a stalwart in the Salukis lineup for two years. 

Simay is a barrel magnet. While it's only average raw power, Simay finds the fat part of the bat at an impressive rate. He's got super-quick hands in the box and has a hitterish look to his swing. It's a flatter path that limits his ability to hit the ball over the fence, but a swing adjustment or two at the next level could unlock 15-homer upside if he ever earns a full-time role inside a lineup. As presently constructed, Simay tends to run higher-than-average ground ball rates. He does have an adjustability in his swing, however, that helps him make plenty of contact outside of the strikezone when he's fooled. Simay's experience has helped develop a strong approach at the dish with low chase rates and low strikeout totals. If it all comes together in pro ball, he has a chance to be a reasonably high average, high-OBP shortstop who has the athleticism and foot speed to play the shortstop position at an average level. His average arm strength and lateral mobility suggest a rovering utility role on the dirt would be a fine fit.

One of the best pure bat-to-ball guys in the 2026 class, Myers hits absolutely everything posting elite contact rates both on pitches inside the zone and outside of it. He's a left fielder by trade with limited physical projection and size, but he profile a top of the order slash who can run high average and on-base numbers at the next level. Myers isn't a terribly quick runner, likely only solid average going forward. He doesn't figure to be a huge base-stealing threat.

Taylor saw an enormous growth spurt going into his junior year of high school prompting his stuff to take a major leap. Taylor tacked on major weight and muscle and developed the ability to bully hitters with a big fastball and burgeoning secondaries.

The fastball for Taylor has been up to 97 and it can be tough for hitters to pick up. He hides the ball behind his back thanks to a big, deep arm swing with enormous scap load and counter-rotation. Taylor explodes forward, landing slightly open at foot plant and slingshots the baseball through the zone with intent and tempo. He's got major spin capacity and can sizzle the heater through the top rail with tough angle, tail and occasional carry. It's got the makings of a plus heater, but commanding that pitch with better frequency will be an emphasis if he hopes to reach his ceiling.

A mid-80s slider is his best secondary. It's got diving action and some late lateral tilt. Taylor tends to spin the fastball better than he does the breaking ball, but there's some feel for shape. There's a mid-to-upper 80s changeup that he'll run away from left-handed hitters. It's probably the secondary in his arsenal with the best upside giving his arm action and fastball value.

Taylor has a reliever look for now. There's some effort through delivery, he lands open through release and components to his trunk tilt to be difficult to repeat across several innings while holding control for the zone. Taylor is a physical right-hander whose best role could be throwing gas late in games. He will be 18.5 for the Draft.

Smithwick, another young-for-the-class college bat, is lauded for his approach at the plate and a swing that is balanced. He's shown a willingness to go to all-fields, hitting both velocity and spin with authority in his prep career, though he's thus far shown streakiness in his ability to make consistent contact, especially in terms of battling off pitches outside the black. Smithwick has struggled considerably against advanced spin, a hole in his game he simply must rectify if he hopes to go in the top ten rounds in July. Most of his power is to the pull-side, showcasing some organic loft and extension when he can get out in front. 

Smithwick has athleticism and above average tools at the plate with a prototype body that should lend well toward the Oxford product sticking behind the plate. He was a mainstay behind the plate for Ole Miss from the jump thanks to strong receiving skills and the ability to smother grenades that bounce in front of dish. He hopped in the transfer portal and headed to Oklahoma State following the 2025 season.

Talavs is a very interesting starting pitcher prospect who checks a ton of boxes from the conventional scouting lens for his position. He has considerable fastball value with a heater that's been up to 96 and, at times, flashed extreme amounts of carry through the zone. He's struggled to repeat his release and his shapes will zig and zag all over the place, but when Talavs stays behind the baseball he can really hop a baseball through the zone. There's all the makings of a 'plus' fastball here with further time and seasoning. 

Talavs has mostly been limited to relief opportunities but should see extended reps and starts as his draft-date approaches. He produces above-average extension and repeats his operation well across all three of his pitches. The breaking ball has taken serious strides over the last twelve months and is now a legitimate weapon against right-handed hitters. He's also shown above-average control for the strikezone despite his arsenal being hit a bit harder than he'd like at times. 

Finding consistency in his release will unlock an entire new level of production for Talavs and that should surface in due time.

Bell has a lot of fans in the scouting community. The bat is a work in progress and adding impact in the box will be a priority, but on the dirt he's among the most polished, soft-handed infielders in the class. He projects to stay at shortstop and can make every play and every throw with buttery actions. There's a fluidity about Bell's game that can be difficult to find in the states, generally reserved for players who developed in Latin America. He's a name to track and a high-ceiling defender.

Lee is an extremely athletic righty up to 95 mph with some of the most impressive metric traits you can find in this class. The fastball has near perfect four seam efficiency with serious ride coming out of a low launch release. The split/changeup fizzles out at the plate and falls off the earth, tumbling in at less than 1000 rpms at times. Lee can spin a slider in there too, flashing above average with strong velocity, up to 85 mph. There's starter traits here and projection as well. To this point the performances haven't matched the "stuffiness" of his arsenal, though scouts in Southern California are convinced he's one of the better blocks of clay on the West Coast.

Laurel is an explosive, powderkeg athlete with loud tools all over his reports. There's a ton of strength packed into his 6-foot frame and it really shows offensively. There's big bat speed and lightning quick hands. Potential here for considerable power and it's already showing up in games. Laurel has a quiet setup with high hands and drops them into the slot, on-time for velocity and adjustable to spin. He's really muted his leg kick over the last year as well and it's helped the overall hit tool take a leap forward. Some of the highest level offensive tools in the class here. Laurel stands out on defense with double-plus arm strength and the ability to holds runners at their stations on fly balls hit his way. He's a fringy runner who doesn't figure to be dynamic tracking balls deep into the gaps, but Laurel makes the routine play with ease and does a nice job putting himself in a position to fire back into the infield coming through the baseball. He plays a violent, aggressive brand of defense on ground balls that get into the outfield with long strides toward the infield and a "test me" mentality. A really strong combination of tools here only lacking foot speed. Laurel will turn 19 years old a couple months after the draft.

Originally an East Tennessee State commit, Crabtree elected to go the JUCO route after not getting drafted in 2023. He landed at Pearl City CC, a program that has vaulted buckets of good arms into the Division 1 ranks after a year or two. A freshman campaign saw Crabtree punch 105 tickets and walk just 28 batters in a workman's campaign where he threw 76 innings as a teenager. He was the first pitcher at Pearl City to punch over 100 tickets in a single season in more than 15 seasons. And he did it as a freshman. That performance, alongside his projection and components to his pitching arsenal landed him in Knoxville. Unfortunately he didn't get the level of opportunity he was hoping for at Tennessee and once again transferred, this time to Southern Miss. 

Crabtree is more of a strike-thrower than a natural punch out artist. Everything coming out of vertical over-the-top slot, Crabtree works north to south with his arsenal. His fastball is 89-91 after the second or third inning of work, but he's been known to snag 95s here and there early. He'll hop the heater over the barrel and likes to work at the bottom of the zone. It's a fastball not too dissimilar from Stanford's Matt Scott from 2025. He pairs the heater with a diabolical upper-70s curveball with big, sharp break. Crabtree can on occasion get over-pronated on the breaking ball and create a screwball action. It's a unique look for hitters and it's a pitch that has consistently locked up good bats. There's also a mid-80s changeup that he likes to show left-handed hitters. It's a complete arsenal.

Crabtree has a loose arms and throws plenty of strikes. His stuff has continued to trend upwards and could work in a number of roles as a pro.

Gainous saw his stuff absolutely explode during his junior year. He tacked on some weight and muscle throughout his frame and saw the fastball velocity jump and his spin rates climb. He now represents one of the more physical, effective right-handed pitchers in the state of Georgia for 2026. 

Gainous has been up to 96 and will mix things up between a four-seam and two-seamer depending on the handedness of the opposition. The four-seam is most effective out of his over-the-top slot. There's some late life and hop when he stays behind that pitch and is landing it at the top of the zone. The two-seamer is launched from a lower three-quarter slot and features tail and some sink. Both pitches flash above average. 

The changeup is Gainous' best secondary. He sells it with arm speed and can tumble and fade that pitch away from lefties and has shown a willingness to throw it at the back foot of righties. Gainous has feel for killing spin too. 

There's a curveball and a slider, however both are mostly average for now. The slider is firm and short with average spin traits. The curveball has some hump in it at this stage, however he spins that pitch over the top with a bit more action. 

This is four pitches and enough strikes to warrant consideration in a future rotation. Gainous has a loose arm, feel for tempo and a durable frame. He's one of the more effective high school arms in the state of Georgia to track for the 2026 class.

Silicz is as projectable as they come from a starting pitcher perspective. He's long, and lean with broad shoulders and strength in his lower half. He looks like the kind of pitcher who should settle in closer to 230 pounds by the time he's done fully maturing. Silicz has an effortless delivery with an arm-slot slightly lower than what would be considered conventional for a pitcher of his size. He's up to 92 with some carry and late tail, but more commonly sits 89-90, pounding the zone with his fastball. He's shown promise from a curveball that possesses slightly above average spin rates and deep break that plays well off his heater. Considering the ease of the operation and the frame, Silicz has a chance to skyrocket up draft boards if his stuff blossoms in the months leading up to the event. He's one of the better arms on the West Coast this year.

Draft-eligible for the second year in a row, it came as a bit of a surprise that Andrews went unselected in 2025 considering his metrics and data-friendly pitch mix. 

Andrews is a physical right handed pitcher with a great body, and repeats his delivery well. The fastball currently sits in the low 90s, up to 94 with heavy sink and tail coming out of a high release. That steepness and strike-throwing ability has teams intrigued by the uniqueness Andrews could bring to a staff. 

His mid 80s sweeper is especially effective featuring considerable horizontal tilt and vertical depth. He spins the hell out of the baseball and has the tools to own a plus breaker. It's one of the more impressive metric breaking balls available in the 2026 class, especially valuable when taking into account his ability to start at the next level. Andrews has worked hard to establish a more impactful changeup, however he struggles to get to a shape that comes far enough off his fastball to make it a true out pitch.

This is a loose arm, a strike-thrower and a pitcher with moxy. While Andrews may never become a punch-out artist, his sinker/slider combo should provide him an impactful role at the next level.

A well-traveled righty, Pallares enters the 2025 draft just months away from his 24th birthday. He has zero leverage in this class, however he's certainly done enough as a redshirt senior to get an opportunity in professional baseball. Stops at Glendale Community College, UCLA and Cal State - Northridge led him to Loyola Marymount in 2025, an opportunity that he has seized and excelled with. 

Pallares is finally pitching in a starting role this year after doing the hybrid song and dance for much of his collegiate career. Fringy control for the zone has long held back his extended opportunities, and while his control and command haven't dramatically improved in 2025, they are better. Strikeouts are way up this year too. 

This is five pitches with a fastball up to 98. He'll sit 93-95 with some carry and tail, moderate spin and a launch slightly higher than league average. He throws the fastball for strikes at a healthy clip and misses enough bats and generates enough chase to suggest it may be average-or-better as a pro. The changeup is his go-to secondary; a mid-80s cambio with solid depth, killing spin effectively. It's a solid-average, maybe even above-average changeup despite a general lack of velocity separation from the heater. 

His arsenal is rounded out by a slider, curveball and cutter. The slider projects best. It's firm with some cutter-like bullet action. The curveball is a strike-stealer when he throws it in the zone and the cutter more often than not melts into the slider. 

Pallares' has found newfangled strike-throwing ability this year and is mixing it up with hitters. He's got a shot to be selected as a dramatic under-slot option on day two or three saving a team something in the range of $100k with the pick. The stuff is likely good enough to go right to High-A, and he'll have to due to his age.

Farr has a startling amount of projection left in his frame with long levers and a high waist. His best baseball is certainly in front of him. Farr is hitter-ish now, though he's turned up the bat speed this spring and is flashing game power, but there's more on the way given his current frame. He's showcased considerable raw power in batting practice, and scouts think he could grow into solid average (north of twenty bombs) homer upside at the next level. There's more whip and stretch from the left side of the dish, more hitterish as a right-handed bat. He's got solid zone-coverage and fights off or puts in play strikes he pulls the trigger on. There's some chase in his game, but it's not at alarming levels by any means. Scouts love what they've seen on the dirt where he's a glider with quiet actions and a legitimate chance to stick at shortstop.

LaSalle is a long, lean, strong performer with buggy, twitchy hips and explosive torque in his offensive game. A 19th round pick by the Royals in 2023, LaSalle elected to go to school where he's flashed big tools and even bigger projection at times. 

The raw power here is tremendous, though tapping into that raw power has been streaky at best. LaSalle extends beautifully through the baseball and showcases tangible physical upside in his swing. He can be an eager hitter with some chase in his game. He can get a little anxious at the plate and has a tendency to go after spin off the black at times, but it's more of a streaky habit than a player trait. LaSalle is an above average runner and could play second base, though most scouts like the bat a bit more in left field at the next level.

Smejkal is a well-rounded athlete with an athletic build and the ability to contribute and add value in a number of ways on the field. Most like the upside on the mound where a lightning fast arm has scouts forecasting mid-90s velocity in the future. It's a compact arm action that's worked up to 94 mph with some arm-side tail and sink. 

There's a slider and a curveball that melt into each other a bit, but at their best it's a low-80s slider with deep two-plane tilt. There's also a mid-70s changeup that'll he'll show to lefties, though it hasn't been as effective or utilized much in tournament looks. 

Smejkal has some effort and head-whack at release, something he'll want to clean up to help his durability going forward, though at just 165 pounds, that ironing may take place naturally with added strength. Some scouts like Smejkal at shortstop and at the plate where he showcases a simple swing, direct to the ball with a gap-to-gap mentality. He's technically sound on the dirt with a strong throwing arm and a real chance to play the shortstop position going forward. 

This is just a ballplayer whose best baseball is ahead of him as strength and maturation do their thing. Smejkal will be 18.5 years old for the draft.

O'Donnell has big arm talent, if not quite wrangled in yet. He's jumped between schools the last three years. Originally an Florida State signee, O'Donnell ended up enrolling at Florida SouthWestern State in 2024, but struggled to throw strikes and found himself transferring once again. He pitched a the State College of Florida, Manatee-Sarasota in 2025 and showed off big radar gun readings. That attention got him looks on the Cape and in the MLB Draft League, but O'Donnell went unselected in the Draft. Still just 21 years old, O'Donnell is looking to elevate his draft profile at South Florida with July in his sights.

A big, physical frame, O'Donnell can chuck the pill. He's touched 99 mph in the MLB Draft League and will sits 94-96 in his game outings on campus. O'Donnell's fastball owns a ton of ride and is plenty capable of missing bats inside the strike zone. It's a potential 70-grade heater if he can get the strikes in check. 

Walks and command woes have slowed O'Donnell's development in college. Entering the 2026 season, O'Donnell had 66 walks across 54.2 innings pitched. That has come alongside 67 strikeouts. It's well-below average control. 

O'Donnell has a big arm and a big fastball. At a minimum, he's going to be an undrafted free agent signee for a team looking to take a shot on the traits. If he can tap into even 40-grade control, he's got a shot to make a nice chunk of change toward the end of "Day 2" or on day three.

Bobo's athleticism stands ou in a big way on the bump. He's a quality mover with solid extension. It's a drop-and-drive operation with a fast arm that comes through on time. Bobo throws strikes with a three-pitch mix.

The fastball will get up to 93, however Bobo more comfortably pitching 88-90 after the third inning or so of work. There's some ride and tail on the heater, however it's not innately a bat-missing pitch right now. It serves its purpose inducing soft contact, filling up the zone enabling Bobo to get to his secondaries. 

The slider is bigger in nature. It's generally 75-77 and will climb up to tickle the low 80s when he shortens the pitch up. There's two planes with some late depth to get ground balls. A low-80s changeup is his go-to weapon against left-handed hitters. 

Bobo is a quality arm. He's a good athlete with athleticism and actions that project on the bump. The stuff will need to climb to hear his name selected in July, but it's a bright future regardless of his next stop.

After two seasons under Coach Savage at UCLA, Kim transferred to Fullerton seeking full-time opportunities in his draft-eligible 2026 season. 

Kim is an offense-first profile with a big, tall, strong presence in the box and a willingness to own the plate. Scouts would like to see him shorten up the swing a little bit to stay on time against tough secondary stuff, but the impact in his swing as currently constructed is without question. Kim carved out a role for himself within a deep Bruins program from the start and has received at-bats as a freshman, but never developed into a lineup mainstay. There's raw power in the profile that could eventually lend itself to average game power by the time he's draft-eligible. Kim has feel for getting the baseball in the air, however he expands the zone at an unhealthy clip causing his strikeout rate to bloat during colder streaks. He's especially susceptible against arms with polished secondary weapons. 

On the dirt Kim as continued to add weight and no projects to third base or first base going forward. The actions are still smooth, rhythmic and under control.
