He's a fringy runner with a fringy arm across the diamond, but it's enough to stay on the infield and should improve with added strength and maturation.

A big year at Mississippi State helped Sullivan elevate his draft profile in 2025, but he went unselected. Game power has trended backwards since transferring for USC Upstate, but the hit tool has proven plenty capable in the SEC. 

Sullivan is a bat-only prospect. He makes tons of contact, hardly never expands the zone and has flashed solid average raw power. He's more of a barrel magnet than he is an outright slugger. He's unlikely to be a guy who pummels 20 homers per season at the next level, but he should run steady batting average and on-base clips. His feel for the fat part of the bat should push his extra-base counter up too. 

Sullivan's biggest wart is his lack of defensive value. He's a designated hitter who has played sparingly at first base and in the outfield. He profiles as a "day three" bat-only prospect who could be used to save a team some money considering his age (23).

The younger brother of 2024 first round pick Bryce Rainer, Colten is a force on the mound with a better chance to pitch than hit going forward. Given his premium 6-foot-6-inch frame, he's a player worth betting on. 

The stuff has ticked up for Rainer as he's gotten bigger and stronger. Already touching 95, he projects to throw a good bit harder with his big-time athleticism and frame on the mound. It's a fastball that tails away from left-handed hitters and can miss bats at the top of the zone thanks to a lower-than-expected slot from the 6-foot-6-inch righty. Rainer has a longer arm action with a wide elbow spiral. His command will come and go. If he can get to average control/command, his stuff will play.

A mid-80s with bullet, diving shape is his best secondary presently, however a mid-80s changeup is rapidly closing the gap and will likely end up his best secondary in due time. It's a pitch that works well with how his fastball behaves. 

Rainer is going to throw pretty hard. It may end up in the bullpen due to his feel for the zone and quality of strikes, but he's got plenty of time to buck that perspective label. Rainer will be 18.6 years old for the Draft.

Hamilton has long been considered a big prospect in scouting circles thanks to his abilities on defense, as well as his bloodlines. A premium runner with soft hands on the dirt, Hamilton best projects at second base where his throwing arm won't be tested quite as much, but his lateral mobility will be valued. Offensively, Hamilton shows flashes of line-to-line power, but too often relies on his speed to get on base. More impact at the plate could push his stock up boards. 

He missed much of his freshman campaign in 2024 recovering from a torn ACL. Hamilton struggled to earn full-time run in 2025 recovering from that sam injury and was mostly used as a pinch runner. He went 0-for-3 in his three at-bats at Vanderbilt as a sophomore. That prompted a move into the transfer portal landing him at Duke.

Takeuchi has a beautiful right-handed swing, and has increased his physicality over the last calendar year. That said, there are still questions on the overall impact in the bat, and whether he'll be able to stay at second base. The hit tool has been streaky on campus and he's shown a more aggressive approach at the plate than he had during his prep days. Proponents of the profile see a short, compact swing with equal power to all-fields and budding athleticism and strength. The final product may be a solid-to-above average defender at third base with an average hit tool and fringy raw power.

An immediate force at Louisiana-Monroe as a true freshman, Winfield showcases a pretty left-handed swing featuring above average raw power and more polish than most players his age. Winfield posted healthy contact and chase rates as a teenager in the Sun Belt Conference en route to an invitation to play for Texas in 2025, but he struggled resulting in him landing in the portal once more. Houston is his home in 2026. Winfield is hoping to clean up whiff rates and chase rates that ballooned on him as a sophomore, nullifying the raw tools that make his game so exciting. 

He is a choppy runner with above-average speed and shorter strides, but he's a strong athlete who takes clean routes to the ball. Despite his already stout, physical frame, Winfield still has projection in terms of raw power. He has an average arm and likely projects into left field as a pro, though some evaluators are bullish enough on the athlete to consider the thought of giving him run in centerfield now and again.

Blessed with a big, physical frame and an even bigger fastball, Calhoun has the clay of guy who could see his stock soar. He's pitched primarily out of the bullpen for the Rebels during the early parts of his career, but is taking on an expanded role as his draft approaches. 

Calhoun looks a bit like Emerson Hancock on the mound. It's a slingshot three-quarter slot with a fastball that explodes out of his shoulder. He works down the mound very well with impressive extension, athleticism and tempo. Calhoun has been up to 96 and comfortably rests 94-95 with carry through the zone. Over extending-inning showings, Calhoun is more 92-94. His capacity for spin stands out helping generate some of the bigger shapes he's imparting on the baseball. Calhoun's heater is a bat-misser and a pitch that should take to professional baseball well. 

The breaking ball has teeth upside if its usage takes a jump. He'll sit 82-83 with enormous two-plane shape. It's an exceptionally deep breaking ball that he'll sweep away from right-handed hitters. He tends to broadcast the pitch a bit by shortening his stride and changing his slot a tick, but with tinkering the capacity for a plus breaking ball is in the tank. 

Calhoun has also flipped over a handful of changeups in Oxford and he's shown the ability to create some arm-side tailing action too. It's too firm as presently constructed, but there's some foundation to build upon here. 

The biggest thing holding back an ascension in Calhoun's draft stock is below average control and command. He's walked to many batters in his Ole Miss career. Should he learn to iron that out and show the ability to work through a lineup twice without his stuff and feel deteriorating, he could see his name climb higher up boards.

The book on Jensen is the hit tool and the frame. Scouts are super-intrigued by just how much more physical Jensen could eventually become. While his lower half has filled out, there's still room in his shoulder and upper-body to add muscle and strength. The long levers and high waist point toward a hitter who could eventually play the game closer to 230 pounds and the subsequent power gains should come with it. His long, athletic frame stands open in the box facing the opposing pitcher, closing off his front shoulder and lead-leg during his stride allowing him to use the entire field. He's an intimidating presence.

To this point in his career Jensen has lacked the raw power you'd expect from a player of his size. It's been mostly fringe-average bat speed. Jensen has seen a jump in his bat speed this season after spending six weeks at Driveline during the winter. He'll need to flash more consistent exit velocity peaks if he's to become a priority in the top-ten rounds. The hit tool is reasonably polished. He could stand to sacrifice some bat-to-ball in an effort to hit the baseball harder.

Jensen has split time between first base and third base, the former being the more likely outcome at the next level. He is a sneaky athlete who can post fringe-average run times. That said, Jensen lacks first step quickness and his arm strength likely won't top that of a more polished defender in professional ball.

Jensen is draft-eligible for the second time after going unselected out of Cornell as a junior in 2025.

It's been a rollercoaster for Bing. He tore his UCL and required Tommy John surgery during his junior year in his high school. He used his senior year to recover and decided to enroll at McLennan CC to get back on the bump. After throwing over 70 innings as a freshman, punching 75 tickets along the way, Bing committed to the University of Texas and enrolled in Austin in 2025.

Bing is a low-slot lefty with a low-effort, repeatable delivery that allows his arsenal to carry deep into his outings. He demonstrates a natural feel to pitch with a four-pitch mix, all of which he lands for strikes. The fastball will touch 91 with some carry and tailing action. He'll manipulate the shape depending on the batter too. Evaluators think Bing could reach back for the occasional mid-90s radar gun reading as his arm-strength continues to come all the way back.

Bing's arsenal consists of a low-to-mid 80s changeup that flutters as it approaches the plate. It darts off the fastball tunnel late with decisive fading action. It's got a shot at becoming an above-average weapon. Bing likes to play with the shape of his breaking ball too. It's generally a low-80s sweeping slider that he'll throw at the back foot of right-handed batters and will swing away from lefties. It too has a chance to blossom into an above average pitch. 

Bing's natural feel for pitching and his ability to land everything where he wants points toward a high floor starter or swing man at the next level.

Marsh is a twitchy middle infielder who derives his value from his ability to play on the dirt as well as run. The defense is sound at shortstop with quick-twitch actions, range and the ability to play under control. Marsh gets a great first step in either direction, gobbles up ground balls with consistent hands and footwork and slows the game down on his throws to first. It's solid-average arm strength, but his throws possess carry and are on-target. 

The speed plays well on the offensive end where Marsh can burn down the baseline and steal extra bags once on. He's a fidgety hitter who stings baseballs into the gaps and the speed makes allows him to take the extra base. Marsh has below average raw power and doesn't figure to be the type of player to slug beyond balls hit down the line and dropped into gaps. He can occasionally turn and burn on a mistake heater or a looping breaking ball, but it's unlikely to be a large part of his game at the highest level.

Moore is an imposing righty who can rush it up to 96 in bullpen sessions. He's more commonly 91-92 and can carry the ball a bit atop the zone. It's an average fastball with average utility. 

The breaking ball that can exceed 3000 rpm with big downer shape and sweeping tilt. He throws it hard too, 80-83, up to 86 at times. It's an above average breaker that has generated impressive whiff and chase rates throughout his collegiate career. There's mid-80s changeup with strong two-plane tilt and some late depth as well, however he hardly throws it. 

Moore's strike-throwing ability has improved year after year, however injuries have slowed his ability to gather momentum. He transferred from Virginia to Florida State after the 2025 season seeking a fresh start and a new voice after Brian O'Conner left the program.

Lessard reclassified from the 2027 class into the 2026 class and will be 18.8 years old on draft day. He's a bat-first prospect with huge raw juice from the right side. Lessard is a sight to take in at the plate. He sets up from an unorthodox squated setup with an open orientation to the pitcher. He anchors extremely hard into his back side and generates a ton of rotational torque off his back hip/heel. There is some noise in his swing with waggle and wrap that can get him out over his skis against spin, but when Lessard is on a pitch there are few players in the class who can tattoo the ball like he can. He'll battle the pitcher at the plate fouling off several pitches in the zone to stay alive in anticipation of a mistake. He's susceptible to chase outside of the zone and presently lacks some of the adjustability necessary put those balls in play, but when he's swinging at pitches in the zone he hardly ever whiffs. It's a steep path with the goal to lift and launch to the pull-side. 

Defensively, Lessard has plenty of arm strength and profiles just fine into the outfield if he's forced to shift out there over time. His arm action behind the plate can get long at times prolonging his catch-and-release, but at this stage in his baseball career he makes up for that hitch with pure arm strength in many cases.
ATHLETIC TESTING

Ty Tillery is going to throw very hard. It's still coming, but the velocity ceiling is clear as day. Already up to 94 with late tail and sink, Tillery abuses the strike-zone with a barrage of fastballs that feature late teeth and knuckle-breaking shape. The arm swing is long, but it's ultra-athleticism and Tillery consistently puts him in an explosive position at foot plant. The release has some crossbody to it, but that does help him hide the ball better than most of his peers. 

Tillery also throws a low-80s slider with late action and two-plane bite. It'll be an important pitch going forward as Tillery's fastball isn't necessarily a bat-misser as much as it is an effective weapon to induce weak contact. This is a very fast arm with reasonably low effort. It could end up a bullpen arm in a high-leverage role, but Tillery will certainly carve out a role at the next level in one manner or another. He's very fun to watch.

Everly is a rhythmic hitter with wiggle and twitch in his swing. He's short into the zone and creates stretch, long through the zone with power to the pull-side. Everly does a nice job of getting his foot down and reacting to what's thrown his way. He's adjustable and has the ability to keep his hands back, firing when a mistake presents itself. Everly has been a swing tinkerer the last couple of years. He seems to show up to the yard with a different swing every weekend. At times he's got a neutral, traditional setup. Other times he'll stand more straight up and slightly open his stance to see the pitcher better. Settling into a consistent routine will be important as scouts work to decipher the offensive tools and upside. 

Everly is at least an above average runner and may be a tick quicker than that. He's got strong actions on the dirt and projects to end up at either second or third base at the next level; the latter being where most evaluators forecast. 

Everly will barely be 18 years old on Draft day and has a chance to get paid in the Top 100 picks if he presents a polished product as July approaches.

Allen arrived at Wright State and immediately became a force within the Raiders pitching staff as a freshman. In 2024 he threw 25.1 innings and punched 29 tickets, issuing just 11 free passes.

Allen is primarily a two-pitch merchant. It's a big fastball that's been up to 97 and will comfortably rest 91-94 across multiple innings. It's not the sexiest heater from a metrics perspective, but Allen has still manage to post close to elite whiff rates with the pitch. He's an exceptional athlete and a fast mover down the bump. He creates a ton of extension and hides the ball nicely with an early hand break and tight arm circle. His velocity seems to sneak up on hitters despite not overwhelming them with dynamic shape. Allen does spin his entire arsenal, including the fastball, quite well, so there may be some low-hanging fruit to get the pitch performing even better with more formal development.

Allen's slider has real teeth and it's got a chance to eventually present as a 'plus' weapon. He can really spin the breaking ball, approaching 3000 rpm at times, but comfortably sitting north of 2800 rpm. Allen leaves that pitch in the middle of the plate too often severely dampening its effectiveness. Finding more feel for the glove-side should unlock far more effectiveness. 

Allen has a changeup he's barely thrown. If he's to start at the next level, showing scouts the ability to move the baseball to the arm-side against left-handed pitchers will be critical. His athleticism and explosiveness can be something impossible to teach. He's pretty clearly a draft prospect and a player development ball of clay.

Tucker Long is precisely what Iowa pitchers look like these days. It's nasty. He's a ultra-low launch righty who hides the ball well with a three-pitch mix; all of which are present and effective. The fastball will grab 93 and live 88-90 with tremendous life through the zone. Long's mid-80s sweeping slider is tough for hitters to pick up out of the hand and he'll deploy it to either side of the plate. It'll end up a plus weapon in due time. The changeup might have the highest upside of any of his three weapons though it's still being developed. It'll flash plus and could project better than that. Long has a super fast arm and athletic qualities in his delivery that are next to impossible to teach. Better still, he'll barely be 18 years old on draft day. If the velocity ticks and Long can prove he can start, it's day one characteristics. It's similar profile to Levi Sterling from the 2024 draft. High-octane upside.

Solis is an arm-talent reliever with a fastball up to 98 sitting in the dead-zone with shape. Solis doesn't fool hitters too much with his velocity despite living 94-96. Part of that is due to below-average extension. He also has a tendency to show the ball early in his delivery. Solis does have a highly-effective low-80s slider that features considerable diving action. It's been particularly effective. He's a fringe-average strike-thrower who can go through cold snaps issuing free passes. Considering his general lack of athleticism on the mound and lack of fastball production to this point, Solis projects as a low-leverage reliever at the next level.

DeCremer is nightmare fuel for hitters. He features a lot of moving parts and deceptive elements in his delivery. He's got a lightning quick arm with tons of life on his fastball. He's been up into the mid-90s with electric shape. He hides it well and it explodes at the plate. He'll really keep hitters off balance with a low-to-mid 80s slider with depth and some horizontal tilt. It comes out of the same slot as the fastball, but goes the opposite direction. 

For now, DeCremer has the look of a reliever, but he's a very good athlete and could end up in a rotation. It's not all that dissimilar from the operation that has made Mike Clevinger successful throughout his career.

MacDougall is a steady receiver of the baseball with strong framing skills, especially laterally. He's got softness in his hands and controls the temperament of his pitchers well. It's average arm strength and pop times that are on the fringy side. 

MacDougall's bat-to-ball skills stand out in a big way. He's a mature hitter with a patient approach. He hunts fastballs and doesn't miss them. It's fringy raw power at best, however his pitch selection and emphasis on elevating the baseball does help get the most out of his raw power. 

MacDougall projects a platoon catcher at the next level with bat-to-ball skills and some ambush tendencies that could help him lose a handful of balls over the fence each season. His arm strength will be tested in the new meta of Major League Baseball, but he does many other things as a catcher well.

Reeder is a fiery competitor with one of the louder track records of any profile in the 2026 class. He's a distinguished starting pitcher prospect with several complete game shutouts on the back of his baseball card and a propensity to pitch long outings with high pitch counts. Reeder has touched 94 but will generally rest 88-91 with arm-side run and sink. He's tinkered with working in a four-seamer at the top of the zone as well. It's a full arsenal featuring a changeup that fades hards into the feet of right-handers complimented by a slurvy breaking ball with more depth than lateral tilt. 

Reeder's delivery likely needs a new coat of paint if he's to start as a professional. It's arm-talent heavy with more of a thrower operation rather than conventional pitching mechanics. It's a short-extension slingshot delivery landing way open helping to generate the arm-side life he achieves. As he continues to add strength and works to polish out some directional inconsistencies at release, Reeder could be a guy who sees his velocity explode, especially in a relief role. He will be 19.2 years old for the draft.

Winston possesses some of the best bat speed in the class. It's a ferocious right-handed swing that produces top-of-the-charts exit velocities and premium game power. Pennant isn't growing into the ability to hit the ball over the fence, it's already very present.

His profile does come with swing and miss, as it to be expected from a player of Pennant's size and archetype. He sells out for impact and that can leave him susceptible to spin. Pennant's swing can get long when he's fooled, causing him to get off balance and finish over his toes. Still, when he works the count and gets ahead, the results can be jaw-dropping at times. Pennant will need to refine his approach and become more consistent, but the physical tools are here.

A primary outfielder, Pennant projects a fringy defender with heavier steps and mechanics in a corner. He's got average arm strength, buoyed a bit by arm accuracy that stands out -- he puts the ball on the bag. He's got a chance to stick in the outfield, however a first base outcome is possible.

Pennant is a fringe-average runner.

The right-right high school outfield prospect is a tough demographic, especially when it comes with swing and miss. Still, Pennant's production has been so impressive at times, his name could get called in July, especially if he's willing to take an affordable bonus.

Stanley is a long, lanky righty with a ton of growth ahead of him in a lean frame. A big-time athlete on the mound, Stanley has a electric, whippy arm action that is a little long in the back, but he controls four pitches well and maintains his balance through finish. The fastball works up to 93, sitting 89-91 most days with natural cutting action. He flashes a deep curveball in the upper-70s, as well as a low-80s slider with two-plane break featuring more depth than sweep. He'll show a changeup, though it's firm and lacks the separation off the heater to be a real weapon right now. Stanley is a projection arm who could work into the mid-90s with time and added strength. A 20th round selection by the Rays in 2023, he elected to head to BYU. He has since transferred to Utah State.

Hachman offers one of the better fastballs in the entire class, especially as a left hander. Operating out of an over-the-top vertical arm slot with a ton of arm speed, the Missouri Tiger will live in the low-90s with arm side run and has touched 97 in the past. He's shown impressive feel for both a curveball and changeup that work well off of the fastball and miss a ton of barrels. Ton of projection left in his long-levered frame combined with high-level pitchability. Hachman was called "one of the toughest at-bats you can imagine" by his peers in high school. Commanding the baseball with more consistency will be key toward determining where he fits in the draft. He tore his UCL months before his freshman campaign at Arkansas and missed virtually his entire first year with the program. He then transferred to Kentucky in the summer of 2024.

One of the most gifted athletes in the 2026 class, Horvath can do a little bit of everything on the baseball diamond. Scouts are split on whether his future is on the mound or in the field, but a case can be made on both fronts. 

Offensively, the tools are big. He's a plus runner with a long, projectable frame. It's plus-to-double plus arm strength that plays in all three outfield spots. His possesses raw bat speed in the plus to double-plus range. It's an unpolished, brutish swing that generates big exit velocities and ringing extra-base hits with over-the-fence impact. His operation in the box seems to vary from swing to swing, but he's shown feel for the fat part of the bat. There's a path to project an impact hitter here. Questions remain on where the hit tool will buoy but if scouts are convinced he can ever get to an average hit tool at the next level, he'll be a popular name in the Draft. 

On the mound Horvath has been up to 93 but more commonly sits 89-90. Strikes have been an issue from the righty in tournament settings and he's yet to hone in on a consistent breaking ball. The arm talent is fairly obvious, the polish is what'll need to come next.

Maybin, son of MLB veteran outfielder Cameron Maybin, possesses some of the same tools that at one point made his father the No. 1 overall prospect in baseball. It's a long, lanky, athletic build with strength and projection tip to tail. There's considerable bat speed here with budding power being showcased in BP settings already. Maybin continues to add strength and is one of the more imposing bats in the class at this stage when he's putting the ball in play. Maybin crushes fastballs, but has been streaky in terms of identifying and impacting spin. Patience and continued reps against high-level pitching should conceivably see his overall hit tool jump. Maybin's speed really plays in-game too. While it might only be above average foot speed at present, the body and overall athlete point toward a guy who should keep his value on the base paths into pro ball and could grow into 'plus' speed. He's also a flashy defender who figures to handle centerfield or shift to a corner where he'd be a valuable asset as he adds more strength and mass. Maybin has the look of a Justin Upton type of player at the next level. The hit tool still has something to prove, but this is high-level traits. Maybin will be 18.8 years old on draft day.

Alm is a tooled up hitter with traits to impact the baseball, and project more slug on the way. He's got athleticism to burn in the field too.

Alm sets up with an open stance in the box and creates big stretch with an exaggerated forward move and bigger leg kick. He separates hard at foot plant and rotates as good as anyone in the country. The intent and violence in Alm's swing can get him disconnected at times when facing pitchers that can spin the baseball, however he's shown very well against velocity in his amateur career. It's a longer swing, something he'll need to shore up as the stuff continues to trend upward.

Alm's greatest strengths may be in the field. He's a plus runner with above average arm strength and full-bore aggression on how he attacks the baseball. Alm can play a bit out of control at times, but when reeled in, his athleticism shows out in a big way.

As Alm gets stronger and doesn't have to work quite so hard to get to his impactful tools, the whole package should come together.

Nolan Souza is the rare, premium prospect coming off the islands of Hawaii. He's got a buttery smooth swing with elite-level hip separation, suggesting he's going to age into serious game power. He's already impacting the baseball, but it could continue to develop more and more as he adds weight and physicality. Up 15 pounds since arriving to campus, he's flashing plus raw power and that could eventually reach a 70 grade. Souze has had trouble with his bat-to-ball on campus and that's exacerbated his ground ball rates too. While he's hitting the ball extremely hard, making contact has been a challenge at times, as has been impact the baseball with backspin. Souza has particularly struggled against bigger velocity and spin leading some to believe it's just an entire adjustment to the collegiate game that's taking place. He's a big frame and will almost certainly slide over to third base or a corner outfield role as he fully matures, but he moves well and could stick on the dirt longer than most anticipate. This is a pretty premium athlete with most of his upside still ahead of him. 

A nasty shoulder injury sidelined Souza for much of the 2025 season. He'll look to get back on the saddle in 2026.

A transfer by way of the Palouse in the Pacific Northwest, Johnstone put together a steady career at Washington State before transferring to Nashville for the 2026 season. He is 23 years old and finds himself draft-eligible for the third year in a row. 

Johnstone is an elite bat-to-ball artist. Whether inside the zone or outside of it, if Johnstone is swinging, he's likely putting the game in motion. He's a patient hitter who hardly ever expands the zone, however he can get antsy late in counts and hasn't yet shown a willingness to turn his patient approach into impressive walk rates. Johnstone seeks to put the game in motion, but he's more than willing to see a few pitches before electing to pull the trigger. There's not much raw power or bat speed to speak of here as Johnstone owns underwhelming exit velocity data. That said, he's got just one full year of playing time under his belt and some believe that consistent playing time may allow him to unlock more 'A-Swings' in 2026 and beyond. His swing plane is ultra-efficient allowing him to back-spin pitches to the pull-side and uncork the occasional homer. That said, Johnstone more commonly uses the whole field and doesn't aim to lift-and-launch.

Johnstone does have solid-average arm strength and is a solid-average runner with a quick first step. He takes good routes to the baseball and is comfortable in the outfield. He may be forced to left field by a more dynamic defender in due time, but he's more than capable of handling the role at the '9'.

Veasey was a true two-way player entering Alabama but has since dedicated himself to a bullpen role at the collegiate level. And for good reason, his stuff is sick.

Veasey's fastball has a chance to be a dynamic out-getter at the next level. He's capable of inducing some pretty sublime shapes on the heater. Veasey will grab north of 20 inches of induced vertical break regularly with the fastball, cutting the baseball at an extreme level. It's huge stuff, however unrefined. Veasey control and command are both below average, costing him opportunities to showcase his stuff in leverageable spots. If he can get the heater to even fringy command, it's big value on the pitch. 

Veasey's slider has a chance to be equally dynamic. It's 82-84 with big depth and some lateral movement. Veasey generates above average spin on the breaker, however he tends to shorten his stride and broadcast the pitch a bit resulting in more command woes. He's struggled to land the breaking ball in the zone. Finding the ability to repeat his operation will be key in approaching his ceiling. 

Veasey's athleticism, spin capacity, extension and fastball value on paper all check a lot of boxes. His rawness on the mound is stopping him from becoming a bigger weapon. That will come in time. Veasey will be 20 years old for the Draft, but turns 21 just a week later.

The younger brother of Angels first rounder Reid Detmers, Parker is another broad-bodied righty with a budding fastball up to 93 and a breaking ball that features enormous sweeping action and some depth, generally thrown in the 76-77 mph bucket. Detmers has a short-arm release that presents some natural deception. He's more polished than most of his peers at this same stage with feel for the edges of the strikezone.

Dietrich is a long, lanky lefty with stuff that has slowly ticked up over the course of his amateur career. Scouts are projecting a velocity jump in the coming years due to his arm speed, athleticism and frame. Dietrich has been up to 92 with a gnarly sweeping slider and a changeup that possesses some fade off the fastball tunnel. It's all about projection with this one and the ability to command the baseball in the future.

Robert is a true four-pitch starting pitcher prospect who has gradually added better and better stuff since enrolling at Coral Gables. He possesses above average athleticism, a long-strider down the mound and throws strikes. He checks boxes. 

Robert has been up to 96 with a fastball that lacks bat-missing shape, but the velocity continues to trend upwards. Unless he scraps the four-seamer and commits to a two-seam sinking heater, Robert is unlikely to ever possess better than an average fastball. Robert's sweeper and curveball are both very good offerings. The sweeper sits 81-84 with considerable lateral sweeping action, as well as strong vertical depth. His curveball is even bigger and nearly just as firm. It's performance stimulated by a higher-than-average release height. Robert also throws a changeup that has been average and slightly effective thanks to how closely it resembles his current fastball shape. 

Without a more definitive fastball, Robert will likely struggle to become better than a mid-leverage reliever or quad-A starter. Should he commit to sinking the baseball, a future exists as a No. 5 starter or swing-man in a bullpen. Robert missed most of the 2025 season and expects to miss a good chunk of 2026 with an elbow injury.

Menendez is a big, burly lefty with a fastball that has seen tremendous gains in recent years, now brushing 97. He'll live 92-93 with life and will mix in a big, power breaking ball in the low-80s. Menendez really hides the ball holding coil in the back and utilizing a short-arm action that keep the ball behind his ear until release. It's a tough arsenal to pick up out of the hand.

The first thing that pops when catching Jake Hooker throw is just how easy the ball comes out of his hand. It really explodes and sneaks up on hitters late. In bullpen settings, Hooker has been up to 95, sitting 92-94 with some armside run and sink. Hooker will need to find a bit more dynamic shape in his fastball going forward as it too often can sit in a dead zone. His best pitch is a mid-80s slider with hard, sharp, two-plane bite that really profiles off the fastball well. That breaking ball has been up to 87 and projects plus if he can continue to command his two-best weapons. He'll mix in a mid-to-high 80s changeup that lacks separation and definitive shape, but has flashed fringy/usable at times. Hooker has a live arm and a bit more projection, though command and feel for quality strikes currently holds the profile back. Tons of maturation ahead of him in the coming years.

Black finds himself draft-eligible for the second time in two years after going unselected as a junior at Georgia in 2025. 

Black burst onto the scene as a true freshman in 2023 providing impact and polish to a Texas-Arlington lineup that shined. He has since transferred to Georgia where his tools continue to flash. A left-handed hitter with a line-drive approach, Black boasts some of the most impressive overall contact rates in the country, even moreso when facing top-shelf velocity. It's a simple left-handed swing with an upright stance and moderate leg lift. He has some rhythm and waggle that helps trigger his timing. Black is one of the more demonstrated hitters in the country capable of using the whole field with some opposite-field power in the bat as well. He can get beat on pitches in on the hands, but he's done a nice job fouling those pitches off, extending his plate appearances. He's a cookie killer who boasts massive slugging numbers on pitches down the middle-third of the plate. However, when he offers at pitchers pitches there's way too many ground balls. Improving his ability to do damage on pitches on the corners will be a point of emphasis as the draft approaches. 

Defensively, Black is a sure-handed second baseman with a flair for the highlight reel play. He's only a fringe-average runner, and his physical frame will likely keep him in that bucket going forward. It has sometimes limited his ability to get to foul pop-flys behind the first base bag, but when he can get to the spot he's shown good field awareness and makes the play. He's got solid average arm strength capable of making just about every play at the position. His athleticism holds him back from making the tough backhanded ranging play to his right at times. Black has demonstrated a strong internal clock and hardly ever rushes things on the dirt. There is a lot to like in this player and profile. If the raw power ticks up and Black is able to improve his ability to barrel balls on the corners as July approaches, it's potentially a top-ten round pick.

Scouts love the pure stuff and intensity Keenan brings to the bump. It's a fastball into the mid-90s that explodes out of hand, though his shape wavers as the game moves along. Command for the pitch has been hit or miss. Keenan has the ability to break off a big, slurvy breaking ball that's made guys look foolish as he possesses conviction in the breaking ball. It's a fairly long arm action in the back, so shortening that up and tightening his elbow spiral may help scouts convince themselves this is a long-term starter profile, as well as improving control and command for his arsenal. Mechanics aside, the pure stuff here is awfully good and the projection is obvious.

Fisher has been a loud performer going back to his high school days. He can really hit, and the added muscle he's packed on since arriving to Tallahassee has only added to the offensive impact potential he possesses. He uses the gaps and has tremendous extra-base power, with almost all of his over-the-fence power being to his pull-side. Fisher does a great job of getting extended and putting the barrel on the ball, sending his hands through the zone much like how Matt Holliday used to operate.  Fisher is a below average runner with a fairly maxed out frame. He's likely to end up at second base where his lateral burst won't be tested quite as much. He's got quick hands and is a good enough athlete to throw from multiple angles. There's a shot Fisher is a DJ LeMahieu type of performer, though admittedly much smaller in stature. You're buying the bat here and betting it's polished enough to result in a big league regular.

Bell is a promising young left-handed prospect with pitchability on the bump. He'll live 91-93 and will mix in a changeup, a curveball and a tough cutter/slider. Bell is lauded for his ability to pound the zone, mix things up and keep hitters off their feet.

Parker is a smooth operator on the dirt with some bounce to his step and explosive actions across the diamond. He projects to stick at shortstop where his tools really play. Parker has some bat speed and has added some physicality this winter. He projects a hit-over-power bat. He's an average runner.

The University of Hawaii has quietly become a pretty competitive program from a pitching development standpoint. Magdaleno has a chance to be the top arm out of the Islands in some time. 

A breakout prospect in the West Coast League in 2024, Magdaleno carried his success back into college pitching boasting impressive control and a well-rounded arsenal to keep hitters uncomfortable. He's one of the better strike-throwers in the country and it isn't limited to just one pitch. 

Magdaleno's fastball will grab 93 on occasion but he's more comfortably 89-91 with generic shape. It's not a bat-misser, but Magdaleno does get his fair share of weak contact. He works the corners like a true artist.

Magdaleno has an above average changeup in the low-80s that dances off his fastball and generates his swing and miss. He creates plenty of separation off his fastball and tumbles his cambio into the dirt resulting in impressive whiffs. There's also a curveball in the upper-70s, but it's more of a get-me-over than a true weapon. Magdaleno isn't a guy with a top-draft pick profile, but he's certainly the type that plays in the big leagues for several years thanks to his control, command and unwillingness to get himself in trouble.

Emerged as a draft follow in high school and has only elevated his profile in college. He's been up to 97 with a four-seamer that features generic shape, and he'll hold 92-94. There's a two-seamer that some scouts believe is likely to end up his primary heater. Buursema is a supinator that cuts the ball. That release profile has led to one of the more intriguing sweepers in the sport featuring velocity and huge lateral tilt. He works hard to get to his velocity on a more stout frame, but strike throwing has improved on campus. There's a more natural low-90s cutter and an upper-80s changeup as well.

McKinney spent two years at Baylor, though he didn't get on the mound until 2024. He was a punch-out artist as a redshirt freshman knocking down 60 hitters in just 49.2 innings. But those strikeouts came alongside 35 walks as well. Still, McKinney pitched exclusively as a starter at Baylor and has pitched extended innings at Arizona as well. 

At this stage, he's more of a one-trick pony than anything. But that's not a bad thing. McKinney's fastball is up to 97 mph with considerable riding action, best when he's getting through the pitch and generating some slight cutting action. It's a bat-missing weapon and every bit that of a 60-grade pitch. McKinney forced hitters to swing outside of the zone with his heater in 2024 and he's doing more the same this spring. It's a pitch complimented by above average spin rates and above average extension down the bump. McKinney simply knows how to blow it by hitters.

McKinney's slider is firm and short. It's a mid-80s bullet spinner, though he's had trouble getting to that pitch and executing it in games. He had a tendency to short-arm the breaking ball too, cutting down his stride by close to eight inches, ultimately "aiming" the slider rather than getting down the bump and letting it rip. There's some low-hanging fruit to get the slider performing at a higher level and it should eventually mold into an above-average offering if his command as a whole improves. 

McKinney has also shown a changeup, though it lags behind his one-two combo and generally lacks conviction and command.

This is a big-body righty with a fast arm, and tight elbow spiral and good direction down the bump. There are components here to believe in the ceiling on the horizon, but it's unpolished. He's certainly a draft arm, but where he fits will likely be dictated by the strike-quality and the developments of his secondary weapons this season.

Rizy is a huge right-handed pitcher with an intimidating frame and stuff that has continued to tick up year over year dating back to his high school. For now, he sits 93-94, touching 98 early in outings with an upper-70s breaking ball featuring two-plane tilt. Rizy has a smooth operation and impressive body control considering his size and levers. If the command continues to surge leading up to draft day, he's got a shot to go early. Rizy has always been on the older side and will be a draft-eligible sophomore at 21.7 years old.

Jaylen Walker is a massively naturally talented two-way athlete guy who could have a future in the outfield or on the mound. Most scouts prefer him with a bat in his hand. It's effortless juice out of a high hand setup. Walker creates a ton of space in the box with a long stride and whippy swing. He's got twitchy hip and has shown the ability to pound the ball to the opposite field. When he gets one, it's loud. There's some consistency in contact quality still to be desired and his operation at the plate seems to change from plate appearance to plate appearance; all common for a player his age. Most scouts see that coming as the body gets more physical and mature. 

Walker projects a fringy runner in a corner outfield spot. He's got plus arm strength befitting of a right fielder. 

On the mound, the arm strength is fairly elite. Walker was already touching 90 mph with a Brusdar Graterol-esque all-upper body delivery. It's mostly pure arm speed and velocity over pitchability, but he certainly has late-inning capabilities, especially at this early stage. Walker will be 18.3 years old for the draft, younger than most of his peers.

Clement, the son of former MLB pitcher Matt Clement, played well as a freshman striking out 23 batters in 21 innings. 

Madden will run the fastball up to 93 mph with carry and some tail. His curveball is a slurvy breaker with considerable depth and swing-and-miss traits. Clement is still working to firm that pitch up and remove a hump when he leaves it in the zone. There's also a cutter and a changeup, neither of which he throws too often.

Given the bloodlines and strike-throwing ability, Clement has a chance to rise in 2026.

Yehl missed the entire 2025 season with an arm injury after being considered a potential top-ten round talent entering the year. He had surgery in October 2024 and is expected to contribute to the Mountaineers in 2026.

A massive youthpaw with long levers and projection ahead, Yehl is a relief prospects with one of the better breaking balls in the class. His mid-80s sweeper has been up to 88 mph with considerable lateral tilt. Yehl is still working to control the zone and command his arsenal to allow his stuff to play up to its potential, but from a metric standpoint it's a pretty darn good breaker. Yehl has a good sinker too featuring strong vertical traits and it too has performed well on campus. He's been up to 94 and will rest 89-91 over two-inning outings. 

Yehl needs to throw strikes with more consistency. It's assumed his fastball velocity will see an uptick as the draft approaches. He projects a priority bullpen add in the 2026 Draft unless he shows signs of starter potential.

Wittmer has the look of a legitimate power lefty with unique release traits and a one-two punch arsenal that could get college hitters out today. He'll work up to 96 mph with carry and tail producing considerable in-zone whiffs at the top of the zone. The slider is tunnels with low-80s two-plane tilt; more vertical plane than sweep.He's demonstrated the ability to fill up the zone and features a reasonably low-effort operation. Wittmer is close to physically maxed and doesn't have a whole lot left in the projection department, but it's 'now' stuff and a definitive starter look.

After losing some of his prospect shine with an injury in 2025, Leaman is looking to rediscover some of the exciting velocity gains he found during the winter of 2024. He saw a monstrous transformation that winter jumping from a guy chucking 89-90 mph cookies into an explosive mover topping out at 98 mph. 

Leaman's fastball features sink and tailing action that can shatter barrels. He pairs the sinker with a very good slider in the mid-to-upper 80s, touching 90 mph at times. It breaks with cutter shape -- short and inconsistent. Still, playing off the fastball it's a pitch that's produced plenty of whiffs. He's worked to pull off that pitch a bit to create more sweeping action this spring. There's also an upper-80s changeup that he'll flash to lefties. 

Leaman has an explosive delivery that inherently possesses some effort, though it doesn't look as though he's overdoing it on the mound. There's not much head-whack and the operation looks sustainable. He creates huge extension for a pitcher of his size and certainly looks the part of a big-league caliber arm. His draft upside will be dictated on whether or not he can re-find that velocity he flashed in the fall of 2024.

Simply put, one of the better breaking balls in the class. It's an upper-70s hammer with enormous depth and sharp, late, bat-missing shape. Harris is a nightmare to deal with if he gets ahead in the count. Harris has been up to 95 though he doesn't get as much value out of his fastball due to its shape. The changeup is a legitimate third pitch to round out his arsenal as Harris kills spin and creates parachuting action with a willingness to throw it to either-handed hitter. There's considerable velocity separation on the pitch. 

Harris does have some uniqueness in his release with some effort and a lead leg block that collapses on his breaking ball and occasionally his fastball too. It's not a delivery that promotes total durability as scouts look toward the future, but to this point he's been a strike-thrower and hasn't missed any time with any ailments. As he gets stronger and continues to refine his craft, Harris has a chance to develop into one of the most dynamic pitching prospects in the class with stuff that rivals few. He will be 19.2 years old for the draft.

Jones was one of the most physical frames in the 2022 high school class and remains ultra-intimidating today. He already destroys the baseball. On the data side of things, he's a monster. It's among the most outlandish barrel-speed/hand-speed combinations in the 2026 class. Despite the 70-grade raw power, Jones has struggled to get to it in games as the hit tool has consistently lagged behind. 

Jones is a primary third baseman but has been utilized more and more in the outfield the last two seasons in college baseball. Jones has stiffened up a bit as he's gotten bigger and stronger leading some to question if his future lays in a corner outfield role or first base going forward. He certainly has tools on the dirt. Jones is especially adept charging the baseball and he'll flash above average arm strength moving to his left and coming in on the dirt.

The fear with Jones is the hit tool will never buoy at a level that makes his raw power and physical/athletic traits play on the field. He's gradually gotten better as the years have gone on in college, some believing he's got a chance to own a 40-grade hit tool when all is said and done.

Adelmann was one of the most impressive relief artists in the country as a sophomore at Bucknell. He ran up huge strikeout rates on the back of a devastating breaking ball and enough fastball value to keep hitters honest. The big frame leaves hitters waiting for velocity, but it's not something presently in his bag of tricks.

Adelmann creates steep angle down the mound. His tall, burly frame helps create a way higher than normal launch height. That arm slot coupled with his ability to create cut and sink gives him a unique looks that hitters never see elsewhere. Adelman spins the ball very well and that cutter helps setup the aforementioned breaking ball that neutralizes the opposition.

The breaker is a sweeper with considerable lateral tilt, thrown 83-84, up to 86. He's shown strong command for that pitch and lands it glove-side on the black with consistency. Adelman does tend to shorten his stride when throwing the pitch, something that could get him in trouble with professional hitters who are better at identifying pitches out of the hand. He'll fold in the occasional changeup, but it's hardly part of his natural menu of pitches and lacks distinct shape at this stage.

Adelmann's frame, plus breaking ball and unique fastball traits will surely get him drafted in 2026. Whether he fits inside the top ten rounds or as a priority "day three" add will be largely dictated by how much more velocity he can add and how much cleaner he can get in terms of consistent strike-throwing ability.

Teasley is incredibly young and won't turn 18 years old until well after the 2026 season comes to an end. He'll play the entire 2027 season as an 18 year old. Teasley is built like a powderkeg -- thick, durable and bulldog-like. He's got strength aplenty in his core and lower-half. He's been up to 94 but lathers in the 90-91 range with some carry and tail late through the zone. Teasley tends to favor pitching at the bottom of the strikezone. His breaking ball has hammer tendencies with well-above average spin rates that'll approach 3000 rpm at times. He's shown feel for keeping that pitch in the zone and will dance with it off the fastball. For now, it's mostly two pitches.

Teasley has an athletic delivery that really leans hard on a deep hip hinge and considerable torque. Teasley closes off to the batter in an extreme way and hides the ball well because of it. There's some inversion in the back as he comes to a firing position, though he mostly finds himself on time at foot plant. He does a very nice job repeating his delivery and his landing point. 

For now, Teasley has more of a relief look to him, though that may be largely in part due to his two-pitch mix and unorthodox coil. Those sorts of mechanics have worked for players like Johnny Cueto in the past, though Teasley lacks some of the looseness of the latter. Given his age, his stuff, ability to spin the ball and strike-throwing ability, he's an extremely high-follow as July approaches.

Darden has some of the most exciting clay in the class with swing metrics and athletic testing that point toward a sky-high ceiling if it all comes together. Per Blast Motion, Darden rotates faster than most in his class -- a trait that allows hitters to make later swing decisions and get to top bat speed quicker than their peers. He rotates very hard through the zone and flashes 'plus' raw power. Darden can fly on the bases and in the field and has the athletic tools to handle centerfield. He may be the fastest player in the class with borderline 80-grade speed. He'll need to polish up his ability to see and handle spin in the box as he matures, but if he shows some aptitude in that department it's not out of the question to hear his name called in the top three or four rounds.

Volmdering has held down an extended role for the Mustangs going back to his freshman year. He's a strike-thrower with three pitches he can land in the zone.

The arsenal is led by a fastball-changeup one-two punch that can be highly-effective. Volmerding has been up to 94 with the heater but more commonly sits 89-92 after the first couple innings of work. He generates moderate carry through the zone from an exceptionally high slot. It's not a pitch that projects better than fringe-average going forward, so his secondaries much thrive. Thus, the changeup...

Given the high slot, any steepness and downward action Volmerding can create will be effective. His changeup is a low-to-mid 80s cambio that he sells well with solid arm speed and tunnel. It generates solid separation away from the fastball and plays very well at the bottom of the zone. Volmerding may eventually get this pitch consistently sitting above-average, especially when one considers his feel for landing the pitch in and around the zone. 

Volmerding likes to throw a mid-80s cutter with short, firm break to keep hitters' barrels off the fastball. It's a pitch that plays nicely off the fastball/changeup combo. There's also a big sweeping breaking ball that he'll throw in the upper-70s to left-handed hitters. He's also shown a willingness to backdoor that pitch to righties early in counts.

While Volmerding may lack prototypical fastball value he makes up for it with three pitches that flash solid-to-above average at times. He's a good athlete who extends well down the mound and should continue finding success, specifically with the changeup going forward. There's some projection remaining in a long, lanky 6-foot-4-inch left-handed frame too.

Grant had a really big summer in 2022, impressing scouts with his stuff and physicality, but went undrafted as a prep due to some mechanical inefficiencies and signability concerns. Primarily a two-pitch guy, Grant can rush it up to 96, sitting 92-94 in longer outings with a solid low-80s slider that gets plenty of swing and miss. Grant is a bit of a tweener as it pertains to starting or relieving, but it might not matter as the stuff is presently good with more to come. You draft this sort of talent as a starter and let it ride. Grant missed the 2024 season due to an elbow injury.

Atkinson certainly has some uniqueness to his profile. A tall, gangly right-hander, Atkinson presents a high-slot with a higher-than-generic release point creating steepness to the plate. He supplements that high slot with a sinking fastball that at times flashes true bowling ball shape. He creates one of the steepest approach angles in college baseball when he's landing his pitches at the bottom of the zone. He's been up to 96 and will rest 90-93 into later innings. Atkinson doesn't spin the ball particularly well and doesn't induce a great deal of whiffs with his fastball, but the ground ball rates are healthy as one might imagine. Atkinson's slider has promise with strong chase rates from the opposition thanks to tunneling action off the fastball and further depth. It's a firm breaker up to 88 mph and routinely 84-86 mph. It likely projects in the solid-to-above average category as a pro once he establishes a bit more polish and value on his sinker. Atkinson has worked hard to establish a changeup in his repertoire though he's been reluctant to show it too much. His feel for command that pitch has been rather spotty to date. It'll be critical if he hopes to capture his starting pitcher ceiling at the next level. When considering the uniqueness in his delivery, the sublime ground ball rates, the looseness in his delivery and his size, plus his well-above average extension, Atkinson presents a starting pitcher prospect going forward so long as his development remains on an upward trajectory.

There's something of a Matt Chapman quality about Reynolds' at-bats. The mannerisms, the body control, the pull-side loft, it's all reminiscent of how Matt Chapman moves in the box. Unlike Chapman, Reynolds is an outfielder with athletic tools he's puts on display in showcase settings. A plus runner with a long, physical frame, Reynolds fills out a uniform well and looks good on the field. He checks the boxes. He's got quick hands and generates tight coil in his load. It should eventually turn into solid-to-above average raw and game power at the next level. Reynolds aims to lift the ball to the pull-side and that's evidenced in his baseball card. 

In the field, his speed more than makes up for what are largely average routes to the ball at this stage. It's fringy arm strength as well. Reynolds has a chance to stay in centerfield if he doesn't outgrow the position, though he'll likely slide to left field if he gets to physical to stay at the 8. Reynolds will be 19.3 years old on draft day so there'll be pressure on his bat to outshine his peers in the year leading up to the event. If he ends up at school, he will be draft-eligible again in 2028. Reynolds is also committed to play football at the University of Clemson.

Granse recently went through a dramatic growth spurt lengthening his frame to his current 6-foot-4-inch profile with plenty of strength gains on the horizon. The lanky southpaw works from a closed setup with a high moderate leg lift and a long stride. Granse has some cross-fire in his delivery with a really whippy motion. The fastball will touch 87, though Granse has a tendency to overthrow the heater at times causing some command issues. He's generally in the strike zone, though he'll scatter it a bit. Granse, whether by design or otherwise, tends to lower his arm slot on his slider and changeup to create more depth and overall action on both pitches than a more vertical slot would. The breaking ball is a low-70s sweeper that can be tough for hitters to track through the hitting zone. The changeup comes off the fastball tunnel with fading action into the LHH box. The fastball and changeup particularly have proven efficient in inducing soft contact. As Granse adds weight and strength the arm action and effort at release should polish up and subsequent velocity will arrive. He will be 19.2 years old for the draft.

Picot gets extremely high marks for his bat speed and ability to impact the baseball. It's a bit of a flatter bat path with some rigid athleticism in the way he attacks the ball, but he's always on time and has a knack for blistering line drives all over the field. Picot can certainly turn one over the fence when he finds the upper-grain of the bat too. Scouts are looking to see the hit tool trend up on campus. Picot is twitchy and rangy in the field with an above average arm, likely destined for a corner outfield role in the future.

Chirello finds himself draftl-eligible for the second time as scouts patiently wait for his long, wiry frame to add the physicality folks have expected for a few years now. Chirello is tooled up, but his lack of noteworthy strength gain has left his physical tools lacking in the box. 

It's hard to get much more projectable than a guy like Jackson Chirello. He's a long, lanky, high-waisted athlete with a whippy left-handed swing built for damage. As a freshman he showed massive exit velocity potential, and found the barrel more than most of his peers. 

Chirello has played some time at third base, though some evaluators believe his frame and long strides will eventually fit best in the outfield. He possesses a strong arm that will play anywhere on the field. His 6-foot-5-inch frame will likely add upwards of 20 pounds of muscle before he becomes draft-eligible.

Sauser saw his stuff take a big jump after arriving on campus and is now a more explosive mover with a fastball that'll creep into the mid-90s, living a tick or two below that. Sauser pitches with moxy, conviction and tempo with a competitive attitude and bully tactics. The fastball features late life and carry through the zone with bat-missing traits. He'll mix in a low-80s slider he's proven can play to both lefties and righties, though it's shorter shape relies on tunnel to get whiffs. Sauser figures to throw a good bit harder as we approach the 2026 draft thanks to his leaner upper-body strength and god-given arm speed.

It's not often you see a player born and bred in the state of Utah, developed in Utah and stay in Utah during his collegiate years only to transform himself into an upper-tier big league prospect. McChesney has accomplished that. 

McChesney slashed .340/.478/.547 as a freshman with seven extra-base hits. It was a taste of what was to come. He’s solidified himself as a top-shelf centerfielder as a sophomore. McChesney possesses an athletic build and double-plus speed that is quite evident in the field and on the bases. 

McChesney is growing into more raw power as he's matured and added weight, but as things stand it's well-below average. He doesn't necessarily have the build or explosion in his swing to project better than 40 raw power as a pro. While the hit tool is coming on, he still struggles in general to make a lot of contact and identify the slider out of the hand. 

McChesney has the athletic traits and and speed in centerfield alongside a distinguished glove to make him an interesting pro prospect. He'll need to make considerably more contact if he hopes to go inside the top-five rounds, but the building blocks are there.

Detlefsen played two seasons in 2023 and 2024 with Dodge City JC racking up 90 hits, 15 doubles, four triples, and 20 home runs. That production landed him in San Antonio for the 2025 and 2026 seasons where his game has continued to blossom.

Detlefsen's best tool is his raw power and bat speed. It's real. It's juice that plays to all fields with the ability to hit the ball out through the opposite field gap. While Detlefsen has done a nice job avoiding strikeouts, there are considerable holes in his swing, specifically spin at the bottom of the zone. He absolutely punishes fastballs but adjusting to the breaking ball on the bottom rail has been difficult in this his junior campaign. He's had a tendency to expand the zone on those pitches as well. It's a fairly straight-forward scouting report for pitchers and an area of his game he'll have to refine if he's going to find much success with the bat from Double-A onward.

Detleftsen is a primary left fielder with 40-grade speed. He does take very strong routes to the baseball and looks mighty comfortable tracking the baseball. He flashes an average arm that has a chance to improve in pro ball considering the athleticism in his arm action.

Detlefsen may never possess better than a 40-grade hit tool and the power will be key toward his ability to reach the big leagues. He's talented enough in the outfield play out there full-time, even if he won't be the most dynamic glove.

Farris is a massive 6-foot-4-inch slugger with tremendous bat speed and game power. Already 210 pounds, Farris has weight well-distributed throughout his frame and should have the ability to put on 10 or even 15 more pounds of strength without losing too much athleticism. Farris has immense physical tools, including a plus throwing arm that plays both in the outfield and at the hot corner. To this point, most of his run has come in right field where Texas State thinks he fits best. Farris has some bat-to-balls skills, but a hand hitch and late coil in his load has led to occasional timing issues on more advanced breaking balls. This is some of the most impressive raw power in the 2026 class, and far more athleticism than you'd expect from a player of his stature. Farris was a Detroit Tigers 18th round selection in 2023, but went unsigned.

The whole story on Nienaber is huge projection. Squared off shoulders with a lean frame and a high waist, he's exactly how you draw them up at this stage. Tons of upside on the horizon. Nienaber is already up to 91 from an athletic, short-arm delivery with a lower slot that his frame would generally suggest. There's some deception here. Fastball shape flashes plus, though it can melt into dead-zone shape as he fatigues. Nienaber is an aggressive mover who lacks effort. The operation and arm action really work. It's mostly an upper-80s fastball, a curveball that'll flash solid average, a changeup with teeth when thrown with conviction featuring some late dart and depth. He'll need to be a bit more efficient in throwing strikes and avoiding free passes, but there's a lot to like and dram on here. Nienaber will be 18.5 on draft day.

Webb has a chance to feature the best fastball in the entire prep class. Already touching 93 with north of 22 inches of induced vertical break, there's almost zero high school bats who can handle that pitch on the top rail. He's got a downer curveball with tremendous vertical separation off the fastball and nearly perfect pitch mirroring. As a two-pitch mix, it's one of the best combos in the class. Webb has good tempo and shows athleticism in his delivery. If a strong third pitch ever comes along it could be mid-rotation or better potential at the next level. Webb will turn 19 years old roughly a week after the draft.

A big, long, lanky right-handed that oozes projection, "PVE" features a ton of traits scouts want to see. He's already flirting with 93 mph heaters featuring considerable sink and tail. 

The slider has the makings of a real weapon, an upper-70s sweeper with huge two-plane tilt, lateral frisbee action. There's a bigger mid-70s curveball that he'll show earlier in counts as a get-me-over offering as well. PVE's changeup has upside too with late depth and some characteristics that allow it to play up off the sinker profile. 

Also a talented hitter with surprising athleticism on the dirt; a full-time shortstop when he's not on the mound. PVE will be 18.8 on draft day.

Sandford certainly looks the part of a future frontline starter. The 6-foot-6-inch righty comes action-packed with a 96 mph fastball, immense extension down the mound and elite fastball shape featuring tons of carry through the zone. His best secondary is a sweeping slider with above average spin in the low-80s, though it plays up at this stage thanks to Sandford's feel for commanding the pitch away from righties. There's also a project-changeup in his arsenal, though it's a ways away from being at the level of his top-two offerings. There's a good deal of head whack in Sandford's delivery at the time of publish, something he'll need to iron out if scouts are to trust he can hold up and survive the rigors of pitching in a rotation.

Cain's bat is currently ahead of his defensive prowess, but the offensive game is fairly advanced for his age. He's a left-handed hitter who has shown the ability to impact the baseball with above average exit velocities. He deploys a wide-open stance with whippy bat speed, the entire operation reminiscent of Chase Davis at Arizona. At this stage of his career Cain has a bit of a grooved swing with a streaky track record of being able to get to velocity at the top of the zone. He pummels just about everything below the belt with a pull-side emphasis. Cain will need to carve out a role defensively somewhere on the field over the next few years otherwise his draft profile will be muted a bit.

After a year at Nova Southeastern, Valentin transferred to Texas State for the 2025 season where he saw his stuff and performance take shape. 

It's mostly two pitches for Valentin who relies on a dynamic breaking ball to get outs. The fastball is up to 94 but features pretty vanilla shape and release components negating its effectiveness against college bats. 

The sweeper is big and firm. He'll throw that pitch almost 30 percent of the time. It's been up into the upper-80s, but usually sits 81-83 with darting, diving shape. 

There's also a changeup in the tank, however it's fringy and only thrown about seven percent of the time.

Schlaegel is an outfield prospect with present bat speed and well-rounded athleticism. He's an above average runner who takes good routes to the ball and features a plus throwing arm. That combination of tools projects Schlaegel into any of the three outfield spots, though most believe he'll be forced into a corner by a more superior runner once fully matured. Schlaegel has a line-drive approach and a flatter swing plane that presently limits his game power, though bat speed is present and with a few tweaks could unlock fringe average, maybe even average game power at the next level. He's an instinctual player who is solid on the basepaths and could eventually be a weapon at the next level in that regard. Schlaegel was a day three pick of the Boston Red Sox in 2023 but went unsigned.

Sharp is an exciting two-way player, though his future will be on the mound where his athleticism and operation really standout. Sharp hasn't yet seen his expected velo bump, sitting in the upper-80s grabbing 92 with a banger breaking ball. Some evaluators believe Sharp will ultimately be a guy that can sit 92-94 with a plus curve and polished command inside the zone. Sharp's mechanics work really well on the bump.

Molinaro has enjoyed a big three-year stretch with the bat. It got him drafted in the 17th round by the Nationals in 2025, but Molinaro decided he had unfinished business on campus.

Molinaro has active feet and hands at third base with solid average arm strength. Multiple arm angles create varying ball flights across diamond. Internal clock can rush at times. Arm accuracy gets wide when he hurries. Makings of a fringe-average defender with continued reps. Tools present.

He'll be used as a leverage money-mover in the 2026 draft.

Hetlzer spent his first season of collegiate ball at Cal Baptist before moving to Auburn in 2025. He's already up to 97 mph with a lower launch fastball that possesses marginal carry. Hetzler's low-80s sweeper is a good one despite dropping his arm slot even lower and broadcasting the pitch a bit. There's also a changeup that is in production and not yet a reliable, finished product. A lot to like in the arm talent, athleticism and strike-throwing ability here. Hetzler will have plenty of pro interest.

Newmann has tremendous projection in a long, lanky 6-foot-6-inch frame. The slider is his bread and butter at this stage; a low-to-mid 80s two-plane sweeper with some late, sharp bite. That pitch has done well in producing whiffs and chase from the opposition. The fastball has been a pitch to get ahead in counts but hasn't been terribly effective in terms of missing bats. It's a low-90s heater with generic shape. Newmann will need to continue working to extract value out of the heater if he's to start at the next level as it's key to getting to the sweeper. There's a bigger curveball in the upper-70s as well as a mid-80s changeup that are both deployed depending on the handedness of the opposing hitter. Neither pitch possesses polish yet, but both have distinct shape and could eventually become average offerings. Newmann's control has been fringy to this point in his career and his release point can get lost at times. As he continues to mature on the mound both physically and intellectually, he's got a shot to develop into a strong back-end of the rotation option at the next level.

Fay finds himself draft-eligible for the second time after not getting selected in the 2025 Draft. 

Fay redshirted as a freshman but jumped into a huge role as a redshirt freshman in 2024 earning starts and extended innings for the Crimson Tide. Fay is a low three-quarter slot righty with a fastball that'll work up to 96 mph and will sit 93-94 into the fourth inning and beyond. There's heavy sink and arm-side run on his heater; a ground ball specialist with weak contact as a major selling point in his arsenal. Fay spins a mid-80s slider with some sweeping characteristics. He's immensely projectable and should establish himself as a prized college arm for the 2026 draft by the time July rolls around.

Taylor missed draft-eligibility as a sophomore in 2025 by just five days but had he been eligible he'd have had a pretty good case to have gotten paid. It's a three-pitch mix and they all dance differently around the zone. 

Taylor's fastball isn't overwhelming. He'll run it up to 92 with reasonably ordinary shape. He's at his best when he's generating more carry than tail as his low-launch makes for a tough look for hitters at the top of the zone. But while the fastball may only be fringe-average at best, his secondaries are more. 

The sweeping breaking ball is a good one. Few in the 2026 class can match the velocity and shapes Taylor produces on the sweeper. It's 82-84 with two huge planes of movement. It's every bit that of a plus pitch.

Taylor's changeup, while nascent, flashes good shape and separation away from his fastball. It's too firm for the time being, but Taylor effectively kills spin and should be able to develop that pitch to solid-average or better in professional baseball. 

Taylor is undersized and throws with high intent. It's a relief look. There's an argument to be made it's one of the more underappreciated breaking balls in the class.

Knight raised his stock after adding a bunch of good weight and subsequent impact in his offensive game. He possesses a well-balanced swing with organic loft and serious pull-side juice. His game is definitely catered toward hitting the ball in the air, but his present raw power has provided value in that approach. Knight has some swing and miss in his game, and he can get in trouble in lefty-lefty matchups. That said, he's a solid runner with a solid average arm in the field. He profiles as a power-corner outfielder; likely a left-fielder at the next level. Knight can also pitch a little bit, up to 91 from the left side.

Boylston is a tremendous athlete. His physical tools scream in the outfield where his plus speed and obvious feel for routes to the ball stand out. The bat is largely unproven, though there is bat speed present and scouts are bullish on the power potential if he hits enough to garner regular ABs. 

He became an immediate starter at FAU upon arriving and has produced from the outset.

Schaefer is a projection righty featuring a low-90s fastball, up to 94 with hop, above average spin rates and the inherently feel to spot the pitch on the rails to the glove-side. Schaefer has the ability to land an average slider and curveball low-and-away to right-handed hitters, the former featuring shorter, firm shape. He also flashes a changeup as well. Schaefer has some two-way upside as he's a strong athlete and awfully young for his class.

Rodriguez just looks the part. He's got an insanely quick arm with a clean release and hopping traits on the heat. He's been up to 96, but settles in 91-92 on most occasions. The velocity has a tendency to dip after a couple innings, so he'll have to show more consistency on that front if he hopes to start in the future, but the pure arm talent here is significant. While the heat is impressive, it's his mid-80s slider that fools hitters most. It's been up to 86 with serious tilt. Rodriguez missed his freshman season with the Gators recovering from TJ, but is expected to play a large part on the later in the 2025 season.

Holland has a fastball up to 96 with heavy boring sink, though he's generally 90-93 over long innings. The slider is the most interesting weapon, a mid-80s tilt that has been thrown to lefties and righties alike. Holland shows considerable feel for pitching and commanding the baseball. He'll throw plenty of strikes and, while he doesn't yet possess a third pitch, his current two pitch mix features interesting tunneling traits and more upside to come.

Bradley has tremendous size with wide, squared off shoulders and a ton of strength across his entire frame. He's got the prototype physique traditional scouting measures have looked for in a young starting pitching prospect. His entire arsenal comes launched out of a low slot with some natural deception. The fastball will touch 93 with late tail, an especially difficult pitch on the hands of right-handed hitters. A sharp low-to-mid 80s slider features depth and occasionally will generate a bit of horizontal tilt. It's a bat-missing two-pitch mix. The arm really works with looseness and control through release. If Bradley can add in a reliable changeup or splitter to live off the life of the fastball, he's got a very interesting starting pitcher profile, especially considering his unique release traits. There's a ton to like here. Bradley will be 18.8 on draft day.

Pitzer was a prized get for the Gamecocks coming out of high school, but a lack of opportunities led him to Starkville for the 2026 season. 

He's an explosive, quick mover with decisive tempo on the mound and a natural deception about his pitching style that keeps hitter uncomfortable. The fastball is high-spin offering with more carry than arm-side run. He'll work up to 94, but generally settles in 90-92. He features a quality low-80s slider with big, sweeping break. There's also a fringier curveball that he's used for get-me-over strikes and seldom put-away pitches, spiked.

Cropper really began opening eyes in 2022 as a high schooler featuring a mid-90s fastball coming out of a deceptive low launch. He mixed in a low-80s slider with short tilt, though he had a tendency to slow his arm down a bit to land it. Since then, he's grabbed 99, sitting 94-95 over short outings. The slider still has a ways to go, but the athlete and operation here are awfully impressive. If Cropper continues taking steps forward developing his secondary offerings, he's got a shot to start. He's still reasonably green and there's plenty of development ahead of him, but this is good clay. Cropper missed the entire 2023 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery.

Wendt's operation is the selling point. He projects to throw pretty hard with his loose, whippy, three-quarter delivery. He's a solid athlete who extends well down the mound with fluid hips and plenty of rotational torque. Wendt works in the low-90s now, but evaluators believe he has a shot to throw into the upper-90s with late arm-side darting action on the heater. He'll mix in a low-80s slurvy breaking ball that tunnels well and has been a real swing-and-miss weapon to this point, though a lack of competition in his district hasn't tested him to this point.
