One of the more projectable arms in the 2026 class, the 6-foot-6-inch Gholston weighs in a tick over 200 pounds and already showcases the arm-speed and athleticism to suggest there's a lot more coming in the tank. Gholston ended up a 17th round pick by the Brewers that year, but elected to head to Norman. He'll live 90-91 on most days, grabbing 93 every now and then. He operates out of a short-arm delivery and hides the ball very well. His slurvy breaking ball is an upper-70s offering with two-plane tilt and conviction. The changeup might be his best pitch with late, darting action that he's willing to throw to both lefties and righties alike. Gholston certainly looks the part of a future starting pitcher at the next level with three pitches that could all eventually grade out as above-average or better, but commanding the baseball and improving strike-quality will be an emphasis in his development in Norman.

Simply put, Seiber has one of the heaviest, nastiest sinkers in the 2026 class. It's elite two-plane break with firm downward action and heavy tailing arm-side run. It's a pitch that creates a ton of chase outside of the zone and due to its movement profile, more swing-and-miss than your run of the mill 2-seamer. Seiber doesn't throw terribly hard yet just brushing 94 and resting in the low-90s, but that unique action on the fastball lets the pitch play up. Seiber has peculiar secondaries menu with a changeup that spin harder than his slider. The cambio has good action, but it's firm compared to the fastball and actually possesses more lift than his sinker. That variation is inherently different for hitters to see, but does open Seiber up to giving up homers. The slider features well-below average spin with bullet shape and solid depth. Considering the action on his fastball and changeup, the slider does play well with close to a foot-and-a-half of horizontal differential. Seiber will gradually need to throw harder as he matures, and his long 6-foot-6-inch frame suggests that velocity will come. He's got back-end of the rotation upside at the next level if he can find a way to improve the overall action on a breaking ball. The physical frame, the length, the projection and the strikes... Seiber has some exciting clay.

Brittain is a tall, projectable righty, though projectable may not be an appropriate description for a kid already flirting with triple digit heat. Brittain has been clocked on as hot as 100 mph on radar guns, though Trackman has him touching 99. It's a hellish sinker-ball profile with impressive depth out of a higher-than-average launch height and some late, sharp tail. It's one of the more productive and impressive sinkers in college baseball. 

There's a lot of effort and arm speed on the profile, and it appears more relieverish than starter at this stage. His best secondary is a high-80s changeup with some late tail and depth. Brittain has been described as effectively wild, though the arm talent and frame here are pretty undeniable, especially for his age.

It's been a winding road for Elliott with injuries and inconsistent performance lengthening his collegiate career.

Elliott is another crafty lefty with four usable pitches and a ton of deceptive qualities. Elliott can flirt with the low-90s, usually settling in a tick under that, but the heat plays up a bit with solid late hop from a tough angle. Elliott's best secondary is a legitimate double-plus changeup with immense fading action, falling off the table. It's been murder on righty bats. He's got a big, slurvy breaking ball that he uses against lefties, as well as a fringier slider that can tunnel off the fastball at its best. Elliott projects a back of the rotation southpaw unless the fastball ticks up a notch. 

Elliott is a very solid prospect, but he's dealt with injuries that have sidelined a good chunk of his collegiate career. He will turn 24 years old about a month after the Draft.

Johnson is a talented projection righty with a low-90s dead-zone fastball, a deceptive delivery and a changeup that really gives right-handed batters fits. Fastball command continues to be an emphasis in Johnson's development as his margin for error with his current fastball shape is small. He likes to pitch inside and his misses are often to the arm-side. The arm action can get a little late at times causing the miss arm-side, but he's a good enough athlete that it should clean itself up over time. There's also a bigger curveball in the profile that is currently more of a get-me-over offering. Johnson is a scout favorite in smaller circles who watched him coming up through high school baseball.

Hunter Watson is going to strikeout a ton of batters in his career. Metrically, it's one of the most unique arms in the 2026 class. Watson lets it rip from a low, vertical arm-slot featuring considerable carry through the zone; a bat-missing monster fastball that's already grabbing 93. It's a super-fast, compact arm action with twitchy, athletic hips pointing toward more velocity on the way. 

Watson will flash a changeup with hard fading action out of a similar slot with arm speed. He's had a difficult time commanding the pitch, but there's 55-grade upside there. The slider will flash in the upper-70s with some late depth and gyroscopic spin. There's also a fringier curveball that projects to be his fourth-best pitch if he's keeps it in the arsenal. 

Watson has thus far shown fringier control and command of his pitches, a point of emphasis in his development. Still, the point stands, it's some of the most unique pure stuff in the class with top-three round upside if polish comes as the draft approaches. If pitching doesn't work out for any reason, he's also a decorated catcher with a solid hit tool. Watson is on the older side and will be 19.1 years old on draft day.

A high-level performer in high school, Delamielleure found a ton of barrels. He's an accomplished defender who likely profiles into a corner at the next level, potentially staying in centerfield during his minor league career. Delamielleure has a premium frame with the potential to grow into some power, though presently he works mostly gap-to-gap, occasionally juicing a ball out pull-side. Evaluators believe he could grow into a solid average power bat with solid average speed. Delamielleure gets extremely high marks for his attitude in the dugout and his leadership qualities. His grandfather is in the NFL Hall of Fame.

O'Connell is a talented left-handed projection arm with a calm demeanor, a quiet operation and he fills up the strike zone. O'Connell has been up to 92 with a firm fastball that he'll throw to all four quadrants. At his best, he'll generate carry at the top of the zone and work some arm-side run away from right-handed hitters. It's a lower, deceptive slot, so the velocity plays up at this level of competition. There's more in the tank in this lanky frame, though he'll probably peak into the mid-90s. 

He lands a variable slider that he'll add and subtract depth from depending on the handedness and the situation. There's also a nascent changeup that scouts like the upside of strictly due to O'Connell's pronated release. There's at least average upside on the pitch. There's some inversion in the delivery, and that will give some scouts pause, but O'Connell's low-effort, high-volume track record may dissuade those concerns. 

After a year at Vanderbilt, O'Connell elected to transfer to Duke for the 2026 season.

Tarpley Jr. was an 18th round selection by the Oakland Athletics in the 2023 MLB Draft, but went unsigned. He's an extremely physical, projectable outfielder with a long 6-foot-4-inch frame and a high waist. To this point his offensive performances at Youngstown have been uneven featuring an aggressive approach, some chase and streaky bat-to-ball skills. Tarpley Jr. has clocked plus run times with a long gait and can clock a bit quicker than that underway. In terms of the tools, it's an above average throwing arm in center with budding raw power at the plate. Tarpley continues to get stronger and his barrel awareness at the plate continues to improve, but this is a physical specimen with a bright future.

Graziano is a smooth operator at the plate with a line drive approach to all fields and a budding power tool. He handles velocity well, but has shown some holes in handling spin. He's a plus runner coming from a strong, lean, powerful body. He possesses a solid average arm in the field and is routinely on target. The selling point here is the bat with the speed combo. He's got the chance to really develop and get better as time goes by in ways other do not thanks to the swing, the frame, and the trajectory of his tools.

Davis finds himself draft-eligible for the third year in a row after playing two seasons at Samford and two more at Vanderbilt. Now at Penn State, he's looking to recapture some of the spark that made his profile so enticing during his Samford days. 

He's a hit-over-power type of bat with strong bat-to-ball skills and a refined approach. There's some sneaky pop here, though most scouts don't believe it to be more than fringy at the next level. Davis hits the ball on the ground way, way too much and will need to start elevating the ball with more effectiveness if he's going to be a productive big leaguer. 

He's an average runner who generally doesn't put his wheels on display on the bases. Davis' bat has been the calling card, though the leather at second base has surprised some folks, some throwing solid average grades on the glove.

Gaffney looks like Jeff Bagwell in the box with his squatted, ultra-closed stance, high hands, aggressive back elbow and physical frame. Gaffney can produce plenty of bat speed and doesn't get cheated. It is an aggressive approach, and Gaffney will expand the zone, but he still boasts strong contact rates and his exit velocity numbers have continued to trend up since arriving to campus as he's added more and more muscle. Gaffney will need to find a way to elevate the ball with more consistency, but the athleticism and strength are both present for his name to get called early in July. 

Gaffney is a below average runner with a short stride. He is destined for first base at the next level.

After spending his freshman year at Texas and receiving limited playing time, Richardson transferred to Jacksonville State in search of more opportunities. 

Richardson is among the most physical pound-for-pound athletes in the class features premium bat speed and real impact at the plate. He's an above average runner with a strong arm at either third base or in the outfield. Most scouts believe his future is in the latter thanks to longer strides and strong route running ability. Richardson will need to continue refining his hit tool should he hope to see his stock take off before July. Too often would he expand the zone against better arms, and his contact rates suffered because of it. Richardson is a draft-eligible sophomore.

Miller has huge strength in his hands with a low-effort operation built to do damage. It's serious intent at the plate with juice to all-fields, occasionally flashing massive pull-side game power. Miller has rhythm and waggle in his swing and does a nice job getting his foot down, staying on time. He's become more athletic and a bit quicker in the last couple years on the showcase circuit, now an average runner with a lighter-footed gait and a longer stride. Speed will never be a huge part of Miller's game, but he appears to be heading into a direction where he can stay in a corner in the outfield and hold his own. The carries this profile, but it's a good one.

Hanes got a jumpstart on the 2026 class back in December 2023 by re-classifying up from the 2027 class. Now more age appropriate, Hanes will be 18.3 years old in July 2026 with a chance to be one of the more model-friendly arms available. It's a full arm stroke with a whippy release. Really sturdy frame with a high waist and broad shoulders. Hanes has a reasonably low-effort delivery with some head-whack at release on the fastball. While he's been up to 94 and the fastball projects, it's his breaking balls that could rank near the top of the prep class come draft day. The first is a massive sweeper with huge lateral tilt and late, sharp, diving bite in the mid-70s. The second is a more firm, low-80s slider with shorter tilt to get hitters off the heat. The upside here is tremendous so long as the strike-quality continues to develop forward. The highest type of arm to follow for 2026.

A former 2-way guy who elected to commit to pitching as a freshman at Binghamton, Griffin checks a lot of the prototype boxes scouts look for in a big league arm. He's got the size, length, levers and athleticism that project going forward. Griffin really gets down the mound with well-above average extension that should allow his fastball to translate to the next level so long as his command for that pitch improves. Griffin has tickled 98 and will sit 93-95 with cut and a bit of carry, though his fastball is more of a traditional cutter with late-spinning depth. He compliments the heat with a low-80s gyro slider that he'll have to throw more firm as he matures, especially if he wants his cut-fastball to improve in terms of effectiveness. It's a supination profile with considerable arm talent. There's a lack of a third pitch and he's yet to get stretched out to the point where scouts can project what it looks like as a starters profile. Regardless, if a third pitch never comes it's a reliever profile who could go 50/50 fastballs/sliders working away from right-handed hitters.

Brown is a long, large infielder with a broad, mature frame and a high waist. He projects to add plenty more strength in good ways as he matures. Brown gets a good deal of raw power out of a wide base and stretch out in front. He's got athletic hips and really projects to hit for quite a bit of power at the next level. There's some moving pieces in Brown's load that scouts will be conscious to track approaching draft day, specifically as they pertain to his ability to purely hit, but the tools on the offensive side of the ball here are pretty loud. The moving pieces have certainly contributed to what has been well-above average chase rates to this point, though Brown does battle and foul off pitches frequently. Defensively he looks like a third baseman long-term where his strong lower half, his low squat and gait, as well as his longer arm action will most comfortably play.

Marshall is among the most physical bodies in the 2026 class. He's particularly strong at the point of attack with heavy hands and wrist strength that generates big exit velocity readings into the opposite field. He's short, compact and quick into the hitting zone, though he's shown a susceptibility to spin in tournament settings. Marshall projects to hit for power at the next level. On the dirt he's a primary third baseman with average tools. He could ultimately end up in the outfield at the next level if he outgrows the infield. While the offensive tools are strong, Marshall does have a good arm on the mound and could be used as a reliever in college. He will be 19.2 years old for the draft.

Gonzalez is a first-base primary defender with a big projection bat and age on his size. A young 21-year-old for this class, Gonzalez already possesses serious game power from the left side thanks to compact, tight turns on the baseball. His pull-side power is noteworthy, and his 6-foot-3-inch frame points to more coming. Gonzalez does a good job leveraging into his back hip and looks to launch the baseball. He's limited defensively and is a fringy runner, but if a team buys the bat, he's got a shot to sneak into day two as a power-over-everything profile.

Ortiz is an athletic left-handed pitcher with a fast, loose arm and polished operation on the mound. He gives hitters a deceptive look with a steep angle, hiding the ball late. The fastball is largely an average offering at this point, up to 90 with some sink and tail. He'll vary the shape at times, though his release points to a future sinkerballer. The breaking ball is an absolutely hammer biting with significant depth and some late sweep into the RHH box. It's a true weapon despite it usually sitting in the mid-70s. There's also a changeup that's flashed, but requires further work in consistency of execution. Ortiz has considerable upside, especially as he'll be just 18.1 years old for the draft.

Duncan is one of the highest level defenders you can find in the 2026 class with elite-level speed and sublime route running skills in the field. On top of that, it's a plus throwing arm that plays in every outfield spot. Duncan doesn't yet possess a ton of punch at the plate, but evaluators like the frame and believe some juice could develop as he develops his swing.

Vanek burst onto the scene as a sophomore at Chipola bashing homers and finding barrels at an exemplary rate. His play quickly got him noticed in the D1 ranks racking up scholarship offers to play all over the country. Florida State would end up his eventual landing spot.

Vanek is a first-base exclusive profile who produces plus bat speed and has shown impact to the pull-side as well as the opposite field gap. He's an average runner with an athletic gait for a player of his position. He won't hurt a team on the bases, at least early in his career. Vanek is nimble at first base however his footwork and technique continues to be a point of emphasis in his development. He's got a chance to eventually become an average glove at the position.

Whether he hits and mashes in Tallahassee will ultimately dictate his draft position in 2026.

Wolff is a big, sturdy, 6-foot-6-inch righty with a low-90s fastball that'll bump 95 at peak. His bread and butter is a firm splitter in the low-80s that flashes above average and should be an out-getter at the next level. Wolff is still learning to hone his arsenal in and around the zone, but there are some starter traits that teams like if he puts it all together.

A talented right-handed pitcher and shortstop alike, scouts love the upside of Moore on both sides of the ball. He's a tad undersized from conventional measures to project as a starting pitcher at the next level, but several arms 6-feet and under have bucked the prototype trend in recent years and Moore could be the next. He's a deceptive, low three-quarter arm with a two-seam fastball and sweeping slider that pair nicely off one another. The fastball sits in the upper-80s (up to 91) right now but it possesses considerable bore to the arm-side. Moore will pitch inside on righties and lock them up. The sweeper flashes 'plus' but will need to add firmness as he matures. He routinely sits north of 15 inches of sweep on that pitch. 

Offensively Moore has an athletic frame with strength in his lower half and levers. He stands tall with rhythm and waggle and is consistently on-time with some organic loft in his swing. There's power upside here, though Moore is yet to blossom into the player who flashes the bat speed scouts expect to eventually see out of his frame. There's some looseness in his hips and Moore creates space in the box. The best is yet to come offensively. 

On the defensive end Moore shows solid range and enough arm strength to play shortstop at the college level, though he's likely to make the move to third base or into a corner outfield spot at the professional level. He is a fringy runner whose throws generally do not possess the natural carry you'd expect to see from a full-time shortstop in the pro game.

Evans is a toolshed with a ton of twitch and explosive movements in his game. He's a strong athlete with plus speed in the field and above average routes in centerfield. His frame should allow him to stick up the middle, so long as he doesn't get too muscled-up and slow down. Evans possesses bat speed with above average raw power and an attack angle that allows him to access in right now. He's become more dynamic in how he approaches at-bats in the last calendar year and is forming into a more complete offensive option. He can get a little swing-happy and his approach can waver now and again, but if a team is looking for unpolished upside, Evans is really fun clay with a definitive big league regular ceiling. He'll be just 20 years old and draft-eligible.

Ohland is a switch-hitting catcher with pull-side power from the left side and line-drive, gap power from the right side. He's a polished receiver who does a fantastic job framing his pitches. Above average crouch and explosive with a solid average throwing arm. Ohland has struggled against premium pitching, but is revered by his pitchers and staff for his ability to handle the game. He transferred from the University of Washington after his freshman year.

Haferkamp is an ultra-physical outfielder with broad shoulders, a high waist and considerable strength projection ahead of an already strong frame. He's a bit raw in the field, but offensively there's tons of impact potential. Haferkamp presents big, crude bat speed and uses it to all-fields. His swing plane is repeatable, though he's working through eliminating a nagging arm bar in his swing that can sap some of his game power. This is fairly typical with young, lanky players. He's committed to UC Santa Barbara.

Best is a physical freak with huge bat speed and athletic tools smattered throughout. He's got a short, compact swing with feel for the barrel and organic loft that creates majestic game power. Best can put it over the fence to all-fields. An above average runner, Best has tools on the bases and in the field. He's got a plus throwing arm that features plenty of carry. This is a pretty intriguing prospect with some unpolished parts of his game that should improve as he matures on campus. After spending his freshman campaign at Florida State, Best transferred to New Orleans for the 2025 campaign.

Harrahill certainly looks the part with a tall, long body and plenty of athleticism on the bump. He throws a low-to-mid 90s fastball that's been up to 96 with extreme armside run and some sink. It moves so much, Harrahill struggles to control or command the pitch with much authority, though he's consistent with missing to his armside. Harrahill throws a beautiful changeup that tunnels and separates off the sinker very well, flashing above average. He's got feel for it and it could eventually end up plus if he can add a bit more depth to it. Harrahill throws a below average curveball that can flash average when tunneled with command. The name of the game here will be whether he can harness his stuff and find more of the zone. If he can, Harrahill could be a draft steal.

Brasseaux works in the upper-80s, up to 94 with an long, albeit easy arm action and real feel for the strikezone. His slider is his best weapon with strong tunneling characteristics and short, two-plane shape. Brasseaux is a projection arm with upside. Brasseux shows upside at the plate too with a loose, hitterish left-handed swing and a gapper mentality. Brasseux is an average runner, but does possess a huge arm in the outfield and could profile into either corner.

Chatterton is a physical-frame righty with a quick arm who projects to throw very hard in due time. Already grabbing 98 with life on the top rail, Chatterton can absolutely dazzle at times. He is a big scap load guy who really rocks and rotates in the back, exploding through release. He loves to throw a budding changeup that lives off his fastball, though he has a tendency to broadcast and tell the pitch at times. Still, finding arms with feel for separation and killing spin can be rare. Chatterton has a slider and curveball, though both lack feel and firmness at present, however there is distinct shape on the former. The effort and operation point toward a reliever at the next level, but it's very real *now* stuff and radar guns don't lie.

Ryan has a pro-built body with plenty of strength spread out tip to toe. He's got a sturdy lower half and broad shoulders that point toward a starter's profile. The stuff has steadily come along for Ryan over the past 12 months with a fastball now grabbing 91 with late life in the zone. Ryan has a track record of pummeling the strikezone with his arsenal supporting the notion he'll pitch long innings at the next level. His best secondary is a heavy breaking ball with vertical depth that plays nicely off the fastball. It's usually thrown in the mid-to-upper 70s and projection an above average weapon as he continues to add firmness to the pitch. He'll flip in a low-80s changeup with fade and depth as well to keep left-handed bats honest. Ryan is going to start at the next level and his pitchability to durable frame only help support that notion. He will be 18.8 at the draft.

All Waid has done from the very beginning is blister baseballs at every single stop. The kid just mashes and posted some of the gaudiest numbers of any high schooler back in 2022. He'll split time between first base and catcher, though most believe he's destined for first base as he moves forward into higher levels of baseball. He's got the making of a potential plus hitter with plus power, though his athleticism and lack of versatility will be a hurdle he'll have to grapple with as he moves up the ladder. Still, you're buying the bat here and it's a good one.

Kepo'o-Sabate's athleticism immediately stands out both at the plate and on the mound. While he's been a strong hitter to this point, most foresee a future on the mound. He's already touched 92 mph with some carry and arm-side run from top shelf arm speed. Kepo'o-Sabate's seen growth over the last 12 months in terms of shaping the breaking ball. It's an upper-70s slider with sharpness and two planes. There's solid-average upside on that pitch. He's also developed a changeup that lacks arm-side action, but does dive a bit at the plate. It's still a work in progress. Kepoo-Sabate continues to show projection in a reasonably raw package. His arm speed may push him into the mid-90s, though the intent and inconsistencies in commanding the baseball may push him to the bullpen. He will be 18.4 for the draft.

Reyes has a beautiful line drive swing with sneaky juice to the left side. Reyes possesses the long, lean frame teams like to see too, though he's begun to pack on muscle at Miami and is approaching his fully-mature form. He's a solid average runner with a solid average arm in the corner as well. In Reyes, you're buying the bat speed and the ability to handle all three outfield spots in a pinch. He should be able to develop into a solid average power hitter with a hit tool that'll let it play. Key for Reyes will by syncing up his lower half and getting the foot down on time against velocity. 

Reyes spent the first two years of his collegiate career at Rutgers before transferring to FIU for his draft-eligible 2026 campaign.

Randle is a smaller framed infielder with a sweet left-handed stroke and a line-drive approach. He's got a track record of hitting good arms, though he may ultimately lack the projection of some of his peers.

It may be difficult to sign Smith away from his commitment to NC State as his two-sport talent has the Wolfpack salivating at the upside on the gridiron as their future quarterback. On the baseball field it's two-way upside with tons of athleticism and arm strength on the dirt with a quality right-handed bat that projects to hit for power. The swing is unique with body-swaying rhythm and weight transfer oddities in his setup and load. He presents a lagged barrel with deep-set hands, though he puts himself in a good position to hit and can get the barrel to any zone with fast hands. Smith is up to 90 mph on the mound with a clean arm action mixing in a traditional curveball with depth and some tunnel. A lot of avenues for this profile to find success going forward. Smith is on the older side for this class and will 19.4 years old for the draft.

Waiolama is a physical righty with a rigid, jerky, yet athletic drop-and-drive delivery, working downhill aggressively to the plate. One keen evaluator compared the way he moves to Gabriel Hughes. He's been up to 95 with some deception in his secondaries, most notably a low-80s slider that showcases some bite as it works off-tunnel. Waiolama is an athletic righty with a big body, though his final role is to be determined as some see the effort in his delivery as a developmental emphasis at the next level.

Schwartz is a big, physical catcher with an imposing, sturdy frame and loud tools scattered throughout his scouting report. It's comfortably above average raw power and most scouts think he'll eventually live in the 'plus' raw power bucket. He's getting to a lot of it in games already despite some noticeable swing and miss in his game. Behind the plate, his pop times are strong. They're buoyed by an above average throwing arm with his footwork and technique requiring some polish into the next level. Scouts are split on whether he's a catcher long-term, primarily due to his overall size, but his other tools should help take the pressure off his ability to catch. Schwartz is an explosive, violent athlete who posts average run times and features a very strong first step out of the box. He has a plus throwing arm in the outfield and some in the eval industry would like to see him take more reps at third base. Offensively, Schwartz has a high hand setup with jittery, anxious hands a la Jose Altuve. He's mostly open and upright pre-load, sinking into his hips as the ball approaches. Those dramatic changes in plate may have an adverse effect on his ability to time his triggers consistently, as well as cover velocity at the top of the zone or spin under his knees. Adjustability is a concern in the box. When he's on-time, the pull-side power and back-side leverage can be jaw-dropping. There's been a fair amount of strikeouts in his game so quieting things down and letting his physical tools do more of the talking in his swing will be a developmental emphasis at the next level, wherever that might be.

Konstantinovsky was reasonably unheralded coming out of high school, but Rutgers loved his tenacious competitive fire and ability to pound the strikezone for multiple innings. A true strike-thrower, Konstantinovsky is up into the mid-90s  with a slider and changeup that both flash average offerings going forward. He's a weak contact machine and has a knack for getting the big strikeout when he needs it, despite not necessarily holding the label of a punchout artist. The book on Konstantinovsky is his polish and starter upside.

Dickerson is an imposing infielder with a long, athletic frame, broad shoulder and tons of projection. He moves well on the dirt, though most scouts see a move to third base or the outfield as his body continues to fill out. Already an average runner, Dickerson could get stronger and maintain that speed. His throwing arm is largely average as well. That said, the potential and upside for damage offensively certainly exists. Dickerson works to the pull-side, but he peppers balls into the RCF gap in BP. There's considerable bat speed here, and the raw power is fairly obvious. There's a bit of an arm-bar out in front for Dickerson, so cleaning that up and extending through the ball could really unlock what his frame is capable of.

Jackson is a power-first catcher with big bat speed out in front and a propensity to pull and lift. The juice is the carrying tool here, though Jackson does have an average arm behind the plate and some quick defensive actions. Jackson also has upside at third base with some bounce to his game. Developing consistent bat-to-ball skills and a more refined approach would elevate his game into another tier as far as scouts are concerned.

Martinez flew under the radar a bit approaching the 2023 draft, but really showed well with a loud bat and a more physical approach to the game. Martinez can cover the entire zone and has a bat path built to do damage. He plays a sure-handed brand of infield defense. He's likely destined for second or third base and should be a sure-handed option with a bench role at the next level.

Lape features massive bat speed and still has the long limbs and lean frame to project more power in the future. Evaluators believe this will comfortably turn into plus power as he ages, maybe more. Lape is more solid average in other parts of his game, though he's a good athlete and could develop more tools as he matures. He's an average runner with an average arm for third base.

A tireless worker with infinite enthusiasm to get better according to scouts in the know, Smith is a highly projectable righty with a lean, lanky frame, a high waist and squared off shoulders. He's an explosive mover who figures to throw very hard some day. He's been up to 89 with bat-missing shape and a tight slider with sweeping shape. There's also an upper-70s featuring some tail. Smith continues to get stronger, and as he does, continues to polish out some of the effort and head whack in his delivery. As pitching and the game begins to come to him more naturally with strength gains, his profile could skyrocket. This is a really good arm whose story will likely fully unfold with more muscle and time. Smith will turn 19 a month after the draft.

Wadas has plenty of pull-side power and has had no issues demonstrating it in games and side sessions. The bat speed here is real. Wadas may be a bit positionless as most expect him to end up at first base where his glove is fringy. You're buying the power here and hoping the projection and development in the field advances.

Sarna will be young for the 2026 draft but evaluators like his pitchability and feel for three pitches. He's primarily a fastball guy with sink and feel for the arm-side, generally in the low-90s. He'll throw a low-80s slider with two-plane tilt, more depth than sweep, as well as a changeup that he's been working to fold into the rotation with more consistency.

Alexander is an imposing hitter to his prep peers thanks to big leverage and bat speed. It's a long, physical frame that's been able to add a bit more strength in the lower half over the last 12 months resulting in loud exit velocities to all fields. Alexander can create damage to the opposite field better than most in this class thanks to his short, compact stroke that holds barrel speeds on inside-out swings. There's some swing and miss present on spin and elevated velocity, though he punishes mistakes and has shown the ability to keep his weight back. Alexander is an average runner who projects into a corner at the next level where his average arm strength will comfortably play. He will be 19.2 on draft day.

Larson is a barrel-chested righty with present stuff and some projection remaining in a higher waist, long-levered frame. He's been up to 97 with heavy, boring action into righties hands. Changeup shows promise, though it's his high-spin breaker, approaching 3000 rpm that has scouts intrigued. Larson has some starter traits in his athletic delivery and feel for controlling his body on the bump. He'll be just 20 years old on draft day. Many have said off the record Larson would be in pro ball already had it not been for a broken ankle suffered in the months leading up to the 2023 MLB Draft.

After a wildly successful freshman year at Wofford, Wicker became a huge point of emphasis for teams bidding in the transfer portal. Wicker landed at LSU where the Tigers will hope to unlock the infinite upside of the 6-foot-6-inch righty. Wicker is up to 94 at this stage with huge arm-side tail and some sink. He launches from a low slow, especially considering his size. The fastball hasn't been terribly effective at this early stage in his career, though analysts are bullish on the upside if he changes his zone approach to pitching. Wicker's bullet slider is comfortably his best pitch with near-perfect gyroscopic spin and some solid vertical plane. It's not yet a 'plus' pitch, but it could get there with more value out of the fastball and the additional velocity he's likely to gain with added strength. Wicker throws a fringy changeup as well and considering his arm angle and release traits it'll likely be a pitch he'll need use more going forward if he hopes to realize his starting pitcher upside at the next level.

Bryce enjoyed a massive freshman campaign with Merrimack where he broke the school record for hits in a single season. Bryce has tremendous length and plate coverage with long levers and an athletic operation in the box. He'll use all fields and possesses some sneaky juice as evidenced by his 16 frosh homers. There's some swing and miss in the game and he'll need to improve his willingness to take walks, but there's some pillars to build on here in an offensive profile. A third baseman by trade, Bryce is an average athlete with a heavy-footed gait and will likely be a fringy runner by the time he is draft eligible. It's solid average arm strength that will comfortably stay on the left side of the infield or into a corner outfield spot.

One of the best power bats in the Northeast out of high school, Jaros looks the part of a middle of the order slugger with his strapping and projectable 6-4, 220 frame. The power he generates is effortless and he can drive the ball a long way without getting off his best swing. He mashes fastballs and has shown improvement handling spin and offspeed. Jaros has more than enough arm strength for third base but his heavy feet may push him to right field or first base.

Mitchell is an imposing switch-hitter with power that really plays. He's a natural athlete in the outfield who takes good routes and can handle any of the three positions, though he's likely destined for a corner where his average arm and average speed play best. Mitchell has plenty of projection and could develop into a power-first bat.

Dale has a sweet, low-effort, left-handed swing with a propensity to shoot baseballs to all fields. He's got some pull-side juice and quick hands that project well into professional ball. Dale is an average runner with an average arm, though he has an athletic gait and clean arm action in the field and makes accurate throws to the bag.

Williams has a ton of raw, pure stuff. He's been up to 99 with a high spin fastball and a high spin breaking ball, as well as a reasonably repeatable operation. Despite his size (just 6-foot, 190 pounds), Williams lacks the effort many of his hard-throwing peers do. Williams also struggles with commanding the baseball, as well as feel for his secondary offerings. The frame is a bit of a concern moving forward, but he's got the makings of a dynamic weapon in college ball, or a guy that could move to the bullpen at the next level. 

Williams spent the first two seasons of his collegiate career at East Carolina before transferring to Maryland in search of extended innings and the chance to start.

Marx is a hard-throwing transplant out of the state of Utah. He can rush it up to 96 in early innings, but generally sits 91-94 if he's getting stretched out over the course of a start. He's touched a bit higher in side sessions, but bottling that velocity into games has yet to show. Marx has a repeatable operation with fantastic arm-speed and tilt in his hips. Because his lower half and plant leg are a little stiff, coupled with his size, some scouts see a reliever at the next level. Still, amped up, Marx has the making of a guy who sits in the mid-90s with a breaking ball that can approach 3000 rpm with sharp bite.

Haeger has a ton of bat speed and barrel wrap with significant burst out of the box. He's a true power-speed threat, the latter being the more present tool. It's a flatter bat path, but with age and strength should lend to over-the-fence power. In the field, Haeger has bounce with an average arm and solid range in the corners. He's still getting feel for baserunning instincts and his ability to consistently steal a bag, but there's a lot of building blocks here to project a big leaguer with sparkplus traits.

Robinson is a massive, imposing slugger in the box with the immense bat speed you'd expect from a player his size. A premium, elite football prospect, many consider Robinson the top tight end in the country, the 5-star blue-chip should get drafted in the NFL Draft. Robinson is a solid average runner with a sprinters lean and tight steps. He's been clocked in the neighborhood of 4.3 seconds home-to-first, though that could tick up a bit if he dedicated himself to baseball and straight-line speed. He's a supreme athlete considering his size. Robinson is an unpolished ball of clay on the baseball field and until he gives up football to pursue his ceiling as a baseball player, his applicable upside may be muted.

Armstrong possesses a ton of thunder in his bat for his size, and he's begun learning how to translate that bat speed into a more formidable hit tool in recent showings. He's a super-athletic infielder with a great first step on the dirt and plus speed to go along with it. He features a fringy arm that may push him over to second base at the next level. Armstrong's stock and development will depend on where the hit tool eventually settles.

Brauner has serious hitterish traits with burgeoning tools elsewhere on the field and a track record of performing against high-level pitching. Brauner uses all fields and has some juice to the pull-side, though his frame may limit his power output at the next level. Brauner is an average runner, but he's a high-level baseball player with big instincts and the ability to impact the game with intangibles. He's likely destined for left field at his peak.

Glasscock has touched 93 and showcases two distinct breaking balls, as well as feel for commanding and spinning the baseball. He's got a smooth, repeatable operation and is a very good athlete on the mound. The body has immense projection with long, lean limbs and a high waist. Glasscock could be living in the low-90s as a starter, touching the mid-to-upper 90s when all is said and done. There are some similarities to a Walker Buehler type of profile here. He'll miss the 2023 season with injury.
Smaller frame, up into the low-90s. Really fantastic athlete and creates a super-vertical arm-slot to let to fastball eat.

Boehm is a physical infielder with soft hands and feel for tempo on the dirt. He'll fit best at third base where his lateral mobility and bigger frame will be less-tested. That said, Boehm features above average arm strength moving toward first base, and average arm strength moving to his right. He has a tendency to drop his arm and throw a bit more three-quarter moving away from the diamond. Boehm's biggest tool will be the bat where his strength plays. Boehm extends well and possesses plenty of whip in his barrel sending rockets to the pull-side. Boehm makes a lot of loud contact and the bat has real upside.

Bakes is a compact, bulldog-build catcher with considerable arm strength and a chance to hit for some power. He gets high marks for his ability to frame pitches and to this point in his career he's held runners station to station for his pitchers. Bakes is still developing consistency in his ability to smother pitches in the dirt and limited passed balls and wild pitches. On the offensive end he's shown a decent bit of swing and miss in his game at this early stage in his career, but coaches and scouts like what they've seen from the young bluechip in batting practice and believe he'll eventually grow into a bit more consistency in his at-bats.

Lawson got extremely physical during his high school career packing on tons of strength and added physicality on the mound. The arm works really well. While it's a longer action, it's loose and whippy with controlled recoil through release. McLeod has some head-whack through his delivery that scouts hope will slowly dissolve over time to help justify his starting pitcher ceiling. In terms of the stuff, McLeod has been up to 96 with steep downward angle and ride. It works well at the top of the zone despite a lack of deception. McLeod possesses above average spin rates and will deploy a short mid-70s slider with some tunneling traits. There's a lot to like here. McLeod will be on the younger side, just 18.3 on draft day.

Hyde is a thick, bulldog-framed righty with budding stuff and strong feel for throwing strikes. His fastball has been up to 95 though he'll more commonly settle in the 89-91 range with some late carry through the zone. It's a fastball that has performed well in the zone, but doesn't induce much chase outside of it. Hyde does possess above average extension and athleticism, so forecasting out more effectiveness on that pitch isn't out of the question. His changeup is his most-used secondary; an average weapon with fairly generic shape lifted by above average execution. Hyde has produced a near-30 percent whiff rate on that pitch and it's been especially useful in getting left-handed hitters off his heater. There's a slider and a curveball as well, the latter being the more projectable weapon at the next level. Hyde will need to blossom and throw all of his pitches more firm in the coming years, but he generally misses bats, throws strikes and has feel for a full menu of secondaries.

Sos is a third baseman, a strong athlete with the power bat/power arm archetype at the hot corner, though scouts are bullish on the hittability here too. He's got plenty of projection to go in his 6-foot-3, 200+ pound frame, and is already impacting the baseball.

Link is a two-way guy, but his home is on the mound. He's a good mover and pretty athletic with some upside to project more on the way. He's been up to 96, but ordinarily sits 90-93 with an average breaking ball with more in the tank.

Lucas possesses a long, lanky frame with lean limbs and a ton of room to add strength as he matures. His tools on the dirt are presently fringy, but his athleticism and projection really leaves a lot to dream on. A lot of scouts have Lucas a future power arm on the mound rather than an offensive prospect, but we like the line drive swing and willingness to take the ball to all-fields. If he adds a bit of thump and the athletic tools tick up with development, he could play second or third base at the next level.

Denby is a firecracker shortstop with a budding hit tool and some power projection in a compact, lofty swing. He moves well on the dirt with quick hands and a strong arm for the position. Denby's footwork is still cleaning itself up, but this is a potential 50H/45P bat with a 6 arm. That profile projects anywhere on the field, especially with Denby's frame and athleticism.

Luzardo is a funky right-handed reliever with some interesting stuff and a live arm. His fastball has been up to 96 with some carry and tail, though he's struggled to miss bats or induce chases out of the zone in part due to his delivery showing the ball early. It's a fastball that's easy for hitters to track despite it's wide release. Luzardo doesn't particularly extend down the mound well either; another leading cause for hitters picking up his velocity early. Luzardo will drop his arm-slot to throw a pretty encouraging sweeper that's been featured upwards of 16 inches of lateral tilt at times. He also throws it firm for its shape; a mid-80s breaker. It's got the makings of a potential 'plus' breaking ball at the next level, but he'll need to work to command it more efficiently and will likely need to extract more value from his fastball if he hopes to get the breaking ball playing up to its potential. Considering the athlete on the mound, the extension down the mound and the strike-throwing woes, Luzardo projects a low-leverage reliever who generates whiffs by throwing the sweeper early and often.

Griggs has good size and has packed on a ton of strength over the last calendar year. Griggs' profile is buoyed by a sweet left-handed stroke with balance and fluidity. He's shown game power in league-play and projects to add more bat speed as his leaner frame fills out. It's fringe-average arm strength at third base and fringy speed. Griggs is destined for first base or third base where his soft hands should be apt for the assignment, though he's unlikely to ever feature gold glove caliber tools. The bat has scouts talking and he's squarely a day-two prospect.

After a freshman year where he didn't get much opportunity at Alabama, Griggs transferred to Stetson for his 2026 sophomore campaign.

Liedel is a well-built right-handed pitcher with broad shoulders and strength in his frame. He's largely worked in a bullpen role at his most efficient, though the stuff could be stretched out and given multi-inning looks. Liedel has a fast, loose arm that works. Everything is pretty easy, if not "controlled violence". The heater has been up to 93 with late life and some tail. He's not afraid to pitch inside to RHH and will buckle them off with a hard, vertical breaking ball with late, heavy tilt. He's a gritty competitor with an edge about him on the bump. It's definitely an "I dare you to hit it" mentality. Liedel will need to develop a third pitch and scouts will want to see extended outings before throwing seven figure numbers his way in the draft, but this is a tremendously talented arm who could be living in the mid-90s by the time the draft rolls around. He's also young, barely 18 years old for the draft.

Olivera is an athletically built righty with a strong frame and a three pitch mix. The fastball routinely sits 91-92 capping at 95 in short outings. There's a slurvy breaking ball that he can melt into a shorter slider with in the upper-70s bucket. There's also a low-80s changeup with hard parachute action. Olivera possesses a good arsenal and pitchability.

Gomberg is a metric monster with a low-launch heater possessing high spin rates and hop at the top of the zone. He mixes in a two-plane slider with sweep and feel for a fringier changeup with some tunneling attributes. Gomberg can rush it up to 94 and most believe he is a reliever profile due to the effort in the operation.

Devooght has a live arm up to 97 mph. The shape of his heater is currently rather generic and isn't a whiff-generator, but he may end up flirting with triple digit velo by the time he's drafted. He throws a firm mid-80s slider with gyro shape and a bigger low-80s curveball that projects the best of any of his secondaries. Devooght tends to see his velocity dip as he works into his third and fourth innings of work, but could be a dynamo in a bullpen role. It's a loose arm with some effort at release. Devooght projects a hard-throwing reliever who could buck that label with further refinement. He certainly has a workhorse frame and average control for the zone necessary to start.

Sanders has prodigious batting practice power and it leaks into games at times as well. It's more power over hit right now, but the sheer bat speed is among the very top of the class. Sanders is a fringy runner with an average arm behind the plate. He's already a big, strong, barrel-chested kid, so his fitness as he develops into pro ball will be worth watching, but he's got a decent shot at staying behind the plate with the right discipline and development program.

Scott is a very, very strong kid with strength throughout his entire frame and lumberjack hands. He's short and compact through the baseball and still delivers a load at the plate. It's plus raw power and he's got the strength in his upper body to deploy it to all fields. Scott is an above average runner with an average-to-solid average arm best set for right field. He's also got a flair for the dramatic, seemingly delivering big hits at every stop he's played. Some Jermaine Dye comparisons here.

Hoffberg has been a dynamic bullpen arm for the Bulldogs during his collegiate career. The sweeper is his gem, a low-80s banger with considerable depth and well-above average spin rates. It's been a whiff machine. He's been up to 90 with reasonably generic shape, though he's reluctant to throw the heater with as good as his breaker is. He's been working to fold in a splitter more in games and exhibitions though it presently lacks arm speed and general conviction.

Hernandez sure looks the part on the mound with a long, athletic frame and the fastball that misses bats. Hernandez can rush it up to 93, usually sitting 88-91 with some real life on the heat. He mixes in a breaking ball that flashes with barrel-missing capabilities and two-plane tilt. Hernandez is still getting stronger and continues to look more and more athletic each time out.

Hogg is a toolsy player with steady leather on the dirt and fundamental actions in all his game. He's an average runner with burgeoning bat speed, growing past his gap-to-gap profile of his younger years. Hogg is more of a gap-hitter at the plate with a quick, flat attacking plane, using the gaps to his advantage. When he wants to get into ambush mode, he can get a bit more aggressive with his launch angles and bat speed, though Hogg tends to focus on putting together a mature at-bat and not selling out. He's got a long, decorated history of handling velocity, and handling it well, so transitioning to the pro game should be rather smooth, at least in terms of seeing arms that throw hard on a regular basis. Hogg is a third base/outfield prospect for now. His steadfast approach toward the game will serve him well anywhere on the diamond.

Harrington stands out in the field for his defensive prowess in centerfield. He takes strong first steps and his routes to the ball have always been polished. He's got a shot to player centerfield at the next level. He's got some unorthodox, twitchy actions in the box with something of a Nolan Arenado aesthetic to his setup and swing. Harrington's swing can get a little long at times and he can get disconnected, but he's largely performed in tournament settings. Those swing mechanics may iron themselves out over time as he adds more muscle. Harrington is also a decorated wide receiver for his school. One of his triplet brothers, Alex, is also draft-eligible as a premium shortstop prospect. Both players will be 19 years old for the Draft and are expected to be tricky signs away from Stanford.

Extremely physical infielder with big bat speed and *now* power. Schmidt moves well for his size and should have a future at either second or third base as he matures. The bat is the selling point here.

Athletic delivery with a rocker step and good tempo. Gets into the backside well and moves down the mound. Repeats well and can land the slider really well. Shorter tilt, but hides it well and tunnels off the fastball nicely. Changeup has sinking action. Above average fastball command, up to 94, sits 90-91. Solid strike thrower with obvious velocity upside.

Lyons has a long, lean, powerful frame with the bat speed to go along with it. He's a prototype third base profile with an above average, maybe plus throwing arm on the left side of the dirt. Lyons has a flatter bat path and works gap to gap right now, but evaluators believe the frame and present bat speed suggest a future power hitter at the highest level. Lyons remains fairly lean and could stay at shortstop early in his pro career, but that won't matter to teams who are buying the offensive upside.

A natural shortstop, Kelley has seemingly made the switch to being a pitching prospect of late as he's continued to add strength and his operation has gotten better and better. The delivery is the selling point here as Kelley is only up to 92 mph. He is working to develop a spin profile, though he'll flash a solid average changeup. Kelley figures to live in the low-90s and flirt with mid-90s peaks in due time.

Copper is a unique righty with a lower, short-arm release and a dynamic two-pitch mix that tunnel brilliantly off eachother. The fastball has tremendous arm-side bore and he'll push 95 with the pitch, though he's more commonly 89-91 when tasked to throw multiple innings. He works in a slider with two-plane break that's extremely tough for right-handed hitters to track when he starts it off the outside edge. Copper has a reasonably loose operation, though he likely projects a reliever at the next level. Still, the pitch shaping here is interesting and could have teams calling in July.

Arms is certainly on the older side for this class and will turn 20 years old before opening day in 2027. He's a slappy hitter from the left side with the ability to carry the ball into either gap and spray mistakes down either line. He's smaller in stature but runs well and carries below average raw power that does present itself on occasion thanks to his feel for the barrel. Arms is a strong runner and has the look of a decorated defender in left field.

Good sized athlete with plenty of present strength. Average runner. Primary shortstop, could move to third base. Has good quickness and has body control to go with burst. Throwing accuracy can waver at times due to lower arm slot across the diamond; affects the carry of his throws. David has a strong internal clock and is a high IQ player. Right handed hitter, some strength in his hands with loose wrists through contact. Hit tool upside.

Garza has one of the most decorated hit tools in the country featuring elite bat-to-ball skills to go alongside as mature an approach as you'll find in the college ranks for a player his age. Garza covers velocity better than almost all of his peers and takes what the pitcher gives up. He smothers pitches in every quadrant and at times has flashed some sneaky pop, though most scouts agree it is below average raw power, unlikely to ever be a prevalent part of his game. Garza can cover shortstop in a pinch but is best suited to stay at second base where his arm action will be less tested. He's a fringy runner who doesn't like to steal too many bases, so continuing to run high batting averages and on-base percentages will have to carry his game.

Kane's future is uncertain as he's equally enticing on the mound as he with a bat in his hand. On the bump it's a loose, super quick arm with a low slow and natural deception that has proven difficult for the opposition to pick up. He's up to 88 now, but should creep into the low-to-mid 90s with added strength and reps. Kane teases a mid-70s slider with tight, short and sharp depth and a changeup he'll float to lefties and right alike. Offensively Kane is a line drive hitter who uses both gaps to find space and extra-base hit opportunities. There isn't much natural raw power to speak of but Kane puts the game in motion and allows his solid average speed to contribute, applying pressure to the defense. He's shown good actions on the dirt and likely projects a second baseman or outfielder at the next level should he keep hitting. Kane turns 19 years old one month before the draft.

Valdes is a hitterish centerfielder with tools that could keep him at the "8" at the next level. He's an above average runner with high-level instincts and runs solid routes in the field. He makes a lot of contact and doesn't chase too much, though he's unlikely to ever hit for too much power. Despite his size, Valdes makes things happen on the bases and in the field and could translate to a top-of-the-order table setter at the next level.

Rogers is a physical right-handed pitcher hailing from the great state of Mississippi. Rogers features a low-90s fastball that's grabbed 95, though his command for the heat comes and goes. He struggled at times to repeat his delivery, specifically his timing as a stabbing jab in his arm action gets him off rhythm at times. Rogers has shown the ability to flip over a mid-70s slurvy breaking ball, but his spin rates are a tick below average and need refinement if he's to develop anything more than an average get-me-over spinner. Rogers has fantastic arm speed and above average athleticism for his size. Polishing up the whole package is his next frontier.

Matson has a reasonably elite frame when it comes to projecting on a starting pitcher. The shoulders are wide and there's plenty of strength spread through the lower half. Matson has a super loose arm and the ball really explodes through release. It's a full stroke that's been up to 91 with considerable carry and arm-side run when he comes around it a bit. The fastball is the selling point here, however a low-70s curveball has been shown early in counts as well. It's a pitch that needs more firmness and arm speed, but that likely comes through added reps and understanding of his craft. He does repeat his release point well. Matson has a chance to live in the mid-90s and flirt with more than that by the time the draft rolls around. Better still, he'll be just 18.1 years old for the draft.

A primary outfielder, Erickson projects a plus runner with a corner profile, likely left field thanks to an average throwing arm. Erickson packs a punch at that plate with extra base-hit juice and plenty of power to his pull-side. He's demonstrated opposite-field ringing gap power as well. Erickson operates from an open stance with high hands and whippy barrel speed through the zone. His bat path can vary from event to event, so finding consistent triggers and hand work will be an emphasis moving forward. Erickson is a high-level performer who gets more out of his tools than most of his peers. He's a grinder.

Sorrel is in the argument for the most talented player coming out of Louisiana for the 2026 class. A tall, broad, super-talented right-handed pitcher, Sorrel is already touching 92 and won't dip below 88 over long outings. It's a buttery operation with a loose arm, steep angles and tons of tunnel in his arsenal. Sorrel makes pitching look effortless. It's mostly a two-pitch combo with a mid-to-upper 70s slider featuring depth and some late two-plane tilt. If the strikes continue to point up as they have in recent months, and a third pitch gets stapled down, Sorrel has a chance to develop into a special arm with rotation upside at the next level.

Antolick wasn't much of a prospect his junior year of high school, but blossomed late, so much so that the runway wasn't long enough to get selected in the 2023 draft. Now an Aggie, Antolick has been up to 96 with a 92-93 mph fastball with late finish. He also throws a breaking ball with fringy spin rates and feel for shape. Despite being a strike-thrower, Antolick projects a reliever at the next level due to some effort at release.

Hayden Morris comes packed into an extra-large, physical, athletic 6-foot-9-inch frame, and the stuff you'd expect from that sort of profile is as anticipated. Before tearing his UCL in 2023, Morris could rush it up to 95 with significant carry and some arm-side run. His fastball includes well above-average spin rates and projects to jump into the mid-to-upper 90s as he gets into pro ball. Over long innings, Morris is more 90-92. He tunnels a mid-80s curveball with late depth and above average spin rates. There's also a changeup here, though it's clearly a tertiary weapon. Morris has had an interesting path in baseball as his commitment to the University of Texas was rescinded after his injury. He is currently uncommitted with no school affiliation.

Gibson is a gritty arm that competes with a three-pitch mix, mostly working east-to-west. He's been up to 94 and will dance his slider and changeup off of his sinking heater. He's smaller in stature but has the pitchability most of his peers lack.

Walker is a slasher at the plate, but that works with his top-of-the-scale speed and burner mentality down the line. There's bat speed present, though his bat path isn't conducive of over-the-fence power. Walker's speed projects well in centerfield, though some believe he could grow off the role and shift to his right into left field.

One of the more unique looks in the 2026 class, Lyons is a low-launch righty with a fastball that features a flat VAA and it eats at the top of the zone. He'll grab 92 at peak, but sits 88-90 mostly. There's also a sweeping slider in the 79-81 bucket. The whole product is deceptive and unique, a la Paul Sewald. He is a draft-eligible sophomore with a reliever look.

Lara, as his age might suggest, is one of the more advanced, polished bats available in the 2026 class. He sprays the ball line-to-line and goes with what the pitcher offers him. He's a solid-average runner with a swing that projects into the next level, whether that be college or the professional ranks. Most scouts like his upside in left field. He'll need to tap into more game power if he's to capitalize on his draft stock. He will be 19.6 years old for the draft.

Britt oozes projection. His long legs, lean levers and high waist all point to a pitcher who could soon throw gas. For the time being he's mostly living 88-90, touching 93 with solid carry and arm-side run when he wants it. He'll throw two fastballs depending on the plane he wants to target. 

There's also two breaking balls with tight spin and commanded in the zone. Britt has a super loose arm and an athletic high leg kick that helps him generate torque. The profile could really surge with added strength. An extremely high follow for 2026. He'll turn 19 years old the week of the draft.

Pearson has drawn comparisons to former Royals slugger Billy Butler and current big leaguer Ty France. He's a talented hitter with considerably more bat speed than his same-age peers, and could develop into above average game power when all is said and done. Pearson has a discerning eye at the plate and strong bat-to-ball skills, though can get fooled on spin against more premium competition. Defensively, he projects best to first base moving forward, though he's a better runner than many give him credit for any can deploy average speed in left field. Pearson's profile is carried by the bat however. He will be a draft-eligible sophomore but will be 21.7 years old.

Bradley Stewart is an awfully interesting left-handed arm. He comes to the plate with a long arm swing and a deceptive low launch. There's something of a Madison Bumgarner or Anthony Solometo look to the young lefty. Stewart isn't a hard thrower just grabbing 92 at peak, but he hides the ball well and mixes in a short sweeper and a budding changeup that allow the fastball to play up a bit. The sweeper is an absolute yakker with huge depth and lateral jets. He needs to throw a lot more strikes if he wants to be in play on day two of the draft. It's elite bat-missing stuff if he can get there. He projects into a bullpen at the next level and should represent a unique look for a team hoping to build out a staff of differing arms. Unfortunately, he underwent Tommy John surgery in 2025 and has missed his entire sophomore season and may miss time on the mound in 2026 as well.

Wilson is a gritty middle infielder who always seems to have the dirtiest jersey on the field. He can rover between shortstop and second base, though he's likely to settle in at the latter at the next level. Wilson has a short, compact swing and drives the ball to all fields. It's impressive bat-to-ball skills despite a lack of slugging thump. Wilson projects a nice utility piece at the next level buoyed by a high on-base percentage and low strikeout rates. He's also considered a dugout favorite by teammates and coaches. Wilson was a 20th round selection by the Kansas City Royals in the 2023 Draft.

Everything Van Assen does is extremely easy. Maybe to a fault. There's not much stride and there's certainly zero effort in his delivery. Van Assen pitches to contact with an upper-80s sinker that features plenty of arm-side run and some sink. His slider is comfortably his best weapon, a breaking ball that jumps off the sinker tunnel late and hard. It falls off a cliff. It's only a low-80s pitch at this stage, and it's a pitch that may struggle to perform against more premium competition, but Van Assen carved up the opposition as a true freshman with that pitch. He's also been working to incorporate more of his splitter, a pitch that flashed as a prep. He's not an arm that will overwhelm batters with velocity or stuff, but he's tough to hit and could have a bright career as a swingman or no. 5 starter.

An loose righty with an extremely low release, Horwat is tough, unique look for opposing hitters. He'll touch 92 with tremendous sink. He still manages to jump above barrels at the top of the zone. There's a curveball and a changeup, though neither is a refined offering just yet. Horwat is not a strikeout pitcher but rather a reliever who pitches to weak contact.

Simply put, Carrillo is one of the more uncomfortable at bats a prep will take in the 2026 class. One of the more premium pure arm talent guys in the class, Carrillo has a longer slingshot arm action that induces a ton of movement on his pitches. The fastball has been up to 91 with significant arm-side tailing action. The slider and cutter are both tunneling monsters with north of a foot horizontal separation off the fastball. He'll manipulate the cutter into a gyro bullet spinner at times as well to create depth. Carrillo will flash a low-80s changeup that tumbles late off the sinker line. The looseness and athleticism on the mound really stand out. Has a chance to throw a good bit harder as he matures. Carrillo will be 18.4 years old for the draft.

Taylor is a primary catcher with big raw power and a strong approach. He's physically maxed, but already impacting the ball. Average receiver and average athleticism/crouch. Solid average arm strength.

Unbelievable arm speed and projection on the mound, Turner is a guy who could eventually flirt with triple-digit velocity, but feel for the strike zone will need to improve. There's some effort in his release that could improve as he matures into his craft. The fastball has been up to 90 mph with late fuzz at the top of the zone. It's one of those fastballs you can hear. It's complimented by a mid-70s slider featuring extremely hard, sharp lateral tilt with easy plus projection. Turner also throws a fringier mid-70s splitter that he's been working to help sell off his heater. If the strikes improve, it's Top 100 pick upside. The floor here could be a mid-leverage reliever at the next level. Really high-octane stuff. Turner will be 18.8 years old for the draft.

Ladd breaks a lot of conventional cliches for 6-foot-6-inch right handers. It begins with his release height, a launch two or three inches low than the average big leaguer regardless of their height. That's not a look hitters are expecting to see from such an imposing frame. Ladd will run the fastball up to 93, but more commonly sits 89-91 and he's struggled to miss bats with that pitch. He'll need more velocity if the release traits are ever to play in his favor. But considering his size and physicality, some scouts believe more could come. 

Ladd's sweeper is his best pitch, and it's a good one. He'll run that breaker away from right-handers at 81-84 mph and he's touched 86. It features above-average lateral action and will dive at the plate as well. Those two planes and reasonably firm velocity band have given hitters fits. Ladd works in a mid-80s cutter right in-between his fastball and sweeper to keep hitters off the barrel. And it's been effective in doing so. It's every bit that of a plus weapon. 

Ladd will need to add a changeup or a splitter to get something going the other way if he hopes to start at the next level. This, plus he'll need to add velocity. His strike-throwing ability has improved this year and he'll have suitors in the 11-20 round range, if not a couple rounds sooner.

Garner is a physical lefty with a loose arm and a sturdy lower half built for long innings. He's a well-built southpaw with a fastball that's been up to 92 featuring arm-side tail commanded east and west with ease. He'll work in a heavy tilt slider with left to right sweep to lock up righties and get whiffs from lefties. The slider works well off the fastball. Garner has good arm speed and should be working into the mid-90s flirting with numbers a bit higher than that early in outings before he's draft-eligible. He's a guy who pounds the zone and has feel for the glove side and arm side to get hitters out. An LSU commit, Garner will be 19.7 years old on draft day and will be among the oldest preps available. If he gets to Baton Rouge, he will be eligible again in 2028.

Rathmann has athletic tools that stand out in the field. He's a double-plus runner with an above average throwing arm, a profile that fits in all three outfield spots. Rathmann is still developing at the plate to engage his lower half, but the body has taken physical strides of late and looks considerably stronger. Rathmann will be 19.2 years old for the draft.

A hitter-ish outfielder whose performed at elite levels throughout his prep career, Barber is a spark plug. He's got feel for the barrel and looks the part each time he steps in the box. Barber is one of those hitters who seems to have patience and a plan at the plate. There's looseness in his hands and wrists with the ability to manipulate when fooled. Barber has some defensive tools including average run times and steady routes in the outfield. There will be pressure on the bat to perform, but he's produced at just about every stop to this point. He will be 18.4 years old for the draft.

The case can be made for Wes Peterson eventually owning the best sinker in the 2026 class. He's already up to 92 with elite arm-side run and sink, a true knuckle-breaking righty. He'll pair the sinker with a hellish deep upper-70s sweeping slider that can deviate three entire feet of horizontal separation off the fastball line. Peterson has a full arm swing and a whip-like release of his pitches. He's a premium strike-thrower who has the look of a reliever at the next level. If a third pitch comes forward it's not too farfetched to project out a starter's profile. Peterson will be 18.6 years old for the draft.

A physical catcher, Conte is revered for his defensive polish and arm strength. He's got a good shot to catch at the next level thanks to a high-level IQ, advanced understanding of the position and training over the years. It's among the best catch-and-throw traits in the class. Offensively, there's raw power and he's shown it in games, though he can get a little trigger-happy at times expanding the zone. Conte be a draft-eligible sophomore at 21.5 years old.

Lopez is lauded for his sweet left-handed swing and calm demeanor at the plate. It's an open setup with even balance featuring rhythm and waggle. Lopez has some extra hand load in his swing and can get out on his front side early, but he does a nice job keep his hands back and delivering a heavy load through the zone. He's purely a feel hitter who swings down through the baseball and does a nice job creating backspin resulting in above average pull-side raw power. Lopez is mature enough to eliminate his stride entirely in two strike counts. He's an old-school hitter. Lopez is a below average runner, though he's a bit more efficient underway and can stretch gapper into extra-base hits with ease. Defensively he may be forced to first base over time, but for now he possesses the frame to catch in college. Lopez is a draft-eligible sophomore.

Demetree has a plus throwing arm at the hot corner and considerable feel for the barrel at the plate. He's got a well-developed lower half and he uses ground force well to impact the baseball and produce bat speed. Demetree has a promising bat and is an average runner. He projects to stay at third base. He'll be an exceptionally old draft-eligible sophomore, already 21.7 years old.

Myers comes to the plate looking to do damage with serious intent in a violent swing. That steep attack angle has led to some contact quality concerns against upper-tier pitching, but also some prodigious shots. Myers has a bat path not too dissimilar from a guy like Kris Bryant. He'll need to improve his ability to handle velocity at the top of the zone, but Myers absolutely smothers soft stuff left in the zone at the knees. Myers has a strong arm at third base, and is a decorated pitcher in his own right, up to 91 on the bump. Defensively, Myers handles the routine play at the hot corner with ease, though scouts would like to see his hands work a little more out in front, but he projects a third baseman moving forward so long as he doesn't outgrow the position.

6-foot-6-inch lefties don't grow on trees. Stribling has already tickled 95 and will sit 91-92 over multi-inning showings. He mixes in a slurvy breaking ball with huge sweep coming out of a high-three quarter delivery in the upper-70s at its best. There's a changeup here as well, but it lags both in consistency and feel. Stribling has a sky-high ceiling, but it still learning how to properly use his frame and athleticism. He'll be a draft-eligible sophomore.

Enright has one of the more aesthetically appealing swings in the 2027 class, a simple left-handed stroke with natural loft and not wasted motion. He absolutely abuses anything in the lower-third of the zone, but can be susceptible to elevated velocity at times due to a steeper shoulder set at address. Enright possesses a physical frame with average raw power and potentially another half tick more on the way in the projection department. He is an average runner with average arm strength for the dirt, potentially set to shift to third base as he gets more physical. He is a draft-eligible sophomore.

Continuing the long line of talented infielders to come off the dirt at Yucaipa HS, Arambula is an offensive-oriented prospect with a strong mix of hit and power. He's mostly a gap hitter now, but figures to grow into more power as he matures thanks to compact bat speed and a knack for lifting and back spinning the baseball. Arambula operates out of a wide, squatted setup and really explodes on the baseball. He's a strong kid with a well-built lower half, pointing to a future at third base as a pro as he continues to fill out.

Young is your prototype table-setter with a quick, slasher swing and a solid eye at the plate. Scouts would like to see him develop a bit more impact in the swing, but he's one of the better approach & bat-to-ball hitters you'll find. He should run high walk and batting average rates early in his career. He's quick out of the box and posts above average run times, a nuisance on the basepaths. Young could end up at second or third base at the next level.

Manuel is a power righty who's shown feel for a two pitch mix. The fastball catches the headlines up to 95, settling in 90-92 over starts. There's a bigger upper-70s bender in there that Manuel lands for strikes, but scouts want to see a firmer slider or a tighter secondary as we approach the draft. He is a draft-eligible sophomore.

Cole Hansen is a well-liked catching prospect out of California with many fans in the scouting community. He's a big, physical backstop with compact strength and a strong arm. He's lauded for his leadership skills. He swings a heavy barrel with demonstrated power to the opposite field. Hansen could eventually hit in the middle of an order. There's something of a Mitch Garver comparison here. 

After a year at Oklahoma, Hansen transferred to Cal Baptist in 2026.

Cleveland is a long, lean left-handed hitter with a ton of projection left in his lower half. He possesses average bat speed, but scouts and analysts see a whole lot more impact coming thanks to his well-above average rotational acceleration and connectedness at the dish.
